ToME might not be a graphics wonder or a story-driven epic - though, don't get me wrong, it does come with a ton of interesting and often funny lore to discover. What it is instead is a classical steep-learning-curve, hard-to-master roguelike with some surprisingly deep, well thought out game mechanics.
If you're looking for a challenge or even simply an ARPG with an incredible replay value - randomly generated zones, huge number of interesting races and classes with their unique gameplay, 3 gameplay modes between the campaign, the arena and the infinite dungeon - you're looking in the right place. You can even choose your own flavor away from difficulty setting by deciding not to play a roguelike at all but instead venture into exploration mode and simply discover the world of Eyal with lives to spare. Oh, and let me mention the wonderful, always spot-on soundtrack too. You'll know what I mean when entering the arena.
Now, as far as flaws go.. ToME comes with surprisingly little (and even less that some addon, readily available in the workshop, can't fix for you). There's the odd balance or fumbling with the UI issue and 'graphic that could have been this tad better' but these minor troubles do tend to pale in comparison to the overall expirience and the number of for-your-convenience features the game brings, some of which - like the 'auto use when' function that for example automatically starts up your sustained abilities under specified conditions - I would have wished for in AA genre titles.
Overall ToME is an incredible achievement not only but especially by an indie developer and I would highly urge every genre fan to give it a spin. Just beware: it might suck you in and it probably won't let go again any time soon. ;)

What I have played of this game has been absolutely amazing, and I wish I had more time in my day to really delve into all it has to offer. This game entails the heart of what makes many love Roguelikes. All the features of a true Roguelike are in this beautiful game, and if you don't wish to go the hair-pulling route (that many of us are masochistically fond of,) you can set the lives distribution from permadeth to limited, or even infinite if you so desire. The art style is simplistic but beautiful, if not nostalgiac. Those who have been playing Roguelikes for a while or who know the genre from its roots may find a nice feel of classics such as Nethack and Iter Vehemens ad Necem (IVAN) in this game, as it keeps elements of those games, as well as the genre's originator, ROGUE itself intact, while throwing in a few modern entities that work very well.
For those who like the classic roguelikes, whether it's the retro ASCII or the Tile-set based games, you'll find a lot of enjoyment in this game. A high recommendation to any pure Roguelike or Roguelite fan.

It pains me to say this. I've played Football Manager since it was Championship Manager. I've enjoyed each iteration of the game immensely and have always appreciated the understanding and implementation of realistic and believable football strategy in the games. This year's version, however, is the first one that truly irritates me for the first time.
The changes in this year's version compared to the last are both hit and miss. The new Dynamics system is a welcome change and I do like the fact that you can have a better understanding of your sqauds overall atmosphere. It's simple to understand and makes phasing out long-term servants more interesting. I also like the new Medical Centre which gives you a better overview of your players' risks of injuries and how to best avoid them. Of course, my favourite addition this year is the new scouting system and how much more believable it is.
Now for the bad part though, and the reason I can't honestly recommend this game. The game is terribly hampered by bugs. This is nothing new but this year it is definitely too much. Yesterday, my game crashed 6 times while playing. I needed to replay matches and renegotiate contracts multiple times. Sometimes, the pitch was entirely black and I couldn't see the actual matches until I restarted the game! It is simply unacceptable to ship a game in such a state and bad service to the fans who have supported these games for many years.
I love the Football Manager series and I hope that SI keep improving on the tried and tested formula. Football Manager games are wonderfully strategic and this year is no exception. The additions that have been made truly make sense and work simply but effectively in the game and helps you better immerse yourself as a management genius. It is just such a shame that the game is plagued by unnecessary bugs that sully the overall experience and leaves you simply not wanting to keep trying out of sheer frustration. Hopefully, these bugs will be fixed with patches but for now, I'd recommend holding out on buying this game.

A conspiracy theory involving the creation of man, his purpose, his nature and most importantly, his rulers. The game talks about the origin and evolution of religion, objective truth and how history can be shaped and molded into creating truths that better suit humanity's rulers. Important philosophical questions are raised and never truly answered because maybe they're not meant to and you're supposed to find your own meaning and purpose in the world. The game was designed to make you think and reflect on these things by yourself and I believe that makes Assassin's Creed 2 one of the best and most important games of our generation.

RAGE is a very well designed game, it has its own style similar to how Pixar or Studio Ghibli have their own style. I read somewhere that it’s the last game programmed by a famous developer working for iD Software (Doom, Quake and Wolfenstein). The weapons are really fun to use and there is a different type of cool weapon for every situation. The cars feel nice and meaty to drive too, I enjoyed revving the engine and speeding around the wasteland.
This game does not perform well without some tweaks but there is a lot of help available. I got it running and looking great after following some guides and making some easy changes. The textures look great from a distance but when you get up close they lose fidelity. The game still looks amazing though with all sorts of physics effects and cool lighting.
A lot of people seem to think this game is not worth playing but there are also a lot of people who say that it’s great. I remember playing it back on the PS3, I liked it a lot then so I wanted to go back and experience it again. It is clearly influenced by great games like Metro and Half Life 2 while it also definitely feels like an iD Software game. It does feel unfinished though, the Scorchers DLC tries to rectify this a bit but it’s not a complete solution. So in the end, Rage feels like it could've been much better with more development time. It is still a great game though and I really like it, if they ever make a sequel it could be absolutely amazing.

DoD messes with TfV's autonomy system for fascist nations, making some of the Together for Victory focus trees unplayable. Additionally, DoD seems somewhat half-arsed, it only adds features for four nations, skipping over Austria, Slovakia, Albania, Greece and Bulgaria completely (probably saving them for a later DLC). Over all good game and definitely worth the cost, the only problem I really have is that the AI is below average even for a Paradox game, but that's more of a pet-peeve than a serious complaint.

It may sound corny, but OneShot is more than a game. It's a very unique experience, and that's what makes it so mind-blowing.
On the surface OneShot is a fairly simplistic RPGmaker puzzle/adventure. You control a young child, named Niko, who wakes up in a foreign world and now has to save it by bringing the world's sun (actually just a lightbulb) to the top of the tower. To do so Niko will cross the land, meet a bunch of colorful characters and find some items that will help them on their journey.
Except it's not all there is to it. Noticed how I used the word "control" instead of "play as"? That's because you aren't Niko - you are
, a person controlling them, and the game will acknowledge that during the very first minutes of gameplay. From that point onwards there will be literally no fourth wall - Niko
will communicate to you directly. This alone makes the experience unusual, but there's even more to come - to tell the story it wants to tell OneShot uses a very clever narrative, and it does so just perfectly. It would be a shame to spoiler even parts of it, so I'll just say that it's not like something you've ever seen before - and when it comes to this game, that's not an exaggeration.
If you're still not sure whether you should buy OneShot, I will also say that Niko is incredibly likeable, and the way they talk to you and respond to your commands will likely make you get attached to them pretty quickly. The game also has very atmospheric art and great music.
Just play it.

I could just say that Salt & Sanctuary is Dark Souls in 2D and be done with this review. But it's not that easy, so let’s do it properly. I enjoy my time with this game and co-op is tons of fun too in a way that Dark Souls doesn’t really offer.

As with all of my reviews, these are my own opinions and experiences; please check out other reviews too!

You can't pause the game and it can be really frustrating if you just suddenly have to go afk during a bossfight or bigger groups of enemies. There is no PVP other than fighting your own friends in split screen which is a bit disappointing. Some bosses can be really frustrating since they have unusual hitboxes and you often have to wait until they are done with their animations to be targetable again.

Sanctuaries and shrines let you save the game to refill your health and potions or level up and expand the skill tree, but using them will respawn previously slain monsters (not bosses). Choose between 7 different factions called creeds which all have different rewards for offerings. Expand your sanctuary with offerings to gain shops and passive bonuses to that specific region, the choice is limited to 4 offerings per sanctuary so chose wisely. The areas are not procedurally generated but instead crafted by hand and with care. Kick down ladders or open doors via switches to open up shortcuts that will help you traverse the rather huge levels faster.

Chose between 8 completely different classes each with their own stats and weapons which serve just as a basic layout, but you can just do whatever you want afterwards thanks to the rather huge skill board where you can branch off in the desired direction. Weapons have strength and dexterity scaling which tells you how good they are for your current class or rather chosen skill set. Manage a logical equipment system where having more weight on you slows down your entire movement, including rolling and ledge climbing. A basic stamina system for dodge rolls, blocking, and attacking which when empty renders you vulnerable to attacks. The smooth combat system features light and heavy attacks that can be chained together is very well done and response. Smash enemies to pieces with body parts flying all over the place and a good amount of blood everywhere with fitting sound effects. You can even throw enemies up to do some sick air combos! Claim passive upgrades to further enhance your gameplay like the ability to jump off walls or walking upside down.
Monsters drop salt that can be used to level up as well as upgrading your gear but they also drop gold which is used for buying equipment or paying the cleric who drags you back to the sanctuary after being defeated. Getting hit by monsters decreases your maximum health until you either use mending or visit a sanctuary shrine which should be avoided by all costs. Dying at bosses will cost you a bit of gold and will reduce your salt to zero but each salt lost this way is accumulated and can be regained after you come back and finally kill it. Dying twice to everything else however will lose you the previously dropped salt forever. Finishing off monsters with glory kills feels just great and you have to be very quick in order to execute them correctly. Salt & Sanctuary presents you with dozens of boss fights which are both challenging and interesting and can actually be pretty hard since they will change their attack patterns several times throughout the battle.

Thanks to its online functionalities, you can see players messages in form of bottle messages which tell you of dangerous areas ahead of time or just help you with telling you where the secrets are. Occasionally, you can see other players in the sanctuary as they mind their own business. Graves left behind near other players’ deaths will warn you about upcoming encounters. You can even see the corpses and sometimes just heads of other players hanging around in certain spots.
The game offers local co-op that can also be used for online play via hamachi and in-home streaming which worked like a charm; no screen or input lag at all. Your co-op partner will be a second character from your save file and keeps all the loot and dust he gets while he won’t disappear after each boss and you can safely play the whole game together. Additionally, enemies will be a bit stronger while playing together as compensation for the additional firepower.

You know nothing about the world and the game won’t tell you much about it, this mysteriousness really helps to keep up the atmosphere. The rather dark aesthetic mixed with flashgame-like graphics covered up with nice effects and multi layered back and foregrounds gives it a very dreamlike feel.

Huge parts of the game simply have no music at all, which combined with the presented artstyle works just perfect to set the tone the game is aiming for. Boss battles, sanctuaries, and some specific areas are the only exception to this so you always know when something is going on or in case of the sanctuary, when you can relax for a brief moment. The songs that are there are very subtle and fit the situations perfectly.



There isn’t much of a perceivable story but rather one that has to be learned through the game’s world and characters. You are presented with a basic premise of what you have to do but additional story is for observant people only, and if you want to fully understand everything that is going on you will likely have to check out some story analysis online.

While borrowing a lot of things from the Souls series, Salt & Sanctuary can easily stand on it’s own thanks to having distinctive features and charm. I recommend it to fans of the souls genre who are not against the idea of it suddenly being in 2D and people who enjoy action oriented metroidvania games. Definitely check out the co-op too!

Star Wars Jedi Knight Dark Forces 2 was a long awaited sequel for me.  By that, I mean I bought it last Christmas and couldn't get it to work properly.  Basically, the music wouldn't play in the levels and me being a Windows 10 user was a bit frustrated.
Thankfully, on August, there was a music patch, but that meant I had to start a new save file to hear it, which I didn't mind since I just gave up on the second level back then so I didn't get too far.
And now I finally beat this and it's an improvement over the first Dark Forces.  The familiar weapons like the blaster and the Stomtrooper rifle return.  So do the mines and grenaids.  Plasma rifle and pulse rifle.  They work just as they did in the first game, but the movement feels more fluid than ever.
Not only that, but the level design is a lot less confusing and more straightforward.  And the addition of the lightsaber as well as force powers is a welcome addition to combat.  I ESPECIALLY love how depending on your actions in the game, you will get different Force powers.  Jedi have non-lethal powers like blinding and invisibility, while Sith have Destruction and Force LIghtning.
It adds some replayability, even if player choice is basic.  Don't expect Mass Effect or Deus Ex levels of it.  All it really changes other than what Force powers you do have are some of the Dark Jedi boss battles and some cutscenes.  You don't get brand new levels for different choices or anything like that.  Just a different ending and a few new cutscenes that just come out of nowhere (like the ending just feels so out of character for a guy who just wants to avenge his slain father).
And the Star Wars soundtrack is awesome, given how this is long past the days of MIDI soundtrack.  Not that I hated the first game's soundtrack since it was pretty charming, but I think it goes without saying that most would prefer CD quality.  Me being one of them.
But the only thing about this game I can qualify as a negative is that, depending on how tolerant of the visuals you are, they haven't aged the best.  Thankfully, the cutscenes are in FMV, but even those look grainy on HD monitors.  I'm very tolerant of dated visuals, but I didn't find anyting particularly novel of the art style.
Nothing really immersed me into its environment unlike games such as Quake, that while had dated 3D visuals, it at least made the most out of the lighting effects and coloration to still immerse me into it.  But to give credit where credit is due, it looks like a game set in the Star Wars universe.
And I think the bosses are garbage.  They involve a duel against a Dark Jedi, and all of them just amount to avoiding their lightsaber and tapping them, hoping they don't block them.  It sounds cool on paper, but the execution leaves a lot to be desire.  Some bosses are just outright annoying, like Boc where he just jumps around, being a constant nuisance.  Just wait for him to slash, then go forward and tap him while his guard is down, do it again, that's all the bosses amount to.
But the positives heavily outweigh the negatives.  And given how they patched the music, I highly recommend buying this and its expansion I've yet to play, but they usually come in a bundle so why not give that a try as well.

I love this game to death, and really want to see it grow. I have 75 hours as of the review, leagues more than anyone else I've seen with a review, and I've loved playing every hour.
First off, as a warning, this is an
, think of back when Minecraft was still in Alpha, for example, it's come a long way. This game still has many bugs and a lot missing but there is still plenty to work with.
Starship Corporation has three main parts to it, you're always doing one of the following:
It needs to be said, the management is most just picking contracts and researching new tech to work with. Management is still very much in the works, but it's not the main draw of the game, anyways, I personally feel.
Building your ship is one of the big reasons you'd love the game like I do. If you've ever wanted to build all the inner workings of a space ship then you're going to love this game. While you're not building the perfect personal spaceship with everything you'd want (You're not making your personal dream ship here), you get to make everything you'd need to have a real functioning spaceship that you're going to be selling to other companies. You'll be making many types of ships, from military transports/vessels, cargo ships, tankers, mining ships, to even private racing vessels. You'll be placing every room, corridor, and power line in the ship with a lot of different types of rooms and requirements.
After you finish that you'll take your blueprint to the actual testing room and send it through the grinder to see how well it functions. You will have a crew size of your choice, normally 7 or more, to make sure everything is working as it should be. You start off with simple functionality test, seeing how well the design works overall, and move to the extremes of the scale; Large scale collisions, asteroid fields, large-scale system failures, up to pirate attacks, ship-to-ship combat test, and full-scale marine boarding parties coming at you. There is even some spec-op assaults and minefields test to really test your high tier designs. These can last anywhere from 2 minutes to 10 and you will want to do as much as you can.
which will do it's best to get you a good score if you wish to skip them. You can even select how well you want the auto select to be at the start of the game if you want more of a challenge.
Again I'll warn, this is an Alpha and still has a lot of work to even get to beta but I do urge you to get the game to help support it's development. Updates are regular, about one a month, and help add new content each time.

An hour into this game and I'm really impressed. The tutorial was easy to follow and guided me step by step through the process of designing my first ship.  The tutorial itself is well done and has an attractive female voice to aide you as you go along, and that's a good thing because this is a very in depth simulator that has a great amount of detail and thoughtfulness put into it. On one of the tutorial steps, I'm advised to be careful of electrical nodes that power various systems and to place them inside room of the ship so that if they ever fail they can be repaired. Also, to design redundancies in case of failure so multiple ship systems don't all go offline at once, and then to realize there is a power drain for every extra node that can require more power generators and all the while everything costs money adding to the price. Another was about putting on space suits for the crew during efficiency testing so they can survive in the case of a hull breach. Just little nuances like that go to show you how much depth this game has to offer.
Right now Im in the process of learning how the placement of my hatches and rooms affects the crew during standard operation when something goes wrong and how they have to zig zag around the ship to get to where they need to perform maintenance, put out a fire, seal a breach or get a wounded crew to sickbay, just to name a few. It's detailed, engrossing, and fun to the extent that I cant wait to see what battle testing my eventual designs will be like...
To imagine that I'm not only building a ship, but a company that with careful attention to detail and some time, will become the primary ship building construction company in the galaxy. Beware, Megalodon Galactic Inc. will rule the stars!
TL;DR: Love this game so far. For an early access game, totally worth the twenty bucks. The replay value is in building your company and outbidding rival ship builders, becoming adept at how best to design a given ship class, as they are all drastically different and require various astute strategies to work effeciently, and refining those designs as you progress toward being able to build the hugely expensive and powerful warship classes. And then finally, testing the designs in actual missions to be able to get a rating for the ships which you can then sell on the market. It's starship construction bliss. If you don't like ship building, design and construction games, then this game isn't for you. For me, it's an awesome reprieve from the likes of Fallout 4 and Skyrim and my various 4x strategy games.

So. Football Manager 2017 is still my most played game in my library, and I loved it, but FM2018 improves upon it in almost every way.
PROS:
Dynamics - This adds so much more challenge to the game, and cranks up the realism a bit more.
Better 3d - Looks better, is smoother, and the player animations are much more realistic.
Medical centre - Good for if you are not sure whether to start a tired player, also offers some good infographic stuff.
More stats - So much more analysis can be done, and it is presented beautifully.
Tactics screen - I like the coloured boxes showing strengths and weaknesses, and the links between players. Also, shirts again instead of boring boxes, which is always a plus.
CONS:
Some player interactions are still a bit stupid. Praise a striker for scoring 4 goals? He says "I don't think my performance was that good", and morale drops. Only occasionally though, far less often than in FM17.
Need a more powerful laptop to run it - you can't get by with a potato anymore.
UI - Some things take a lot more clicks to get to.
OVERALL: I have only touched on a few things, but they are the most obvious things I have noticed in (almost) 200 hours of gameplay. I definitely reccomend upgrading from FM16 of below, but if you are completely happy with FM17, wait for next year since there are still some issues. However, if you are tired of FM17, FM18 introduces a whole lot of new features that will keep you going.

That quickly becomes annoyingly tedious and you're left with a feeling of wasted potential. Speaking of which, the ending was a major letdown and ended in a maybe 30 secs video sequence. *sigh*
Until then however everything was fine. That's one of the few occasions where I would have  preferred to give a neutral rating because it's hard to go either way.
+ surprisingly good enemy AI, dodges bullets, takes cover and even retreats if things go bad
+ nice battle animations and details. Enemies shoot around corners and over cover. They react to situations and comment them (for example when they lost a leg)
+ good selection of weapons. they are fun to use, feel different enough and even offer different ammo types to adjust to your needs and situations even more
+ conveniently shaped maps usually lead you back to where you started, preventing unneeded backtracking
~ about average main story. it has some good moments and certain locations are well made, but it feels a bit shallow
~ many different missions and minigames, but they become redundant after a short time
~ story- and sidequests tend to send you back to places you had already finished, even though with new enemies this time
- bad case of silent protagonist
- no decisions whatsoever, very linear
- very little selection in car parts and weapons
- very weak ending
- no replay value
Altogether the world of "Rage" felt like a mix between Fallout and Resident Evil. It was fun to watch and play and I enjoyed most of the battles and some locations, but it's nothing I'd want or need to play twice. Grab it when it's on discount. And make sure to get "The Scorchers" DLC. It felt almost more worthwhile than the main game.

The game has beautiful scenery and great music, with simple mechanics and a simple story. I just finished the game, and although I recommend this game, it does have some flaws that would stop me from playing this game again. The world is really empty, and aside from finding those stars which are scattered across these empty maps, there isn't much to do to occupy your time. The fox travels extremely slowly, and I found myself going on my phone while holding W to pass the time, as getting anywhere took forever. There is also a level where you have to find these 3 rocks, and I found all 3, but the "interact" button didn't do anything on the first rock, except for show me this diagram of a fox with 0/3 underneath, which made me think I had to find 3 objects. I spent the next half hour scouring the map for...something, only to find that I had to spam the "interact" button to get the rocks to register that I had found them. This level was incredibly frustrating, as the rocks were scattered across the map, and the travel time was just incredibly long and boring. If the levels were filled with wildlife, maybe it would've been more interesting, but I'm sure even that would have gotten boring after a while. I would rather have had smaller levels with more content than large open levels with nothing to do. I wish the music would play more often, because spending so much time walking around doing nothing got pretty dull, and the music, which was fantastic, might've made it more interesting.

Pros:
The First Tree is an incredibly beautiful game with amazing art and a tragic story that you quickly become wrapped up in. It is just so, so pretty. And the voice acting and soundtrack are fantastic. The trees and grasses and lighting effects are so pretty and very different in every level. It's very obvious how much love the creator put into this games visuals.
Cons:
I payed The First Tree on launch day so I really hope the creator fixes some of these problems with future patches and updates. Basically, I found this game unplayable on the steam link controller as of 17/09/2017. The camera has to be controlled manually, so you end up constantly scrolling around awkwardly on the terrible steamlink touch pad. I also couldn't get the "action" button to do anything, and couldn't get past the first digging sequence. They show you the keymapping for about 10 seconds at the very start of the game, and there's no way to access this later in the game to make any changes.
Additionally, there are a number of extremely buggy platforming parts that left me so annoyed I turned the game off. I've never seen a game with such a buggy double jump, the height you jump seems completely random when using the controller. Once I switched over to playing on the PC with a keyboard and mouse these sections were less impossible, but there were still several parts of the game where I got stuck in a random crevice and had to turn the game off to restart the level.
I also would have liked it if the music looped more. There were a lot of times I was running around in silence which is a bit of a shame considering how good the music is when it's playing.
Verdict:
I really enjoyed this game despite the problems. The artwork is some of the best I've ever seen in an indie game, the atmosphere and story are really engrossing  and I'd definitely recommend picking this cute and short game up, especially on sale. However, save yourself some aggravation and don't bother playing this on your steam link, I wouldn't call this game controller compatible in it's current state.

First thing first, this game is fun. It is a LOT of fun. That said, it does need a whole lot of work. That is stating the obvious, as the game literally just came out a few days ago. Do not get discouraged by the glitches and bugs, as these are very normal. That said, my experiences have been mostly negative.
I started the game, which loads amazingly fast and runs like a dream for me, and found myself a nice quiet server to play on. The people on the server were extremely kind and quick to help me learn how to play and what to do with things. So off I go, mining up debris from the shore and being completely lost and confused in this amazing archipelago when I realized.. I'm about to starve! But that's ok because I have a busicuit! So I eat my tasty little bit of bread and realize.. I also have a raft! Sweeeeeet!
A tiny bit of trial and error and a few embarassingly silly questions into map chat later.. and lookout world, I am afloat on the most AWESOME rigged up raft ever! Then things get even better when I find floating trash. WOO HOO! I got myself  some string and a car battery, couple other odd things.. and now I can make a fishing stick! I won't go into detail on how long it took me to figure out that cooking the fish makes them much better to eat.. but it took a while. I will go mention that at one point when I got off of the raft, I was attacked by a shark. I know what you are thinking.. "Hey, stupid, you just get out of the water." but no.. I tried that. You see, this shark was ON A MISSION! So there I am, squealing in panic, as this shark HOVERS out of the water and up a hill after me. It was very intense for a little while, but I did manage to pickaxe said smiley shark in the face.. to death.. and got some super tasty "Shark Chops" for my effort. Yummy.
Now at this point I have a pretty good stockpile of resources from my adventures, and I will tell you now that it does not take long at all to build in this game. Four hours into the game and I had enough resources to build anything I wanted. So I build a small base and figure out how to make a small shipyard, and I made a jet ski. That's right! SPEEDY BOAT! And boy is it fun. There are whales too.. and you can jump these beefy guys with your jet ski for almost endless fun! And then.. get shot in the head from half way across the map by someone with a sniper rifle who you never even saw. Well that's ok, it is a "survival" game after all. Just.. you don't have to survive the world, you have to survive the people. That's fine.
Back to the base finally because I forgot to build a cot, but the devs are kind enough to respan you with another super raft AND A BISCUIT! I found my jet ski again and got it home and then built myself the big ship yard. Now things are getting VERY good. Took me less then two hours to be in the big gunboat. I got to say.. driving that thing is FUN. It actually takes one person to steer while someone else runs the engine for you, making it a loooot of fun. Puttered around for a bit, refueled it at the refinery, went to head back home in the pitch dark. Now I didn't think much of this because I had a friend on the front of the boat with a flashlight.. then I am suddenly looking at the respawn timer again. Another headshot.. IN PITCH DARKNESS INSIDE THE CABIN OF A BOAT!
By now I am somewhat annoyed.. but what the heck.. My buddy and I respawn and get the boat home.. only to find two guys waiting for us outside the base. Only.. we didn't know they were waiting for us. Because while we leave our game settings normal, meaning when it is night time it is DARK.. some people can still somehow see well enough to get two head shots almost instantly. They kill us, steal our boat, and leave.
This should give you an idea of the player base. There are diamonds in the ruff, but within four hours I have been killed a half dozen times and every sintle one was a headshot. That doesn't seem like a coincodence to me, so be ready for that if/when you do start to play. All the same, we trundle on. By now I have about.. 12 hours in the game and I've built and driven pretty much every single vehicle in the game. Some are more fun than others, but all of them have their uses. I've also had most of them stolen from me. The game desperatly needs some sort of anti-cheat. Not to mention that the moment you log out, someone will come by and somehow demolish your metal walls in a few minutes, take everything you worked for, and be gone before you get back.
Pros : The game is FUN. Really fun. Even if you do loose everything, it doesn't take long to get it back. It is fast paced and when you loose something, it really is not a big deal. Aside from the sea plane, the vehicals are realistic to drive and a lot of fun to use. Flying sharks! Yes, I am counting that as a pro because it was so absolutley terrifying and hylarios to see that I think everyone should experience this.
Cons : Cheating. Watch out for the players. A lot of them are legit.. but the cheaters are out there. No lights for your base. This means the cheaters can see you in the dark but you will not be able to see them coming for you. Base defenses MUST be manned to work. There is no automation so the moment you log out, everything you have is forfeit and will be taken from you. Not might be.. not could be.. but WILL be. You will have to start from scratch most days.. but at least it doesn't take very long.
I would gladly promote this game to anyone who wants a nice fast pased game, but I would never label it as a survival game. It's very much more a FPS game with construction elements in it and a food bar you have to keep full with a very occasional bite to eat.
***UPDATE***
I logged back in after a good long break from the game just to see what was going on and wow has it been updated. They have overhauled the UI, worked over some of the crafting, and sadly.. the sharks no longer fly. I do miss the free shark meat delivery, but I suppose I don't mind dipping a toe in the water now and then to kill another one. Sadly, thef is a HUGE problem still, even on PvE servers. They do seem to have some sort of anti-cheat as well which is nice, though I'm not sure it works. Honestly, nobody plays this game any more. I suppose it was a combined issue of not enough content and rapid progression. You can build everything in a few hours if you put your mind to it and have some help and then you find yourself with nothing else to do. The development team seems to be extremely small, another sad factor which has drasticly slowed progress of the games development. I still hold out a lot of hope for the future of this title and the forums have a little activity on them here and there so at least someone else is enjoying it.

A dungeon crawler rpg roguelike. I think its awesome.
Its accessable and easy to get into. numerous races and classes to play as, and you will unlock more of both as you play, even with just the base game!
Even workshop classes you can download, havent tried any of those though.

Another thing I find sets TOME apart from other roguelikes is the selectable difficulties, they not only have easy,normal, hard type selections but also there is exploration,adventure,roguelike choices where roguelike gives your character only 1 life (unless you can find magical items that add to it)  to live through the quest, Adventure gives you a 'free' life after certain level milestones, so when you die with an extra life you get to choose if you want to respawn where you died or outside the area. And exploration gives you unlimited lives.
There is a lot to loot here too, all types of weapons and rarities.
All in all id recommend this game to anyone looking for a good rpg or roguelike,

Ambitious to say the least. Starship Corporation has great potential to grow into something great. Despite all flaws and missing features I still enjoyed playing this game. I enjoy micromanagement and, to a point, tedious tasks. However, this game does take tedious to a new level. For one, the need to move rigid rooms can become very bothersome when you get to the end of a ship design. Having to move nearly every room and hatch one square along to fit what you need turns an enjoyable task into a labour. After finishing designing a light cargo vessel I found myself mentally exhausted but, at the same time, I felt a good amount of achievement. Testing the vessel showed that I had created something that was above and beyond all other competitors. I applaude the developers for having the foresight of adding a testing mechanic to this because without it I would have probably dreaded the next design trial and given up on this game completely.
Other issues I have is the lack of transparency when it comes to elements such as the marketplace and research. I imagine as time goes on and I get more aquainted with the systems in place and how a game plays out researching new modules and rooms would become almost instinctual. However, for a new player, the lack of forgiveness for looking at a contract and wasting time and money to research everything it needs only for the contract to expire, could be a deal breaker. I understand that this is a game about being smart with what you have, but more time on contracts to research crucial rooms would be very much appreciated. Furthermore, having similar, if not the same, contract reappear within a shorter time would help. It could easily end up playing out in a vicious cycle of research, lose contract, new contract needs something else, research, lose contract, ad infinitum. Such a problem would lose people after negative reviews are written.
Also, the UI tends to get a little opaque with information that sometimes doesn't necessarily have a need. Yes, if you want to micromanage down to last coin then it helps but I found myself paying very little attention to the amount of electricity a powerplant produced or how much coolant I have. If I needed more power I made more plants simply by seeing if my grid powered everything.
While this game needs a lot of work, polish, and more features, I am pleased with the amount there right now. Albiet an expensive time wasting puzzle game so far, I find very little that would be a deal breaker. However, if you are not a fan of micromanagement, obsession over details, and an unforgiving economic system and market, I would avoid this game. You will not enjoy it. If, however, you are an obsessive with a great deal of patience and an almost zen like attitude to design you will enjoy this game.

If the original Dark Forces was undeservedly compared to a DOOM clone, then Jedi Knight: Dark Forces 2 can be equally considered a Half Life clone due to the level design and its scale as well as the overall engine and textures that makes it appear like a Star Wars adaptation.
While this is also an oversimplification of JK’s merits, the emphasis of its similarly handled level design that funnels the player through environmental direction is something from the original Half Life that adds to the experience that was already refined in its atmosphere from the original Dark Forces. While it’s nowhere near as immersive as the Tie Fighter/X-wing flight simulators or the Knights of the Old Republic RPG, Jedi Knight manages to still convey the sense of scale of the Star Wars galaxy in its compactness of an experience.
Out of all the Dark Forces games, Jedi Knight manages to have the best of both approaches that have divided the expectations between the Dark Forces games and the future Jedi Knight games. The FPS gunplay of the original as well as rudimentary Jedi powers and lightsaber encourage a more thoughtful approach to be a Jedi rather than making another power-fantasy in the Star Wars universe. This approach goes beyond its narrative merits as it mechanically adds to the realness of Kyle Katarn’s character as an experienced bounty hunter who happens to become the most compelling, inept Jedi who ever lived.
Note: In order to avoid compatibility issues, follow this guide for JK Hub to install a launcher to make it run on modern hardware:
Back in the mystical era of the ‘90s, videogames touted this forgotten gem of an approach to add storytelling to games through full motion videos (FMVs) that can only be replicated in cheesy YouTube fan movies. The experience added hilariously bad acting to the point where the practice became weirdly charming much like watching heavily dated cyberpunk films from the ‘80s, and Jedi Knight is perhaps the greatest schlock that ever graced the Star Wars universe that manages to tell a story that is equally as nostalgic as it is compelling. Had the game been remade without these cinematics, the game wouldn’t nearly be as amazing without these Star Wars cheese.
As for the narrative itself, Kyle Katarn continues his journey from Dark Forces in uncovering the details surrounding his father’s death as his pursuit to redeem his Empire’s history takes him along the path of the Force as he must decide whether to become a Jedi or a Sith as he stops various Dark Jedi from claiming the power of the Valley of the Jedi. Unlike Outcast that retold a similar story, Jedi Knight emphasizes the mechanical transition into being a nerf-herder with as much charm to his wit as his skill with a blaster into the Jedi Knight or Sith Lord that he will become. The major difference is that growth is earned through player skill, and the journey never truly favors the player taking one approach for granted, which makes the game play distinctly from the original as well as future games.
Characters beyond Katarn himself are also given notable improvements by hamming them up as well as creating truly unique characters like 8t88, the scene-chewing Boc Aseca, the king of Hamlet Jerec, and the hilariously fabulous Yun are all cartoonishly excessive in their personalities yet make the game as distinct in its storytelling. Katarn himself has perhaps improved the most of all returning characters as he embodies the more charming personality with his unique perspective on matters concerning the Jedi and the Sith. Jedi Knight truly solidifies his character through his story-arc, and it creates as enriching of an experience for him as for the player much like Max Payne.
As previously mentioned, the most notable change from the original is the emphasis on growing into a Force user over the course of the journey that determines the player’s affinity based on the Force abilities they choose, a hidden karma system when playing, and rewards the player with cinematics that show Katarn redeeming himself or being consumed by his past through the Force. These aspects may surprise players who find themselves ending up on the dark-side without realizing they started down this path, and unlike Dishonored the changes never penalize the player to the extent that it becomes a concern if the player is mindful of where they swing their lightsaber when in public environments.
Changes to other areas of gameplay capitalize on the transition from a DOOM-inspired 3D game into a true 3D experience. The most notable of improvements is the greater sense of verticality that impacts its sense of scale, which leads the player through funneling the environments towards an intended goal as well as utilizing the lighting system for direction. Areas remain still as complicated as the original but because of how careful these areas are designed the lack of direction is never a problem. Each mission slowly expands the scope and scale, and while they appear like open worlds their linearity is disguised through the vastness of these levels.
As for its combat systems, gunplay remains largely the same as the original while offering the lightsaber as a double-edge sword for given situations. If players are accustomed to Jedi Outcast or Jedi Academy, they will probably find the lack of polish and complexity of the lightsaber to be a black mark on the game when narratively as well as mechanically, the lightsaber is one of many tools in Katarn’s arsenal with an appropriate time and place to use them. Even when in the case of boss-fights, explosive weapons are a useful means of fatiguing enemy Jedi to make the lightsaber combat less frustrating. Similar to the problem of Max Payne, Jedi Knight becomes notoriously difficult beyond Easy towards the end of the game without proper Force powers to make up for the emphasis on playing as a Jedi.
This is the only criticism about its gameplay I agree is an issue, and the way in which the game adopts a total Jedi or total Sith playstyle whether you want to have one power from another side makes the replayability a concern. Had the game established neutral Force powers like the KOTOR games perhaps the game’s difficulty could be smoothed out from its current state. In spite of this lack of balance, the core gameplay and mastery of skill for the player and for Katarn is a compelling reason to replay the game with two distinct paths with small and large changes to the experience.
However excellent and refined of an experience, mechanically as well as narratively, Jedi Knight is as a sequel it ultimately began the path towards the dark side for the series as it strayed further from the Dark Forces roots of an FPS and focused more on the power-fantasy of the fanfare of Star Wars. Mysteries of the Sith, a harmless expansion to Jedi Knight, manages to also be an extension about what makes the original games so distinct and great as they expanded upon new stories within the mythos of Star Wars, not reveling in the fans-service of being a Jedi amongst the biggest names. The story of Katarn is something inherent to video-games as an original character much like the iconic characters of Agent 47 as 007 as well as Max Payne of John Woo and Noir films.
As a result of this fact, as much as I love Jedi Knight as the best in the series, its deviation towards the Jedi focused path began in this game and that holds it somewhat responsible for the lackluster follow-ups from another developer, and much like the future of Max Payne, the memories of these classics can never be tarnished much like the original Star Wars trilogy.

Had a great time with this one, one of the better Star Wars games, and shooters in general. It is a sequel to Dark Forces, another excellent old-school shooter from the 90s.
First of all, the level design is just amazing. The levels are massive, vertical, hold a ton of secrets, and are always built in such a way that makes them believable and not just maze-like.
Second, the gameplay. This is one of the first (if not the first) SW games that lets you wield a lightsaber (both from 1st and 3rd person perspective) and run around cutting droids, imperials and other scumbags. Running into a room full of stormtroopers and slashing them within seconds. The game also lets you use a number of Force powers such as Force Jump, Speed, and, depending on your choice, LS or DS powers like Force Heal. The gunplay is also great, and, if you want, you can play the game like a traditional shooter, blowing away enemies with a concussion rifle, or mowing them down with the imperial repeater.
The atmosphere of this game is also stellar in quality. The original John Williams's soundtrack is used perfectly throughout the game, the sound effects are also true to the source material, and the in-game cinematics, which are composed of live-action segments filmed on a greenscreen fused with CGI effects are simply epic. The actors portraying Kyle, Jerec and the other good and evil Jedi all did their roles in a pretty believable way, and, although these cinematics may not be Oscar material, no one can deny the amount of effort, devotion and pure love that went into creating them, and for me personally, they will always trump the modern over-dramatic epileptic crap developers and publishers shove into modern shooting (and other) games.
The only downside to the game can be the dated visuals (it was released in 1997 after all), and that it can be a bit of a hassle to run it on a modern operating system. However, there are mods that fix these issues and give a nice visual overhaul, so the complaint is pretty much redundant.
All in all, if you love Star Wars, and if you love shooting games, play Dark Forces 2! Pay no attention to the mixed reviews, most of them are the aformentioned complaints about the visuals and compatibility issues.

A friend of mine at the time this was released was playing the game and gave me the idea to try it out, and I was highly, highly skeptical of it at first.  I deferred to his taste and judgement in games however and decided to buy it from Walmart.  The first thing I noticed was that it was based on the Unreal 2 engine.  This lead to some of the similar graphical capabilities.  I was amazed with the complexity of this game at first not understanding how to play it.  I thought it would be a simple terrorist shooting affair, which didn't appeal to me very much.  The surprising aim-mechanics (reticle snapping) were also one of the first things I noticed about this game.  You get control of an entire squad, which you'll want to bring back intact.
But when the goal isn't to rack up kills but is to finish a mission objective, and you inherit some sense of self-worth from how well you achieve that objective, it changes everything.  Soon you are meticulously approaching every door ready to use all of squadmates and weapons in your arsenal (and you feel guilty for the stupid sob's whose lives are about to end).
You drop in, kill everything that guards, get your hosties, and get out, and it's much better than the Counter-Strike approach ever was, because whereas Counter-Strike inherits from the Half-Life engine and the Quake engine, this actually inherits from the Unreal engine.
And if you think back to all the things Unreal engine did that Quake never did, you'll start to realize this engine has some intersting capabilities.  Unreal had vehicles implemented during this engine cycle, large maps, and high-res textures.  Quake never implemented vehicles, and it still doesn't do that well (they're usually just static objects.)

I could just say that Salt & Sanctuary is Dark Souls in 2D and be done with this review. But it's not that easy, so let’s do it properly. I enjoy my time with this game and co-op is tons of fun too in a way that Dark Souls doesn’t really offer.

As with all of my reviews, these are my own opinions and experiences; please check out other reviews too!

You can't pause the game and it can be really frustrating if you just suddenly have to go afk during a bossfight or bigger groups of enemies. There is no PVP other than fighting your own friends in split screen which is a bit disappointing. Some bosses can be really frustrating since they have unusual hitboxes and you often have to wait until they are done with their animations to be targetable again.

Sanctuaries and shrines let you save the game to refill your health and potions or level up and expand the skill tree, but using them will respawn previously slain monsters (not bosses). Choose between 7 different factions called creeds which all have different rewards for offerings. Expand your sanctuary with offerings to gain shops and passive bonuses to that specific region, the choice is limited to 4 offerings per sanctuary so chose wisely. The areas are not procedurally generated but instead crafted by hand and with care. Kick down ladders or open doors via switches to open up shortcuts that will help you traverse the rather huge levels faster.

Chose between 8 completely different classes each with their own stats and weapons which serve just as a basic layout, but you can just do whatever you want afterwards thanks to the rather huge skill board where you can branch off in the desired direction. Weapons have strength and dexterity scaling which tells you how good they are for your current class or rather chosen skill set. Manage a logical equipment system where having more weight on you slows down your entire movement, including rolling and ledge climbing. A basic stamina system for dodge rolls, blocking, and attacking which when empty renders you vulnerable to attacks. The smooth combat system features light and heavy attacks that can be chained together is very well done and response. Smash enemies to pieces with body parts flying all over the place and a good amount of blood everywhere with fitting sound effects. You can even throw enemies up to do some sick air combos! Claim passive upgrades to further enhance your gameplay like the ability to jump off walls or walking upside down.
Monsters drop salt that can be used to level up as well as upgrading your gear but they also drop gold which is used for buying equipment or paying the cleric who drags you back to the sanctuary after being defeated. Getting hit by monsters decreases your maximum health until you either use mending or visit a sanctuary shrine which should be avoided by all costs. Dying at bosses will cost you a bit of gold and will reduce your salt to zero but each salt lost this way is accumulated and can be regained after you come back and finally kill it. Dying twice to everything else however will lose you the previously dropped salt forever. Finishing off monsters with glory kills feels just great and you have to be very quick in order to execute them correctly. Salt & Sanctuary presents you with dozens of boss fights which are both challenging and interesting and can actually be pretty hard since they will change their attack patterns several times throughout the battle.

Thanks to its online functionalities, you can see players messages in form of bottle messages which tell you of dangerous areas ahead of time or just help you with telling you where the secrets are. Occasionally, you can see other players in the sanctuary as they mind their own business. Graves left behind near other players’ deaths will warn you about upcoming encounters. You can even see the corpses and sometimes just heads of other players hanging around in certain spots.
The game offers local co-op that can also be used for online play via hamachi and in-home streaming which worked like a charm; no screen or input lag at all. Your co-op partner will be a second character from your save file and keeps all the loot and dust he gets while he won’t disappear after each boss and you can safely play the whole game together. Additionally, enemies will be a bit stronger while playing together as compensation for the additional firepower.

You know nothing about the world and the game won’t tell you much about it, this mysteriousness really helps to keep up the atmosphere. The rather dark aesthetic mixed with flashgame-like graphics covered up with nice effects and multi layered back and foregrounds gives it a very dreamlike feel.

Huge parts of the game simply have no music at all, which combined with the presented artstyle works just perfect to set the tone the game is aiming for. Boss battles, sanctuaries, and some specific areas are the only exception to this so you always know when something is going on or in case of the sanctuary, when you can relax for a brief moment. The songs that are there are very subtle and fit the situations perfectly.



There isn’t much of a perceivable story but rather one that has to be learned through the game’s world and characters. You are presented with a basic premise of what you have to do but additional story is for observant people only, and if you want to fully understand everything that is going on you will likely have to check out some story analysis online.

While borrowing a lot of things from the Souls series, Salt & Sanctuary can easily stand on it’s own thanks to having distinctive features and charm. I recommend it to fans of the souls genre who are not against the idea of it suddenly being in 2D and people who enjoy action oriented metroidvania games. Definitely check out the co-op too!

I played this game over 40 hours on steam and at least twice as much from dev's website for free.
I definitely recommend this game for anybody who has an appreciation for rougelikes.
It has everything that a rougelike needs; huge replayability value, good combat system,
randomly generated locations. The list goes on and on.
Online chat is a brilliant feature and it's quite awesome that the developer launches some special events for people in game from time to time.
There is one thing that bothers me though, and I dislike it so much that I have decided to write this review.
This game is not fair. It's imbalanced, there are classes not worth putting time into. And you need a lot of time to try to pass the game.
After investing a few  hours in the character you created, you are going to die because of some stupid reason.
E.g. playing a reaver lvl 25 I was killed by a creature immune to 90% of my attacks in a main-quest location.
I grinded every other lower level zone before exploring this one, but it did not matter. Dead. Nothing new unlocked on this run (at least 6 hours spent on it).
Playing berserker, above level 30, lost my last life because I was teleported during life-saving skill which could not work in this location (Using unstoppable and being thrown to fearscape). Boom. Random death. Hours gone.
Countless deaths while playing archmage, killing myself with my own fireball blast hitting invisible enemies who were too close.
Some of those deaths could be avoided, but there are ones against which you are helpless. "Memento mori" is not my favourite thing to be reminded of while playing a game.
If you like spending way too many hours only to lose and start again, apparently you are a true rougelike fan and this game is for you. If you care about the time you spend on games, go play something else instead.
TL;DR: game is awesome and addictive, but you will die a lot in unfair ways and you will probably wast countless hours.

Ahh, Tales Of Maj'Eyal. What is there to say about it? Well--
-Odyessy was hit for 50 nature, 50 temporal, 30 fire-
-Killed-
~Spoiler Free Review!~
--------NOTE---------
This review is based off the majority of my play with mods. For around 90% of my hours on the game, I have spent it with mods. I shall list what mods I used at the bottom of the review, but none are extreme enough to change any of the core concepts of the game. The mods I've used made information easier to understand.
Oooh boy. I absolutely love this game. I really, really do. If I had to pick a single game to bring with me into, say, Space, this game would be my pick, hands down.
You know what's strange for a Rouge-lite game? Having encouragement to directly talk with the community. Yeah, strange, isn't it? Whenever you're in the game, and you're online...you're connected to the community with a button-press away. There's a window on your screen (that isn't intrusive) where people's achievements within the game and conversations are. You can link items and monsters you find to show off to others the items you've found, or to ask for strategies on creatures you've never faced before. I do reccomend a mod called "Die In Obscurity" so you don't see how every single person dies. It can overflow the chat at times. Afraid of spoilers from the community? No problem! The moment someone types something that's considered spoilerly, they will be sent to ToME Spoiler Chat. It's an automatic system, so you won't even see a glance of spoilers. I've NEVER had a issue with the community, and have had quite a few conversations with the dev himself, Darkgod. The moderators are absolutely awesome as well! Good on all of you!
So, yes, this is indeed a positive for the game. I encourage you, as well, to take part in the community!
I'll talk about the story in a bit, but I believe this is to be the BIGGEST draw to the game. The combat.
You see, Tales Of Maj'Eyal is complex. This, sadly, can be a heavy drawback for those who would rather actually enjoy it. In every single turn (every single move you make) has a LOT of things considered, from the speed of projectiles flying at you, to how spells affect the enviorment are re-checked to apply their affect again, and how everyone runs around. This is perhaps one of the only turn-based RPGs I know that has a heavy emphasis on mobilty. You CANNOT, I REPEAT, CANNOT run around without a plan. You. Will.
Doesn't matter if you have badass armor and defense-increasing skills on. You cannot block everything or tank everything. Even TANKS in this game have to consider mobility, and know when it's time to run and reposition themselves. The only class that can remotely do this is Bulwark, which I feel is "THE" class everyone should play first. They have a rediculous amount of defense, but it won't get you too far in the game alone. Learning the game takes time, and many deaths.
On the bright side, this complex combat is actually very satisfying once you understand how it works. There's SO MANY WAYS TO END YOUR FOES. From
to
The amount of classes is purely absurd, and to this day I've STILL not tried them all. On top of that, you have Races. Humans, Elves...There's many more, and each has sub-species within it. The reason why I won't say who they are, is because it's considered spoilers. Sorry. Although, I will say there's only a few races that have classes usable only by them, you can mix and match pretty much anything. There's a lot of depth in a single class, and with so many, there's a lot to learn here. On top of that, the loot is satisfying to obtain. I've even carried some things I couldn't use because it just sounded so badass. I ain't giving my Corpsebow to a mere shopkeeper!
Also, the difficulty settings are very varied. You have two different kinds that come into play when you play the game. Difficulty, and the Style of the Difficulty.
{Easy}
{Normal}
{Nightmare}
---and so on---   Those difficulties change how hard the game is. How strong foe's talents are, the level of the zones, and so on. The higher the difficulty, the more EXP you earn. There are three difficulties locked when you start the game.
And the Styles:
{Exploration}  Infinite lives. You are beyond death! The difficulty I say you should NEVER play, it ruins the experience. But if you don't like having a bad time, I won't judge you. There are a lot of gorgeous sights to see in the game.
{Adventure} You gain lives on select level-ups. Simple, not overpowered, but not the core experience.
{Rougelike} "You ARE your character." You only have one life. The moment you die, your character is immediately deleted. :gameover: However! You can still find ways to revive yourself in game, such as a rare-as-it-can-get vial. THIS is the Style of difficulty I always play on. It's my preference.
It's visuals....are alright. It's your typical fantasy style, but it's not too distracting for me, actually. It's the enviorment I'm in, so I roll with it. It's great for what it is, there's a LOT of variety here! You'll be in space, heaven and hell, wintery landscapes, swamps, and volcanoes! Personally, I like it. But I can see how people might be "turned off" by it. Honestly, there's not a lot to say. One of the few games I say imagination works in it's favor!
It serves it's duty. Spells sound like spells, fists sound like fists, steel sounds like steel. There's no glaring issue with the sound, but nor is there anything that stands out as supreme. The soundtrack? Well...The music in the game is the same, it serves what it's meant to do. I honestly have muted the music for a long time now, and have other things in the background, like the news or music. It's one of THOSE kinds of games, despite it's complexity, where you can focus on other things while playing it. It IS turn based, as well.
On that note, like how I feel with Sanctuary RPG, once I've played long enough, I'm "in tune" with the game, reading information at only a glance, making actions with speed and care. Even when I set the game down for a few weeks, I was very easilly able to get back into this state.
The story of Maj'Eyal is a fantasy, what would you expect? If you can suspend disbelief, you will find so much to read and learn about the word. Well written poems, stories, and last words of daring adventurers before you. There are several campaigns, but the one with the most amount of story is, well, "Tales Of Maj'Eyal". There is also the Arena and the Infinite Dungeon. Personally, the Arena isn't very fun to me, but I absolutely LOVE the Infinite Dungeon. You and the endless dungeon crawling experience that this game offers, with nothing in your way beyond blood thirsty monsters and glorious loot. It feels alive.
All in all, there's not too many RPGs like this. Where it manages to be...a community driven single player game. It's definately unique in that regard. With such a cheap RPG, why not buy it? Well, the initial ramp of difficulty (and throughout the game, regardless of skill) requires stategy over going wild with a sword, so this isn't the kind of game you can sit down with if you have little time. It respects your time, however, and the community is very helpful, VERY alive...The sound and appearance will not satisfy everyone, but it serves what it lives for. Things sound exactly like they would. I don't think giving it a "Score" would satisfy myself with the review, so I'll simply give the answer of "I highly reccomend this." To ALL RPG fans!

I jumped into this game purely out of curiousity and my experience was alright actually.
First thing I noticed going into the game was the graphics. I definitely felt like most of these textures and objects were some of the default textures but I looked past the graphics since the game is in alpha. If you want to build bolts to build a door you can, otherwise if you have the material needed to build the bolts and the door already then you can just build the door and the bolts will be constructed automatically as well. It took me a while to figure out how to build a base in order to fully feel safe in this game but I appreciated how blind I felt to everyhting. For still being in alpha I can recommend this game. It is the right amount of challenging and fun and as long as the developers keep to their word about the future additions I can see myself playing more of this.

Edit: to clarify

Dishonored is sort of like a mix of Hitman, Thief, and Deus Ex in equal parts. The mission style gives you a target to assassinate and a playground of ways to do it like Hitman, the overall FPSRPG structure is pretty remniscient of Deus Ex, and you're encouraged to steal everything that isn't bolted to the ground like in Thief. If you like any of these games you'll probably also like Dishonored, though there are a few catches.
The first hangup is that the AI is fine when it's left alone, but gets a little schizophrenic once anything out of the ordinary happens. If you pull a whale oil tank out of its socket to turn off a barrier a guard may casually shrug it off as the tanks not lasting long enough, then proceed to spend the entire duration of your stay in that level yelling for you to come out of hiding and never "cooling down". Sometimes guards will just become triggered for no reason and start running around levels with their swords drawn, even if the level finish screen confirms that neither you nor any bodies were ever found.
But the more important thing that I noticed a lot more on subsequent playthroughs is that the game is very heavily built for the nonlethal/stealth player, and it has the subtlety of a brick to the face with it. The game specifically warns you in multiple tutorial tips that not killing anyone is the "best" way to do things and gets you a better ending, and the dialogue isn't much better. At one point you meet Slackjaw, a gang leader who gained power by killing every previous leader in the territory, and he instinctively acknowledges you as an assassin coming to kill someone. After you help him out he offers you a deal, and the only thing he offers in return is to get rid of the targets in a way that
kill them, and he makes sure to make it a point that he won't kill them several times in the dialogue, even though to him there's no logical reason why you would care about that at all. The combat itself is built a lot more with Thief in mind, and while you can play it like an action game it's just not really that fun, due to the low enemy variety and low weapon variety.
Despite these hiccups I still think Dishonored is a great game, but if you're expecting a Deus Ex-style experience where you can play actiony or stealthily and have fun both ways you might be disappointed. But if you're a fan of stealth games, Dishonored is a pretty solid choice, even if it is a bit easy.

walking around searching for things without any hints about what to do, collecting stars which is extremely frustrating, trying to get through the horrible and unpolished platforming you have to sometimes endure. That's it. Now, let's move on to the actual review:
So, I really don't know what to think of this game. It's a good idea, it looks good and it has everything it takes to actually make you buy it in the first place. BUT, even though I usually love games that are just about walking around and listening to or finding out about a story, I didn't quite enjoy this game as much as I hoped I would. I'll just start with some positive points about this game:
-
, it looks great. The atmosphere is amazing and it feels really immersive,
-
, really adds to the atmosphere and especially impresses at the end of the game,
-
is sort of interesting, but mostly on paper, due to some of the negative points I'll be listing now.
-
aren't consistent, the ends of areas look blunt and undetailled, you can even tell when an area ends before you get to the trigger that teleports you to the next.
-
has a lot of flaws (for the record, I played the whole game with a controller, but I imagine the same problems about the controls also count for keyboard & mouse players). I often found myself trying to collect a star (the white things you see in the trailer) multiple times, just because the hitbox of them wasn't large enough or the controls/camera angle made it hard for me to catch them.
This is really irritating, as the movment speed is pretty slow, you have to walk long distances in this game and turning the camera with a controller is excruciatingly slow, without an option to change it. You also can't invert the camera's y-axis, which only increased my frustration with the camera and general movement.
In addition to that, the jumping is confusing, as you can do double jumps, but you can only do them in a non-disclosed timeframe after the initial jump. You also jump higher if you hit both jumps right after each other, which I haven't ever seen before, I don't get the reason behind and doesn't make any sense to me.
Often enough I found myself trying to get somewhere, but couldn't do so due to the controls or because the game didn't tell you how to get there at all. I once spent 10-20 minutes (due to the slow movement speed) on multiple tries trying to get up a cliff, just to be disappointed with nothing significant being on there, even though the game made it clear there was something there.
Another time I had to activate certain things to open up a path, but the game didn't tell me how to do it. The first two times it worked just fine, but the last time I had to search for 5 minutes to find out what to do, and what ended up working wasn't what I had to do before.
There are hardly any Settings in this game. No mouse/camera sensitivity, no inverting the y-axis, no advanced graphics settings, no volume settings, no keybinding settings, nothing. It only has the very minimum you need to be able to play a game, and I don't think that's enough.
It might seem like I'm a little nitpicking, but this is a 1-2 hour game for 8€, and all these flaws really add up to have made my experience with this game a lot less enjoyable. It tries to be some sort of platformer, but it absolutely fails at that. The movment flaws also require you to retry some jumps multiple times, which takes ages due to the slow movement speed. If you are looking for a game to have fun in, please move on, I don't think you will find anything here. If you want a game with a good story, then in my opinion, you're wrong here too. Let me tell you why:
-
Probably one of the main points why anyone would buy this game, except for the graphics and promised atmosphere (which it mostly delivers).
Let me make it short: I don't like it. It is told in a very cliché way, it is sort of generic and had nothing to it that made it stand out to me. It was a little interesting, yes. It really was. But that's it.
I thought that just the story of the fox, which the main story doesn't focus on too much, was a lot more interesting, and it was the only thing that actually got to me.
The only thing that makes the story interesting is that it was artificially blown up to try to hit you right in the face, but you really feel that it's forced, and the narrators don't do a good job at delivering it, especially because it doesn't feel genuine and real at all. If the story gets to you, it's because it tries really hard to make you feel something, but for me it didn't quite work out.
This still doesn't contain any spoilers, but just be aware I will talk about what the story is about in this spoiler:
"The First Tree" is a nice game. I didn't hate it, but I didn't like it. I didn't really have fun while playing it, but the graphics, the soundtrack and the story of the fox you play made me keep playing it, and after finishing the game, the ending made it worth my time for me.
BUT; In my opinion, this is not enough to justify buying this for 8€. You could spend that money on better games that deliver an even better experience, and often even look better. I would not play this game again, and I would not advise anyone to spend money on this. If it is on sale really cheap, at least 50% off, and you are fine with only good graphics and a nice atmosphere, go for it. I, as someone who luckily doesn't need to worry about spending 8€ on a game he doesn't like, don't regret buying it. But if these 8€ meant ANY more to me than what they currently do, I would probably refund this game after finishing.
If you buy this game, just don't expect to have a flawless experience that's fun to play - expect to have a relaxing time, some distraction from your surroundings and a semi-interesting story to guide you through it. If that's the only thing you want and you're fine with unpolished, partially annoying gameplay mechanics, this might be worth it to you.
EDIT: I read a few people say that you should go easy on this game because only one person made this, but what should I care? I spent 8€ on this game and it should be able to be criticised just like the game of a AAA developer.

As a perennial player of FM, my experience has been that FM 2018 is the poorest incarnation of the game because of the following:
- Far too many mindless long shots.
- Overpowered goalkeepers. In several career games Man Utd rule the PL and Atletico Madrid rule La Liga. Put simply it's because De Gea and Oblak rarely concede.
- Penalty conversion is really poor (Aguero missed all 8 penalties we got in a season until I was forced to switch to a player with lower pen attribute. Conversion rate improved but we miss more than we score) that I would prefer not to get any during a match as it affects my players morale.
- At corners I like to have one player lurk outside the box. This results in most corners being passed to the player lurking outside of the box (irrespective of corner instructions) and then shooting wide. The AI does nothing about it so it becomes repetitive and boring. So why don't I just remove the player from that position? Because it allows the AI to counter me.
- I feel that it requires more mouse clicks to get to places as opposed to FM 17
I've managed to live with these issues by playing only 3 seasons with each team, before moving to another team and league and creating a different tactic.
But all the above issues are present each time, which has caused me to lose interest already by January (usually FM keeps my interest until March/April).
Most likely I'll buy FM 19, but it's a shame that FM 18 has been such a disappointment.

I usually buy FM every couple of years and have been playing the series since the Champ Manager days.  FM2018 looked really promising and the game itself, in my opinion, shows a lot of progress and promise for the future.  However, I'm going back to FM2016 for now.  Here's why:
1) The game is too buggy at the moment.  I started a new game with Walsall FC in the English League One and the right back (who was playing in Scotland the previous season) was carrying a one match ban.  That's fine, it happens.  The problem was that the red card prevented him playing in any pre season friendlies, even in the under 23s or under 18s matches.  That meant that I had to wait for the first match of the season for the card to clear before attempting to build up his match fitness.  Reds cards picked up in the league or cup do not affect friendlies.  Bugs like this should've been spotted before people were made to pay £38 and reading the forums there are many other bugs still to be dealt with.
2) I miss FM Touch.  I know that not everyone likes it, but why remove it?  It's great to have the option there to play a more streamlined game and I personally want it back.  I didn't play FM2017 so i'm unsure if it was removed then or now, but sometimes I just can't be bothered with the extreme, realistic, 'hands on' approach and just want to speed through seasons.
If the bugs are wiped from this game I will probably pick it back up again and change my opinion to 'recommend', but until then I'm back on FM2016, which is a shame.  I was looking forward to this game.
