Starship Corporation is an ambitious mix of several game genres. The game certainly has a great deal of potential, and brings together some interesting and innovative gameplay ideas.
Now let’s talk about the cold vacuous reality of this game and its current state. It’s been in development for YEARS, and seems of have made very little progress on many of the core features beyond basic pick-and-place ship layout, a shallow/buggy market system, and a badly designed “ship simulation game.
It’s an unbalanced and buggy mess, with a “Full Techtree” victory achievable in just a few hours of gameplay (once you master the crude and mindnumbly repetitive gameplay tasks). I encountered countless errors and bugs simply through the course of playing the tutorial and several sandbox games.
There is no strategy, virtually no resource management, and limited room for creativity, and zero re-playability. The techtree is little more than a halfassed speedbump – in virtually every situation the next technology/module is superior to its predecessor (in some cases comically superior re: Storage Modules)
You will likely spend 70% of your playtime in the “crew training” module (Since each new ship design requires you to play through over a dozen repetitive tasks), it seems to be the most fleshed out portion of the game. Here you will find such exciting features as:
- Zero AI for your crew, and virtually no automation.
- A Buggy and challenged interface
- Hours of frustration.
Sadly, that does not instill confidence in the team’s capacity to deliver a good game.

I didn't do enough research on this game before I bought it.
Note to self:
Do not search for games when you are bored just as you shouldn't go to the grocery store when you are hungry.
Do not buy games on the first day they come on Steam.
Game Summary:
1.) Build ship
2.) Test it
3.) Sell it
Most of your time will be spent testing the ships. It didn't take long before I began to feel like I was 'working' instead of 'playing'. you basically set up "routes" for your repair guys to "maintain" the different pieces in your ships.
Each part in your ship has a certain time frame they must be visited by a repair guy before it starts to take damage.
Felt like I bought a pacman game.
After buying the game, I repeatedly saw demands where people were asking for AI (artificial intelligence) to take care of ship testing for you.
There were aspects such a energy, heat, fuel, oxygen, water, and storage on your ship, but I didn't feel as if there was much more strategy with placement of those ship parts outside of making an efficient route for your crew to run around and maintain parts.
The "Sell" part of the game where you sell your ships might as well been something put together in a Microsoft Excel spreadsheet. The criteria for who a customer choses as the contractor for their bid did not go into details of anything I would assume should be part of the decision making process. Lowest bidder was the only rationale I saw. Not.... your ship is more expensive, but it has more storage and is more durable than the other ships.... or, your ship is 1% more expensive, but has military capabilities, whereas the others don't.
The Galactic Civilizations III game I already have gave a much more gratifying ship building experience than this game does, and that wasn't even the sole purpose of that game. Galactice Civ 3 didn't go into the depth of as many ship parts as this game includes, but at least I got to fly my ships around and watch them wreak havok on my enemies. Perhaps this Starship Corporation has something of the sort in mind for future development, but as it is now, I feel like I bought an alternate version of Pacman. If the game looks different in the future, I will add another section with an update to my review.

So I haven't played this game for long, but I have played it enough to recognise its problems, and they are pretty fundamental and damning.
The game is basically 3 games, which are a business simulator that's a little inconsistent and buggy so far, a ship blueprint designer which, at least at the start, is much more like a puzzle game than a way to get creative or clever about design (as an aside, you have to power staircases but you can't run a cable or pipes downstairs? What?), and as a third element, an overtaxing but underwhelming ship simulator.
People have compared it to FTL, but it's more like if you had to constantly move your crew around every room for ten minutes per sector in FTL or your ship explodes before it can even do the first jump. And your crew never shuts up when you're telling it to do this. If that sounds like a great idea, you might just be the target market for this game.
Anyway, the main, crippling problem with this game is that after you've picked a contract and designed a blueprint suitable for its requirement, if you change your ship designs even a little bit (even literally rearranging a few doors and readjusting the wiring so they work right), you have to go through the stressful-yet-tedious process of recertifying the ship, which is a ten minute  simulation of the ship running (real time, you can pause and slow down).
Now you could theoretically turn the speed up, but you have to direct your crew to maintain your vessel, and even on a tiny seven-man ship (the smallest possible), that requires near-constant input because there's no automation whatsoever. And if anything goes wrong eight or nine minutes into the process, you really have to start again because otherwise your rating for how well the ship performs gets tanked, and you need a certain rating for your ship to get bought.
Until you've done that, you also can't access the more theoretically enjoyable parts of testing the ship, where you try to prove it's safe in a series of emergency situations. But too many of these have the same patience-testing ten minute time limit, and if you discover that there's some kind of flaw in your design when it comes to dealing with one problem or another, welp, guess you have to do the original certification all over again, plus everything else.
Oh and incidentally you still have to maintain the ship in the ten minute emergency certifications, just like the "sit here and make sure the ship doesn't break down by clicking and listening to radio barks a lot" mode. Brill.
Now in a game called Detroit from 1994, you had to do something like this too. They've somewhat similar games, in fact. Same big map screen with (eventually for this project) different markets, and your factories and labs, with a designer and a related test function.
Big difference between this game and Detroit is that in Detroit, it doesn't take three f*cking hours to not quite be able to sell your first car, because although you tuned your gear ratios and connected up your brake fluid just so, you didn't optimally design your automobile to sustain an attack by tommy gun wielding gangsters that you as a CEO have to survive for nearly a quarter of an hour, so it's back to the drawing board (and then test centre... again...).
I might actually like this game if they started excising big parts of what it currently is. But that's not the usual trajectory for an EA project, so I can't recommend it in good faith. Sorry, boys.

i don't even know where to start with this game. i haven't played it in a few months because i put in 23 hours the first two days i had it and decided i should take a break. if that tells you anything.
so i guess i should probably start with the gameplay. you'll spend most of your time in-game fighting one thing or another, and the combat feels fantastic. the game is played entirely at your own pace, so death can come in the blink of an eye, or at a miserable agonizing crawl. whatever the speed, death is inevitable and frequent. the difficulty options are nice however, and there's both a casual mode and a pretty solid tutorial to help ease you in. the ui is great and you don't really need to use hotkeys at all, though a few of them are nice to have. it's perfect if you like rogue-lites and want to try something a little more traditional without some of the more annoying aspects of roguelike.
moving on to graphics and story. look, i know you've probably already looked at the screenshots and said, "really?? ehhhhhhhh" and that's fair. honestly though, they've really grown on me, and while a lot of it is "generic fantasy", so much of it isn't, and it subverts the genre in just the right places. the sprites and environments have had some nice work put into them, and despite looking like they're from 1996, they really bring a unique atmostphere to the game. the worldbuilding and music fit well with the visuals and add a lot to the immersion. the dialogue and found notes are all worth reading and give insight into the world, whether it's a small scrap of comic relief in a hectic dungeon or the detailed history of a faction bought from a bookseller. everything is  well-written (if a little... campy in places. not sure if that's the right word) and usually breaks up the pacing in the right places.
what will keep me coming back to this game tho (most likely for years to come) are the amazing moments you just can't find anywhere else in gaming. this aspect of the game is reminiscent of skyrim in a lot of ways. despite any flaws the game might have, there is nothing like coming out of a cave in skyrim and knowing an entire world is out there for you to explore. ToME is the same. there is nothing like the feeling of slowly suffocating to death under sand and knowing there's no one to blame for yourself. there is nothing like discovering what lies beneath Lake Nur for the first time. it's a game that lets your imagination run wild in a way "prettier" games can't.
tl;dr play this game. you'll probably get more hours out of the 10 bucks you pay for ToME + Ashes of Urh'Rok than you'll get out of the $120 you spent on the Witcher 3 and MGSV.

German AI declares war (DOWs) on Poland and struggles to take it. It then DOWs the Low Countries and does not attack them. Truly, the Dark Souls of not comparing things to Dark Souls
I had just finished breakfast and walked over to my personal computer station, brush in my mouth. "Brushing really is the Dark Souls of oral hygene", I thought as I checked my E-Mails. There was a notification by my boss at Journagaming 2000, which I read intently: "We need a review of Cuphead", it said "and please, don't do the gimmick of comparing that game to Dark Souls just because it's unforgiving". I installed my copy and proceeded to launch it.
Immediately, the title screen and opening cinematic made me feel as though I was back in Lordran, the Curse Of The Unded (or as they call it in Cuphead, the devil stealing your soul over gambling debt) being explained to me. After clearing hurdle after brutal hurdle in the tutorial and dying about a dozen times, I couldn't help but compare the dash jump required to advanced to the manitically difficult patterns of the Asylum Demon, but avid a gamer as I am, I was succesful in beating the tutorial without comparing the game to Dark Souls.
Immediately upon finishing the tutorial I was thrown into Inkwell Isle with multiple branching paths to take which would take me to the next boss. "What is this, Dark Souls?" you may be thinking -- I KNOW, RIGHT? But no, this is merely Cup Head, sporting some beautifully fluid animations that I do not get tired of and a very rewarding gameplay style that will make you throw your hands in the air in victory the instant you hear that "KNOCKOUT!"
The game's theme is clearly very well thought out. While it is well cartoony and bubbly, it follows suit on themes most present in old school cartoons with dark undertones, showing itself very self aware in being a game that is marketed to adults who want to feel as though they are playing a kid's game that gathered a cult following. This, of course, reminded me of the way Dark Souls did its take on the inherent darkness in man's soul. Ironically, I found that as well animated as Cuphead was, some visual cues weren't as good as they could've been. Many times, enemies did attacks that covered the entire screen and force you to dodge small pellets, but the enemy's animation while they do these attacks sits on your peripheral, making it really hard to concentrate. Despite this, the controls are very responsive, very unlike Studio MDHR who completely ignore my requests that the game be retitled Cup Souls. Sure, I did find that every enemy playing the same puff of smoke animation when killed could be inconvenient at times, such as when trying to dodge an attack that is cued by a similar puff of smoke, and some fights felt were only beatable through the use of the right items, but none of this is a game breaking problem when compared to the utterly rewarding nature of playing Cuphead and avoiding comparing the game to Dark Souls.
But ultimately, what I liked the most is the core mechanic of fighting boss after boss with very little chaff in between. Short and to the point, I was very reminiscent of fighting Gwyn, Lord of Cinder while I tried to beat a giant floating bird complete with its birdhouse as it fired eggs and smalled pidgeons at me. Most bosses having several forms made getting to see the next form a lot of fun as the design alone was often super interesting and almost for a second made me forget about Dark Souls, and my nearly pathological need to compare everything to it.

There's a Reason why the Reviews are very postiive, while the top reviews are all negative. It's a mixture of people not getting "the game they wanted" which is a small but loud minority, and people complaining about how Paradox breaks their games into a good base game, and DlC that always update it and improve the base game. The game itself is just plain fun. It's not oversimplified, but not too hard to teach a friend either. It will surprise you and definitely is fun alone or with a friend.
Now I'll be completely honest. Their first DLC definitely had a bad idea of making the "spearhead" battle plan a paid feature. So all of the complaining about it are correct that it was a bad idea to make it paid content, but they have every right to charge for it. If not, just go back to playing their previous games which had either None or very basic AI for telling AI to control a Front.  It's still further work they put into the game, so don't go crying about the entire game being bad just because of them charging for it. The rest of the features both free and paid with the DLC are wonderful and make the flow of battle much easier to understand and keep track of.
Speaking of AI, let's talk about the bad ai complaint. The biggest reason this is a good game even with the AI doing some crazy things sometimes (AI completely abandoning a front because of a new war!? sure I can declare war early to abuse it!), is it sometimes does some crazy good things! I've seen the AI do some very interesting things, and it's led to some awesome fun alternative history moments (Poland create their own Alliance, Russia Attacks! Germany and Italy send tank divisions as Volunteers and are barely holding the secondary defense lines, France joins the Comintern and Declare war on Germany! UK now has to choose wisely whom her allies really are. Strengthen the Axis, but save the Polish Alliance? Or Create a Massive Comintern to help crush the Axis early, but lose europe to an entirely newfuture enemy)
The biggest flaw that usually messes everyone up is Germany... the way they made the game, Germany gets lots of free go to war buttons. The AI are like the Orks in Warhammer 40k... they WILL push that button when they see it. This can sometimes cause the early defeat of Germany if the player does not support them. This is a known issue though, and they've already taken steps to help fix this and it's become a rare event (like an alternative history where Hitler went crazy earlier!)
Remember though, this is still "Logistics: the game". The fun comes from making sure that your researching down the path to your victory, keeping the industry building the path to victory, and your nations defending your industry so you can actually keep up! You're setting up battle plans to punch through, encircle the enemy and crush them with maneuvers, not just Get Big Tank, blow up everything. You creating the right Alliances, pushing the right neutrals to your side, trying to grab as much as you can without waking up the sleeping giant that is America with too much war, too quickly (Though Japan will always ruins it by taking over China and creating a 100% world on fire <.< ) and keeping your trades going so you don't slow down production.
TL:DR - The game is just plain FUN. I've been playing since Hoi1 and I'm honestly quite impressed and enjoying this game. I've finally taken over the world as Romania, and feel proud at my understanding of the game. Seriously, it's a the first game in a long time that I've enjoyed learning it over several plays and feel rewarded in the end by being able to take small nations to greatness. I'm loving seeing this game franchise played by more people so seriously... just buy it!

To review Plug and Play is a really hard task, cause I have no idea how to review a game in which I have no idea what I'm doing, but I'm gonna give it my best shot, so here goes.
Plug and Play is a game about Plugs and love. There's no traditional story telling here as it's all random sequences which make up the entire game.
The gameplay consists of dragging and clicking the entire time. The entire game's goal is to plug something in or plug something out.
The art style is weird looking and it just creeps you out at first and then it weird's you out, how strange the game becomes in a short amount of time.
The game is also incredibly short. It took me 10 minutes to finish the entire game and after you finish the game the first time, there's no replay value what so ever, so keep that in mind if you're planning on buying this game.
In the end, there's not much to say about the game apart from what I already said.  Plug and Play is a great little art title and I highly suggest you check it out, but only on a discount since I recommend spending 3 euros for 10 minutes of content. I do suggest getting it on a discount though and you will not be disappointed.
Final Rating:
7/10 Wait for a discount

for a star wars game, and for its time, this game is (or was) unbelievable. even by today's standards as far as the story goes, this game has everything a star wars game *should* have: new jedi, new sith, the use of lightsabers and force powers...and to top it off - RL cutscenes (although not *brilliantly* acted out) which makes this game incredibly unique in that respect. as both a shooter and a hack and slash game, this game is pretty well balanced, and the levels are quite well designed too. if I had to fault it fairly on a few things, I'd say the story was quite weak, especially if I'm comparing it to the star wars movies. but star wars games are never brilliant for their narratives and in that respect this game is one of the better star wars stories, especially given that there are sequels that develop upon it. in my opinion it is far better than the sequel in most respects, and it's *definitely* a better story than jedi academy.
the graphics by today's standards are pretty dreadful, but thankfully you can mod the game out to fix that somewhat. if you're looking for an original star wars game that is more than just mindlessly swinging a lightsaber about, this game is brilliant. but if you're looking for more of a traditional "star wars" game where you're not using blasters for half the game, and where you're not expected to have to put in an ounce of thought here and there, maybe stick to another star wars game. 7.5-8/10 - definitely recommended if you can forgive the game for looking more like lego than the *actual* lego star wars games...

Tool up, dumbos! Here's the deal... We're Americans, so we're the good guys. They (any other nation, but heavy accents obligatory) are clearly the bad dudes. So, camo on, scope lids up.  Let the banalities begin!
Maybe I'm alone in this, but I like games to have at least made some attempt at a moral issue, where the sanctity of life presents at least a crumb of doubt in what you are doing. Shooting peoples' brains out is simply less fun when you start thinking, 'well what did he ever do to deserve that? How is it helping this imagined world if I stick an unapologetic slug through two brains at once? He's just a guard, probably on a zero hours contract, trying to get by, and I'm going to knife him in the neck. Bummer.'
The other thing is, if you play a character who is already highly trained, a 'special ops' uber-killer, there's no way up from that. Gordon Freeman was a gentle scientist who expanded his skill-base. If you start at the top, where can you go, narratively speaking?
Sniper Elite at least has that WW2 setting, so even though Karl Fairburne is a one-note macho dullard with all the wit and wisdom of a folding trench shovel, you still feel you're fighting evil. Anything based in the 21st Century, especially involving US forces, you feel sort of faintly sick, being part of some over-funded bullying world police.
Why can't the hero be Swedish? Or from Belgium?
These problems would be solved by not being so goddam Tom Clancy about everything. Or by maybe having a level where you merely have to serve Halal lunch through the slots in the doors at Guantanamo, just for some perspective on your life choices. Instead of an end of level boss, you could meet Henry Kissinger and get lectured on why covert, illegal military operations in other peoples' countries are actually good for the world.

It’s enjoyable to play but feels like the ending was rushed and leaves me with no desire to want to play the game a second time. Get it only when on sale, tinker with the config to make it look and play much better, and you shouldn’t be too disappointed – not until the end anyway.
I did enjoy the game. Like many older games there is a certain amount of configuration modding required to make it work properly, but there are plenty of guides describing how to do that. The texture quality reducing as you get closer to stuff is something you can’t fix though, but if you can learn to accept it then the game becomes much more enjoyable. I quickly learnt that if I approached something and it started to look like it came from the Amstrad era... just move on - it’ll be of no importance to the game anyway.
It claims to be open world – I’d dispute that. The game directs you through the main quest quite aggressively, with most NPC’s doing nothing other than telling you to get on with the main quest, so there isn’t any incentive to go exploring. If you do (like I did when the game ending told me I could still go and explore the world) there’s nothing to do. A couple of hints are made during the game about there being other settlements around the world which might need my help too. Is there? I couldn’t find any, and most of the settlements previously visited during the main quest are locked down if you go back to them later. Quite disappointing.
The ending is the biggest disappointment though; even Sarah is bored with being in the game at this point! The end city is supposed to be huge compared to the towns already explored, but you only get to see a small bit of it in what is a repetitive
quest. But worse than that, when you do complete the game and
… nothing changes. If you go back and revisit the two main towns then they are both stuck in time, waiting for someone to
. Huh? Didn’t I just do that!
It’s a real shame the game is near impossible to mod, as I’m sure the modding community could have easily added a more fleshed-out ending to the game and turned it into something worth playing again and again. But no. I’m glad I played it, I’m glad I completed it, but I don’t think I’ll play it again. :(

I've come around to this game after a few false starts. I definitely recommend getting the 2.0 mod for this game, as it's a vast improvement over the original layout. On to the game: I'm sure you've heard this game takes place in two parts - planning and action. Both are incredibly well done and are borderline simulation territory, but definitely still very gamey. The AI is pretty good, but not perfect. You can tell your squad to go clear a room and sometimes they will bunch in the doorway, ignoring terrorists. Another favorite is missions where enemies may not be armed, but are trying to complete some objective (like deleting data from computers). Many times, the AI would be told to clear a room and ignore these enemies, leading to a mission failure. For this reason, I feel there are a few missions that are just bugged and don't reflect the base game (namely mission 11, where it's unclear what is causing a mission failure, as all weapons were silenced and all enemies were killed upon entering a room). For missions like these, it's nice to have access to the developer console and just 'completemission.' This game is far from perfect, but it's really fun when everything comes together. The Gold Edition comes with the expansions, too, so you get a lot (around 30 missions?) for your money. SWAT 3 and 4 are still my favs, but this has an addicting element to it, as well.

This is definitely one of the best games in the Assassin's Creed series and an absolute classic. The gameplay has aged decently. Combat isn't as good as later entries and at times Ezio seems to jump in a completely different direction to what you wanted, but overall it's a fairly solid experience. The story is the strongest point here, and the protagonist, Ezio Auditorie, is arguably the best in the entire series. The events of the game take place starting from his birth until he is about 40 years old, and you will notice him mature greatly as the story progresses. There's also a lot of different cities and areas to explore, my personal favourite being Venice.
Try to get the game in a sale if you can, but I strongly recommend this to anyone who wants to get into or already likes Assassin's Creed.

Ok, some people seem to have trouble running the game, which I can´t confirm. So far I haven´t had a single crash and I have fullfilled my first contract without major issues. Only bug I had so far was that during one mission a crew member got stuck on an airlock, that´s it.
The game itself isn´t fast paced strategy or a real tycoon simulator (at least not yet). It´s just pick a contract, which demands a certain type of ship. For example a freighter that can load 3000 tons and handle a small boarding. Then you choose a fuselage and place the rooms you have researched on it while trying to balance things like electricity, crew size and so on while also keepign in mind that for example exhaust and loading doors can be places where boarding takes place. So do not place the bridge, the target of every boarding crew, right beside those, for example. There are many things to consider.
Then you control the crew through a varity of simulations, like the above mentioned boardings or a meteor storm or a fire in the enine room etc. The better your ship handles those the better the rating, and the more money oyu can ask for it. Of course you could also create a shity ship which barely has all the rooms it needs and places it´s crew in mortal danger, but only costs half as much as the other company? There are different tactics here.
Note that every ship can try every crew simulation, but a lot of ships won´t and don´t need to handle all these. Your 3000t frighter with a crew of 10  for example doesn´t have to win a boarding manouver by 25 special forces soldiers. Your contractor won´t expect it anyway.
So as oyu can see there is a lot of thought involved here, so for the love of god: Don´t buy this game and drag the ratings down if you can´t handle that. The game is not too hard (in fact it´s gotten easier since the first demo from a few years back on desura).
Which brings me to my final point: The game is already in development for several years, so while it´s unlikely that it will be abandoned at this point, it´s also unlikely that it will leap forwards in huge steps I think. So if you want to support the developer, buy it, it´s worth it I think, but don´t expect the finished game next month or so.

Reviewing the Alpha.
The concept of the game is awesome really so this will be a positive feedback assuming the game gets the necessary upgrades. It's more a thumbs-up for the developer so that they carry on.
But the game is really in an alpha state so I wouldn't recommend buying now, you will see a large chunk of cons but they didn't stop me from playing, it's just that if you don't have time or curiosity to deal with them, you should wait for a later version of the game.
Pick a hull, build the rooms of your ship and stress it under specific use cases like firestorm, piratery, or simple normal operation.
Sell your creation in the galaxy by answering speficic requests from companies.
Research new modules for new features.
The game content is quite complete right now. Or at least sufficiently large anough to make the game interesting to play.
All the situations are playable, a lot of different rooms to research, a whole galaxy with tons of systems where you can build an office and start answering specific needs and a final mission.
I'm sure most of the cons will be corrected at some point but here they are
The cons :
- You don't get much personal satisfaction until you've finalised a complete ship and its tests so, unlike most other game, you will be frustrated of doing and doing again until you make the perfect ship and go through the numerous tests. So I guess it's lacking simple objectives to start with and get a hold of the game. Like a non manned ship for instance or a single seater fighter...
- Building your ship can be a pain due to corrifor management. I think there should be a free draw corridor system. Though, it works...
- Very bugged at the moment, but well, it's an alpha, lots of in game error pops or crashes but its playable anyway.
- I find the time you spend on just planning the route of your crew to optimize necessary maintenances very painful. Your team is slow, maintenance stats go down very quickly, difficult to synchronise all of them when they have to meet back in the same room cause this room needs 4 crew to maintain and so on. This game should not be a patrol tycoon :-)
- I was kinda confused by the breaches. Still haven't figured out how to not kill the crew while attempting rushed repair  or not having the rest of the crew die with lack of oxygen while you suit up or loosing a whole area of the ship by sealing it off with little expectation to retrieve it some day.
- Lack of indicators and bars so that you understand the status of the rooms in one glimpse.
- Couldn't find a way to make the crew escape in the emergency evacuation system
- Interface is annoying, like when you want to go to previous menu ingame, you'd prefer starting over from the 1st menu cause it's clumsy. Or not really intuitive. You often wonder where to click at the start.
- Tutorial is just enough for the Alpha, Still images. It needs to be improved for the final verison. Though without it I would have never figured out how to maintain rooms in the ship...
- If anything happens on your ship, then your technicians go away to deal with the problem and all your maintenances get disrupted = chaos. Yes, you can have an army of technicians though to deal with that but not really efficient.
- Sounds need to be balanced or reviewed. Like the hard breath when soemone is about to die. And it's even worse when ALL your crew is about to die... Just die quietly please, don't overload my ears.
Your ship has a flaw ? You need to change the plan ? A
tooo bad, you'll have to start all the tests over even if you add a screw in the captain chair. So, piece of advice, think ahead  and assume the consequences. Maybe this flawed design version of a ship can be sold at good price anyway !
To conclude, you'll probably wonder why a thumbs up with so many things to correct! Well, simple, I don't know any game that puts you in this "design and test" situation where you honestly feel like you're a ship manufacturer with the difficulties it brings.
It's just missing the production line setup in the factory ;-) joking
Lot of work ahead though !

After the first update, I am changing my review and am now cautiously recommending this game. It still has lots of bugs... but the game breakers in the basic functionality are gone... now I am able to reliably design a ship and save it, and run the various crew simulations on it. Does it still take a long time to load?  Yes... but I don't care as much now that the game doesn't crash nearly as often.
There will be more bugs found (I have an unfinished bug report to do after writing this review), but the developer fixes them quickly. I'll be thrilled when he adds new content, but the ship design and simulation content is there... and it's good, and it's fun.
Some people have complained about having to micromanage the crew in the simulation part (specifically the routine operations simulation)... I don't find this is the case. When the simulation starts, I pause it and give orders to the crew (including a maintenance tour for the technicians)... the crew pretty reliably goes about doing those orders, so as long as you didn't miss something in the initial orders, you are good. I pretty much give the orders, unpause it at 2x speed, and then just keep an eye on it for anything I missed.
I am keeping my initial review below.
----
This game has unbelievable potential... it's everything I've wanted in games where I design my own starship... I've dreamt about being able to design my own power routing, cooling systems, etc., and route them how I want to... this lets you do all of that.
The problem is that the game is horribly buggy still... you first notice this when you load it... it takes 2-3 minutes at least to load. This is way too long of a time to wait around waiting for a game to load. Then, when I tried to run the tutorial, I got about 2/3 of the way through the ship design process, and the tutorial tried to have me save the game. Well, I did it, but then the interface went away and a debug console message came up and poof... the last hour disappeared because the auto-save didn't work, and the save ship dialog locked up the game.
Then, I tried going directly to the next stage of the tutorial... it immediately crashed to desktop with another debug message.
I really want to love this game, and I hope that these issues get resolved in a timely manner... I will be back, but I can't recommend it for anybody in its current state of development.

I love the concept behind this game. It was just added to early access so clearly there's a lot more development to be done. The core of this game is laying out floorplans for space ships. You need to consider not only cost and avoiding wasted space, but also where rooms are in relation to one another, and how defendable the ship is from various threats. Once you finish a blueprint, you switch to a mode where you test your ship in various scenarios in order to earn a score. A higher score increases your ship's value on the market.
There is a meta game, with different types of contracts. Most of the contracts are to buy a ship from you, and have specific requirements. There are also contracts where you use one of your own ships to complete a task, such as transporting goods from one system to another, or salvaging a derelict ship.

My reccomendation for this game is completely unrelated to my own personal opinions. It is a very niche title which is difficult to outright recommend to anybody. This is a WALKING SIMULATOR, so please do not purchase it it expecting any form of gameplay as there is virtually none.
I completed the game. Wasn't really what I thought. Came into it expecting Fox Simulator 2017. Instead what I played was more akin to Dear Ester (which I have also completed). Using Dear Ester as my only comparison as I have not played any other walking simulators, this is my critique:
I can't but feel a little disappointed personally with the ''story'' behind it. This game follows the narrative between a man and a woman. The fox is only used as a means of advancing the story as opposed to being a focus of it. This could have had literally any other theme such as a player controlled toaster traversing a junkyard and still be inconsequential. There was no immersion factor or relationship between the human narrator and the fox outside of the narrator mentioning that the fox is simply a dream he is having (and another moment that I won't spoil). What is constantly talked about as you hit certain invisible checkpoints throughout the level is the narrator's real life problems. Personally, this does not interest me in any form.
The level design was obviously made to stretch out the length of the game. Expect to be walking for a long time across minimally textured surfaces for minutes at a time with nothing going on. You cannot interact with any of the environment outside of collecting glowing point orbs which do nothing other than award steam achievements for collecting them, and one particular level's extremely basic mechanics to unlock a door. The few rabbits that I actually found run away from you as you draw close and cannot be interacted with. The entire time you will be moving between glowing white point markers in the distance which, for the most part, naturally lead you towards the end of each level.
The music was extremely loud. Not my personal taste but I can't exactly rate it since it is entirely subjective, but the lack of basic options settings in the menu meant that I had to lower my headset volume since in game sounds cannot be adjusted. That includes the voice of the narrator. The music also does not loop, so as you are slowing making your way across expanses of nothingness expect to hear nothing but the crunching of leaves and rain. The options menu also lacked the ability to adjust the mouse sensitivity. By default it is extremely low. Apart from AA you cannot alter any of the graphics options outside of ''low, medium, ultra high, etc'' presets which I have no idea what the technical differences are between them. I played on ''very high'' but I don't imagine that, in a game as graphically simple as this, will have much of a performance impact. ''ultra high'' did tank my framemrate below 60 though, but without being able to see what each preset altered, I could not determine why that was.
In conclusion I feel as though this game is almost strictly worse than Dear Ester. Good first attempt for the small development team behind it though. But if you were going to have to choose between either it would have to be Dear Ester. This game is graphically inferior with a rather questionble story and artifical pacing. Unfortunate since the ''Walking Simulator'' market is very niche and there are other popular, more established titles that have been out for years already. If you came here because you like foxes like me then you might not find this game to be as fulfilling in the fox aspect as you wish.
As I said at the beginning, my choice to not recommend this game is independent of my own personal opinion of it. Unfortunately though, if I were recommend this game BASED ON my opinion then it would also have to be a ''no''. Dear Ester just does it better I'm afraid.

I can recommend this with a disclaimer: this game is the dev's first. It's an ambient, story-driven collectathon. If you play games for the story, you'll enjoy listening to Alaska-man talk about his daddy issues while you run around as a fox in some pretty scenery. If you play games for mechanics, you'll probably get hung up on how barebones the content is and how the fox handles like a tricycle. Also the music shuts off after half an hour in any given area; not sure if this is intentional but it'd be nice if it looped, elsewise you're stuck with nothing but nature sounds and your own thoughts which for me inevitably turned to "I wonder why the fox doesn't make the Stuka dive bomber sound when it jumps off cliffs". Not sure where the price point comes from, $8 is a bit much for about an hour and a half of content and story. All this in mind though I did enjoy it and for the dev's first game it's not bad.
Some suggestions if the dev reads this:
-Lots of empty space in the game that could be filled with just a bit more stuff. Other collectibles, other animals, etc. The minimalist thing is nice when it comes to UI but not so much when it comes to content.
-Maybe this is just me but I couldn't find anywhere to change the sensitivity for the xbox controller and it's default set to be extremely low.
-It may or may not be a stylistic choice to have shut off the music after a half hour but I'd rather have a continually looping variety of ambient songs and if the player wants to only hear the nature sounds have an option to turn off the music. It's especially key to a story driven game like this without a lot of other stuff going on to have nice atmospheric components.

For instance, people told me not to make a rouge/ranger as they are "useless" well that just motivated me to make one even more.

Which mean's RIFT is basically a game of DPS and Healer (maybe support if you know how to do it properly).

It's not pay to win (P2W), you don't need to pay to be the best in the game. Paying just really helps you get more powerful in a shorter amount of time. Like for a redicilous amount of money you could buy all the top tier armors/weapons but can also earn those items the normal way by grinding.
All in all it's a very good game, they update often and I'm glad I found it.
Overall Rift gets a 8 out of 10

The Typing of the Dead: Overkill is an offbeat first-person puzzle-action game for the PC that lets you fight hordes of gruesome zombies by quickly typing out words that appear onscreen. This unusual game actually has a history: It originally debuted on Sega's Dreamcast console in 2000 and was itself a modified version of Sega's previously released light-gun arcade game, The House of the Dead 2.
As with most light-gun games, The Typing of the Dead is played "on rails"--that is, you can't actually move your character or choose where to go next; the game determines that. However, depending on how quickly you defeat your enemies, you may be able to rescue innocent bystanders, uncover bonus items, and choose alternate paths through a level, though you'll always finish each level by fighting a powerful boss monster. These boss monsters will actually challenge you in a few interesting ways. For instance, one will force you to figure out and type in the correct answer to a simple question, while another will come barreling at you with a giant chainsaw and will strike you if you can't type out a full sentence in time.
The Typing of the Dead is an unusual game that might not have amazing graphics or sound, but its gameplay is unique and extremely fun. Despite its strange, silly premise, it does have a few explicitly gory sequences--some zombies turn into sloppy messes when shot down, which is why it's an M-rated game. But if you like action-packed games or horror movies, you'll probably enjoy The Typing of the Dead...and even if you don't, you might want to give it a try.

I told myself not to write a review before I've actually beaten the game, and while it took me longer than expected (admittedly not in small part due to me fooling around instead of playing serious builds), this is it.
This is hands-down my favorite game ever.
Before i begin: You can play the game for free by downloading it from
(the official website).
Purchasing the Steam version will get you a few perks you would otherwise get by donating. (those aren't major, however the DLC is and is in my opinion definitely worth it)
So do test it first before buying and then buy it if you want to support the creator (mostly a single guy by the way).
Things that are great:
-It's in many parts a traditional roguelike (which I am a fan of), that means: turn-based combat, procedurally generated dungeons.
-It's in some parts more forgiving than traditional roguelikes: option to choose between permadeath, a limited number of lives or unlimited lives (while the last takes away from the fun imo), multiple difficulty settings (easier, which will not get you any achievements, normal, which is pretty hard, on to various degrees of insanity)
-the most interesting choice of classes i know from virtually anywhere: There are the classic Berserker, Archer, Archmage but also things like Mindslayer, Oozemancer, Brawler, Solipsist.
-Every class is played differently: due to completely different sets of skills and build possibilities, each class has its own unique playstyle.
-no grinding: all dungeons can only be cleared once, there are no respawning mobs. Additionally there are no consumables, these are replaced by "inscriptions" which are infinitely usable, but on a cooldown, meaning there is nothing you have to save up for a big bossfight, but you still have to think about when you use what in that fight.
-impressive gameworld: The sheer amount of lore there is for you to find is impressive. This is a point where it differs from many classic roguelikes: It has a main quest, a story, and lots of backstory, all of which I personally found to be interesting and engaging. The various dungeons feel interesting and different.
-it's challenging: You actually have to either think about what you are doing, or prepare to die a lot. You might die a lot even if you do until you figure some things out. To me that is a good thing, to others it might not be i guess, but that's what exploration mode (unlimited lives) is for: figuring stuff out.
-great community: Why is this important? While it is not a multiplayer game, there is an in game online chat. It shows character deaths and character achievements (this can be turned on/off) and can be used for chatting. This is extremely helpful for asking about things you might need to know, and in my experience the community will be more than happy to help.
The things you might not like:
-Graphics: This is a Tileset-based game. It doesnt feature great animations or anything like that apart from spell effects. If that is extremely off-putting to you, i'm sorry. As to the tileset itself, I like it, others might not.
-It may not be easy to get into: There are many stats to keep track of, sometimes making it hard to decide which items to take over others, the GUI is great in my opinion, but at the start it can take a bit to get used to it. So if you have any questions while playing: dont hesitate to ask in chat!
-it's challenging: see above
-If you are an achievement completionist, you might get into problems with this game. Just a warning.
All  in all, i very much recommend to try it.
And dont give up after a few deaths :P

I’ve been waiting for Cuphead since it was first revealed in 2014. Now it’s finally here. Cuphead, a super difficult platformer/run & gun game with outstanding visuals, one which mimics the aesthetics of 1930s cartoons to perfection. The game is pretty, but we knew that for the last 3 years. But is the gameplay any good?
Cuphead is basically a series of boss fights with the occasional run & gun level in between, all accessible via an explorable map. It was originally designed as a purely boss fights game, but when it got a lot of attention at the 2014 E3, StudioMDHR decided to make something bigger and better. And I, for one, am glad they did. Nothing in the game feels as if it was just an afterthought. Every boss and every level is well thought out and just feels great.
If you look at the screenshots, I’m sure you will agree they are absolutely stunning. The game doesn’t just look similar to 1930s animations. It looks exactly like it. Not only is it drawn perfectly, it also mimics the animations spot on. Combined with a nice filter that simulates the flickering of an old film, the illusion is complete, you really feel like you are in an old cartoon.
The sound is equally convincing. The game plays an original song on the title screen and right away it feels like this is a very authentic re-imagination of the cartoons of yore. A style that extends not only in regards to the visuals but also the audio. All sound effects, music and voices sound like they were taken directly from an old film reel.
But how does it play? Responsive controls are very important for this type of game. And they are. Responsive that is.. You have just a few actions, the basic movement itself, a dash move, standard and special attack and a movement lock which keeps Cuphead in place while shooting. Aside from that you can switch through your available weapons, while in the air combat missions you also have the ability to hold down a button in order to morph into a smaller version of yourself that is more agile, just doing lesser damage. That’s as far as the controls go. The game is not about complexity. Quite the opposite. You have a very limited set of moves but need to execute them perfectly in order to succeed. If you die in a level, it’s most likely your own fault.
You may already have heard that Cuphead is supposed to be quite difficult. Indeed, it is. Both the bosses and the run & gun levels are extremely challenging. Sometimes so challenging that it took me 20 or more tries to get it done. So, don’t let yourself be fooled by the kiddy graphics, this game is hard and you will get bogged down on certain stages. If you don’t enjoy fighting a boss over and over just to get a little better every time until you eventually beat him, just barely, better think twice before getting Cuphead. As brilliant as the game is – it is certainly not for everyone. It might look mainstream and even childish when looking at the screenshots, but the reality is that it is a niche title for a niche audience. It is fast, pure and unforgiving. It won’t hold your hand, it won’t help you on the way. However if you can handle the difficulty, you will enjoy Cuphead a great deal. Nothing is more satisfying than beating a boss that you really got stuck on for the last hour.
Cuphead is the game we were all hoping for. The presentation is unique and nearly perfect in both video and audio. The gameplay is simple and precise. It is challenging and addictive, I suffered from ‘just one more try’ syndrome quite a bit. For those who don’t mind challenge and brutal difficulty, it is nearly perfect with very few things to criticize. It may be a simple game, but what it does it does extremely well. If you are even remotely interested in this kind of game and don’t mind the difficulty this is a must-buy.
+ Gorgeous Visuals: A beautiful re-imagination of 1930s cartoons, they couldn’t have done it better.
+ Sound Design: Music, sound effects and speech all feel very authentic.
+ Boss Design: Every boss fight is different in both, the look, and mechanics.
* Difficulty: A welcome challenge to some, but a deal breaker to many others.
- Hectic Gameplay: You have so much to dodge on the screen and the game is so unforgiving that you don’t have the time to admire the beautiful art style.
5/5

So, overall this game is great. Great music, great aesthetic, and all that good stuff. I just wanna say that before I go into my little ran- I mean review...
However, as a game dev myself, I noticed some things that were generally irritating about the gameplay. By no means is the gameplay bad, but these things just generally peeved me. First off, the parry system, allbeit the backbone of combat in this game, was basically luck based. Not really, but it sure as hell feels that way some times. You go for a parry, you think you've got it perfect, and it decides to ignore you entirely and you take the damage for it. It wouldn't be so annoying, but in the end of each level, parrys are a big part of your score. Maybe I'm just bad at the game, I thought, but even in tool-assisted (frame by frame stepping) attempts, it seems almost random what qualifies as a parry and what doesn't.
Secondly, in the development world we have something known as hitbox gratuity. Essentially, hitboxes on good things are big while hotboxes on bad things are small. It's a way of giving the player a little benefit of the doubt, since unlike real life, frame by frame rendering can cause problems with accuracy in subtle ways you might never even have noticed, and because the hitboxes are invisible, and don't always wrap the sprites in a perfect fit. Well, this game has none of that. None. It's not that bad, until you get to the first bullet hell level and realize everything you do has to be frame perfect.
Third, there's the inescapable damage. There's so damn much of it. Partially because of the hitboxes being generally unconventional, but also because the game has a tendency to back you into a corner at the worst of times. Even in games like the original Ninja Gaiden, unavoidable damage wasn't as frequent as in this game. I know it might just be me, and that there's always someone who can get through the levels first try with the best possible score, but for the general populus, the damage is just unavoidable.
Complaints aside, I still really enjoy this game, and recomend it 100%. Just make sure you keep what I mentioned in mind while playing, otherwise you'll meet the same gruesome fate over and over again.

I think this may be one of the most poorly optimised retro releases to ever be pushed onto the steam storefront.
Let me get this out of the way by saying this is solely a judgement of the Steam release, there is a good chance that the GOG release actually works.
When I initially bought this, the game had no soundtack, constant graphical glitches (Turning the entire screen into something the Lucky Charms Leprechaun would throw up) and extremely stiff and jerky controls. And by Stiff and Jerky I mean that actual aiming was nigh impossible and I had to resort to playing with the arrow keys to aim. It wasn't fun.
However today, I learned that the steam release recieved a patch mid-this year that fixed a lot of the issues that plagued the game upon release. But...
It's still broken. The controls are still floaty and the game constantly changes between screen resolutions when you press pause. Only this time there are no windowed cutscenes. The Menus are filled with options that are convoluted and even when attempting to modify in order to make the game run better, don't help.
The base controls themselves are bizarrely mapped, there is an underlying disconnect when having to cycle through two mimi-menus containing Force Powers and Items, each with different buttons, and weapons (which you cannot cycle through with the mouse wheel) are awkward to switch between, so I guess you can add a third in-game menu to that as well.
Even though using a lightsaber in combat is persuaded, It is not fun to use in a first person perspective and the aforementioned botched controls make it tiring to use and player death is constant when using it.
This all come to a conclusion when I entered a Dual Boss fight with two Dark Jedi; one a Damage Sponge Boss (a trope I despise in games) who has an unavoidable choke attack, the other a little gremlin guy who could turn jump around everywhere and turn invisible of all things. To quote a certain lovable rogue "That's not how the force works!"
After emptying all my rockets and thermal detonators into them, they were somehow still standing and I was forced to jump and slash at them with a lightaber. 'This is not a good boss fight', I thought as I broke my legs from falling down a suspened platform, again.
I quicksaved a lot until finally winning the fight. Nothing happened so I assumed that a door had opened somewhere, the broken and floaty controls made me fall down the aforementioned suspened platform and die. After defeating the boss again. I quicksaved, only for the game to go into a cutscene an promptly crash.
I will not be playing this game again.
What else is there to say? The Soundtack is typical Star Wars, orchestral and epic, the graphics are from 1997, no point in judging them. Everything else about this release is a disaster though. Please do not buy the Steam release of Dark Forces II. If you really want a good Star Wars game, try the original Dark Forces, at least that game works.

RAGE: An approaching meteor triggers an apocalyptic end-of-the-world scenario that eliminates most of humankind on Earth, reducing civilization to a post-apocalyptic state of scrabbling for survival amongst the few remaining people and those lucky enough to be secured in pods of safety, called Arks. Waking up out of an Ark, your character is attacked by wasteland survivors, and rescued by one as well. Thus begins your journey. You swiftly find that your kind - Ark survivors - are bound to be hunted by the Big Bad, the Authority, for the ancient tech that you hold, access, and represent.
This game desperately wanted to be Quake crossed with Red Faction: Guerilla and skinned with some kind of Wild West/Mad Max sci-fi mashup setting. It achieved none of it well.
Its characters were stilted and uninspiring, dialogue was clunky, the Old West feel was a mistake, the fps gameplay was dated and stale, and even the driving portions were awkward and trite.
The audio engineers did a good job on the cars, though. The driving sound effects are good and actually do have a Mad Max feel to them. That's probably the only redeeming factor to this game. The NPC character modellers did a great job, too, with very detailed models, although they're either incredibly grotesque or just so cheesily written (or both) that it doesn't really matter.
The worst sin, though, is that there's so much texture popping. It's incredible that this game shipped without it being fixed prior to launch, or at least immediately patched on day1. It's _awful_. And this isn't just a "works on my machine" issue -- this is across the board, everyone experiences this. You can kind of tweak the video settings, set the buffers up, enable vsync, and I guess get used to it to some degree, but holy sh*t, man. This is a tech issue that should've been fixed by the end of beta.
The card minigame is interesting, and the Tombstone gambling game is very innovative, but the Five Fingers knife game is the worst.
All in all, the story is pretty basic and boring, the level reuse is incredibly bad - you can learn all of the environments you're going to drive in for the entire game by doing races - and the ending is anticlimactic as hell.
Do not buy this game.

If you like
and you like 2D action games, buy
.
is unquestionably a game for fans of Dark Souls, particularly Dark Souls 1. S&S ports the core experience of Dark Souls 1 to two dimensions quite faithfully, warts and all. While this includes things like a satisfying combat system and a growing sense of wonder and exploration, it also includes annoyances such as unexplained mechanics and a tendency to leave you struggling to figure out where to go and how various mechanics work. Many elements have direct equivilencies: Dark Souls' Covenants take the form of Creeds; Bonfires are Sanctuaries, and Souls are Salt. The equipment upgrade system is also lifted nearly directly from
.
isn't afraid to show its influences.
does offer some innovations compared its inspirations. Rather than a singular currency,
splits its drops into Gold, which is used to purchase items, and Salt, which is used to level up and upgrade gear. Level progression takes the form of a skill tree rather than plain stat increases, and weapons and armor require specific skill nodes rather than raw stats to equip. Creeds also have more wide-reaching effects than even Souls 1's rather involved Covenants, although as
makes little effort to explain them many players will likely find themselves in need of wiki guidance.
biggest weaknesses are its enemies and levels. While the combat is fun, there is little variety in both standard enemies' and bosses' behaviors, meaning that you'll likely repeat the same strategy for enemy after enemy and boss after boss. The levels are detailed and challenging, but the similarity of many rooms, the limits of the 2D perspective, and the lack of a map can make navigating a pain. The platforming sections can also be unnecessarily frustrating, especially when platforms start collapsing or popping in and out, and a missed jump or an enemy projectile sends you falling to your doom and loses you both time and resources. Luckily, the hardest platforming sections tend to restrict themselves to inflicting moderate falling damage rather than killing the player outright, but it's not guaranteed. Another problem with the levels is that the traps - usually in the form of pressure plates and tripwirse - are often frustratingly hard to see against the busy textures of the floor, even when you know they're there.
also makes the decision to spawn ambushing enemies from nothing rather than having them visible in the world to a careful observer, which can interfere with the sense of fair play that Soulsborne games tend to cultivate.
While that may seem like a lot of complaints, they are not severe, and I had a lot of fun in my first playthrough and plan to do another. It took me just over 25 hours on my save to beat the game, which is likely on the long side as I spent a significant amount of time wandering about looking under every corner for secrets. For dedicated fans of
, especially fans of the original,
is a must by.

Starship Corporation is a gem that puts you in the shoes of both designing your own starships, blueprint and all - and then having to prove that your design is "good".
My most recent ship had a beautiful design, well structured, symmetric (to a point), easy to maintain, inexpensive and fulfilling all the customer's desires. All was good.
So I went to prove the designs quality.
Standard operations (keep everything running) was a breeze, as were the various yellow alert/red alert/evacuation drills.
When the "How well does your ship handle e.g. an astroid field" question came up, I went in boldly - durable hatches to isolate hull breaches, redundant pathways and subsystems - what could go wrong?
Turns out it is a bad idea to put both of your (redundant) nuclear generator at front of the ship, where asteroids (and other objects) tend to arrive first. In addition it is a very bad time to discover that losing one not-really-redundant generator forces you to shut down either the engine or the life support, and losing both means that your ship is now dead in the vacuum, with the crew soon to follow... Oops...

I don´t know what to say... it´s like the work of a crazy inventor, a magnum opus of sorts and at the same time the lack of automatisation (or maybe I only did not understand how to automate anything) turns it into tedious micro management work where even a small contract often involves hours of careful planning and trial and error... its learning curve is like the mount everest and even thou the tutorials are not bad at all, it still feels a bit like you are working/studying for a test and not playing a game...
At the current stage I cannot recommend it (only to "special" people maybe with some insane attention span and love for detail) but I will update once the gameplay changes to a bit more automated and user-friendly experience.

Starship Corporation will let you run your own shipyard, where you try to earn money designing ships for various applications (cargo, military, mining, etc.) and test them both against the internal battle (asteroid hits, fires, and technical malfunctions) and the external battle, consisting of hostile boarding teams and enemy ships.
I'd split the game in three very interconnected but separate parts: Firstly the business management part, where you run a shipyard trying to be awarded contracts building ships. This part of the game isn't very wide in scope yet, but it provides a solid base for the rest of the gameplay. Clients post a call for bids for ship designs with specific requirements (cargo, military, racing, etc) and you'll be able to gain money if you get awarded the contract, allowing you to research new technology and take on more advanced designs. The game doesn't really allow you to
your ships yet, only test them (more on that later) and sell the design, but apparently that's in the works.
The second part is the ship designing phase, where you fill pre-constructed fuselages with the internals of the ship. You'll need to implement the required capabilities of your ship, while also balancing crew requirements, support systems (power, cooling, and life support) and strategic placement of all of them for when you'll actually use the ship. This part of the game is already quite fleshed out and I look forward to seeing how it will be expanded in the future.
Now, the contracts also specify a requirement for the performance of the ship, and the crew management part allows you to test it. Using a series of missions, you will use your crew (the amount and speciality dependant on how you designed your ship) to manage the internal battle inside your ship, including hull damage, fires, techical malfunctions and hostile invaders. This part of the game plays a bit like FTL, and while this game has more depth than FTL in the battle damage repair side of the game, it's not quite as elegant due to the somewhat clunky interface...
... which brings me to my biggest critisism of the game: the interface. Though everything is
, it is just that. Now of course this is a very early version of the game and everything is still due for improvement, but the way the text looks and scales on larger resolutions, the somewhat unresponsive crew selection and command and the general aesthetic of the UI make it look like the game was developed in the early 2000's. I do hope the developer considers a facelift for the interface.
The gameplay, however, is great. I backed this game in its crowdfunding campaign back in 2012, and it's great to see it taking shape like this. Starship Corporation scratches a very specific itch for me, even in this age where computer spaceships are appearing everywhere again.

I haven't finished The First Tree yet, simply because I don't want it to end too soon. So, first of all: Yes, I can highly recommend that game, but not to anyone. Why? Though if you're a fan of Firewatch or Shelter, like exploring and can appreciate love for detail and a beautifully created little world with stunning atmosphere, great soundtrack and (so far) deep story, you're going to love that game! When you encounter bugs (which I haven't yet) keep in mind that The First Tree was created by just one developer, who obviously put a LOT of effort and love into his project and I've played games that weren't even half that good but created by a horde of developers.
I've been waiting half a year for The First Tree to be released and all the waiting paid off.

Beautiful, poignant, touching. The First Tree is yet another incredible work of art by David Wehle. If you like narrative games, walking simulators, or just cute foxes and gorgeous visuals, this is the game for you. There's even a nice hidden bonus if you played his first game! Amazing work, I'm a fan for life.

So I've just finished this lovely game. It took me just under an hour and a half non-stop. It left me with that lingering feeling of awe, something similar to how Abzu and Journey left me feeling.
What a beautiful game to look at though. The use of colour and light is gorgeous and there were 3 or 4 particular moments in the game that really popped - I won't spoil it for you here.
The voice acting and narration was very well done, the voices were soft and the recording was crystal clear. More importantly the acting sounded genuine and not forced.
It's not all great, the jump mechanics and animations are a little wonky and there were two or three occasions where I lost my way and didn't know where to go. But this entire game was made by one guy on his own, it doesn't have a team of developers or deep resources behind it.
Let's not pretend it's a triple A title like Journey, but For £5 it's a very worthy use of 1.5 hours. Don't expect action and explosions. Clear your mind, sit down, let the story unfold slowly at its own pace.
Once you find the rhythm of the game and the visuals and audio start to wash over you the experience is really a lovely thing.

Despite my abiding love for the Elder Scrolls games - this may be my favorite computer game ever.
Whether you prefer an aggressive/violent playing style or a stealth/pacifistic style the game will accomodate you and react accordingly.  I have completed full playthroughs with both styles  and several more playthroughs that were a mix. All of them were very interesting and rewarding in their own way.  It's rare for a game of this genre to have fully fleshed consequences for your choice of gaming style, but it definitely added to the experience for me, especially the replayability.  My only criticism is that I hope they find a better mechanism for this in Dishonored 2 - maybe with  more noticeable gradients of gameplay impact between the two extremes, as this felt so binary sometimes.  Still, when you add this to the standard game modes options  (beginner to expert) you have a lot of room to grow and rampup your skills.
I found the DLC content (Knife & Witches) to be as fun as the game - and definitely saw an improvement in how the developers approach level desgn/ There are also some excellent new weapons and powers in the DLC I hope will translate into the next game.

Pros:
- Amazing Graphics
- Runs like a dream
- Fun, easy to learn gameplay
- Can pick up and put down easily
- Very good Free to play system
Cons:
- Horrible Matchmaking system
- Monsters are at a large advantage
- Party making system is buggy
- Very little diversity in gameplay
- Tutorials don't really teach you anything
Explanation:
Evolve Stage 2 is a fun game, it requires little time to learn and can supply you with a lot of hours of enjoyment. The game has amazing graphics and runs very well with little to no graphical problems. For a free to play game it's system is remarkable where everything and anything in  the game can be acquired by just playing the game. Matches are quick ranging from as low as a minute to as high as 15 minutes, making it a great game for those who do not have a lot of time.
Unfortunately there are major problems with the matchmaking system. Higher level players will queue with lower level ones creating a frustrating team dynamic where one person has no idea what their doing. Monsters in the game are also at a large advantage because of this as the game is very team oriented and if one person does not do their job accordingly the whole team suffers because of this. Also, there are countless bugs within the party making system, parties are dropped and you end up getting into a match alone. Other times people will leave and it will put you in a solo match with all AI enemies and teammates, and the post game "continue" option never works requiring you to back out and reinvite your party every so often. I think that if the matchmaking system was improved this game would benefit greatly. The gameplay in Evolve stage 2 is fun but there is very little difference in matches and only two game modes to choose from, as such the game can get boring really fast for lack of content although this is not so much of a problem because of the abundance of characters and monsters in the game. finally, I feel as though the tutorial system is very lacking within evolve stage 2. The tutorials teach you the bare bones basics of the assualt class and monster class in the game and I think does go enough in depth on the other classes and how to play as and with them. This adds to the skill discrepancy between higher level players and lower level ones and makes it that much harder on the team when these players queue together.
Overall:
I think evolve stage 2 is an amazing game and I would definitely recommend it to other people, although I tell those people to take caution when approaching the game because there are major matchmaking problems and To try all of the hunters , hunter types and monster or run the risk of the game getting stale.

Despite its age, Jedi Knight has held up well over the years. By today's standards the graphics are rather blocky and textures pixelated. But somehow those low-res textures perfectly capture rusting metal and dusty rock. The gameplay still works well with the player able to choose between shooter and hack-n-slash, in either 1st or 3rd person view. The physics engine is simple, but effective. There is also a hint of an RPG element as you get to choose and develope your force powers. But you can't rely on just brawn to get through, there are puzzles built into the envoronment, and some levels can be mazelike.
One of the highlights is the live-action cutscenes. It was like getting an Episode 6.5 back in 1997. What I found interesting is that there are no characters from the movies in this game. Most Star Wars games at least have a cameo from a movie character, but the Jedi Knight cast is all original or was introduced in Dark Forces. The galaxy is a big place, with adventures and events independent of the movies. Technically Disney has rendered this game non-canon, but its still a great Star Wars game, as is the entire Jedi Knight series.

First off, you might as well ignore the story. Spoiler alert:
The guy giving orders before/during the missions is your typical "Dammit man, get it done at all costs! I don't care about your emotions!" obnoxious military general. Just to drag it out, on multiple ocassions you have your finger on the trigger about to do the deed and captain-impatient tells you there's no time and you have to do something more important.
The cutscenes are full of bad voice-acting, worse motion-capture, and half are entirely useless.
All in glorious 480p resolution.
The gameplay and AI is just horrendous. During one mission, your first target is a sniper who's standing (yeah, standing) in a bell tower, totally motionless. I take the shot, bullet passes right through his head, no damage, suddenly everyone in the whole town knows my GPS coordinates. Eff this, reload last checkpoint. Try again, this time the bullet goes THROUGH HIS FACE, blood splatter and everything, he falls out of the goddamn bell tower AND LIVES. My character comments something to the effect of "Dang, I missed and now he knows I'm here." 'KAY. Reload checkpoint, try again, exact same outcome. No idea what's wrong with this game.
And for a sniper game that involves a lot of crouching and prone, they sure as hell made it impossible to do that. Let's say Z is crouch and X is prone, right? If you're crouching and hit the prone key, nothing happens and nothing indicates that your posture has changed. But when you hit the crouch button again, you go prone. Press crouch again, you stand up. Crouch again, you crouch. Press prone twice while crouched, you stand up. You wind up just pressing Z and X in random patterns to eventually wind up in the position you were looking for. It makes no sense at all.
As for the missions, for more than half you are hand-held by an ally as you follow them needlessly-close to enemies and have no choice or challenge in taking a different route or finding your own way. It's just bad. Let me sum up how the game plays: During one mission, you go through a parking garage packed with hostiles. You are tasked with shutting down the lights and sneaking out using your night vision while the enemies are blind. You have one route to take to the fuse box, thereby forcing you to perform a scripted knife kill along the way. Stab enemy (the stealth kill animations are also atrocious btw), look to the right,
, there's another hostile not 25 feet away looking right at you with no visual obstructions, and he doesn't notice. Alright then. Proceed to the fuse box, RIP THE WIRES OUT BECAUSE THAT'S HOW FUSE BOXES WORK, and head for the exit. All the way to the exit, you can pass 5 feet in front of enemies and they can't see you because it's pitch black. At one point I thought "There's no way I can get past this guy, I'll be 2 feet from his face, I'll just kill him instead". Wait for the area to be clear of other enemies, stealthy knife kill from behind in the inky black darkness, suddenly EVERY ENEMY KNOWS I'M THERE AND CAN MAGICALLY SEE ME, I get lit up and die next to a rusty old car.
That's this game.
4/10

Where do I begin with Salt & Sanctuary...
This is one of those games that takes the concept of being rewarded heavily by not dying, getting to "checkpoints/safe zones" to spend those rewards, to become more powerful; and is constantly referred to as the "2D Dark Souls". I hate to agree, but it is... and that is GREAT!!
Salt & Sanctuary makes you feel alive (ironically) and forces to you to focus on your every move; whether it's movement, timing of your melee swing or dodge rolling to avoid most certain death.
Yes, you may die a lot. Yes, if you die twice in a row you lose ALL "experience" (known as Salt) and can never regain it. Yes, you find really incredible armour but can't use it because you have to increase stats to actually have the strength to equip it and become stronger. BUT! Putting all of those positives aside, the biggest reason to head to the Store, Click Add to Cart, Put your details in and Purchase this game RIGHT NOW... is, you want more from the game as soon as you log off to do something else with your life - and THAT is powerful.
No game I've played in a long while has made me want to play it more and more.
I've only played through 50% of the game with about 7 hours played, but that's only as one class type (Paladin).. and there are about 7-8 total to choose from on character creation; making the game replayable on numerous levels with different play styles. There are also Challenges which I haven't even started to look at yet!
Boss mechanics are great & always keep you on your feet with new twists throughout the encounters... and you just know that one tiny little undead waiting in the doorway of the last room before a Sanctuary safe zone will, infact. Kill you. :D
Would recommend highly & definitely play with a Controller.
