Aurelien Regard’s The Next Penelope is a futuristic reimaging of Homer’s Odyssey; old meets new in a stylish yet retro world of neon race strips and mechanical monsters.
Upon starting the game we are transported to Ithaca, Penelope’s home world. We soon learn that it is under siege by Poseidon who is seeking revenge for the death of his son at the hands of Odysseus, Penelope’s husband. After a brief tutorial, Penelope makes a deal with Poseidon to track down her love in exchange for sparing her kingdom, and the odyssey begins.
While the story shows promise, it quickly becomes little more than a quiet backdrop. Characters from Greek mythology such as the Minotaur or Arachne are introduced only to be killed off soon after. The conversations between Penelope and these characters also reveal very little about the plot and offer minimal insight into the characters themselves. While this is hardly essential in a title such as this, when employing such rich subject matter, it feels like somewhat of a wasted opportunity. The developer is to be commended for attempting to incorporate such lofty inspiration, and with more of the themes and characters crossing over into the gameplay this could have been an interesting tale, but sadly, what little story there is on offer is largely forgettable and likely to go over a lot of player’s heads.
The gameplay is split between racing sections, which will often include enemy pilots, and large-scale boss fights. The racing mechanics are very simplistic, your craft will accelerate on its own allowing you to concentrate on steering and attacking. This was the first thing that seemed odd to me – it felt as though a lot of the control I would normally have in a racer was taken away by not allowing me to control my own speed. Braking is another option which is alarmingly absent and makes drifting on courses without barricades incredibly frustrating – on these levels it becomes a matter of memorising when and where to drift as opposed testing your reflexes and steering. Additionally, I felt the tracks were zoomed in way too much, making each upcoming turn a gut-wrenching experience.
Racing against CPU opponents does however involve an element of strategy, as Penelope’s arsenal of weapons and upgrades will be essential to claiming first place. These power-ups include a laser beam, which can bounce of walls to hit foes, a grappling hook to clear debris and life-stealing mines to name a few. Smart use of weaponry really is the key to success, and failure is often the result of missing a shortcut, or recharge point. Energy will be required to use any of Penelope’s powers, but also doubles up as her health bar; this encourages ‘tactical’ use of powers and smart racing. The energy mechanic is sadly, far from perfect. Energy is all too hard to recover with too few recovery points on the tracks and too many necessary powers.
The boss battles are a mixed bag. Some of them test your racing abilities while throwing in obstacles or time limits; these are the most effective as they play off the mostly solid racing mechanics. However, a couple of the bosses are fought in enclosed arenas where the constant acceleration becomes your worst enemy. The inability to brake or even slow down makes it very hard to hit bosses and colliding head on with a wall will likely result in death as it is all too hard to turn around while your ship keeps bloody accelerating. These fights feel laboured as energy/health is too hard to recover; the result is a slow paced battle while you gradually claw back lost energy needed to attack the boss. These really are the lowest ebb of the game, which is a shame as they could have been an enjoyable challenge had the ship controls been altered to accommodate them. Thankfully, the final boss fight does just that and plays out as a side-scrolling shoot-em-up. This is exactly what the other bosses should have done – completely mixed up the gameplay rather than forcing the standard racing mechanics into an arena unsuited to them. This boss-fight is definitely one of the best parts of the game and it’s a shame the shmup sections didn’t feature as a bonus level.
Visually, TNP is a joy to look at. It takes the best of retro arcade design and blends it seamlessly with high-resolution backdrops and animations. The overall aesthetic is comparable to other 80’s arcade style games such as Pac-Man tournament edition which uses the neon glows and particles on darker backgrounds to great effect. Penelope, enemy racers and bosses are all very simplistic polygonal renders which would look right at home in a Star fox game. The characters within TNP are all represented in a pleasant animated style, which effectively apes a western, 80’s representation of Japanese art style. Some character designs are more striking than others, with Penelope herself being a clear standout. The soundtrack is also suitably 80’s in its influences, incorporating elements of techno, synthwave and dance into a bass-heavy, adrenaline fuelled sound which perfectly accompanies the art style while never being too obtrusive.
There is something very retro and charming about TNP, and its visuals and sound design are definitely some of its stronger assets. One fantastic feature in particular is the option to activate scanlines and a simulated arcade cabinet haze at any time by pressing (L3)/(F10). This highlights the game’s fantastic retro visuals and makes it feel like a genuine arcade experience. My one gripe is that after each death, this option seemed to reset and had to be turned back on -this quickly became a pain as I died a lot, which brings me neatly to my next point.
The Next Penelope is hard as♥♥♥♥♥♥ Now this isn’t necessarily a criticism: I’m no stranger to old-school arcade games and am even partial to a bit of masochism, but TNP demands perfection. Slip up once or twice and you will fail, particularly on the Acheron stages where there are no barricades. But when you finally manage beat a level, it feels great. Like all good arcade games, the true appeal of the game shines when overcoming a challenge. While the difficulty may not always be particularly fair (some levels and bosses were just cruel), overall I feel that the challenge on offer is solid enough to please arcade fans and even offer some replay value when attempting to beat time trials and unlockable missions.
A bonus local co-op mode is included and plays a bit differently to the base game. Only one weapon is available and using it will place you immediately in critical condition. Additionally the camera will focus only on the player in first; fall too far behind and you’ll be wiped out. This mode is a nice little addition and offers some variation on the racing mechanics. What this game really needs however is an online mode. The single-player content, while fun, feels like a precursor to a greater challenge, which an online racing tournament would suit perfectly.
Overall, The Next Penelope was a pleasant surprise. It pays homage to its arcade roots both stylistically and in terms of difficulty while presenting a sleek, polished experience with a variety of game modes on offer. The challenge borders on unfair and made me angrier at a game then I’ve been in a long time, but the achievement of completion outweighs the frustration. While I would have preferred a more focused experience, this variety helps to highlight each of the mechanics while offering a unique and diverse slant on the racing genre. The boss battles are a definite low point and the game is thin on single-player content, but the retro aesthetics and (mostly) smooth controls are enough to make this Odyssey one voyage you’ll want to embark on. For the work of a single man, The Next Penelope is a truly impressive example of what indie games can offer to the industry.

UPDATE 2017-02: Tested 3-player couch multiplayer with friends, THIS IS A TOTAL BLAST. Unless you have only "close" friends that dislike Micromachine like racing, this is a must-have to pile on that top 15 of "couch fun gaming evening" list.

Didn't quite finish the solo yet (some missions are hard ;)) but spent time enough (several hours, although many offline) to get a good opinion.
This game is GOOD (but hard)! You could view it as a mix of several games. The solo campaign makes you follow a tragicomic story of Penelope trying to find her husband throughout the universe. On each planet you'll visit, you'll get access to a special equipemnet that you'll have to use to finish a specific challenge, a classic race against opponents or defeat a boss: laser, teleport, trip mines and such... The level design of each planet nicely revolves around the specific item, making it easy to understand. With that said, you'll still needs good skills and concentration to win!
Didn't have a chance yet to fully test the multiplayer, it's more like a traditional Micromachines with equipment: choose a power then race to the point of being a screen away from your opponents.
UPDATE: Tested multiplayer: even with only less than 10 different maps, the great design of each and the originality of each "bonus tool" makes it a great fun time with at least 2 other people!
All in all:
- Story: Nice. Although plot keeps basic in writing, dev put much effort in making the story funny and distracting, and the idea of reusing a classic mythological story in such a way gives it a nice refresher.
- Graphics: as anything related to taste, you may or may not like it. In any case, every detail (character design, races, ships) follows a coherent design and gameplay-related objects (like energy) is easily identifiable.
- Music: I'm not particularly fond of the genre, yet it is well adapted to the settings. Serves the gameplay well.
- Gameplay: while I regret a bit that you cannot manage yourself the ship's speed (it's at constant speed), the variety of powerups and evident effort in designing original challenges makes up for it and far more.
- Multi: local only (for now?), but probably as fun as Micromachines/Rock&RollRacing could be... Which is great! :)

The Next Penelope is top down racing game that has RPG elements. The story has you playing Penelope, the wife of Ulysses who is on a mission to find her husband and save her people from all sorts of techno space versions of ancient gods. In the game you use the left and right buttons, or triggers, to steer your vehicle. As you play you unlock new powers by defeating bosses, and just like Megaman you’re free to explore and decide which powers you want to unlock first. The teleport power is great, it slows down time and lets you cheat your way around the levels. This boss fight with a minotaur has you warping around avoiding dangers while waiting for prime spots to attack. Each mission rewards you with experience that can level up some unique skills, like zooming out the screen to help you see farther. This game is amazing, fast, fun and the challenge ramps up perfectly. It’s like F-Zero and Megaman decided to play the speeder bike level in battletoads.

I really want to make comparisons to F-Zero, yet I cannot. I feel the perspective difference (top down) alone is enough to not, but there are clearly F-Zero influences in The Next Penelope. While many of them are obvious in game-mechanic behavior (energy charging strips and boosting), there is also new abilities introduced, with the most notable and fun, weapons. While the game-play isn't too original, this game implements them spot on for a very fluid and enjoyable experience.
While I can't say it's a F-Zero successor (again, due to perspective differences), it most certainly seems to be for Micro Machines. Micro Machines was a great classic game from the NES I never really got into too much. However, The Next Penelope grasps my attention for a racing game immediately. With great art, music, and game-design, it's hard not to recommend this game.
I personally think the game is great fun. This was my first Hearts of Iron game and I found it great fun.

I have played all HOI games. HOI4 in itself isn't a bad game. It has good points and bad. Many features missing compared with previous iterations. Many balance issues and the depth and details are missing to really immerse a player into the game.
In truth I think this is a bare bones of a game and not quite complete and not a respectable standard for the price. I play the game because I enjoy HOI games and the basic sandbox format of Paradox "stratagy" games.
The issue I have is it seems unlike HOI2 which is still the best HOI game as a whole where the business model was straight forward and the game was finished to a high standard flaws and all with the technology of the time; HOI4 will be likely "fixed" and modified in installments that masquerade as DLC instead of decent comprehensive patches.
For the overall base price and likely additional costs to DLC I cannot honestly recommend anyone to purchase this game.
Certainly not speculate on the quality of so called "expansions" by purchasing the DLC upfront.
What is typical of this business model is the reliance on the modding community to create content for a bare framework of a game.
For this conduct by Paradox, I regret I must at this time give this game a negative response.
Until such a time as the game is available at a respectable base price for the content provided and support from the developer that is reasonable to be expected for such a price, I will stand by this assessment.

As a veteran of the Soulsborne category of games, I can say with certainty that this masterpiece is worthy of being called a 2D Dark Souls. It has everything you'd want from a good souls-esque game, only in side-scrolling form.
Pros:
-Enemies/Bosses are tough, yet fair.
-The Lore snippets on gear/skills, combined with the graphics and eerie music, make for a satisfying ambiant trifecta.
-Safe areas have as much to offer as you want them to (for example, offer up a Blacksmith idol to make a blacksmith available at whatever Shrine you're currently in).
-If you normally get sick of games after a two-hour session, that'll change. I could probably play this for an entire day and not get bored. Aggravated from certain bosses, yes, but never bored.
Cons:
-Just like any Souls-esque title, the path of your adventure isn't directly stated, and then you lose your sense of direction with all the different paths and traversal options, and then before you know it you've spent half an hour just trying to figure out where to go next. It's a small issue, but I dare say it adds to the fun.
Overall, I give the game a 9/10. It's well worth a small stipence like $17,99. I'm less than 7 hours in and I feel like I haven't really gotten anywhere. It sounds accurate but, in a game like this. 7 hours can seem like an eternity.

Have not played much yet, but the game is enjoyable for what it is. To me, it has a rise of nations feel in terms of border expansion, watchtowers, and resource gathering (which is a very good choice by the dev). It stays true to its name in which you can literally fracture the flag by flinging rocks via catapult and destroying your enemy's plans of expansion. Catapults fire fairly accurately with an upgrade which is both good and bad. Considering that walls can be constructed using stone and then tore down brick by brick, a bit more variety in the flinging of the ammo (higher and lower shots, rocks breaking apart etc) could go a long way to make this game feel surprsing and chaotic in PVP battles.
But I think that is where this game has true potential. The price is fair for what it is, and the good choices made by the solo dev thus far show promise that this game could head in the right direction.
A few additional suggestions for the dev:
1) A way to repair walls more easily.
I haven't played much yet, but rebuilding a new wall in front of the old one or behind the old one isn't the most fun way to repair when resources are limited. I think a key to save a wall in a current "state" to which workers can be assigned to repair that state would help a lot.
2) Ability for workers to turn resources in at flags. I understand the point of the warehouse, but if it is destroyed when you have too few of resources, you have no means to rebuild it. Perhaps make the flags a capable spot for turn in so long as there is no warehouse, but create a cap for how much resources can be stored there.
2) The obvious stuff: larger maps potentially with fog of war, custom maps, more upgrades with some choices that are permanent. Just makes the game feel more strategic to have to choose your strategy with limited information about what your opponent is doing.
Great work thus far!

After several years of this game being completely broken on Steam, Disney Interactive has stepped up and released a patch.
Despite the fact that it predates their acquisition, despite the fact that it probably isn't a huge money maker, they did this. For that, they've earned my respect.
Before the patch, the game didn't work in fullscreen properly, the music was entirely missing, and was highly prone to crashing. The update has fixed all of these issues. There are still issues with 3D Acceleration mode, limiting you on the color depth, but I'm hoping those will be fixed as well.
Beyond the technical aspects, my review of the game follows:
This is an old game. It is not a pretty game, and it is not a polished game. It is a very good game for the time, and if you either grew up with it, or can go back and appreciate classic titles, it is well worth full asking price, let alone sale price. I grew up with the Jedi Knight series, so I'm applying a heavy helping of rose-tint nostalgia paste to my goggles.
That said, it is still a fun, though at times puzzling and confusing game. It's from that era of shooters where we were just starting to experiment with platforming elements and puzzles, and as a result, it can get very frustrating on both.
Quicksave is your friend, you will need it. The Medium and Hard difficulties are brutal, par for the course at the time. Those of you who grew up with 90s-early 2000s PC shooters know what to expect, and the game is a blast if you enjoy that kind of run-and-gun gameplay.
The story is fairly cheesy, read the accompanying novels, if you can find and stomach them, as they shed light on a lot of details the game glosses over.
Overall, before the update, I probably would only recommend this to hardcore fans of the series, but now that it works out of the box, I think I can recommend it for anyone who's interested in the history of the series or PC gaming in general.

This review is of the single-player campaign.
Rage is what we would get if Fallout 3 and Quake got together and had a kid, with Borderlands as the mid-wife. Excellent shooting mechanics, decent story and fantastic level design set in a debris-filled post-apocalyptic wasteland littered with bandits. What seems an “open world,” though, is really a set of corridors connecting the various hubs, enemies are endlessly reused, and pointless crafting slows the otherwise swift, deft gameplay. Recommended at a discount of 50% off (for the game + DLC) or more.
Total size on my hard-drve: 23.8 GB
++ Level design. The Dead City, the Distillery, Jackal Canyon… Simply great all round.
+ Excellent characters. They’re never explored in depth, but everyone is unique, with few re-used voice actors.
+ Great selection of weapons. A variety of specialty ammo was a nice touch.
+ Good driving mechanics.
+ Great atmosphere. Walk into a bar in Wellsprings and there are people chatting, a jukebox is playing in the corner, yellowish light filters through the dirty windows, and a dusty haze hangs in the air.
+ Excellent soundtrack.
+ Excellent voice-acting.
+ Excellent facial animations and body language (especially for its age). Not normally something I’d notice, but I played Rage right after playing Mass Effect Andromeda. What a breath of fresh air Rage proved to be.
+ Well-optimized on PC. Plays at a silky-smooth 60fps on my Radeon RX 470.
+/- Story works, but is hardly special. Our hero was locked in cryostasis when a threat to Earth materialized. The threat happened, we wake and enter the “new” world. We join a Resistance movement, fight bandits and Authority. Fairly standard stuff. Sequel-bait ending right as things are getting interesting. Rage is six years old. At the time of writing, there is no sequel in sight.
+/- Fun mini-games, but there aren’t enough of them, and they’re repeated in each city hub with no variation.
+/- The textures. Up close, they’re awful, some of the worst I’ve seen. Stand a back a bit, and they look amazing. Forcing 8k textures via a config file helps, but doesn’t solve the issue. Landscapes and vistas look impressive, but wall switches don’t.
+/- Racing seems shoe-horned into Rage. It’s a welcome change of pace, but it seems like it would be a waste of resources in a post-apocalyptical wasteland.
+/- No day / night cycle while you’re out in the wasteland.
+/- Almost all the women are hawt. It took an asteroid slamming into earth to turn almost every woman you meet into a model. But hey, I’m not complaining. Though it does feel a bit weird to rescue this one (hot) woman from bandits (who had tied her up in a very suggestive position); she then takes up residence in your trophy room as... one of your trophies?! Wtf.
- Frame-rate is capped at 60. Unlocking it will require a mod (called “id5 Tweaker.”)
- Level paths might be well-designed, but too often they feel tight and narrow.
- There’s no point to crafting except to pad the gameplay. Why not stumble across grenades? You do a few times, but more often you’ll be looking for the four components needed to craft grenades.
- There are a few bosses, but no final boss – surprising in an Id game.
- Enemy AI is extremely predictable. Soldiers tend to stick behind cover; mutants will charge your position relentlessly. Once you know who you’re facing, combat rarely surprises.
- Aside from your initial dune buggy, no customization options for your vehicles.
- Not many enemies. Mutants, Authority, and bandits. That’s it.
- Not a true open world. Hubs connected by corridors that you will traverse repeatedly, fighting the same re-spawning bandits over and over. Most buildings require a loading screen.
- Fetch-quest missions. Most of the side-content is fetch-quest filler that frequently involves...
- Re-used levels. Expect to play some levels twice. The second time is sometimes in reverse of the first time.
- Awful mouse acceleration. There is a Mouse Sensitivity slider in the options that helps (there is partial controller support).
- Alt-tabbing out of the game disables v-sync. After you alt-tab back into Rage, you’ll have to visit the options menu to turn it back on.
Rage turns out to be a mixed bag of good and not-so-good in nearly equal measure. It’s definitely possible to have some fun with it in a shoot-y sort of way, but it’s an “over fast, on to the next game” experience instead of wanting to immediately return to the world for another playthrough. I’d love to see a sequel – the world building is first-rate – but I hope we see more than a thin plot used as an excuse to shoot things in obviously re-used levels. There is real potential in the Rage franchise.

This game is more than just a SOLID roguelike -- it's also a pretty damn close to being a cRPG because of the turn-based combat, immersive story elements, and character-building.  The popular user-defined steam tags for this game are 100% spot on.
Don't let the game title or graphics put you off. I think the title is too silly for a game this good.
Don't listen to people who say this game is too hard -- there's multiple difficulty levels and modes -- one of the modes makes it just like Diablo 1 in terms of difficulty (exploration mode).
Exploration mode -- there's no fail state (think of the Diablo series).  It literally can't be too hard in this mode.
Adventure mode  -- The perfect compromise.  You start with one life, and get a handful more as you level.  Death still sucks, but it's not too bad.  When you die, the game is telling you to Get Good -- It's not just because you didn't pray to RNGesus enough.  I think the game is balance tuned to this mode for normal human beings.
Roguelike -- One life.  It's Ironman mode in a game balanced for multiple lives -- without the ability to grind in increase survivability (think Diablo).  So, you need a _very deep_ understanding of the game mechanics to succeed in this mode.  Like, looking at the code deep -- or at least benefiting from the knowledge of others who have, in some way.  Not that the game is totally unfair.  It's pretty damn fair.  But there are things in this game that will most likely result in your death if you're unprepared, and there's no way to know to prepare for them without having encountered it before.  In many cases, you do get very good hints about this through the ingame Lore/Story bits you find -- but not always.  That's my impression, anyways.
The above modes are on top of additional difficulty settings, so it's rather fine-tunable (I started playing on Normal-Adventurer, and I'm still playing in that mode at 100 hours /played -- and I haven't beaten the game yet).
High points as I think of them:
Gameplay is amazing.
Itemization is top-notch.
Class ability balance is pretty damn good -- most games I feel like I'm beta testing class balance, but not here.
There's an actual story, and there are immersive pieces of lore that you find that are well-written.
Extremely moddable, but not in a "bad" way like some games where you'd need to spend 100's of hours modding before you start playing (I'm looking at you, Fallout 3 and Skyrim.  Morrowind would be in the same boat, but it gets a pass from me because that game has style).
Loving the Z key.
Escort missions are brilliant.
The Devs removed the grind for consumables -- which is one of the major departures from classic rogue games.
The Rogue class is fun as hell for me.
You can tell that the Devs are true gamers -- what is optimal is also often enough the most fun way to play.  I get the impression that this is not merely serendipitous.
After/If you beat the game, you can take your character into a true infinite dungeon to see how far you get.  That sounds pretty awesome, even though I haven't done it yet.
Helpful ingame chat (you can link items into it, and there's an ingame browser).
The only downside is the graphics.  They could be better, and with how moddable the game is, I'm actually pretty surprised it's not already.  There's a certain amount of charm to them, but it's not like Fallout 1 level charm -- but then again the only game that comes close to that (or exceeds in some aspects) is Diablo 2, so I'm being a bit unfair.  There is a DLC for like $1 that does improve the UI graphics some, and I think it's worth getting.
I could improve the graphics substantially and release it as a mod, but I'm too busy playing -- it's that good.  Mayber everyone feels the same way.
Get this game because it's great.
Get the DLCs to support the Devs
I'd rate this 9.9/10 if the price was irrelevant.  At its current price, it's an honest 11/10 ((before you say anything: YES I know).
TLDR: It's great.  This game deserves to be more popular than it already is.  The Devs deserve your money.

You make a basic character and class from the limited selection available to you. 2/3rds of the other possibilites are locked, but you hope you will eventually acquire them with time and diligence. You start your playthrough on the easiest difficulty. You die a lot, but you slowly learn the ropes.You start over, this time with a more refined build. You begin to learn the dungeon order. You move faster and die less. The challenge is gone, and you move up to the next difficulty.
It's a different game. You lose within an hour. You try again. This time you don't even get through the first level. You re-learn the game, and slowly improve. Your build is more refined. You become more cautious, more perceptive, and you start to make real progress. After numerous do overs and deaths, you finally surpass your prior characters. You're in uncharted territory. Your first bout with the final bosses ends in seconds with your champion in pieces with your honor. And so you start again. You progress, you die, you repeat. You start over a lot, but each character gets further than the last.
Finally, after many gruelling hours, you have beaten the bosses and won! Your palms are sweatng, your knees feel weak, and you feel so elated you could fly.
You move up to the next difficulty. You lose within moments. You re-learn the game, and you do it all again.
You beat the bosses on this difficulty. You know the ins and outs of this characer so well you could write an encyclopedia. So you start a totally new character, with some of the new races and classes you have unlocked. You start on the easiest difficulty and lose within seconds.
So you do it all over again.

Admittedly I'm pretty tired of the demon souls combat+exploration+mysterious story formula: learn by dieing, and explore for items that are mostly useless for your character (unless you look up what you want and go searching for them).  And I'm tired of reading item descriptions for the "lore."
But this game can kiss my♥♥♥♥♥  First, you have the dark souls conceit of having to learn enemy attack patterns (usually by dieing first).  Second, you have platforming (and other than Ori and the Blind Forest, I'm not a platforming fan).  Gravity will kill you often.  Third, you have a confusing map with way too much backtracking and areas locked off by keys or requiring skills you get later.  And finally you have controls that often respond in weird ways to the environment-- or you have to ask "can I do that?" and risk death for the sake of experimentation.
Some of the crap they put in here is just to♥♥♥♥♥♥you off-- traps that knock you off platforms, enemies that disapper when you swing at them, unicorns that one shot you which you cant POSSIBLY know until they do...
The skill tree is silly-- its just a fancy way to pump your basic stats.  I picked a 1 hand + shield from the start, and combat remained unchanged as my character progressed.  I just got bigger stats.  Switching from an axe to a mace was slightly different but the choice was really based on my enemy's weakness, not playstyle.
If you like the idea of getting your♥♥♥♥♥kicked like Dark Souls, platforming, and looking up what to do next, this game is for you.  For me this game was not fun, I'm burned out on Dark Souls, and I would have rather replayed Ori.

Open, sprawling adventure, rich in lore and style.
You can go in the front door nailing every last enemy to the walls with your crossbow and pistol. This style has consequences later on in the game, and plays-out differently to if you play it by becoming a shadow. There is extra challenge in taking the 'non-lethal' route too. Your choice.
I'm a simple person with simple tastes, and normally take the front-door heavy-weapons approach, but the sneaky shadow style beckoned this time and it's been a blast. I've found myself holding my breath a lot while playing this game.
Equipment and skills can be modified and upgraded to suit your style.
The game has been intelligently designed with fields of vision simulated for enemies and intrusion detection systems. Hit an enemy with a sleeper dart intending a non-lethal run through and watch them plummet to their deaths in the water or break their necks down stairs. That's still counted as a death on your shoulders so you'll have to find another angle or creep up behind them and choke them.
An engrossing challenging masterpiece.

This is the benchmark for tactical shooters on the PC, and has yet to be surpassed by any other game. Raven Shield and the other original Rainbow 6/Rogue Spear games are true tactical counter-terrorism simulations, based on real weapons and tactics used in modern day counter terrorist operations. You plan your mission, you don't get to save during a mission, and it's one-shot and you're dead. No regenerating health, and when an operative dies it is final. I love Raven Shield because of the punishing difficulty, and emphasis on being the first to spot your opponent and quickly aim for the head. I think this is a good representation for close quarters combat, as close as you can get to real life.
I love this game, and it's sad to see the Tom Clancy and Rainbow Six licenses being sold down the river. Everything after RVS and Athena Sword has been dumbed down garbage for the masses. Rainbow Six was never meant to appeal to the call of duty or counter strike crowd, it was in a class of its own. I got this game when it came out in 2003 and I just re-installed it, and it's as good as ever. I've beaten the single player 4 times, twice on elite, and it doesn't get any better than the feeling of successfully completing a mission with no fatalities. I have spent countless hours on multiplayer, which is also great too. I can only hope they make more games like this, because there are no modern games that come close to realism and tactical depth like Raven Shield does.

I love this game. I enjoyed Vegas 2 immensely as well but Rainbow six 3 is just superior. It is so amazing when you set out a complex plan and have your team execute it successfully.
The shooting in this game is also quite fun and there is a good challenge to it. This game is all about setting up a strategy for your 1-8 team members (each are unique and have their own stats like sniping, electronics, etc), in which you can create 1-3 fire teams and set up complex orders for them in the planning stage. You can set "go codes" which mean a team will wait for a player order to set up a synchronized attack (such as having gold team breach and clear and green team toss a tear gas grenade in, while red team sets up a sniping potion to protect the flanks).
The missions are fun and have excellent map design where multiple different strategies can be executed. There is perma-death for everyone so you must be careful with their lives.
The AI while basic at times can be quite intelligent. It can flank you, toss grenades, retreat to a different area and even surrender (careful sometimes a surrendering enemy will have an enemy their to flank you when you try to cuff the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥).
This is a game for a more intellectual FPS gamer and is the best Rainbow Six game out there (I've played them all except siege but that is nothing like this game at all). This game runs perfectly at 1080p (although the menus/movies don't but it is still fine) and I have not had a single issue with it at all (I have mostly played on a non-steam version but have just bought this one for the included expansion pack).

It's basically turn-based Diablo 2.
10/10

This game is more than just a SOLID roguelike -- it's also a pretty damn close to being a cRPG because of the turn-based combat, immersive story elements, and character-building.  The popular user-defined steam tags for this game are 100% spot on.
Don't let the game title or graphics put you off. I think the title is too silly for a game this good.
Don't listen to people who say this game is too hard -- there's multiple difficulty levels and modes -- one of the modes makes it just like Diablo 1 in terms of difficulty (exploration mode).
Exploration mode -- there's no fail state (think of the Diablo series).  It literally can't be too hard in this mode.
Adventure mode  -- The perfect compromise.  You start with one life, and get a handful more as you level.  Death still sucks, but it's not too bad.  When you die, the game is telling you to Get Good -- It's not just because you didn't pray to RNGesus enough.  I think the game is balance tuned to this mode for normal human beings.
Roguelike -- One life.  It's Ironman mode in a game balanced for multiple lives -- without the ability to grind in increase survivability (think Diablo).  So, you need a _very deep_ understanding of the game mechanics to succeed in this mode.  Like, looking at the code deep -- or at least benefiting from the knowledge of others who have, in some way.  Not that the game is totally unfair.  It's pretty damn fair.  But there are things in this game that will most likely result in your death if you're unprepared, and there's no way to know to prepare for them without having encountered it before.  In many cases, you do get very good hints about this through the ingame Lore/Story bits you find -- but not always.  That's my impression, anyways.
The above modes are on top of additional difficulty settings, so it's rather fine-tunable (I started playing on Normal-Adventurer, and I'm still playing in that mode at 100 hours /played -- and I haven't beaten the game yet).
High points as I think of them:
Gameplay is amazing.
Itemization is top-notch.
Class ability balance is pretty damn good -- most games I feel like I'm beta testing class balance, but not here.
There's an actual story, and there are immersive pieces of lore that you find that are well-written.
Extremely moddable, but not in a "bad" way like some games where you'd need to spend 100's of hours modding before you start playing (I'm looking at you, Fallout 3 and Skyrim.  Morrowind would be in the same boat, but it gets a pass from me because that game has style).
Loving the Z key.
Escort missions are brilliant.
The Devs removed the grind for consumables -- which is one of the major departures from classic rogue games.
The Rogue class is fun as hell for me.
You can tell that the Devs are true gamers -- what is optimal is also often enough the most fun way to play.  I get the impression that this is not merely serendipitous.
After/If you beat the game, you can take your character into a true infinite dungeon to see how far you get.  That sounds pretty awesome, even though I haven't done it yet.
Helpful ingame chat (you can link items into it, and there's an ingame browser).
The only downside is the graphics.  They could be better, and with how moddable the game is, I'm actually pretty surprised it's not already.  There's a certain amount of charm to them, but it's not like Fallout 1 level charm -- but then again the only game that comes close to that (or exceeds in some aspects) is Diablo 2, so I'm being a bit unfair.  There is a DLC for like $1 that does improve the UI graphics some, and I think it's worth getting.
I could improve the graphics substantially and release it as a mod, but I'm too busy playing -- it's that good.  Mayber everyone feels the same way.
Get this game because it's great.
Get the DLCs to support the Devs
I'd rate this 9.9/10 if the price was irrelevant.  At its current price, it's an honest 11/10 ((before you say anything: YES I know).
TLDR: It's great.  This game deserves to be more popular than it already is.  The Devs deserve your money.

You make a basic character and class from the limited selection available to you. 2/3rds of the other possibilites are locked, but you hope you will eventually acquire them with time and diligence. You start your playthrough on the easiest difficulty. You die a lot, but you slowly learn the ropes.You start over, this time with a more refined build. You begin to learn the dungeon order. You move faster and die less. The challenge is gone, and you move up to the next difficulty.
It's a different game. You lose within an hour. You try again. This time you don't even get through the first level. You re-learn the game, and slowly improve. Your build is more refined. You become more cautious, more perceptive, and you start to make real progress. After numerous do overs and deaths, you finally surpass your prior characters. You're in uncharted territory. Your first bout with the final bosses ends in seconds with your champion in pieces with your honor. And so you start again. You progress, you die, you repeat. You start over a lot, but each character gets further than the last.
Finally, after many gruelling hours, you have beaten the bosses and won! Your palms are sweatng, your knees feel weak, and you feel so elated you could fly.
You move up to the next difficulty. You lose within moments. You re-learn the game, and you do it all again.
You beat the bosses on this difficulty. You know the ins and outs of this characer so well you could write an encyclopedia. So you start a totally new character, with some of the new races and classes you have unlocked. You start on the easiest difficulty and lose within seconds.
So you do it all over again.

Fantastic top-down racer with an interesting story to boot.
Gameplay Video:
You play as Penelope on her quest to find Ulysses (her husband), making your way through the galaxy trying to avoid being captured or worse. Game progression is non-linear and up to the player as you can select any planet you like to explore but they are marked with advised difficulty settings. Each planet has a variety of race formats and some of these require much more strategy then pure race skills due to the game mechanics. Basically as you use weapons they drain energy and if you run out of energy it's game over, so it becomes somewhat of a balancing act between not crashing into walls and using power-ups efficiently. After completing events you will be rewarded with XP which can then be used for permanent upgrades.
Anyone familiar with F-Zero/Micro Machines will feel right at home with this game.
Responsive controls, great soundtrack and addictive gameplay (just one more turn!)
Recommended and impressed given it's a one man team and early access. Cheers. :)

Admittedly I'm pretty tired of the demon souls combat+exploration+mysterious story formula: learn by dieing, and explore for items that are mostly useless for your character (unless you look up what you want and go searching for them).  And I'm tired of reading item descriptions for the "lore."
But this game can kiss my♥♥♥♥♥  First, you have the dark souls conceit of having to learn enemy attack patterns (usually by dieing first).  Second, you have platforming (and other than Ori and the Blind Forest, I'm not a platforming fan).  Gravity will kill you often.  Third, you have a confusing map with way too much backtracking and areas locked off by keys or requiring skills you get later.  And finally you have controls that often respond in weird ways to the environment-- or you have to ask "can I do that?" and risk death for the sake of experimentation.
Some of the crap they put in here is just to♥♥♥♥♥♥you off-- traps that knock you off platforms, enemies that disapper when you swing at them, unicorns that one shot you which you cant POSSIBLY know until they do...
The skill tree is silly-- its just a fancy way to pump your basic stats.  I picked a 1 hand + shield from the start, and combat remained unchanged as my character progressed.  I just got bigger stats.  Switching from an axe to a mace was slightly different but the choice was really based on my enemy's weakness, not playstyle.
If you like the idea of getting your♥♥♥♥♥kicked like Dark Souls, platforming, and looking up what to do next, this game is for you.  For me this game was not fun, I'm burned out on Dark Souls, and I would have rather replayed Ori.
The combat system is awesome, the skill tree is massive, it has so many locations to explore, art and animation are amazing, and i started a new playthrough immediately after the final boss.

This game is an amazing Single Player Campaign.
Being framed for killing an empress and kidnapping her daughter, and being given powers from a powerful and mysterious person to get revenge on the people that really killed the empress.
Dishonored takes your actions into account. Whether you think you should kill every enemy and target to pass the level, or to find other ways to deal and sneak past your enemies to reach the target. There will be consenquences to killing a man, rather than letting them live, even if they are the enemy in Dishonored. (The Chaos System)
Playing the game using Lethal, or Non-Lethal ways.
Dishonored was made to test and ask you:
"Would you take the High Ground? Or surprise them from underground?"
"Should you unlock Time Stop? Or upgrade Dark Vision?
"Should you kill the man that helped assist the death of the Empress kidnapping of her Daughter? Or find another solution..."
This is a type of game that won't grab your hand and lead you through the level, but give you freedom to do what you want. The freedom to experiment, interact, and plan to how do deal with your targets. But it will remember your actions...

Open, sprawling adventure, rich in lore and style.
You can go in the front door nailing every last enemy to the walls with your crossbow and pistol. This style has consequences later on in the game, and plays-out differently to if you play it by becoming a shadow. There is extra challenge in taking the 'non-lethal' route too. Your choice.
I'm a simple person with simple tastes, and normally take the front-door heavy-weapons approach, but the sneaky shadow style beckoned this time and it's been a blast. I've found myself holding my breath a lot while playing this game.
Equipment and skills can be modified and upgraded to suit your style.
The game has been intelligently designed with fields of vision simulated for enemies and intrusion detection systems. Hit an enemy with a sleeper dart intending a non-lethal run through and watch them plummet to their deaths in the water or break their necks down stairs. That's still counted as a death on your shoulders so you'll have to find another angle or creep up behind them and choke them.
An engrossing challenging masterpiece.

I've always looked at this game and wondered if it was worth the purchase or not and through multiple sales I have decided to sideline this game due to the low player count and all I can say is that the game was worth the purchase the entire time. The gameplay is fantastic and good fun, playing with friends both monster or hunter is good and coordination is always key. Due the game being free to play it has seen a huge rise in player count, making it one of the most played games on steam right now and I definitely hope it withholds this place.
For those who don't know, the matches are 1v4 with the 1 being a massive creature with the 4 being a Support, Assault, Healer and Trapper. The game boasts a good feeling of team work in your hunt for the creature and combining each of the roles to the fullest makes it tremendous fun. The matches aren't too long winded which makes the game even better in my eyes and if you want to play alone then the monster is a good solo option. Often times people will question the balance of the game and in my eyes the monsters / hunters are an even match in the right hands and that makes the battles feel 1,000 times more epic and hard-fought. Any PVP game will have something to complain about balance wise so it's expected for people to feel hard done by by a more experienced / skilled player.
If I were to say that the game is optimised I wouldn't be sure if I was lying or not, I've seen that many people have been complaining about framerate issues but for me it has been flawless, I feel as if people with lower tier PCs expect to run this game smooth on max settings and suffer the consequences. I and my friends run this game perfectly fine, smooth as butter above 60 frames per second on max settings. That's the least I can say for other people but due to the game being f2p now I can only advise that you try it out to see how it performs for you. That's where I mention that the graphics are phenomenal, one of the best I've seen on a game in a while and that makes the game just that bit better.

I picked up HOI4 for £24 after using a voucher I got for free. £24 = 6 beers = 3 hours of fun.
I've played, at time of writing, 467 hours of HOI4 since purchase. 467 hours of fun.
467 hours = 934 beers (467*2) = £3,736 (934*4)
Nearly 4 grand worth of enjoyment for less than 25 quid, and no hangover or liver failure to show for it.

Salt and Sanctuary is a 2D soulslike RPG with a focus on creative platforming. The story has you as a protector of a princess stranded on an island inhabited by all manners of weird and disturbing creatures trying to find your charge.
The gameplay is very smooth, making combat and platforming - the two main focuses of the game - an enjoyable experience thru and thru.
The art design of the game is very dark and twisted for the most part with memorable style to it that looks very hand drawn and deliberate.
RPG elements come in the form of armor and weapon choice aswell as Rings and Charms. The game has an interesting leveling system that reminded me a lot of the sphere grid from Final Fantasy X. Instead of increasing your stats in a linear manner you invest levels into nodes that can give you access to better weapons or armor or spells or give you more healing potions or just give you points towards your stats.
Speaking of weapons, the game has a nice varitey of weapons, ranging from your standart swords and axes to greathammers and even pistols. The game also has two seperate magic schools, magic and miracles. This wide range of arms in conjunction with the multiple endings and ability to go thru the game as many times as you want to with one character gives SaS a lot of replay value.
Lastly I would like to point out the games amazing world design. Many of the areas are interconnected and many hidden pathways can be found by those who are willing to find them (or look them up).
Overall, I can recommend the game wholeheartedly for any fans of the soulsborne genre, fans of 2D action RPGs and fans of metroidvania style games.

Pros:
+ The game looks stunning at a distance (see cons)
+ The story is good, if not original.
+ Gun mechanics are fun, with a twitch aim feel, and high difficulty makes the game challenging.
+ Sounds are chunky, and feel vibrant.
Cons:
- Textures look awful at close range due to the engine.
- The game has a 60FPS lock, and FOV lock, and texture pop in, which can only be worked around with mods.
- Lots of bugs, and stuttering, with poor performance on a high end system.
- Steam cloud saves don't work, I lost my save data and have to start the game again.
- 'Open world' is not open, the game is very linear, and often restricts your movement around the map, creating a false sense of reality.
- Game doesn't feel authentic, a lot of the ideas are cliche, and similar to a Borderlands/Fallout theme, which has been done to death.

JK: DF2 was one of my favorite games back in the day and easily one of the best Star Wars games ever but it does not play nice on modern systems. I would recommend tracking down the CD version instead of buying the Steam version if you can, as that version is compatible with a fan patch that can get the game running.

Do I recommend this game based on the game itself? Of course, it's a worthy sequel to Dark Forces and an excellent transition to a tridimensional engine. The graphics are very weird and too "pointy" even for its time. The gameplay is very fast paced, and eventually you get your own lightsaber to hack enemies away! Of course, like its predecessor, there are some levels in which the level design makes no sense whatsoever, and some impacient folks will probably skip to a walkthrough. The FMV cutscenes are very weird but kinda cool, I guess.
Do I recommend buying it here on Steam? Not so much. This game is notorious for having compatibility issues on every Windows that came after XP, so prepare to lose some time testing fixes, patches and whatever the hell else to get the game working. I would recommend that you get it a very, very low price, like I did, so in case you can't run it, at least you won't be losing too much money. Brotip:

I recieved this game for 99 cents, thinking it was a steal.

I played all of this game today, from beginning to end. It went from entertaining and satisfying to frustrating very quickly.
I'll give a few good things about this, then get going with the crap show that this game is.
The following will contain spoilers.
Pros:
The interactive sniping is relatively good. I felt somewhat immersed and satisfied with what I was doing and the kills I made.
That is it. That is the only good thing I have to say about this game.
Cons:
The sniping is good, sure, but let's be real. I know nothing of real military operation, as I have never been deployed or been through boot camp or any other such measure. But, even I could tell that this game was absolutely terrible at replicating a real military operation. If you pulled the kind of BS that the main character does, you would be slapped in prison with a dishonorable discharge VERY quickly. Not sent out on "one last mission" to get revenge on your ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ spotter from years past.
Despite most of the sniping being pretty good, your spotter is a damn liar. The game does this so poorly. But you have to follow his instructions to THE LETTER or you WILL die. A few times, he makes calls for targets that you can't see yet, but when you move your vision to where he says the target is, it will be a floor up, or a floor down, from where the target actually is.
This next one absolutely shattered any remaining hope I had as I finished up the game. In the last act, in the final two missions, your spotter makes a few calls. "You take one, I got the other." In the previous times this happens, he follows through. The game scripts his shots and the other enemy dies. In the last couple, this breaks. You make your shot, but your spotter does not fire. Period. But your shot blows your cover and you have to kill the other guy for him. This happened to me 3 times.
The animation is awful in the cutscenes.
The story is a steaming pile of♥♥♥♥♥♥ I felt no emotion toward any of the characters. I just wanted to get the game over with, because I'm a completionist and I finish what I start. The main character is an idiot and an ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥.
At a few points, it is scripted to the story that you blow your cover and the enemies spot you. This wouldn't be an issue, if it weren't for the fact that you can only take 3 hits of damage (on normal difficulty) before you die, and also for the fact that, unless scripted otherwise, the NPC's have what is essentially aimbot. I had to camp a corner to kill some enemies because I couldn't do it before I blew my cover, and the first two tries at it, They turn the corner, their character models instantaneously turn, fire one shot, and you die, despite my previous assumption that it took more than one hit.
This game is wholly terrible in almost all of it's aspects.
You want a good stealth game? Dishonored. Best stealth game I've ever played.
You want a good sniping experience, but outside of the multiplayer hellhole?
Battlefield: Bad Company 2 had the most refreshing and satisfying sniping experience that I've had to date, with a wonderful story and memorable characters.
Please do not buy this game, even if it's just 99 cents. It is not worth your time.

Paradox always tends to make good games and this is really on that way. The way to manage your army and fronts has greatly improved from HOI III, requiring less madness micro and making great powers like USA or USSR available and not just the "autistic mode on".
Economy has been a bit simplified too, but it still requires mastering, expecially playing the Axis forces you will have real struggle to obtain some vital resources: rubber (for aircraft) and oil (for anything that isn't base infantry).
Naval and Air combat are cool and ACTUALLY a thing: with certain nations (UK, Japan, Italy) you really want to have a strong navy and airforce.
Pretty much all the game is about being efficient. Being efficient on gathering resources, on placing your forces where they are needed, on production, on trade and on coordinating national foci with researches. So if you don't like using your mind to think about how to do things efficiently, this is not for you. Math and logistics are vital parts of the game, because this is modern warfare, and being optimal is the key to victory.
The game is also deep in the managing of supplies, so you can't send all your 150 USA division to invade Sicily or you will get wrecked. You can't send even 10 division in Sicily if you don't get a port.
Many people criticize the AI of this game, wich sometimes is a bit lacky. But not every game is perfect, and it's not a problem so big as someone make you believe. There is no such thing as "Germany sent all his divisions fighting in Egypt and got wrecked by USSR" unless you have messed up doing something gamey. If you remain historical, AI will be good, the more you derail, the more it gets confused.
I'd give this game a fair 8/10 for now, but I believe Paradox will release patches and make it a 9/10 for sure ;)

I rate a computer game based on a custom-built formula to discern its real-world value. It's quite simple, but an effective way to record my enjoyment of said game. It is:
2 Beers = 1 Hour of Fun.  In my town, a beer costs £4, so you tend to take your time with it...
Anyway... 2 beers = 1 hour of fun. And 2 beers = £8. Therefore, a game that costs say, £20, is equal to 5 beers (or 2 1/2 hours of fun). Still with me?
I picked up HOI4 for £24 after using a voucher I got for free. £24 = 6 beers = 3 hours of fun.
I've played, at time of writing, 467 hours of HOI4 since purchase. 467 hours of fun.
467 hours = 934 beers (467*2) = £3,736 (934*4)
Nearly 4 grand worth of enjoyment for less than 25 quid, and no hangover or liver failure to show for it.

Other reviewers had me eager to recapture the magic of Dark Souls with this game, but Salt and Sanctuary is excellent in its own right.  Unforgiving combat, balanced character classes, grand exploration, gorgeous design, a great community, and a sensible plot are perfectly mixed here.
I particularly enjoyed how the game's world of vast forests, plains, and lairs were so tightly interconnected with the sprawling palaces, temples, and monuments.  Exploration felt that much more real and meaningful, which added to the accomplishment of triumphing over bosses, overcoming traps and hazards, or simply surviving.
There are very, very few games I enjoyed replaying as much as I did the first time through.  This game is definitely one of them.  Salt and Sanctuary isn't perfect (some monsters can easily stunlock you to death, rolling doesn't work as well as it should in two dimensions, and no camera movement means you'll have to take more than one blind leap into potential death drops), but has so much going for it that I'm happy to overlook the flaws.
The _only_ thing I wish was different is that (except for the final boss), the same track is played for all boss fights.  The varied and often epic boss themes are what sealed my love of Dark Souls, and this game entirely misses that.  Think of the Ornstein and Smough fight without the monumental brass, Dark Sun Gwyndolin without the haunting vocals, or Knight Artorias without the brooding strings and choir.  Much of their personality is lost without these themes - a lot of why I remember them years later is because of the music that set them apart.
This game relies just as heavily on lore and interaction for back story, and one area guardian after another who is different only in appearance and move sets tend to blur together or be forgotten.  I still thoroughly enjoyed this game and would strongly recommend it, but damn if the dev didn't miss the chance to make Salt and Sanctuary absolutely perfect.

This was easily my favorite game of 2016, and there was some tough competition. As you may have heard, this game borrows heavily from Dark Souls, and if you haven't played Dark Souls, you will miss all those amazing references. For me, Salt and Sanctuary does a few things better than Dark Souls. But that's an argument for another time.
What you get with Salt and Santuary, is a game with challenging combat, a Metroidvania style map that is fun to explore, and build options and NPCs that will keep you coming back for more. The bosses can sometimes be more or less challenging, depending on your build, but I found them all enjoyable to fight.
Basically, the hype is real. This game is amazing. If you like good, challenging combat, whether or not you are familiar with Dark Souls, you need to play Salt and Sanctuary.

"The Next Penelope" has a F-Zero vibe mixed with micromachines gameplay. The ship is always accelerating so you can focus on turning and using the weapons/skills. Using those weapons makes the racing way more complex and deep.
There's a campaign mode with different missions and bosses, these stages have different goals (it's not always about racing), so there's a lot of variety. There are different difficulty levels, my first impression was that it would be a bit easy but there are some pretty hard and enjoyable challenges in "The Next Penelope".
It's still on early access and has some minor issues, but even on its current state is a wonderful game. Can't wait to play this with my friends on multiplayer.

I love top-down racing games, but I also love games with a story. Well, The Next Penelope is a racing game with a story that actually makes sense. That's enough for me to highly recommend it, but there's even more.
An open galaxy with unlockable weapons to give you a good amount of freedom. Beautifully stylized graphics with retina-burning colors (retina-burning colors are a great thing — retinas are just an urban legend and we don't really need them). A weapon system that is actually smart and allows for some fast-thinking strategy. Plus it's fun. No really.  FUN! Just play it.

The Next Penelope is a sort of top-down, sort of on the side view (but mainly top-down), fast paced action racing shooter game that's full of color, an interesting classic looking story, and challengingly fun.
The game's really polished with minimum issues that usually accompany games in beta or alpha, so it left me playing the game in its entirety, at least the main campaign of the game, smoothly, and I enjoyed most of it.
The look of the game is a mix of beautiful and colorful visuals, and an art style that reminds me of the late 90's / early 2000's for some reason. The games characters, and the way they are portrayed, coupled with the graphical effects, sound effects, great soundtrack, and the whole presentation, really emits a strong charm from the game which really reminds me of Mega Man X because of it's presentation, and that's kind of awesome.
The gameplay is fun and smooth, with the driving controls being simple, steering right or left, and considering your momentum while making turns to not bump into walls which will slow down you movement, or fall off and lose, but while it is simple, it's also challenging with how you have to time your movements with boosters, dodging bullets and missiles from your enemies or traps, know when to use your power, which is connected to your life-energy fuel where if you use a power, you're also using up your life-energy, so you have to conserve and collect energy to not get yourself destroyed.
Aside from reasonably good races, and challenging tracks, and the good progression going from easy to "impossible" difficulty, with a nice level selection menu map, the game has boss battles which at first made me confused as I thought this was a racing game, but nope, it's a racing game with apparently boss battles, and they're fun and definitely changes the pace of the game from always racing, and each one is unique in a way that you have to use what you have learned from previous races and the ability you've again from it, to defeat / help defeat the boss you're battling against, so no boss battle is the same.
The only thing that's bad I have to say about the game, is that since the game is in 2D, some parts of the track is designed in a way that makes me think there is a turn to make, leaving me confused every time I come across those certain part(s) of the track, unless I've played through that track so much that I've memorized it to not get confused.
Overall it's a great game, and I love everything about it so far, and will probably enjoy the upcoming 4-player coop that it will have, and the extra content upon release or through its development, and for the price, it's a polished - in-development - goodness with an awesome charm.

Fracture the Flag is a very cheap but very enjoyable multiplayer RTS Town building game. At £2, you can’t really complain about the price and the game is coming along very well.
In essence, you build a lumber mill, a warehouse (to store your resources), and then spawn some workers that you then assign to different jobs such as miner, lumberjack, quarryman etc. The workers will then go off and collect these resources and bring them back to your warehouse which adds them to your available resources. You then build other buildings which have a range of different purposes. Such as a barracks for turning workers into swordsmen, spearmen etc. The game also has an unlock tree in which you gain points while playing and use said points to unlock different abilities or buildings/units. Such as a faster worker speed to gather resources quicker or to unlock military units such as spearmen and catapults.
For an early access game, this plays really well and runs very well. It has some issues you might expect in an E.A. title such as some U.I. issues, but I am assuming those will be polished out as time progresses. From looking over some of the forums, the Devs seem to be very active in the community, replying to questions and accepting criticism/advice on how the game could be improved.
Personally, I have a few suggestions on how the game could be improved. These are:
-	Make workers have different coloured shirts depending on their jobs. For example: Blue shirts for Mine workers, red shirts for lumberjacks etc. Just so it is easy to distinguish who is who rather than it looking like a mosh pit of blue shirts.
-	Polish the U.I. Yes I know this is probably a given, but some of it needs more improvement. Such as the Barracks for example. You click on the barracks, then click the sword icon and any unemployed workers will run to the barracks and become swordsman. This needs to be much clearer and more obvious.
Apart from that, it is refreshing to see an E.A. title such as this and puts my faith back into the E.A. project as this is a fantastic little gem for such a tiny price.
Well worth a look and I hope to see this as one of the very few E.A. games that make it out of E.A.
EDIT: The recommendations I have put in this review I also submitted to a Fracture the Flag message board in which you can suggest improvements. This is the reply I received from the Developer.
“@TribalHarry Some visual difference could be possible. At the moment the colours are reserved for different players. Worth a thought for sure. Thanks for the suggestion.”
I cannot recommend this game more. With a Dev that’s in the community willing to listen to feedback and take it into account while updating the game. Well worth buying even if you don’t plan on playing until the game is out of E.A. just to support this Dev. We need more like him/her in our community.

Even though I went light side on my first play through I know you can go dark and get different powers and maybe even a different ending which means the game has replayability.

My Advice, even though I didn’t, before you play this game go look for some mods. So before you play this just go online and find some mods to help make this game more of enjoyable experience for you.

It's a pity, really, that Jedi Knight tends to run badly on modern OSs. I don't recommend it for WIndows 8/10 PCs as it usually runs pretty badly. My WIndows 7 rig ran it without a lot of issues.
It's a pity, because the game is just absolutely fantastic. Levels are huge, but not empty, and make great use of verticality. The automap is great at showing you where you're supposed to go, and really gives you a much better idea of how big levels are. There are a lot of nooks and crannies to explore throughout. The guns are satisfying, not great (Dark Forces I had better looking and feeling weapons IMO) , and the movement is really great, kinda like Quake's movement but with less momentum, handy, as JK tends to have more platforming and tight passages of which you don't want to fall out of. Force Powers are nothing special (This was before the prequel Trilogy, though), but some of them are well used in levels (especially Force Jump, but also Speed.) There are Dark Side (mostly damage-dealing) and Light Side (buffs/healing) It also has a lot of battles with Dark Jedi, but they're quite lackluster, since the lightsaber combat is pretty clunky.

The cool thing is that on about the last third of the game, you get locked into either Dark Side or Light Side. After a few seasons of midtable Football Manager has finally returned to form. Yes - football puns.
I've always been a huge fan of Sports Interactive, going back to their time with Eidos when they made the Championship Manager series. Recently, I discovered that I've spent several years of my life playing all the various editions and versions of Champ Man and Football Manager and there's good reason for that - the games are deeply immersive when they're done right.
At its heart Football Manager still provides the same management/simulator experience based around managing a football team. This has never been Football Manager's problem, the sheer depth and scale of the database covers a vast majority of the most popular leagues from around the world. Those that aren't active can soon be made active through the use of the editor, and a quick look of the official forums will show you there are plenty of people working on league extensions already.
In recent years Football Manager's crux for me has been the Match Engine, the very brain that drives the match results and helps determine your fortune as a manager. The level of detail and effort that goes into the Match Engine cannot be understated. It's almost a never ending cycle of development and review, and no matter how many eyes review it once it's released there's no going back. In previous years the Match Engine has been released with poor marking, poor closing down, full backs running riot, goals galore from crosses, corners to the back post exploits. Exploits that once become apparant become almost impossible to ignore and deter from the overall enjoyment of the game.
In an ideal world these would be patched out instantly, rather than adhering to SI's current stance of key patches  (Often a Post-Release patch around Christmas and January transfer update in Feb/March). After this only the MAJOR gamebreaking issues looked to be fixed, which sadly doesn't include Match Engine oversights or exploits. I understand this, and appreciate that level of effort it takes to make changes to the Match Engine, balance, and rebalance and check for the ripple effect those changes have had on other parts of the Match Engine that previously worked fine.
Thankfully this year all seems well. There's perhaps a slight overeasy feel to scoring goals down the middle, especially with a front three (or a fast striker that can get in behind), but for the most part the Match Engine looks and feels as close to a game of football as Football Manager has achieved to date.
There's a good mixture of goals from various areas of the pitch, long and short range, crosses and throughballs and well worked build up with a change of pace to the passing play instigated by playmakers. It also feels as if Preferred Moves have finally been given some extra spice within the Match Engine too, further allowing you to customise and train players to your preferred style of play.
The other major overhaul to Football Manager this year is the introduction to Dynamics giving the manager some insight and feedback into how their man management is having affect on the players they're coaching. A welcome addition for me, as I like take time out to talk to players personally and build relationships with players I trust even if they're not 'good enough'. The best feedback I can give this new feature is that it makes sense and it's useful, something of a rarity on new additions to Football Manager over the itterations.
It's possible to build a strong core of players that all get on well, think you're the bee's knees of a manager and will run through walls for you despite being technically very poor players. It might not sound important, but once you've played a game as a lower league team, with limited funds, you'll see the appeal this can have.
The only area of the game I still feel is lacking is the transfer module, with players not really being aware of their locale when thinking about finding a new club, and the cost of wages/transfer fee being 'odd'. Granted, SI couldn't have foreseen the hectic transfer window that happened before release, and this one is just a matter of opinion, but hopefully it's something that gets the care and attention it deserves.
Overall Football Manager 2018 has me hooked again, where once FM16 and FM17 had me disappointed and going through the motions. I'm firmly invested in my career save (I often start unemployed with the lowest rep and see how far I can go as a manager) this time around, with two seasons under my belt with Clyde - So far I've got them into the Scottish Championship after back-to-back promotions and I'm still using the original squad all thanks to good squad management and dynamic building.
So for those who felt perhaps a bit jaded by previous releases of Football Manager now could be a good time to return. Those new to the series, I honestly can't think of any point where to start as each version grows in scale upon the last. Thankfully there is a 'toned down' version available called Football Manager Touch, which you get when you purchase Football Manager, so that could be a good place to start.

Rage is a typical Id Software FPS. Poor story (but much far elaborated than any previously done by the studio), nice looking graphics at least from far distances and solid FPS gameplay, simply said the shooting is awesome, some missions are much better than another but in general is a great shooter.
Id Software began the developing of Rage in the most darkest times for PC gaming when piracy, changes in retail channels and beginning of internet gaming stores plumped down PC retail sales.  Those dark times when XBOX and Playstation began to drain all PC exclusive franchises (COD 2, BF Bad Company 1, Medal of Honor and a long list) that studios/publishers skipped the PC.
Then Id Software took a decision to focus Id Tech 5 in optimize developing times between ports. This is the interesting part because Id Tech 5 engine games (Rage, Wolf New Order, Wolf Old blood, Evil Within)  look awesome from far distances and like crap when getting closer. So bad that is unbelivable that someone released a game with those graphics in 2011 !!!!.
Even is a urban legend that original Rage textures were about 1TB in size (In comparison Rage takes 23GBs in disk) is this is true should be interesting if someday those textures become released. (Do you imagine a SSD 1TB disk full with only one game? hahaha)
About the gameplay: Typical master piece in shooting from Id Software, frenetic shooting, solid gunplay, weapon selection, interesting levels and never gets boring when you start a new mission.
In a plus they tried to add some kind of RPG elements, side quests and racing (Even some players found more fun racing that the shooting ?!?!)
With modern hardware and proper configuration you can run Rage at Ultra graphics without texture popping.
If you like shooters you're going to like Rage that's for sure.
Solid and enjoyable FPS, but it's easy to see why it has been forgotten.

A fine shooter with rather poor story and terrible driving sections.
Rage seems to be suffering from trying to fit too many genres into single game. While some of them feel absolutely fine - some do not. And the game suffers for it.
At it's core Rage is a first person shooter set in a post-apocalyptic world. The earth is devastated by an asteroid while humanity takes shelter in underground vaults - I mean arks. Due to sabotage a certain group of people wake up first and claim the land for themselves - they call them selves the enclave... no wait - the Authority. Your awake later with no memory it seems and try to find your way around in this new hostile world.
So story wise this game is nothing spectacular. The premise is pretty much similar to Fallout. The world is destroyed, you get picked up and suddenly you have to kill the bad guys before eventually mixing up with resistance. Not really complicated - and doesn't get better.
Visually the game is fantastic. This is how Fallout 3 or New Vegas should like. And it runs quite smoothly at that.
Rage pretends to be a open world game but it's not. The open levels which you traverse by vehicles are just a bit bigger levels. The fact that you don't really get out of the car during them - you could but it's pointless makes it feel all the worse.
As a fps game it's doing very nicely. It feels a bit like the new Doom with the movement and the shooting. The guns here do have iron sights but it's generally easier to just run around and shoot stuff, and certain levels do actually remind Doom's arena like combat. Enemies similarly take more bullets to kill than my preference but it's not as bad as I feared prior to picking up this game.
Guns themselves are quite well designed and the fact that you can use different ammunition for each makes the combat all that much interesting. Additional crafting mechanics do add a bit to the whole experience as well.
The really poor thing in this game is the driving. Especially at first with the quad it feels just so stiff and artificial. The fact that the game makes you do some races doesn't help as I didn't really find them entertaining. The handling seems off and the general vehicle combat is just not fun.
The mission breakdown doesn't help as well. The world is designed in a way that there's a central location in the open world level that mostly break into different points of interest. Generally the missions look like - get a mission, travel to certain spot, kill bad guys, go back to talk to mission giver, go talk to another character, go back and report. Each time you travel trough the center. Each time there are banding there - and they re spawn every time you enter certain spot. So within a single mission you can fight four or five times with them. Unless you choose to ignore them which you probably will very quickly. But it's annoying all the same.
In the end as a FPS it's a pretty fun game. As all else not so much. And while the story is rather weak it's still a fun game to play. The locations and encounters are just enjoyable and if you're looking for some mindless shooter - Rage is a nice fit.
