My first roguelike was Dungeons of Dredmor, which was fun, but in terms of gameplay options and experimentation, it just wasn't enough.  This game is more than enough.  There are 26 classes in this game, most of which have unique playstyles and minimal overlap.  Between those, there are many ways to build most of them with endless opportunities to experiment and die horribly in different ways.  The UI is confusing at first, but very functional once you get the hang of it.  There is a significant mod community for those who are into that.
The game comes with most of the classes and some races unlocked.  This is somewhat controversial but for me was highly beneficial for my enjoyment of the game.  Making the classes unlockable makes the game much less overwhelming to pick up and provides a significant sense of progression even when your character fails to win the game.  Once those classes are unlocked, higher difficulty options and mods continue to extend the game's life.
Healing potions and most consumables are replaced by cooldown-based "Inscriptions" and "Runes," which is perfect because it removes any sort of "saving for a rainy day" hesitation players tend to have in combat.
There are a couple of issues with this game.  Some rigs may encounter excessive memory leaks with the default graphics settings.  Graphics and sound are expected to be minimal but there are a few obnoxious sound effects and themes in the game and some volume imbalance.  As commonly seen in these games, early level progression with many classes at higher difficulties is extremely frustrating.  But these issues are minor.  Stop reading and get the damn game.

i really wanted to enjoy this game. but heres my few problems with it.
for a game that kinda bills itself as speedy in general, the actual movement in game is pretty slow. consider it like Jet Grind Radio, instead of Jet Set Radio Future. same attitude, but much slower in all aspects. if they made the boost speed standard speed, and made boost faster, it might be more fun.
but then theres the modifiers. "cement shoes", "slow thuggin". these pop up very rapidly, often just as the last one is ending. i had a match where the entire game was in slow motion because we got slow thugging over and over. these *might* make the game more fun, if they didn't happen so often. as it is, they kill the pacing.
lastly, theres the "closed area" rule. where less than a minute into a game, half of the level gets closed off and kills you if you go in. this might be better as a more gradual effect, but no, its a big nope stamp coming all at once. on one level, in the last 3 minutes of a match, everywhere was closed off except for a narrow platform suspended between two buildings. locking off areas of a free running game sorta seems like a mis-step to me.
in any case, this game has a serious problem of too many mechanics. cut out any two, and the game might be a lot more enjoyable. maybe future patches will help. as it stands, i cannot reccomend it.

Best WW2 strategy game. Some improvements could be made, but those will come in time. All hail Paradox!
War! What is it good for? Absolutely everything!

Paradox always tends to make good games and this is really on that way. The way to manage your army and fronts has greatly improved from HOI III, requiring less madness micro and making great powers like USA or USSR available and not just the "autistic mode on".
Economy has been a bit simplified too, but it still requires mastering, expecially playing the Axis forces you will have real struggle to obtain some vital resources: rubber (for aircraft) and oil (for anything that isn't base infantry).
Naval and Air combat are cool and ACTUALLY a thing: with certain nations (UK, Japan, Italy) you really want to have a strong navy and airforce.
Pretty much all the game is about being efficient. Being efficient on gathering resources, on placing your forces where they are needed, on production, on trade and on coordinating national foci with researches. So if you don't like using your mind to think about how to do things efficiently, this is not for you. Math and logistics are vital parts of the game, because this is modern warfare, and being optimal is the key to victory.
The game is also deep in the managing of supplies, so you can't send all your 150 USA division to invade Sicily or you will get wrecked. You can't send even 10 division in Sicily if you don't get a port.
Many people criticize the AI of this game, wich sometimes is a bit lacky. But not every game is perfect, and it's not a problem so big as someone make you believe. There is no such thing as "Germany sent all his divisions fighting in Egypt and got wrecked by USSR" unless you have messed up doing something gamey. If you remain historical, AI will be good, the more you derail, the more it gets confused.
I'd give this game a fair 8/10 for now, but I believe Paradox will release patches and make it a 9/10 for sure ;)

Tom Clancy's Rainbow Six 3 Gold by Tom Clancy is a third game in Tom Clancy's Tom Clancy's Rainbow Six franchise. Which was realistical tactical shooter, where you would create your own plan for the level and then execute it, being excited to see how your dumb AI teammates will get slaughtered this time. And yes, it uses "one shot, one kill" system, almost. Released in in 2003 by Red Storm and Ubisoft, it also had console ports for Xbox, PS2 and Gamecube. Consoles ports were different: no planning, you command only one 4-man squad and each got few hitpoints.
This is Gold, meaning that it comes with inclusion of original Raven Shield game and the first expansion pack - Athena Sword, that mostly adds few more levels, released in 2004.
There also was a second expansion pack, which was almost finished (probably meaning that it just didn't go through debugging), Iron Wrath. It was released for free in 2005 on Internet anyway. Meaning that people were happy, aside from 56kb modem users.
So, technical stuff. While main menu and planning phase work at 4:3 resolution, gameplay itself supports widescreen resolution. But it doesn't change FOV, so you will be seeing chubby people. But it crashes sometimes when you change between planning phase and execution phase. So always save your plans!
Expansion packs are a bit weird in that they will not play their new sounds, that are briefing voice acting and new sounds for new weapons. To fix that, you will have to go to mods folder, find folder of needed expansion pack, and then copy "Sounds" folder from there to the root directory of the game.
You also will have problems installing free Iron Wrath, as installer will not recognise Rainbow Six for what it is. To fix that just check Steam Guides. In nutshell, you will have to create new key in Registry where retail version of a game keeps all the needed info about itself. You don't have to screw the system itself, don't worry.
As for multiplayer, well, you could play in either coop or competive. It used old Ubi service, but as of now, multiplayer is technically dead. I heard that at some point you was required to use UPlay account instead, but it didn't work for me.
EDIT: Because turns out that my actual login, that is email, is way too long for the game. HA!
In this game you play as anybody of Rainbow Six squad, the point of which is to make terrorist think that they are dealing with six pony-loving hippies, only to be met with eight aim-botting hard-try top operatives. But because it's a top secret squad and it's actions are written off as actions of special forces of whatever country they are in, the shock tactic of the name just never works. Just use flashbangs for that.
Well, in this part you are dealing with neo-nazi terrorists who love taking hostages, listen to briefing and watch occasional cutscenes that make you feel good and even heroic for a job well done. Which is nice. It has ending video, so that's enough.
Another thing to note is that Rainbow Six is full of only top-top-top people, only the best individuals from separate parts of world. And then, after collecting them all, no one bothered to teach them how to work as a team. The only thing they ever learned is that they are supposed to walk in a line. And even then it can go wrong in small hallways, where a leader of a line will turn around and start pushing the tail out, as it refused to turn around, until his heavily armored butt slides out from the doorway and gets filled with bullets, while you scream at the screen in observation mode. Good bullets. Shiny, sturdy, can survive from -50 to +50 degrees of temperature. Must be 7.62x39mm ones. A bit outdated, but good bullets indeed, tactical-realism fans approve.
No, really, I got to see that few times.
But really, AI in single-player game can do a lot of things to sabotage the fact that game relies on squad-based tactics.
And well, let's say that Rainbow Six 3 isn't as best ever as fans tend to call it.
Or at least it didn't age well.
And when I say "didn't age well", what I mean is "SWAT 4 came out". Which was not only more tactical, but implented proper AI teammates. No planning phase though.
At least graphics and music in this game are still nice. Even got ambient music sometimes playing during mission and such. And ragdolls look funny nowdays, just crashing onto floor. Blam.
Anyway, since fans of tactical-realistical games always brag about such games and on question "what is tactical exactly?" they answer only "ummmm... you are too stupid to get", here is what you get to expect: Abuse leaning around corners when you are controlling a soldier; Abuse the aimbotness of AI teammates and place them in such way that no one walks behind them; Throw smoke grenade to become invinsible for AI; Try to come into difficult room from few directions with different teams. Those four rules is what makes this game. And planning.
You get into mission and first thing you get is briefing. After that, you are going to set up a plan. And oh boy, that's the main feature of the early games of franchise, as you get to put waypoints for up to three teams. You can also coordinate them together by setting go-codes. Tell them to throw grenade or breach the door. Actually, you can either try to beat level with no plan like generic realistical shooter, use pre-made one, use pre-made one and edit if neccersary or just make up a whole new one. And it's just awesome that you can make the map play out the way you want.
Until you will find out that AI can't open door slightly and throw grenade in, like players. Or bounce grenade at the wall, limiting the usage of flashbang. Or that they have tendency to never stop at waypoints and fire full-automatic while walking. Or that they will never decide to wait for enemy come out if they hear "huh, that's strange". Or the way you can't order them to throw smoke grenade down the tunnel in the third mission, so it's only up to player. Or just find out that some tasks AI does really badly.
In other words, while it DOES require tactical planning, but for dumb AI. Through trial-and-error of execution you will find what AI does best and judging by this you will build your plan for dummies. Which takes away some enjoyment.
If you try to pull something clever in this, you will have to do dirty job with your own hands. And even if you build a good plan, there is a bit of randomness on placement of some terrorists, so it can sometimes go wrong anyway.
After that, you set up a squad, pulling 8 members for a job and separating them into teams. While wondering what's the point of Demos, who just make some objectives complete few seconds faster, and recons types. After that you look at huge list of samey weapons that you don't care about, pick the strongest/favourite assault rifle and put silencer onto it, as there is no real tactical choice. Unless sniper rifle. Then you look over some more useless devices, including multiplayer-only, which are in campaign for some reason, or like tear gas grenade and gas mask.
Then you start execution and watch the new way your team getting slaugthered in some wacky way on the first minute, then beat remaining mission as a lone wounded machine gunner, slumbering with broken legs and getting through by abusing leaning, which is how I did pre-last mission. Actually, that was slightly fun. But only for once.
But really, the main reason to recommend it is the lack of alternatives. No other tactical FPS outside of Rainbow Six has detailed planning, as far as I am aware! So it's sad that Ubisoft wasted this part. New R6 games are still nice, but should have kept feature that was making franchise unique.
Not as sad as lack of SWAT4 on Steam though.

The end of an era, it marks the last great tactical shooter on the market before this series descended into mediocrity. Nothing else since this has come close to equalling its quality of brutal, unforgiving tactics. This is a game that wears its realism on its sleeve and isn't afraid to let you drop dead from one bullet fired from a guy you couldn't even have seen coming. You move slowly and even walking throws your aim way off. Repeated autofire might as well be fired with your eyes closed. Guns feel weighty and impactful, dropping enemies in one or two torso shots.  It's harsh and doesn't feel remotely fair at times, but having smooth, flawless success in this game is more satisfying than any other shooter I've played.
Unlocking all the maps requires playing through the campaign mode, where the iffy team AI and permanent injuries/death to the squad members can make things frustrating, but if you take the time to plan things out they usually go well. The game has no tolerance for the slightest mistake, for even a single corner left unchecked, and requires awareness and caution you rarely need in other games.
The real fun comes with friends. Competitive modes are fine, but nothing's better than the sheer teamwork it takes to clear out a whole map in co-op. And the sheer disaster that can strike if any one of you slips up for a moment. Multiplayer no longer functions out of the box, so you'll have to take alternate methods to get it work, such as Hamachi or Tunngle, but it's well worth the effort. Still one of my favourite coop games of all time.

I see you did not listen.  On the assumption that you are still not convinced of Rift's awesomeness, allow me to tell you why it is just so awesome.
To begin with, it's like World of Warcraft, but FREE.  In fact, I would go as far as to say that it is superior to WoW (World of Warcraft)  under numerous accounts. After about 4 playthroughs and 80 odd hours of the game, I can confidently say it is exceptionally well done and well worth $15.  Very easy to pick up, and very easy to put down.  You can save any time, and there are plenty of checkpoints to avoid you doing much needless backtracking at all.
Story:
The story isn't openly told to you besides some basic vague details - but instead much of the depth of the world of Salt and Sanctuary is hidden among items/equipment descriptions, discovered by interacting with the NPCs (repeatedly), and experienced more fully with successive playthroughs giving it great replay value, in my opinion.  The mysteries and lore to be discovered are fascinatingly dark.
Skill Tree:
The level-up mechanics I found to be very versatile.  There's no hand-holding so I do recommend looking up guides for how to build your character or at the very least, planning out what you want to do.  I strongly recommend focusing on Heavy Armor, Magic, and Greatswords though and packing on as much Endurance and Willpower as possible.  The fact that you lose salt when you die / have to recover it neither added nor subtracted from my experience.
Gameplay/Fighting:
I found it very smooth and fun.  You develop a wide variety of defensive and offensive options which you can switch between before battles - especially boss fights - to prepare yourself.  You're always given a warning when a boss is near and often tips on how to best fight it.  Along with resistances you can also use Heavy Armor to increase your Balance to increase your stagger resistances to help avoid getting stun locked by enemies.
2 Player Co-Op
No, it doesn't allow online play.  Only couch co-op.  If you have a buddy you can likely cruise through the game in a day or two together though.  It was a lot of fun doing so and the 2 player game mechanic worked well.  Enemies are scaled up in HP to balance the difficulty somewhat and it felt about equally as challenging on 2 player and when I went through on single player.
Art:
I really enjoyed the dark art style.  It goes excellently well with the grim and melancholic tone of the game.  It never felt out of place, and I honestly wish I could find more like it.
Bugs/Exploits:
There are a few minor bugs mostly related to co-op play, such as maybe 2 or 3 items not being obtainable for whoever is 2 player when they go back to their own game.  One of which I encountered was a Key that is needed to proceed in the game - but, this is easily bypassed by summoning a character that has the key you need, using it, then moving on with the game.  There are also some level up and item duplication exploits that are really easy to perform if you want to.  These I felt added value to the game though in case you felt it was too hard or just really wanted to easy-mode the game for the sake of feeling omnipotent.

Chances are, if you made it past the trailer and the preview pictures, you're going to like this game.  This game and genre isn't for everybody and you know it.  Personally, I was just looking for a low graphics game to have for play on my laptop... only to find myself putting in tens of hours on my desktop as well.
My first roguelike was Dungeons of Dredmor, which was fun, but in terms of gameplay options and experimentation, it just wasn't enough.  This game is more than enough.  There are 26 classes in this game, most of which have unique playstyles and minimal overlap.  Between those, there are many ways to build most of them with endless opportunities to experiment and die horribly in different ways.  The UI is confusing at first, but very functional once you get the hang of it.  There is a significant mod community for those who are into that.
The game comes with most of the classes and some races unlocked.  This is somewhat controversial but for me was highly beneficial for my enjoyment of the game.  Making the classes unlockable makes the game much less overwhelming to pick up and provides a significant sense of progression even when your character fails to win the game.  Once those classes are unlocked, higher difficulty options and mods continue to extend the game's life.
Healing potions and most consumables are replaced by cooldown-based "Inscriptions" and "Runes," which is perfect because it removes any sort of "saving for a rainy day" hesitation players tend to have in combat.
There are a couple of issues with this game.  Some rigs may encounter excessive memory leaks with the default graphics settings.  Graphics and sound are expected to be minimal but there are a few obnoxious sound effects and themes in the game and some volume imbalance.  As commonly seen in these games, early level progression with many classes at higher difficulties is extremely frustrating.  But these issues are minor.  Stop reading and get the damn game.

It demands a lot of thought, and rewards you with deep and engaging gameplay with important choices to make on multiple levels. As you progress through the story and unlock more races, classes, and skills, the number of possible play styles available multiplies. It takes a lot of time to even begin to master, but is compartmentalized in a way that allows you to play in short doses if your life is generally busy.
One warning: don't get this game if you're a compulsive completionist. There are close to 1400 achievements; it's simply impossible to do more than a relative handful of them unless you're one of those lucky YouTube entertainers who plays games for a living.

Excellent.  This is a really gorgeous, and fun game.  It's reminiscent of the old castlevanias, you have bosses you have to memorize the patterns of, and run-and-gun stages where you're fighting weaker enemies.  Everything was put together excellently, the progression is done via coins you collect, and you can pick the upgrades to what you think will support you best (and the different guns tailor themselves  to different playstyles or conditions).  The game is not long, it'll probably take about 10h to finish, but it doesn't feel short, and even after 10h there are likely achievements you haven't gotten (to be fair if you're really good you can probably beat it in about an hour--I needed a number of tries to beat many of the bosses).  Overall, the bosses were excellently done, though i did find a few (2-3) where there was too much randomness and winning felt more due to luck than actual improvement (not to say that i didn't improve, but even with the improvement i don't expect them to be a cakewalk).  The run n gun levels are a nice way to break the flow, but like others I do wish there were more (though I'm not sure what other rewards would really fit the progression system to make them).  The music was excellently composed, each one being tailored to fit the boss.
Overall, and excellent package, and well worth the asking price.  Unless you hate difficult games, then it should be a must by.

Cuphead is a fair challenge, not artificially difficult, and that makes it very satisfying to learn and beat.  There aren't too many that have challenge of this quality and artwork this elaborate, or boss fights that are this creative and still well-designed.  Additionally, because you just jump straight into boss fights at will there's basically no fluff or boring/annoying segments.
Don't listen to anyone who complains about RNG; I completed it on Expert and virtually all deaths were my fault.  This game is all about learning from your mistakes and being better next time.
There are a few attack patterns that are barely telegraphed, fast/instant and especially cheap the first time you see them.  They're a bit of a negative, but not time consuming to learn.  I mean, we're largely talking about ~2 minute fights.

TL:DR: I rate it a solid 8/10.
If you are a fan to the Football Manager series, then you know what you get with Football Manager 2018. The best football sim on the market and amazing stats from pretty much every league in the world. The game works in the same way as usual where you can take over as manager for a club of your choice and try to lead them to glory. Or to relegation and gloom if you are managing your rivals. The choice is yours.
New to the series is the Dynamics. A feature that will allow the manager to more closely man manage their players to maintain a coherent and happy squad. Player interaction is more refined and, while it have some balancing issues to iron out, is pretty well implemented. Other new features are a new scouting system and the medical senter. What those do speak for themselves, though they are supposedly more realistic than before. Scouting is not as possible to abuse as before and players will be more injury prone if you don't manage their training and rotate your squad.
This version also feature a new graphics engine, but the graphics themselves are not that much better, but for most long time fans the graphics are not the bread and butter of this game. The match engine have gotten a touch up, and seems to be much more stable than ever before.
Football Manager 2018 is a solid game in the series with no major problems, but some small things here and there. If you enjoy the series then the game is right up your alley. There are no major news in the game, but some good improvements all around. And of course all the latest transfers and staff movements are covered down to a ridicoulus level of detail.
As a long time player with countless hours wasted on the series I enjoy it and recommend it. Score: 8/10

TL;DR: Looks great, but the gameplay is incredibly annoying to the degree that I now consider it terrible.
The art style is really cool, and was the main thing that excited me about playing this game, but it's in service is nothing. The gameplay itself is a mish-mash of old-school and new-school elements, but they managed to pick the worst of both.
Initially the weapon crafting and exploration elements of the game seemed like they were going to be interesting additions, but in reality, the former was just extremely incremental min-maxing combined with grinding (because you have to purchase/build each part of a gun with earned money/farmed crafting elements), and the latter runs dry, because you run around the same few levels with different objectives for different missions.
Boss fights in particular are heavily based around multiplayer, as the damage required to beat a boss doesn't scale to the number of people playing, and you only have a limited amount of time to attack them before they run off to another location on the map. That would just be really annoying if the game didn't also have a timer for the completion of each level, which is completely arbitrary in a game like this, and elevates the boss fights from annoying to unfair. The only way in which the timer improves anything is when you just can't find something on a level, and you'd rather die than spend any more time looking for it. Other than that, it's purely a pain.
Oh, and if you thought it was dumb to bring back level time limits, you also have a limited number of lives for each mission, as well.
The active reload system is an interesting complication of basic platform-shooting, but it adds yet another control element that ultimately tends to weigh the game down more than make it engaging.
Also, the fact that enemies endlessly respawn is good for farming crafting items, but that's about it. The combination of enemies with shields or awkward placement (you can’t shoot diagonally) can really eat away at your time, not to mention the fact that healing items are really limited in the game.
Ultimately, I really wish that the game lived up to its art style. I’m glad that I got this in a Humble Bundle, or it would have been all the more frustrating. For $21 I would be piiiissssssed.

Three and a half hours was all I needed to make a verdict.
I played this game on the PS4 when it came out, there were some balance issues but that could have been ironed out. I used the Wraith because I liked being sneaky. I remember running away at low health and coiling up inside a bush, they ran right past me, Inches away from me and they ran past me. I was able to get away for just a little bit longer (They still got me though). THAT was one of the things that made this game a hunting game.
I tried using the same tactics from before in this Stage 2 version, run full sprint in one direction then just as the hunters arrive, sneak off in a different direction, giving me some extra time to munch before the hunters got wise to me and followed the corpses instead of tracks. But they didn't need to do that, they found me pretty quickly,
In the older version, I still had to outsmart the trapper, each one had a way to find me which justified the classes existence in the first place. But the planetary scan that each trapper now has, what use is Maggie's hound now? What's the point of using the hunter with the bat? Why use Griffin's sensors? Why tag wildlife with Abe's dart gun? You don't need to, the scan can be used so frequently, you don't need anything else. And because of the damn scan, there's no hiding, there's no point in trying to out think the hunters, there's no point in sneaking, there's no more hunting. It's just a cage match with a lot of running.
Monsters might as well sit at the start and die, maybe if TurtleRock sees a sharp decline in monster victories, they'll do something different. They may not do something right but it'll be different. I was on their side when they tired convincing 2K not to release the expansions too early(They still did, those asshats), which is one of the things that screwed the game. They've lost my sympathy, especially when they said the stealth aspects of the game were toxic and needed to be removed, that means the planetary scan wasn't just some stupid idea, it was deliberate. IGN may be kissing TurtleRock's♥♥♥♥♥for it but it's just a big middle finger shoved right in my face.
EDIT: By the by, I will still continue to play...BUT do not expect me to use the Planetary scan as a Trapper. When I'm the the Trapper, we're playing Evolve Classic. And as the monster, I'll do exactly as I said, screw around at the start and let em kill me(That is, unless the hunters decide to screw around with me instead :D )

I rate a computer game based on a custom-built formula to discern its real-world value. It's quite simple, but an effective way to record my enjoyment of said game. It is:
2 Beers = 1 Hour of Fun.  In my town, a beer costs £4, so you tend to take your time with it...
Anyway... 2 beers = 1 hour of fun. And 2 beers = £8. Therefore, a game that costs say, £20, is equal to 5 beers (or 2 1/2 hours of fun). Still with me?
I picked up HOI4 for £24 after using a voucher I got for free. £24 = 6 beers = 3 hours of fun.
I've played, at time of writing, 467 hours of HOI4 since purchase. 467 hours of fun.
467 hours = 934 beers (467*2) = £3,736 (934*4)
Nearly 4 grand worth of enjoyment for less than 25 quid, and no hangover or liver failure to show for it.

An incredibly good idea fallen to some lazy production.
What is this game? Basically, it is Dark Souls in 2D. Souds cool, right?
What does this game do well? It has quite and intriguing beginning, giving tons of quenstions and pretty much 0 answers. It has a painfully familliar combat system of dodges-blocks-parrying-slashing-smashing-fireballing etc (alas, no backstabbing, although in 2D that could've been stupidly overpowered). It has a nice (i.e. creepy. I.e. gothic. I.e. it is good) atmosphere, some neat (or at least unique) visual design. After all, it provides this feeling of madness when you end up losing all those souls you carefully gathered for level up due to some low-level monster or trap you didn't see.
But what does this game do wrong? Oh, boy, where to start.
First of all, I really disliked how much S&S tried to rip off DS. I know it is the same genre, but do we really have no other ideas for it? We have salt (souls), obtained from monsters, we have creeds (covenants minus PvP), we have DEX/STR/MAG builds, we have sanctuaries (bonfires), we have stamina management, we have little to no explanations about the world, we have kind of convoluted maps with shortcuts... Etc, etc, etc. Again, I perfectly know it is the genre, but sometimes it occured to me the game tries TOO hard to be JUST LIKE Dark Souls.
Why is it bad? DS is a great game! Yes, I know. But S&S is NOT Dark Souls. Heck, it is not even 3D! And to add some difficulty to the game (because 2D can't fully provide hardcore-experience and stuff, i guess?) the creators decided to add some elements which I see only as artificial difficulty.
1) Freaking platforming. Personally, I don't like platformers. I hate meticulously calculate the length of a jump. try to find which platform to jump onto next etc. I guess no 2D game can really do without at least some platforming elements. But why do it so stupid? In this game we have several Brands (platforming abilities, basically), we have several types of surfaces (solid, breaking, fading...). Frankly, this is mostly subjective, because I suck at platformers and I've lost a lot of souls by just falling. But there is some objectivity to it. And you know what I mean: second-to-last level. A hell of game design. I will get back to it later.
Also, knockback from the enemies. Countless times I've been knocked back into some pit. That is, in my mind, also a questionable design. Especially when it is a boss fight.
2) Unfair bosses. Bosses is one of the things that made Souls cool. They were difficult, they were unique and they were extremely satisfying to defeat (except for Bed of Chaos, a stupid thing). Each had a unique set of moves, but they were at least fair. Even if you screwed up once in a fight, you could win anyways. well, here... First of all, I disliked design of majority of the bosses. They are plain and provide 0 volume to the world, to the atmosphere. Secondly, most of them are simply unfair. If you screw up and they strike you, there is a nice chance you will get stunlocked and die: while you recover from a boss' attack, they wind up another, so when you get up you are getting hit once more. And again, and again... A lot of boss fights come down to what attacks boss will be using, since there are easily dodgeable attacks that are also punishable by you and there are attack with almost 0 preparation time and recovery animation. Stupid RNG is stupid. I will just throw in a couple of names: Tree of Men, Witch of the Lake, Dismembered Husk. Boss fights are also really dependant on your gear, which bring us to my next point...
3) Unpolished RP system. All of the bosses has some weakness to some types of dmg and some defense against others. They also tent to use 1-2 types of dmg. Therefore, oftentimes can equip sets with high defense and use an appropriate weapon to make your life easier. The funniest thing here it often doesn't really matter, how you build your character. Especially since there is some unbalance in class potencies: e.g. my DEX thief struggled with majority of bosses (since they have an incredible poison resistance), but some STR builds have almost 0 problems with any boss. Huge favor towards STR and high-level magic builds? Probably. Not sure about that, but I did have some troubles (git gut? Maybe, frankly).
4) Game design and last levels. At first I really enjoyed the game. It felt fresh, it was interesting. But towards the end of the game I noticed it got... more stupid? Often it felt like the developers got bored and tried to finish the game faster. As a result we have really half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥second-to-last level. Extremely stupid platforming section with little to no navigation help and some really questionable game-design solutions, like forcing players to lose part of their HP in platforming section right before the boss... And the story in the end felt really underwhelming and disappointing.
Also the music wasn't that great. I did not remember any of the tracks (if there were any), and I hear the sound of feet on the sand in my nightmares.
On top of that we have few bugs and glitches, like losing all your salt forever after being devoured by mimic (bug or feature? Bug, really, because it says some monster has taken the salt, but no one has it).
All in all, I liked the game. However, in the end I am really disappointed in it. What started off big and promising turned out to be meh. I am a huge Souls fan, and this is a 2D Dark Souls look-alike. The problem is, it is NOT DS. It feels really different: Dark Souls was challenging and rewarding, Salt and Sanctuary is frustrating.
I could recommend, however, getting this one. I did enjoy it, but the frustration sometimes was too overwhelming.
Hopefully someone at FromSoftware plays this, and finally realises that the Dark Souls games will never be this good, I've been waiting for a new Chromehounds for way too long.

Graphics: Using a heavily modified version of the Unreal 3 engine, Dishonored portrays the steampunk city of Dunwall with a style and flair that hooked me instantly. The models and textures are as high-resolution as a PC gamer could ask for, and the unique shaders and strong, hard shadows conveyed a strong, graphic novel-esque sense of visual atmosphere. The world's grim visual glory was even further enhanced by the spectacular art direction, taking queues from Half-Life 2 and blending that aesthetic with elements lifted from steampunk subculture to create a unique, rich, and enthralling visual experience. 9/10.
Gameplay: It's difficult to address the gameplay and story separately, as the two are inexorably intertwined, but I'll do my best. Missions fling you into vast, open environments littered with hidden nooks and crannies, open windows, and rooftops just begging to be explored and immersed in. As you explore, you come across runes, coins, and whale bone charms. Runes are used to unlock elements of a supernatural toolkit, handing you various new strategies with which to engage in combat or exploration, but never overwhelming you with too much at once. Coins are used to purchase upgrades to your more physical gadgets, such as new lenses for your clockwork mask, or an automatic reloading system for your hand crossbow. And lastly, whale bone charms are equipped to give you small perks of a sort, such as gaining token amounts of health from drinking water, or swinging your sword slightly more quickly. Charms are randomized as well, so you'll rarely find one in the same place between playthroughs. Taking the elements the game gives you and combining them is where the real gold is, and every solution you come up with is something you created, not you being funneled through a narrow pathway or being told to do things a very specific way, as is common with modern games. This isn't a game where you're disappointed by hitting yet another invisible wall - this is a game where you're thrilled by discovering that yes, that did, in fact, work. 10/10.
Story: And this is where the game truly gets into its stride, and this surprised me. Before I played the game, I was expecting a thrilling experience, not really a complex story, or good characterization. Dishonored had the courtesy to hand me everything. I'm not going to spoil anything, but the story is intense and emotional, despite the fact that it can only really be advanced between missions. But it's not the pre-set story that's the best element here, no... it's how the player's actions impact the curve of events. The game gives you tools of death; it gives you a pistol and crossbow, it gives you mines that fling razor-sharp shrapnel in a metallic tornado, it gives you a power that summons a swarm of ravenous plague rats, but it also gives you a warning: if you take too many lives, the story, characters, world, and even you will change for the worse. Many disregard the warning, much like I did... and were left distraught when, at the very end, the game solemnly held up a mirror. There are games with intense stories and endings that make you tear up, but there is NOTHING as harsh as this. Games like Mass Effect or Spec Ops: The Line, as much as you can impact events in the former, are sending you along a predetermined path. The ending isn't a product of your actions - it's simply affected by them. When Dishonored came to a conclusion, I knew that all the horrible things that had happened were MY fault, not because I'd been forced to take lives, but because I'd CHOSEN to. 10/10.

Conclusion: Dishonored was everything I'd hoped for and so much more. This game is a work of art, and you owe it to yourself to play it any way you can. It doesn't matter what the magazines say, this is my game of the year without a moment's thought.

I am a fan of Star Wars and I have been since I was very young. This game came out when I was just a child and I never actually played this game back then, but I did enjoy countless hours of repeating the demo mission from the old free Mysteries of the Sith demo (MotS is the standalone expac for this game) over and over again, as well as the original Dark Forces. I then began playing Jedi Outcast a few years later, then Jedi Academy. Needless to say, I'm a HUGE fan of the Jedi Knight series as a whole.
This game has to be one of the most unique shooters out there for the sole reason of force powers and a lightsaber. For the time, this game had beautiful graphics, a remarkable art style that very strongly captured the Star Wars atmosphere, and combine that with the lightsaber/force powers, you take what would be an average 90s shooter and turn it into one of my favorite games of all time.
When I purchased this game two Christmas sales ago (with the Star Wars pack), I excitedly hopped onto Steam and installed this game first, and since then I've probably played through it over 50 times. It's not as if there's a lot of choice, as there isn't. Basically, you choose your force powers (and how proficient you are with them) as well as whether or not you kill innocents/droids. No, is is neither the choice nor secrets that keep me coming back to this game. It's purely because this is a GREAT game, even by today's standards.
Graphically, this game is definitely straight from the 90s with FMV cutscenes, blocky polygons, and low-res textures, which leads many people to opt into downloading graphical overhaul mods but I have not once wanted to change the graphics. Sure, they're an eyesore compared to today's games but they still have a nostalgic charm. Plus, as an aspiring developer myself, I am in awe at how they pulled off some of the effects by tapping into their creativity-- something modern devs need to take a look at. My favorite effect is the lightsaber, which uses animated sprites in just the right way to achieve the proper effect.
Gameplay-wise, this game runs pretty similar to modern shooters. The number keys select your weapons, you have jump, crouch, run, and activate buttons, you fire using your mouse. The only major difference between this and modern shooters is that there isn't an ironsights feature, nor do you have a separate key for grenades/explosives.
If you can get past some of the compatibility issues (I can't run in fullscreen on this PC which uses Windows 7), this game is worth every penny if you like Star Wars, shooters, and/or classic 90s games. In fact, the whole Dark Forces/Jedi Knight series is worth a purchase, as they're all great games with great stories and addicting gameplay/level design. I'd say this is my personal favorite in the whole series followed closely by Jedi Academy.

Fracture the Flag version 1.0.0 Early Access is a real time strategy game ... or at least it wants to be one some day. The game mechanics are very similar to "The Settlers".
Although the basics of the genre are in the game there is currently almost no balancing or tactics involved. Also, as far as I noticed, there is currently no unique selling point in the game. Everything you do you have done already in other games - only better.
If you want to play the game as a single player game you will be forced to collect a given number of resources and compare your achievement time with others. That's it. There are no tutorials, no missions and no A.I. Basically, you don't want to play the game alone.
As a multiplayer game things look a little different. There are two maps included (2 players and 4 players). In the current state of the game there is not much to do. You collect resources, you build an army, you attack - everything on a very basic level. It might be fun to play the game with a person you know personally. Sadly, you don't have the option to select your opponent. As an anonymous multiplayer game there is currently not enough content,
You can very easily rush your opponent. Buildings can be destroyed far too quickly. I managed to destroy the enemy baracks with only two swordmen while my opponent failed to kill them with 6 swordmen on his own in time. Combat is a chaos. If two armies attack each other they share a 1x1m spot. There are no spacial tactics involved and you can't even see who is winning until all soldiers of one side are dead.
The game may have potential (at least it's stable) in the future but there is a lot of work to be done. Currently, it's more of a prove of concept than a game.
Unfortunately, I cannot give a neutral review in Steam. At its current state I can't recommend the game even as an early access game. It needs at least another year of development before players will enjoy the experience on a regular basis.
My improvment suggestions:
- Please support the mouse wheel to zoom in and out
- Give buildings more hitpoints or don't allow basic ground units to damage them
- Implement a fighting system where not everyone fights at the same spot
- If you can afford a building don't use a red text color to show the needed resources
Finally: I don't think that it's a bad game but it's far too soon to be playable.

First of all, something about myself.
I have started playing the series ever since it was Championship Manager 2004, not skipping out on any year.
I am completely disappointed in this year's edition of SEGA's Football Manager 2018. To me, as a customer, it feels they are not really putting in the work, quite possibly because there's no real competition to the product.
Why is that?
- The match engine has the same bugs as the years before it. Balls hitting in player's backs, way too many crossbars, never one that goes in off the post. The same players chasing down the ball to the touchline stopping the ball and having the opponent take the ball, etc. The match engine is simply all the same maybe with a animation or two added, but with the same bugs encountered in previous editions. No lessons learned there from SEGA.
- Network games come with quite the challenges this year. I've literally had to try over and over again with my friend for over an hour in order for him to be able to join my server. To this day I do not know the cause of that. Then there's the game basically splitting into two separate instances. I've had a friend of mine spectate my match, only to see that I was playing a totally different match than what he was playing.
- I want to emphasize again the amount of bugs and bad touches the match engine gives. It would otherwise be an okay game, but I really feel like the match engine ruins a lot of the experience with stupid plays and unrealistic sequences.
I would honestly recommend on skipping out this year or simply waiting until the January update and getting it for 10$ or something.

I give this game a 4/5.
Pros:
- Wide variety of classes that play dramatically differently.
- Classes are fairly well-balanced, although some are considerably more complex and require more careful play than others.
- Lots of loot, and items can have a wide variety of buffs or even debuffs.
- Mod support.
- The game is long.
- Decent default tileset, and many more available in the workshop.
- Transparent numbers for the most part, so careful planning is possible.
Cons:
- Death is frequent and often feels random.  Because of the wide variety of abilities, status effects, and damage types, it is very difficult to build a character that can effectively defend against being one-shotted.  It's not fun to see a boss and instantly die.  There are also far too many ways to be stunlocked.
- There's no way to grind experience or equipment.  There is a fixed amount in the world and you get what you get.  Resistances are key and largely only come from equipment.  Gold is very limited, so despite the plethora of shops it is very rare to be able to afford anything useful.
- Some of the class mechanics are very complex and not well explained.  Or explained at all.  I'm looking at you, chronomancer.
- Some classes are very equipment-dependent, which means if you don't get the right artifact drops you cannot play effectively.
- The game is easy for the first couple hours and then it suddenly spikes towards the end of the second tier of dungeons.  Every game starts with the same run through the same 6-10 dungeons before the "real" game starts.

metal slug meets scott pilgrim, with a bit more depth.
while mercenary kings is a fun platformer, with beautifully drawn characters and backgrounds, it is a fairly different sort of game compared to the metal slug games. what really sets it apart is the litany of options when it comes to weapons, as here, you could actually craft your knives and even guns, part by part. each part carries with it a different attribute, allowing you to build custom weapons to suit your playstyle into the missions.
it does have a lot of charm and novelty to it all, but in the end, the game stretches out a bit too long, and with a bit too much grind especially when it comes to getting materials for crafting. that in itself could be a deal breaker for some players, depending on what they were looking for i suppose.
if you expect the run-and-gun, side-scroller style of metal slug, you just might end up a bit disappointed with this. but if you loved metal slug, but had always wanted a bit more depth when it comes to customization, then this might be right up your alley.
while i dont particularly enjoy the grind, i did quite like the experience of it overall. a bit on the fence maybe, but i suppose i'll lean towards thumbs up for this.

Post-apocolyptica... Has been done many a time and therefore is quite hard to get just right in a game. However, I feel 'id Soft' got it right, which isn't a surprise with Bethesda publishing (for those of you unaware, Fallout series was created by Bethesda; another post-apocalyptic game). RAGE is a game I think you play and complete once or twice and re-visit a few months later and not feel disappointed. The gameplay has a distinct 'Borderlands' feel to it, in that at times it can feel like an arcade game, yet the story has enough meat to it to forgive this. It also has a touch of 'Mad Max' blended into it with the cars that you drive around in and the various packs of human tribes. Its not something you have to get tied into like 'Fallout' or 'The Forest' where you need to spend vast amounts of time in game.
The opening video to RAGE is intense and really throws you into the atmosphere of "The world is about to die". It was brilliantly executed, how it was brief but impacting enough to last in your mind. Especially focusing on the role your character will be playing out in this epic journey. As you begin the game, you get a very good taste of the graphics that are to be expected throughout the game as well. The other characters in the game feel real, their speech and movement is indicative of their background.
One problem that shows during the game is finding where to go. When travelling outside a town, you can view minimap in the corner. In town you do not get this luxury. More than once, I was caught out trying to find a location, only to realise it was not in town. Also the end of the game seemed a little rushed. Which is a shame because the start really builds such a dramatic climax, towards the end it seems to "loose its wind".
During the game there are two sets of controls to learn. Human and Vehicle; in either function, the controls are relatively simple and easy to learn. However, when controlling the vehicle, I noticed steering can get clunky at speed, due to using a keyboard (advise a controller). Gameplay is great, its fluent and fast paced. The enemies are varied and will often catch you out with their dodging. But I warn you; pay attention to the advise given on what ammo to use per enemy unit. Otherwise you will end up feeling like the game is severly unbalanced. Although a fast paced shooter you still have to be tactical in your thinking and using cover wisely.
Gameplay/Interactive: 7/10
Graphics/Asthetics: 8/10
Controls/Ergonomics: 9/10
Atmosphere/Enticement: 7/10
Price/Value: 7/10

For a veery long time I hadnt played any game that made as much fun as this one. When I started playing video games about twenty years ago, each game seemed to be exciting. I was eager to explore, discover new locations, find secrets, solve the puzzles and so on... Time passed, the amount of time I spent playing video games grew and the excitement of playing games got lost somewhere. Even such great games as "Witcher 3" couldnt awake the passion I felt years ago.
So I never expected a 2d-platformer-Rpg-game to be able to excite me.
But it did!

Some older players might still remember the first Prince of Persia. It was such a simple game, but it had so much in it (secret potions, secret rooms, puzzles). "Salt and Sanctuary" is similar to that. The maps arent big, but you have the feeling, that there is so much stuff hidden somewhere (new items, new paths, secret rooms).
The gameplay manages to stay interesting until the end of the game. The old combination of monster-slaying and platforming somehow becomes exciting and interesting....
Generally I hate boss-fights. But I enjoyed the challenge of fighting the bosses in "Salt and Sanctuary". Graphics: Using a heavily modified version of the Unreal 3 engine, Dishonored portrays the steampunk city of Dunwall with a style and flair that hooked me instantly. The models and textures are as high-resolution as a PC gamer could ask for, and the unique shaders and strong, hard shadows conveyed a strong, graphic novel-esque sense of visual atmosphere. The world's grim visual glory was even further enhanced by the spectacular art direction, taking queues from Half-Life 2 and blending that aesthetic with elements lifted from steampunk subculture to create a unique, rich, and enthralling visual experience. 9/10.
Gameplay: It's difficult to address the gameplay and story separately, as the two are inexorably intertwined, but I'll do my best. Missions fling you into vast, open environments littered with hidden nooks and crannies, open windows, and rooftops just begging to be explored and immersed in. As you explore, you come across runes, coins, and whale bone charms. Runes are used to unlock elements of a supernatural toolkit, handing you various new strategies with which to engage in combat or exploration, but never overwhelming you with too much at once. Coins are used to purchase upgrades to your more physical gadgets, such as new lenses for your clockwork mask, or an automatic reloading system for your hand crossbow. And lastly, whale bone charms are equipped to give you small perks of a sort, such as gaining token amounts of health from drinking water, or swinging your sword slightly more quickly. Charms are randomized as well, so you'll rarely find one in the same place between playthroughs. Taking the elements the game gives you and combining them is where the real gold is, and every solution you come up with is something you created, not you being funneled through a narrow pathway or being told to do things a very specific way, as is common with modern games. This isn't a game where you're disappointed by hitting yet another invisible wall - this is a game where you're thrilled by discovering that yes, that did, in fact, work. 10/10.
Story: And this is where the game truly gets into its stride, and this surprised me. Before I played the game, I was expecting a thrilling experience, not really a complex story, or good characterization. Dishonored had the courtesy to hand me everything. I'm not going to spoil anything, but the story is intense and emotional, despite the fact that it can only really be advanced between missions. But it's not the pre-set story that's the best element here, no... it's how the player's actions impact the curve of events. The game gives you tools of death; it gives you a pistol and crossbow, it gives you mines that fling razor-sharp shrapnel in a metallic tornado, it gives you a power that summons a swarm of ravenous plague rats, but it also gives you a warning: if you take too many lives, the story, characters, world, and even you will change for the worse. Many disregard the warning, much like I did... and were left distraught when, at the very end, the game solemnly held up a mirror. There are games with intense stories and endings that make you tear up, but there is NOTHING as harsh as this. Games like Mass Effect or Spec Ops: The Line, as much as you can impact events in the former, are sending you along a predetermined path. The ending isn't a product of your actions - it's simply affected by them. When Dishonored came to a conclusion, I knew that all the horrible things that had happened were MY fault, not because I'd been forced to take lives, but because I'd CHOSEN to. 10/10.

Conclusion: Dishonored was everything I'd hoped for and so much more. This game is a work of art, and you owe it to yourself to play it any way you can. It doesn't matter what the magazines say, this is my game of the year without a moment's thought.

A very good introduction to classical roguelikes. TOME streamlines some things while keeping true to the formula of old school games like Nethack, ADOM, and Brogue. There's a free version that's basically the same as the paid version - you can download it from the TOME website if you're not sure you want to buy this yet.
TOME has automatic identification. You also get an item called a transmogrification chest, which basically cashes out your loot while you're still in the dungeon - reducing the risk of overencumbrance or loot saturation. TOME also has a modern engine and tileset, although the tileset is rather ugly. Most importantly for new players, there are five difficulty settings and three permadeath settings. The permadeath settings are especially useful, because they provide the option to 1) explore with unlimited lives, 2) play the game as intended, but with limited lives, and 3) play with permadeath like a true roguelike.
While it has convenience features, TOME is still an old school roguelike. Beating it without spoilers is a large undertaking, although not as difficult as Nethack. The different dungeons/areas are all different types of difficulty and as a level one character you might wander into a powerful monster's lair and get immediately annihilated. This is the kind of game where you'll need a wiki open most of the time if you're not a masochist.
TOME is also very feature-complete. Not only is there a standard story/open-world mode, but there is also an arena and endless dungeon. The Steam Workshop opens up modding opportunities. There is a huge amount of lore (my estimate so far is at least the length of a full book). There are lots of classes, many of which only become avaiable to you once you've reached a certain point in the game, which ensures there's always something fresh. It has over a thousand achievements, which is the highest out of any game on Steam (when it first came out Steam couldn't even handle it, the devs had to work with Valve for a few weeks to get them working properly).
One thing that really spices up the game for me is the ability to play as anti-magic. There's a faction in the world of TOME that is violently opposed to arcane magic. You can join them as long as you don't use any arcane magical items or cast spells. It's not as much of a challenge as it seems because there are non-arcane "natural" enchantments too, so anti-magic is a valid choice for story, roleplaying, or gameplay variation. It makes melee classes quite a bit more interesting and immersive.
I highly recommend Tales of Maj'Eyal for people who are interested in getting into classic roguelikes, or old roguelike fans who want to play something newer.

Tales of Maj'Eyal (ToME) is a turn based RPG with many roguelike features. Overall, the story isn't relevant (although there is a lot of lore to read). It rather concentrates on fighting, looting, and leveling.
Instead of writing an in-depth review here are the apects that I like the most about it:
ToME has a whole lot of classes to offer. Sure, there are the archetypes like Warrior or Archer. However, you will also find many crazy and interesting classes. Examples for this are the Paradox Mage who controls time, the Oozemancer who draws his powers from oozes and slime, and the Wyrmic who uses the powers of the dragons.
Most skills (called "Talents") in the game have cooldowns. IMO this is great because it makes concentrating on one or a couple of talents an irrelevant strategy. Just the amount of talents in the game is staggering. In addition, many talents of a class allow for synergies. Also, you have to be well prepared for a number of different situations.
The cooldowns make combat so much more interesting. It is always a good idea to carefully consider using which talent in which situation. Just nuked a standard enemy with your most powerful spell? Well, you won't have it available for the next 20 turns.
Some enemies can have the talents of one (or even multiple!) of the classes available to the player. This will put you repeatedly in extremely dangerous but also very interesting situations.
The game offers tons of randomly generated loot. The items can vary in their stats heavily and may change your playstyle a lot. There are also items with predefined properties (called artifacts).
Hovering over an item shows a very detailed description (same with talents).
I highly recommend ToME.
Btw, you can even legally get the game for free. Buying it on Steam will unlock a number of donator bonuses which are honestly dispensable. Did I regret my purchase, though? Not at all! The game is well worth the asking price and I am happy that I could support the dev a bit.

I won the war as Britain in the game and I do not feel that the game was very fulfilling. The best part of the game for me was 30 something hours in and I droppped 15 nukes on Japan for them to surrender which they did not. The game feels like an extreme resource and technology race. The game is fun at first but I prefer Stellaris to this game because the stories in that game feel more compelling. If I were to enjoy this game more I would like more quests with more diversified wording for the news headlines other than "the cowardly enemy capitulated because they were cowardly". I want more of a narrative of how that invasion was and occupation of the capital in the real war or how it could have been. LIke occupations and invasions to Japan were feared to be very bitter fights to the last man woman and child rather than face the "American Devils". Which makes me think that propoganda is an untapped opportunity that this game could use. There are records of civilians killing themselves rather than surrendering.
The game has a lot of potential but for now is a very basic template and I hope to revisit it again after so major improvements (that should be free). Furthermore there does not seem to be any worthwhile war goals or challenges for the game. For instance, I would like there to be a challenge for lose less than X amount of your manpower in the war. After winning the war there is not a compelling reason to continue (technology stops, and the wars are over). There does not seem to be an endgame or goal to the game. There needs to be some way to research faster from buildings and resources rather than technology to research technology faster. I am trying to avoid saying that the game feels pointless. Also, for volunteer conscription the percentage should go up as the war progresses for patriotism for events in the war or, as I mentioned before, from propoganda. Like the attack on Pear Harbor, the Miracle at Dunkirk, successful invasions, etc things that surged volunteers and patriotism in the real war. It would feel more immersive if there was a news alert that said that due to this event in the war there is an influx in volunteers and faith in the war effort. Something I found strange is that there is no food shortages or needs for food. If you have an army of over 1 million you need a way to feed them other than building guns and factories. "Bullets or bread?"
To sum it up, put some challenges or goals to the game for each nation and more narrative. The achievements in the game are not compelling enough. At this point the game feels like a glorified resource manager and not a very good WWII simulation. Finnaly, General Macarthur was an idiot, put an impressive and historically enigmatic General like Patton on the front like he deserves. Another interesting change would be if yoiu choose not to punish Patton for insubordination and having him lead the Ghost Army in England instead having him lead the D-Day invasion and some possible consequences written for that decision. Even the Nazis were surprised that we punished our best general like that! Also the story of the man that never existed with the false invasion plans that the Nazis recovered saying we were going to invade in different place besides Normandy like Italy and another coast. Or how Rommel said that if the Americans were successful after D-Day that the war was lost. Or the decoding of the enigma machine by Allan Turing in Project Ultimate! So many stories about the WWII campaign that were untapped and unmentioned in this game that should have been. Even the air Battle of Britain was missing from this game. Especially Churchills decision to sacrifice Coventry rather than let the Germans know we had decrypted their code!!!!!!!!! So many consequences could have been written for that decision! The Germans never even tried to bomb me. :(

Currently this game is pretty bare bones but the mechanics are very unique for an RTS game and it definitely has a lot of potential. There's a surprisngly large but unfinished skill tree/unlock tree that you can use one of the 4 resources to unlock. There is Stone, Wood, Minerals, and Build Points. All resource harvesting is self explanitory except build points. Build points are produced via flags that can be places to also expand your build radius. The unlock tree is built in a way that each unlock will increase the price of the next, meaning you must be sparing and choose your unlocks strategically. It is very difficult and time consuming to unlock all of them, currently. There is plan for naval and air units as show in the unlock tree but is not yet implemented. The base building is similar to that of Age of Empires but differently paced and currently lacks defensive structures beyond walls. The current units consist of, workers, (upgradable) swordsman, catapults, and ballistas. There are currently 2 maps, a 1v1 and a 2v2.
----------
- Really nice developer who is very active with the community and development
- Runs well, which is expected with Low Poly
- Real time destruction mechanics
- Unique and intuitive mechanics
- Graphically pleasing
- It's $3
----------
- Quite buggy
- UI sometimes doesn't fit on the screen depending on where the building is location on the screen when selected
-Upgrade tree information for many items does not work or has wrong information
- No resolution select or support for higher than 1080p resolution*
- No singleplayer campaign, skrimish, or bots*
- No private/hostable games yet*
- Very low player count
- Only 2 maps
----------
The game is definitely fun and unique.  I recommend picking it up if you want a new take on RTS games, to support development, engage in alpha testing (report bugs, suggestions, etc.), or have $3 laying around. I don't recommend it if you want a very polished and functional game and don't want to wait for that to change.

Rift is pretty great. I say this as a longtime fan of the genre and a veteran of many similar MMOs. While it still doesn't quite reach the pinnacle of combat design polish of a game like World of Warcraft, it gets damn close, and I'd easily call worthy of the silver to WoW's gold. The class or "soul" mechanics that are used in developing your character's abilities make for a wider variety of potential characters than any mainstream MMO I can think of, while retaining a reasonable level of balance (no MMO is ever completely balanced, sadly).
More importantly than those two things in playing it today though is the question of whether going F2P has changed the game for the worse. I've been playing since shortly after release, and I feel pretty confident saying that the game has constantly improved since that time, and shows no sign of slowing, even after the change to F2P. The "restrictions" (as all F2P games tend to have) on what you can access without paying any money are pretty reasonable. You can access all zones and raise your character to cap (60, as of this writing) and then continue on and participate in endgame content as you please. You won't have access to the Storm Legion souls (new souls, one for each class, originally added in the expansion, now available by themselves, as the remainder of the expansion content is free), but that's about it (as far as I understand it, I've continued to be a paying customer since the conversion).

Fantastic game! Don't care about the graphics. It is outdated yes, but the gameplay makes you forget all about it as it is just amazing to be an officer for Rainbow Six.
This is the last best game in the series (Still waiting for the cod version of Rainbow Six, aka Siege), and is a must if you love S.W.A.T. 4 or any of the Rainbow Six games before Siege. If you love tactical shooters in general, this is a must buy.
Rainbow Six 3 has a really systematic and a fantastic planing phase, where you decide all the orders of what Teams Red, Green and Yellow shall do (if you have more than one team). You get to decide movement, actions, aggressiveness and order other teams/your team to wait until you give the command to move or the other team is ready. The enemy A.I. is not great, they react poorly to sounds and friendly corpses. If you run, they'll hear you through floors, if you shoot, they'll only hear you if your standing next to them. If they witness someone die, they don't care, why should they?
Shooting feels great and realistic. It is really hard to hit something if you're not aimed down your sight. If you spray, you'll miss your target and probably die. Bullets are deadly, meaning you'll die in just a few bullets even with the heavy gear. You're not a bullet sponge, be careful around corners.
Leaning, leaning around corners is REALLY important here, and they've done a fantastic job with that. There is the standard q and e to lean, but also ctrl. With controll, you can lean how ever you want, it makes taking cover a much easier job than in other shooters.
RS3 has the standard gamemodes, Terrorist Hunt (killing terrorists), Hostage Rescue, Bomb defusal and so on. However, in RS3, hostages can and will be shot by Ts, if not careful. If they're alerted, they'll shot them without hesitation. Plan your moves, don't run and gun, and be f#cking careful.
I love the Rainbow Six series, and fully recommend getting all of them. They are fantastic games, and hopefully Siege will be as well.

It took me a bit to decide whether I should recommend or not recommend this game, but I eventually settled on "not recommended", even though my opinion is more in the middle.
On the one hand, RAGE is a fantastic tech demo of the idTech 5 engine, a huge update from idTech 4, which was used in Doom 3 and Quake 4. The engine uses "megatextures", which means that every single texture is unique to that specific area. From a distance, the graphics look astonishing, but up close they're very blurry.
Characters have exaggerated and unnecessary animations during their dialogue, which sounds annoying, but it gives the game a feel of something akin to a Disney/Pixar film, which I quite liked.
As per every id Software title, you get a fixed arsenal, starting out with a pistol, then acquiring a shotgun, a machine gun, an assault rifle, and all kinds of weapons and new ammo types. The shotgun, for instance, can fire out arcing explosive shots and plasma, and the game actively encourages you to use these new ammunition types by giving subtle hints in the environment. Going back to the shotgun, there are instances where you need to use its plasma ammo to take out small units that power force fields in order to progress.
While the gunplay feels great to me, the combat sequences aren't so fun. The combat isn't fun, it's boring. You only get to fight two enemy types -- the type that runs at you with a melee weapon, yelling they're "gonna carve you a new one" Borderlands-style, and the type that stays behind cover and shoots. Remember that this is from the company who was almost always a step or two ahead of the game industry in the 90s.
My biggest complaint with RAGE is the health. This is an id Software game, is it not? So then why are you able to go hide behind a rock while the big hole where your face used to be patches itself up? It's ridiculous, no id game would have regenerating health. It removes any and all challenge RAGE has, and Nightmare and Ultra-Nightmare become a cakewalk if you hide in just the right spot.
Overall, if you're a person looking for a fun experience, this might be up your alley. I wouldn't know, as I can't read minds. I haven't been able to convince myself to finish RAGE, it's just so boring to me.
Also, if you want to check out RAGE, get it during a sale. I've heard it's a short game.

It's difficult to review this because the more I say, the more is spoiled.
Everything in this game, from the visuals to the mechanics, are there to aid the story, which is excellent.

OneShot is a good game. And Niko is the best boy.
It has a great atmosphere and tone. The music and soundscape captures it perfectly. It is in turns funny, whimsical, threatening, hopeless, and joyful; it's a credit to the game how quickly it brings you to identify with, and care about, your charge.
The story is a relatively simple affair, but it delivers on its key themes and messages, and the odd bits of meta-gameplay make it an intriguing one to be a part of (quite literally).
Gameplay is fairly standard fare; explore environments and collect things you can combine in your inventory to solve simple puzzles. They are rarely taxing, and you won't have to search hard for the right pieces of clues. Everything you find is necessary. I appreciate that much of the fat that can plague these puzzle adventures has been trimmed, as I feel elevating the potential for frustration would destroy the mood carefully built by the game world, and be a detriment to the players relationship with the protagonist. I did find a few places a little frustrating, mostly because of the controls (especially menuing) and the way the levels work, but nothing that stuck around for long.
If you can, I would recommend trying to set aside four or so hours so that you might finish the game in one sitting. I had to do it in two pieces, and it still worked very well. I just think maintaining the atmosphere would have been better.
Technically, this game isn't going to be winning any awards. The 90's engine is a design choice, but even with a Titan X and i7-5820k, the game mostly ran at about 40fps. It was a bit jerky, but it is bearable due to the style of game.
I would also highly recommend re-sizing your monitor to 720p whilst playing, especially on a >1080p screen. This is easily done in either Nvidia Control Panel, or just right-click on desktop>Display Settings. It changes back and forth instantly, but I wish the devs had found their own way to scale the game properly on screens bigger than a small laptop. I would consider that their job, not mine. Still, it is a most minor grievance.
That aside, Niko is a completely adorable, sympathetic and likeable character. The pixel animation so full of heart and character. The world is full of NPC's whose small roles are so well written you'll wish you could just keep talking and hanging out with them. I'd recommend you give it shot... maybe... OneShot (boomboom!).

Fantastic top-down RPG.  A little old school style, a lot of charm and a healthy dose of humor among countless little secrets, bits of lore, and subtle surprises.  Gameplay is quite deep, with each class enjoying different styles and tactics, as well as the flexibility for various builds and playstyles within a given class.  The classes themselves are unique, and all in all ToME gives a unique RPG experience that's reminiscent of rogue-likes but with a breadth and depth all its own and quite unlike anything else I've come across in the genre.

Short version: This is a wonderful roguelike and well worth the price.
Longer version:  Tales of Maj'Eyal is a nicely balanced turn based roguelike set in a well written world filled with lore.  The graphics are nice and simple, with many similar roguelikes using ASCII instead.  There is a nice selection of classes and races with a large amount of unlockable classes that all have interesting differences to set them apart.  For 2 examples, you could be a defensive tank with the bulwark class, or an alchemist, lobbing magic infused gems as explosives while your golem protects you.
Another nice detail is the differentiation between arcane, nature and psionic abilities, including the presence of items "Infused by arcane disrupting forces", which can mess with any arcane abilities.  And what roguelike would be complete without randomly generated gear, with a nice amount of pre-generated artifacts(with written lore/descriptions) to add to the mix.
Lastly, this game also has a good selection of difficulty level, with normal, easier and nightmare unlocked by default, along with the for exploration mode, adventurer mode or roguelike mode.  As the names might suggest, the roguelike mode is permadeath, with a rare few exceptions, while adventurer mode gives you a couple lives, along with a few more as you reach the higher levels, though enemies do fully reheal if you respawn.
If you're a fan of roguelikes or turn based rpgs, then this is a game well worth looking into.

An incredible game, better than most games which make usage of small figures without a constant means of animations...

There is also so much Lore hidden around the game. Either from completing quests, slaying unique entities, finding documents, or reading wall and statue inscriptions one can discover all a manner of things about the world, its inhabitants, cultures, races, monsters, relics, and more!
Finally, all the unique particle effects for the spells, and all the new unique effects on the HUD, add a bit of insight to a world you would otherwise rely solely on text and figurines to understand what is going on. Things turn darker when you are influenced by an effect that decreases sight range, things blur if your stunned, dazed, and such, the screen tinges a different color based on whether you are bleeding, frozen solid, standing in fire, poison muck, or acid... this is highly useful since you'll need to resolve effects, some of which you might not realize your under the effect of without of this.
Also, the game is so VERY detailed that they have different difficulties for both realism and complexity. Want unlimited lives? Explorer style is best for you. Want a limited set of chances based upon your successes and failures? Try the standard experience. Care to put your life in the hands of fate? Choose Roguelike, for a single life, with the potential for another if you discover things like becoming a Lich or Reincarnating in that specific life!
