almost 800 hours of playtime and several wins and i still play this game and love every minute.
Have you ever play Angband? Nethack? Roguelikes? Old cRPGs?
Tales of Maj'Eyal could something you are looking for.
ToME offers a wonderfully diverse cast of races/classes and various difficulties to play on, providing high replayability.
Each race/class provides a unique assortment of skills and abilities talents that are all chosen as you progress and level-up through out the game, allowing you to effectively be in control of the strength and development of your character.
The graphics are very remenant of old-school rpg gaming with some new polish added in.
I find the style of graphics and presentation to be one of the endearing and strong aspects of ToME.
the simple gaming feel with a complex system in root, where your success is uniquely determined by your choices, actions, and strategies.
As a roguelike at its heart, death in game is no stranger.  Sometimes it comes a bit quickly and unexpectedly.
Other times you can see your mistakes play out and see where things could have gone better.
Death is a natural course of the gameplay, but each subsequent playthrough provides an opportunity to hone your tactics or knowledge to help your next character out.
You are rewarded for learning from mistakes and improving your strategies, I feel this is one of the defining strengths for ToME.
You can however play with extra lives if perma-death is a bit daunting =)
The asking price of $6.99 is extremely generous in my book, as i have spent ten times more money for AAA games and have often played them a fraction of the time that i have spent on ToME.
I very highly recommend Tale's of Maj'Eyal anyone who is a fan of older style rpgs, tactical combat, or rewarding skill systems.

The other point is though.. they will update this game for years. Two years from now this game will be amazing and you will comeback after each update to see how it effects the game in different ways and what new thing can be done. SO... in finally note I totally recommend this game. Its one of my personal favorites. And if you are looking for a hardcore WW2 strategy game, this is it.

Dark forces 2 was the first star wars game I've played. I rememeber going to the library, burrowing and playing through it. I couldn't get past the first level back then though... After over a decade and having played the rest of the jedi knight series (Played a bit of dark forces 1 and completed the rest), I thought it would be nice to return to this game. In Dark forces 2, you play as Kyle Katarn, an ex-imperial stormtrooper who is trying to get some payback on the people responsible for killing his father.
- Wide range of weapons = including pistol, blasters, smg, grenades, bowcaster, rocket launcher, lightsaber etc.
- Light Sabre battles
- Good environment variety = You will go to canyons, farmsteads, imperial bases, Nar Shadaa and many other places across your adventure.
- 21 single player missions = composed of around 7 boss battles and 14 standaard levels.
- Lots of hidden secrets in each level
- Different endings based on force allignment
- Decent number of force powers
- Classic star wars sound effects
- Decent, although cheesy, story = Mainly due to the not so great acting by the characters.
- Has multiplayer mode
- Wide range of foes = Including stormies, officers, rodians, gamoreans, bugs, walkers.
- Constant crashes when launching game for windows 8 and up (can be fixed though).
- Constant crashes when choosing to restart level.
- Ocassional crashes when saving/loading.
- Menu screen and cutscenes does not have wide screen support (can be fixed apparently).
- May need walkthrough as you will get lost trying to find where to go.
- Some annoying/unfair boss fights.
- Missing background music = You can mod it back in, but doesn't loop.
- Poor map = you can't use it to navigate where you are or where you need to go.
- You can only upgarde force powers at the end of the level = becomes a major problem in boss fights when certain powers can make your life alot easier.
- No quick saves
Surprisingly, I enjoyed my playthrough of dark forces 2 despite the constant crashes and other obstacles I had to jump over. However, I strongly recommend you purchase the GOG version over this as it has better support for newer systems, runs better, DRM free and fixed a ton of glitches.
Annoying to get it to actually work (at least for me) but it's still a really fun, difficult game. (although the cutscenes and menus play in windowed mode :I)

This is my first review that I am aware of. If this is your first time playing a HOI game, then you should be happy with it. It's interesting and you will invest a lot of hours into it.
However, if you have any of the previous HOI's, this game is a joke. Once again, publishers feel they need to dumb down games in order to make more money. This HOI is incredibly simplistic and takes away a lot of the fabulous complexity in previous versions that made the game stand out. Research is simple and visually looks stupid with the fat buttons to make sure you follow the obvious linear trees. By 1944 in my first game, I had all national focuses, and 90% of technologies filled. The AI is dumb and very direct. They removed the complex diplomatic/intelligence structure. Warfare is simplistic with the front system, although some of it was interesting. I quickly ran out of generals, only to find out as I "bought" new ones, the same face pic came up for several of the generals. I had 4 with the same face. Why do you buy generals with diplomatic experience versus army/navy/air experience? I had 400 army experience, and could not use it for anything really. I didn't want to create a new template, so it just went to waste. You should be able to use it to get generals, improve technology speed, get combat bonuses, etc. No air commanders??
I did like the way they designed Air combat. I thought overall it was better than the cumbersome air system from previous versions.
Verdict. I am giving it a negative review based on my experience playing previous versions. If taken without any previous knowledge, the game would be enjoyable.

Although Assassin's Creed 2 dates back to 2010 and some people may find the outdated graphics and such offputting, I have to say this game still amazes me today, alongside Skyrim.
The storyline and side quests provided substantial game time which I thoroughy enjoyed. Even after completing all of these missions there is still plenty to do for those who want to 100% the game, such as locating treasure, exploring tombs and solving glyph puzzles. As the storyline progresses, so does time which provides availability to new areas and technology, which I found a logical way to unlock better equipment and gear rather than being granted availability from 'getting good'.
Although I mostly love the game, there are admittedly negatives that did make the gameplay a little bit unenjoyable at times. The game is played in third person which I don't have a problem with but there are certain points during a parkour sequence where the camera will either look from a really obscure angle so that it made me unsure with which direction I should go to move forward to reach the next point in a sequence, or the camera will suddenly change position and make me suddenly move in the wrong direction. I also found a lot of the time while free-running I thought, "I didn't want to do that". For instance, there's a Borgia messenger I'm chasing down on the rooftops and instead of leaping to the next building, I dive into a conveniently placed haystack below. Nice. There is also a very annoying game breaking bug I unforunately stumbled across. Just a little warning: DO NOT RETURN THE 100TH FEATHER WHILE WEARING THE ALTAIR OUTFIT GIVEN VIA ONE OF THE UPLAY REWARDS. YOU WILL HAVE TO RESTART THE GAME ALL OVER AGAIN. I found this one out the hard way.
Other than this, I didn't encounter many other important problems, and overall for a 2010 game, this is fantastic.
And another little note for players, when you arrive in Venice, be ready to give your mate a hug once the tour has concluded ;)

Truthful in its nature of strategy and action, R63 is quite undeniably the last true tactical game to have come in the series.
Pitting you in a what-would-be a spec op's worst nightmare scenarios too crazy for real-life, you're given simple objectives that usually encompasses rescuing hostages, preventing certain destruction, and all the while killing everyone else in sight (enemies do rarely surrender though). The levels are great and complex, but some may prove to be too much of a challenge, with some of the most unforgivingly tough gun combat you'll face. As hard as it can get, this instead left me craving for more for some reason.
Enjoyment is however, marred by a few technicalities to the likes of the occasional dumb but crazy aimbotting enemy AI and slightly underwhelming gunplay. What's more annoying is the incompetency of your own teammates, who may fare well in the easier levels but get completely obliterated in certain, more assault-oriented levels. Ultimately it doesn't matter how much strategic map planning comes into play, it all boils down to the player's own level of FPS skills for the best success, which puts into question the real importance of the
aspect.
Regardless, this game goes far behind SWAT 4 as one of the best tactical shooter I've ever played. And given the state of the Tactical Shooter genre that has since died off in gaming trend, this position will always remain as such, sadly.
This is the last great Rainbow Six game developed before UBI turned the R6 brand into a steaming pile of garbage.

I came expecting somewhat of a Dark Souls clone, with unique mechanics, boss battles, and elements that are reminiscent from their past games, what I got instead was a mix bag that introduces several different mechanics of Dark Souls, leaving frustrating one's of their own.
The level design alone made me quit this game, it's so large, and massive, with not that many enemies from the start, that really, the few spaces that you get in between each fight end up making the game an incredibly redundant experience, which I dislike because the overall feel of the combat it's great, I would compare it to something a bit more like Bloodborne than Dark Souls tho, it's faster than Dark Souls, it's simpler, I guess given that this is made in a 2d perspective, and the aesthetic and boss battles are great, tho, a bit terribly paced if I may say so, at first at the very least, the boss battles happen simply to often, and while they don't become that frustrating because of their difficulty what kills it for me is that their frequency makes them less surprising and unique, they just seem clustered after a while, and I find that the game should have had a better paicing when it comes to that.
Maybe it gets better later as you progress.
Having said that the game's level design, as I said before, it's what killed the game for me, I found it immensely frustrating to play through, after a while of just dying from falling, traversing corridors and ladders that go on and on and never seem to have any direction at all, I just got flustered, it's not the fail of direction that makes it frustrating, it's the fact that after playing it for a while, and traversing the same old boring corridors without that many enemies to fight, or secrets to discover, or generally speaking, stuff to do, the game ends up becoming a bit of a chore that eventually in your next encounter or so, picks up the enjoyable and absorving combat mechanics, bringing you right back, and really incentivizing you to keep playing.
But it's not enough of an incentive to me.
After a while I understood that the game was trying to retore to reminiscent aspects of even the core level mechanics of Dark Souls, but the beauty in that game it's that the level it's constantly changing, even when you don't know where to go, there's always something new to see, something new to explore, even while not progressing to the next area, even while being stuck, there's never anything that's the same, just on the top of my head, in the first Dark Souls you start in a dungeon, you move to an area that seems like a church, you fight, or escape a boss, then you head to a massive structure similar to a tower of somekind, with graves, and enemies around you.
In this game there's a point in which you reach a certain part that it's simply conformed by ladders, and nothing more, just ladders, and enemies, nothing else at all.
I just... Couldn't stand it after a while.
Just not my coup of tea I guess, just don't have the patience, not anymore.

Before I get into too much detail I'm going to try to give a general idea of how I felt about this game. I've heard of this game being like a 2D version of the Souls games, but it just isn't. It does share some qualities, but I honestly enjoyed the Souls games much more than Salt and Sanctuary. Not to say it's bad, I have enjoyed playing it so far. It just isn't polished well in too many places. The detail put into the lore and all the little details in the item and monster descriptions is great. There were some tough spots of platforming but nothing that I would ever say was unfair. The combat mechanics overall also work well. Now I'm going to go into detail on what I felt was wrong though. While this will most likely be a larger portion of the review do not take it as the negatives breaking the game.
What could be fixed up:
Inventory: This is a rather big problem for me. So you have hundreds and hundreds of items in your game. Why in the hell did you build the inventory system to store everything in one big line based on order of picking things up without any way to sort it?! Sure you have category tabs, but that just isn't good enough when there are so many items in the weapon or armor categories. Also your line order isn't set by category from what I can tell. That might not seem like such a big deal until you use up a consumable and then pick up a weapon only to find it showing up in the middle of the list instead of at the end like expected. It is so hard to even manually sort the items yourself thanks to this weird system where if you use up or drop an item it leaves its space in the line open and the next item you pick up automatically gets put into the first open spot.
Shields: Now obviously having shields makes sense. Somehow having your shield up blocks all attacks from all angles, but that isn't even the problem here. The problem is that there are only a few shields you'd ever really need because they make you a near invincible fortress. Becoming immune to all damage except the handful of enemies with a grab/impale that ignores shields makes much of the game a joke, including almost all the bosses. Sure players who aren't as good could use some help, but making shields so good you can ditch all armor just doesn't feel like the way to do it.
Materials: For the most part the upgrade materials don't feel too crazy to go for. I'm not even saying the curve on the difficulty of obtaining them is too steep. What feels weird is that the rare high end materials have such varied availability compared to each other despite how it doesn't really feel like the high end weapons follow any kind of pattern in using them. For example why does a mid-tier Reaper weapon use the once in a playthrough material gained after an optional boss while the high-tier Reapers use a late-game farmable drop or a new game farmable drop?
Challenges: There is no real point to any of them. From what I saw when I looked up if it was worth it they don't give you anything for completing them, you can't turn them off even in new game plus, they lock the character out of coop, and the Hardcore challenge even locks you out of a faction in the game. Since there is no reward for any of them anyways then you're better off just doing a normal game and setting rules to challenge yourself, that way you can actually opt out of them if it isn't fun anymore.
Recovering Salt after Death: For bosses it works wonderfully. Having to remove a set percent of the health of the boss (it looked about 25% or so) means you can't just run in to pick it back up before warping out. Environment kills spawn a salt bat where you were last safely standing, and that works well. With normal mobs though there is a problem. If you get killed by a normal mob you have to kill it to get back your salt. That's fine so far. Why does it get stronger though? If I just died to a mob, why do I have to kill a strengthened version of it when I died to it before it was strengthened?!
Character faces: This is really more of an opinion, but still I figure it is worth pointing out. Something about the character face designs just feels off with the art of the rest of the game. Now this only applies to the normal human faces, and even varies for me from character to character.
_______
In conclusion:
It is still a good game, I plan to get all the achievements for it in fact. Many people talking about it as being like a 2D Souls game just made me give it more scrutiny I think. On it's own it does some right, some wrong, but overall gives a positive impression. If a developer happens to read this then if nothing else please add inventory sorting.

I got this very cheap, which is great.. but unfortunately this game is pretty bad. The only things I actually enjoy are the moments when you get to find a vantage point and pick away at enemies, while adjusting for wind and gravity etc. That element is kind of fun. Pretty much everything else is not.
Graphics aren't great, but I don't even care about that. The real pain in this game is movement, everything feels very clunky and slow. Apparently there are things to find, judging by achievements.. but the game seems to actively discourage you from exploring. It's so straightforward in what you have to do, and the checkpoints are either needlessly close together or stretched oddly far apart. This forces you to replay some pretty boring areas again and again if you fail. Nobody wants to crawl on their belly along one side of the map again. That's pretty much what passes for stealth in this game. It gets old fast.
There is also very little variety in options and gear, it's just your rifle and pistol. You can pick up ammo (which you won't need) and medkits (which you'll rarely use - maybe more useful on hardest difficulty?), but can't pick up enemy weapons or have any real variation in your combat. If any enemy is face to face with you, you're pretty much dead in a second. You are so slow and gimped it's a bummer.
Granted I'm only on Act 2, but I'm pretty much done with this game. It's just too annoying to play, and the good parts don't make up for the bad.

Tales of Maj'Eyal. -sigh- I said I would write a review for this game when I beat it. Well I just edged over six hundred hours and finally have won. There really isn't much more to cover. The tags show it's a rogue-like, the videos give you a solid understanding of what to expect, and the user base has voted it overwhelmingly positive. So instead, I'm going to explain the emotional aspects of the game.  TOME (Tales of Maj'Eyal) will make you feel dead inside. I've litteraly taken a skirmisher over the course of thirty hours into the second to the last room and died. Boom, save deleted. Can you handle that? I couldn't, that was around hour mark 400. I couldn't sleep, I'm not kidding, when you die TOME plays this little dun dun dunn tone. I had no idea I was about to die, the moment the screen flicked red and that tune played, well, I broke out into a sweat. My friend was over visiting from the other side of the state and that is the only reason I didn't freak out into a felonious rage. Now you gotta understand, that was one death of many. Your victories are few and far between in TOME, you refight the same bosses over and over and over, it doesn't matter how much content there is in the game, you will feel almost no reward for killing alt minotaur for the hundreath time. You'll rage through the sandworms annoyed that you have to think with every move rather than autopiloting. When you're sucked into the fearscape with a fire specd character you'll understand fear and if you get out alive you just return to the motions. After hundreds of hours of hundreds of deaths you finally get to the last boss. Then you win. I've been smiling for two days now, I think on winning and just grin. I can't help it. It's probably the most rewarding victory I've ever had in a game. Puts emerald or ruby weapon to shame. Six hundred hours for this feeling. Then you take it off normal mode and switch to nightmare difficulty and die in the starting area. So basically what I'm saying is, how well do you know yourself? Is this a goal worth your time? It was for me.

As far as I'm concerned ToME is the best roguelike made so far. With the expansions it has two story campaigns to go through, an infinite dungeon and a wave fighting arena mode. The main campaign has tens of zones (and random generated zones using the farportal) and Embers of Rage featuring over 20 zones as well.
With 14 races and over 30 classes each featuring their own talent categories (some can share some categories with other classes) there's an insane amount of replayability as you try different class/race combinations and master their playstyles. Granted a lot of them have to be unlocked by doing different objectives in game, if you're not into that theres a mod that lets you unlock all of them.
Main reason why ToME is THE roguelike to play is the nature of it's combat. As you play you will gather abilities from talents and items, some of them having multiple uses (like Rush being good for: attacking, repositioning and escaping). Enemies also use the same abilities depending on their class and by inspecting them you can learn how to deal with different enemies as different classes. It plays like a turn based tactical RPG and it's great.

To be clear, I actually enjoy Cuphead because I'll take any kind of challenge, no matter how ridiculous or unfair. This review is looking at the game as a whole as opposed to my opinion.
The #1 rule for a game to be both challenging and rewarding is for it to present you with difficulty based on how skilled the player is. That may not sound like it's a rule that can actually be broken, but Cuphead breaks that rule in almost every way. How, exactly? By incorporating a large element of random chance because of the game's many problems. Before I cover that, i'll just say that one thing Cuphead has going for it is it's 1930's cartoon- styled graphics; no game looks quite like it. With that said, here's what all is wrong with this mess- this includes both technical errors, as well as developer oversights:
-No matter how powerful your computer is you will get INSANE frame dorps CONSTANTLY. This alone causes at least a third of my in-game deaths.
-Loading times- did Bethesda develop this game or what? Sometimes it's fine, and others it takes a whole minute to switch between isles.
-Enemies will not always appear on screen, but they can still damage you
-Ex attack does not always work on an Xbox controller
-Controls are severely delayed at times (primarly when switching between ducking and jumping)
-Parrying mechanic never works the same- sometimes multi-parry doesn't work, and sometimes parrying doesn't work at all.
-Holding down A does not alway result in a high jump
-Lobber shot doesn't always deal damage (in my experience at least, not everyone has this problem)
-Ememy projectiles will function off- screen, so they can harm you if you are at the edge of the screen with no time to dodge it
-some bosses' attacks have no predictable animation, making it random chance as to whether or not you dodge that attack
-some boss fights contain platforms to jump between- their positions are random, which can sometimes make enemy attacks unavoidable
-Seeker shot will sometimes attack things that don't exist
-Hitboxes are WAY off- sometimes a man's hat will damage you, and other times you can stand insie of an enenies' mouth and take no damage
-Cuphead focuses on bosses, while any good game usually has either an equal number of bosses to stages, or more stages than bosses- this makes nearly every playable section stressful.
-Taking damage can cause you to fly back into another enemy attack- which causes you to fly back into another enemy attack yet again (mostly a late- game problem). It could be intentional, but it's seriously just annoying.
-Many boss fights are based on trial and error because of how sudden their attacks are, forcing you to die so you can memorize them for next time. I never had to do this with another video game before- not even in any Dark Souls game!
-No online Co-Op; this option should be a given in the modern gaming world.
-I understand that some parts of a game are meant to be brutally difficult, but a single boss fight shouldn't be so difficult that it takes me 2 hours and 30 minutes to beat them. The platforming genre and Shoot 'em up genre aren't exactly new things to me, either.
-Here's a personal complaint: the music resets every time you die, and this can get obnoxious to me in minutes.
I can think of more problems with Cuphead, But they are either nitpicks or irrelavent to other players. That's what I've got to say about Cuphead.

First, I played this game back in the day and as such my Steam play-time does not reflect true play time.
If you are looking for an old-school Star Wars FPS experience, the Dark Forces series is surely worth checking out. This is the sequel to the original Dark Forces(also worth checking out), a more Doom-esque FPS. In Dark Forces 2, we see 3D accelerated graphics and the introduction of cut-scenes.
Performance-
The steam port is somewhat unstable and there are some quirks that will have to be ironed out to get it running smoothly and in the correct resolution. I had to reverse my Y axis input on my mouse, as well as reduce all mouse sensitivities. You will also have to enable 3d acceleration and find a resolution that works for you.
If the game crashes continually when starting a level, visit
and download dgVoodoo. Extract D3Dimm.dll and DDraw.dll to your jedi knight game folder. This fixed the problem for me and hopefully for you as well.
Graphics-
Naturally the visuals don't hold up that well, as this game was one of the earlier FPSs to feature 3d-accelerated graphics. The textures were well-done and the game doesn't look horrible and is quite playable. If you attempt to play the game at 1920x1080 you will find UI elements such as health and ammo gauges become too small to read. When you pause the game and enter the menu, the game will go through an awkward transition where it becomes windowed and small. Annoying, but manageable.
Gameplay-
The default controls are archaic, as this game predates the modern WASD layout that has become standard. All keys are rebindable, so this too can be dealt with. The level design isn't quite as impressive as I remember it being, but the maps are expansive and have plenty of secrets to find and clever enemy placement. There are a variety of weapons to employ including a lightsaber and rocket launcher. The gameplay is fast-paced and fluid. I found it enjoyable.
Story-
The storyline is somewhat campy, but it follows the same protagonist as Dark Forces 1 as well as later jedi knight games. If you enjoy Star Wars you will enjoy the story, though the cinematics can seem a bit goofy.
Opinion-
If you are at all interested in classic FPS or classic gaming in general, and have a soft spot for Star Wars, this game is well worth checking out. It represents an important step in 3d graphics development, and is fun in it's own right. For the complete Kyle Katarn saga, be sure to check out the original Dark Forces as well as Jedi Knight 2.

So Meta, Even This Acronym.
OneShot is cute, imaginative and, at times, simply mind-blowing—and blowing the jaded mind of a modern gamer is not an easy task. The meta nature of the game is highlighted by its name: you only have one shot at it, and then the save file becomes corrupted. There won't be a second journey.
Only... how is it fair? Whatever you do, you will have to face a dilemma in the end, and choosing either of the cruel options is reductive and simply wrong. Can you... rebel against the whole thing, perhaps?
These, however, are the thoughts you'll deal with by the end, but even before it the game is littered with charming meta-humor. The main character needs to sleep, for example, and when she does, the game closes. Some puzzles require thinking very much out of the box and using unexpected approaches. All the while the touching and lovely story of a hero stranded in a strange land and carrying a lightbulb to light up the local sun continues to unfold.
The game is at its most poignant during the moments when
The execution of OneShot leaves something to be desired: while very sweet in terms of visuals, it's often clunky and makes you do a lot of unnecessary walking back and forth solving various puzzles; coupled with imperfect location layouts, it gets frustrating sometimes. La oferta que encontramos en Streamline es sencilla, donde eres un Cazador o Corredor, si fuiste seleccionado para comenzar la partida como Cazador te ves en la necesidad de buscar a los demás jugadores para golpearlos y poder convertirte en Corredor, si te toca ser Corredor tu objetivo es conseguir puntos. El juego es desarrollado por el equipo independiente Proletariat Inc.
Quizás la característica principal del juego sea el enfoque que tiene hacia la plataforma Twitch, que por si no lo conoces, es un servicio gratis para realizar o mirar streams de juegos de video, etc. El juego esta diseñado y creado pensando en ofrecer streams calidad. Stramline permite a los jugadores que utilizan Twitch para transmitir sus partidas interactuar con sus espectadores; los que estén viendo la partida pueden participar directamente en las rondas, apostando por sus jugadores favoritos, cambiando las reglas de las rondas en tiempo real y competir en mini-juegos.
Lo mencionado en el párrafo anterior es posible gracias al Streamote.tv, un sitio web creado por los mismos chicos de Proletaria, una herramienta que permite a los streamers y espectadores interactuar entre ellos mientras juegan Streamline sin tener que hacer un desmadre en el chat de Twitch.
El título se juega en linea, en partidas de hasta 16 jugadores, donde ya sea como Cazador o Corredor nos vemos enfrascados en partidas donde las reglas del juego cambian a según las elecciones de los espectadores de la partida, con game changers chistosos, como por ejemplo: uno de los cambios en tiempo real nos limita a solo poder caminar como un cangrejo, de medio lado (y haciendo pantomima de cangrejo), otras nos ponen a brincar durante un minutos (sin que lo queramos), otras ralentizan el tiempo y todo va en cámara lenta. También existen cambios en el mapa, como que empieza a llenarse de lava en el suelo afectando los jugadores, o el mapa se empieza a hacer más pequeño poco a poco. Acá pueden ver un video del juego que subimos a nuestra pagina de Facebook.
Otra característica es la posibilidad de poder cambiar la ropa y accesorios de tu personaje, con cientos de combinaciones posibles dándole un toque mas personal, con distintas ropas y muchos colores divertidos.
Streamline es un juego que podría ser más divertido, pero se queda un poco corto. El problema no es que sea poco divertido, el asunto es que el título es un poco lento, la jugabilidad se siente lenta, y se atenúa aun más cuando todo en el titulo se centra en correr. Para mi gusto los jugadores tienen poca velocidad, y eso le resta emoción. Los saltos, piruetas y plataformeo serían más emocionantes si el desarrollador le añadiera un poco más de velocidad a los personajes, convirtiendo la experiencia en algo más vertiginoso y dinámico.
Los gráficos de Stramline son regulares, con un aire a Team Fortress y Battleborn, no son ni malos ni buenos. El audio es sumamente molesto para mi gusto, pero no es peor que el “reggaeton” de la vecina al frente de mi casa, así pues, es recomendable bajarle el sonido al audio y poner tu propia música para evitar algún cáncer en el tímpano.
En corto, Streamline no lo hace mal, las cosas que merman la experiencia son fácilmente corregibles y con el tiempo podría ser un juego regular-bueno, vacilón para jugar con los amigos. Un juego que cuesta originalmente $20, lo cual es caro para la experiencia que ofrece, asi que mejor agarrarlo mientras se pueda.

So... it took me 63 hours to finally manage to beat the game in Normal/Adventure mode for the first time. Now it's time to write a review... wait, gotta buy the DLC first... including the one that doesn't do anything, to support the dev. I felt like a criminal for how much I paid for ToME from the start...
Ok, done. Now... where was I?
Oh, the review. I paid 10 times more (each) for 2 or 3 games during summer sale than I paid for Maj, just a couple of days before getting it. What happened was I didn't play any of the others (AAA stuff) once after I started ToME, and now I'm writing this review while thinking about what class to play next.
If you haven't played any game like this one before, and by looking at the screenshots feel like it doesn't look (literally) good enough for you, keep in mind that the point is: while it doesn't have the fancy, modern graphics, it does right everything most games these days do wrong-- everything that makes it a GAME is great.
I'll try to keep it short:
Roguelike - It is, but on Adventure mode you get about 7 lives (+some items you may find that can resurrect you once). You can go hardcore, 1-life Roguelike if you want.
Races/Classes - Several of them, unlockable. I'm still missing 5. They are very different from each other, with many different and interesting skill trees. You gotta put some thinking into figuring out what you are gonna make and how you are going to build it.
Items - Diablo-like, random drops and attributes, different rarity and tier levels. You feel the thrill of finding good loot. Lots of uniques too. You can stash them and retrieve with another/new character, boosting them hard on your future playthroughs. Just 3 at a time tho, which is annoying, but you can re-do it as many times as you want and so distribute any number of items between your dudes.
Map/Dungeons - Always the same dungeons, but spawning on random locations across the map and with randomized interiors. Some minor events and sub-dungeons are also randomly generated.
Quests - Not a lot of them, always the same, but some are very interesting and give nice rewards.
Lore - LOTS of lore scrolls to be found, telling the game's universe story. I didn't read them, I never do, I don't have the patience, but if you like immersing yourself a bit deeper, you won't have a problem with that.
Elite/Rare/Unique/Boss Monsters - These are the ones who usually take those 7 lives away from you... along with the rare multihued wyrms... and magic wielders... and map encounters...  and everything else if you are a Mage.
Gameplay - You gotta build your character right, position yourself right, pay attention, have an escape plan... some parts are really though until you get a good hang of the game-- which is great, and a good part of the fun.
Graphics/Sound - They work perfectly, the visual effects are nice and the music is pretty good.
Bugs/Crashes - I got 3 in 63 hours. Fixed a "0 turn duration skill" by going back to the main menu and then continuing the game, fixed both crashes by clicking "Close" on the in-game dump note. I had to kill one of my temporal hounds on the second one though, otherwise the dumps kept coming, but it was easily fixed.
This is a great game, awesome cost/benefit. I'm usually skeptical about old-school graphics, but they don't take anything away from ToME, and this baby does very well what most modern games screw up - the part that really matters.
And now... I'm going Paladin next. To see if I can get that holy gentleman past the freaking Master...
EDIT:
My paladin died on the last boss fight. I'm still mourning him... or rather all the items he took along to his grave. I hope he is in hell... forever...
Doombringer, the DLC class, is awesome.
I also found out I'm not man enough to face the Atamathon.
On the downside, Temporal Hounds always end up glitching somehow (and Time Warden is the s**t, my best dude). I had to edit and repack some of the game's files to fix one of them. It worked, but required some effort. And now, doing the Prides on Nightmare with that very same TW, the game began freezing hard, forcing me to reopen it to keep going every 20 minutes or so.
So... avoid Temporal Hounds if you can. I can't, I like puppies. On the other hand, I didn't have any problems whatsoever with the other classes... my summoner (who spawned a lot more stuff than 3 dogs) worked fine until he got♥♥♥♥♥♥♥by The Master.

A lot of action games and shooters seem to glorify violence and bathe the player in it in mindless, yet entertaining, way, but Rainbow Six 3 (like its predecessors) abandon this concept for a more realistic perspective on violence.
The gameplay is brutal. You're not a bullet-soaking hero that can kill wave after wave of enemies. Instead, you're a fragile human with only his squad and tactics to guide you through. A single bullet can end your character's life, and it is because of this that violence in the game is more often feared and respected. Everything from the planning of the mission to the way you enter of your room is in your control, but a slight slip-up can leave you with multiple casualities—all of which are permanent for the rest of the game.
If you're looking for a game that focuses more on tactics and realism, rather just pointing and clicking on enemies, then look no further.

Before I begin this review, I should make it clear I have in total bought 9 copies of this game. This review will be written starting with a pros and cons summary list followed by an in depth look into the game. This review will conclude with a final rating.
Pros
- Fidget Spinner Spins
- Well Paced Progression System
- Decent Music
- Good Graphics
- Lots Of Spinners To Choose From
Cons
- No End Game
- NEEDS MORE SPINNERS
- No Longer Have A Life Or Friends
Written Review
Now that we have the pros and cons of the game covered, we may begin to delve deeper into the true review of this unparalleled and unprecedented game, possibly the greatest of the century (or maybe even of all time).
Overview
When you open up this innovative masterpiece, you are greeted by a beautiful, captivating main menu, the likes of which grabs your attention and holds it both visually and audibly. The exquisite layout of different fidget spinners provides but a taste of the fidgety goodness of which you are about to be immersed. These are tastefully interspersed with a few quirky comments, a couple of social media buttons and the main menu UI. One could say that this UI is somehow lacking, however I feel as though it feeds nicely into a minimalistic theme of sorts. As amazing as the visuals of the main menu prove to be, they incomparable to the stunning audio of the main menu. You are instantly mesmerized by the spellbounding power contained within the extraordinary and thrilling lyrics you are met with when you first open this game. This is, however, only the main menu.
Once you somehow manage to drag yourself from the perfect and somehow utopian main menu, you are met with the actual game screen itself. The words previously used to describe the main menu would only understate the game screen itself, doing it both a disservice and an injustice. Neither the English language, nor any other, contains words which could even begin to describe the perfectness of which is this screen. As such I shall simply describe it. In the top left corner lays your money count next to a green money symbol. Underneath this a black bar which counts how many spins your spinner completes each round. If you reach certain milestones by filling this bar, you get more money per spin every round. In the bottom left, there is round button containing the picture of a fidget spinner. This allows you to change the look of your spinner once you level up. In the middle bottom, a round button with a dial on it. This allows you to use money to increase the speed of your spinner, allowing you to reach higher and higher milestones. The bottom right button allows you to change settings (currently only sound as all your graphical settings are open for change only when you open the game). Above this is the main menu button, if ever you feel the grasp of the immaculate main menu pull you back in. Up next is a funny. In the top right corner is how many spins a minute your spinner is doing, or in layman's terms, how fast your spinner is currently moving. In the middle of your screen is how many swipes you have left this round. Finally, above this, you have your spinner itself.
Gameplay
Every round you are blessed with 5 swipes. These allow you to move the spinner in a clockwise motion, with each spin being counted underneath the black bar on your top left. You must figure out the best methid to gain the most amount of spins possible. Some people are natural spinners and will get how to do this easily and quickly. Others have not been so blessed and will require hours, if not years of training. However I strongly believe it is possible for all to spin to the highest level possible with the right trainer and training. While I would never claim to be the best spinner in the world, I am certainly happy to point people in the right direction towards getting more spins on their spinners.
Overall, gameplay is smooth and the progression sytem is very well paced. Whenever the game feels it is just beginning to get a little boring, you unlock a new fidget spinner and the flood of excitement rushes over you all over again as if it were are new game you were beginning to play, even though at this point it has taken over your life, you have lost your job, your wife and your kids. The only gripe I would have with this game is that the end game is somewhat lacking. You eventually reach a point where the milestone needed to fill the black bar is massive and it takes a long time to unlock all the speed unlocks to progress to the next milestone. Now, while I would usually accept this as a very good feature as it adds an element of perseverance and extra challenge, basically adding hundreds of hours, if not an eternity, of gameplay to this game, it causes me to look up from my computer at the homeless shelter which has become my home after recently losing my apartment after not being able to pay rent after I quit my job to become a full time spinner.
Conclusion
This game is literally perfect in every single way imaginable and many that cannot be imagined and must be seen to be seen. It is because of this I have determined that this game is created by a being higher than ourselves. While I have lost my wife, kids, job, apartment and life thanks to this game, I still recommend it highly as I now consider it to be my wife, kids, job and life as well as the only shelter I need. I no longer need actual human interaction or meaning in my life. Honestly, this is all I need.

The game has its flaws, but no game is without such things. To give a game grief for not being flawless is setting a standard bar well beyond realistic expectations and there for being unreasonable. Also most of the negative reviews have hardly clocked enough time to really get into the game.
The short:
This is a great time killer and if you like making prospect of making tons of whacky weapon combos and personal perks to enhance your character's speed, jump and other stuff then you'll love this game even if there are some spelling errors in text and the occasional bug.
The long:
This game is not a Metal Slug clone, it takes a lot of inspiration from it like character designs, setting, some minor game mechanics and combat from Metal Slug but its not a fast paced side scrolling shooter. The game actually reminds me more of the old Castlevenia games with
with its multi layered levels and hidden areas.
This is not a game where you'll forever be blasting your way forward (like how Metal Slug games play) without turning back, you will need to take time to farm for materials to build better weapons and perks. The repetiveness of farming can be troublesome for players who just want to rush on ahead but for players who actually enjoy all the benefits of being able to craft more weapon parts it pays off in spades (90+ hours and I still haven't made everything or done all the side missions).
This coop in this game is also really fun, my advice is wait till its on sale and buy the 4 pack for yourself and 3 pals.
In fact as much as i love this game I don't think its worth almost 20USD, its a time sink sure but thats mainly if you want to make and try out new weapon sets and combinations (the farming can really eat up time).
So do I highly recommend this game but not at full price and only if you can handle grinding for crafting fun stuff.

So Meta, Even This Acronym.
OneShot is cute, imaginative and, at times, simply mind-blowing—and blowing the jaded mind of a modern gamer is not an easy task. The meta nature of the game is highlighted by its name: you only have one shot at it, and then the save file becomes corrupted. There won't be a second journey.
Only... how is it fair? Whatever you do, you will have to face a dilemma in the end, and choosing either of the cruel options is reductive and simply wrong. Can you... rebel against the whole thing, perhaps?
These, however, are the thoughts you'll deal with by the end, but even before it the game is littered with charming meta-humor. The main character needs to sleep, for example, and when she does, the game closes. Some puzzles require thinking very much out of the box and using unexpected approaches. All the while the touching and lovely story of a hero stranded in a strange land and carrying a lightbulb to light up the local sun continues to unfold.
The game is at its most poignant during the moments when
The execution of OneShot leaves something to be desired: while very sweet in terms of visuals, it's often clunky and makes you do a lot of unnecessary walking back and forth solving various puzzles; coupled with imperfect location layouts, it gets frustrating sometimes. However, I'd say the game itself is charming and unique enough for it to be easily forgivable.

7/10.  While the game is fun, there are many areas where it suffers.  It is compared(rightfully so) to Payday, and does have some similar qualities, however there are a lot of things this does that Payday does a lot better.  The enemies and level design are the most glaring.  There are either no or at least very short breaks between waves, and each wave contains an obscene amount of enemies.  While mowing Nazis down by the hundred is a trope of the nazi-killing genre, the game throws SO MANY at you so frequently  that the game starts to lag out on an otherwise powerful computer.  And to make matters worse, the lag doesn't improve.  The game neglects to remove dead enemies, and while I don't like it when games remove bodies as soon as I turn around, the massive piles of ragdolls cause the game to get slower.  And slower.  AND SLOWER.  It's something that I think could have been easily avoided.  The bugs in the enemies don't stop with performance.  They glitch through walls, players, doors, furniture, I've literally seen them get stuck ON TOP of an open door.  It's an issue that makes the game feel very frustrating as I'll be spraying my Sten into a corridor full of Nazis, only to turn around to find some grunt meleeing me from behind.  Bugs aside, the gameplay feels generally less complex than Payday.  For example in Payday 2, when robbing a joint, you'd have an oppurtunity to get set up, sometimes even barricade a few windows before the SWAT teams arrived.  Not here.  From the moment combat starts you get absolutely swarmed with wave after wave of crazed soldiers with almost no relief in between them.  Again, I know that's a trope of the genre but it's something that could have been a little more refined than it is.  Overall the game is fun, but I'd still grab it when it's on sale.

If you like solitaire, you will certainly get your money's worth here. Part of the time you are rebuilding King Arthur’s castle and compound by collecting resources to protect it from a goblin attack. You gather food, gold and material resources. Once you finish Merlin's tower, you can buy power-ups with your resources (some with one-time use and others that you can continue to use). However, you can repurchase a maximum of 5 wild cards and 2 jokers, each hand. You can also go back and replay hands, especially if you want to complete the game with all perfect (3 star) achievement. Lots of achievements you can complete. Very enjoyable and nice graphics.
Once you get the castle and compound built, there doesn't seem much interaction with the characters and not much to do except to get through hands or go back and try to get perfect hands. Then again, you can pile up money to finish buying all the power-ups and wild cards.
The only problem I had was getting a random exception error, especially after playing several hands. This crashes the game. The other bug I noticed, which does not affect the game, is the background is skewed or doesn't show up at all (the background appears solid white or black.)

It's a solitaire game with a twist -- you have three different resources (gold, food and building mats) you spend on upgrading your castle (buildings which either provide resources or unlock further "tech") and magic (which affects the card play or increases buildings' output). What else to wish for?..
... Well, the game being half as long. Because it has 300 levels, and you max out exactly about level 150. After that, you have nothing to do with your resources at all, except brute force grind through the remaining 150 (!) levels by buying wildcards or jokers when you can't perfect finish right away.
Don't worry, you will have more than enough income to not even bother trading food/bricks for gold while doing that.
That is, if you are obsessive enough to do the chore.

I got this a while ago but didn't get around to playing it until recently. Coming from the Soulsborne series, this game is a refreshing take on a great formula. By my guess I'm about 1/2 to 2/3 of the way through the game, and so far it's been a great experience.
I'm going to assume whoever reads this is familiar with the Soulsborne games. If you aren't, read another review, because I'm not really going to talk about that too much. Instead, I'm going to talk about how the 2D format impacts the Soulsborne formula.
From a gameplay perspecitve, the 2D format allows for some very fun and creative platforming that isn't possible 3D. The game constantly rewards the player for noticing objects and places and keeping their location in mind in order to access them later. I was worried that two dimensions would limit the level and world design that I love in the Soulsborne series, but it certainly does not; in fact, in some places I'd say the world and level design, filled with interconnecting paths and shortcuts, far exceed that of other Souls-like games and the Souls games themselves.
Another concern of mine was how the combat would feel in 2D, but again, that concern was unfounded. The combat is fun and rewarding, despite the somewhat wonky controls.
My only complaint about this game is the boss fights. Unfortunately, most of the bosses in this game have very limited movesets and are very easy to predict. I don't know if I've simply been overleveled, but up to where I am in the game, there have been only 3 or 4 bosses that I didn't beat on my first attempt. This is somewhat disappointing, not only because I'm a veteran of the Soulsborne series, but because this game itself hypes up the bosses with challenging levels, areas, and enemy combinations, and then the bosses, which are meant to cap that experience off and whose defeat rewards the player with an achievement, are unfortunately underdeveloped.
That being said, that is my only complaint with the game. The 2D platformer formula is merged almost perfectly with the Soulsborne formula, and I recommend this game to anyone, not just Soulsborne veterans.

I am a huge Souls fan. Played and finished Demon's Souls, the Dark Souls series and Bloodborne, and when I saw a 2D souls like game it was a must buy for me. The beggining of the game was a lot of fun, but 5 hours in some enemies and design decision started to become extremely frustrating:
-Enemies started behaving erraticaly: I learned in all Souls games to study enemy attacks, tells and breaches to attack them back, which almost every enemy I encountered so far I was able to defeat by studying them. The thing is, some enemies seem to behave in a random way, one example is the Axe Knight who has 2 consecutive swings that does sometimes track you, if you roll behind him, and sometimes doesn't which made me die quite a few times, one other inconsistencies is that he can stop his consecutive attacks and immediatelly start a new one.
-Questionable design decisions:
+not only this game has the punishing difficulty of Dark Souls, it also adds another element which is not the focus of Dark Souls: platforming. In later stages you will end up dying a lot because of falling, which is a huge pain because you lose all your currency, go back all the way to the last sanctuary and you have to deal again with tough enemies.
+some enemies require you to have a certain item to be able to properly defeat them, like an invisible enemy that floats around you and can kill you in 2-3 hits, requiring you to drink a sight potion so you can see him (problem is, there is a huge chance you won't have the potion, and you are left attacking the air hoping that you will kill him).
It's hard for me to write here everything that is frustrating about this game. I had a lot of rage-inducing moments playing the Souls series, of course, but this game just went too far. If I didn't spend all those 8 hours playing it I would refund it for sure. I feel like From Software is the only company truly capable of creating a difficult but fair game unfortunately.

Basics:  A "bump" game with some semi-random determined areas.  (Bump in to monsters to attack)
Likes: Range of character classes and races that can be unlocked as you play.  Each class and race feels unique and challenging.  Game is challenging, difficult and frustrating at times. I believe this game to be a true, natural evolution of the roguelike genre. It has all the fun and challenge of a classic roguelike but updated with modern conveniences. Not to mention this game is just sopping wet with lore that, if you actually take the time to read through, is pretty damn interesting. In short, it's been an amazing experience so far. If you're a fan of the classics like ADOM then I couldn't recommend this enough.
One of the things I absolutely adore about this game is all the unlockables. In a genre in which you can die fairly quickly or lose hours of progress over one stupid mistake, you need good amounts of replay value to keep you rolling characters. This game does that pretty well with tons of unlockables. You not only have races, classes and talent trees to unlock, but also prodigy unlocks that'll give every character you roll items like the transmogrification box which automatically picks up junk items and turns them into gold.
There's a fairly good variety of dungeons in this game. Not only in style and layout but in the ways you can go about progressing in them. I found myself in a cave with no hallways filled with passive worms that chewed up sections of the wall. In order to go to the next room you needed to follow one of these worms and if you stuck around in one of its tunnels for too long it could collapse on you. Made for a really intense boss fight at the end. Not to mention each dungeon is filled to burst with it's own lore which is definitely a plus. A lot of them have little challenges too in the form of rooms behind stuck doors. If you choose to open these doors you're usually faced with tough monsters and traps, but also some pretty fancy loot. It's completely optional so if you're struggling to get through a dungeon then it's just not worth it.
In the time I've been playing I haven't been able to find a whole lotta quests. It seems like half the people you talk to early-game are all looking for potion ingredients but the rest were actually pretty interesting. I found a secret door in the overworld that took me to a rogue's den where they captured a merchant. You have the choice of joining the rogues or freeing the merchant which unlocks a rare items shop in one of the towns. Later-game quests get more interesting as well.
Teaching someone how to play your game is very important. It's something I think about every time I play a game and it can ultimately ruin a player's experience early on if they have no idea what they're doing. Now this is especially difficult with games like this that are filled with content and complexity. The solution? Unlockables. This game gives you the basics of each different type of class to start off with. This keeps the player from being overwhelmed with options at the beginning or the advanced know-how to play the more strategic classes. It also gives the player a goal early on to keep them playing. I had no trouble at all learning how to play this game. If you're new to roguelikes then I don't think you'd have troubles either.
I think my only real gripe with this game is the random escort missions you get on some dungeon floors. They're great in that if you do manage to escort them to their portal, you get a pretty decent reward. However, their ai is absolutely ridiculous. They tend to blindly trudge slowly towards their portal and tend to get themselves trapped between monsters or just refuse to run away from some of them which is double bad if you're a ranged class. There's a mod in the workshop that helps with this problem but the problem's still kinda there, you're just able to make them wait in one spot for x amount of turns.
All in all, this game is fantastic. The amount of content you get in this game is astounding, too. Even it's DLC is soaked in content. Not to mention the price is pretty damn reasonable. If you're into roguelikes then there's no reason not to pick this up. If you're trying to get into roguelikes but are left feeling empty playing roguelike-likes or games that claim to have "roguelike elements" expecting to get that same rush playing NetHack then you owe it to yourself to play this game. You can tell the developer put a lot of love into it and they deserve every cent they get.

tl;dr This game is a tactical shooter, so it may not be for everyone. It can still be fun to play with people, granted they know what they are doing. The game may have some technical flaws (it being old). If you want to play good old Rainbow Six without wrestling with the Original's engine, pick this one up.
Rainbow Six 3 is a squad based, tactical shooter. This game allows you to take control of the elite counterterrorism unit RAINBOW (yes, that's the name of the unit).
This game is not something you rush into. You need tactics. The game has an entire planning phase where you can modify how each group of operatives moves. You can tell them to wait on your mark, then when you give the go-code, open the door and flash through it.
Multiplayer still works, however you have to have a uPlay account. You could try lan or hamachi, but I didn't test that.
The game has a mutlitude of weapons and armor for you to choose. You can use silenced smgs with flashbangs and go full on stealth, or use 50.cal snipers and M4's with frag grenades to go all out.
This game is also not as easy as your usual FPS. You get a maximum of 1-3 hits before your dead. Everyone follows this rule. Once someone's dead, they can no longer be chosen, so make sure your teammates don't die.
The game also has some mechanics that I've never seen any other FPS have before, or after. These are the fluid lean and door opening. Using the mouse, you can adjust your character to lean at many other angles other than one. Fluid door opening allows you to open doors halfway, a tiny bit, or just enough to let a grenade through.
That said, the game has flaws. The planning stage is locked at ~800x600 (the game isn't but the menus are). The game can sometimes be a bit hard to get into, and you may have to do levels over and over to make sure your preferred teammates didn't die. This game is way different than alot of FPSes out today (Call of Duty, Team Fortress, and Battlefield aren't very comparable. Counter-Strike is a bit comparable, but still has alot of differences).
It's a shame this style of PC game play has disappeared over the years. Remember when the in-store PC game section had 5,6 or more aisles available, not just this years 5 or 6 new releases.
Still one of the best tactical shooters even after 11 years.

But what makes the game unique is planning and executing the plans. You need to pick at least one soldier (up to 8 with 4-men limit per squad) and here is your choice. You may plan exactly your actions, so that you do not need to even touch the keyboard, because the soldiers will do everything for you. You may play it as a shooter (though a much harder one, than the new ones) or play a 'hybrid' version - plan some key actions -e.g. synchronize the assault of one room (with a hostage being kept there for example) and attack it from two sides. It doesn't matter, which playing style you enjoy more, because it will be great anyway.
If you're a fan of a true gameplay and enjoy playing tactical shooters - this game is perect for you!

This game was the peak of Ubisoft's Rainbow Six franchise. Here is why;
-Realistic AI. The enemy AI will execute hostages if they see the player, run if they are outnumbered, and even surrender to trick the player into letting your guard down, so that their friend can shoot the player in the back!
-Lots of weapons, gear, and customisability. One can customise not only their own soldier's weapons, gear, and armour, but their teammates as well.
-Planning. The game allows the player to set waypoints for their team and AI teams, and the AI teams will automattically follow. One can even set "Go codes" to make the AI wait for the code to begin an action, such as breaching.
-The multiplayer still works. One can set up their own dedicated server in a few simple steps. See my discussion post for help.
-Lots of fun game modes and maps. This game has many fun game modes, such as Lone Wolf (terrorist hunt alone); Terrorist Hunt (kill all the terrorists); and Hostage Rescue (self-explanatory). It also features classic maps such as Peak, Presidio and Prison.
-Fairly good graphics. While these graphics aren't amazing, they still hold up well today.
-Non-linear maps. Play your way.
So, if you have played Rainbow Six Vegas 1 or 2, come see what the classic games were like! If you've never played Rainbow Six before, now is a great time to start!

World was nearly wiped out by an asteroid and you emerge from an underground vault. Most of those you meet in Rage desperately want to kill or capture you, and gradually you begin to find out why. Despite the presence of upgrade systems, mini-games, side quests and car racing challenges, Rage is primarily a shooter.  You can ride around in buggies and heavily armored cars, blast rockets at bandit vehicles and speed over jumps to smash floating beacons and earn extra rewards.
In your adventure through corridors and interiors lined with hiding spots as mutants erupt from unseen spaces and bandits fire pistols and shotguns. Combat encounters build in difficulty and throw a variety of increasingly difficult enemies in the mix, forcing you to be creative with your weapons. Eventually you'll acquire all the basic gun types, including a sniper rifle, rocket launcher and two assault rifles. Though only four can be active at a time, you carry everything in your inventory, so weapons are never left behind. The creative element comes into play once you gain access to all the different ammunition types and crafted items.
Though so much of the world wants to kill you, inside the main towns you'll find vendors to buy and sell items, dig up side quests and participate in racing circuits. It's easy to lose track of what they say as you're distracted by the high quality of their movements facial animations, accentuating the care that clearly went into each and every character model.
Co-operative play is also possible in standalone missions separated from the main story mode. With another player you can mow down enemies in pursuit of a high score. You get bonuses for headshots and skilled play, and a multiplier climbs so long as you continue to get kills and avoid dying while point totals pop up all over the screen like you were playing a slot machine, increasing the sense of reward.
The studio knows how to make great shooters and deliver incredible visuals and animations. Despite the lack of genuinely exciting context, all the content packed into Rage is still a blast to play, including the surprisingly entertaining car combat mode and co-operative challenges.

From a historical standpoint, this game is a great secondary source. The NSDAP was the leading party in Germany during 1933 to 1945. The leader of said party, Adolf Hitler, had grown to be a very controversial leader through this period of time, due to his political stances and policies. During the 30s, Germany had grown to be a leading military power in the world, and first struck against Poland in 1939, before conquering the majority of Europe. In the 40s, though, the military advance saw a steady decline, and in 1945, Germany lost, and NSDAP along with it. During the wartimes, the NSDAP was responsible of persecution and genocide of many minorities, mainly jewish people, along with many other warcrimes. In this game, you learn of many well-known high officers of the NSDAP, such as Gabe Newell, Donald J. Trump, Pewdiepie, Rollsafe and Mr. Bean.
From the fantastic graphics, true 1080p HD resolution, beautiful controls, to a lesson on philosophy and history, this game has a lot to offer and will truly stand the test of time in terms of game quality. GOTY.

I have only played this game for a short while, and so far I have mixed feelings about it.
- The graphics are not great. The character animations behave strangely and don't always give the response that you expect from your actions. For example, killed enemies fall in random directions and sometimes it is hard to tell if an enemy is actually dead or not.
- The gameplay gets tiresome after a while. It feels repetitive as you are just constantly running around shooting at endless streams of respawning enemy soldiers, and there is no real challenge in each fight. You have a lot of health and don't have to worry about dodging bullets or any surprising elements, and can literally take on wave after wave of soldiers without ever risking to lose face-to-face in any single fight. The only real "threat" is that you can get overwhelmed by enemy soldiers if they spawn faster than you can pick them off, can't find enough ammo or medkits to sustain your slowly decreasing health through long lasting battles.
- The mission objectives are annoying at times. They aren't very challenging, it's just that sometimes you get lost trying to figure out the one and only possible way to progress. It's often a bit unclear how to perform the objectives, and if you don't perform the objectives exactly as the devs have scripted them, you'll get stuck and run around cluelessly for ages trying to figure out what to do, while constantly spraying down new respawning waves of enemy soldiers. There is usually only one single way, and no alternatives to make progress and therefore the objective line feels very linear.
- Initially I and my friends had technical issues and the game wouldn't launch, but we found a solution on google. Maybe not relevant to the game itself, but it says something about the professionalism of the developer.
The game isn't horrible, but maybe it's just not my kind of game. I can only speak for myself. I'd have appreciated it more if the game had involved more tactical play, focused more on fun objectives, and if they had added more challenge to each fight instead of leaving you to spray down easy enemies in masses. But I guess it is fun if you appreciate a lot of constant shooting and spraying.

UPDATE:
I own both the Steam and GOG versions of this game, and natively, neither one plays nicely with Windows 10.
For the Steam version, on Windows 7/8/10, the functionality of this game is a crapshoot. Even if you are willing to try the various fixes, patches, and moving/renaming of various installation files, it still feels like the game will only work on its own terms, when it wants to. When I still had Windows 7 back in 2015, I was able to get the Steam version of the game to function after some doing. However, what worked for me in 7 did not work for me in 10.
The top-rated customer review on GOG says that the GOG version works well on modern systems - this may be true for Windows 7, but on Windows 10, I'm having headaches similar to the Steam version.
The best luck I've had on Windows 10 has been using a wrapper that helps smooth the relationship between modern operating systems and the old Voodoo graphics API used in a lot of early 3D PC games. It's called dgVoodoo and is referred to in this Steam discussion thread:
. You can also download it from the developer's website:
. It's not perfect, but if it works for you, it will make the game much less frustrating to load and play.
* You can try using Compatibility Modes in Windows, and nVidia users may be able to make use of a legacy driver. Check out this guide for more information:
* Turning off 3D Acceleration / Hardware Acceleration in the options menu may help solve color/functionality issues with your game. It will limit your resolution options, but it may make the game playable for you. Sometimes the game has crashed while I've had this enabled, and sometimes it has crashed while I've had it disabled.
* Adding the -devmode runtime option enables a debug menu that may have some helpful options. More information in this discussion thread:
As for the game, it's a classic. An FPS that puts a lightsaber in your hands was mindblowing in 1997, and the platforming controls still feel good to play with. Once you get maximum points in Force Speed and Force Jump, you can zoom all over the enormous levels and play in big vertical sandboxes. Kyle Katarn is basically a mix of Han Solo and Luke Skywalker, and in the Expanded Universe he's supposed to be the best lightsaber fighter out there, so that's cool too.
ORIGINAL REVIEW:
I love the game itself, but the Steam version is not optimized to run on modern computers and is a real headache to get working, if indeed it will work at all. Seek out alternative purchasing options. I hear the GOG version works well on modern hardware.
Get the GOG version. It works outside of the box, but this one requires modding that doesn't always work when its done. The GOG version also has the expansion included.

While I do not have an abundance of hours clocked on this game, I did have the disc when it came out in 2003. Since then, I have played that thing to death: memorizing enemy locations, the stats of certain characters, and the best weapons combinations. Why? Because not only does this game have excellent gameplay, but no matter how many times you beat it, you can always find better ways to play, or cooler ways to succeed.
The positive aspects of the game are inherent to the gameplay - being a tactical shooter, Rainbow Six 3 (Raven Shield) with its expansions let you use maps to guide ally movements and actions. An example: I know that there is a hostage at the room on the right above the stairs. I can map Green Team, the group I have equipped with heavy assault rifles, to breach the double doors in the center while Red Team, with their silenced weapons, push through the exit in the back, cutting them off quickly. This all happens while I send Gold team to snipe from the runway, ensuring no tangos get the jump on us. We go on the call "Bravo."
It's the most fun I have had playing a Tom Clancy Game.
The negatives come only with the age of the game. It was made in 2003, so the graphics, compared to today, are sub-par. That also means the the AI is a little slow and flawed. Sometimes terrorists can pinpoint your position and pull off a headshot without ever knowing you were there, and sometimes your allies will walk into a full warehouse of badies walking backwards, continuing the slaughter. This can be incredibly aggravating, but these occurences are few and far between.
You have a lot of freedom with gun customization, especially for a game of this particular era, and a lot of freedom with how you plan and execute your missions. This is a must play for any Tom Clancy fan. 8/10
If you enjoy tactical shooters, this is a must.

This is a Parkour game.
There are some resolution sizes available.

There is a master volume slidebar available.
There is a sound volume slidebar available.
There is a music volume slidebar available.
There is a mouse sensitivity slidebar.

The game is fun at some points but at some points really stupid.  You are either a runner or a hunter in an arena, if you are a hunter (which is randomly selected at the start of the beginning), you will have a stop sign as a weapon. You have to find someone and hit a person with the weapon in order to insta kill it - when that person that has died is going to respawn back, he will become the hunter. The runners have to collect points (that looks like pacman balls) that is scattered all over the field. Hitting someone else, will steal some of the collected points in that match. There are 3 rounds, and each time a round is about to end. There will be sudden death.. Here comes the fun part.... If you have died before the sudden death has started. You will remain dead and you can't respawn back. If you get stunned or whatsoever before the sudden death has started. You will be in a disadvantage and most likely die. everyone has an insta kill weapon in sudden death and only has 1 life. At some time the arena match is getting shorter and some zones will be unable to play.
If you are staying in these zones, you will slowly lose HP and eventually die.
Character customization.
Objective less/aimless wandering.
Has sudden death but can be unfair at points.
Level progression.
Matches are relative short.
Alot of loading time (joining/leaving lobbies and finding connection to server)

Great game, fantastic graphics, superb music, great gameplay.
Best played with friends, but beware:  Local co-op is a joke, and the the way that split-screen / menu management works out looks and behaves terrible.  Mutiplayer co-op is a far better experience.
Overall a fun and enjoyable game, but it has some flaws:
- It can get very grindy and repetitve around mid-to-late game.  It picks up quick enough for the end-game content, but that mid-game stretch is exhausting.
- The levels are repetitive.  The level design is largely superb, but get used to playing them over and over again for different missions.
- The crafting system is a great addition but also increases the grindiness tenfold as certain rare materials have depressingly-low drop rates.  A small gameplay change could fix that, I think--giving the player the ability to combine mundane materials together to get quality materials comes to mind--but in lieu of that, get used to checking the wiki early and often.
Despite the grindiness, the game ends on a great note, and I highly recommend it.  Here's hoping for a sequel!

One of my very first forays into the inescapable depths that is the roguelike genre. I've put hundreds of hours into this game (not on the Steam version) and still pop back in every once in a while when I want to experience a true roguelike game. I would highly recommend this as a gateway drug into the realm of roguelikes for any newcomers to the genre. It's got a very easy to use GUI (no need for all the crazy keyboard commands), a talent tree which many gamers are used to seeing when developing characters, and a tileset, for those that can't read ASCII.
While I haven't played it as much, some of the common complaints are that the early game feels a bit grindy. The lack of a hunger clock sort of encourages visiting all early level dungeons, even if you can stomp over them. Some "unfair" deaths by some combinations of powers that some rares/uniques have. This can be especially frustrating, but TOME's adventure mode gives several lives (Gasp, the horror!), which does help to at least mitigate that frustration a bit.
The game is fairly lengthy, and the replayability of the game is amazing. Many of the classes have a very distinct feel to them, which makes it fun to experiment with various character builds. The most frustrating thing about this game is that it takes a while to build up a character the way you want it, and then a harsh combination of a boss can easily wipe it out if you are like me and refuse to skip places and come back to it later.
Overall, a great game to try out and play. If you're on the fence about "buying/donating" to this game. You can play this game for free on
. You will get access to nearly everything that a donator would so you really won't be missing much, but if you enjoy it, I recommend you toss some $$ towards the DarkGod since he's done an amazing thing with this game.

I bought this game in the steam sale, looking for a small indie game to play in the holidays, and I have to say I think I'm in love. I've honestly not made this much fun playing a platformer since the sonic games on the mega drive, and it may be my favourite indie game ever.
Goods
-Amazing level design (on par with Hidetaka Miyazaki's level design)
-Very unique magic system
-Interesting level up system
-Clever mechanics (in the form of brands)
-Enjoyable platforming sections, that aren't forced upon you
-Draws from the souls games, but remains unique
-Non-linear progression (areas can be tackled in many different orders)
-Enjoyable story if you look for it
-Fun local co-op
Bads
-Initially clunky gamepad controls (however these can be remapped)
-A fair few glitches (I managed to make a boss fall through the floor, killing it instantly)
-Large disparity in difficulty (difficulty leaps and dives between areas)
-No Online Multiplayer
Overall, I'm having great fun with this game, and strongly recomend it.
