This game is phenomenal. A 2D RPG Dark Souls  platformer.
The levelling up system uses a talent sphere like FFX or PoE. Different builds feel very distinctive. You can branch any starting character into anything you feel like.
There are a number of secret areas and bosses which reward exploration, although there was nothing which felt like a game breaking item which was a must have, so I felt like I could explore areas naturally whithout a demon on my shoulder telling me to go everywhere and get everything. This also made other play throughs a lot more enjoyable as I found areas and items I didn’t the first time through.
The atmosphere, lore and theme is excellent, and the game feels very well polished.
I think the fear factor is also implemented incredibly well. Starting the game I pooed my pants a few times, but then later in the game, as my confidence built, felt perhaps the game wasn’t as fear inducing as the Dark Souls franchise. Then a couple of giant spiders would drop on my head, I’d scream like a little girl and reflexively throw my controller at the screen, then spend some time gibbering before stepping outside for some fresh air and sunlight.
My only complaints would be the limited soundtrack (which is excellent, just very repetitive) and areas which feel small after you’ve been through them a few times. There are loads of very distinctive bosses though, which is awesome.
Tl;dr Excellent 2D RPG Darks Souls platformer. It’s amazing. Buy it.

First of all. This game suffers from an obvious rushed release. It runs on a dated engine which has none of the improvements from the updated Diesel engine of Payday 2 despite the fact that it has the same publisher behind it.
Singleplayer, you ask? The squad/friendly AI is completely brain dead. Instead of improving the squad AI because of how utterly useless it is, they went out of their way to significantly buff the enemy AI despite all of the feedback they received. From higher HP to damage output to downright aimbotting. The AI, in general, is just awful. Hence those blunt, amateur changes. Don't bother getting this unless you have somebody to play with from the same region. Joining a game from across the globe is fraught with latency issues (rubberbanding, teleporting enemies etc.) thanks to the game's wonderful peer to peer netcode.
The grind is atrocious and the game does very little to reward you for it. Yes. They've added a couple of new weapons but to unlock any of the primary weapons requires a considerable amount of grind. It's ♥♥♥♥ing absurd how grindy it is and rivals free to play titles in that regard. I made it to the 20's with all of my 4 classes/characters and just simply got tired of it. If i need to farm specific maps to earn a reasonable amount of XP, your game is ♥♥♥♥ing broken! And it most certainly is. In many ways.
Boy, is this thing prone to random crashes and it's getting worse with each new patch. And these amateurs can't even point you to the crash log of the game. This is a glorified and highly unstable Payday mod with a hefty price tag. And that's me being complimentary.
It went on sale for $10 a month after its release for a reason.
Also, i think it's safe to say that most of their budget went towards John Cleese's performance fee.

Fidget Spinner has sheer freedom and sense of adventure is a remarkable achievement. Right from the start, the vast landscape of Blue Planet is thrown completely open to you, and it constantly finds ways to pique your curiosity with mysterious landmarks, complex hidden puzzles, and enemy camps to raid for treasure and weapons. The fact that you can tackle any one of these things at your own pace and almost never get pulled to the main path is liberating, but the way all of Fidget Spinner's systems fit elegantly into complex light survival game is even more impressive. I’ve been running around for over 11 hours and I still have plenty of mysteries left to track down and lots of wonderfully crafted puzzles to solve. I’m in awe of the scope and scale of this adventure, and I often find myself counting the hours until I can get back in.
The untamed, post-apocalyptic, techno-fantasy land of Hitler is the main character in this title. Not only is it vast, beautiful, and filled with a diverse set of locations from grassy fields to craggy alpine mountains, but it follows surprisingly realistic rules that let you pull off solutions so intuitive that you might be surprised they actually work. The trees bear fruit, grass fields can be set ablaze, and even enemies and animals behave in a believable manner, based on the skittish and aggressive reactions I’ve seen in the wild. But the realistic touches don’t end there. Each object you encounter, from sticks to apples to rocks and metallic blocks, is made of a material, and those materials usually respond to forces like fire and magnetism as you’d expect.
But what elevates Fidget Spinner is above its open-world contemporaries is its sheer freedom, both in its non-linear questing structure and in your ability to climb almost any surface and travel in any direction once you leave the starting area. It is the heart of what makes this action-adventure game truly special and addictive. Like many open-world games it delivers on the implied promise that if you can see it out in the distance, chances are you can eventually reach it – but here, figuring out how to get there is more often than not a satisfying puzzle in itself, and one that never gets old. For instance, a tantalizing island far off the coast of the mainland was just out of my paragliding reach for the first several hours until after I’d upgraded my abilities. When I finally did, what took place when I finally reached my objective was a great twist that blew my mind – including finding an easier alternate route I’d missed.
The Gaben fidget spinner is easily one of the most useful tools in the game because it's so versatile. You can use it to effortlessly glide across lakes and gaps or ride updrafts into new areas, and I often used each long trip across the map as a way to scan the marvelously lit horizon in search of clues or meditate on what I need to do next.

Before I begin this review, I should make it clear I have in total bought 9 copies of this game. This review will be written starting with a pros and cons summary list followed by an in depth look into the game. This review will conclude with a final rating.
- Fidget Spinner Spins
- Well Paced Progression System
- Decent Music
- Good Graphics
- Lots Of Spinners To Choose From
- No End Game
- NEEDS MORE SPINNERS
- No Longer Have A Life Or Friends
Now that we have the pros and cons of the game covered, we may begin to delve deeper into the true review of this unparalleled and unprecedented game, possibly the greatest of the century (or maybe even of all time).
When you open up this innovative masterpiece, you are greeted by a beautiful, captivating main menu, the likes of which grabs your attention and holds it both visually and audibly. The exquisite layout of different fidget spinners provides but a taste of the fidgety goodness of which you are about to be immersed. These are tastefully interspersed with a few quirky comments, a couple of social media buttons and the main menu UI. One could say that this UI is somehow lacking, however I feel as though it feeds nicely into a minimalistic theme of sorts. As amazing as the visuals of the main menu prove to be, they incomparable to the stunning audio of the main menu. You are instantly mesmerized by the spellbounding power contained within the extraordinary and thrilling lyrics you are met with when you first open this game. This is, however, only the main menu.
Once you somehow manage to drag yourself from the perfect and somehow utopian main menu, you are met with the actual game screen itself. The words previously used to describe the main menu would only understate the game screen itself, doing it both a disservice and an injustice. Neither the English language, nor any other, contains words which could even begin to describe the perfectness of which is this screen. As such I shall simply describe it. In the top left corner lays your money count next to a green money symbol. Underneath this a black bar which counts how many spins your spinner completes each round. If you reach certain milestones by filling this bar, you get more money per spin every round. In the bottom left, there is round button containing the picture of a fidget spinner. This allows you to change the look of your spinner once you level up. In the middle bottom, a round button with a dial on it. This allows you to use money to increase the speed of your spinner, allowing you to reach higher and higher milestones. The bottom right button allows you to change settings (currently only sound as all your graphical settings are open for change only when you open the game). Above this is the main menu button, if ever you feel the grasp of the immaculate main menu pull you back in. Up next is a funny. In the top right corner is how many spins a minute your spinner is doing, or in layman's terms, how fast your spinner is currently moving. In the middle of your screen is how many swipes you have left this round. Finally, above this, you have your spinner itself.
Every round you are blessed with 5 swipes. These allow you to move the spinner in a clockwise motion, with each spin being counted underneath the black bar on your top left. You must figure out the best methid to gain the most amount of spins possible. Some people are natural spinners and will get how to do this easily and quickly. Others have not been so blessed and will require hours, if not years of training. However I strongly believe it is possible for all to spin to the highest level possible with the right trainer and training. While I would never claim to be the best spinner in the world, I am certainly happy to point people in the right direction towards getting more spins on their spinners.
Overall, gameplay is smooth and the progression sytem is very well paced. Whenever the game feels it is just beginning to get a little boring, you unlock a new fidget spinner and the flood of excitement rushes over you all over again as if it were are new game you were beginning to play, even though at this point it has taken over your life, you have lost your job, your wife and your kids. The only gripe I would have with this game is that the end game is somewhat lacking. You eventually reach a point where the milestone needed to fill the black bar is massive and it takes a long time to unlock all the speed unlocks to progress to the next milestone. Now, while I would usually accept this as a very good feature as it adds an element of perseverance and extra challenge, basically adding hundreds of hours, if not an eternity, of gameplay to this game, it causes me to look up from my computer at the homeless shelter which has become my home after recently losing my apartment after not being able to pay rent after I quit my job to become a full time spinner.
This game is literally perfect in every single way imaginable and many that cannot be imagined and must be seen to be seen. It is because of this I have determined that this game is created by a being higher than ourselves. While I have lost my wife, kids, job, apartment and life thanks to this game, I still recommend it highly as I now consider it to be my wife, kids, job and life as well as the only shelter I need. I no longer need actual human interaction or meaning in my life. Honestly, this is all I need.

In more detail:
I have a love hate relationship with this game.
90% of it is great. It could be my favorite strategy game of all time. However the other 10% (namely bugs, a couple of broken/illogical mechanics, and terrible AI) completely ruins it.
Its one of those games where you endure hours of frustration thinking youre doing something wrong, or that it will somehow get better, only to eventually find out youre not doing anything wrong, and it does NOT get better. Game is just broken.
On one hand, UI is VERY well designed IMO and most game mechanics are well tought out. Graphics are beautiful, music is superb, and the game is relatively easy to understand.
However, for me the following points turn the game into a frustrating exerience rather than an entertaining one:
- No point in using the excellent tactical & strategical systems the game provides, when the AI is so utterly useless that you can just select every unit you start with, order an attack, and watch the game "win itself".
- Serious bugs in the game have made it impossible for me to finish it. A country has dissapeared from the map (because it has no more land), and is both my enemy AND a member of my faction! (a member of the axis like me). I cant kick it out of my faction, and i cant attack it. So the game wont end because there is still a war going on. There go 40 hours of play out to the trash.
- When you defeat a country (it capitulates), if this country is part of an aliance you dont really defeat it. Its goverment "goes into exile". In reality what it means is that the country dissapears (it holds no more land) but the game does not credit you for beating it, untill you defeat ALL members of its alliance. This leads to you fighting poland (as germany) untill 1946.
- Dont bother thinking of defence, game will never be a real threat to you.
- For some season, The land you conquer does NOT go to your country if you launch the attack from an allied territory, it will go to your ally. Add to this the unrealistically short range of paratrooers, and how cumbersome naval invations are, the result is that you end up spending time conquering africa to see it go to italy, or india to watch it go to afganistan. Most of the land you conquer does not go to your country.
- Complete lack of ability to set victory conditions. This and the fact that most of the time you dont get what you captured (as described above), make the whole war efford feel pointless. You feel you dont ever "win" or capture anything.
- No user manual exsists for this game. For a game with so many concepts and things to know such as this one, there is no documentation! Instead you are to rely on some "wiki" wich is mostly incomplete, and with lots of empty pages. I guess it was too much trouble to actually write and mantain a users manual.
- Airforce is pretty much useless. It doesnt make almost any diference to attack with it or not.
- Where other asects of the ui are great, managing your naval forces is cumbersome, unintuitive and troublesome. You cant even select units on the map!
- No concept of reconnaissance in the game. You can have your airforce flying over enemy land, and still you wont know what is there.
- This
game has no concept of fuel or money. Im not kidding!
Yes there is the concept of oil, but you only need it to build the tanks, planes, etc. Once you built them, you can use them at will even if you have zero oil.
Money? nah, armies are payed for with popcorn right? and trade? you pay for traded goods with... "factories". Because that makes perfect sense right?
But you know what the WORSE part is?
Paradox greedy, arrogant attitude. They are more concerned in selling us DLC than fixing the bugs.
Yes, yes, they say "they are working on it, and will release a free patch WITH the DLC". But months and months go by and we have to wait untill they finish their dlc before we can play the game we allready paid for.
They seldom intervene in the forums (even their own), and when they do is to block threads and defend their product. Never to help, issue an ETA on the "patch" or do anything helpfull.

(In future may write a longer review, but as it is on sale right now, here is my recommendation in short form)
Tales of Maj'Eyal (ToME) is extremely good at what it is- a roguelike of the dungeoncrawler RPG type, that can also be played as a more regular RPG with limited or infinite lives. Combat is a fairly quick turn-based system, that requires a decent amount of care as death is quite easy to come by. Items, statistics, and talents are complex yet fairly easy to parce, with items especially having a wide variety of possible enchantments and special effects, along with many unique items. There are a wide variety of character classes and races, some of fairly traditional RPG stripe and some highly unique, most of which unlock with play.
Both as a roguelike and as an RPG, ToME has extremely high-quality lore and worldbuilding- every unique item has some kind of description or history, many of the bosses and areas have reasons for existing, and Maj'Eyal, the world, itself has an interesting history and substantially long questline (which is also quite difficult- while playing without infinite lives, I have never come close to beating it)

I love this game. This game was one of my very first gaming experiences. Before Neopets. Before Pokemon. Before my PS1 and Xbox. Before Warcraft 3 and Diablo and all the other good stuff. I used to play this all the time with my dad, and as such constitutes some of my fondest childhood memories.
Anyway, let's dive right in.
This game has technical issues. The menus are locked to 800x600 (?) resolution, though the game itself supports much higher resolutions. It did 1080p just fine for me. However, due to the different resolutions, your resolution will fluctuate whenever you enter/leave the menus. Kind of annoying, but no big deal. You better get used to the low resolution though, because you'll be spending a lot of time in the planning menu. Which brings me to my next point...
This is not your typical action FPS. It's relatively slow paced and you spend a lot of time planning things out. There are 3 teams you can customize. You can outfit each team member with different armor, weapons, weapon attachments, various types of grenades, and various utility tools. During planning you can dictate where your teams go, how they go there, what they do when the reach there, etc.
For example, you might want green and gold team to wait for your signal ("Alpha, go!") before they clear a particular room.
- Want one team to throw a smoke and the other to throw a flashbang before doing storming the room? Done.
- Locked door? No problem, tell them to breach it first.
- Hostages? Throw some tear gas in. Don't worry, you can outfit your guys with gas masks.
There is a ton of ways to complete missions. You can take control of a team as well, and co-ordinate with the other teams in clearing a level.
AI sometimes spotty. On occasions the AI will get stuck bumping into one another, or they'll be looking in stupid directions while taking fire. Most of the time though the AI is quite capable. You'll see your teams moving in formation, covering for one another. They'll strafe into rooms. I've actually been saved by my AI companion more times than I can count, so they're certainly not a burden.
There is auto-aim, but you can turn it off. You can also configure how sensitive you want the auto-aim to be.
There is a lot of trial and error. Your plans will not work on the first try. You'll be going through the level halfway when one of your teams starts getting killed off. Then you'll go back to the planning stage and try to rectify the flaws in your master plan. Maybe green team should throw a smoke before storming this particular room. Maybe you should reposition gold team so that they can better cover fire for green team. This is as much a strategy game as it is an action one.
Another this is that death is permanent. You have a roster of soldiers, and if they die during a mission, they will not be available for subsequent missions. This gives you an incentive to complete missions with minimum casualties. Soldiers can be wounded too, making them move slower and have slower reflexes. Wounded soldiers recover after a couple missions.
This game is fantastic, but it's not for everyone. It can't really be compared to anything else on the market. Unfortunately the Rainbow Six series is no longer the tactical shooter it once was.

Before you read this review, I'm not going to go over much gameplay at all or even mention the new features or anything like that, but rather point out an issue that has sucked a lot of enjoyment out of the series for me, firstly with '17 and now even more-so with '18. I've commented on the discussion forums about it, and then shared these concerns on the Sports Interactive forums, both fell on deaf ears, hence this review.
I've put countless hours into FM over the years, but the past two editions meant I've found myself less immersed due to the simple fact that regens and how they look must be way down on the list of importance for Sports Interactive. Last year we had the alien looking faces like something straight out of Middle Earth, now we have clay-like faces and mud for hair that Maddame Tussaud herself wouldn't even exhibit.
I understand that the gameplay/3D match engine is a big deal for the developers at the moment, but for someone like me who enjoys long saves where the whole of my team will be regens, having about 6 or 7 hairstyles that all look terrible and faces that look like less detailed than their 2008 counterparts takes the personality and immersion from the game.
What makes it worse is that with the new 3D face models (most pointless feature ever because the majority of players don't zoom right in on player faces in game) you can't even use talented modder's resources to make them look more varied, such as Emil Debski's fantastic hair pack. This game has actually forced Emil into retirement, that's how bad the graphical steps backward are, one of the most talented modders in the community has boycotted the series.
Maybe SI are trying to make them look better for the long run, the 3D models will have a lot more flexibility regarding future tweaks. For now though, it clearly isn't ready to be implemented yet. The old regen style from FM'16 and before looked way better, and with added hairstyles from content creators, helped players feel distinguishable from one another which really helped the immersion-factor.
It might not be a massive issue to some but it's practically ruined the prospect of long saves for me, knowing that all my players are going to look incredibly similar and have the same play-doh hairstyles. Thanks SI. Thanks a lot.

First, Evolve Stage 2 is considered a new game compared to its predecessor. The overall tone of the game has been altered to support more action, rather than a game of hide and seek. While I prefered the old way, this new variation is for the better. Heres why:
To start, Evolve is difficult to describe.The people at Turtle Rock Studios have made a game that is akin to an orchestra. Everything is thought out and well rehearsed. The terrain, wild life, characters, vegetation and monsters all come together to form a game that is truely special.
However, Evolve was something people didnt really appreciate. The formula wasnt right for many. From my prior experience, it felt a bit like a walking simulator. You would spend alot of time walking around following trails, searching for the monster. Trapping was considered a skill because monsters were very good at hiding until they got stronger. In otherwords, there was alot of idle time within matches if you werent very skilled.
Personally, with a game this beautiful, I enjoyed the idle time. You had a moment to breathe and take in everything.
Now, Evolve Stage 2 took away this element. They took away the hunting and replaced it with the hunt. Hunters are constantly chasing the monster due the ease of tracking. Monsters can still run, but they can no longer hide.
Ultimately, Evolve Stage 2 feels like it has taken a step back because it still feels like its trapped in an old shell. The new gameplay itself doesnt work with the atmosphere they had created. I understand the need for change when going F2P, but TRS could have added new content to support the new game.
Hopefully they add such content soon. There is an empty spot in my trophy room, waiting for that snapshot. You know, the one of me arm choking the monster's carcass.
TLDR: Its better because there are players....

TL;DR: Mercenary is a 2D platforming shooter that's reminiscing the classic such as the metal slug with a hint of Scott Pilgrim vs. the World to it's art style. If you're a fan of metal slug you should definitely try this title. If you're not a fan of metal slug that's probably because you've never played it before then you should definitely try this title to see what you're missing out on *wink* *wink*
I do however have a few criticism to make on this title. Keep in mind that these elements are, for the most part, optional, therefore, it's completely possible to avoid doing them and just focus on the core element.
Firstly, the concept of boss arena. In short, some of the later bosses that you must kill in order to clear the level. However, they could spawn at any one of the several spawning spots, which forces you to track them down, dish out as much damage as you can, then maybe watch helplessly as the boss decides to move to a different location which forces you to track them down again. Thankfully, the second time the boss is marked on the mini map. On top of that you can take on a mod chip that marks the boss for you. Which takes up a valuable mod ship spot. Which leads me to my next point.
The Grinding. There's a lot of weapon in this game. Which in turns required a lot of materials to build them. Which in turns requires a lot of grinding. Again, if you're one of those people who hates grinding. You can simply Google one of those top weapons guide. Focus on acquiring a set or two that works for you and forget about the rest.
To sum it up. The grinding is a bit tedious. But it's mostly optional. To enjoy the core experience you probably just need to acquire one or two sets of weapon and probably won't use anything else for the most part. A must buy. 8.5/10.

This is an occasionally interesting but really flawed action game. Several things about Mercenary Kings are great, but the whole package is ultimately bogged down by a series of odd and sometimes flat-out awful design choices. Let’s start with the good: the graphics are great and the art direction/character design work by Paul Robertson is awesome. It’s obviously not as gory, scandalous, or surreal as his usual stuff, but it’s still fantastic and it’s what first drew me to the game. Every sprite has tons of personality; I almost didn’t want to kill the bosses because they look so great (otherwise, interacting with the bosses isn't that fun, but more on that in a minute). The crafting system in the game is also quite deep and there are a lot of cool ways to create a wide assortment of unique guns and knives. If you’re into collecting a bunch of materials and creating your own gear, you should enjoy this feature.
However, these positive aspects aren’t enough to make up for the drawbacks. The game looks at first glance like a fast-paced run and gun along the lines of Metal Slug, but it’s actually very slow, plodding, and even boring. The whole thing is really repetitive – you find yourself in the same jungles, mountains, and enemy hideouts over and over, facing a relatively small variety of enemies. Most of the common enemies are bullet sponges that can take a long time to kill, and they respawn extremely quickly. I mean, if you even breathe near the edge of the screen, everybody you just killed will instantly come back. The maps are really big and the game wants you to explore them – many of the missions are fetch quests or hostage rescue missions where you have to look all over the map for captured prisoners. However, the enemies have so much health and they respawn so quickly that I didn’t want to bother getting to know the maps.
All of this respawning makes the maps really uninviting. This becomes a problem when you fight the bosses; at a certain point in the fight, the bosses run away, and you have to slog through the map, which includes all of the same old enemies that you just labored through, to track the boss down and kill it (unless it runs away *yet again*). It just feels like a chore and it wasn't fun at all. On top of this, every mission has a time limit. Couldn’t find that last hostage because the map is too big and every part of it just looks like the same generic jungle? Couldn’t find that boss again after already fighting it two times? Too bad – time’s up! I felt like the game didn't really respect or care about my time as a player.
So yeah, I know the art looks great, but I'd recommend just appreciating it from afar. The game itself is annoying at best and aggressively boring in many ways. There are aimless fetch quests, repetitive stages, frustrating design quirks, and it all felt like a slog instead of a fun, fresh, compelling adventure. I'm pretty disappointed to give this one a thumbs down, but the problems are way too deep.

I have 100+ hours on this game already - and that's on Steam only;  you can get a free non-Steam version of ToME on its website - so I feel it's time to make a review.
First things first, it's a roguelike alright: permadeath, randomized world, tile-based graphics, yadda yadda. And yet it's a great introduction to the roguelike genre, because there are options to play it with a number of lives, or even unlimited ones, to get the hang of the game! Not EVERYTHING is randomized (there are fixed artifacts, fixed locations, etc but it still feels like a roguelike). Also, it contains intuitive UI and gameplay. For example, there are practically no consumables like potions and scrolls - not in the sense we're accostumed to. Instead, your powers (and some items) have cooldowns along with, naturally, some resource management (stamina, mana, psi, etc.). Cast X spell/move? Wait Z turns to use it again. Or, maybe, use some talent that can reset some cooldowns ;-). That cooldown system is really intuitive and just one of the many reasons I'm in love with ToME.
Now let's talk about the world. I'm not an old ToME follower but unless I'm mistaken, it used to be set in Tolkien's Middle-Earth, until it was changed to a more original lore. And it's a great lore: the continent of Eyal was, some time ago, devastated by catatrophic used of magic (i.e the Spellblaze), there are still mage hunters (Zigur), there are political issues (Halflings are militaristic and even used to slave Yeeks); heck, even the demons have a touching and fantastic backstory! So, in terms of lore, the game has good stuff to offer. Some of the actual places are very creative, too: tunnels of sand that can collapse and swallow the uncautious adventurer, underwater ruins, necromancer dens, forests, deserts, and so on...
In terms of races/classes, there are 11 races and 26 classes, allowing for tons of builds. There are your classic warriors (Bulwark, Berserker), mages (Archmage, Necromancer) and even exotic classes that can manipulate things like their foes' dreams (Solipsist), draconic powers (Wyrmic) and even time itself (Temporal Warden, Paradox Mage)! Most of the races and classes are unlocked as you progress in the game and do certain tasks, which aren't too hard, honestly. But if you're impatient, then you can look for an addon (mod) that unlocks everything right out of the bat. ;-)
Anyway, it's getting too long. I typed all of that to convice you to PLAY THE GAME. Seriously, play it. It's great, no matter if you're a roguelike veteran or new to the genre (like me, actually)!

This game was and is the pinnacle of tactical shooters, it was a serious improvement on the already amazing original Rainbow Six games and it was the last installment of the Rainbow Six series that kept the spirit of the original. Though I did enjoy them, The Rainbow Six Vegas games were a little watered down to cater to the casual gamer compared to Raven Shield and Athena Sword. In fact, I believe this was the last decent and truely "realistic" tactical FPS. There are tons of maps in this game that allow for play styles varying from precise, patient and meticulously planned long range engagements to savage, fast paced and adrenaline fueled Close Quarters Battle. There is a massive selection of weapons, attachments, class specific items and even ammunition types allowing the player to tailor their kit to their play style. The armory is bigger than any game that I can think of. Because of this, the replayability of this game is endless.
While it continues to be surprisingly entertaining for a game released in 2003, it is beginning to show it's age and lacks some of the innovative features seen in modern games. The player cannot look down the iron sights of the weapons. Unless optics are mounted on the weapon, the right mouse button only causes a zoom effect. Also the graphics are a bit obsolete. The installation of the Ravenshield 2.0 mod fixes this, however, by improving textures and adding many of the features (including iron sights) that we as gamers have become accustomed to in the last decade.
To summarize, if you haven't played this game and you crave a challenging, thinking man's tactical shooter over the mindless run and gun FPS' you get these days you need this in your Steam library. If I can play this game consistently for over a decade without it getting old, I'm pretty sure you can get at least 100 hours out of it. Do yourself a favor and pull the trigger on this one, you won't regret it.

RAID: World War II is a co-op, 4 player vs Army of AI type of game, my personal favorite genre.
It has ties to Payday 2 in the sense that it uses the same engine, so if you played PD2 then the controls, gameplay mechanics and all are the same. In my opinon making the game easy to pick up because the skills learned in PD2 apply well here (such as shooting, tactics, and controls).
I have heard a lot of pessimism with the release of this game, mostly including that it's a re-skin of Payday 2. While I can understand why people get this vibe from the game, it is simply not true. RAID: World War II is a game about stopping Hitler's advancement to world power. You play as a special ops type group, cherry picked from the best of the best, to execute plans to stop Hitler's rise to world domination...while stealing some gold along the way :P (This is NOT the main goal of the game and was added to give players some extra things to grab while on missions)
Payday 2 on the other hand is a game about bank robbers who's only goal is to make lots of money and become uber rich. Also Payday 2 takes place in the modern world, while RAID, obviously takes place between 1939-1945, during WWII.
Which gives the game a completely different vibe than PD2. You use guns and technology from the WWII era in RAID, which is cool.
I'm not trying to put this game above or below PD2 because I think RAID: World War II is a game in it's own right, seperate from anything.
In conclusion: I highly recommend this game! :D

For the time being, I'm not going to recommend this game. This could change within the coming months but for now I'll share some of the major problems with this game and look at the reason why with some improvement it can really take off.
The raids themselves are excellent for the most part but lack replayability, even on the higher difficulties they don't have any major challanges in them, they feel more suited to a single player campaign game because there is an undeniable flow to the objectives with almost no resistance or challenge in most cases which is something the likes of Payday managed to overcome. Really it just needs some extra obstacles adding to some Raids and more basic raids adding, something on a smaller scale with more objectives, simillar to Paydays bank heists for example.
The characters, classes and special abilities are cool but feel very out of place all things considered. The characters are designed and voiced great, they got this spot on to be fair. Each special ability works well on it's own but considering it's a co-op game there's no real benefit for using them at the same time, not to mention some a clearly far better than others. The class system is pointless, completely pointless and kills a lot of the fun for me. In a blatant attempt to break away from the mould Payday set they spoiled a lot of aspects. The skills are dreadful, there's no real enhancement to survivabilty in any of the trees, just skills that slightly enhance character and weapon stats or speed up timers making the clear grind to level up so much more painful. But by far the biggest problem of this is how simillar each set is so every character plays the same which in turn, chucks the weapon and weapon unlock system under the bus.
Moving onto the weapon system I have very mixed feelings. The weapon unlock system is boring and makes an already terrible grind even worse. The game launched with too few guns and there isn't enough haste to add more sadly. With specific guns being locked to classes or working best with specific classes the clear early staleness of the game gets even more stale especially since you need to grind each character to use specific weapons. Since the game lacks any economy and everythings techincally free except cosmetics they're needs to be more requirements to unlock these weapons such as finding weapon parts or actually allowing us to buy them with gold. I actually really like the attachment unlock system, yaaaaaaaaaaaaaay.
To mop up a few final thoughts, I found John Cleese's cameo forced and an unnecesary ploy to sell the game as he appears for about a minute total. I find the camp/base ugly, realistically if I can have the option to buy a golden toilet cosmetic I should be allowed to remove some of the rubble and fix some walls. Finally, the community is honestly stellar, as a very long time player of Payday 2 and seeing how the player base transitioned over time, this feels like Payday when the BBQ pack was released, which in fact was my favourite time playing Payday so I'm very thankful towards the player base as well for being so pleasant.

If you ever felt like FPS games today were just shooting galleries, then you should probably pick up this game.
I was there, I fought the war against Supersoldier-Nazi-Terrorists from the future. I played Rainbow Six on the console and I beat it once... only once. The game has you playing against Supersoldier-Nazi-terrorists from the future, seriously you should watch the intro... that's the only way I can explain the story, for America. You thought CoD: World at War was deep? This game is deeper. This game is about fighting for America.... in Switzerland.
As a fun, challenging game, Rainbow Six has you taking control of up to three teams and with you planning out their movements along with placing checkpoints yourself. As you start the mission and having your teams following their pre-constructed paths, they will all inevitably die to the incredible aim of the Super-soldier-Nazi-Terrorists (I always manually take control of teams and members to make sure no one dies). Still, it was much easier than the console version which basically had you and three other guys (or four, I forgot) with no backup and running into a whole lotta crossfires and traps. Men get blown to pieces by Terrorists with their grenades and you will get cutdown mercilessly by molten metal fired from the barrels of hidden guns.
This game is easier, with the ability to pre-plan your movements and the ability to take control of multiple teams and team members. This game isn't about twitch shooting or aim, it's about precaution. Precaution as in, "Don't run in clear view of a sniper you dumb♥♥♥♥." The game doesn't hold your hand and requires a lot of luck at times, but in all honesty it is how you plan and how you plan to execute it along with a plan B if everything goes wrong. If you find firefights too frustrating, the game even allows aim assist (the equivalent of aimbotting). You have to anticipate the ♥♥♥♥♥iest situations and how to deal with them. I like the weapons, most of them have different stats and have situational advantages during some missions. However, shotguns are completely inaccurate unless you've got a scope on it (which I find strange).
Team members also have stats and it somewhat rewards you for keeping them alive. The more men survive through missions the better stats they get, so they can aim better, run better, etc. Always keep stealth team members with other stealth team members otherwise the other dudes in the group will give them away. Having a balanced number of team members and organizing their equipment is actually.... fun.
I get to choose what weapon to use, what grenades I want and who I want with me. Yeah, the game can get frustrating at times, but mostly it is your fault if you lose. You have to observe enemy movement, study their patrol paths and watch them intently then plan actions accordingly. You can't run in every room throwing a smoke grenade because of your limited supplies. The heartbeat sensors actually make the game easier because you can see where terrorists are going through the walls and doors (console game had thermal vision). You're never supposed to fight the enemy head-on not unless you've put yourself in a advantageous situation (i.e. smoked room enemy can't see you, flash bang renders terrorists unable to fight back etc.).
Multiplayer is also a blast, if you ever get to play just use your Uplay account username and password. I had to play with three or so other guys against hordes of terrorists in the other room with us throwing tear gas this way and that. There are plenty of wonderful pvp and pve levels that has you killing terrorists on top of buildings, in cities, on boats and wherever the strange and unique level designs take you. Did I tell you I got to fight Nazi Terrorists... IN SPACE?!
Go buy it but keep in mind it's tough difficulty and sometimes frustrating nature.

Bottom Line (Updated 07-2017):
If you want a complete/"complex" strategy wargame, but with mechanics that actually make sense, is not full of bugs, with AI that actually works, and expect at least some support from the devs, I suggest you check out Gary Grigsby War in the East, or Decisive campaigns: Barbarossa.
Not only are they both (in my opinion) far superior games, with better mechanics and FAR better AI, the customer support by the devs of those games is
ahead of paradox.
Bottom line:
This could be a GREAT game, but its NOT.
Dont waste your money.
Wait a few years untill its patched, bundled with the sure to come 50 paid DLCs, and with a high disscount.
In more detail:
I have a love hate relationship with this game.
90% of it is great. It could be my favorite strategy game of all time. However the other 10% (namely bugs, a couple of broken/illogical mechanics, and terrible AI) completely ruins it.
Its one of those games where you endure hours of frustration thinking youre doing something wrong, or that it will somehow get better, only to eventually find out youre not doing anything wrong, and it does NOT get better. Game is just broken.
On one hand, UI is VERY well designed IMO and most game mechanics are well tought out. Graphics are beautiful, music is superb, and the game is relatively easy to understand.
However, for me the following points turn the game into a frustrating exerience rather than an entertaining one:
- No point in using the excellent tactical & strategical systems the game provides, when the AI is so utterly useless that you can just select every unit you start with, order an attack, and watch the game "win itself".
- Serious bugs in the game have made it impossible for me to finish it. A country has dissapeared from the map (because it has no more land), and is both my enemy AND a member of my faction! (a member of the axis like me). I cant kick it out of my faction, and i cant attack it. So the game wont end because there is still a war going on. There go 40 hours of play out to the trash.
- When you defeat a country (it capitulates), if this country is part of an aliance you dont really defeat it. Its goverment "goes into exile". In reality what it means is that the country dissapears (it holds no more land) but the game does not credit you for beating it, untill you defeat ALL members of its alliance. This leads to you fighting poland (as germany) untill 1946.
- Dont bother thinking of defence, game will never be a real threat to you.
- For some season, The land you conquer does NOT go to your country if you launch the attack from an allied territory, it will go to your ally. Add to this the unrealistically short range of paratrooers, and how cumbersome naval invations are, the result is that you end up spending time conquering africa to see it go to italy, or india to watch it go to afganistan. Most of the land you conquer does not go to your country.
- Complete lack of ability to set victory conditions. This and the fact that most of the time you dont get what you captured (as described above), make the whole war efford feel pointless. You feel you dont ever "win" or capture anything.
- No user manual exsists for this game. For a game with so many concepts and things to know such as this one, there is no documentation! Instead you are to rely on some "wiki" wich is mostly incomplete, and with lots of empty pages. I guess it was too much trouble to actually write and mantain a users manual.
- Airforce is pretty much useless. It doesnt make almost any diference to attack with it or not.
- Where other asects of the ui are great, managing your naval forces is cumbersome, unintuitive and troublesome. You cant even select units on the map!
- No concept of reconnaissance in the game. You can have your airforce flying over enemy land, and still you wont know what is there.
- This
game has no concept of fuel or money. Im not kidding!
Yes there is the concept of oil, but you only need it to build the tanks, planes, etc. Once you built them, you can use them at will even if you have zero oil.
Money? nah, armies are payed for with popcorn right? and trade? you pay for traded goods with... "factories". Because that makes perfect sense right?
But you know what the WORSE part is?
Paradox greedy, arrogant attitude. They are more concerned in selling us DLC than fixing the bugs.
Yes, yes, they say "they are working on it, and will release a free patch WITH the DLC". But months and months go by and we have to wait untill they finish their dlc before we can play the game we allready paid for.
They seldom intervene in the forums (even their own), and when they do is to block threads and defend their product. Never to help, issue an ETA on the "patch" or do anything helpfull.

The animations are farely good but you won't get to see many of them in the demo (which I recommend playing before purchasing the full game). There are barely any cutscenes in the first act but in the third act they take up easily 30% of the gameplay.
There are a number of negatives but most people over exaggerate on how bad they are. For example if you are walking through a forest path you might get stuck on an invisable object for a second. One thing i found interesting was in different scenes 'Diaz' was voiced by different people. Last issue I have is that they didn't sync the character's mouth animations with the words they were saying which looks odd.
I haven't played the multiplayer much at all and I'm not a big fan of what I played but I never had high expectations for it. I suggest playing the demo before purchasing it. Now the price; I bought this through the Sniper Ghost Trilogy pack for $2.99 US at the christmas sale (without sale it is priced at $19.99 US). I don't recommend that package because the older Sniper Ghost games aren't nearly as good as this one and plus the new one is coming out this year. By its self this game costs $9.99 US which might be a little pricey but if its on sale its a great pick up (it will probably go on sale soon because of Sniper Ghost: Warrior 3 coming this year). I want to point out that its not a complete copy of sniper elite thats a little worst for a cheaper price. I think people got this idea because of the slow-motion bullet cam that are very similar in both games. The system requirements definitely aren't crazy considering you don't even need a single gb of ram to run it.
A tip of advise, when following Diaz or Gomez to dodge enemies they might walk into an area where you would think they would get spotted. Don't then take another path around the area because it looks safer because you will get spotted somehow so just always follow them whereever they go in those parts of the missions.
Lastly the singleplayer will last you a few hours with the great highlights and the multiplayer is average. I was disappointed that it only took about four hours to finish singleplayer I really wanted to continue playing more missions (e.g. don't expect plenty of hours of gameplay). I rate it 8/10, I would of rated it higher if there were less bugs and glitchs but I rated it this high because it keeps you on your toes the whole time.

We used to shrug them off as just being "a little different upstairs," and exclude them from society. We eventually figured that it wouldn't hurt to include these people in society. We were wrong. Good take on the "souls" genre and fixes some of the issues the souls games have, though it creates other problems.  A few things that stuck out to me:
- Build diversity is fixed in that you can't be a "havelmage" or other goofy builds that were obviously unintended in souls games.
- Less weapon selection, which allows more focus on said weapons.  Transmutations aren't inherently improvements, so there's good build variety in weapons.
- Map is very expansive and exploratory, though I felt more easily lost than I did in souls games.  There were times I didn't know where to go next.
- Dodging mechanics are finnicky.  The iframes are generally bad and throw you off if you're used to the iframes given to you in a souls game.
- Certain enemies are flat out unfair (skeletons that teleport to you forever, and never fully form if you have your shield up, as an example), and can move themselves into a boss fight and make the fight worse.  Obviously not intended.
- Magic is strong with possible feedback damage as an offset.  Magic spells aren't too flashy or interesting, but do their job.
- No online mechanics, which hurts long term investment in the game.
Overall I think its a good game and would put it up there along with other souls games.  Its certainly different, but has a good enough feel that would warrant replays.

This is one hell of a good metroidvania / action-RPG.
+ The controls work great, with quick response times and no feeling of clunsyness during combat (I'm playing with Keyboard, not using the default keybinds - the game lets you change them as you wish, I removed mouse keybinds and play with just keyboard).
+ The combat has a great feel to it. Hits feel impactful, different weapons have different swing times, range, impact effect... weapons are more than just numbers.
+ A high number of different hit types and defense types, allowing you to prepare yourself against specific areas or enemies when needed. Say, some enemies might be more resistant against blunt weapons, others might deal heavy fire damage, etc. You can change your equipment accordingly.
+ A sphere-grid-like character development system.
+ While leveling up and equipping new items definitely makes you more powerful, the combat is still primarily focused on actual skill instead of just numbers. If you make mistakes, even considerably weaker opponents can kill you. And if you play it well, you can kill stuff much stronger than you.
+ An open, metroidvania-style map that is heavily interconnected and feels very well-designed.
+ Many little subsystems like Creeds and Devotion that add more depth and replayability to the game.
- While the setting is somewhat interesting, there isn't much of a real narrative or storyline. It's mostly just backdrop to establish the proper atmosphere.

I've played a lot of roguelikes before. Most of them feel like one long dungeon run. Some of them have a sort of level select (crypt of the necrodancer) or progress through different levels (rogues legacy/binding of isaac).
But none of them had the feeling like you were an adventurer, going on YOUR OWN adventure. They kind of drop you in a dungeon and say "have fun, here's your dungeon".
But in TOME (tales of maj'eyal) you got an overworld map. You can go to really difficult areas or fight random adventurers who just roam around. There's towns you can visit and tons of shops.
It's very immersive, especially for a roguelike. It makes me want to play some pen and paper D&D again.
And there's a ton of skills and items you can get. And lots of random events. Many random bosses / minibosses who will destroy you. There's just a TON of content. It's not difficult to get into, although discerning what loot is useful or not is definitely beyond casual.
You can chat with other players, which even in a single player game can add a lot. You can see when people die, which even if you aren't talking to them, is interesting to watch.
And my personal favorite feature is that you can have multiple lives. It's not a great feature in the spirit of roguelikes, but in the spirit of gaming it's fantastic. This is usually an instant "omg this game sucks and isn't a roguelike". But I love everything about these type of RPGs, EXCEPT for the permadeath.
For some reason, finding a mix of roguelike aspects in a non-roguelike RPG is impossible. That is, things like traps, random events, deep character customizations, random/persistent effects, and just general "I have no idea what this will do, but I'll try it". The ONLY game that ever came close to that which I know of is Din's Curse. Although TOME has the feature as a gamemode, so that's fantastic.

As of writing this I have a mere 14 hours. For a game of this magnitude, my limited gametime is a drop in the comparative ocean. However in these 14 hours I have enjoyed countless adventures and hence feel the need to express my feelings towards this game.
TOME is a Roguelike in its purest form; that said, it is the formula of dungeons within dungeons and static set pieces that allow its narrative to shine. This is not a game of simply smashing your way through numbers to obtain numbers to increase your numbers this is seen in many RPGS and hack'n'slashes;  there is a rich layer of lore found in conversations as well as scrolls and other objects that add a level of depth and immersion that many other "have a quick go" Roguelikes lack somewhat. Make no mistake, this game is a labour of love.
Despite the level of depth and complexity, TOME is incredibly easy to pick up and play; most aspects of playing are self explanatory. Items and their inherent effects are explained concisely and character sheets are detailed but not cluttered to the point of being rendered unusuable. The inventory is forgiving and even offers to empty itself for you after every floor of a dungeon, eliminating annoying overencumbered messages.
As stated previously I have amassed 14 hours in this game; in this space of time I have had a measly 1 character exceed level 10. This is a difficult game, an attribute which may put players off but attracts me all the more. Sometimes deaths leave you feeling cheated, especially random encounters in the overworld where an enemy caster can easily 2 or 3 shot an unprepared player from afar; this is countered by the player being transported to another plane upon death by a being of great power. The player then has the choice of being teleported to somewhere safer or dropped back into the fight rejuevenated. I would be lying if I said the latter act of manning up didn't cost me more than one decent character.
WIth the huge amount of races, talent trees, classes etc character creation is a powerful tool and allows you to progress in many different directions. Want a Cursed Elf? Check. Dwarven Alchemist with his own pet Golem? K. Halfling carrying out his own Hellish agenda of slaughter? Got it. Options such as these, the item system and the procedural world give the game practically unending longevity.
If you can say yes to enjoying Roguelikes, turn based battle, thoughtful strategy, massive replayability and a deep fantasy setting, TOME is a worthy purchase for you.

A bit late to the party, and probably not a lot of value to just throw my "yea!" atop the mountain of positive reviews already here, but none the less, I'll drop this in.
I will say, first and foremost, the game is mostly a narrative. There didn't seem to be a lot of branching or sneaky things or whatnot first time through, though I am fairly sure I missed a thing or two. It's also a game that, despite that, I simply don't feel like I want to replay again.
I won't say much because, obviously, this is one of those games that needs to have little said, but I will strike out on a tangent here.
I think that we're seeing an interesting trend of sorts with games in the recent years. There's a lot of slapstick, badly written, lame humor indie games out there - and don't get me wrong, some of 'em are actually pretty fun, but a lot of people just want to make a game, a system, mechanics.. they don't have a story or an idea for the contents of it, they just wanna make it, so I realize that a lot of devs just won't produce anything that really lasts.
With that said, I think that some of these games in recent times - most obviously Undertale, Night in the Woods, and several more that go further back.. I think in some way it's the younger generations searching for meaning, finding our 'God', and all that deep philosophical stuff. And I think they can have a great deal of value to someone who is open to the story and ideas and wants to consider them.
So, this is another one where you shouldn't snatch it up for the stellar gameplay. Don't grab it with the expectation of mashing buttons, leveling, or anything else.. it has some thinking, and some fiddling, and some of the more 'creative' puzzles weren't super complex, but I understand why the devs would play it a little safe there for the less technically capable.
Ultimately, I didn't know much about it and had it on my wishlist, finally grabbed it, played it, and I'm thoroughly satisfied. It didn't strike me as hard as some of the other couple I've mentioned above, but it was still good. Very solid. I look forwards to further exploration from the devs out there with stories to tell and worlds to build - but most of all we need to all continue to keep searching within ourselves and asking questions. I think the younger generations are more or less lost when it comes to standard religion - and as such, we have to find our own ways to seek comfort in the universe. This game is one such comfort.

I've never posted a Steam review before even though I've played multiple games on here. Portal, Octodad, Undertale... all of these games have introduced me to new characters, new worlds, new stories and adventures. I've escaped the labs with Chell, did... whatever Octodad does... with Octodad, and saved- and destroyed- the world with Frisk. All of these games and stories have stayed with me, but that's all they were, stories. Sometimes the characters have lived on and danced around in my head, even for months after I put their game down, but not like this. Never like this.
Never have I befriended a character before. Never has a character felt so real to me. Never has it been so hard to say goodbye.
I won't tell you anything about the content of this game, beyond the fact that it's highly innovative, that the soundtrack is spot-on, and that the pixel graphics feel very nostalgic and cool. What I will say is that you need to come to this game clean. Don't look up videos or Let's Plays beforehand. Just come to it with no prior knowledge other than a friend's recommendation or the official trailer. Avoid the temptation to look up walkthroughs as you play. Let the game lead you, even when it's difficult, even when it takes a bit of time. The answer's always hidden somewhere, and it's never too hard or too frustrating to find. Just look around, the solutions are all there somewhere.
This is a game like no other. Even beyond Steam, I have played many games, played as many characters. But here, I didn't really play as the character, not like in other games... The character was my friend and ally. He was the one saving the world. I was just there to show him the way, really. There to be a helper by his side, not the real controller of the world.
This isn't just Niko's story. This isn't just the world within's story. This is your story, in a way no other game you have ever played before is. It's waiting for you, Player. It's time for you to not just be the distant controller on the other side, but a character within the story. It's time for the Player and the Hero to fight side by side, saving the world hand-in-hand together.
Don't hesitate.
Don't be afraid.
Let the game tame you.
Pay the $10, and be ready to never see video games the same way again.

Up front, the largest failing of the game is that it never explains the Transceiver item, which pinpoints the boss and airdrops key items like C4, Shock Bombs, or First Aid Kits. I got to the final chapter of the game before realizing you could call people other than Miss Zero. A lot of complaints about the game can be solved outright by it. Also, the game plays a lot more like Megaman than Metal Slug, so expect that going in.
It's true that every mission is timed, but with the exception of a handful of rush stages, you have plenty of time to explore and search for secondary objectives and hidden items. I ran out of time twice in the entire game, both times because I didn't realize you could just call in a C4 airdrop. Missions with specific objectives mark them right on the map. Bosses aren't marked until you find them, but appear in specific marked areas. You can call Cadillac on the transceiver to locate them, if you want. Bosses will move between arenas if you take too long to kill them (usually because you die), but their new location is automatically marked on the map.
Gathering missions can be annoying, because there is no objective except to scour a level for crafting materials. They're always found in guaranteed chests throughout the levels, but can be completed faster if you get lucky drops from enemies. They mostly exist in case you want to grind for materials, because they add guaranteed items to the map.
As for crafting, yes, there is some grind. A LOT if you're a completionist. Absurd, even. But if you're not dead set on getting every part of every weapon set, it's not bad. There are hundreds of weapon parts; some are incremental upgrades, most are just tradeoffs—more damage per shot, but a smaller clip. Better accuracy but heavier weight, etc. You might not get the materials for a part you want as soon as it's unlocked just by playing casually, but you can probably get something similar.
When crafting guns, the big differentiator is weapon type and ammo. Certain combinations are better for certain levels; shotguns for levels full of mandrakes or bats, bouncing for levels with awkward enemy placement. Machineguns tear apart certain bosses, but their weight and low burst damage make them worthless in other levels. When in doubt, use Armor Piercing—it's (almost) always useful and has little downside. Elemental types are hyped up a lot, but make really no difference. Use Caustic if anything; it deals slightly more damage to most bosses, and chip damage to hard targets. If you're having a hard time with a level, try a new weapon type. Bringing the right class of weapon has far more impact than stubbornly grinding up a slightly stronger version of an ineffective weapon.
Oh, and get the Dodger biomod. Invincible rolling makes things much, MUCH easier.

This is definitely one of my most favorite games of all times!
I used to play it since it's been released, and occasionally come back to play it once in a while.
From all tactical shooters I played, this one is definitely the best.
(in my opinion at least)
It has a lot of maps, game modes, tons of weapons (like... I haven't seen this much weapons in most other shooters).
There are usually lots of ways to approach a mission, so it never gets boring to me.
More importantly, this game is REALLY great at coop-gameplay. (so I'm focusing on that)
In fact it's one of it's big strenghts were it excells vs. other shooters in my opinion.
The AI is fully functional (no bugs AFAIK) and coop-missions with other players against the AI are really a lot of fun.
Usually the AI is occupying some building, and you and your squad (up to 8 players) need to clear the building or rescue hostages or whatever else there is to do, depending on the game mode selected.
You have to work as a team, coordinate actions etc. in order to win against up to 35 (or even 40?) terrorists.
No annoying "spawns" of enemies behind your back, like it's in the newer Rainbow Six Vegas games.
Every enemy is placed on the map right at the start of the game, so no one "spawns".
The only way they can end up behind you is either if they are patroling or if they spot you and "escape", they usually try to flank you or they run away and cause trouble for some of your teammembers.
But there is no way they can "spawn" behind you, as they are placed on the map right at the start of the round.
(enemies that spawned behind my back were a huge annoyance in RS Vegas 2 to me...)
Anyway, this game really gives me the impression that I'm working in an elite squad consisting of 8 members, that has to take out a bunch of terrorists.
There is no other game that's better at delivering this "feeling".
At least I don't know of it, if there is any equal or better at all.
I recommend this game to anyone who likes to play tactical shooters with coop-gameplay.

So this is a bit of a mixed bag. I enjoy it but I am thumbs downing it. Hopefully the below explains why.
First, the Payday 2 connection. There are both pros and cons here so I am separating that section out by itself here...
The game, for the most part, is different enough from Payday ( I was one of the people calling it RAID the Heist before i actually played it). The asthetics are much the same (probably due to engine constraints) but the gameplay has a different enough feel. There is no stealth in this game... at all. It tries to tease you that there is a legitimate stealth mechanic... but there isn't. This could be a pro or con depending on who you are. The missions are different enough from payday and I honestly quite like them (except that I got an outlaw raid today that is the EXACT map and layout of the jewelry store heist from payday. LIke dejavou. Not cool.)
Pros:
- WW2 setting.
- Some weapons from that era that i love.
- No drill babysitting.
- Interesting missions.
- John Cleese. Although it feels like he kind of phoned in this appearance for a paycheck.
Cons:
- Diesel engine.
- Diesel engine.
- Graphics. See 1 &2.
- Clipping. See 1 & 2.
- Enemy LOS. See payday 2 stealth bit and again 1 & 2.
- The grind. YOu have to level up each character individually and each weapon individualy. Character by xp and guns by acheivemnet goal (e.g. "headshot 250 people with weapon x). It is grindy as heck. The main collection goal of the game in collecting loot is to get nazi gold bars with you can use to upgrade you hideout. The options for upgrading that are terribly limited and unispired. You can also use it to buy one or two cosmetics for your character. Thing is though, getting these bars is grindy as hell. In 10 hours (of solo play), I have earned 13 bars. The average purchase is 100-300 bars. YOu do the math.
- Lack of customization. You don't get to buy or find weapon upgrades  like in payday 2. You unlock the upgrades as mentioned earlier by acheiveing goals. The upgrades are not mutually exclusive so basically if you earn an upgrade, you equip it. There is not building weapons out for different scenarios or playstyles. There is also no character customizations like the masks from payday. I used to think it was dumb but I miss it here. Sure you can earna different jacket or pants for your character but they are for the most part all grey/beige/olive green/tan in the ww2 fashion and so even thoughthey are different... they all pretty much look the same. You don't get to customize them with patches or stencils or color selection or any of that. That type of custom build feel to this game is completely lacking. On that note, the skill "trees" aren't really tress and feel kind of uninspired. Every level, you get your choice of 3 different skill at each level. You don't lock yourself out of different plaths and the skills, at least at the low level I am , don't really differ from eachother all that much.
- I mentioned that I like the weapons. I do, it just feel like there are not very many of them to choose from for each class.
TL;DR
I am enjoying the game. I like the setting and the weapons. I like the missions. However, I am hard pressed to call it a "good" game and a lot of it feel uninspired and has issues. I cannot recommend it for the general populace to buy.
The game is currently only average. Hopefully they add more content and build on it like they did with Payday 2. I can recommend this game, but only when it's on sale.

From the little amount of time that I've played it, RAID: World War II is a pretty good game. Although it does have the same engine and glitches as PAYDAY 2, those glitches don't show too much, and the similarities between the two games are distinct enough for RAID's mechanics to be considered unique. For example, instead of a level 100 level cap, and resetting for an Infamy level, you can have different classes and characters, all capped at level 40. Some classes have weapons unique to them, while also having certain weapons locked from them.
RAID does have it's bugs though. This may just be me, but I'm experiencing some crashes at random. It could be while choosing a Raid, or in the middle of one, and the game will just quit. It doesn't happen all the time, but it's happening enough to consider it an issue.
Another problem I have with RAID is the downing system. You can only go down 3 times, with the fourth time you go down instantly ending your game, (if you're playing alone, that is.) This was also the case in PAYDAY, but with that game, you could recover your downs by using a piece of equipment. In RAID, there doesn't seem to be any way to recover your downs, from what I can tell.
Enough with the negatives, however, there is something that I really like about how you upgrade your weapons. Instead of choosing what mods go with what weapon, you have to complete challenges to upgrade a certain stat. For example, if you wanted to decrease the recoil of a certain weapon, it may have a challenge where you get a certain amount of kills while hip-firing, or if you want to decrease the spread of a shotgun, it'll have a challenge where you need to get headshots with it. This ensures that you're using the weapon to upgrade it instead of just getting the weapon, upgrading it, and never really using it again.
Another good thing about RAID is the difficulty system. In PAYDAY, you could choose whatever difficulty you wanted to go on at anytime, provided you had enough cash to do so. However, in RAID, you start off with two difficulties, (Easy and Normal,) and you need to beat the raid on the hardest difficulty available to you in order to unlock the harder difficulty. This ensures that you know what you need to do in order to beat the raid before reaching the harder difficulties, which is an amazing decision on the developer's part.
A lot of people say that they don't like raid simply since it has the same engine, format, etc. with PAYDAY 2. While I can see that, and say that it is a bit of a downside, I wouldn't toss the game aside just because of that.

So I just defeated the final boss of this game. The whole game took me about 15-20 hours (I have 30 hours logged at this point because I restarted the game once and I also tried to S-Rank certain levels which took lots of time) and these 30 hours were honestly amazing. This game is probably the best platformer I've played and I've always been a big fan of platformers.
Story: Obviously, there isn't much of a story. It's quite short and snappy: Cuphead and his brother Mugman stumbled across the Devil's casino and tried to deal with the Devil, and now they must pay the price. They have to retrieve all of the Devil's contracts from the devilishly difficult bosses scattered across the 3 Inkwell Isle's.
Gameplay: Cuphead moves so fluidly and I never felt that he was sluggish and unresponsive. There are 6 main guns you can play with in the game, including the starting gun. I found that the only good guns were the Charge and the Spread and that the others were pretty bad, this issue of balancing is a recurring problem with the game which I will get onto later. The game has two types of levels, Boss Fights and 'Run and Gun's'. Run and Gun levels are typically what you would expect of a platformer, you have to reach the end of the level while a swarm of enemies try to kill you. In these levels, you can unlock coins which can be used to buy guns and perks. The perks are fairly unbalanced as well, sadly, and the one I used throughout the game was the Smoke Bomb, which allowed me to stay invisible when I dashed. Despite this OP perk and the Charge and Spread guns, the boss fights were challenging. World 1 has some pretty easy fights, but after that the fights were quite challenging and at times, I took 20 attempts to do a fight. Sadly some of these boss fights are ruined by an unfair RNG system, which decides a lot of the attack patterns in this game, sometimes they can be very challenging, but I stil pulled through because of how fun this game is. Even when you die and rage, you still feel like continuing.
Art: This game looks absolutely gorgeous and it has all been hand-drawn to simulate a 1930s cartoon. The bosses all have unique and strange designs which always surprised me. As the boss fights moved through their respective phases, I was consistently amazed at how creative Studio MDHR could get. For example, once, I fought this bird who was trapped in a clock and after you kill him, it turns out his son is was in the clock and comes back to attack you. Also in early levels, when I fought a crying onion and a carrot. It's obvious that the developers of this game put so much love and effort into it, and I think all the awards this game has won so far were completely deserved.
So in conclusion, please, please buy this game. Anyone who likes platformers will love this game and for a small price of £15, it's basically a steal.

This version  is - unfortunately - by far the least compelling and enjoyable in the series, and for the first time I actually regret buying the game. In their attempts to make the game more realistic, it seems to me that the designers have simply gone too far - the time required to set up tactics for corners etc alone is incredible. There are actually just so many issues - players asking for new contracts every year, irrespective of how long they have remaining on their current ones; constant press conferences and tactical meetings; completely unrealistic injury crises....
All of this I could deal with, as you can pass a lot of stuff on to your staff if you so choose. However, the single biggest issue with the game is the AI matchplay itself, and again - unfortunately - problems that have existed for a few years now simply haven't been addressed. Players continually smashing the ball into team-mates when attempting a pass or shot, inexplicably running past the ball or ignoring obvious passes, the number of missed penalties and shots which hit the woodwork, strikers with high levels of composure and finishing missing open goals time and again and - most annoyingly - crosses which the oppostion keeper has to save at his near post which your player "might struggle to claim he meant". Do these things happen in real life? Yes, of course - but with nothing like the regularity with which they happen in every single game in FM2018.
Finally, this version seems to take absolutely no notice of the "secret attributes" of footballers - Professionalism/Consistency/Big Game Mentality etc; anybody who has ever used the editor or FMRTE will know what I'm talking about. Yes, there are those who think using these tools is cheating, and fair play to them for trying to do things the honest way. However, many of us diehards want to occasionally live the dream of taking our clubs beyond their wildest ambition. FM2018 has ruined that. The series is supposed to be - at essence - a game, a fantasy, a way for armchair enthusiasts to pursue the impossible. The developers would do well to remember that. It needn't be such a slog.

I strongly dislike roguelike games. All too often, they throw a million different obtuse mechanics at you, including but not limited to hunger (discouraging exploration), unidentified items (discouraging the collection of loot, which serves as a major incentive to crawl a dungeon to begin with), or cursed items (discouraging the use of higher quality gear because you'll never be able to unequip it, or equipping it literally kills you)
DarkGod (the developer of the game) decided to try something different, here. Understanding that mechanics like cursed items and hunger are relics of the past, he did away with them. This entire game, conceptually speaking, takes a good, hard look at what makes other roguelikes unapproachable messes and tries to understand what the real meat of the genre is, and he has spent years polishing his vision to a fine shine.
DarkGod has given you a a huge variety of archtypes, each with their own subclasses that specialize in one thing or another. Simple "bump" based combat that dominates other games in the genre has been replaced with a rich skill system that encourages you to carefully consider not only the positions of yourself and your enemies, but what skills to use in order to ensure your survival. Rather than relying on hard to find or expensive to purchase consumable items, you will find "runes" and "inscriptions" that are infinitely re-usable, but come with a cooldown, demanding that you make strategic use of them. The skill tree system forces you to make careful decisions in regards to pumping skills that make it easier to not die, or pumping skills that make it easier for you to kill enemies, which is itself another valid form of survival. Many skills combo together in ways that you can't easily imagine, which, if you slow down and take enough time to think it through, a situation which appears hopeless at first glance can be turned around through sheer determination and enough tactical thought.
I will readily admit that I am not well versed enough in the genre to elaborate any further on what this game does better than its competitors. But I do know that I have avoided playing roguelikes for years because of obtuse mechanics, and this game did away with enough of them to captivate me for dozens of hours already, and will almost certainly rob me of even more of my time as the days go on. If you've played games such as Nethack, Pixel Dungeon, Desktop Dungeons, or Dungeons of Dredmor and were turned off by them, I believe this game is accessible enough to be worth giving a shot, even if you have otherwise given up on the genre.
