I highly recommend this game.
Firstly to lovers of the gendre, but really, if you want to try a good stealth game that will challenge your skill and intelligence, you must try Dishonored.
At the eve of Dishonored 2 I believed it was high time to give this acclaimed gem a try. And I must say I was not disapointed.
Don't get me wrong, all games have their flaws, but Dishonored has the rare quality of having very few of those.
To me the negative points never surpassed the positive ones, or I wouldn't have played the game in full :)
Before I go into specifics please keep in mind this is my own personal opinion.
What did I like?
+ The story
+ The characters
+ The graphics
+ The artwork
+ The challenging missions
+ The world
+ The non kill option
+ The longevity
+ The powers
What did I dislike?
- The ambiance
- The rats
- The unbalanced game style
- The extreme demands of stealth mode
- The clichés
- The absence of a radar
- The dark vision power
More details on those positive points:
While Dishonored doesn't have the most original storyline it still has enough plot and twists to it to keep you firmly seated at you PC screen. But the main atraction is it's gameplay.
The main character may be silent, but all those around him help to build a world full in variety, color and depth.
The other characters all have their stories and secrets, you don't spend much of the game speaking to anyone, but the use of a particular item will tell you much more. Abuse it, it's worth it! But don't worry, the game won't provide any spoilers. :)
The graphics have some good textures and shapes, very correct and respectful of the standards of 2012 frankly still looks great today.
A pity the world of Dishonored looks so static at times. The character motions also leave a bit to be desired but nothing major.
The actual artwork (on paper) is very good in my opinion but it doesn't fully translate into the game. However, the somber clothing and hairstyles totally respect the game world. As well as the angular faces, a look I wasn't familiar with but which I enjoyed in the end, plus beautifull scenarios to enjoy at times from the rooftops during sunset.
The game is non-linear in it's gameplay, all paths lead to rome true but there are many of them. One mission goal equals at least 5 ways to go about it.
Depending on whether you prefer to go unseen, or wish to cause as much 'chaos' as possible. The game will measure how much of a mess you made and Will punish you for it.
It's dificult to create an original world in which to place your characters, this game studio found a clever mix between steampunk and broken utopia, very original. Hint, read all books.
As mentioned briefly before, there are two ways to play this game, kill or not kill, each with it's dificulties and rewards. Naturally it's never so simple.
You will obtain achievements for killing all, for killing some, for killing Only some and killing none. Even the bosses! Which is a much apreciated novelty!
One important distinction to learn early on? Ghost and Shadow. You can not get seen and can not kill, or you can not get seen while still going for the kill.
Naturally, one playthrough won't be enough, which, is another positive point!
Me, I took over 41 hours thus far. Reduce that by half if you're an expert in stealth games. :)
The abilities or powers awarded the players are frankly a breath of fresh air. Blink gives you so many original and cool ways to get about, and Dark Vision is pratically indispensible!
The rest? Well, that depends on how you wish to play the game, and I won't ruin it for you. But note that collecting certain items will be essential for acquiring those powers. Rather than a nuisance it will help you know your misions levels all the better.
More details on the negative points:
Dishonored is dark, in more ways than one. There are no rosy cheeked kids no puppies and no flowers.
Of course it was integral to the game, but you can only stomach so much disease and death, regarless of the cold truth it depicts.
Rats? Why rats? Distasteful to say the least. You best not suffer from this particular phobia or you Won't be able to play the game. On a slightly happier note those are one of two things you Can kill without saction.
Killing is the fastest way, stealth becomes madatory later on however, so you can either be very patient or triger happy, the game takes into account both choices and delivers it's consequences.
But I can't help but feel that those who choose 'kill' are hindered more than the non-kill, more rats for one, more agressif 'people' on the streets, more security and guards.
Stealth much? Knock out a guard, hide him in a dark corner for fear of discovery, need to do the same with the guard dogs for another dog will go on alert at the sight of it's sleeping canine friend, and careful where you place your sleeping beauties for someone on the below floor may hear you!
But by all means slash your weapon at the back of your unsuspecting victim at two feet he won't hear a thing... logic is not Dishonored's strong point.
Did you say 'cliché'? As I said before, the story is not the most original but some events might have you griding your teeth. I can't say much more without spoiling the game.
You must unlock a power to see through walls (Dark vision), but the game offers you an achievement reward if you don't get it, hmmm... but if you have no radar to begin with this game becomes a tremendous headache without it.
Can it be done? Yes. Is it worth the headache for one achievement? No thanks.
And speaking of Dark vision, yellow... why yellow and why do their eyes need to glow like flashlights?
I could go on about it at lenght, but I think each futur player of Dishonored should focus on what good they can take from the game and from there pick out what they like the most and the least.
Especially since this Is a good game and a game worth playing at least once in your gamer life. Like many rare pearls out there Dishonored has earned it's place in legend.
Enjoy your game!
Kind regards,
Keiyan

I didn’t know if I liked Dishonored until the last third of the game. Leveraging the Unreal Engine, and set to the default brightness settings as directed in the initial startup, Dishonored is a washed-out low resolution mess. Individual pixels can be discerned within groups of shaded art making up a wall in a mess of greys and browns. I dropped the brightness down a few notches to create deep black shadows, hiding the transitional colors.
The art style is distinctive and inspired, but initial off-pointing. Thick angular extremities taper towards the body, with odd features over-emphasized as they jut from a character’s head. Turn of the century architecture of brick and glass reaches for the gloomy sky as steampunk technology inspired by a world run on whale oil provides energy weapons and barriers. A terrible plague burdens the city/state of Dunwall, leaving the poor to be dumped into quarantine zones as they transform into walking shuddering wretches that vomit black clouds on the unwary.
Playing as Corvo, the titular bodyguard framed for the death of the body he was guarding, Dishonored initially guides the player through a linear path of escape. Only as Corvo mutely joins a merry band of insurgents within a hub level of sorts does the game open up. Environments are reused to good effect though the scale of the game seems small until the final map, a sprawling island fortress. Until that point, four or five of the base levels are visited at least twice, allowing Corvo to stretch any newly acquired abilities gather along the way.
Blink is a fundamental necessity in Dishonored and as a mechanism fixes the single largest issue facing first-person platforming, traversal. Functioning as a nearly instantaneous teleport, Blink allows Corvo to zoom from perch to perch, ascending or descending the environment at will. Only the highest heights are unreachable, though the indicator of what is scalable can often be confusing. Other abilities include stopping time and possessing animals and people, and all of them can be leveled by gather charms and runes within the environments. More a scavenger hunt than the chore many games make of collectibles, it offers opportunity for multiple play-throughs, as does upgradable equipment. Upgrade paths taken can determine possible strategies, but this concept is not communicated well by the game. Only by finishing it does one fully realize the depth of the paths not taken.
What is unfortunate about Dishonored is the empty shell of a narrative that is offered. Borrowing from Bioshock 2, a surrogate daughter learns from how Corvo conducts himself in the world. Play as a violent murderer, killing everything in sight and the girl becomes ruthless in her world view. Practice mercy and stealth, she become benevolent. An excellent mechanic is robbed entirely of meaning as there is no emotional connection to the girl or to any character in the game. Drowning in bad writing delivered in a vacuum by bored or confused celebrity voices, Dishonored is done a disservice, rendering the game an exercise in strategy rather than an experience to become immersed in.
Heady with upgraded powers I raced through the final moments of the game, skipping an environment entirely and accidentally triggering a scripted event. I chased the event and when presented with an ultimatum I simply executed a multi-power combo that resulted in the enemy killing himself literally in a blink. By this point the game I was so highly leveled the final encounter was a trifle, and that is a shame.
Dishonored is a fine successor to Thief and Deus Ex, offering player agency, and open environmental puzzles but is ultimately hollow.

In the memory of Serious Sam...
I like the idea to make a mix of FPS and TD genres. It looks like Coffee Stain Studios was the first who realized this idea (Orcs must Die released later).
Actually, I am not big fan of FPS games, but i found this one really engaging. I like the setting and visual. It's not just usual aliens. They have their own charm. I like killing them  :D
So what about the game? There are 6 different weapons and ~10 different buildings. You choose and take some of them into the battle. A build phase starts. There is the core where enemies head in the battlefield. So your first objective is to make the best maze with the longest path of the monsters. It's quite interesting, because the game made in 3D with stairs, bridges and etc.
So when you placed blocks to increase the path of the monsters, you have a choice: build/upgrade towers or upgrade your weapon. Actually, you need constantly to make this choice during the mission. Your goal is find the perfect balance.
When you press Enter and enemies’ are approaching. While your towers attack automatically, you need to move, aim and shoot. The idea with having 3 weapons at once is awesome. Every weapon has recharge system. For example, you have a rocket launcher with 1 shell. When you used it, the weapon need about 7 seconds for reloading. You swap weapon and take the plasma gun, you make 3 shots and you take the shotgun. You make 4 shots and take the rocket launcher again, which is already reloaded. I like this idea very much.
When you upgrade weapons it gives extra damage and extra shots. So Rocket Launcher on level 2 has 2 shells. It's quite effective. Upgrading of towers are usual for TD games.
There are 5 levels in the game. You can buy extra with DLC. But the mission is really long to take. I have spent 3 attempts and 50 minutes for the last one to just pass the first mission. Actually, I played on Insane, but it doesn't matter, I just wanted to say, that levels are really long. Yeah, there are 4 difficulties. It's good feature.
There are no big strategic potential and differences in monsters and levels. Usually, I consider it as really bad in TD games. But this game doesn't need it, because It's extraordinary with FPS elements.
The game is pretty old now. And there are better TD games now. So the game doesn't cost a full price.
But if you will take it with 80% discount, I am sure you will spend some hours at this. I recommend!

Mercenary Kings greatest downfall is that it is on pc rather than vita or 3ds.

TL; DR: This game is awful. I cannot recommend buying it, at any price.
Some say this game is alot like Payday 2. It is not. It is more like Payday: The Heist. Except this game is designed significantly worse. It has the same cover-to-cover shooting, where you can only take so much damage, which does not regen over time like with some Payday 2 skills/decks, but the maps are more open so there is never enough cover available, and there's always snipers and flamers everywhere ready to flush you out into the Karabiners of the common grunts.
It has more guns and levels than Payday: The Heist, so there's that, but it also runs like crap, has terrible balancing in both classes and weapons, has enemy AI that is♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ and friendly AI that is even worse than♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ Even the AI in Payday: The Heist, which is also♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ was more useful, because most of those maps where not as open, and thus the AI did not get confused as often.
Let's take the comparisons to Payday 2 next. Most of the mechanics that are similar, are done worse here. Don't you just love arbitrary wait objectives, or having to do objectives that could have been prepared before awakening the hounds of Hell with guns and explosions? I remember going loud on Art Gallary (which is literally a retexture of Jewelry Store from Payday 2), and after waiting a while for the objectives, one of the bots commented "It's been three minutes now. The driver is taking the♥♥♥♥♥♥", and I couldn't help but feel it was actually the developers that were taking the♥♥♥♥♥♥ since the map was so small yet somehow needed an arbitrary waiting objective, literally just to give the enemy enough time to bring in a Tiger tank, which was totally a reasonable response to a robbery.
There's also the specials. In both Payday games, the specials are there to spice things up, but will usually only make things harder if you screw up yourself. As annoying as a Taser is, he only tazes you when you're open, and requires direct line of sight. Dozers can hurt you up close, but can be taken down with reasonable fire on all difficulties, not so with specials here, all of which are obnoxiously present, to the point where you are never safe until they're dead, and even then they respawn within half a minute on anything above Normal. This is mostly due to the fact that the ROF and calibre of weapons is lower than in Payday 2, but still doesn't explain why entirely armourless Officers, and even armourless non-special SS grunts, take multiple shotgun blasts to the face to kill, or why Flamers can fire longer than any flamethrower can, and somehow manage to burn the ground for 30 seconds regardless of the surface, even concrete remaining lit for an unreasonable amount of time. And please show me the WWII gas mask that could protect you from a Nagant or Springfield round to the face.
And why does an Officer need to be physically present on the battlefield, and have to radio in, before the Germans will send in their elite SS?
The stealth, don't get me started. Just kidding, too late. If you, like me, hate Payday 2 stealth, you will find yourself forgiving Overkill after trying this♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ The stealth mechanics over all aren't bad, except that it obviously needs a throwing knife or something for stationary guards you need to get past. The real problem is the screaming mechanic. If an enemy detects you, the 15 nearest guys will too, even though he hasn't fired his gun and there is no verbal shout to be heard, just instant detection by half a platoon. Even if this did work properly it would be very bad stealth design, but it bugs out, to the point where if a guard is slowly noticing you as you stab him, it will instantly alert everyone, even if he didn't fully detect you.
Standing up also causes anyone within a few metres to instantly detect you, whether you moved or not, and trust me, you will want to stand up with the slow crouch speed. Guards also have an insane view distance when facing you, like easily 50 metres.
The weapon upgrade system is one based on challenges, but of course they are incredibly tedious. Things like having to pick up 2000 rounds for sniper rifles, which fire 1 round every 3-4 seconds, so it's hard to decrease them from max ammo, and 500 kills at 20 metres, in a game where all enemies charge suicidally at you in close range, and one-shot kills are rare even if you can get the distance and aim right.
I cannot recommend enough that you pass up this game. This is the kind of thing that would appear on TotalBiscuit's "Steam Sells..." series if he still did those.

First off, let me just that I love Rift. It's a great example of the MMO genre done right. I have played since beta testing began and I have been a fan from day 1. The developers listen to the community when it comes to features and they are constantly updating the game.
One of the best features of RIFT is the class system and skill tree's. The system they use allows for almost any class to fill any raid / group role and makes for a lot of customization. Ultimately, this adds a lot to the game as you can continually change your roles and keep the action and play style fresh and entertaining. If one day you want to DPS and the next Heal, you don't have to roll an alt. This is refreshing and a welcome addition that I hope other companies will take note of.
The only downside to RIFT at this point is the loss of subscribers which forced a turn to F2P. The cash shop isn't pay 2 win, but it also isn't very reasonable either. Lately they have started pushing it more and more to the point where it's getting a little overwhelming and I feel like the developers are on the brink of crossing a line into territory I wouldn't want to be involved with.
At the end of the day, any issues with the cash shop do not alter the core gameplay and fun that can be had throughout the game. Whether you play through the main storyline quests, do instant adventures, PvP, or Raid, RIFT has a lot to offer the MMO diehards. I highly recommend giving it a try, especially since it won't cost you a penny!

I got the digital deluxe edition waaaaay back when the game first came out, and poured a decent amount of time into it over the next two months.  I stopped playing right about when the first hunting season came out, because there was just nobody to play with.
Now that the game's gone F2P, I'd definitely recommend it to people.  You can actually find games now, which is amazing, the hunters and monsters that you could never play before due to the lack of people are pretty fun (Behemoth in particular was one I was hyped for, and is probably my favorite monster now.)
But let's talk about what's changed.  They removed Evactuation, alright, probably not a good idea.  My guess, considering that it's very clearly marked "Beta" wherever they show the name "Stage 2", is that they're reworking Evacuation, considering that one of the big criticisms was that a bunch of mutations does not unique games make.  Makes sense, especially considering that you can't buy Behemoth right now, as they're reworking him since he's a pubstomper.
They removed achievements and reset everyone's progression.  Fair enough, they're likely reworking achievments to work with the F2P aspect now, makes sense if you ask me.  Reset progression?  Oh no, you lost your badges or your skins that nobody actually saw outside of the lobby.  Boo hoo.
You get 3000 funbux for being a founder, an amount which, admittedly, will buy you Lennox's rocket punch and not much else.  But considering that you're a founder, you already have most of the hunters.  You probably got to tier 3, and might've even bought the tier 4 hunters, not to mention the freebie adaptations you get.  Hell, if you're like me you're probably one of the relatively few people who can play Behemoth right now!  So there's not as much for you to spend money on.  I admit, the amount could've been bigger, but it's nothing that'll break the deal if you ask me.
All in all, I'd probably up my prior rating to a 7.5/10, room for improvement definitely.  What people need to remember is that it's in a beta again, which means that things are going to change.

2D Dark souls like RPG, I've heard of worse ideas :) I wanted to like this game, but so far, I'm disappointed.
There are things I like. All the weapons I've tried feel distinct, like they have their own purpose and aren't just a set of numbers. The bosses are where I think think the game shines the most in my opinion. They're well designed, for the most part, often requiring you to think of your position, when to dodge, when to heal, when to strike and with what weapon. It captures the spirit of Dark Souls combat with 1 less D to work with, which is impressive. There's also some clever use of movement abilities in some of the platforming sections.
But there are problems, many problems. Some items names are almost copied from Dark Souls exactly, not itself a problem, but they've been made completely useless. Throwing knives, don't go more than a few feet. Fire bombs do no damage, sometimes literally. And if you're going to copy dark souls, maybe Don't copy the horrendous hitboxes, your attacks will pass right through enemies sometimes and some enemy attacks can hit you even if they miss completely. Enemies can sometimes hit you after they're dead if the animation triggered. Enemies sometimes skip their telegraph or wind up animation before a strong attack, which will always catch you off guard and is completely unfair. It's impossible to tell how close an enemy is to dying so it's difficult to weigh up whether it's worth risking another hit. Be prepared for your character to occasionally fall right through thin platforms for no reason. The ledge grabbing mechanic simply does not work 80% of the time which can make simple traversal really frustrating. Some enemies (the Armour mite for example) can knock you to the ground with their first hit and stun lock you before you stand up over and over until you die. But even small enemies can stun lock you to death. One alien like enemy has an infinite combo so blocking is pointless since, you have limited stamina (enemies do not) so they can attack over and over and over until your stamina is completely depleteld. You also have a cooldown after attacks, but enemies do not. I regularly see enemies starting an attack as soon as their first attack ends, which for enemies who teleport means sometimes you cannot catch them.
Also, the menu UI is a bit of a mess, it's difficult to tell what you're looking at sometimes.
If you're a player coming from dark souls. Your muscle memory will screw you over a few times as the controls are similar, but not identical.
And I've encountered a complete game breaking bug, one of my brands (The Hardlight brand) simply does not work. I can't interact with the platforms and so can not progress any further. (An uninstall/reinstall seems to have fixed the issue)
Sadly, I can't recommend what I've seen so far. The more I play, the less I like it :( Still I wish I could give it a "Might Recommend" If you were willing to put up with the frustration, I can see the fun. But to me, it feels like the game wasn't tested enough. This game is not difficult, it's punishing

I can see the hard work that went into Salt and Sanctuary, but it’s a game that’s plagued with many issues. I plan to go over every single one. The game does have its good points too when it comes to the combat, the skill tree, and some of the writing. Everything else just failed to impress me, especially when it’s so heavily inspired by Dark Souls yet not able to deliver a similar experience in some key areas that the DS series is known for. The game does do things with the 2D perspective to establish its own identity, but you can feel the DS ooze out of it in the UI, item descriptions, and more.
I’ll start with the art style. S&S had only a few vistas and one location that I could call beautiful. Everything else double downs on that dark and smeared look. Torches play an important role with maintaining visibility at the cost of an off-hand and even have a traversal aspect when the Brands (platforming skills) unlock during play. What the torchlight reveals is a somewhat low resolution, muddy, slightly blurry mess. Even the player character and NPCs are ugly. Some of the bosses have a neat look and certain pieces of equipment look okay, but the drawn backgrounds and figures just do not look good overall.
The music is a weak aspect of the game. Besides the menu music when you start the game, I only liked one other song. The rest of the soundtrack is forgettable and all the bosses except one have the same theme. That’s one quality of DS that I would have appreciated here. I ended up tuning out the music during the boss fights.
Speaking of bosses, the fights themselves vary in quality and balance. You’ll run into a couple easy ones, a good chunk of fair ones, and some truly frustrating encounters that can easily result in a dozen or more deaths depending on your class. I should state here that I went with Strength melee with a dash of Prayer the whole way through. These three bosses that I’m going to name are the worst ones that stand out the most: Mad Alchemist, Tree of Men, and The Witch of the Lake. Mad Alchemist was the only fight of the Big Three that I won purely due to luck. His attack pattern changed during what was either the 12th or 15th attempt and allowed me to win since he did the 6 projectiles shooting out of the ground spam only once. Earlier attempts saw me trying to manage the slimes he would summon, only to die fruitlessly. Tree of Men is a very large boss with a painfully specific weak spot near the top of the arena (platforming required) that’s located over a pit. That boss will knock you into the pit. The Witch of the Lake fight is when the game temporarily decides it’s a bullet hell, a great time.
The combat controls for the most part function well with a few problems. The bindings for Light Attack (X) and Parry (LT+X) lead to errors when trying to attack out of a block. Occasionally, you’ll end up accidentally attacking in the opposite direction. Both issues can lead to a free hit for the enemy or a lost opportunity for damage. I noticed the direction one in boss fights mostly. I also never understood dodging/rolling. It felt inconsistent, especially when many enemies, especially the pouncing ones, go for where you’ll be versus where you are which leads to plenty of coming out of roll into a hit or terrible mauling. Heaven help you if you’re trying to escape from multiple pouncing beasts. I was never able to truly have a good grasp of the mechanic and I even remember some rare instances where I could sometimes take damage in the middle of a roll.
Combat in general feels fine, but certain sections of the game are much worse than others. The woods are filled with slimes. They’re a pouncing enemy and when more than one is around, they can chain their pounces together. Dodging is the only reliable way to escape since any pouncing enemy will snatch you from the air and eat your face. Also, blocking is ineffective against those types of attacks which makes how they move based on your speed very annoying when they’re on top of you at the end of dodge. The game has too many enemies that love grabbing or pouncing on you. There was even an enemy that I didn’t even know could grab me that managed to grab me and ruin my day. It’s a common enemy tactic that I hated.
The other thing that I absolutely despise about this game is that unlike a Souls game where you can pretty much spot all the enemies with cautious camera work, enemies will appear out of thin air or crawl out of the ground at will. Heck, some enemies are even invisible and will greet you with death. Just as annoying as spawning and invisible enemies are the teleporting enemies. Those teleporting types
. Sometimes they’ll just take their hits and die or teleport five times in two seconds and appear right behind you for a quick stab.
Additionally, there are too many situations where you die due to platforming woes or being launched by an enemy to your doom. The platforming isn’t very refined which makes those very tricky areas depressing, especially that one place with the horses (that “grab” you to death). Enemies can still bat you away even with your shield up during a jump. I also noticed the wall stick for wall jumps working against me sometimes when descending.
Here are some final remarks. I don’t think the game explained enough when it came to some pretty important mechanics. I had to use a guide to learn about fatigue/wound mechanics and that you could air dash twice. The lack of a map for a metroidvania-esque level design meant using a guide to cut down on time wasted being lost which happened more often later in the game.
What finally made me stop playing was dying to a Bloated Monstrosity in NG+. I was happily smashing the early bosses and only needed a couple tries for Mad Alchemist due to my great shield and camping a platform (those slimes are #1 at being the worst). Afterwards, I fell to my death due to the BM’s massive hammer. I went back to collect without a worry, but the BM sprayed poison on one side. I rolled to the other side of him, but then he turns around with more poison and fills the meter. The poison status killed me in three seconds from full health. My high resist gave me no time to chug an antidote mid-combat.
After that, I decided to skip the rest of the experience. The loss of souls didn’t bother me as much as the realization that I didn’t want to be miserable since the future was pain. For other people, there’s still an incentive continue playing since you can upgrade all your gear and climb even further in the skill tree. The salt payouts are increased for all monsters and the boss rewards are much more significant. Unfortunately, the items appear to be all the same and the salt items give the same amounts.
I did think some of the item descriptions were good, especially with the lore and bosses. Some didn’t have any significant writing to them. The story bits and the ending I received were satisfying.
I think there’s a good game in there buried underneath all my grievances. I’ll leave it up to you to decide if this game is a good fit for you. You can’t come in expecting the level of polish and production that a Dark Souls game has. The difference in team sizes is as big as some of the bosses in both series. You’ll have to accept the flaws and possess incredible patience to climb over any humps and obstacles that don’t always come from good game design. I had higher hopes for this title and wanted it to be better. I cannot recommend this game myself and I suggest reading in-depth positive reviews to balance this one out and have a comprehensive view.

Dishonored is one of those games that I thought was just another stealth game and boy, was I wrong. This was one of those games that made me invest in stealth games again, whose image was largely ruined by games like Thief and Assassin's Creed series. The plot was linear, but in no way boring or bland. The lore is very underrated, and the characters are dark, brutal and interesting. The setting, Dunwall is one of those unsettling dystopias I would never want to be in real life. The perpetual, mono-toned annoucements on the intercom as you try to take guards out, is one of those memorable if not iconic gaming moments. The gameplay is near-perfect. The powers and abilities are really unique. What I loved about this game was it's chaos system, where you're really rewarded for being a pacifist. I took the low chaos route in my first playthrough, but replayed missions with high chaos and both are equally satisfying. I pre-ordered Dishonored 2 recently, but that game is in a mess with its framerate issues. Hopefully they fix it soon, because I cannot wait to play as Corvo again.
Oh, about the DLC's, they're wonderful. Daud is brilliant and his storyline was more gripping than the main storyline. Also, the DLC's are vital if you are looking to buy Dishonored 2. So I hugely recommend buying the DLC's as well.

This is one of my all-time favorite games.  Seriously one of the best gaming experiences I ever had.  The Steam release, however, is not a good presentation of the game.
In Jedi Knight, the sequel to Dark Forces, you once again play as Kyle Katarn, a mercenary sometimes employed by the Rebels.  His father, once a Jedi who left the order, is killed for a secret he kept by a group of dark jedi.  Kyle must avenge his father and stop Jerec from rising to power as an omnipotent new Sith lord
This game stood apart from the FPS games of its time because of some innovations.  The use of a lightsaber, which serves as both an offensive and defensive weapon, was a bit deal.  Lots of games had melee weapons, but the lightsaber handled differently.  The force powers let you do things you could not do in any other FPS.  A rudimentary morality system allowed you to kill NPCs to change the outcome of the game, in an attempt to add a role-playing aspect.
As an FPS the game is satisfying enough.  There is actually a good story, told through cheesily acted cut scenes that still are more Star Wars than the prequels.  I find the focus of the Single Player campaign less about perfect aim (some of the weapons are kind of random, actually), but on cleverness and reflexes.  More often than not, the game insists on a stealth approach to some fights.  Like DF, JK is more interested in mental puzzles than being yet another Doom.  Every once in awhile, the game takes a break from the FPS mold for one-one-one (sometimes more) Jedi battles.
The game really shined in Multiplayer, though, back in its heyday.  A thriving mod community (thanks to a simple modification system) expanded on the already great gameplay.  Fighting an AI with a saber and force powers was one thing, playing a deathmatch against fully-powered Jedis was something amazing.
Unfortunately, this release, the Steam version, is not that version of the game.  Single Player is intact, with the exception of the music, which was redbook audio of John Williams' score.  It does leave something lacking to the campaign, as a result.  The Multiplayer system no longer works at all.  While this is not Steam's fault, it is something you should be aware when buying the game.  With the exception of painstaking modification and router configuration, this is now a single player game.  Which is a crying shame.
The executable for the game is also not always compatible with some patches and mods.  It can be frustrating trying to get the game to work with customizations.
Not all of the differences are bad, though.  The Steam version defaults to a windows GUI for menus, which might seem annoying, but addresses a bug in the original version of the game.  Instead of manually setting the workaround, Steam auto-applies it.  The game contols have been changed to WASD as default, as well.  And while this is not exclusive to Steam's release, this also applies to retail, the game has full native Widescreen support, and always has.  This seems a bit unusual for a 1997 game.
The two sequels that followed were worthy successors, but this was one of the best titles LucasArts made in their heyday.  It's definitely worth playing if you've never experienced it before.

I grew up with this game absolutley amazing.... that said you can start the game, but once in the actual campaign all the colors look like they are trying to give you a seizure.I got angry when i first started it, but walk a few steps out of the first room and it should fix itself.

What is it with Nar Shadda? The place has featured at least three times over the course of the Dark Forces Saga and once in KOTOR II, and it was the weakest part of the game every time. There's just something about the Smuggler's Moon that lends itself to rubbish level design.
Anyway, after checking a few guides on getting the damn thing to run, I finally got Dark Forces II to play. The game starts out a bit rocky, as most of your ammunition is scavanaged off of your fallen enemies, an ineffective strategy when about half of your enemies come at you with good old fisticuffs. This led to a few occasions when I had to take out a dozen enemies with six blaster shots and my own punches, and sadly it seems Kyle hasn't been working out quite like he used to as the fists that could once drop a Kell Dragon are barely enough to put down passing thugs.
Fortunately once you get off Nar Shadda, enemies are universally packing heat, and the game starts to come to life. Ugly, early full-3D life, but life nonetheless. The level design is somewhere between the original Dark Force's nonlinear approach and Jedi Outcast's straight shot from start to finish, and manages to have the strengths and weaknesses of both. The levels are truly impressive in size, and lead to some memorable setpieces (most dramatic, if relatively brief, of which is a scene when you're left trying to sprint for the hangar bay of a ship in freefall), but they also follow a highly specific thread of advancement that, while not so bad as Dark Force's tendancy to block off progression to people who can't use sideways moon logic, still can leave you poking around a level for half an hour looking for the solitary path forward. Perhaps they felt the necessity due to the actual presence of maps in the game, but the locations beat out Jedi Outcasts in that their layout actually seems to have something to do with the location you're alledgedly visiting (for example, a starship whose rooms are actually laid out in the shape of a starship).
However, despite the strengths I mention, I ultimately can't recommend the game because its sprawling design isn't quite as good as Dark Forces, and its storyline isn't as good as Jedi Outcast's, lacking relatable characters and quite often much of a plot at all. For example, once you aquire a lightsaber from your father's droid, you start using Force powers without training, or indeed any exposition that you had any Force potential at all (the lightsaber isn't even your father's, so a hereditary connection isn't implied either). Just "here's a lightsaber, start using superpowers." Not to mention the lightsaber is basically useless in this game. Sure it can deflect blaster shots if you're facing in the right direction, but I ultimatley wound up using my normal weapons for 99% of the game, only pulling out my lightsaber to cut open grates and fight the bosses.
Speaking of which, apart from the game's tendancy to dump you somewhere with not much more than a cursory mention of why you were there (such as letting me run around in a fuel depot for an hour before I actually realize that I'm trying to use it to sneak onto a ship through the fuel lines), the bosses are also generally pretty weak. Unlike the first enemy you make in the game, the sleazy protocol droid 8t88, who obviously can't put up anything resembling a fight, all of the bosses are the main villain Jerec's Dark Jedi cronies, who mostly just stand around in the background of expository cutscenes until they randomly turn up at the end of certain levels for a boss fight apiece. Who are they? Dunno. A smug twit, a domanatrix, a big-guy-little-guy alien duo, and a giggling Twi'lek who I'm reasonably certain was brain damaged. That's about the extent of characterization you get. As for the fight themselves, they weren't as luck-based as Jedi Outcast and Academy's Dark Jedi fights, but they gave very little indication of how well you were doing so I usually just jumped around clicking my very slow attack button until the bad guy fell down.
Ultimately, between the compatibility issues with modern machines, the weak plot, and the occasionally frustrating gameplay (looking at you, rocket Stormtroopers), I can't really recommend bothering with this entry just to enjoy its middling-quality level design.

I recently went back to play this one, and at first I thought it might be a similar case to Jedi Outcast, where a second playthrough was giving me a better outlook on the game. This, however, turned out not to be the case. Nar Shadda was a pain as before, for the same reason of simply not having enough gun-toting enemies to supply your ammunition needs. However, things picked up again afterwards, roughly up to the point where you reach the planet where the Valley of the Jedi is located, maybe halfway through the game.
I should clarify my old remark on the game's "middling-quality" level design. It's not middling-quality. In fact it's remarkably good, giving you a firm sense of scale, location, and continuity. I'm legitimatly impressed that they managed to stretch a single starship across two or three levels without ever giving you the impression that you've visited the bulk of it. Sure it's very game-y in the sense that navigating them is far more complicated than one could reasonably expect the people who actually belond there to put up with, but compared to the cramped squiggly hallways and bottomless pit abuse of later entries it does its job very well.
However, this falls apart around the halfway point of the game. Once you reach the Valley of the Jedi, the entire rest of the game is spent on that planet, and consists entirely of navigating narrow cliffs and Imperial outposts whose existence is never explained, given that the vilains would never have had a chance to set up this elaborate series of bunkers, ventilation shafts, cardo areas,and drills before you got there, seeing as how they explicitly reached the planet at the same time you did.
But more importantly than that mild bit of fridge logic, the real failure of the latter half of the game is that it's just bland. The sets are just as big and interconnected as before, but they now lack context, being little more than a meandering series of setpieces with no obvious purpose, simply stalling time between you and your actual destination. The temple itself, which you spend the entire time trying to reach, is also pretty small by the game's standards, basically just three or four floors of tight corridors until you reach the end and get 'rewarded' with two boss fights in a row and the game ends.
So in conclusion while a second playthrough gave me a renewed appreciation for the level design, the latter half is dull enough that I still can't recommend it, especially given how crash-prone the game is.

There are many things that classify a game as good. You need to look at the characters and the plot, the gameplay and controls, the message and the feelings it invokes in you, even the soundtrack can separate a good from a bad game. There is no other video game that I have ever played that fits everything as perfect as Oneshot does. Oneshot is a game where you play as Niko, a gender neutral sweet kid that has a resemblance to a cat. They wake up in a house they don’t recognize and eventually come across a lightbulb which turns out to be the sun of the world that's every flat earthers dream. The world is a large circle with a tower in the middle where the sun is supposed to go. Niko must return the sun and save the world or else the world of the game will fall into eternal darkness. However, things are not that simple as you must make choices revolving around the fate of this world, and the fate of Niko.
Of course, it isn’t a book, it’s a game, a puzzle game to be exact.  Throughout the game, Niko is faced with a variety of different puzzles that cause you to think outside the box… literally. More on that later but I think that the whole puzzle element is really good. There are many different types of puzzles in the game causing you to really think and although it may not be everyone’s cup of tea, puzzle games have been one of the most classic games along with shooter games and thus can be enjoyed by a lot of people. About the controls, although Oneshot is strictly a computer game, it can be played with either a mouse and keyboard or a controller, whichever suits you the best. Controller is probably better as the default controls are a bit strange on keyboard and I ended up changing them. This is probably one of the very few hiccups in the game but that doesn’t mean the game is bad. Far from it actually.
The place where the game shines is definitely the very, very interesting mechanic of the fact that
as well as one other character who remains shrouded in mystery throughout most of the game but will help Niko in his journey by presenting you with solutions to unbeatable puzzles in very unethical manners. These elements in the game make Oneshot unique and amazing to gamers like me. Many things in a lot of games are the same while Oneshot truly thinks out of the box with new and interesting things I had never seen in a puzzle game.
The last thing I want to talk about are the characters and the soundtrack, which could be better. Yes, the soundtrack is really really good but compared to other games, it seems a bit mediocre. Even still, it’s catchy and memorable and I’ve found myself humming the tunes quite a bit before. Most of the characters aren’t extremely developed in the first half of the game. In the second half when you revisit all again, they seem more memorable than before but they could’ve been a tad bit improved with their first impressions.
That does not mean Oneshot is bad. These miniscule flaws are no match to the amazing story behind it all, the ending is truly bittersweet and truly makes you feel happy and sad and satisfied at the same time. This is really what makes Oneshot memorable as a whole, the amazing, impactful, meaningful ending that I truly loved, just like every other part of this game. It only costs ten dollars on steam and it really is ten dollars well spent. It is completely worth it and unless you really don’t like puzzle games, it will truly be one of the best games that you will ever play. Period.

Very much like Undertale, OneShot is a game that involves you as the player to an extend that is (to my knowledge) unmatched yet by any other game, even of similar genre. There are major surprising elements that you need to experience for yourself to truly understand the smart inner workings of what initially seems to be a rather simple shell of a game. It also helps that Niko (the protagonist) is driving the plot well and acts as a very cute / likeable character to keep you engaged in the plot. The pixel-art is simplistic, but overall coherent and moody, excelling especially at the small little cutscenes. The musical score also is fittingly paced and transports the mood well, but also remains simple and not memorable enough to persist after playing.
Overall the presentation is simple but "gets the job done" just right.
HOWEVER, before you start this, keep in mind that there are some major caveats that need to be named: OneShot is 100% walking and talking - there is little to no "game" existing - no failure states, no challenge, no elements of skill. There is fast-travel, but also a ton of backtracking and walking involved, which can get tedious in a world that is overall not so rich on details, items, characters or even easter-eggs to justify the extra distance. Even with a very limited set of items in your inventory the puzzles can get boring or confusing at times, but those are rare moments which are mostly caused by the sometimes very indistinguishable look of the world.
IF you can stomach the downsides, OneShot surely is worth the venture, because there ARE some great moments that you need to exprience first-hand to understand why this is rated "Overwhelmingly Positive" on Steam. For all these reasons alone and the special ideas in particular the game cannot be praised enough and SHOULD be played by anyone that loved Undertale or similar text-based adventures.

This is the first game I have ever done a review for on Steam.
What can I say about this game...It's beautiful. If you're a fan of cartoony kind of games with tons of action (I mean tons! It's crazy hectic) then this is the game for you. It is, by no means easy. The game can be incredibly difficult and at times frustrating (in the best way possible!) sometimes the bosses will make you rage so hard you want to break your controller. that's the type of game this is.
I would definitely buy this game again. I haven't had this much fun with a game for quite a while. All the boss fights, I mean all of them, are difficult from start to finish and all of them have at least 3 stages to them and have some pretty cool mechanics. The bosses are crazy original and the artwork is friggin awesome. I haven't seen a boss fight I haven't loved so far.
The creators of this game put a ton of love and heart and soul in this game. The moment you play it, you'll see what I mean. Everything looks like it just came out of a 1950's Disney cartoon. The rubberhose art style is incredibly perfected in this game. Cuphead is definitely one of my favorite games of this year. Of course there are some cons to it that I will list.
Pros:
Incredibly beautiful and completely original art style that you won't see in any recent games, yet it's not TOO cartoony to be childish.
A large amount of boss fights that range from difficult to incredibly difficult. :)
Decent amount of customization for Cuphead. You can change out his weapon and give him a secondary weapon to swap to as well as choosing one of three supers (you use that if you fill up your super bar all the way) and a slot for a trinket (I think that's what it's called) you can use this slot for extra health points or neat bonuses on your moves. For example, one of them gives you brief invisibility when you dash.
This means you can dash through a bullet or an enemy and take no damage. (Incredibly useful, imo)
Runs incredibly smooth and every enemy you kill explodes into smoke and little firework looking thingies. Sounds like a small thing but it looks really cool when you start killing multiple enemies that are clustered up in one spot.
Cons:
Not too many weapon choices to choose from. There are some cool ones but I would have liked to see a lot more.
Sometimes the parry mechanic is a little bit unresponsive. Take this with a grain of salt. This could just be me, this game favors precision so I am most likely not pressing the jump button at the correct time when I hit something to parry. In fact, i'm 90% sure.
It's really darn short. Again, I would have liked to see A LOT more bosses and I would have really really loved to see more of the little mini-missions where you get coins. Those little missions are ridiculously difficult but incredibly well thought out and enjoyable. I would have loved to see a lot more of everything in this game.
-----
That's about it. I couldn't think of much more cons to this game. It's beautiful and wonderful to play. It's incredibly creative. You know what it reminds me of? Megaman.
Flippin' Megaman.
Not Dark souls (but has dark souls level difficulty) but Megaman. That is why I enjoy this game so much. I know you'll love it too. Give it a shot, it's definitely worth it.

Streamline is a game that's nailed the party game format, but the most I can say is I'm glad I got it for free - It's mildly entertaining for about 30 minute sessions, but the problem with games based around Twitch interaction is that they're entirely throwaway.
It's an incredbly simplistic game that already feels dated due to some of the terms in game (Ripperoni/Crabcore etc.) that are meant to be hilarious, but aren't funny the first time (Nor anytime after that) and ultimately makes the game feel like it should be played soley by the very audience it's going for; screaming Twitch users and their teenage fans that are entertained by random gameplay and XD humour.
It's clear from the beginning that there's very little depth, in part due to the random nature of the modifiers that thrown in, which frustrate more than they entertain (Which I'm sure is great for the twitch audience, but not much fun for the player). The parkour mechanics are OK at best - the levels work relatively well around them but if I don't feel certain that I'm going to wall-run everytime I attempt to wall-run then you have ultimately failed at creating a good parkour game. The levels are a decent size but the way they're slowly closed off is frustrating and should probably only start in the sudden death section. The aforementioned section itself is quite annoying too, as the attack with the stop sign seems to hit enemies after the swing animation is finished prior to the sign being placed on the characters back again, resulting in unsatisfying kills and frustrating deaths (I can't say that for certain, nor do I intend to go back and test if that is the case). I can't see the multiplayer community sticking around for long either (Especially with no in-game chat function or mode to just run around the maps with others).
To sum up, it's not worth £15; maybe a fiver at most. If you manage to see this while the game is free for the day give it a download and see what you think, you might enjoy it more than I do. Maybe I'm reading too much into a game where you're supposed to just turn your brain off and have fun, but that just brings me back to my main point; it's a throwaway game. As my main interest in it was the parkour system which isn't particularly good, I won't be playing much more of it and I can't see many others playing it either.

Quite a few people have this issue with no way to fix it: Getting stuck on a black screen at start up or at the start of a mission or the end of a mission. At that point the game must be forced off.
Why is this crippling bug still around?

No, Mercenary Kings is not like Metal Slug. If you want Metal Slug, just go play Metal Slug.
Mercenary Kings is a 2D action-platformer with a variety of missions to undertake with generally non-linear level design. Yes, many of the missions share the same maps which I admit is a bit of a bummer, they could use some more variety since there is typically only 2-3 different maps per rank. Still, they're large and fun to explore and, with different types of missions including extermination (kill x amount of y), neutralize (kill boss), gathering (fetch items) and rescue (self-explanitory), among others, the different tasks do mix it up enough to keep it from getting completely stale.
What? Grinding? Yeah, there's grinding. You will need to grind materals to upgrade your gun's parts and upgrade your melee weapons. You will end up repeating missions over and over for mats. However, after the first run or two on a mission, you'll memorize the pattern of where everything is, making it much easier and faster to complete, so it's not as bad as it may sound.
The tunes are good, visuals are splended and charming, humor is amusing, characters are likable and the story works well for what it is.
Controls are responsive and both my old PS3 controller and my Logitech F310 work perfectly...do NOT attempt to play this with your keyboard or you're gonna have a bad time. I cannot stress that enough, do not use the keyboard, use a controller. Game client is stable; constant 60 FPS and no crashes to note.
The gun upgrade/mod system is fun and quirky, but could've been more refined and balanced, as the biggest changes to note are appearences, semi-auto/auto, clip size and reload time. While in theory this sounds nice since it boils down to preferences, many combanations lack fire-power so if you want major damage, you're limited to a few choice combanations. Considering this was one of the big selling points/features, it feels like it was unfinished and rushed.
I wish I could comment on the 4 player co-op, but I've never had the opportunity to try it.
Mercenary Kings isn't a game you can pick up and finish in an afternoon, it requires patience, time and investment. I recommend it, but it's not for everyone.

This game is the benchmark against which I measure all other tactical shooters and trust me when I tell you that practically no other game that has come out after Raven Shield measures up to it. SWAT 4 is very close but RVS comes out on top. In Rainbow Six 3 you take control of an international counter-terrorist unit called Rainbow and your job is to prevent terrorists from doing whatever it is that they are trying to do. To achieve this you use the powerful mission planner to plan your mission to the finest detail, coordinating up to three teams or a maximum of eight operatives. The planner will let you do anything you need to do to get the job done. For example you can set up go-codes to clear a room from multiple directions simultaneously. You can define how the teams make entry into a room: should they breach the door using a breaching charge? Should they throw in a flashbang or gas grenade before entering the room? You get the picture. You can also define the rules of engagement and movement speed of your teams for any waypoint. You can command them to be stealthy and only fire when fired upon for example or you can make them run and shoot on sight if you need to cover ground quickly to get to a hostage or bomb. The planner is awesome.
After you've finished planning your mission you can equip your teams any way you want. There's a lot of gear to choose from. There are light, medium and heavy armor and they affect your stealthiness and speed. Light armor is quiet and stealthy but does not offer much protection. Medium is a great balance and heavy armor looks kind of like riot gear and gives you extra protection but all your actions like switching weapons, turning around etc take a little longer to complete. You'll also be louder when you move. Then there are the weapons. There's a huge selection of SMG's, assault rifles, shotguns, sniper rifles, pistols, machine pistols, grenades etc. There is also a selection of tactical gear like heartbeat sensors, demolition kits (to speed up defusing of bombs), lockpicking kits etc. You can equip each individual operative however you want.
When you get in the mission itself you can switch between teams and operatives to control them at any time or you can stick to controlling your guy and let the AI do it's job according to the plan you've set out for those teams. The friendly AI is very good. The trailing guy will cover the rear of your team and they are very aware of their surroundings and they are accurate as well when firing. They're also good at clearing rooms. They get through the door quickly and each operative will cover their own area of responsibility in the room. You can command your AI team mates on the fly to perform actions like clearing rooms using breaching charges, flashbangs, gas grenades etc. You can also command them to pick locks, defuse bombs or to escort hostages out of harms way. You can perform these actions yourself also. The damage modelling is pretty awesome. You suffer different effects depending on where you're shot (if you're lucky enough to only get wounded that is). Your aim suffers a lot if you get hit in your arm for example. You can't run and your walking slows if you get hit in the leg and so on. Good mission planning is crucial because you want your team members to survive the mission so you can use them again. You have a limited number of operatives of varying skill levels and specialties and if they get wounded they will need time to heal before you can use them again. If they die you lose them for the rest of the campaign. The sounds are awesome too.
The enemy AI could be a little better although there's nothing in their behaviour that would get really annoying during gameplay. Sometimes one of them will drop a grenade as he dies and after it goes off you can hear "huh, what was that?" from the next room as if you can't tell when a frag grenade goes off in the hallway. They're pretty good at coming to investigate noises and stuff like that and they will use cover and get backup if you miss your shot and they get away. On the hardest setting they can be pretty brutal and it's tough to complete missions without any casualties to your team unless you've planned it perfectly.
After you get the hang of the game you can get online and you'll find there are still people playing. You can play adversarial modes or you can play the campaign missions co-operatively with your friends, coordinating take downs etc. using teamspeak for example. Multiplayer requires a
account and the game does lack voice comms of it's own but those are not big minuses.
The game is still every bit as awesome as it was when it came out. The graphics are a bit dated but it will run like a dream in very high resolutions and with ridiculous amounts of AA and AF on. With those kinds of settings it looks pretty good. Also you can get a mod called Raven Shield 2.0 that will enhance the realism of the game to even higher levels adding things like iron sights and it also has higher resolution textures for the operators and terrorists enhancing the look of the game. Tom Clancy's Rainbow Six 3 - were to start? I have infinite praise for this game.
This game is undeniably aged, but the gameplay mechanics still remain a pillar of tactical shooters to this day. Whether you go on a mission with a team of expert counter-terorist operatives, or you head into a mission lone-wolf, alertness and strategy is key to success - your life, your team's lives and the lives of helpless hostages all depend on your execution, which cannot be anything less than perfect.
Before each mission you may chose from a range of multi-national Rainbow Operatives to accompany you on a mission. Each operative has his/her specialty - be it alertness, stealth, leadership or skills with various equipment from breaching charges to sniper support to clearing rooms in close-quarters combat. It is up to you to decide each member's loadout (primary, secondary, type of ammunition, accessories, armor type, etc.,) You may chose to go in with a single squad or split up into 3 separate squads. Then comes the fun part - mission planning: drawing up a master plan takes time and dedication to carrying out a successful mission with zero casualties. Doing so you can rely on your fellow squad members to carry out your plans perfectly automatically - while you are sweeping the basement another squad that you assembled will sweep the roof for you, according to plan. But beware, everything relies on perfection.

i dont go out of my way to post reviews unless a game is really bad or they stole my money, but im going out of my way to recommend this game to support the devs and this 'genre' of crpgs if you could call it that.
my friend that i play dominions 4 with told me about it and how it used to be tales of middle earth. im a big fan of neverwinter nights 1, which is probably my favorite game of all time next to deus ex, so i thought i'd check this out.
i had never played an ASCII style rpg and that threw me off at first. i was like 'wtf is this' because i was ignorant and i didnt understand. i died over and over before even getting to the damned troll king or out of the first area, but with every new character i made i learned a little more. i slowly figured out the stat system, how the mechanics work together to create synergy, how to kill and stay alive, when to fight and when to run, how to avoid pitfalls and confidence traps. eventually i grew strong enough to go out into the world of maj eyal. being someone who cares a lot about lore i read every scrap of paper, i read the inscriptions on the statues of the king and queen in the capital city and learned about the weird oppressive history of the place. it blew my mind.
although its something thats off the beaten track - dont be scared. this is a diamond of a game if you like dungeons and dragons or crpgs in general. difficult, deep, satisfying. i would highly recommend this game. it is one of the best crpgs i have ever played.

RAID: World War II had a bumpy open beta period, but after putting in ample time and following it from release to now, I can safely say: support LGL and RAID.  It's a very good game.
From veteran engine, level, and gameplay devs on PAYDAY 2, RAID brings staples of the beloved PAYDAY 2 formula into a new time period.  While parts of it are quite similar to PD2, I feel that it's found its personality.
With a progression system similar to that of PAYDAY: The Heist, with more modernized ideals from its sequel, I'd attribute RAID with a comparison as a "PAYDAY 1.5".
Difficulty progression is a bit rough, but they've smoothed it out over time and it's felt more and more accessible.  Plenty of levels to keep you coming back for me, and plenty of upgrades, unlocks, and trophies will keep the grind-happy players in the game longer and longer.
LGL seems intent on keeping the community and game alive, with a few free content updates (there's already 3-4 new weapons introduced post release!), and more new raids on the way, I'm excited for the future of it.
I recommend bringing at least one friend along for the ride, or hell, grab three friends for a full team.

I got the digital deluxe edition waaaaay back when the game first came out, and poured a decent amount of time into it over the next two months.  I stopped playing right about when the first hunting season came out, because there was just nobody to play with.
Now that the game's gone F2P, I'd definitely recommend it to people.  You can actually find games now, which is amazing, the hunters and monsters that you could never play before due to the lack of people are pretty fun (Behemoth in particular was one I was hyped for, and is probably my favorite monster now.)
But let's talk about what's changed.  They removed Evactuation, alright, probably not a good idea.  My guess, considering that it's very clearly marked "Beta" wherever they show the name "Stage 2", is that they're reworking Evacuation, considering that one of the big criticisms was that a bunch of mutations does not unique games make.  Makes sense, especially considering that you can't buy Behemoth right now, as they're reworking him since he's a pubstomper.
They removed achievements and reset everyone's progression.  Fair enough, they're likely reworking achievments to work with the F2P aspect now, makes sense if you ask me.  Reset progression?  Oh no, you lost your badges or your skins that nobody actually saw outside of the lobby.  Boo hoo.
You get 3000 funbux for being a founder, an amount which, admittedly, will buy you Lennox's rocket punch and not much else.  But considering that you're a founder, you already have most of the hunters.  You probably got to tier 3, and might've even bought the tier 4 hunters, not to mention the freebie adaptations you get.  Hell, if you're like me you're probably one of the relatively few people who can play Behemoth right now!  So there's not as much for you to spend money on.  I admit, the amount could've been bigger, but it's nothing that'll break the deal if you ask me.
All in all, I'd probably up my prior rating to a 7.5/10, room for improvement definitely.  What people need to remember is that it's in a beta again, which means that things are going to change.

This game is wholly responsible for my interest in the soulslike genre- Having enticed me with it's nuanced yet easy to learn combat, the morbid beauty of the 2D world which you are nudged to explore, and the lore which chronicles the bleak storyline. It's an amazing love letter to not only the Darksouls games, but also the metroidvania genre as a whole.
Taking the role of the 'covenants' in souls, The various creeds presented in S&S are distinctly interesting - each faciliating certain playstyles via the consumable items they provide, and the modifications they make to the equipment made available to the player (as well as mildly impacting the ending).
My only lament, is that Co-op is limited to Couch Co-op, and furthermore- there is not the random invasions that added that certain element of fear and uncertainty to other entries in the soulslike genre.
I can only hope this game is revisted in the future to provide a more nuanced online experience, and to see an expansion or sequel. Nonetheless, even as it is, it's thoroughly worth a -number- of playthroughs.

Full Review:
Assassins Creed 2 is, for me, still the most enjoyable game of the AC series. The game follows Ezio Auditore ,an Italian descendant of the first games protaganist Altair, as he goes from a young man who witnesses his family killed as part of a Templar plot to an experienced member of the Assassin order. The game has some beautiful locations with the cities of Florence and Venice as well as some smaller countryside areas. Theres a lot of side stuff to do like assasination contracts or doing up your villa but the main story is still really enjoyable with some great missions thrown in.
Good points:
-Florence and Venice both look amazing and feel completely different to each other with the beautiful buildings and streets of Florence and Venice having its famous canals.
- Ezio is a great character as he's both likeable and charismatic and its easy to sympathize with his journey. Compared to Altair or Connor from the other AC games he's still by far the best protaganist.
- The story missions are both fun and enjoyable a lot of oppurtunities to put your assassin skills to work as well as the variety of gadgets and weapons Ezio acquires.
-This version comes with both DLC expansions, The Battle of Forli and Bonfire of the Vanities.
Bad points:
- Combat is a bit too easy. You can win most fights by countering enemies and hammering the attack button. Enemies also tend to stand off and attack one or two at a time so its easy to take on big groups of enemies.
- The parkour free running is good but canbe frustrating as it tends to be a bit inaccurate at times. I'd often have Ezio jump the wrong way or crash into a wall which is especially frustrating when your chasing someone or trying to flee from guards.

After sitting down with Streamline for just a few hours, I know this is definitely a game to watch. It's still in early access, with a few rough edges, but Proletariat looks to be pouring additional support into the game, so I'm guessing we'll see a lot of improvement. In the meantime, it's a pretty great game for some quick multiplayer sessions.
First off, player movement is a blast. While it's super easy to get the hang of wall-running, double-jumping, and boosting around a level, the best players I faced were able to pull off some amazing moves. (Very much in the "how the heck did they do that" vein.)
Rounds are also quick, and eliminated players don't have to just sit and watch the remaining runners play. They can interfere as "ghosts," stunning other players and chasing after "haunt" targets for extra points in the round. (Yes, you can keep scoring points when you're dead.) Some of the game mods play around with ghosts as well, like giving them the ability to eliminate other players or even come back to life for a short time.
I did have a few issues with the game: between each game you have to wait a few minutes while stream spectators place bets on the players and use their stream currency to purchase what game mods will appear in each round. If you're not engaging with the stream, (which as far as I can tell requires running Streamote in the background,) this part of the game can drag on. More integration of the stream tools and chat with the game itself is something I'd look forward to in the future.
The game mod system in general also adds some great variety to each round, but otherwise it's mainly there to give spectators a way to interact with the game, since players don't interact with it much themselves.
If you're a streamer, this game is a must, even in Early Access, but even if you don't stream, there's still something here for you. I imagine it's especially good for LAN parties or played wherever you and your friends can smacktalk each other.

Tom Clancy's Rainbow Six 3 is, for my opinion, the best game in Tom Clancy's Games series.
The plot in the game is really simple: some bad guys want to rule the world and we must stop them.
But the story isn't important in tactical FPS. The main thing is gameplay. And gameplay is really great.
At the beginning of every mission, we have briefing. In the briefing we'll know our objectives, how many terrorists on the level and other information. Then we should choose who will go on the mission. There are more than 50 persons in the game. We can choose evryone from the beginning, we mustn't unlock them during the game. Then we equip our operatives.We change their uniform, weapons, gadgets and others. After equipping our team, we should have a plan. This is the most interesting thing in the game. We make checkpoints to our team. Our team will go to these checkpoints. Also we can point, where should operatives throw grenade, or where should they wait another team.
After we are ready, we are going to the "battlefield". We can control EVERYONE in our teams. Usually on missions there are 2 or 3 teams. Usually you should kill all terrorists or rescue all hostages. Sometimes you should deactivate the bomb or  plant bugs in the computers. Terrorist die from 1 or 2 shots. But you also die from 1 or 2 shots, so this game is hard.
The graphics are still good for our days. Yeah, not Crysis, but Raven Shield is from 2003! The controls in game are not comfortable, because there are a lot of options: open doors silently, order your teammates, change operative and etc.
Also there is cool multiplayer. There is not a lot of players, but it is not hard to find them. Usually on servers you should eliminate all terrorists. Also in Gold Edition includes Athena Sword, short campaign with new objectives, operatives and new missions with time limit.
This game is very cool, the best tactical FPS of all times. People who love such kind of games will love it. Other players should also try this game. And it's cheap - $5.99!

Out of all of the games in the Rainbow Six series, this one is my favorite. The graphics are decent enough, and the gameplay is fun and addicting. Slow stealthy cautious strategies tend to win the day over rapid reckless Rambo-style running-and-gunning. The game has a vibrant map making community and there are many custom maps available after the official maps have been mastered. If you join a game that is using a map you don't already have, the game will automatically download the map from the server for you.

Rainbow Six 3 is considered the best installment in the Rainbow Six series by many, and for a very good reason. It is a one of the last true tactical fps's that makes a good attempt at being realistic instead of cinematic and flashy. Rainbow Six 3 is unforgiving and challenging, however, it does not solely depend on your twitch skills like many newer tactical fps's, instead you must use cautious strategy to clear each individual room. One of my favorite features in the game is terrorist hunt which gives each player in a multiplayer game a team of men that they may order to do things such as frag and clear a room. If you are looking for a tactical fps that manages to be extremely intense while requiring a slower but much more intelligent and cautious decisions than you will surely enjoy Rainbow Six 3.

You choose your team from a roster with different classes, loadout (weapon variety is above average by today's standards and easily trounces its sequels), and plan per mission after the in-depth briefing.  The pre-mission planning system is legendary.
The gameplay is more intense than any other shooter.  Deaths are permanent and it is so easy to die.  This and its two predecessors perhaps are more tactically challenging than any other shooter in existence.  Be sure to use this mod.
Seriously, shooters like this no longer exist, and it's a shame.  The command system is beyond most other shooters.  It reminds me of XCOM but in FPS form factor.  No stupid story tacked on, just difficult scenarios that you must overcome using smart tactics.

A true roguelike that got rid of some of the arguably unnecessary and frustrating features of roguelikes (e.g. cursed armor that just randomly kills you) and minimizes off-time with it's auto-explore feature.
The thing that really shines about this game is the character progression and creation though. Unlike traditional roguelike different classes play COMPLETELY different and indroduce new and interesting mechanics (like the manipulation of time for example). Almost every style of play is to be found here; from being a nasty necromancer and summoning skeletons and bone giants to slaughter your enemies to the time manipulating bow - dual weapon hybrid to the anti-magic "slime mage" that posisons his enemies, summons slimes to control the battlefield and uses PSIBLADES (F***ING PSIONIC LASERSWORDS).
In addition to the HUGE amount of classes, the classes themselves are extremly complex by having many different skill-trees to develop and unlock. While some people might see this as a negative I feel like this adds a lot of complexity of depth to the game and makes you able to play classes in completely different ways.

One of the first games I played for PC was nethack.  I loved that game and played it over and over, although I never had the discipline to beat it.  Tales of Maj'Eyal stands out from the plethora of mediocre 'roguelike' games that are so trendy recently. TOME is a worthy successor to the likes of rogue, netHack, Angband, and Slash'Em in every way.
Not only does the game offer a large, procedurally generated world to explore but there are also many very well-designed classes to do it with.  Where the game really shines is it's ui.  The fantastic use of color makes item details readily appreciable despite their complexity.  The auto-explore feature reduces the tedium of fully mapping a level, while sacrificing none of the level of tactical control required for difficult fights.
Since TOME uses a scaling level system (within ranges set by the zone), there is no need to have the type of food/hunger system used to force the player to advance deeper in the older games.  I always found a system that forced me to rush (or rely on random spawns for food) to be irksome.
The character classes are really diverse and unlocking them provides amusing challenges outside the central goals of the game.  Spells, abilities, and customization within a class all dramatically affect the playstyle.  Abilities feel like they have a real impact and boss/rare monster fights require tactics tailored to the encounter as well as the player's build.
The Steam login and chat system now work very well so you can chat with other players.  This can be very helpful and amusing.
All in all, a great game with enormous replayability.  As an update to my review, I finally got through the whole main campaign on a character (Temporal Warden) on normal mode.  A few minutes later I started again with a different class for a totally different experience.

However, what they did is done well, and there's some fun to be had.  So I would say you'll feel like it was worth $2.50, at $5 you'll feel like you paid full price, and at $10 it's expensive content.
To sum it up, the game sizzles, then it fizzles.  I walked away from it feeling really disappointed.
