Similar to Payday 2 in some respects but different enough to be its own with amazing, hardworking developers to match.

It's a WW2 themed cooperative heist game made by a studio (Lion Game Lion) with experience working on content for Overkill's Payday 2. If Payday 2's chief inspiration was heist movies like Heat, then RAID is a bit of Dirty Dozen and Inglorious Basterds. In short, you and three other allied misfits will be conducting commando raids and illicit heists in nazi territory. There's usually a chance to do it the sneaky, quiet way, or to just start blowing things up and shooting your way through. You can play as one of four characters, play them as any of the four classes, level them up, choose which skills to advance, and unlock visual and statistical upgrades for your weapons. Also shared with it's cousin Payday is the added difficulty of special units, in this case things like Officers and a very pulp action style armored flamethrower nazi.
It's had a bit of a rough start, mainly due to some balance issues that need a bit of polishing (as of this review, chiefly the slow grind of the second half of leveling up your characters) and a low playerbase (which you, a prospective buyer, might actually be fixing), but the developers are prompt in changing things for the better and seem to believe in what they're making. They patch regularly, and don't seem to be burying their heads in the sand when players tell them something needs work, which is nice.
All in all, had I not been lucky enough to snag a promotional code from the developer, I probably would be hesistant to buy it at the normal $40 price point. On sale (at as low as $10, as of this review) I would consider it a good buy for anyone who enjoyed the Payday games' formula and either enjoys it solo or can persuade 1-3 buddies to pick it up with them.

Rift has some interesting things going for it that sets it apart in the theme park mmo genre. First and foremost, it is completely free. None of the content is restricted upon creating an account and making your first character.  The cash shop in the game is little more than xp potions, crafting buffs and aethetics.  What I like is that for $20 I can buy a really nice wardrobe, a fast mount and some smaller things and my character will look pretty nifty right out of the gate.  Gameplay is wittled down to accepting quests from npc's, running about 500 feet in some direction, killing mobs or looting items and then turning the quest in to someone, usually the same npc you took it from.  This sort of gameplay has been seen dozens of times in other games but Rift manages to keep it fresh with the group rifts dynamic that spawn every few minutes on the map.  You and a group of other players fight to close rifts to other worlds when they open. They vary in difficulty but usually aren't difficult.  Rift caters to casual players which is where the money is nowadays.  With a moderate amount of play time each week, one could easily hit max level and get some decent gear.  PVP is a grind sad to say.  If you don't play defiant (the bad guys) then you will be playing with bots most of the time, which is illegal in mmo's and consistently lose nearly every match as a guardian.  This is a great time sink if you don't want to spend tons of money on an mmo.

even though the graphics are somewhat outdated by today's standards this game remains to be one of the best starwars games ever made, improving on what darkforces did right and adding 3D graphics this game I would highly recommend. that being said, if you are running windows 8 there are a few tricks you may have to use to make the game run properly. for starters you will want to run the game on Windows XP service pack 3 (2 works alright but crashed more in my time playing around with it) secondly you will want to disable 3D acceleration as on newer machines it tends to cause a black screen issue that the forums are literally packed with questions about, I run mine without the 3D acceleration with the display set too 800x600 and it runs just fine. and thirdly I would recommend setting it to back buffer, this makes the game run much more smoothly. as long as you boot the game from the actual .exe file instead of the steam shortcut you will be able to play in full screen, if you have any further issues the forums are of great help and the community has been very helpful, even with the hardware issues I would definitely reccomend 10/10

Jedi Knight, the follow up FPS to Dark Forces was and still is one of the best FPS games to date.  The only thing that didn't age well in this game is the graphics.  The models can look horrible at times, but overall the immense levels create a sense of immersion rarely seen in games these days.  The level design is top notch, the length of each level is very long, and the variety of weapons is perfect.  This is a Star Wars game at its best.  The storyline is well done too, though the video produced cutscenes are cheesy at best, but at least they keep the story going, and the story gives you reason and meaning to why you are fighting.  I did have some issues with the game.  The amount of times that I died and had to restart from a save from a long time ago was very frustrating.  I wish this game had auto save, which would have been perfect when specific goals on your objectives were completed.  Also, the lack of the audio music from Star Wars (which was played from the CD in the original format) is absent in this Steam version.  I watched the credits without any Star Wars music, and throughout the game it was the same.
This game is a classic.  If you love Star Wars and don't mind the dated graphics, you're in for a great adventure.  Highly recommended.

Typical Ubisoft game: fantastic art design, uninspired story, shoddy development.
The art is fantastic, drawing you into an imagined 15th century Florence. By far, this is what drives this game, since the plot and game mechanics are generally tepid. The power of the art is make feel empowered to explore a fantastic world, though this feeling is somewhat stifled after the first few hours by the only semi-open world feel. The game obviously goes through great lengths to make it feel like you have the kind of open world choices you get in games like Skyrim or GTA, but the somewhat lackluster side-games, the limited travel area, and the vanilla storyline causes it to fall short in this department. In fact, AC2 feels far less open-world than AC1 and several times during gameplay I was screaming out for a chance to just wander the city and take assassination contracts out on people, but alas, you are railroaded pretty heavily into the main generic story. The illusion of choice exists all along in this game, but actual choices are somewhat limited. Each "quest" you get you have the choice to accept or not accept, but not accepting just means you start the cut-scene over and get a chance to try to accept again. In short, the only choices you get are to play or not to play, and after hours of wandering around Florence's stunningly drawn back alleys looking for pieces of parchment and birt feathers, I generally leaned toward the not-playing side of things.
As with most Ubisoft games, AC2 suffers from lazy development, though mostly in the port to PC -- though I did find myself several times cursing the poorly designed camera rotation that often rotates mid-run to cause you to veer unexpectedly is other directions. It was also fun finding the numerous other spots in the game where I got the♥♥♥♥♥♥kicked out of my by Florence's overly ubiquitous town militia after I got glitched halfway off the map, unable to move. And don't be too creative about how you approach your targets. Once I decided to be sneaky and come down from above, only to trigger a cut-scene back with me on the street getting robbed. Oh yeah, and the cutscenes. So after a few hours, when you're desperately bored with the plot, then use the cutscenes to get up and stretch and get a snack because you can't skip them.
If you're playing the PC version the biggest complaint is typical lazy console port that Ubisoft is so famous for. Most of the game plays all right, but the controls for PC are hideous. If you prefer Keyboard and Mouse, don't even buy the game. It's maddening. The controls make a lot of sense when using a gamepad, but I spent a number of frustrating hours trying to get my controllers to work with the game. I have a XBOX and a more generic Logitech controller, both of which work fine with other games, but they were frustrating glitchy in AC2. I basically had to mod around the XBOX one and re-maps keys for my logitech one. And, to make matters worse, whever I found a new viewpoint in the game, for some mysterious reason, the game would re-map my controllers again. So, stupid.
In spite everything, I still somewhat enjoyed this game, though not as much as AC1. In general, if you get lucky and get everything to work well, and can ignore the crappy port, it's not bad for a somewhat mindless romp through Renaissance Florence. But in the end, I probably wouldn't recommend it as one of my more favorite games.

Basically, OneShot is about its protagonist, Niko. He wakes up in a strange world and eventually finds a lightbulb. When placed atop a tower, this lightbulb acts as a sun, and Niko must bring it there.
This game is amazing. Rather than sucking you into the world with interesting or fun characters that you just want to care about and be with, you ARE a character in this game, and the character you play as constantly talks to you in his dialogue, and is also just a lovable character. It makes you feel more like a part of the world. And a lot of the music in the game's soundtrack is low and melancholy, fitting the games (literal) dark atmosphere. there's still plenty of humor to be found though. As for how long the game keeps you entertained. Beating the game should take around 4-5 hours depending how good you are at puzzles. but it's similar to games like Undertale. One playthrough is shorter than your usual one, but things change after one playthrough.
. However, Undertale is a quirky, more cheerful game most of the time, OneShot tells a rather dread tale of a doomed world that is accepting its death.
and one more thing. You have to break the 4th wall to solve certian puzzles, like going into files and stuff. And that's pretty cool.
But every game has it's flaws. As the name "OneShot" suggests, the replayability is pretty bad. In fact, you can't replay the game until
In the end, I absolutely loved OneShot. It's got an amazing story, charming characters, good humor, and the game breaks the 4th wall in unexpected ways. I'll always recommend this game.
Buy it. Play it. Now. If you have the money, buy it. EXPERIENCE IT. You will absolutely not regret it. It's brilliant in so many ways, endearing as all hell, and I love it to pieces.

Ho-lee Pancakes, where to start with this one?
How about the graphics? While rather simplistic, it's still found to be rather beautiful and pretty. The facial portraits of the different characters are all of high quality, and some of the reactions, especially from Niko themself, has got me cracked up more than a few times. Though where the visual aspects of this game truly shines is in the artwork and pictures by Nightmargin, typically shown in transitions from areas to areas or dream sequences. Overall, the artstyle lends itself to be very attractive to look at.
The gameplay meanwhile, is rather simplistic as well. You can make Niko run faster, move, interact, combine objects to complete puzzles... And that's about it, which makes for the groundwork of most of the puzzles of the game, many of these are rather simple, but not too simple that you can just look at it and figure out the solution without thinking just a bit. But that's only for most of the puzzles... Sometimes you need to think, and look, outside of the box.
The music fits the tone of the game rather well, with much of it being melancholic and down-tone in nature, as the world is slowly falling apart, but with enough upbeatness to instill a sense that not all is lost, and that the world can still be saved. Some tracks are darker, some are more somber, some are lighter, some are more cheerful, and I can not recall a single time I felt a soundtrack was out-of-place, and merely enhance the feel of the environment and the characters. Speaking of characters...
They are in my personal opinion the strongest part of the game, Niko in particular. But every character that you find yourself talking to more than once or twice are very distinct in their personality, and many of them are rather likeable. And I can't stress just how adorable and lovely Niko is as a person. And I find myself wanting more of these characters, and, again, Niko in particular.
Now that I've praised the game, do I find any faults with the game? Well, yes. Especially one fatal flaw that sticks out like a sore thumb. One that I still can't get over.
It's so short.
You're likely to get 5-6 hours out of this game in a single playthrough. But trust me when I say this, those 5-6 hours and 10 dollars/euros are going to be worth it. I do not have buyer's regret in the slightest. But it still pains me that it ended so quickly... And speaking of things that pain me... Some spoiler-filled material below. Do -not- read it unless you've actually finished the game. And I'm not talking about watching someone else play through it. I want -you- to play through it.
Besides these little gripes, it's a stellar game. One I can proudly recommend to everyone. Even people who aren't fond of puzzle-adventures. If only to meet the lovely cat-child that is Niko.
And for the love of that precious lightbulb, do let the poor thing sleep and eat, will you?

Raid: WW2. Oh boy, here we go. A game almost as hyped, yet a letdown as Duke Nukem Forever, or Guns N Roses Chineese Democracy. Yet, like that game and album, there is some hidden gems hidden deep in the flaming bag of dog♥♥♥♥♥♥ This is almost a hard game to review. Is it a AAA game? No, so you cant review or compare it as such. Does it live up to its big brother Payday? Again, no. Has it got a ton of unfair hate because of this? Maybe....
There IS some fun to be had in this game, and there is alot of potential here. You just got to dig deep and find it. If you take it for what it is, and what it isnt, all in all its a...well..average game. Alot of people thought that this was just gonna be a payday game with a WW2 reskin. For better or worse, this is NOT the case. Yes it was made by some of the people who did the dlc for Payday 2. Yes it was heavily inspired by the sub genre that payday is in. Yes it runs on the diesel engine. But the game does have its own system, play style, and does things in its own way.
Gone are the equiptment such as med and ammo bags, along with regenitive health and armor. The game has taken on a more "retro" style, where you must find ammo and med packs during gameplay, and you cant heal by just staying out of the line of gunfire for a few seconds. Depending on what your looking for, this could be a con or pro. Old school gamers may appriciate being takin back to the time before you were basically invincible. As a matter of fact, most of the gameplay and style seems to lean more towards the early days of first person shooters then it does payday.
The controls are fairly basic, but they work good enough. Nothing super complex here. Which again can be a plus for people looking for this type of gameplay. The perk system is setup to where you have to be careful in what you choose to unlock for each level, as you only get one choice per tier. This encourgages not only teamwork but working and making builds to complement your teammates/friends. You can however respec your skills, though It does cost some gold to do so.
I think the biggest cons with this game can be remedied with a large patch. The AI is crap yeah. There is very limited content, like Payday the Heist limited. Of course, this game hasnt been out for long, and with all the hate and lack of sales the game is getting, who knows if or when we will get more. Of course they are not going to put alot of time and money in making DLC if no one is going to buy the game in the 1st place. So keep that in mind before complaining about the small amount of heists (around a dozen or so) and weapons.
The next thing is the graphics. Yeah yeah they may not be everything, but its one of the biggest complaints I seen. Look, it was no secrete that it was built on the desiel 2.0 enegine. Everyone knew that going in. So buying the game and complaining about it afterwards is stupid and pointless. However, they look alot worse then Payday 2. The really do need to be polished up. Again something that im sure can come with an update, if enough people buy it in the 1st place to make it worth while. Its a buisness. And no one is in the buisness to lose money. Plain and simple. And if everyone refuses to buy it, all its goin to do is hurt the people who did. Instead of being improved its gonna get no support.
The devs have released alot of patches and updates already since its release, and it has seemed to address alot of the bugs and glitches in the game. How much more they will update, at the end of the day, is up to sales. What I would like to see would be 1st an improvement in the AI and polsihed graphics at least up to Paydays standards. Then more content. Hell release one or two free dlcs, then for early supporters give them the 1st one or 2 paid ones for free. Make everyone happy and keep people playing while bringing in more players.
Overall, its not a bad game, but its not without its issues. However the issues I feel can be fixed, if the dev is motivated enough to do so. Would i reccomend? I say yes, on sale. If you can get it for around 20 bucks, then its worth it. In its current state however Im not so sure about paying 40. They are continuing to do updates and all so time will tell. It has potential. Many games have rough launches but end up becoming really good. I mean, how many people even played the 1st payday? I got it on PS3 when it came out. 20 bucks, it looked interesting. But from what i saw not many people bought it. It too didnt look the "prettiest" and had very limited content. And look what it turned into.
Give raid a chance. It may end up surprising everyone.

Some people are blindly calling this game Payday 2, WWII Edition, and while the game does obviously have some similarities, it has enough differences in my opinion to warrant it being its own game, and hopefully this review clears things up a bit
Let's get the similarities out of the way
Robbing-You obviously have the ability/opportunity to steal nazi treasure, but this is RARELY the sole purpose of a mission, however, it should be noted that the "get the treasure to the exit" element is shared, but as mentioned beforehand, rarely the only purpose
Gunplay and team emphasis-The gunplay and controls feel similar enough that people who played Payday 2 will be used to it and have a general idea, but the mechanics that are not identical may seem small, but they will actually play into your strategies and how you play compared to Payday 2. Obviously the game can be a blast alone, but is even better online or with friends and it's strongly recommended to team up and get missions done as efficiently and best as possible
Some Missions and Mission structures-On occasion, a mission will strongly remind you or basically be modeled after a payday 2 mission (such as the outlaw raid to rob a German art gallery) or how operations are structured similarly to multi-day heists, but the missions themselves 99% of the time are different enough as well as the objectives
That is where the similarities end, now let's get to the differences
Leveling up structure-Rather than the idea of earning skill points when you level up and having them thrown at many skill trees or one skill tree with multiple builds being an option, each character can be trained individually and upgraded individually but each starts at level 1. The upgrades are picked between usually 3 choices (i.e. more ammo with pick-ups, bigger grenade inventory, or less recoil with automatic weapons) however, the kicker is that you can only pick one of these three choices when you level up, and while they can be upgraded by adding more points when you level up again, that may limit your choices
In short, the leveling up system is a lot more like Boarderlands
Stealth-Stealth is played out a LOT differently and goes beyond not getting caught and avoiding things unlike Payday 2. You obviously don't have to worry about pager limits, but at the same time, you have no silenced weapons (obviously) aside from your melee weapon and 99% of the time you will get caught if you fire your gun (the 1% being if you shoot someone and somehow no one else is in range to hear the gunfire, but that’s extremely rare)
With stealth, you need to plan out and explore the map,  learn the patrols routes, and find the most effective way to complete your objective without causing attention and also plan out who to get rid of and when/where, hiding bodies and making sure no one else is around while moving them and hiding them well enough is a major element of the game and is not as easy as hiding them in a dumpster compared to Payday 2 (although dumpsters can be an option during some missions, they are often not around, and you also don't get blueprints of maps)
In short, stealth is harder, has a different approach, and requires more experience or trial and error (the good kind) before you can efficiently keep things quiet. It should be noted that stealth does need some fixing though, some foes can see through a wall or corpses can glitch through ceilings for example
Difficulty-With these other things listed being in mind, the game is much harder than Payday 2, it also is much harder because it plays like older shooters where health does NOT regenerate and does NOT go by the "bloody screen" rule, you need to stick to cover and keep your distance if you want to be alive and hunt down and make use of med packs and ammo either from crates or from foes that drop them on occasion. I very much enjoy the idea of a more realistic shooter in this context, the only time your health can regenerate (and not much at that) is with your war cry, which can be thought of as a Boarderlands style ability where after you eliminate a particular amount of foes, a little bit of health regenerates, and you get increased damage and less recoil for a little bit until the war cry wears off
The biggest factor of difficulty is that health is not the same as Payday 2 in context that patching up does NOT give you more opportunities to get down,, if you go down 5 times, it's game over, and with no armor or regenerating health it can seem like nothing in terms of amount of downs you get. But the difficulty is balanced. People who play Payday 2 on harder difficulties (I managed to beat everything on One Down with a friend and AI) will be in for a treat in terms of a challenge and a game that has familiar gameplay but enough tweaks to be different enough to in turn, be a challenge.
Weapons and Upgrades-With how weapons are structured, Its encouraged to try each weapon a bit (within your class, you can also change your class if you want, but that’s beside this particular point) and stick to a particular set of weapons to your liking, because killing a particular amount of nazis with a weapon (i.e via hip fire, getting headshots, or killing nazis in general) will unlock upgrades such as decreasing spread and increasing magazine size, the weapons upgrades are also in tiers, which means that once you unlock tier 1, you get to a particular character level, and you will unlock tier 2 and you and your "old girl" will have to wipe out more nazis, but this doesn't feel like a chore, because that’s what you'll be doing anyway while doing missions
Missions
Missions in Payday 2 usually are stealing loot, taking someone out, or creating something, these missions are structured objective wise like payday 2 (meaning do  objective, A, then B, then C etc..) but Raid's missions are quite literally more "with the times" and can offer variety with everything from wiping out SS camps to stealing an enigma to decode nazi messages to destroying panzers at a tank depot to even rescuing prisoners at a bunker (which btw, NPC's that need to be rescued can die, so you need to keep an eye on them and have a good eye on whether or not you tell them to move)
Lastly is special foes
Special Foes
Special Foes in itself is common, but the strategy and types of foes are different enough (with the sniper being the only exception, but that's expected)
Flamer-People often compare the flamer to the bulldozer, but other than having heavy armor and needing to aim for the head, there’s nothing similar about it, you need to actually keep your distance and gun it down from cover while avoiding its flame which can linger on the ground
Officer-These can be thought of as similar to Captain Winters, but rather than ending an assult when going away, officers will instead need to be taken down as quickly as possible, otherwise heavier infantry will keep hammering you even after an attack is over, not to mention they are fast and have powerful handguns
Spotter-These ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s will keep throwing flares which you'll have to either extinguish or run away from a bombing run after the flare "goes off" when you run out of time, its best to take these down after they throw their first flare and after you put it out
To conclude this review, this is what I have to say (Mind that this review is coming from someone who played the beta)
Raid WWII takes little bits of Payday  and uses it as a "blueprint" having some similarities, but it adds its own "spices" to make its own  "recipe" to be different or its own type of game, with a more realistic approach (but not too realistic to avoid being frustrating) and feeling more challenging. It's a nice welcome change with how many shooters there are these days and this game can be thought of as a mix of Payday's premise and some of it's elements meets the OLDER (were talking 1999 or early 2000s) call of duty games before call of duty went downhill imo

A game for the ages, Cuphead is a marvel of gameplay and animation excellence. Often described as "2D Dark Souls", Cuphead offers a challenging (but fair) adventure comprised of some Run N' Gun side-scrolling levels, but mostly intelligently designed boss battles. Every level and boss offers great variety, with nothing ever feeling too "samey." From giant, killer veggies to devious genies, Cuphead impresses.
There is no checkpoint system in this game. It expects you to go hard or go home. Thankfully, aside from being fair, each level/boss never seems to go on too long. If you die, the game will show you how far you got in the level, which can lead to addictive "I was so close, I gotta try again"  behavior.
There's a currency system in place for you to purchase alternative weapons and supers with. One particular loadout may give you a little easier time on a certain boss than another. Coins are collected in side-scrolling levels, but there's also some hidden around the world map. There are trade-offs to most (if not all) purchasable items, however. For example, you can buy another health point, but your weapon damage is slightly decreased.
If you want a solid, challenging, addicitve, and stylish 2D game, Cuphead has you covered. So, what are you waiting for? A brawl is surely brewing!

Opinion:**
I love this game- when I found out about it this summer I was blown away that more people weren’t paying attention to it.  As a streamer on Twitch I am always looking for games that get the chat involved- many times the game I am playing has zero integration and occasionally it is nice to provide an experience that is all-inclusive for the viewers.
Here's the basic gameplay description:
There is one game mode currently: Elimination which pits the “hunter” against the “runners” to gather the most points before getting eliminated! The parkour movement allows everyone to get around the level with ease: double jump, sprint, power slide, and dodge left/right.
The hunter is the only one with a melee weapon and their goal is eliminate the runners- pretty simple! The hunter also recharges stamina over time where the runners are vulnerable with limited stamina (runners pick up lightning bolts to refill it). The hunter is normally the host of the game who is streaming on Twitch but you can also choose another person to be hunter or a random choice.
The runners can punch the hunter / other runners if they have good timing and use the parkour movement to avoid them.
If you get eliminate you come back as a ghost to “haunt/grief” other runners. Press G to taunt their failures (or pay your respects).
It’s a tug of war to get the most points with unpredictable rulesets that are voted on in the chat through the proprietary streamote.tv site where you (using a virtual points system) can bet on who wins, buy rules from the rules store, vote on rulesets during the game, and play Bingo!  Chaotic, action packed with an excellent soundtrack that will leave your head bobbing involuntarily. (available on Spotify, Google Play etc.)
How to get started:
Once you launch the game you will connect your Twitch account which is super easy to do- then your ingame name will match your Twitch name.
Click on inventory* to customize your character- before you “get good” you gotta look good. Just sayin’!!
The options menu has the ability to view / rebind controls (I play with inverted mouse).
If you are a solo player you can just hit quick play* and get into the action- you will be assigned to a random party.  Once you find a game you can go to the host’s streamote.tv site- for instance if Kappa was playing Streamline theirs would be

However, where this game shines is the Twitch integration for streamers- using the streamote.tv site that gives everyone something to do- the host (streamer) chooses who is allowed to join the party- open for anyone to join including those who use the “quick play*” feature, invite only to choose specific people, and subscribers only for a quick and easy Sub Sunday event!  The party system even detects who owns the game for ease of use when inviting players.  One of my favorite additions recently was the quick play* feature which allows new players who don’t understand how the streamote.tv site works yet a way to get into a game and meet other players.
And this is a game that can get quite competitive- I was recently at TwitchCon and saw in person how the skill ceiling for Streamline is something that no one really expected.  I got a chance to talk to the best players in the game right now and they are all very friendly but once the game starts so does the competition.
Conclusion / tl;dr:
A fast paced, smooth parkour Pacman where one hunter aims to eliminate the runners asap!  A great game for streamers to involve everyone in the chat and get things hype!  The current game mode is limited and there is a high ceiling for potential other game modes.  Team Elimination will be all I play once that mode is finalized.
Currently there are 5 maps and many different customization options including exclusive Steam items or Twitch Prime items if you end up owning that version too (free on Twitch Prime through October).  As a streamer this is a must play- if you are the competitive type you can try to take the crown from the best players currently.  Best and only game of its type out there. Worth.
*Inventory and Quick Play, other features are this way as of the current version and may be subject to change.
**Objective opinion, not compensated for this review.  I received this game for free as part of the alpha testing phase.

Streamline looks more complicated in gameplay videos than it actually is. Within a few rounds you can get a good grip of the game. The game can include up to 16 players. 15 Runners plus a Hunter. The Hunter has the ability to kill the Runners in one hit. The runners compete for points by collecting orbs of differing values while using a dash meter. The dash meter is filled by pickups and you gain more points if you collect orbs while dashing. The movement in the game is context sensitive, as you can wall-run and do similar acrobatic feats while holding a button. If you are killed, you become a ghost. A ghost can no longer collect orbs, but can gain an increasing amount of points by punching a randomly assigned, still-alive runner. The game is played in 3 rounds that last a few minutes and the point total is cumulative, so if you die early in the first round, you can try to make up for it in the second round (and perhaps sabotage the runners who have amassed more points than you). If you are still alive at the end of a round, ghosts disappear and a sudden death commences, where you are finally able to kill the hunter by landing a hit on him, you just have to survive long enough and land a hit. The Hunter is scored via a letter grade (F- to A+ it seems), while the runner with the most points wins.
There is intergration with twitch, as you can host or join lobbies by linking your twitch account in-game and then using the developer's twitch player at
. You do not have to install anything, as some people seem to be confused on how this works. The end result is that you are able to find lobbies via this website, join a party, and play with a streamer (or if you are a streamer yourself, host). Viewers are able to view the stream of the game and use a point system to influence the game through different global buffs/debuffs that they choose when to activate. They can also bet on who they think will win and rack up more points via bingo in the lobby.
To put it simply it's a competitive score-based platformer with asymetrical gameplay (Hunter, Runner & Ghost). It also involves optional stream integration, so that viewers may influence the gameplay. It's still early-access at this point, but feels solid and I have enjoyed the quirky experience so far. Recommended.

[Player review]
My review of Streamline based on the experience of a player that does not stream.
Streamline is in my opinion an incredibly fun and challenging game because it offers a different experience every time I play. This experience is formed and changed each time by the Players,Viewers and Rules which change every time I play.
The movement in Streamline is easy to jump into but requires some practice to get down, don't be afraid to maybe lose a few matches while getting into the game. Once you get the movement in the game down however it opens the gate to play every match in a diffrent style. Be it avoiding the hunter by staying on map wide distance of him/her or challenging the hunter straight on and getting that satisfying "Bear wrestler" accolade at the end of the match by stunning the hunter throughout the game.
The look of the game is very cartoony which bases on your prefrences can be either a pro or con.
The ability to join and play with a streamer and his/her community can be enjoyable yet for some perhaps a bit scary.
For those who enjoy meeting new people I encourage joining on going streams to chat and play together. For those who do not feel the need for community play there has recently been an update which added a "Quick Play" mode. This allowed for players to play without being forced into a new group of people, this mode even eliminated the dependency on streamers to host in order play the game.
For streamers who have a smaller group of viewers getting a good feel of the game might feel a little bit challenging at first. However it is still possible to get the most out of Streamline.
Streamers are for example able to open their game to both viewers and "Quick play" players, this makes it easier to gain a full party without having a big viewer base. ( The downside is that these players might not join the stream and will thus not join in on the betting and voting/buying rules.)
Another way to gain more players is the publicly open discord from the developers "Proletariat". In the discord Streamers are able to advertise to and communitcate with player and other streamers, this often increases the players who are both active on streamote and in-game.
A last option would be to join with multiple streamers in one hosted game, through using the
. this way each streamer has their own streamote channel and viewers but the betting/voting/buying is shared.
Thus yes, it might be hard at first but there are options provided to help you at it.
Since there has been quite some changes and additions to the game I will not review this until further in developemnt.
I hope this adressed some of the important aspects for players/streamers deciding to play and/or buy streamline.

***I'd like to mention upfront, plan on playing this game with a community to get any fun out of it, otherwise it's going to be a lonely experience.***
So that's out of the way, it can take a bit to get your bearings and understand what's going on. Really after a match or two you'll quickly find out it's basically like a 3d Pacman where a bunch of players are trying to collect points, and one "hunter" is trying to eliminate them. But that's not quite the whole picture; the community portion involves players using an app/twitch to vote on rules on a game in progress. This is where the magic is! Mid-game you can expect floors to turn into ice or lava, weapons to turn into pool noodles, players to randomly explode on contact, just crazy #$#@!
If you can get passed the initial confusion, this game can be a blast. Especially if you are tuned into twitch while playing and getting everyone's reaction to the action on screen. Totally worth it!

I hate roguelikes. I like difficult games but roguelikes are the antithesis of fun to me. I hate losing my progress, I hate not being able to save scum, I hate dying and losing the feeling of satisfaction just when my character is starting to get somewhere. That being said, I am in love with Tales of Maj'Eyal. It's (shockingly) a roguelike turn-based RPG with varying levels of roguelikeness. For example, when I die - and I die a lot - I choose to start over at level 1 with the same character rather than make an entirely new one every time.
At first glance it looks like some college kid's freshman project, but the UI is clean and has all the information you need without seeming overwhelming. The writing is often hilarious and the lore is deep and engaging. Character sheets, stats, and numbers make me gibber and hyperventilate, so if that's your thing prepare to pore over your character until your eyes bleed. The world has a surprising amount of depth with many races and political/social dynamics between them. At 7 bucks it's really a no-brainer if you like RPGs or turn-based combat; it's definitely one of the best games I'd played in the genre.

Played this back on 360 and with it on sale on Steam figured I would give it a go. My perspective is from someone who is accustomed to console games. If you are a PC gamer some of the gameplay issues may bother you more than me.
Pros
- Gunplay is pretty responsive and crisp. It hasn't aged horribly but is a little stiff. This could also be due to it being an older game and I am using an Xbox Elite Controller so I do not know how good the gamepads are for this title. Overall controls well.
- Graphics are still really good. Obviously it shows its age but at 1440p it looks a lot better on my current PC than it ever did on 360. Animations are pretty good in enemies and the player.
-Sound. Gun sounds and enviromental effects are pretty good. Had to turn music down though as it was drowning out the speech
- Setting and style.  I gotta say ID had a pretty good take on a Fallout setting and gameplay style. I love the crafting and the Wingblades (I think thats what they were called lol)  The world is well designed. Levels are pretty linear but the world is somewhat open, definitely focused though.
- Shotgun. Its an ID game and the shotgun is cool. :D
Cons
- That ending... obviously. A pretty big con to what was a pretty enjoyable game up until then. I can't imagine its any different on PC
-Framerate -  This game has had some issues for me staying at 60. Even taking it down to 1080p it fluctuates between 35-45 sometimes breaking 50 and infrequently hitting 60 and staying there. I also needed to turn on V-Sync dude to heavy tearing. Performance wise I am sure the 360 was only at 30 FPS so this is still an improvement but I have become accustomed to 60 on my current rig even at 1440p and nearly 144hz on some games like Vanquish.
Overall for the price I got it, less than 5 bucks I think, has been very much worth it to replay a game I enjoyed quite a lot back on the 360. I would say get it if you like shooters for sure.

OneShot is a unique puzzle adventure game where you help guide a cat child named Nico on his mission to return the sun. What makes this gameplay special is that the game itself acknowledges you the player as a separate entity from Nico, and there are frequent 4th-wall breaking interactions and puzzles.
In addition to the unique gameplay, OneShot has lovely pixel graphics and a wonderful soundtrack that both help set the tone of each location.
Nico's character development is excellent, and by the end of the game, I cared a lot about Nico and what would happen to him.
Overall, this game is definitely worth the price.

Assassin's Creed 2 is the second game of the Assassins Creed franchise , and , said by many, the best one yet.
The scenario is redistribuited throughout various citys like Florenze, Venezia , Romagnia and temporarily the game is located in the XV century more precisely throughout 22 years of the life of Ezio Auditore de Firenze.
Let's evaluate it!
Graphics --- 75/100 : The graphics on Assassin's Creed 2 are ( by the time of this review ) already outdated. While it is very "chompy" for us already,back in 2009 I believe they were astonishing.                                                                                                  I think, nonetheless, that the models of the faces of some characters ( especially the less relevant ones ) could be more detailed despite the age of the game.
Sounds --- 75/100 : The soundtrack in this games offers plenty of pleasure moments especially when the city guards are pursuing you while you parkour in the XV century Florence rooftops. That angelic specific music suits wonderfuly in the parkour moments and I absolutely loved it.
Despite the good soundtrack, some dialogs of the civilians were extremely repetitive and a reason to mock.
Story --- 90/100 : Great Story! You are Desmond Miles, a normal person whose ancients were several generations of Assassin's. You are caught in a war between Templars ( the bad guys) and Assassin's ( The good guys). In the first title you are kidnapped by the templars while in this title you are caught by the Assassin's. Due to the low resources of the Assassin's ( that have to face a source of infinite resources that feeds the Templars) you incarnate as Ezio Auditore de Firenze as a way of seeking more information about the Pieces of Eden , and the  main goal , to train you.
Ezio Auditore de Firenze is motivated by revenging the ones that killed his family and throughout the course continues the work of his father about ancient artifacts called The Pieces of Eden.
Gameplay --- 85/ 100 --- Nothing really new here. Fantastic combat system that , in my mere opinion , could be more punishing.The game feels ,after some hours, repetitive due to a decent length in the story time. The social features of the game are well achieved although they could make it a little bit more imersive.
In the end , the game deserves :   81 / 100

It's like Pacman but with parkour and instead of ghosts you're trying to punch other pacmans to death. The Good:
- Data galore! Possibly too much noisy data to be honest, but I appreciate it being there nonetheless.
- Tactics customization, shouts, match prep, are much more in-depth this year.
- The social and medical tabs will likely become more significant as we acclimate to their usage.

The Bad:
- I'm really not digging the skin layout so far this year. Normally when there's a big change, I chalk it up to unfamiliarity and usually acclimate to it fairly quickly. This year, it just feels worse. More cluttered. Smaller fonts. A glossy look that makes it seems like we're going back to Windows Vista when we've been good on Windows 10 for a couple years.
- Options are hidden away so it takes more clicks to do an action previously. Hiring staff/setting scout assignments for example: you have to click a little edit button, and then play around with the setting, exit the dialog box, and then search through the list. Whereas before, all the options are displayed above and easily editable while you're sifting through options. Hell, even praising/scolding individual performances require you to click the player's name, then move up the screen to select player interaction, then select your tone + comment. I miss having the drop-down next to the player themselves, but again, the new skin is cluttered with stuff so that there's no space for that.
- Speaking of scouting, it's changed quite a bit. Not sure how I feel yet. On the one hand, it's probably a bit more realistic with scouting packages and whatnot. On the other, setting scout assignments and sifting through recommendations is more hassling thus far. I'm keeping an open mind, but as of right now, not particularly enthused about it. I'm not digging these icons of player position or scout percentages with the magnifying glass display. It seems like they're making it more glance friendly for the touch version perhaps? Or maybe shifting the aesthetics away from the excel worksheet look. Who knows.

Negatives:

In summary this is a huge improvement on the series. Well worth price. I'm pleasantly surprised by it so far.

Mercenary Kings is a cynical college art project masquerading as a videogame. In less than an hour of playtime, the game managed to show every possible hint of amatuerism in its design. A design based on games from decades ago that had better control schemes.
The biggest flaw with this "game" is the incredibly poor design decisions. The first mistake was the addition of reload for what should have been a relatively simple run-and-gun experience. It breaks the flow of gameplay and often just leaves you huddling behind some barrels until you've reloaded. Not that taking cover matters; The enemies barely move and the barrels are always taller than you are, so you have to jump into enemy fire anyway. This is compounded by absolutely byzantine level design that makes backtracking endless and goals impossible. It doesn't help that enemies respawn faster than this game being pushed out the door. On top of
, the game often imposes time limits on your escapades. The result is endlessly frustrating. The "developers" clearly haven't taken much notice in the games they were so intent on emulating:
. Even Contra, a game released in the late '80s, allowed the player to shoot diagonally. There's no reason this could not have been done here.
Mercenary Kings is so bad I thought it was an Early Access title because it has no features and is overpriced. It looks like someone took a game with one level and no interesting game mechanics, gave it a nice art style and called it a day. Normally, I would cut the devs some slack, seeing as it's a Kickstarter and probably their first game, but the pricetag is just insulting for the amount of content (that I've read about; Apparently there's a useless crafting system). Only a Kickstarter could raise $100,000 for a game to be $20 and have the same content as a gif of the opening and closing animated sequences. The lack of gameplay coherence and common sense gives me the sneaking suspision that the game was mostly an ego trip for an art student.

There is a lot of side content to be experienced, but one of the big problems with the game is that the areas you drive to all feel like a corridor. The online mario cart deathmatch multiplayer mode is long dead, so forget about that. The two player Co-op missions are ok, and you can play them by yourself, but thye get boring real quick. Especially if you have already played through the missions in the single player story.

Where do I even start with this one?
It's the gold standard of the Rainbow Six series for starters. The game is arguably the funnest tactical shooter ever and this is the game people point to when asked about a more tactical and professional feeling Rainbow Six game than the action games like Rainbow Six: Vegas. Being a game from 2003, the graphics look a bit rough, though that doesn't hurt the gameplay at all. You play as a sort of commander for the elite, international, blacker-than-black ops team Rainbow. Rainbow specializes in counter-terror and hostage rescue missions and are deployed when needed around the globe. This means that the levels take place across a variety of settings. You'll go from saving dignitaries in the Swiss alps to foiling bank robbers in London to clearing a mansion of baddies in the Cayman Islands. This keeps things unique and interesting throughout the game.
Each mission has a set pattern to it. You start by learning about the situation from Rainbow Six, the leader of Rainbow, and the other advisors with him. You then go to the team room where you select which operatives are going out on the mission, select their guns, armor, and other equipment, and choose what teams they'll be on. Then you go to the bread and butter of the game: the planning room. You are given a blueprint of the area and tasked with creating a plan for the teams to follow that will result in a successful mission. The planning system does take a bit of time to master but once the get the hang of things you'll find that the planning system is robust and customizable with a great depth to it. Once you have a plan created you can choose what team you'll be leading, in first person shooter style, through the action phase of the mission.
The action isn't as fast-paced as other games, but the methodical and tactical way that you can move through the area is unique, very enjoyable, and by no means boring. The action gameplay can shift from stealth to sychronized takedowns to all out gunfighting at a moments notice. The operatives and the terrorists all react realistically to bullets, meaning they die near-instantly. If that sounds too tough for the more tactical-minded gamers, you can also choose to observe the plan from a third-person flying camera and let the A.I take control of the operatives on the mission. You'll invariably find your plans don't always succeed, but there's much fun to be had from tweaking your plan until the teams move through the level like a well-oiled machine; to qoute the A-Team, "I love it when a plan comes together." On a related note there are pre-made plans that you can load in if you find the planning system too much to handle or are frustrated with repeated failures.
The last great feature of the game is the custom mission option. This gives you access to all the maps that you've unlocked in the campaign and some that are only available in this mode and allows you to create a random mission from a good amount of mission types. Replaying story missions, terrorist hunt, hostage rescue, and lone wolf wherein you are alone and needing to get to the extraction point. The custom mission feature garuntees that you won't get bored with this game. Add to all the goodness explained already the fact that there's still a thriving modding community keeping this game fresh and adding better graphics and more gameplay to this already massive game and you've got a shining gem of the tactical shooter genre that still hasn't been topped in the decade that it has been out.

Sanctum is a strategy/FPS hybrid game with tower defense tied in, complimented by its exciting and catchy sci-fi soundtrack and awesome environments.
In Sanctum, you play as a soldier known as Autumn Skye, and you must defend The Core, the power source for all of your towers and for your entire base. Aliens of different forms will come and attempt to attack it, and attack you and your friends. Each enemy has different strategies of attacking, and each one has different weak-spots, where hits will do more damage than the hits would on the other parts of their bodies. Some of these enemies are airborne, and will attack from above, and some will attack ground-level.
There are 16 maps in the base-game Sanctum, and each have different amounts of space for your tower bases. You can arrange them however you like, and you and your friends must build a maze to make it so that the aliens, known as the Lumes, will have the hardest time possible attempting their reach to your Core. You must use your resources to build new towers, upgrade old towers, and upgrade your weapons.
Sanctum is a fun game to play with friends, or in single-player alike, and the variation to the enemies, weapons, and towers is pretty cool. I would recommend this game to anyone who enjoys strategy games, FPS games, and tower defense games, as well as those who like sci-fi themes. ^.^

I feel like all the negative things I read about this game reflect some of my favorite aspects of it.  It can be quite difficult and frustrating, especially the leveling/currency system - you lose all your xp since last time you leveled (you can only lvl if you make it to a sanctuary) and 10% of your money when you die - but this challenge just makes the game that much more fun and rewarding (I'm sure there's a quote about how death makes life worth living or something out there somewhere).  I've rarely experienced such a sense of joy and relief as I do after trudging through a dark dungeon full of difficult foes, bloodied and fatigued, sure that my next encounter will cost me my life, my salt, and my gold, and then.. through the next door.. could it be? Yes! Sanctuary!
Yea, the character/class system is sort of simple.. but not THAT simple.. I've definitely played much simpler.  I love building characters and enjoy a lot of options when doing so, and this game still satisfied that desire.  There is still a considerable web of passive skill nodes to choose from, the web is just pretty straightforward in this game and not at all overwhelming. I don't mind overwhelming personally, I like my skill trees as complex as possible, but sometimes its nice to not have to think for 30 minutes every time you level up.  I still had a lot of fun making my character while playing through this game, and I'm already excited about building a different class on my next play through.
The music is awesome.The atsmophere is great.  I've never felt so immersed in a 2D environment before (except when I was playing Hotline Miami maybe). Some people have complained about the lack of map and complicated level design - it's called exploration people. This game actually gives you a sense of it for once it instead of spoon-feeding you every step of the way. The world (island) is surprisingly large and intricate, especially considering it's all 2D. There's all sorts of interesting places to explore, and you have to keep running all over the place the entire time, checking for new paths you might have missed or been unable to traverse previously, instead of just going straight ahead the entire time.
Yea, I don't know what else to say.. this is one of the better RPGs I've played in recent memory (and I play a lot of RPGs). For what it is I would give it a 10/10.  I have no complaints (which is rare, trust me)!

From an aesthetics and design perspective, this game is top notch. It also has a decent kind of humour in it that I enjoy. None-the-less the FPS facet of this game is quite lacking. For the sake of a functional tower defense game the enemies must travel in very specific ways with very predictable behaviour and that is as good for an FPS as the ducks in Duck Hunt.
Anyone who knows what's he/she's doing will be able to emplace a couple of guns at the enemies' spawn point, then make a tight corridor with Amp Fields and Holo-blocks (bullet damage multipliers) and just sit at the end of the corridor holding the mouse button. The gun overheated? No problem! swap to the Sniper rifle and click instead of holding. That run out too? switch back! Needless to say that the protagonist sounds way more into that than me.
In case you're in doubt, yes, there's no ammo count in this game. The sniper rifle and shotgun have between 1 and 6 shots, all other guns are based on "overheating".
If you like either fishing or tower defense games, you might like this one. If you want a solo or co-op game to shoot at waves of monsters which can actually react to you and give you action, then pick Killing Floor 2 instead.

Booring game!  Better graphics that the first Ghost Warrior but that's about it.  Extremely linear, being directed from spot to the...yawn....next.  A little less linear that the first one but you are still being funnelled in one direction.
When aiming the Sniper rifle moves around so much (even with holding your breath) that it almost seems like your character has Parkinson or some other degenerating motor skill disease.  I've got a digital camera with a 35mm telephoto lens that I can hold steadier than the character can.  Regardless the game was repetitive and plain boring with a minimal story similar to the first Ghost Warrior that really didn’t matter.  The voice acting was mediocre also.
As with the first Ghost Warrior they did little with the background scenery.  I always try to explore the background in games and particular this game because you can tell that a lot of time was put into creating the good-looking jungle backgrounds.  However, even the buildings in this game were basically just boxes as they had very little inside them.  In most shooter games you would explore everything looking for loot, ammo or whatever was available in that particular game.  In this game there was little reason to explore as there was not much to find, the odd ammo here and there and the odd Health pack and some in game items.  I never came close to running out of ammo and didn't have to worry too much about my health.
The AI is pretty blind as you snipe an enemy next to another one and he doesn't notice.  For the most part I found this game way to boring and would snipe enemies to make them come to me so I could have a gun battle.  I also notice that in some in some situations that if you didn’t snipe the enemies in the order that the game wanted your compatriots on the ground somehow ended up getting compromised and you had repeat that scenario.  I also got stuck in a couple of places and had to restart that section.  That's the problem when creating linear, corridor shooter game with great backgrounds that aren't exploitable.  At one point I got stuck between the side of a building and a fence that I probably wasn't supposed to be able to explore and therefore could not get out and had to restart that section.
Like the first Ghost Warrior couldn't finish it because I got bored with the linear gameplay, invisible walls and the very limited exploration of the environment usually necessary in most other FPS games.
Similar to the first Ghost Warrior I would give the graphics a 4/5 because you can tell that the artists put a lot of work into creating the jungle and other backgrounds.  It’s a pity they weren't better utilized.
As for its boring and excruciating linearity gameplay I would give it 2/5.  Thank goodness I got both Ghost Warrior games on a Steam sale so I don’t feel so bad not finishing them.  That’s one of the better things about Steam; wait long enough for a really good game sale and if you didn’t like the game it’s not that big of a loss.

I'll put aside technical issues and any other free version mechanic comments since those aren't really the feature of the game, just symptom of remarketing it. Since it's free to play now I'd encourage you to try it out, but I can't recommend it. The Evolve Stage 2 has the same issue the original game had, it is not a team game. Now you might think that you have four people with classes and they need to work together, etc aka team stuff, but this is team versus individual. It's not 4v4 or 6v6 with team work being the deciding factor. The monster has one mind and one life to worry about.
Imagine you are playing a tank/healer/dps game with a boss fight - The tank holds agro. But in this world the boss ignores the tank and attacks the healer and the healer has less survivability than any other class. You only have so much jet pack, you only have so much health, and you have so much time. This is the problem and with an experienced monster, there's no real contest.
Unless they plan to make the hunter roles more fluid then there is nothing to save as casual team. You need a plan, experience, knowledge of the maps, communication, an understanding of cutting off instead of just following, and a regular team to protect the assest that matters most. I only had one idea to solve this without requiring a life commitment: make it so that when the monster takes damage, the person that damages them becomes more visible and everyone else becomes less visible. Make the natural reaction of the monster that of a beast - not a human behind a keyboard and mouse looking for the 'green' energy healing the hunters. Maybe make the monster only see grey scale, or can't actually see all the hunter energy and ability effects - since that's just eye candy for us and would be foolish to use such flashy, eye catching things in reality.
In conclusion - game hasn't changed since first release - still the same imbalanced problem that all 'MANY vs ONE' games have.

However as good as Dark Forces 2 is. It is completely ruined by how shoddily the game runs on modern operating systems. It's to the point where if you try and run it in a 64 bit OS you have to trade between getting the game to render with proper colors vs a playable framerate.
This is a major case of buyer beware. It's near impossible to run on Windows 7 and 8 64bit properly, and the only way I got this game to work was by installing a Virtual Machine. Only purchase if you're willing to put up with how badly this game runs.

Star Wars Jedi Knight: Dark Forces II was the first video game I've ever played back when I used the classic Windows 98. To this day I still have my copy of the game in working condition.
**Story Info|Possible Spoilers**
The game is set one year after the events of Star Wars Episode VI: Return of the Jedi. Former mercenary Kyle Katarn meets an info broker droid named 8t88 who informs Katarn that is father, Morgan, was killed by Jerec, a Dark Jedi with plans of rebuilding the Empire. Kyle is given a disk from 8t88 that only a droid in his father's home can read. Kyle Katarn sets out to find this droid and put an end to Jerec's plans to keep the galaxy at peace.
**Gameplay**
Dark Forces II much like its predecessor is a First Person Shooter, but now you are given the option to use a 3rd person camera if you so desire. The main game is divided into 21 levels, each with an objective and are completed in order.
Given at your disposal are various weapons, explosives, and various force powers categorized as Light Side or Dark. later on you'll get a lightsaber after finding Morgan Katarn's droid.
The lightsaber combat in Dark Forces II is very primitive and therefore feels dated. You can swing the saber diagonally left and right standing in place, swing in the direction you are moving, do a "fury" attack when moving forward, and a power attack using right-click on the mouse.
The gameplay overall is slightly dated, but I think still holds up to today.
**Graphics**
Do not expect the graphics to be outstanding! Since this is a game from 1997, the graphics are blocky, pixelated, and at times messy. However, for 1997 standards, it's good for its time... Assuming you are not playing it with the 3D Hardware Acceleration disabled, then it just looks bad.
**Verdict**
Star Wars Jedi Knight: Dark Forces II is still a blast to play 17 years later, but don't be surprised by its dated feeling. I consider it to be up there with my personal top 5 Star Wars games. As a guy who has been playing it all his life, I definitely recommend you get this game. This is not one you should pass up!

For anyone who's remotely interested in the Star Wars expanded universe is going to want to play this.
It's hard for me to be unbias when writing a brief review because for me, I feel waves of nostalgia when playing this. But I'll try my best to list the good points and the bad.
I should note I finished the game in 9 hours, getting most of the secrets and watching all cutscenes.
Things I liked:
The music. The score comes straight from the films, so it's always going to be fantastic. This is of course if you choose to install the music with a patch, it dosen't come with the Steam version as standard.
The story. This is one of my favourite Star Wars stories, maybe it's the haunting voice of Rahn from the cutscene's or the fact all the bosses are genuinely interesting. I like the whole notion of the Valley of the Jedi.
The cutscene's. Let's be honest, alot of why this game was so popular was the live action cutscene, which were of the quality of something from the films. Wonderful actors like Jason Court bring the whole game to life.
Here's some things I didn't like:
I had trouble getting the game running well on new systems. There's some great guides to help you out there mind.
The cutscenes, for me, would only show in a small boarder window. I mean at least I got to watch them, but it's not ideal.
As I've already noted, the game does not come with the original music, you'll have to add it in a patch (it's well worth it)
As a shooter the game holds up very well, infact it's better than most modern day shooters. If you're worried because you've looked at the sceenshots and you're wondering if you could adapt to such an older game, I'd advise giving it a go.
But you should be warned, as most buying will most likely be running the game on newer systems, you may need to do some fiddling around to get the game running.
Truely a timeless cassic, if you're willing to get past it's age.

So much more content, back story, character development and customization than the first game. One might fall in love with the persona of Ezio and how he matures to become an Assassin and parallely, whatever Desmond learns in the process. Set during the renaissance, Ezio has allies like Leonardo da Vinci and Niccholo Machiavelli, to name but a few. And his story is interspersed so finely with actual history that one might actually believe those events took place exactly like in the game. The connection with the first game, with Altair as well as Desmond, was made flawlessly.
For the gameplay, the dynamics are much the same as in the first game, with some added moves, making combat slightly more realistic and more dynamic. The graphics look amazing. Florence, Venice and Forli look like their real counterparts.
It's a really long to finish and I definitely don't have the patience to complete every mission from the sub-plot, particularly the one involving Subject 16. It's very tedious (and the reason for the 9, instead of the 10). But I'm sure patience would be rewarded because of the video waiting at the end of it.
All in all, I would definitely recommend this game to anyone!

Without a doubt, this is iD's weakest game, but that doesn't make it a bad game at all, if anything this game is still one of the best games I've played.
The story is crap, honestly to say there is a story would be an insult, because nothing is really connected except for the fact the Authority are bad and they're hunting for you. The ending (Haven't finished on PC, but have on Xbox 360) really doesn't reward you for what you have achieved throughout the game, and is just treated as yet another mercenary mission, and that's really all that the game is, you are just a mercenary doing jobs to earn money.
Even with a terrible story, the game is just so fun, the gameplay is simple yet awesome. The guns feel smooth. The driving is good, even if a bit too simple. The controls are mostly okay (Excluding the fact to switch between tools you need to use F1, F2, F3 and F4). It feels as well done as in other iD games.
The world is superb, if anything the vibes of Borderlands and Fallout are a superb combination, sure the graphics aren't exactly brilliant today, but the world that we are given still nails the post-apocalyptic feel. And heck even the enemies have that side of insanity to them which add to the feeling that you are indeed in a post-apocalyptic Earth. Dead City to this day remains as one of the greatest areas I have ever explored, just that feeling back in 2011 exploring this destroyed city with all types of enemies is just a feeling I haven't really been hit with in a long time, and for that RAGE is a game that hits me a strong sense of nostalgia, and is a game I just cannot forget.
Saying that though, the term "Open-World" is really disappointing in the game, the map isn't too big, the separate areas are very linear, something that a lot of games were trying to change out of in 2011, so really RAGE hasn't aged too well for that reason. If it wasn't so linear the game would be much better than it is.
Some complaints I do also have for the game is that the audio is a bit buggy, another issue that has been around since 2011, the audio doesn't sound right, characters will stop talking at times completely, it just ruins the experience at times. The multiplayer isn't great, it's just races, but you'll be sick of them after doing them in the campaign. And finally, the game has for some people been really difficult to run, I personally haven't run into any issues, saying that though this is probably because most of the reported issues have been with AMD users, which I am not one of.
As a whole for £8/$10 (currently just £2, no idea what in $ or euros) I say go for it, it's a great game for its price and you'll easily get your money’s worth with purchasing this game.

Rushed, unfinished, overpriced. Very hard to recommend even if you like shooters and co-op games.
Raid is the WW2 spinoff of the Payday series, made by Lion Game Lion, the guys who were the B-Team for Payday 2 DLC back in 2015 before they started work on their own game. They're mainly level designers, and it shows: Raid has fantastic level design and I still see new variations on the same handful of maps after so many hours.
Now that we got the good out of the way let's get to the bad. There's a lot of it.
This game is grindy as ♥♥♥♥. It's F2P MMO levels of grind. You have an insanely unforgiving XP curve, tied to missions that give incredibly low amounts of XP, and you gotta do it 4 times because each character class must be levelled up individually. The game adds "challenge cards" to alleviate it: it will give bonus XP but there are certain conditions attached, such as "headshots do less damage" or "melee weapons only". These cards come rarely, though, the bonuses suck, and most times they're not worth the effort. This would be slightly less bad if the skill system were interesting. It's not. 90% of the skills are just incremental bonuses to your character stats, except whenever you get to level up your special abilities, called "War Cries" (more about that later).
The weapon unlock system is bad too. Weapons are tied to character classes, so if you want to use a shotgun on a sniper character, you're out of luck. Weapon effectiveness is also gated by upgrades, which you earn by completing weapon challenges, such as get X number of headshots or Y number of hip-fire kills. Sounds good on paper, except the challenge numbers balloon up really fast and take a long time to happen naturally. Challenges also come in multiple tiers, and each tier is gated by level requirements as well. Upgrades significantly change your weapon's performance; you simply can't tackle higher difficulties without having some upgrades on whatever weapon you choose. Combined with the absurd challenge numbers, the game is pretty much encouraging you to drop it down to easy, spend hours to farm kills, then crank it back up to the desired difficulty.
On to the characters classes themselves, they fall into pretty standard arch types. The best class in the game is the medic class, Assault. Assault gets access the widest variety of the game's most effective weapons, and their War Cry ability can heal the team on demand and grants the user reduced ammo consumption.  The sniper class, Recon, is best played without using sniper rifles (sniper rifles are atrocious in this game). Recon's ability increases damage and grants auto-aim, which makes it perfect for using automatic weapons. The explosives class, Demolitions, is good on paper, mediocre to bad on execution. The only explosives that exist right now are grenades, which are not very good. Demolitions is also lacking in weapon unlocks: other classes get a slow but steady drip of weapons; Demo does not unlock anything between level 15 and 38 (the level cap is 40). I don't have enough experience to say much about the last class, Insurgent. It specializes in close quarters fighting and can dodge incoming damage; that's about all I know.
Aside from the grindfest and unbalanced classes, the game also suffers from general balance/gameplay issues. Enemy types are not easy to tell apart - it is hard to differentiate between different types of regular infantry, but elite enemies are easier to spot because they wear SS armbands. The game's main special enemy type, the flamer, needs extensive reworking: its sound cues only work for hosts and its flamethrower does way too much damage and has way too much range. For any Payday 2 players reading this, the game also has a special unit called the "officer" that works similarly to Captain Winters, except done worse in almost every possible way. The officer turns regular infantry into elite units and makes elites spawn more often. The game never tells you when officers are around so you have to look out for that SS armband, and then it becomes a Nazi wack-a-mole as you need to find the officer among the horde of elite units that are now wrecking your team. In general, Raid's approach to difficulty seems to be throwing an absurd amount of enemies (50+ on map at a time) at you, all of whom have unavoidable hitscan attacks. This works in Payday 2 when you have a lot of crowd control skills and weapons at your disposal and does not work at all in Raid.
Even putting aside all of this, the game is just riddled with bugs and UI issues. Remember how people always kept saying that Payday 2 should have used its safehouse level as a lobby? Raid does exactly this, and it's awful in all the ways you'd think. Instead of just making a lobby, you always need to load up the safehouse (which takes forever). You always have to load into this level before playing a mission, or in-between missions.♥♥♥♥♥♥ you can't even look at your characters without having to load into the damn safehouse first. You can't change any of your weapons or skills unless you're in that safehouse; once you're in the pre-mission screen all you can do is ready up or choose challenge cards for the upcoming mission. When you ready up, you can't unready for a mission. The game has the same janky as ♥♥♥♥ weird animation problems and subpar netcode as Payday 2 does because it uses the same engine.
The one complaint I see floating around on the internet about this game is that it's too much of a Payday clone. That's flat out wrong. Payday at its worst and its grindiest was still interesting; Raid is mostly uninspired and dull. This game would actually be better if it took more mechanics and design from Payday. As it is it feels like it's purposely trying different ideas that are bad for the sake of being different, and also makes a lot of the same mistakes early Payday did. There is some delight to be found in exploding Nazi heads with a shotgun or Garand, but this game needs a LOT of work. The developers have a chance of turning it around, but with a microscopic player base only 2 months after release it might be too late.

Tales of Maj'Eyal (ToME) is a roguelike game that has been around in various forms for several years but until the more recent versions might have been a little too oldschool style for many modern gamers. I'm going to try to be unbiased in reviewing this game but it might be tough since I started playing when it was called Pernband.
Graphics: 3/5 The tiles in this game are very well done and for the most part, everything is pretty easy to identify. In some areas it may be hard to see a monster next to an obstacle but this may be by design. It also has ASCII mode for old school roguelike nerds like myself.
Sound: 3/5 Not horrible but not great. The music mostly fits the areas but some of the sound effects just sound wrong to me.
Difficulty: 5/5 Like most roguelikes, this game is not supposed to be easy. ToME does have adjustable difficulty levels to appeal to a broader audience. You can start with a set number of lives or go typical roguelike style permadeath. You can adjust your experience from casual gaming to pulling your hair out.
Gameplay 5/5: ToME is different than most roguelikes in that it has a somewhat open and explorable world as opposed to a single dungeon and maybe a town. The player starts in an area that depends on the characters race. These areas range from simple to brutal. The story is decent and there are plenty of other quests to occupy your time. This game is controlled by keyboard and/or mouse. This makes it easy for an experienced RL player or a novice to jump right in after the brief tutorial. The level generation is done well enough to make each playthrough feel unique and the battles require just the right amount of strategy to keep the game interesting. There are various unlocks that range from things you will do in a normal game to tedious quests.
Overall: 4/5 If you are an oldschool rogueliker, then you are probably already familiar with some version of ToME. If you are newer to the genre and want to play a difficult dungeon crawler with some exploration then this game is worth looking at.
