Having spent over 100 hours on Hearts of Iron III, another few hundred most likely on the non-Steam edition I had before getting the complete pack, and other Paradox games on top of that, I'd call Hearts of Iron IV a big disappointment. The game has plenty of potential and good things in it, but all of it is let down by some flaws and lack of depth.
-Battle-planner. It's something you don't have to use, many surely point this out. But it gives you a slight edge with the plan bonus and most of all, does the work for you. But if you're intent on using -and- actually playing at the same time, it tends to override your commands and making delicate plans, which I've already made up in my mind, is rather hard to do and annoying. It's not a good addition at all, instead people should devise their own tactics and respond to the tactical situations as they develop, not letting the AI do it. That's a big con.
-Armies. Now they're big, one front might be led by a single field marshal who can command an unlimited amount of divisions, in addition to a few dedicated -armies- for armour and possibly other special troops you might have. Having individual division, corps, army, army group and theatre commanders brought much depth and detail into the game, letting your special elite divisions develop more (with their commander), rather than having it all bunched to a few guys whom you'll use throughout the game. The command structure is gone, and with it the old supply system. Now if you're lacking supplies, your front suddenly gets locked down instead of letting the situation worsen over time and develop. But oh wait, there's no fuel. Unlimited fuel for Finnish armour.
-Resources and tech. The last point over there brings us to this topic; now it's possible to get a very developed army with nuclear weapons and rockets whilst playing a third world country. Other than that, the research is very simple and ends in ~1945, thus not giving much advantages for the great powers which had their cutting edge tech (or loads of men to spare, hoh). You can also produce everything you desire whilst having no resources, albeit at a much slower rate. And you cannot stockpile your resources either, instead they'll have to be traded, in addition to your RAD troops deciding to call it a halt whilst they're needed to haul rubber from Indonesia.
-AI issues, which seem to concern many other people. The AI hasn't really offered much of a challenge, the only thing that held of my blitzkrieg for France was RAF's air superiority, whilst for Brazilian invasion of US it was the naval planning AI which deemed the empty Caribbean to be a threat and wholly unknown terra incognita for us. They might've (and surely have) fixed some of the issues, but at least they were still there the last time I played. No cunning invasions and flankings, mainly invasions into Germany's heartland with two divisions. Or not patrolling the seas at all.
-Focus tree. These have been made for few bigger nations, making the game less flavoured (kinda like with the few portraits instead of proper pictures they used in the previous Hearts of Iron games). They also delay and derail some historical gameplay, as the focuses might delay Barbarossa quite a bit, for example. And most of the time they don't work with other ideologies, in case you have a civil war or a coup.
Now, I've enjoyed some of the games I've had so far, quite a lot even. But all these issues and the fact that game is much more arcade-y and simplified simply drive me away from it, and thus I cannot recommend it to anyone interested in the usual Paradox stuff with steep learning curves and lots of detail.

Star Wars Dark Forces II
I'll just start off by saying, this game was a huge dissapointment to me. The original Dark Forces game is a game I played often when I was young, and I still love and play it to this day. I actually forgot about the game for a while, when I started to expand my horizons and started playing more startegy games. Since I've always been an avid Star Wars fan, I was looking through the Star Wars games on Steam and came across this game. I never knew there was a sequel and I was really excited to see what the sequel had to offer.
I'll admit, I started off by really enjoying this game. In the beginning the only thing that really bugged me was the inverted camera. Here comes the first flaw of the game, at least the Steam version.
The camera is inverted by default, and I could excuse this if I could change it but I can't. When I find the option that I think is to change the camera, the game crashes. In fact, this happens almost every time you try to change the options. I'm not sure if this is just a problem with the Steam version or what, but still it gets annoying. The problem with inverted camera though, is that once I get used to it, whenever I try to play another FPS I suck because the camera is correct. Honestly, who thinks inverted camera is ever a good idea?
Other then that, the game was pretty good at first. The objectives were nice, the story (even though lacking) was decent, and the level design was pretty good for its time. Speaking of design, I'm not usually one to care about graphics AT ALL, but there is a such thing as working with limitations and just being lazy and making your game look like crap. Atari 2600 games are an example of games that had primitive graphics, but worked with their limitations and made amazing games like Adventure. Take a game like 'Bubsy 3D', everyone hates it. Sure, the Playstation had 32-bit limitations but masterpieces like Crash Bandicoot didn't seem to have any trouble with looking nice. Bubsy 3D on the other hand was the bare minimum of a game, it was so bland it looked like a game still in alpha. Same with DFII, A game from similar time Thief, was able to look amazing and have great design for its time. DFII makes everyone look like a freaking 90's LEGO Technic figure.
Anyways, back to the important part of the game, the gameplay and story. The gameplay is pretty much what you would expect, except for the addition of the LightSaber. Honestly, I found myself using the guns more then the LightSaber. I didn't really feel anything from using it, I felt like if there was a sword in DOOM that you fought Melee with. There is a reason why it's called a FPS, not a FPM. Anyways, the Lightsaber didn't even work all the time. Sometimes when I tried to block it wouldn't work. The force is another flaw with this game, sometimes it works, sometimes it doesn't. That's a main flaw about this game, it works when it wants to, like an Apple product. When I shoot lightning it works fine, but try to push something good luck.
The story eventually gets really confusing and doesn't really make any sense. At one point I randomly kill the woman who piloted my ship, and some guy with a cyborg eye randomly shoots me with a red ring and says 'You Belong to the Dark Side Now'. This just makes no sense in a Star Wars game, and then I'm apparently so fat that when I fall into a ship it collapses. For me when the story and objectives stop having a point, I stop playing. There's no point to go on any further if there's nothing I feel I should accomplish.
If you happen to like it, good, keep on enjoying it. I honestly would not recommend this game if you were a big fan of the first game. I'm just going to forget about this game and play some good old Dark Forces I.

Jedi Knight: Dark Forces II is the first game to ever allow you to play as a Jedi with actual Force powers, but so far the only one to combine it with old school FPS and a enthralling storyline. While the old engine certainly has its limits and leaves a lot to be desired in terms of eye candy, the leveldesign and ambience of the total experience is far superiour to games like Jedi Academy or The Force Unleashed. Of course, this is also the only game in the entire franchise that allows you to choose between the Light and Dark Side, based on your actions in the preceding levels. So on the crucial moment, it's not as if you make a 180 degrees turn, like in Jedi Academy, but you are instead just following the path you had already descended upon.
The leveldesign is totally old school FPS. It contains platforming puzzles; many secrets (I still haven't found them all) and easter eggs; and, of course, a freedom to travel as you please. Some of the levels therefore are a true maze, such as "Palace Escape" or "The Return Home to Sulon". In both cases you can travel into multiple directions without running into places the game doesn't want you to be, which gives a sense of freedom. The platforming puzzles are sometimes simple cases where you must jump at the proper moment, like in "Double-Cross on Nar Shaddaa"; sometimes the puzzles rely on your Force powers like Force Speed or Force Jump, like in "Into the Dark Palace", which means you can't go on if you have forgotten to upgrade those powers. In other cases, there are physics puzzles to solve, like in the "Fuel Station Launch" level. Hidden within the levels are many hidden areas, some more obvious than others, which adds to the replay value. And on top of all this, there is a lot of variety in the leveldesign. You never have the feeling some tricks are repeated all the time, with the exception of the lightsabre duels, which brings us to a new subject.
The old engine has its obvious limits. Aside from not looking too well, especially not for modern standards, the game mechanics are hopelessly outdated as well. The most obvious problem is the addition of Force powers. While these work smoothly in later games, this game still kind of struggles with the concept of being a Jedi. Once you get the hang of it, it's endless fun, but until such fortune, you will likely wonder why your lightsabre doesn't make you a bit more invincible than it should. Force Jump still requires specific activation in this game, making it hard to control direction and height. Force Pull is limited to items, so you can't Pull enemies over. There is no Force Push yet, which is sincerely missed. Force Blinding and Persuasion generate the same effect, but Persuasion is much more effective, making Blinding obsolete. Force Lightning also is hard to control and slightly disappointing in effect. The lightsabre has limited ways of hitting the enemy, resulting in you sometimes losing a lot of health to a single stormtrooper because you don't manage to hit him while he's standing still. Combined with the right Force powers however, your level of invincibility will rise to endless heights. If you can overcome and accept the limits of the engine, none of these problems will ruin gameplay, but instead make it more challenging.
The variety of enemies and your arsenal of weapons also do not disappoint. Naturally, you grow tired of shooting Gran and Rodian thugs after a few levels, but once you reach "Into the Dark Palace" you will battle actual stormtroopers, Imperial officers and AT-STs. Other hired guns are Trandoshan bounty hunters armed with deadly concussion rifles. And be careful not to run into the monstrous Kell Dragons! And of course the seven Dark Jedi led by Jerec. You can battle most of them with your lightsabre, which is of course the most fun weapon in the game, regardless of its limitations, but the other weapons are not less useful. You can choose from simple sidearms like the Bryar Pistol, but there's classics like the Wookiee Bowcaster or the Imperial Repeater. Even Thermal Detonators can be used to blow up your enemies, and when heavy fire power is necessary you may even call upon the Rail Charger or the Concussion Rifle. The latter weapon has some quirky effects, but once you see its devastating power you will soon forget about that.
One last element that makes this game as awesome as it is, is the storyline. Without spoiling too much, you are Kyle Katarn and you are chasing the droid 8t88 in order to find your dead father's message, which he left for you. He instructs you to follow Jerec, who is in search of the Valley of the Jedi; a place in which hundreds of souls of dead Jedi and Sith are trapped. Jerec intends to absorb their power and become invincible. Of course, he must be stopped. On your way, you'll meet his six servants, all of them with their own unique character and duelling style. Yun is the insecure apprentice, whose loyalties are uncertain; Pic and Gorc are two genetically engineered Sithspawn who always battle together; Maw is pure hatred and muscle and has the unique feature to be able to fly, which makes for an interesting duel; Sariss is cunning and strong with the mental side of the Force; Boc is annoying as hell; and Jerec of course is the mastermind. You can tell by the way I describe the lot that I am pretty fond of them. A game that can achieve that has a great ambience. So unlike in the follow-up titles, Dark Forces II features a very fascinating and realistic storyline within the confines of the Star Wars universe. For the full experience, I would recommend the Dark Forces Trilogy novellas written by William C. Dietz, because those books provide the full background story to the game and each character.
To wrap this up, Jedi Knight: Dark Forces II is hands down the best Star Wars game ever released. The graphic aspect of the game is obviously outdated, but the storyline and the ability to wield the Force are the most important aspects of a Star Wars game. Combine the exceptional storyline with the old school leveldesign and the variety within the enemies, levels and weapons, and the verdict can be nothing but positive. I would recommend this game to all fellow Star Wars geeks!

Fidget spinner
From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia
Fidget spinner
Fidget spinner red, cropped.jpg
A typical three-lobed fidget spinner
Type	Stress-relieving toy
Availability	1993–present
Materials	Brass, stainless steel, ceramic, titanium, copper, plastic,latex etc.
A fidget spinner is a toy that consists of a ball-bearing in the center of a multi-lobed flat structure made from metal or plastic designed to spin along its axis with little effort.
Fidget spinners became popular toys in April 2017, although similar devices had been invented as early as 1993. The popularity of the toy among children and teenagers has led some schools to ban use of the spinners in class for being a distraction, while other schools have allowed the toy to be used discreetly.
The toy has been advertised as helping people who have trouble with focusing or fidgeting by relieving nervous energy or psychological stress. There are claims that a fidget spinner can be used to help calm people down who suffer from anxiety and other neurological disorders like ADHD and autism.[1] However, as of May 2017, there is no scientific evidence that they are effective as a treatment for autism or ADHD.[2][3]

Design
Spinning fidget spinner
Fidget spinners are toys not unlike yo-yo or other skill toys, designed to spin with little effort.[4][5] A basic fidget spinner consists of a two- or three-pronged design with a bearing in its center circular pad.[5][6] A person holds the center pad while the toy spins.[6] They are made from various materials including brass, stainless steel, titanium, copper, aluminium, and plastic.[4][5] The bearings are generally ceramic, metal (stainless steel or chrome), and some are hybrids—such as ceramic balls with stainless races and cages. Each fidget spinner also has two or more weights on the outside that make it spin faster and stay balanced. Bearings can vary to adjust for the design's spin time, vibration, and noise, causing unique sensory feedback.
Being a kind of a flywheel of a gyroscope in principle, fidget spinners come with similar effects enabling a player to pull various tricks and stunts while forces of a gyroscope take hold. A fidget spinner can be balanced on top of fingers, thrown and caught, and so on.[7]
Origin
As of 2017, the patent status of the various fidget spinners on the market was unclear.[8]
Catherine Hettinger, a chemical engineer by training, was initially credited by some news stories to have been the inventor of the fidget spinner, including by media outlets such as The Guardian,[9] The New York Times,[10] and the New York Post.[11] Hettinger filed a patent application for a "spinning toy"[12] in 1993 and a patent was issued, but Hettinger allowed the patent to lapse in 2005 after she could not find a commercial partner.[9][8] A May 2017 Bloomberg News article showed that Hettinger was not the inventor of the fidget spinner, and Hettinger agreed.[8]
In an interview appearing on May 4, 2017 on NPR, Scott McCoskery described how he invented a metal spinning device in 2014 to cope with his own fidgeting in IT meetings and conference calls.[13] In response to requests from an online community, he began selling the device he called the Torqbar online.[13]
Marketing and sales
Google Search popularity of fidget spinners in early 2017.
With the rapid increase in the spinner's popularity in 2017, many children and teenagers began using it in school, and some schools also reported that kids were trading and selling the spinner toys.[14][15][16]
As a result of their frequent use by schoolchildren, many school districts banned the toy.[9][10] Some teachers argued that the spinners distracted students from their school work.[14] According to a survey conducted by Alexi Roy and published in May 2017, 32% of the largest 200 American public and private high schools had banned spinners on campus.[17]
When fidget spinners rose in popularity in 2017, many publications in the popular press discussed the marketing claims made about them for people with ADHD, autism, or anxiety.[3][9][10] However, there is no scientific evidence that fidget spinners are effective as a treatment for children with autism or ADHD.[2][3][18]

It's... honestly not at all what I ended up hoping for. I was hyped at first, considering Lion Game Lion got their start making some pretty nice heists and bonus features for Payday 2, and with the overall rarity of shooters not set in modern or futuristic times, it seemed like it'd be unique if nothing else
But... seriously. When you can manage to make a game like this, and make it unsatisfying to even want to load the game up, you've done something very wrong
Mechanically, it feels identical to Payday 2 without an Armor system. Which.. admittedly I sort of like, because there's no more having to go to one extreme of being a walking tank or someone who relies on RNG to not die. But about five years of Payday 2 gunplay has gotten extremely stale. Nothing feels satisfying about playing this. Stealing gold is either done Bag Throwing Simulator style (and in a step back bots can't help you carry items like PD2) or you have to go on a bit of a pixel hunt like you would for Gage Packages in PD2. I'm A-OK with a little scavenger hunt now and then, but to continue that, your end-of-raid reward is effectively based entirely on how many dog tags you and your friends picked up over the course of the level. Get nothing? You probably got an exp boost for... say, 70. In a game where the average Raid tends to give 1000-1500, even without multipliers
And that brings me to my biggest complaint. It's. A. GRIND. You get up to 5 character slots (mercifully all unlocked already), and each levels up separately. And you might think that with a level cap of 40 (I think?), it wouldn't be so bad, especially since Payday 2 started out infamously grindy and it had a level cap of 100
But no, you'd be wrong. And not only do you have to grind a bit excessively for levels, you have to grind to improve your guns. Yeah, I love the fact that you don't have to pray for mercy from the RNG gods and get the weapon mod you want, when you could potentially get a mask or mask customization item you didn't want, and I love the idea of having your weapons improve with time. But things like "Kill 500 enemies who are 20+ meters away with this weapon to get a very minor recoil decrease" is just... excessive, to me
All this grind says to me, we have nothing to keep our players invested, so let's force them to spend more time trying to unlock things. Grinding's not a problem until it gets excessive, when it takes you so long to get one simple thing that you'd be better off ignoring it entirely, and I wasn't even halfway through leveling up ONE class before that set in for me. And this is coming from a guy who's got at least four Final Fantasy games under his belt
I honestly hate talking this badly about this game, because it's very clear LGL cares for it and they have good intentions. And yeah, it has some great stuff. Decent enough writing, very nice weapon selection (aesthetics from mods aside, dear god it gives cod ww2 a run for its money in how wrong those look. Have you SEEN an M1 Garand with a BOX MAGAZINE?) and animation, and each Raid feels like it has a unique goal from the outset instead of "Hit this place for money, now hit that one", especially since you're not entirely out for cash in them. Plus, changing your jacket/pants is a lot cooler than PD2's lackluster mask customization, and (at least in the case of tops) it's something you actually see for more than two seconds. And the comic that came with it is a bit of a fun read, it's not long and it's not a masterpiece but it's nicely-done
I guess if I had to sum all this up it would be... this game has potential. But it's going to take it a while to reach it, and most of its problems aren't even its own fault. THAT would be the result of using Payday 2's wonderfully bad engine
I mean like all reviews this is pretty subjective, and you're more than welcome to disagree, but.. really, if you walked up to me on a street and asked me "Should I buy this game", I would just tell you no, and all of that up there is the reason why
Though I do have one last thing to mention, one of the game's biggest saving graces. The videos. The live-action bits with John Cleese, all the Hitler videos if you win a mission where he has the most hilarious breakdowns. Those alone, I think, are worth a mention. They perfectly embody the sort of off-beat approach this game has. They add that last little bit of satisfaction to a well-done raid, and it's clear that everyone involved in the videos was enjoying their roles, especially ol toothbrushe stache himself
So that's about all I've got to say. I won't outright call it a bad game, especially with the respect I have for LGL, but it's not one I would honestly recommend. At least not yet. If it gets better in the future I might be able to change this, as I have with many other games (see: Payday 2, Team Fortress 2)
Although uh... Unless you want the really nice-looking Golden M1 Garand, and the extra two melee weapons you get... The Special Edition ain't worth it. Not at all. You get a giant jacket with Special Edition logos on each shoulder, you get a Candy Apple skin for the Kubelwagen (including generic ones on the roadside) and yes it ALSO has Special Edition text.. That one gets a pass because it actually looks cool, but still: seeing the whole "SPECIAL EDITION" logo on EVERYTHING about it gets annoying. If you do want this game, do yourself a favor and ignore the Special Edition. It's not worth the $15 extra (unless, as mentioned, you REALLY want that Golden M1 and the Candy Apple Kubelwagen)

Don't get me wrong, I love RAID WW2. I love its setting, I love the characters and I absolutely love♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥Hitler off.
However, sooner or later, RAID will simply become too boring to play. Right now, I feel that the only reason I'm playing everyday is just to get weapons that I have yet to use and upgrade them. The proficiency system is severely lacking. Yes, you can definitely make your character stronger and kind of make a build with them, but it is not as significant as Payday 2. Theres really nothing I can strive for except for hitting Level 40 and fully upgrading every weapon.
The weapon upgrades also does not feel as significant. Only slight stability/damage increases and thats it. The only big change is practically the magazin size. Don't even get me started on the x metres challenges.
The backstories for the RAIDS and Operations are quite interesting. However, I found the Operations quite disappointing. I expected more, and generally half of the missions all together doesn't seem that it would impact Hitler directly and upclose. I want more RAIDS/Operations where we can target someone that is relatively close to Hitler. This of course makes me a fan of Last Orders and Odin's Fall. Others such as Tiger Trap, Extraction are also my favourites in terms of backstory. Like come on, there were plenty of SS officers that were killed mysteriously/disappeared, maybe put those names in RAID and just have the gang to kill them off. Boom. Instant tie in to History. Mysteriously died? Nah mate, got murdered by the equally mysterious RAID gang.
The XP payout is horrendous. So much games to level up. Especially so after level 15. I know, we are supposed to farm, and if we do not like to farm, maybe this game is not for us. But seriously? Yes, I know that we are supposed to farm. But the XP needed to level up is just absurd. What happens to the Solo players then? In Solo, you barely earn any XP, even on Very Hard. Then you would ask me do go public. Yep, sure thing. Go public where theres only 30 players everyday, and where hosts kick you for no reason at all. If there are no changes to be made to the XP, at least give us another ecentive to level up. Upgrading and unlocking weapons ain't going to cut it. Upgrading your base? Yea, it looks cool. But also not that good of an ecentive to keep playing. The only fun thing about the base upgrades is literally just the playable piano.
There are also not even enough weapons to begin with. So many good weapons from the WWII era are not even here! Wheres the beloved PPSH? FG-42? The Luger Pistol? Shotguns? With the absurd XP system, and so little weapons, people are going to be upgrading their weapons miles faster than levelling up, and players would get bored in an instant.
6.5/10 for me. Such a high-potential game. I said to my friends plenty of times that I will play this more than Payday 2. At this rate, I already am. It is just small problems here and there that are blocking the success of this game. Just wait when RAID drops in price/goes on sale. Not worth the $30 at all. Feels more like a $15 game to me. However, I dp see the determination of LGL and how they are committed to fixing and updating this game with free content. Already, we had 2 updated RAIDS, 3 new weapons(Grenade and melee included) and even a Halloween event added to RAID WW2. Keep it up, LGL. Sooner or later, RAID WW2 would be totally different from PD2, humming quitely to its own special, and unique beat.
And of course, Hitler would become more, and more, and more mad!

This is like the Dwarf Fortress of single player turn based rougelikes.  So much has been poured into it's universe and lore, and that's just the offical main module for the game.  TLDR: Buying this game will be the best thing ever for your rougelike, turn based, strategic, leveling, rage inducing needs.
The world map is consistantly the same, but the dungeons and places are randomized classic rouge dungeons that have themes, leveled content, and many many trolly rougelike goodness waiting inside.
Skills and healing are on turn cooldowns in addition to costing mana/stamina to use, making the whole game really strategic.  The fact everything is turn based yet updates in an instant means the game plays at exactly the pace you can keep up with it.  If you are taking your time reading stats, the game won't do anything till you take action.  But if you pretty much just want to wander down a few hallways to that old room, a single click will instantly have the game "run" you over there, and if anything happens along the way (such as enemies coming into view) the game will stop and go back into "single turn" strategy mode.
Race and Class are seperate in character creation, and all play different enough that you'll be playing a totally different tactic, yet are based on the same stat and skill tree like system, so you'll know exactly how to figure out the new class.
Add in workshop support for many modded race/class/modules, the open nature of the modding, and the existing website's large community of players and creators, and you'll quickly see why this is one of the best things you will ever buy if you are even remotely interested in rouge-like games.
It's also sufficently rage inducing when you die.  Just a fair warning.  It does follow the rouge game logic of "learning by death", so don't become too attached to your characters.  Much rage, followed by "I really shouldn't have done X" moments.  You can start as the same character on death, and the gameworld has ways to get "lives", even in permadeath mode...so it's a tiny bit more forgiving then your usual rouge.  But only a tiny bit.
It should be noted you can play this for free (with some limitations) from the website of the game.  Paying for the game on steam gets you the "Donation" version, with all the limitations removed, same as donating through the site directly.  The steam version can log into an account made with the free version.  So if you are on the fence, give the free release a go for a few hours before coming back and buying the game.

I could use more specific information on tower damage to help me learn strengths and weaknesses vs certain enemies.  How do I know which lane is going to be used next?  The graphics are kinda blocky and bad.  Am I really supposed to get on top of a tower and shoot enemies there?  Many of them run so fast I have to chase after them, shooting them in the butt.  The sound effects are generally headache-inducing, especially the menu ones.  And worst of all, being first person means you can't see what's going on.  Even a Dungeon Defenders style of camera would be preferable.
On the plus side... uh... honestly, I can't think of a plus side here :(

There are plenty of hardcore members posting about how great this game is, hence I gave it a go. I'd say I'm fairly used to the basics of it. Here are my thoughts about why I'm not going to play any more:
Despite an otherwise slick game, the combat is clunky and not very responsive resulting in a taking it in turns kind of combat.
The story is nonsense. From what I have picked up in between all the hilariously bad Tolkein imitation names and places, I am some-sort of evangelical zombie brought back form the dead because I'm... really tough? That's a pretty major role play element to impose on every single player in the faction.
The overly heroic and epic stories have all come across as a little bit 'try-hard'. I have already slain a horde of powerful demons in battle, but does anyone give an iota of♥♥♥♥♥♥ No. Hell, I don't even know where my comrades went after the battle! The starting zone keeps the chosen one theme and sticks to the rigid kill X find Y items quests.
I would have been more comfortable just culling a few boars or hitting a practice dummy to introduce me to the world populated solely by ...sigh... mighty heroes. An apocalypse where I am chosen by the gods to return from the dead to the living world and purge the corruption is too overdramatic for a character who isn't allowed to use the big boy potions.
There are conflicting themes in the game that the graphics don't suit. Rift is some sort of dark satirical fantasy world (nobody can take a giant squirrel mount with a fearsome armored knight riding it seriously). These pseudo realistic graphics already look painfully dated. Sliding all the slideys up beyond the highest standard settings gave me a very bloomy smoothly modelled world with a lot of particle effects and some very detailed character models. Note that this did not improve the overall stylistic asthetic of the game, it just made my graphics card work a bit harder. And no matter how many antistropic filters you use or how many samples your antialiasing takes, the landscapes look like the bland generic areas of Everquest on par with some of the worse looking PS2 environmental designs. You are very aware that would are in a game world and are reminded of this with every stompy footstep the characters take through the world. The game is well polished, but the initial art designs are just bad.
There is no such thing as a free lunch, yet Rift's free to play (F2P) methods are some of the best in terms of balance... so far. However, the F2P model is kind of jarring at times for a beginner. I can't use the auction house (AH) without spending real world money on the game. I would be happy to pay more than a few quid if I didn't feel so deceived by Trions 'every feature is accesible for free' campaign. As I progress through the game, investing more of my time (money isn't the only thing you pay for an MMO with!) I feel that there is no way of telling what I will and won't have complete access to compared to a "whale" gamer with more money than sense.
Original elements that supposedly make the leveling aspect of the game good (random Rift events and instant action questing) don't really work. It's turned the whole experience into a grind-y 'Pug' dungeon where nobody talks to one another and everyone is just grinding through a chaotic mess of quests to get to the sweet nectar of end-game. Those o-so exciting elements are already run of the mill events after no more than a few hours of playing.
The elephant in the room is that Rift is constantly and deliberately putting itself up against WoW: and not beating it. It uses the game mechanics that worked really nicely in WoW and improving on them in very tangible ways, making a slightly improved experience for the individual player. Rift forgets that Mmorpgs like WoW, EVE and Everquest (in the early days), work really well because of the massive, diverse and vibrant community of invested players; not trivial things like the map/quest-helper having good integration etc.

Hands down... my personal "Game of the Year 2016"
Just recently came out on the PS Vita, therefore it is THE de facto, "One and Only" Dark Souls-like game on any handheld console.
I wouldnt try to compare this to the Castlevania games because S&S has its own character, or more accurately it is pretty much a Metrovania game with Dark Souls action RPG gameplay.  So, If you like Dark Souls + Castlevania, then you will love Salt and Sanctuary.
Likes:
The overall world level design is pretty interesting.
The background/zone level designs are all unique and creative making your journey around the island feel less dull and repeative when you grind for levels and loot for crafting.
There are lots of short cuts to open,
lots of zones to explore,
lots of bosses to fight,
a nice variety of routes to certain bosses and certain collecting of "brands" aka key character abilities like in Metroid,
so like in the first Dark Souls game its not completely full on linear progression, but rather it's linear with multiple branches.
Ofcourse there are what I would call, "key PLOT bosses/zones" that are significant enough where YOU HAVE TO BEAT in order to progress.
Also the Boss names/designs are REALLY REALLY COOL, enough said on that, and ofcourse there is LORE descriptions in thier item drops.
Also just like in Dark Souls you can CUSTOMIZE the balls out of your character, so enough can be said about that for sure.
One thing of note, the very first great sword you find is BROKEN (OP'd) as Hell, which makes going through your first playthrough fairly do-able, especially if you use poison builds.
The travel system is pretty conveinant just like in Dark Souls and depending how well you utilize the "Make Offerings" feature at your "Sanctuaries/Shrines" which are your  NPC merchants/crafters/covenenant specific uses.
Well I could on and on about how much I like S&S but its TOO LONG TO LIST lol
Dislikes:
Sadly, the character art design is kinda bad.  It looks kinda cheap/lazy, and character features looks like those animated characters of that electro punk band Gorillaz, except Gorillaz looks WAY better.  I think this game's character creator is probably the worst part of this game which was unfortunately a turn off to some people who look down on indie games like this.
However I do feel the equipment you pick later on kinda makes up for it, like the Bloodbrow set which is obviously a nice inspriational nod to Bloodborne including an NPC you meet who wears the set, and gives you lore about the "Bloodbrow Hunters" fighting "Beasts" lol
It's pretty sick looking, and there are also other good looking equip sets you can find or grind from enemies like the Split Swordsman.
Bottom line the inital character designs are terrible, but you can find equipment that does look cool on your character.
And speaking of equipment, ugh....the Inventory menu is kind of a lazy jank♥♥♥♥♥mess.
Don't be fooled upon first impression look of a "Souls-like" asethetic but whenever you pick up items/gear/weapons and etc. it is sorted in the order of what and when you picked up first.  THERE IS NO WAY TO ORGANIZE your inventory, except drop everything ONE BY ONE in the order you want it as.
Yes, I know this is a very nit picky criticism but damn its annoying as hell for OCD guys like myself that wants my sets in a particularly place and order.
As far as music, not a whole of lot variety, every boss has the same common boss music which is fine,  however this game did do the FINAL BOSS a huge justice by having its own unique music, even the map before the final boss has its own unique music which was really cool upen first visit.  And as you grind levels and loot through out the game you can occasionaly get those sick ambient heavy metal riffs which is something Dark Souls games doesnt have, so that is a nice touch.
Last thing that I didnt like is some of the bullcrap platforming shenanigans in later levels like those platforms where they disappear after 2 3 seconds, and you have to time your self FOR EACH AND EVERY SINGLE disappearing platform, which was ANNOYING AS HELL,  and in some extreme places if you miss the platform YOU FALL TO YOUR DEATH.
However I believe it was just one Zone where you had to deal with the bullcrap disappearing platform garbage, and it is beatable, not impossible but annoying as crap.
Well that's my two cents, and I hope you guys enjoy this awesome game and for reading my insights, and ofcourse apologies to any spelling/grammar freaks for burning your OCD.  Cheers! :)

Gameplay: 10/10 (Smooth and perfectly difficult, with a well-designed learning curve)
Score: 10/10 (Perfectly aligns which each moment and never feels old. The final few locales are especially chilling)
Mechanics: 8.5/10 (Fluid controls on keyboard or controller. Only complaint is the difficulty/inavailability of magic compared to melee that was common in the early Souls games as well. Skill curve on rolling and attacking and memorization and intuition is all an amazing blend. The glitches, most commonly found in speedrun attempts, imo, should be patched, they break the illusion this game has. You will probably only encounter one to two glitches your entire first run though, much less than any AAA title.
)
Overall: 9.5/10 (The same score as Dark Souls 3... if they release a hotfix to correct the bugs it would achieve the coveted 10/10 that I have not yet bestowed upon any game...)

A rather brilliant Metroidvania homage to Soulsborne.
- Satisfying combat that rewards careful planning
- Environments look wonderful and obviously a lot of effort has gone into the world design
- Loads of enemy variety to keep things fresh throughout
- Loads of great, memorable boss battles with some lovecraftian influences
- Interesting character progression system that's flexibile enough to allow for some creative build design
- Lots of playstyle variety with loads of magic to choose from as well as distinct melee and ranged weapon types
- For the most part, the controls are fluid and responsive
- Creed system adds a nice layer of personal world development and customisation
- Great atmosphere and some interesting lore
- There's no inventory management and no external storage, so inventory becomes cluttered and unmanageable
- Soundtrack is very limited which seems a bit of a diservice to the large environment, enemy and boss variety
- Some enemies need some functionality changed. In particular the
are a bit ridiculous and just frustrate rather than challenge. I actually thought this was bugged at first.
- An online multiplayer would have been nice
Apart from those few tiny annoyances I thoroughly enjoyed everything on offer and I'm impressed with the quality of the experience from such a small development team. I'd certainly absorb a sequel or a spiritual successor.

So now with this game F2P alot of changes have been made, abilities became universal, everything is unlockable with in-game currency which is easy enough to obtain, maps and roles have been reshaped and balanced to supply a faster paced and arguably  more fun experience. Its a AAA Title on a Free to play platform with a great currency system and so far, no cash shop or pay-walls.
The balancing seems correct but rough. there are hunters who are obviously better than others, monsters who are insanely better than others. but all in all its all pretty fair when you understand the mechanics.
So far in this first week of F2P you lose and win in about the same ratio regardless of what you play. taking into account the map, the monster, and each individual hunter which there are about 6 options for each of 4 roles.
The biggest issue right now is people dropping out of games when the odds arent in their favor, or before the game even starts if they dont get their prefered class/role. Which then replaces their selection with a Bot, which is all honesty, are absolutely ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. A player dropping out of a game can very well cost you the game, and a monster dropping out of a game is a guaranteed win for the hunters. There of course is the obligatory flood of noobs who trap dome monsters when nobody is around or in a bad arena, who shoot a fully armored  monster who is fleeing only making it faster in turn, Who select prefered as "medic" and end up killing the entire team. But these should dissipate in time.
In conclusion, The game is worth your time if your interested in an immersive first person game of "Cat & Mouse", "Hide & Seek", "Tag", and a little bit of "Follow the leader"

Antaria Online has a lot of potential to be a very-casual MMORPG. It is pretty straightforward and simple, a child-friendly game. During my playthrough of 5 hours I manage to reach level 20 and haven't encountered any problems. All I can say is that it needs more content, Antaria Online needs to be able to ask "what is the purpose of doing this or that" because so far it looks like it's going for a "Grinding" route. Which isn't a bad thing unless they over do it. As of this moment I have ran out of quests to do and places to explore so I and many others are waiting for the new update.

it's early access, but still... I feel like there's a few things that can be said for this game.
1) the quests, even in the starting areas, are just dull as hell. it's a real grind to finish everyquest going as, right now, you kill X things, turn in quest, then kill X things again but this time picking up an item they drop. rinse/repeat til current max level. Take a leaf out of WoW's book with levelling 'zones' and the ability to turn in lots of quests at once to a quest hub of sorts, rather than having to seek out the next quest giver once you hit the next level you gained from the quest before.
2) Crafting mechanics. the mining spots need massively rebalancing. early game content, which is essentially what this mining is, shouldn't take nearly as many rocks as it currently does to craft a single bar.
3) the developer has designed the game around mobile users and microtransactions for progression. You can tell this is the case because the framework is already in place to buy thousands of gems for $50 a throw, even though there aren't actually any items in game that require it yet. Do not be surprised at all when that gem store in game (where you can curently pick up only vanity items) turns in to a store where rings/amulets for additional buffs/etc appear.
4) no grouping/party system. Not that it matters at the moment as there were only myself and my friend online when we played, but no way to add friends/communicate in game at the moment. Group/Party system that share quest objectives/can kill the same enemies perhaps.
5) skills. The adventurer class (default) gets 4 skills in 2 hours of gameplay, and only one of them is actually used in regular combat. you need LOTS more skills. Clicking an enemy, then mashing 1 until it dies isn't exactly entertainment. it's just dull.

I won't do a full review on the games current state, but will instead do a short rundown on what the game currently offers and my opinin on it.
The game looks really nice and cute, which is why I personally picked it up in the first place. There's a lot of asset recycling at the moment, but that's just about what you can expect from an MMO anyway.
This is certainly one of the strong points for the game, as it gives it a unique feeling, taking on a more cutesy artstyle than many similar games.
from a gameplay perspective, there isn't a lot yet, all the combat is done by spamming buttons on your keyboard, and you use the same method on all monsters, even the "bosses", since all of the monsters attack you in the same way. The combat is as such not very complex and the game feels more like a chill game , sort of "clicker"-esque.
The progression system is sort of what you'd expect from an RPG. You start out with simple gear, get gear that looks slightly cooler with slightly better stats, and you keep going from there. Nothing special, but not bad either.
The skill system is very simple, giving you only a current max of 5 abilities at level 15, again leaving the combat very simple and laidback.
All in all the gameplay is very casual, and you're not going to feel any challenge doing anything, but the progression system keeps it "interesting" (~ 5 hours of gameplay so far)
I think at current calling it an MMO is sort of misleading, as the only actual player interaction there is at the moment comes in the form of the market, which at the time of writing is completely empty because there's really nothing to sell to anyone (no rare drops etc.), I suspect that will change in the future. There is no chatting in game which can be seen as a bad thing since it may leave the game feeling more like a single- rather than multiplayergame.
The ingame interface is fairly good missing some key features on pc though, like pointing at skills in your skill menu and pressing the number you want it to be on, instead of the more mobile-friendly drag'n'drop. You'll also bump into a lot of red warnings if you're a buttonspammer like me, when youre trying to do things like spamming a skill, which can be distracting.
It's an Alpha game, so there isn't a lot to do right now, and considering this game has a coin shop button right on the main GUI, it really does feel like one of the free mobile games you might find. If you ask me, I would say it's worth the 1 dollar, as you can expect much more content in the future.
TL;DR: It's an alpha, some things are lacking, some things look promising. It has my recommendation :)

This game is phenomenal.
The best way to describe it is that it is an attempt to catch the same lightning in a bottle that created Undertale. Like Undertale, it seems to be a perfectly innocent RPG, but things are not as they appear to be. Whereas Undertale subverts the expectations of a turn-based battle system, OneShot subverts the limitations of a puzzle game, and clues needed to progress may be found in the most truly unexpected of sources.
The characters, the world, the lore...everything is so well-put together, and it draws the player into a powerful, immersive experience. You have a great responsibility before you, and the choices you make are very real. In the end, you have One Shot to save the world.
As I said with Undertale, go in as blind as you can. Don't look up the story, don't watch any Let's Plays, just experience it for yourself.
The question that arises with all these comparisons is, of course, is the game as good as (or better than) Undertale? I think the answer will vary from person to person, and my experience with the game is still too fresh (as of this writing) to make a balanced judgment. But I can say that you, one way or another, will not be disappointed.

Assassin's Creed II, graphically improved and better control responses, is following up after the interesting journey of Altair, master assassin from the Third Crusade days.
You return where you previously left off as Desmond, still imprisoned inside Abstargo's facility. However, not for long. Lucy returns and helps break you out, just to bring you to an apartment complex where you return to the Animus to discover more of Desmond's ancestors.
Inside the animus you enter a time of Renaissance in Italy. Your journey starts through the eyes of Ezio Auditore da Firenze, a young man full of childish antics and testosterone. From here you live through the years of young Ezio as his world abruptly alters as he witnesses political turmoil and power struggles. This is obviously a sheer jist of what you will encounter.
Pros:
- Another promising story to enjoy.
- Huge graphic improvements from the first game.
- Combat feels more fluent and at times challenging when trying to counter.
- Renaissance time, one of my favorite historical periods.
- There is more to do, as in fortress upgrades, more side-quests, and gear purchasing.
- The world is larger and vastly more beautiful in comparison to Assassin's Creed.
- Ezio, though uninspiring at first, grows on you as you travel through ten years of his life.
- Assassin attire does not disappoint.
- Water doesn't kill you!
- New weapons and armor customization.
I personally recommend upgrading your fortress as soon as possible. It brings in some great cash every 20 minutes of game time. So if you need to step away for a bit, leave the game running.
Cons:
- Side-quests, as normal, can become tedious. However, they are not required to progress the story.
- A few bugs still present, but not largely inconvenient as the first installment.
- Parkour does feel more touchy with the environment.
- I like the gondola, but steering it can get a tad annoying around smaller areas.
Very little cons, I really enjoyed this game. I started it on a Friday night and completed the main story within the same weekend. So don't expect a 30+ hour story. This was a great upgrade from the first installment and witnessing some of Altairs legacy was also rewarding. This game will not disappoint and will definitely give you your moneys worth.

Fans gave this game a hard time when it was first released, but I never understood why. The developer id have consistently given us some of the most iconic shooters in the entire genre, and while Rage is not the best game they ever made, it's very, very good!
Make no mistake, this game is NOT like Fallout - it's 90% traditional FPS that simply allows you to have a say in how many missions you take on and in what order. There is also some mandatory racing, but it's not that hard to get the hang of.
The plot is largely forgettable, simply providing context for the universe you're in. As it is, the setting is heavily inspired by the Mad Max-universe where you play an enhanced human fighting against a variety of evils such as ravaging gangs, fanatical mechano cults, dangeros mutants, zombies and the like.
What makes Rage stand out is the idTech engine and megatextures joining forces to create an extremely detailed universe, where even random NPCs are exceptionally well designed and animated. Rage also features a truly great selection of id-approved guns, all of which can fire a variety of ammunition, and a variety of useable items that you can carry into battle.
The player can dispose of enemies at close range with the classic id-shotty, build exploding RC-cars and drive them into a group of enemies from a safe distance, throw out neck-seeking razor sharp boomerangs, mow down enemies with an actual vehicle, or nail enemies to walls using the rebar launcher as they explore the wasteland. Once your options have expanded a bit, the game can be a LOT of fun, and the AI really helps too as it is smart enough to really keep you on your toes.
I highly recommend getting The Scorcher's DLC as it gives you access to one of the most fun weapons in the game, gives you even more to do in the main campaign and also a sexy sidekick to oogle if you're into that.
Overall, a very, very solid shooter from a legendary developer.

Honestly, some of the most fun I've had with a roguelike, can only name a few that I'd rank higher than it. Unlike most roguelikes, there's an overworld with towns, said overworld and said towns are not randomly generated, but have fixed layouts, only the dangerous areas that would loosely define as "dungeons" are random in layout. Each option feels quite different, and usually has a somewhat unique play style, with race choice as well as class. The game doesn't exactly feel unfair until mid to late levels when the adventure starts getting into ridiculous territory.
Visuals for something as lightweight as this and static sprites are quite nice, there's some 3D effects and 2D effects based on special abilities being used, the sprites are large and detailed enough to know what you're facing before you mouse over it.
Controls are fairly simple, opting for an action bar where you can slot all your different items/abilities, which may deter some of the hardcore players of roguelikes. There's also mouse support, and right clicking on your character or other things allows one to play mostly with the mouse if one prefers.
Sound is present, there's music for every area, sounds for different attacks and special abilities, nothing to really write home about, but it's not bad.
Game mechanics are fairly solid and scale up to the point of more or less halfling going toe to toe with kaiju god-slaying robot of death, though quite a few of the mechanics are not 100% intuitive, difficulty is pretty variable with lots of options. Achievements are a colossal pain in the♥♥♥♥♥♥though, as a result, as getting an achievement in one difficulty setting doesn't unlock it for any others, and a lot of the achievements have 12 variations or so based on difficulty settings. Will say that some randomly generated enemies can be impossible to kill, I had an issue with a named bone giant who was impossible to kill at the level cap with ridiculously strong abilities as a summoner.
The game also has a plot and rewards you for being a nice person or a total jerk as well. It's not super deep, but it's enjoyable.
The engine's moddable as well, I recall the official site having an eastern fantasy campaign.
I made it about halfway through, but it started feeling like a total slog.

I feel quite sorry that I dislike this game, but it's not fun to play to me. It is obvious that somebody put both effort and thought into this game, but unfortunately it still doesn't work.
The game is just super frustrating to play. And actually I don't think difficulty is the reason for that: In general I enjoy difficult games. In Salt and Sanctuary, there are two mechanics which I find especially annoying:
First, if you gain enough experience ("salt") to reach the next level, you don't automatically gain that level, you have to go back to the last save point and click a button. If you die before doing that, your salt is lost (well you can get it back, but anyways). This wouldn't be so bad, but in addition, each time you enter the sanctuary, all enemies respawn.
So I continously find myself in this situation: I beat a hard section of a level, killed the enemies, and got lots of salt. I can now either a) go back and claim my level -- and face the hard secion again immediately without doing anything wrong. Or I can b) continue playing, with a very significant risk of dying before reaching the next sanctuary, having to replay the hard section in addition to losing my level.
Second, the savepoint are not actual savepoints, but respawn points; if you die, you don't load your last save, but instead you respawn, losing some gold, all your XP, and without getting the consumable items back you used since you last respawned. Thus, my character just gets weaker and less resourceful with each death, reducing my chances to beat whatever killed me before in the next attempt.
This is just super frustrating. I think in a jump-and-run game like this where you are likely to die often, you need some "retry" mechanics which doesn't cost the player anything.
If dying would just reset you to the state you were in when you last reached a sanctuary (including gold, XP, and items), and you would gain levels immediately after collecting the necessary XP (this should probably create a savepoint), I think this game would be much more fun to play, at least to me.
Other than that, the sound effects are very nice, the atmosphere is good, and the fighting system is somewhat unique -- so I think there is potential. The keyboard controls feel way more clunky than I think they would need to, though.

However there are ALOT of diffrences between this game and Dark Souls. Firstly is the 2D layout which changes everything in removing a dimension the develeopers added everything that makes this game shine.
The maps are more focused on vertical climbing with a hefty dose of platforming you just couldn't fit into a 3D game.
The map layout is also much much easier to memorise with it removing a whole movement axsis and being desgined in one of the easiest memory formats.
as I said above theres more platforming in this game which is why there are also special ablities called "brands" which are just awesome and fun to use and give the game a sort of MetriodVenia feel as you explore around and aquire the ablity to walk on walls or turn light into bridges or kickflip off walls.

There is very little online interaction, instead you simply get messages from other players online and have to rely on the friend next to you on your couch for help.
There will be some things (like the Witch of the Lake) that actually really are utter ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t and unfair, but honestly...it's up to you to adapt and conquer that. This game has a very steep learning curve, and you will likely hate it at first.
I know I did. I hated the absolute ♥♥♥♥ out of this game when I first tried it. Over time, as I got better and was more comfortable wih how things worked, I began to like it more and more.

This was the first game I bought when I got my new PC, after five years of not playing any games. I saw the reviews, played for two hours, got bored, and bought other games and forgot about this. I could not understand why everyone thought this game was so great.
Then about two days ago, I decided to restart the game, and instead of hacking my way through like I did the first time, I tried to go the non lethal route. I just finished the game today and now can't wait for the sequel to come out in november. Using stealth really changed the amount of fun you have in this game a lot. I still replayed every level running around killing everything, but you really miss out if you don't try to go the nonlethal route at least once, as it makes you really engage with the game and disposing of them in different ways rather than just killing them with weapons. This is a great game. Great story, good gameplay, and a unique feature, the Blink-182 (a shortdistance teleport) that actually adds to gameplay rather than being a useless gimmick crowbarred in for the sake of being original.
The only slight dowsides are that the dialogue sounds like it was written for people suffering from severe amnesia. Like how the NPC's always very ham-handedly mention every story development in conversation to make sure you don't get lost, which makes it hard to connect with the characters.
Also, the guard dialogue is a bit weird. They have a set number of standard responses, and when another guard asks them something, they will randomly choose one of those, without regard to whether it's appropriate for the situation. So you'll hear stuff like:
Guard A: "Let's go for whisky and cigars tonight."
Guard B: "Chances are very good."
But besides that the game is amazing. The level design is great and really encourages the use of your Blink power. The combat is fluent and responsive and stealth is fun and challenging.
Overall, this game isn't as good as Thief II, but it's damn close.

I have such mixed feelings about this game. It has a lot of rough edges, but Lion Game Lion really seem to care about the game, and haven't thrown in the towel just yet. Get this game on sale if you can, at the momment I can't reccomend it at it's $40 dollar price tag, there just isn't enough content to warrent that kind of money. But lemme explain a little.
Now, don't get me wrong, there is a lot of issues with this game. For starters, the "Diesel" engine brings along it's share of issues from the "Payday" series. Desync is a huge problem with this game. The rewards system feels bare bones and not rewarding at all. More than half the time you will be getting XP boosts, and sometimes cosmetics for a character you don't like or don't play. The "proficiencies" is nothing more than increasing a certain stat by 10% every time you level up, and sometimes upgrading your class ability. Leveling up takes FOREVER once you get around level 10. Unlocking upgrades for your weapons starts out simple enough, but becomes a grind. The AI is just bad, I can't really expand on that statement, they are just bulletsponges that don't respawn. Finding the collectable dogtags gets pretty old, pretty fast. Etc..
And yet I keep coming back to this game. Something about it draws me back in. The shooting feels pretty solid, and the dismemberment system can be comical and satisfying at times. The challenge cards system has a lot of potential, and community is fairly nice. The player base may be low, but the people you find seem to enjoy the game and enjoy playing with others. And Lion Game Lion are pumping out updates pretty regularly. As of the day I am writing this, the studio just pushed out Update 6 yesterday, which attempts to fix XP issues and added a new grenade.
I like this game. I don't know why but I feel like there is still hope for this game. I do not recommend it at full price. $40 dollars is a lot to ask for. But if you can get it on sale, I don't feel like you will be disappointed. Or you will. I dunno, I like the game, maybe you will?
TL;DR: Game has a lot of issues, get it on sale and have some Nazi killing fun.

Despite the delicious pixel-art graphics, this game is far from your typical retro game's "feel"
A healthy chunk of the game IS memorizing boss movement and reflexively dodging bullets a-la metal slug, but you'll be spending more of your time grinding old missions to up gather materials to up your dps (among countless other variables depending on the goal of each particular mission and your preferred playstyle) and customize your loadout.

Over all though this is sweet game for the price with tons of content. Don't know if I'd recommend it for solo, but it's definitely fun in coop.

Bayla Bunny is EnsenaSoft's attempt at creating a platforming game that is accessible for all ages (e.g. kid friendly). However, adults, be warned! You'll never be able to get over the nightmares of the piano played 'Heads, Shoulders, Knees and Toes.'
The game plays as a normal platformer where players run and jump among other basic mechanics that players of platformers will be familiar with.
The game adds more and more mechanics to its game over the course of its 27 levels. I would have liked to have seen more than one level between the introduction of some mechanics. Not because I wasn't already familiar with how they worked but rather that reinforcement of skills has proven to work. As a result, I feel that some younger gamers may become frustrated as they are forced into an information overload. Adding more levels would also provide greater value to the title.
The game initially advises you to press the left and right buttons for movement. This does work. However, for whatever reason it felt sluggish. I soon picked up my controller to see if the game had controller support. Thankfully, it does. It also makes the game control a lot more naturally. As a result I recommend that if you have a controller that you play with that rather than the keyboard.
There was, however, one slight problem that I discovered with the controller. I couldn't work out how you are able to move to the next level. Therefore, I had to use my mouse between levels to select the next level. If it isn't possible to do this with the controller then I would advise that the developer update the game with this feature added. This would be viewed as a quality of life improvement.
The game has clearly been designed with a younger audience in mind. Therefore, it is perfectly acceptable to expect a cartoon-like graphical feel to the game. As aforementioned the music throughout the game incorporates a heavy dose of 'Heads, Shoulders, Knees and Toes' into the game. The sound is acceptable as well. Arguably the presentation is the best part of the game as it can definitely be seen to be engaging to its target audience.
It's an EnsenaSoft game on Steam. Do you think it's Steamified? Of course it isn't. Though I do hear that the developers are looking into changing that. Trading cards and achievements would be a great touch that encourages their potential player base to pick up their already cheap titles.
Any self respecting adult will likely pass at listening to the music on repeat. However, for a child's first platformer it's a pretty solid title. I'd like to have seen more time given to the introduction of mechanics but that's really the only gripe that I have with the game. It's really the 'My First' version of platformer.

I've had it on my wishlist since release, I was overjoyed when I received it as a gift from a friend and I had to dive right into it.
3 playthroughs later, time to sing its praises... except, it's actually hard to do so without spoiling anything.
The gameplay is not too different from other similar story-based RPG Maker, with some light puzzle elements in-between talking and exploration.
What makes the game different is the fact that it's heavy on meta- elements (which I absolutely love) and it smashes the fourth wall from the very beginning, making it clear that you, yes YOU the player are as much of a part of the game as any of the other characters.
The story of the game starts with Niko, a kid with curiously cat-like features, that after waking up in a foreign and dying world is addressed as "The Prophet" and tasked with restoring the world's Sun... which is actually a lightbulb.
You, as the literal god of the world, are asked to guide them and aid them in his quest, trying to understand the world and its inhabitants in the process.
I'm not gonna spoil anything more about the game, I can just say that it was a very unique experience that I would recommend to anyone that enjoys meta narratives in games like I do.
I was also surprised by how much the game makes you care about its world and its characters, starting with Niko themselves.
If you pick it up, make sure to stick around and play the game a second time on the SOLSTICE route (which you can access after beating it once). It really explains a lot and completely fleshes out the story.

ot, is a fantastic game, absolutely loved it. OneShot is a simple game with a great story, good music, and art. Your mission is to guide the protagonist, Niko, to restore the Sun of the world. ist, Niko, he is SO CUTE <3_<3
My opinion of the game
-------------------------
When I started playing the game, I started to write down on a txt file every small thing I li
ed or didn't like, but I ended up giving up on that because I got caught in the story. I enjoyed the very first scene when the camera is directly on Niko's e
es, the changes in music, the dark graphics, all the puzzles were fun (except the last ones in the tower... really annoying), and I think I got lost about... 3 times during the whole game and I had to look up a guide, but m
st of it was easy to figure out.

st so so so cute, all the "mhm!", the smiley faces... "Fish! :D", and him talking directly to me made me get attached to him a lot.
The music, while very good, calm, and memorable, lacked a
ew "emotional" tracks, perhaps an orchestra one for a sad moment, or a high-beat
ne for action scenes, like escaping the squares.
The art in this game is great. I like ret
o style graphics, and these ones are done well, except I don't like much Niko's sprite, not sure if the brown color or the way the cat ears are drawn (he looks like a bat), but overall great, and I really like the cutscenes with static images, very well drawn and beautiful!
The gameplay is bad and g
eat at the same time. It's just a "walk and read" game, there are no action scenes where you need to use your reflexes, no mini-games, but the mechanic of br
aking the 4th wall is absolutely awesome. The first time I heard from the computer that I had to look in my Documents folder, my mind blew off. I really didn't expect it to go th
t far, and then it changed my desktop, with the hidden pattern behind the game window... every new interaction with my own computer was just awesome, I loved it.
The story is great, but I did not like the end. When I got to make my
ecision, I wanted 100% to save Niko, but I chose to Save the World since I was told the computer would try to trick me into shattering the sun... And after then, the credits, a few static images and pam! ... the game just unplugs the cable. Such and abrupt ending, with no post-game, you just open the game and you see the room illuminated by the sun. Then, by deleting the save file you can start again, and at that point I was a bit upset because of my confusion. I was not sure what I had to do, did I have to complete the whole game aga
n?? It really did not felt re-playable after that, and I was mad that such a great story ended like that. After research in forums, wiki, guides and youtube videos, trying not to spoil myself, I understood  everything about the routes and the Solstice update.

Antaria Online: An MMO with cartoon-like graphics and an easy to pick up playstyle.
Rating: 9/10
Controls:  They are almost a hybrid RuneScape/WoW controls. Click to attack, then press numkeys to use your skills. Very easy to play, without feeling too dull. They're not reinventing the wheel by any means, but the combat feels smooth.
Graphics: The game is quite cute and runs without issue on my mid-range PC. At this early stage in the development, there are little to no graphics options available. But I can't see much need for it at this point.
Length: Probably the biggest reason the game may receive downvotes at this point is the length. It's very early in development, and thus the game is pretty limited. For the price tag, I still say it's worth it. If only to help support the developers continuing to update the game.
It's still way too early to say where the game will go, but at this point I'm overwhelmed with excitement to see where this game will go in the future. I have high hopes we will continue to see this game updated and fleshed out.

For $5, this is a fun game and a good way to kill a weekend. It has a Borderlands/Fallout vibe, but unlike those games it is a shooter first and an RPG at a distant second. Most of the guns feel powerful, and there's a lot of strategy to be employed. Some guns are more useful for certain enemies than others. A lot of the enemies can soak up a lot of damage, but the smarter you fight the more effective each shot will be. Some enemies you should run up fast and shoot with a shotgun. Sometimes it's worth sniping from cover, even in a close indoor fight. Some items like the boomerangs or RC Car bombs are good in some situations and less so in others. I wouldn't say it's a thinking man's shooter, but it definitely invites more thinking than Call of Duty.
The graphics are okay. Sometimes a vista looks quite beautiful, but close-up objects have muddy low-res textures. It's a very mixed bag. The soundtrack is forgettable, but very functional. The music will essentially tell you if enemies are nearby or not.
The weakest part of this game, by far, is the story. You step out of a cryogenic freezing into a desert apocalypse with no knowledge of anything (like Fallout's Vaults). There's no real purpose or desire for your character, so basically every character puts you to work doing their violent, mercenary chores until the end of the game. Some of it makes sense (save the town from evil bandits!) and some if it doesn't.
Supposedly there's this evil dystopian government, the "Authority," that's super bad, and characters tell you that you're going to join the Resistance at some point. The only thing is, I've never seen an example of this Authority's evil. They don't even appear in person until halfway through the game. When they appear, it's because you attacked them first. And even then, clearly nobody in the towns fear them. They swear at the Authority soldiers, and the Authority soldiers don't even smack them in response. Half Life 2 did a good job of showing a citizenry that's beaten down and defeated by an oppressor. Here, the Authority inspires the same level of fear as the IRS.
The missions are fun, but there's clearly no coherent plot thread. The last mission doesn't feel like the culmination of all your work up until this point. It just feels like one more job in a series of mostly disconnected jobs. I know id Software isn't known for their plots, and that's not necessarily a problem. I love Doom and Quake and Wolfenstein and accept that they are mostly games for shooting and not learning stories. Still, I was able to understand pretty clearly that Hell Demons and Nazis and the Strogg were evil. I can't understand why the Authority is evil, except that clearly all large governments are bad, duh. I never thought I'd accuse a visual work of "telling, not showing."

A bad port of a mediocre shooter.
Tedious, repetitive, unsatisfying.
Gameplay consists of shooting, driving and crafting. None of which are particularly fun or satisfying.
The same locations are reused many times whether you’re driving from location to location. Or when you’re participating in races.
Main mission locations are reused for lame side missions where you just redo the location but in reverse. So you basically enter from the exist, and exit from the entrance. So lazy. You’re usually sent back to a location to find something. Fetch quests.
The game may look open world but its not. Its very linear. There is nothing to explore.
The characters are not memorable. The enemies are not memorable.
Conversations are long. Characters take forever to get to the point. You have to wait through their long conversations before you can accept a mission.
COMBAT:
Switching weapons in combat is more of a hassle than it needs to be considering these guys made doom.
You equip 4 weapons at a time in slots. If you want to use another weapon you need to pause the game and add the weapon to a slot.
This is not a strafe shooter. Just staying crouched is the best strategy. And duck behind cover to regenerate health.
Enemies have invincibility frames. They take no damage when reacting to your gun fire. Meaning you have to wait to shoot them again.
CRAPPY DLC PRACTICES:
The pre-order bonuses can be unlocked by simply creating a folder and copying a text document.
The scorchers dlc is good. But its cut content. It also allows Extended Play so you can continue playing after the game ends. Something that should have just been part of a free patch.
This is not the first time Bethesda has published a game that refused to let you continue after the ending.
BAD PORT:
The textures look bad. The game runs poorly even on new hardware. Graphics options are limited.
Enemy corpses vanish within seconds.
MODDING COMMUNITY DOESN’T CARE:
They allowed modding but you’ll only find one mod. This game apparently wasn’t worth the time.

This is definitely not iD Software's shining star. The audio is a bit rough and the texture streaming, while innovative, is a bit distracting. The game engine though is very well optimized and provides a really large environment to explore without needing a monster gaming machine.
The level design is very cool and convincing. It really makes you feel like you are in a Mad Max film. The combat is fun, especially with the nail gun and its strange attachments. Much like BioShock, the guns all have multiple ammo types to switch between which leads to the combat being so fun and fast paced.
Speaking of fast paced combat, there are several different enemy types. Some shoot at you and try to hide behind furniture or walls and some (those pesky mutants) charge in and try to mob you with melee attacks. The gigantic 'boss' creatures are especially awesome. The coolest enemy of all though has to be "The Authority" which are humans wearing electronic armor. You can shoot off pieces of said armor or penetrate with certain ammo types. You can also disable their electronic armor with EMPs which allows slightly easier penetration with normal ammo types. Very unique.
In the end though, I only played this game once or twice and then set it down for good since the necessity of vehicles in the open world is extremely annoying. The racing missions and pretty much anything related to the vehicles really distracted from the FPS gameplay for me.
