This is, in my opinion, the best roguelike on the market. ToME is an incredibly deep and strategic RPG/roguelike which takes place in an insanely lore-rich world of classic high fantasy.
The game is strategic in that time moves in "turns", meaning time ceases to move between actions or movements. This allows you to carefully plan each action, rather than requiring twitch reflexes. If you want fast paced action, look elsewhere. Animation is minimal, yet the graphics are extemely charming, and convey quite clearly everything that is happening.
Character creation is rich, deep, and super flexible, albeit extremely complex. I've played the same class a million times, but the result is always different depending on how I lay out the stats and skill points, which is probably my favorite part. I am constantly finding fun and oddball builds which get a million times farther than I expect. If you like making characters for tabletop rpgs you'll love this♥♥♥♥♥♥
The difficulty is pretty brutal, but it always feels fair. There are ways to turn this down for chickens, or up farther for masochists and vets. As you play, you get better at making characters and becoming better at survival. But there are a TON of things to unlock too. There are different classes, races, and starting items to unlock in addition to "campaigns", which are essentially different game modes. If you get bored of adventuring around the continent, turn on endless dungeon mode. Tired of that? Arena mode is a blast too.
Basically, this game is insanely fun, super challenging (and therefore rewarding), and the world is written with a very tasteful degree of seriousness. Humor can be found in dialogue but it is subtle and never breaks the immersion (no memes thank the lord.)
If you enjoy roguelikes and don't have this game, do yourself a favor and cop it! If you like it, go get that dlc too. My best character so far has been a halfling doombringer. if that doesnt convince you I dont know wat will

So unlike most "founders" of the game I'm one of the founders of the game that had really appreciated what they had done. Evolve in it's earliest stage was a very interesting and beautiful looking game and had 4 players hunting down a monster that was trying to hide feed then essentially eat the hunters booty (rather quickly I may add). So when the game first released it was a very enjoyable experience and I got to meet many amazing people. However when the so called DLC simulator struck people started to pull away from this game and sure I understand why, but that's all you cared about?! REALLY?! Come on guys show some respect! However even through it all I stayed and here we are at Stage 2. Evolve Stage 2 is literally amazing! Ever since it's reboot I have played this game so much since then with my friends (and don't let my total play time fool you I'm just a busy person) and I can say TURTLE ROCK YOU ARE DOING SOMETHING RIGHT! It's a fun and interesting game and it no longer feels like a "running simulator" as people who only picked up the game for a few hours would call it. Matches are faster paced more intense and no matter what side you're on it overall feels way more balanced than before. Weekly hunter and monster rotations are great for new players to learn and (mind the pun) Evolve, while new players still have the benefits of any characters they had previously before the the game went F2P, but the "Founders" can teach a whole new generation of Evolve players what it means to truly play this game! With that said though it's time for a PROS and CONS list.
PROS:
- Faster paced combat
- Feels way more balanced
- Hunters have passive health regen when not in combat (great for medics because they don't have to wait to heal other players anymore until combat)
- Assaults new defense matrix reduces alot of damage the monster can dish out.
- Getting silver keys (the in-game currency) is fast an easy
- You can know pick 3 perks and if you pick a higher version of the same perk ie Bronze and Silver Speedloader perk the effects stack
- Trappers new planetary scanner shows the relative location of the monster.
- Teamwork is hugely Improved
- and more
CONS:
- Some of the stealth aspects of the game have been removed.
- Monster now has PASSIVE ARMOR REGEN which is a pain and needs to be removed
- All hunters can dome (ruins trappers purpose slightly) and a new player 1v1 in the dome will die garunteed
- Wraith (One of the Monsters) no longer cloaks on deployng Decoy.
- Removed Supports Cloaking ability which was clutch for staying alive against the Monster if you were the only one left.
- Expert players (Unfortunately) can be rude to new players at times.
- Gave Lazurus' Lazurus Device (A heal tool and gives no penalty and can revive dead players) ALMOST A MINUTE COOLDOWN! It MUST go back to the 3 second cooldown for combat purposes (Otherwise LAZURUS is a useless medic)
- Power Relay now has less health (approximately a 75% health reduction)
- Monsters NO LONGER flinch when attacking the POWER RELAY if one person is shooting the monster (You know so they win the game) unless multiple teamates are shooting at it or a heavy damaging weapon is used (NEEDS TO BE FIXED ASAP)
- Some of the stealth aspects have been toned down to much. This took away the one thing that made WRAITH unique (Definitely want Wraith to be stealthy as she has the lowest health of all monsters)!
- EVERY TEAM MEMBER NEEDS A MIC OR WINNING AS HUNTERS IS VERY HARD AGAINST AN EXPERIENCED MONSTER!
Things I'd like to see:
- A little faster progression
- A little more focus on stealth, but at the same time maintaining the intense combat
- Jetpacks using LESS fuel when Jetpack Dodging in combat with the monster.
- A revamped NEST mode.
- More maps (Already planned).
So... that's it really. Take away what you want from this review, but I've been there since the beginning and I can say TURTLE ROCK IS on the right track to making this game what they originally set it out to be! So, I hope to see some of you in-game with me and I'm looking forward to what comes next!

Raven Shield is what many (myself included, if I'm honest) consider to be the best Rainbow Six game, as all the following entries in the series either fail at realism, (Lockdown) or straight-up take the 'arcade' route. (Vegas)
It's often compared to the likes of Counter-Strike, and I'd honestly say that it's better. This is because it adds a lot more to the table in terms of weapons, game modes, maps, decent AI opponents and team mates, as well as allowing you to perform more actions; as an example, you're able to 'fluidly' open doors so you can silently open it a crack to peep through, just swing it open, or even put a breaching charge on it.
In terms of weapons/gadgets you can use, other than having literally a mountain of guns to pick from, (although I always say the FNC and Steyr AUG are the best ;) ) ranging from assault rifles, sniper rifles, sub-machine guns, shotguns, light machine guns and pistols (including automatic pistols), there are a whole load of grenades and other equip-able items you can pick from. For example, there are of course your typical frag and flashbang grenades in the game, but there are also CS teargas (and gasmasks you can take to counter this) and smoke grenades. Not to mention the various other explosives and utilities, such as claymores + remote detonators (no magic hostile presence-detecting ones like in other games), C4 explosives, heartbeat detectors and many more.
Also, the iron-sight haters won't have a problem with R6 3:RS either, as they've still got the good ol' zoom - which shouldn't be an issue for those who dislike the zoom, as there are plenty of choices with scopes of varying types, as well as other attachments for your weapons.
So yeah, essentially if you want to play a realistic and fun shooter with loads of different tactics and choices, get this!

Overall, a positive experience.  Soime thoughts, based in part on earlier reviews I've read here:
1) I've read a lot of complaints about the UI.  Once you get to used to it, I do feel like it's more efficient and you have more options. Maybe it's a question of individual taste?
2) Dynamics and man management are defintely important.  If it's not something that appeals to you this may not be the version for you. I personally quite enjoy it and I think dealing with squad chemistry and motivation is something that has been under-emphasized.
Getting your tactics right remains critical. But getting your players to really gel makes a huge difference. As dyamics (hopefully) improves over time your team's passes appear to be crisper, there seem to be more though balls, and important parnerships form on the field. It's a very satsifying pay-off if done right.  If you don't get it right it's a headache.
Perhaps there shoud be a way to turn off dynamics for those who don't want to deal with it?  I can quite understand if people prefer a more purely tactical game.
3) I do agree about msising some little things, like knowing how many goals a player has every time he scores.
4) How about adding the women's game?  Much fewer games to be sure, but I think it would make an interesting wrinkle.
With all that mind, it's very much worth the purchase.

I've tried so hard to like it, I really have.
It feels like the "Castlevania 2" of Contra-style shooters - you see what it's trying to do, you respect it, but the things it changes ultimately spoil the game as a whole.
While original side-scrolling shooters allow you to wade straight into walls of enemies and bullet-hell, with it all being over in a matter of 30 minutes or less. Mercenary Kings has aimed for slower, longer-form play, giving players a wide variety of different objectives, more broken down missions, plus the ability to collect and craft.
It's an awesome idea, it's great to see, and once you've gotten to grasp what the hell the game wants you to do, you'll find yourself diving back into the jungle to find all the parts you need to customize your hero and their weapons.
The crafting is good, pretty comprehensive and every change you make will be noticeable - all great stuff.
However, the inclusion of varied missions and crafting is ultimately what brings this game down if you're looking for the arcade-style shooter that it touts itself as.
Although there are so many references to the classics, it forgets that a core part of their gameplay was continuous progression - sometimes simply being the very action of scrolling from left to right. With all Mercenary Kings missions being selectable, but effectively mandatory for progression, you'll find yourself revisiting the same maps over and over again, sometimes to shoot X amount of a certain type of bad guy, other times trying to find X amount of an item to craft simply so you can unlock more of the mission types you like - not all are good.
It's the classic bad practice of throwing "gopher" missions into an otherwise small game, in order to make it feel bigger.
Much like the hunter/gatherer style missions, crafting is also pretty mandatory, as you'll want certain rates of fire and certain bullet types to taken on some of the bosses. The addition of gopher missions and crafting is, in essence, how they've made the game bigger and, to be coarse, it's cheap padding.
So with all that in mind, the retro aesthetic, the 8-bit soundtrack, the throwbacks to older arcade shooters like Contra and Metal Slug and Metal Gear - they all just remind you that you'd rather be playing those games, instead of hunting through the same patch of jungle for the 5th time to find 11 specific lumps of steel so you can unlock more missions.
It's got a lot of charm, but the combination of removing directed gameplay, whilst still forcing you down a linear path is a recipe for disaster. If done ever so slightly differently, this could have been awesome.

Yes this review is long, but I really enjoyed lol, there's a TL;DR at the end!
Ooooh where to start? Well let's get the basics down first, Dishonored was definitely a well structured game. It's definitely unique from different stealth games I've played. I know it's been out for a while, but I just snagged it off of humble bundle for a nice price along with the dlc. It's honestly a shame I've waited this long to get my hands on this game. So to start off, Dishonored breaks the paradigm of stealth games to be honest. By that I don't mean it does some whacky off worldly♥♥♥♥♥♥where it changes and contorts "stealth" gameplay. The part that I really enjoyed about dishonored was actually the super natural aspect. The different abilities are new to me for stealth games, although in terms of stealth games I've only played the far cry series, splinter cell series, and theif. Regardless it was a nice refrehser since I am really starting to get into stealth games as of late. What was cool about that aspect was how the powers could be used differently and upgraded to fit your style of play. Depending on if you like to take it quiet, or for some reaason like to go loud and guns blazing in a stealh game (No judgement :D, you do your thing man) it really does cater to a variety of playstyles. This also goes a long way with weapon and gear upgrades as well. Another aspect I really enjoyed (Or enjoy in all games for that matter) was the decision making. Depending on how you play the game, it would actually alter how the game ends with the final cutscene. (If you're anything like me you won't actually replay the game just to see them -.-, instead you'll just look it up on youtube like me ^^) The next on the list would be the storyline. The plot was not the best, but I've definitely played games that have plots with less effort put into them. It was very simple and easy to follow, but there was a certain foreshadow that really gave it away (for me anyways). It was easy to see the "twist" coming, that is also due to the short gameplay. The story advances rather rapidly sort of giving away a decent amount. To add on to that, yes the gameplay was rather short actually! I was hoping for some more without the use of DLC. (This review is being written before playing the DLC, just so I can review the base product.) The game took me roughly 12 hours to complete and that wasn't on a run of just barging through the game and trying to finish. I took my time to try and soak in as much of the story as possible. While there some options to get more gameplay during missions (Won't go into specificis due to spoliers) the game didn't seem very content heavy. But despite there being some cons with the pros, I'd still give Dishonored an overall positive rating! It's worth it for the price it is, and while in my opinion it does not possess the best plot or content quantity, it makes up for it in its quality as well as uniqueness. If you want to have a fun time with a nice stealth expereince Dishonored is definitely a must have.

~25 Hour Review:
This is truly a mixed bag of Salt, while it is clearly worth recommendation it isn't without flaws that people should consider.
Game difficulty isn't dictated by mechanics but instead opting for number inflation. Instead of new traps, tricks, and pitfalls to be concerned, with your only worry is just how hard something is going to hit and in which basic form it comes.
To the game's credit the monster design, visually, is amazing! However, there is a distinct lack of actual combat variation going on. Combat becomes very repetitive with the same mechanics applied really no matter the encounter.
Further compounding the issue of combat being stale is the lack of equipment and items in the game. There is a very limited list of weapon subtypes and a just as limited  number within each of those groups. Individual weapons fail to really feeling unique amongst the peers either.
Almost as slim as the weapons is the "story" behind the game. Very interesting individual elements, but nothing is really fleshed out and you are just left with small bits of each character.
In terms of character creation there are options but the game is clearly balanced to favor two very specific character types. Either a ranged high damage mage or a brick wall knight/paladin, both builds giving you the ability to simply avoid or negate damage.
It just feels as though the game ran out of funding and had to be wrapped much sooner than the ideas behind it would want. The items, the story, the balance all feels shorted. The basis of what Salt and Sanctuary is approaches the quality of Castlevania: Symphony of The Night. It just feels as though its development was cut short and overall the game suffered.
Hopefully we get a Salt and Sanctuary sequel that takes what we have to a new level of refinement and expanse.

Let's get to the point first and ask if is this game worth about 20 bucks.
In my opinion: Yes. I have put more time into this game than into many other high profile games.
(Scroll down if you just want to see the pros and cons)
If you like Dark Souls you probably already heard about it.
And yes, in it's core it's a well done Souls inspired game with a metroidvania platformer getup.
It has punishing enemies, covenants (creeds as they are called), souls like currency, a parry/riposte system, variety in armor and weapons(some work even better in 2d), an interesting artstyle and beautiful scenery.
There are some differences though.
Creeds actively give boni as you level them up, having greater impact on the game than just selling certain spells, weapons or armor. These boni consist out of these as well, but you can also get more healing items, buffs and consumeables. You can choose one out of the later each time you level one creed up by trading in monster drops.
Instead of souls you get salt. It's used to level your character, upgrade weapons and create new weapons from monsterdrops. Similar to bossweapons, but here also from common monsters as well.
You also receive gold to buy anything else
Speaking of leveling up: Unlike in Souls games you don't immediatly spend your levels on base stats. But rather receive a black pearl which you put into a Final Fantasy 10 like grid. Here you can spend this pearl for stats and the ability to use weapon and armor types and classes from tier 1 to 5. You have to go down paths to reach the end tier of each. You can put up to three points in each stat.
Weapon and armors cost as much as the tier number, tier 5 costs 5 pearls (level ups) however they boost one stat just as much as well. So if you buy the abilty for tier 5 swords you also get 5 strength. You get more out of weapon points than for individual stats.
You can also find these black pearls every now and then in the game as well as grey pearls which erase points you spend and then you can rearrange them.
Like in Dark Souls 1 (at least in my opinion), once you are able to parry, you can parry any parryable attack by blocking and pressing attack. Either with a shield or 2 handed weapon (I experienced no difference)
You can 1 and 2 hand any weapon, 2 handing increases your strength by 50%. Instead of a shield you can use wands, the miracle counterpart and 1handed ranged weapons, like crossbows and guns. The aiming does need time to get used to, though.
Some weapon types combine movesets from others. The swordwhip (you guessed it) combines swords and whips for example.
You will have no trouble finding armor sets and weapons you like in terms of looks and usabilty, I am sure.
I have mentioned the artstyle, I personally love it a lot, but it's a matter of taste so take it with a grain of salt.
In combat you will notice that your max health with decrease by taking damage, similar to Dark Souls 2's slow hollowing process and almost copied from Dragon's Dogma.
Same thing happens for stamina and focus (which is new) if you fight long enough. However spells and miracles put a much, much greater strain on these. However spell and miracle users unlock special items to remedy this. Down other skills paths might be one point for this.
Items to regain max health can only be unlocked by certain creeds, if at all (correct me if I'm wrong)
Now what is present in Salt and Sanctuary and not in Dark Souls is the Metroidvania like gameplay.
You have one big map, but some areas are restricted by abilities you will unlock by branding through the game.
Such as inverting gravity (only for you and by activating certain monoliths), I will not tell you all of them...
As you progress through the world, you'll find sanctuaries, save spaces similar to bonfires. By claiming it for your creed you can rest there, level up and upgrade it by offering stone statues. These not only bring npcs to these places, but also give passive buffs to the sanctuary's designated area. And yes, you are always part of a creed. You can freely switch between them, but some might not want to put up with you after you sinned often enough.
Spellcasters will recieve elemental imballance, punishing overuse of magic spells (I had no trouble though)
There is a multiplayer, you can unlock it by offering a sellsword statue to the sanctuary. You can also engage in to pvp if you want.
I will sum things up now:
Pro:
-It's beautiful in it's own depressing way.
-Enemies are punishing
-a bestiary, which keeps up with enemies you have slain and which of how many different drops you have gotten...
-combat is simple, but simply works
-simple combo system for those who can't finish Devil May Cry on harder difficulties ;)
-lot's of variety in almost every way
-interesting new mechanics adding to combat
-Soulslike storytelling in item descriptions and skilltree, as well as some more philosophical and  obvious story
-possible to go through the game in not intended ways
-Optional bosses
-explorering types are usually rewarded
-developer still patches it, implementing new languages and correcting mistakes
-number of equipable spells (which there are 2 of each for magic and miracles) doesn't need to be increased by spending points, you still have to make the right choices, though
-multible endings
-Challenge modes, such as hardcore, no healing, no shields, etc.
Con
-same weapon types all handle the same, some might be faster some slower, that's it
-some types as a whole are uninteresting (imo). I have no desire to play with daggers for example.
-you have to consciously decide not to level up to avoid overleveling (I always feel to strong on NG)
-while some bosses provide a good challenge at least on NG, others just fall flat...
-some enemies have gripping attacks, they are usually pretty strong and are sometimes unavoidable and feel cheap
-ambushes might feel cheap too, as some enemies can just appear without warning, always at the same places, though
-some shortcuts from different areas make no sense
-by teleporting to a sanctuary guide, you can teleport to any sanctuary you visited. Imo he should be tweaked
Overall verdict:
If you can overlook some shortcomings, you can get your money's worth.

I'll start this by telling you that I've been playing TOME since it was Tales of Middle Earth. That's right, originally it was based on Tolkien's work and was an offshoot of a long lineage of games directly related to Rogue, via Moria and then Angband. There was a middle variant in there at some point called Pernband.
Some back story:
At some point DarkGod (the main dev) decided to rewrite the client because the old angband client was full of spaghetti code and it became untenable. So came t-engine. Tome was then written as a module of T-engine (all made by DarkGod for no $$ I might add.)
In Tome 3 there were Jedi!!! and other fun ideas but it was chaotic. Tome 3 was a mess, (Tome 4 was much cleaner.) But it was still pretty opaque as Roguelikes go. I would tinker with it, have fun with lost souls etc and then get bored. So I went the way of many players got involved in other games only came back periodically when I got a yen for playing with Lightsabers again. At some point, I noticed Tome 4 was progressing and downloaded and everything was different.
Gone were most of the touches of the Angband and Tolkien worlds. You can still see a few here and there but TOME had become Tales Of Maj Eyal with an original story and a total reworking of the graphics and mechanics. On and off Ive done some beta testing (though my forums account from then was deleted more than once so I guess being inactive on the forums is a good way to get culled.)
At some point I managed a couple of end games. I won once and once I sacrificed my guy (I still don't know why that doesn't count as a win...)
Every time I came back more and more stuff was added and then I saw that they had finally made the leap to Steam. I wanted to buy it immediately because I believe in the game and the devs and why not support them? But I was reticent with all the other games I have and also had to wait for money to pay for it anyway.
I probably should not have waited but I did and when I did finally get the steam version I was not disappointed with either the basic game or the DLC (which I had no previous knowledge of.)
Divergent note that tangentially relates to this review:
Bob Dylan has said on songwriting that if you can't change a song, if you can't mess with the words or change the arrangements it is dead and you should bury it. That is a paraphrase because I don't have the exact quote on hand. But this is how I feel about games. TOME is a living game, always changing.
Many pay to play games are not. They merely make some stuff they took out initially available for DLCs when the wells run dry. TOME is not like those games. TOME is developed by a caring group of dedicated players and programmers who are making an epic play experience.
Yes epic. You have a ton of races and classes which unlock as you play. Sometimes the unlock is just something you were going to do anyway but sometimes in true RPG fashion you have to investigate and figure out some puzzle or quest to get the unlock you want. And you can unlock them in something like 9 different modes. The game offers 50 levels of experience in whatever build combo you choose. As you learn more about classes and races you find yourself getting deeper into the decision making process and you realize you have many more choices than you will quickly be able to play with. This could take a long time. As is without any further changes. And the game changes from game to game so you may not always get an event or area you thought you might. And different play styles create vastly different approaches and in-game storylines.
There was a lot of discussion when Maj'Eyal became the world of the game about how terribly difficult the game was (is) so now there are multiple modes for discovering the game. The most rewarding depends on your personality and proclivities as a gamer. You can play with Easy and Exploration and virtually never risk death, or you can unlock, insanity and madness modes and play only in true Roguelike fashion (1 life, though there are items you can find to hedge that bet.) Or you could play as I do on Normal with Adventurous. To each player their own. This is an innovation I wish more devs would think about. Multiple play modes for multiple types of players means more fun for everyone.
The game has a few pit falls. It is deep so it is not hard to get into trouble if you are tired, hungry or bored. Don't do that. Play when you are fresh and excited and keep it that way. You won't complete it in a day. (The main quest line takes a minimum of 10 hours I think if you skip everything else and I highly recomend you don't do that.)
You may also find that the game lore is hard to penetrate. This is partially due to writing style and partially because who wants to read so much of it? Yes you should read the lore the first time you encounter it at the very least. You may or may not glean valuable clues from it but if you need to you can go back to it later. Once you have unlocked certain features you will be able to access ALL of the lore you've ever seen as a player.
You may notice that I am not giving a lot of specifics here because part of the fun of this game is playing it unspoiled. You can of course look stuff up or ask for spoilers if you aren't into all that.
I will say the sound effects while fairly professional are not my cup of tea. I am not really a game sounds kind of player though. I typically turn sound off in games I play and I only checked them out in TOME out of curiousity. You might find them entertaining. Apparently, also there is music. Something I didn't check out. (I am an older guy with a very staid taste in music. If it isn't Classic Rock. Folk, Blues or Soul from the 60s-70s then it probably isn't on my mp3 player. Though I do enjoy more varied styles, when I am gaming that's mainly what I listen to.)
I write all this mainly to enthuse about how much I am enjoying playing TOME again and want you to know it is worth every penny to buy it on steam.  The community addons alone make the game extremely customizable.

Rainbow Six 3, like most of Tom Clancy's titles, is a squad-based tactical shooter with a lot of depth. This game favors tactics over action, and you will spend hours planning out each mission before actually playing it. Before a mission, you can choose who goes on what team (Alpha, Charlie, etc.), choose their loadouts (a lot of weapons to choose from, each with their own advantages and disadvantages), and plan out the mission waypoint by waypoint. Once you are comfortable with how the planning stage works, you can coordinate attacks from multiple angles, give go-codes to execute orders, set the rules of engagement, and so on. The game gives you the option to either play through the mission or watch the AI do what you have told them to do. It's a really nice option, because it's basically two totally different styles of gameplay. You can play it as a strategy game, being the man calling the shots, or play it through the eyes of a Rainbow operative. Pick this one up.

The Rainbow Six series has always been a favorite of mine. Not the Vegas series or Lockdown, mind you, but every game up to 3, and 3 is the best installment. It's one of the most realistic shooters you will ever play. You cannot rush into a confrontation without thinking or you WILL die in one or two shots. The best way to go through a mission with minimal casualties is to plan it out beforehand. When you're making a mission plan, you'll need to prepare for any situation, and even then, the enemy can surprise you, and one slip-up could ruin the entire operation. It involves a lot of trial and error, but once you finally make that one plan that has your team blaze through the mission with zero losses, you WILL feel proud of yourself for getting it right. In fact, once you get the hang of planning, you won't even need to control your squad directly anymore. The game allows you to watch the AI carry it out for you, and they're usually very competent. If you love tactical shooters, buy it.

I love tactical games, but I have no patience for this nonsense. I got it for like $1.50 but still requested a refund. I think this game had serious potential but the developers just didn't put enough time into it to balance it properly.
Maybe the game 'gets better' later on, but there is a seriously bad first impression. I couldn't even get a 'gold victory' on the first map on normal, even after playing it numerous times and trying to learn from my 'mistakes'.
Problems
1. The timed victory concept just doesn't feel right. It forces you to just throw everything you have at the enemy, leaving very little options to be truly tactical.
2, The enemies keep auto-retreating away almost every time you hit them, making it very difficult to defeat them in a single turn without going deeper into enemy territory and exposing yourself to new enemies to destroy you. If they could auto-retreat once per round, I would be fine with that, but no, there seems to be no limit.
3. The enemies regenerate. Not like 1 or 2 HP, no, almost completely every turn. This further takes the 'tactics' out of the game. You just have to rush and try to kill units, consequences be damned. If you fail to kill a unit, it's basically gg.
4. My 'hero' got one nearly one shot in the first map by basic enemy units (even while I was on neutral terrain). I couldn't use him to do anything except do the 'killing blow', he was so frail. And the enemies just gang him if he goes anywhere near them.
They should call this a puzzle game instead of a tactical game, because unless you do things in an exact and precise order, you're screwed. I'm fine with timed combat but there has to be some sense and reason to it.

Final edit: I have played through both Jedi Knight and Mysteries of the Sith (the expansion). To do so I followed Steam user -FwG- ^ Bucky's instructions (thanks, man!). I had to roll back my AMD videocard drivers. This means I had to remove all current videocard drivers and install this, older, videocard driver: 13.1 WHQL, which can be found here:
Also, I had to download a DLL file from the JKHub website, which can be found here:
. Put the file in the same folder where you JK.exe or Mots.exe is.
Don't forget to turn on hardware acceleration in the setup menu in-game.
So, does all of this change my opinion? Well, no. Jedi Knight and its expansion are awesome games, but the way Steam provides them to us is unacceptable. The amount of tweaking that has to be done, is quite severe. If you're not very technical or aren't allowed to change videocard drivers the game is unplayable on PC's with AMD cards.
Besides the tweaking, several issues remain. The cutscenes in Jedi Knight and Mysteries play in a minimized sceen in the top left corner of your screen and the soundtrack doesn't loop, leaving out music for an incredible large part of the game (a Star Wars game without the epic music?!).
If the game was playable as it was intended I would give it ten thumbs up, if I could. But in its current state on Steam, I cannot recommend it. The way Steam throws a broken version of a beautiful game online to be sold, without any heart for how much this game means to people, is unacceptable.
EDIT: After toying with videocard settings and in-game resolutions, I was able to get some gameplay out of it. Still, there are the crashes (when going to the menu screen and back), the small windows in which the menus and videos are shown, the ingame music that doesn't loop (tracks stop after one play-through, so the rest of the level is without music) and the lack of 3D accelaration.
So, contrary to what I stated in my review below, the game can be played, but not stable and with a poor audio and video presentation.

Yes this review is long, but I really enjoyed lol, there's a TL;DR at the end!
Ooooh where to start? Well let's get the basics down first, Dishonored was definitely a well structured game. It's definitely unique from different stealth games I've played. I know it's been out for a while, but I just snagged it off of humble bundle for a nice price along with the dlc. It's honestly a shame I've waited this long to get my hands on this game. So to start off, Dishonored breaks the paradigm of stealth games to be honest. By that I don't mean it does some whacky off worldly♥♥♥♥♥♥where it changes and contorts "stealth" gameplay. The part that I really enjoyed about dishonored was actually the super natural aspect. The different abilities are new to me for stealth games, although in terms of stealth games I've only played the far cry series, splinter cell series, and theif. Regardless it was a nice refrehser since I am really starting to get into stealth games as of late. What was cool about that aspect was how the powers could be used differently and upgraded to fit your style of play. Depending on if you like to take it quiet, or for some reaason like to go loud and guns blazing in a stealh game (No judgement :D, you do your thing man) it really does cater to a variety of playstyles. This also goes a long way with weapon and gear upgrades as well. Another aspect I really enjoyed (Or enjoy in all games for that matter) was the decision making. Depending on how you play the game, it would actually alter how the game ends with the final cutscene. (If you're anything like me you won't actually replay the game just to see them -.-, instead you'll just look it up on youtube like me ^^) The next on the list would be the storyline. The plot was not the best, but I've definitely played games that have plots with less effort put into them. It was very simple and easy to follow, but there was a certain foreshadow that really gave it away (for me anyways). It was easy to see the "twist" coming, that is also due to the short gameplay. The story advances rather rapidly sort of giving away a decent amount. To add on to that, yes the gameplay was rather short actually! I was hoping for some more without the use of DLC. (This review is being written before playing the DLC, just so I can review the base product.) The game took me roughly 12 hours to complete and that wasn't on a run of just barging through the game and trying to finish. I took my time to try and soak in as much of the story as possible. While there some options to get more gameplay during missions (Won't go into specificis due to spoliers) the game didn't seem very content heavy. But despite there being some cons with the pros, I'd still give Dishonored an overall positive rating! It's worth it for the price it is, and while in my opinion it does not possess the best plot or content quantity, it makes up for it in its quality as well as uniqueness. If you want to have a fun time with a nice stealth expereince Dishonored is definitely a must have.

Mercenary Kings was one of the most disappointing games I've played in a while.  It looks great and the premise gives off the vibe that it's going to play like a Metal Slug, Contra or any other fast-paced 2D action shooter.  It doesn't and almost every aspect of the gameplay is poor.
You'll notice immediately the intentional jump delay.  I don't know why the devs were so tied into this mechanic, it's terrible in this type of game.  You can get away with deliberate jumping in some titles, but not this one.  The jump delay makes the game feel so off.  MK also has reloading.  Why?  I don't know and having to reload constantly brings nothing positive to the game.  There's also the issue that you have to press down to pick up items, and you'll have to pick up items constantly and it breaks any flow the game manages to create.  I wish the whole crafting angle wasn't even a thing because it doesn't appeal to me in the least and from I've read, it's not any good even if you're into crafting.
Supposedly the game is super repetitive and grindy as well, but I didn't last long enough to find out.  If you're looking for some fasted-paced 2D shooting action on PC, you're much better off with the Metal Slug ports, even though DotEmu didn't exactly do a great job on them.

A dastardly cross of  gameplay from Metal Slug and Contra, with more RPG typical features like persistent equipment, crafting, and character upgrades. Interesting gun mechanics, and pretty slick 16-bit (ish) aesthetics make it a delight to play. The story is pretty minimal, but the writing is very funny, and continual references to other games make for great "AH! I GET IT! THAT'S FROM _____!" moments. Also: local and online co-op. It has both. The game doesn't change at all between solo and co-op play however, so everything becomes much easier with others.
BUT: somewhat repetitive. There are over 100 individual objective based missions, but they take place on a much smaller number of actual maps, and going around the same maps many times can get boring. Add in the farming that inevitably occurs when you're trying to get parts for a specific gun part or implant or knife, and it can get a little tedious.
Overall great game, especially for fans of old school run and gun sidescrolling shooters.

One of the best Shoot'em up I've ever played (probably the best).
Well, really, there's a bad guy who wants to do bad things, and you have to beat his a**.
Mercenary Kings takes place in a wild lonely wild island where a super-vilain has decided to build his super-vilain's base.
It offers (from the top of my head) approximately 7 differents sceneries, from the wild jungle to the full-of-traps temple, or even a high-tech complex.
You like or dislike this kind of graphics, but I actually love it. "Pixel-art"-like graphics are, in my opinon, a standard for this kind of games, and it suits very well with the features and gameplay it offers (even animated boobs, no jokes).
Easy to learn, pretty easy to master (at least master on specific type of weapon / ammo). I personnaly used an xBox 360 controller from the very beginning, so I cannot relly talk about the Keyboard / Mouse controls.
Controls are intuitive, and even if it's not at the beginning, you really have the time to master it.
Mercenary Kings is quest-based, with a "Hunting ground" (aka time / quest-free zone) where you can hunt animals and such to get missings compenents for your gear.
It offers a crafting system for your guns. You have to build from components a parts of weapons, then you can assemble whatever part of any gun you like together, it will make a working gun (probably not as working as you expected).
Some weapons have a certain "synergy", making you able to use special ammo (6 differents types) like shrapnels or rockets, and sometimes two of them at the same time (piercing rockets, omfg).
You can also build knifes, which I thought to be unless, does really matters from middle to end-game.
There's equipable "mods", which makes you carry more, run faster, shoot elemental bullets, or even makes you insensitive to certain elements.
I don't really want to talk about the rest of the features, since it would probable spoil a bit.
I didn't test multiplayer yet, I will update this review as soon as I tested it.
Like I said, probably the best Shoot'em up I've ever played. I did finish the last mission, but I would really enjoy play this more. There's a really great amount of quest, stuff to craft, secrets to discover, and all kind of things.
I didn't find anything that really upset me here.
I'm kinda sad I couldn't test multiplayer yet, but as I see it, it would be as epic as the rest of this game.
Note: 10/10. (Really.)
N.B.: As a non-native english speaker, I apologize for any mistakes / bad words or such in this review.

I have three (3) major criticisms about this game.
1. The AI is horrible and repeatedly takes you out of the experience. In some instances, the AI controller spotter got me killed. In other instances, it is beyond me how a camoflagued sniper, under the cover of darkness, with no natural or artificial lighting, hiding in a bush, is seen by an enemy or group of enemies.
2. In the "training mode" you're not taught to understand the mechanics or rationale behind sniping. So, when playing in the elite or expert mode, you have to be accurate 100% of of the time or face excessive reloads, also taking you out of the experience. It's worse when you add point #1 above.
3. For a game predominantly based on stealth, it is difficult to absolutely avoid enemies altogether.
Overall, though brief, I enjoyed it for what it was. Based on the points above however, I wouldn't and can't recommend this game.

I played Rift since the beta, I usually play rift without steam so I could've gotten more hours on record but anyway, rift. This game doesn't really have a good first impression but once you get the feel of it, it gets addicting and can be a legitimite replacement for what ever MMO you are playing now. (WoW.. Cough.)
It has a unique class system that pulled me right away when I was playing in the beta. The balancing of the classes are mostly turned towards the PvE side of the game. PvP you ask?.. Well, PvP isn't Rift's strong suit... at all. While it can still be fun, the imbalances can make it frustrating and the enormous amount of 'bad' players can really make you bite your lip. I feel as though rift's PvP is more balanced for group play than solo. Also Facerolling is quite common, so it's best to bring a pre-made party.
The PvE side of this game though is exellent, it really makes you think what is the best spec for each situation you are in. Actually, the class system makes the game, it is very good. Once you are starting this game, it is wise to not stick to one build; make a TON of them and make the right spec you see fit to your tastes and works in your favor. There is a lot of things going on the map at all times. Rifts, are a key machanic which the name of the game implies. They pop randomly on the map and when you complete one you could get some wonderful goodies in return. An other cool thing are invasions that wonder across the map, making the game feel alive. But during an event, these invasions can get hairy and could literally conquer a whole area. Your quest hubs will be invaded and even main cities. This encourages group play which is very nice as well. You'll usually be grouped up automatically and fight against the baddies is some type of full blown war.
Speaking of wars, this game is pretty CPU intensive so big wars might make you lag, a lot. Any good mid ranged GPU will run this game well but don't skimp on the CPU, god help you if you don't.
I would love to write more but I am pretty busy at the moment, it was nice to test this steam grading system out.
PS: The ingame store is pretty nice, they put a lot of work into it. Also nothing in the store will give you SUPER MAX ENDGAME MEGA GEARZ. It's mostly costumes and funiture for your ingame home. The lockboxes don't have anything worthwhile inside, though it is good for gamblers or whatever.

So unlike most "founders" of the game I'm one of the founders of the game that had really appreciated what they had done. Evolve in it's earliest stage was a very interesting and beautiful looking game and had 4 players hunting down a monster that was trying to hide feed then essentially eat the hunters booty (rather quickly I may add). So when the game first released it was a very enjoyable experience and I got to meet many amazing people. However when the so called DLC simulator struck people started to pull away from this game and sure I understand why, but that's all you cared about?! REALLY?! Come on guys show some respect! However even through it all I stayed and here we are at Stage 2. Evolve Stage 2 is literally amazing! Ever since it's reboot I have played this game so much since then with my friends (and don't let my total play time fool you I'm just a busy person) and I can say TURTLE ROCK YOU ARE DOING SOMETHING RIGHT! It's a fun and interesting game and it no longer feels like a "running simulator" as people who only picked up the game for a few hours would call it. Matches are faster paced more intense and no matter what side you're on it overall feels way more balanced than before. Weekly hunter and monster rotations are great for new players to learn and (mind the pun) Evolve, while new players still have the benefits of any characters they had previously before the the game went F2P, but the "Founders" can teach a whole new generation of Evolve players what it means to truly play this game! With that said though it's time for a PROS and CONS list.
PROS:
- Faster paced combat
- Feels way more balanced
- Hunters have passive health regen when not in combat (great for medics because they don't have to wait to heal other players anymore until combat)
- Assaults new defense matrix reduces alot of damage the monster can dish out.
- Getting silver keys (the in-game currency) is fast an easy
- You can know pick 3 perks and if you pick a higher version of the same perk ie Bronze and Silver Speedloader perk the effects stack
- Trappers new planetary scanner shows the relative location of the monster.
- Teamwork is hugely Improved
- and more
CONS:
- Some of the stealth aspects of the game have been removed.
- Monster now has PASSIVE ARMOR REGEN which is a pain and needs to be removed
- All hunters can dome (ruins trappers purpose slightly) and a new player 1v1 in the dome will die garunteed
- Wraith (One of the Monsters) no longer cloaks on deployng Decoy.
- Removed Supports Cloaking ability which was clutch for staying alive against the Monster if you were the only one left.
- Expert players (Unfortunately) can be rude to new players at times.
- Gave Lazurus' Lazurus Device (A heal tool and gives no penalty and can revive dead players) ALMOST A MINUTE COOLDOWN! It MUST go back to the 3 second cooldown for combat purposes (Otherwise LAZURUS is a useless medic)
- Power Relay now has less health (approximately a 75% health reduction)
- Monsters NO LONGER flinch when attacking the POWER RELAY if one person is shooting the monster (You know so they win the game) unless multiple teamates are shooting at it or a heavy damaging weapon is used (NEEDS TO BE FIXED ASAP)
- Some of the stealth aspects have been toned down to much. This took away the one thing that made WRAITH unique (Definitely want Wraith to be stealthy as she has the lowest health of all monsters)!
- EVERY TEAM MEMBER NEEDS A MIC OR WINNING AS HUNTERS IS VERY HARD AGAINST AN EXPERIENCED MONSTER!
Things I'd like to see:
- A little faster progression
- A little more focus on stealth, but at the same time maintaining the intense combat
- Jetpacks using LESS fuel when Jetpack Dodging in combat with the monster.
- A revamped NEST mode.
- More maps (Already planned).
So... that's it really. Take away what you want from this review, but I've been there since the beginning and I can say TURTLE ROCK IS on the right track to making this game what they originally set it out to be! So, I hope to see some of you in-game with me and I'm looking forward to what comes next!

I have sort of conflicted feelings about Tales of Maj'Eyal. In short, if you judge it purely as a roguelike, I don't thing it don't hold up too well. Part of the reason I may think that may be my preference for NetHack influenced roguelikes, and my lack of familiarity or appreciation for Angband influenced or Ancient Domains of Mystery influenced rogelikes, but I am not sure how much Tales of Maj'Eyal's design is based on those games.
On the other hand, judged as a RPG Tales of Maj'Eyal does a lot of things right. It has a rather interesting tactical battle system, lots of different character creation options, many ways to tweak and customize your skills, any many items to find that offer a lot of tactical death. It's story, while perhaps presented in a way that relies too much on finding and reading lore text, is at least interesting and presents a few dark twists on the standard high fantasy setting.
No mater how you judge it, the interface is great, mostly easy to use but able to do a lot, the battles are fast-pasted and fun, and it can be very addicting. The graphics are simple but more then functional enough for what they are, and there are enough interesting special effects and visual flare to make up for the more static sprites. The music is generic but memorable and sometimes can actually be pretty fantastic, even if it is more or less all part of free game music packs.
I think that is all that really needs o be said, but here is some more detail about how I think about it as a roguelike:
The big problem with Tales of Maj'Eyal's design as a roguelike is simply that the game is too long, story heavy, and not random enough. There is variation in the loot you get and the monsters you face, but the over all world is basically set. Same world map, same town, same quests. The layout of a lot of the random zones are different but the basic themes of the zones are set, and each zone has a set rank for items, a set number of floors, a set list of enemies and possible bosses. Due to how the game is balanced and how enemies never respawn except in a few cases, it's basically required to repeat every zone and sidequest each run or you end up drastically underleveled very quickly, and due to each zone having fixed level requirements you can't even vary the order that much.
Although you actually have multiple lives before dieing in the default mode, permadeath still is a problem and when it happens you have to start over from he start and go through the same old stuff you already saw again. There is a mode where you can simply have infinite lives, but I kind of wish there was some kind of middle ground, perhaps a way to start over with a new character but with a number of story events that carry over and alter the world. There is a unlock system that adds new races, classes, skill trees, and other things, and that helps, but it still only adds so much and may of the unlocks are obscure or tedious.
I also have a problem with a lot of the streamlining or elimination of a lot of roguelike staples potions and scrolls are gone, and instead characters can equip a number of infusions or runes that can be used over and over again but have a cooldown timer between uses (actually every skill and magic spell in Tales of Maj'Eyal uses cooldown timers, I am not really a fan of them but it works). Wands and other tools work in a similar way as well. This eliminates stockpiling of consumable items, but also eleminates the sort of careful rationing of your resources you need to worry about in other roguelikes.
It's only logical because of this that the whole item identification game is gone and no items have overall negative effects, eliminating the kind of risk vs reward of using items in a panic. Many people may not like needing to worry about identifying stuff but the feature exists in roguelikes for a reason, the same reason randomized levels exist, to make sure you can't just win with rote memorization, and so every action you take has to be done very carefuly. Roguelikes since the original Rogue have always been about exploration and experimentation and the whole idea with unknown items was a big factor in that.
But again, despite all of these things I don't like about it as a roguelike, I still think it's a really good RPG. Maybe there isn't really that much of a difference, most roguelikes are basically RPGs after all, I just thought I would share my feelings on the subject.

The last real Rainbow Six game. I'm not saying this due to opinion. The name 'Rainbow Six', in the Tom Clancy universe, refers to the leader of the multi-national counter-terrorism SOF 'Rainbow'. In every Rainbow Six up to this one (original, Rogue Spear, Covert Ops), you take that role; assigning team members to squads, choosing each member's loadout, creating a plan for each team to carry out during the course of each mission. Then you can either spectate or take control of one of the teams. You really can't even compare or argue the Rainbow Six games that came out after this because they are basically a different genre with different fans.
Post-Rainbow Six 3 (Lockdown, Vegas, Vegas 2, etc.) you only take control of a single protaganist throughout the entire game. You can't plan out the mission because the missions are linear and setpiece-focused, much like traditional FPS games. Your health regenerates in later games, and they have no wounding system. And while the Vegas games were still fun and you were still a member of Rainbow, you did not assume the position of the commander, Rainbow Six, in these games. And unfortunately, no big-name developer has made a game simliar to the old school Rainbow Six games in well over a decade.

Don't be fooled by all the negative reviews comparing this game to whatever other post-apocalyptic shooter and open-world game. Even though it might look like it is open-world from the screenshots, it's not. And this is a good thing! Depending on the player I guess.
For me, I had no intention into investing hours and hours on exploring every nook and cranny of the wasteland in order to find hidden items and side quests. This is where I found the game to be just right. It's quite linear actually. There is no punishnment for not exploring nor an OP reward for doing so. This way you won't have to feel bad that you might have missed something which could have made the combat easier for example.
Other than this you can entertain yourself with a handful of side quests which just yield you more money, which in the end you end up spending on a few (but not necessary) upgrade items but mostly just ammo. There are racing and slaughter mini games on which you can spend more time which yield, once again, just more money or upgrades for your vehicles. Be warned though! Driving in this game is quite bad. The controls are hard and the cars pretty much drive like air. It can get somewhat annoying in certain racing modes, but once you eventually master the♥♥♥♥♥controls, you're fine.
What was surprising to me is how short the game felt and how unsatisfying the ending was. Mind you, there are no bosses in particular. Except maybe slightly more armored enemies but that's it. At the end, there is no ominous boss fight which cumlinates in you saving the world or whatever... no. You just fight of hordes (although you can't even call them proper hordes) of enemies, walk up to a terminal and push the button.
That's it.
Yup.
The final fight is just unloading all your carefully hoarded ammo into some 20-30 enemies and using a terminal. Congrats you finished the game!
Despite the ending being just plain balls, I liked most of the gameplay leading up to it. The characters were also interesting. They aren't particularly deeply portrayed but you can certainly get into some funny conversations with random personas which you meet around town.
There's a ton of achivements on which you can spend extra hours if you're into that.
Had some troubles with graphics though. Despite being able to run other comparable games on high with no lag, I had to find some workarounds for this one. Seems like it helps if you actually start the game as administrator and disabling the motion blur does wonders.
It's odd to have an ID Software game where being in cover is better than trying to keep moving, but nontheless, still a fun shooter.

Regardless, I enjoyed it. It is neat how the levels all react to previous levels (if you clear a level without killing people, later levels will have less guards and vice versa). Combat can feel infuriating but fair and it's always fun to experiment with kills.

It is like a less-serious-more-forgiving Hitman with supernatural powers and more linear levels.

----Spoiler Free Review----
I don't normally write reviews in any depth, but this game definitely deserves it
An excellent game in an unexplored genre.
Stealth and assasination in most games end up being a side thing, something as an additional objective. Normally poorly implemented. Dishonoured combines both aspects into an integral part of the gameplay, however more importantly it gives you choice.
You can go through the whole game never getting involved in any stealth, getting into multi man fights and taking everything head on, you can play as a regular assasin hiding in the shadows waiting for the time to strike.
But perhaps the one thing that seperates this game the most from any other stealth/assasination based game is the fact that you can go through the whole game without killing a single person. A game The achievement "Clean Hands" is also a reward for doing so, never killing anyone in a game all about assasination and extensive combat.
The graphics are stylised although realistic, they are generally very nice although not the focus of the game, all the areas that you will visit are extremely detailed
The story is also excellent, although as this is a spoiler free review I cannot go into depths of what will happen or why it is great. One thing to share is how you act directly influences how the game progresses, you have small dialogue options, although those options will be signifcant and even make you pause to think on how you want to respond. Your actions also play a big role in how the game will play out.
For those that don't want to read that I will also put direct stats of what I think the game holds up to
Graphics: 8/10, instead of going for a real life look they went a stylised version
Combat Gameplay: 9/10, if you love sword fights, close quarter combats or the like, you'll enjoy it here
Stealth Gameplay: 10/10, one of the few games to full on hit the mark in the genre
Movement/General Feel: 10/10, The parkour system works perfectly with all the abilities given
Story: 10/10, the story is excellent, and changes based on even your smallest actions
Overall if this game has interested you in even the tiniest, buy it, its very cheap too even with all the DLC, look around and pick it up.

Salt and Sanctuary is a game made of love and devotion. Created in the shadow of games like Metroid and Dark Souls, this game lovingly crafts its own universe stealing ideas from tried and true series to make something that is unique.
Salt and Sanctuary places you as the protector of a princess on a boat that gets ransacked on your way to... some... place. Your avatar wakes up on an island inhabited by various monsters, such as zombies and flesh eating bats and wolves. Its all pretty standard.
Where S&S places itself apart is the atmosphere; this game is f***ing creepy. Theres tons of blood, mounds of corpses, torture devices, and cities of the dead. Honestly if this were a realistic PS4 game it would be more horror than anything; it even dials up the creep factor many times above Dark Souls (the Queen of Smiles gave me the heeby jeebys!). Graphically this game is phenominal, other than the character avatars which look weird.
Gameplaywise you will progress through an RPG style battle system like Dark Souls; killing foes, collecting salt (aka souls), leveling up, and killing more. Eventually you will get powers like a dash jump and the ability to use obelisks which unlock more places to explore, as well as various fun puzzles and interactions.
Many would compare this game solely to Dark Souls because of its battle system, focus on difficulty, and well... pretty much a lot of its crafting and such, not to mention the story that doesn't really lend itself readily to you. And in many ways they would be right. However, this game lends itself more to Metroidvania style games so much so I'd say this is Symphony of the Night with a Dark Souls battle system.
My sole complaint really is no friggin map. This game is actually pretty massive, and you WILL miss things. And due to being no map, its very easy to get lost. Its hard to tell where to go to get to the next area, and I know for a fact I probably missed a lot of nooks and crannies. A minimap or a map you could open would have been awesome.
Honestly, theres not much bad to be said about this game.
Pros
-----
* Gorgeous
* Creepy as f***
* Huge
* Fun gameplay
* A GOOD METROIDVANIA FOR ONCE!!!
* The leveling up system I actually like more than Dark Souls, I like the sphere system. Made me have to think about my levels more.
* The temples/covens/whatever you call them change a lot of different gameplay areas, which is a nice change because Dark Souls covens don't do much if you don't play MP
Cons
-----
* Needs more minimap
* Music gets old, theres only a few sound tracks
* Avatar models are ugly
Overall I would honestly give this a 9/10. A must have if you love Dark Souls/Bloodborne or Metroidvanias, or if you like deep RPG's you can lose yourself in.

Disclaimer:  I've never actually played Dark Souls, so this is all new to me.  But I've seen videos of it.
With that in mind:
First of all, it's Dark Souls.  In 2D.  Just in case you didn't already know that.
Now the big question is, "will you die".  Yes.  A lot.  It has the difficulty.
The next question would be, does it feel right, and is there the right rhythm and fluidity there?
Yes.  Both are done right.
And then the art style:  The art is going to be different moving from 3D to 2D, of course.
In this case, the colors are very washed out, intentionally I'm sure... but the detail is pretty substantial, particularly on characters, and the animation is filthy fluid/smooth thanks to the 2D skeletal animations.
The heads of your character and NPC's are not right at all.  Which is quite a down-side.
But it kind of works, in portraying this as *slightly* less dreadfully serious than Dark Souls.
The music is splendid!  What music I've heard from it, while obviously not as varied, seems much better than Dark Souls.  A lot of rock.  I'm a sucker for rock.
The bosses work in a similar way to Dark Souls, though limited to 2D.  They are tough but beatable.
I recommend this game if:
A)  you finished all of the Dark Souls games and want to try something else or
B)  you are intimidated by Dark Souls, and feel a 2D version MIGHT be a way to SLIGHTLY soften the process of acclimating yourself to the actual Dark Souls games(that's me). or...
C)  You like "metroidvania" style games.  This game actually works really well as one of those.
For me, it was that second one... starting out a little tamer... but that's not really how it works.
This game may have less dimensions than Dark Souls.  But I don't get the impression it's easier.
And it is definitely.  not.  easy.
Oh and I did not get this game for free.  It wasn't even on sale.  I spent months wanting it, had to have it, then finally paid full price, and no regrets.
Got Dark Souls on sale, haven't touched it yet.  Go figure.
And yes, I'm doing a video series on the game, just look up "the humble hunter" on youtube.

As advertised, this is a 2D shooter / scroller / run around the map a roller with plenty of gun customization.
The music is pretty good and the pixel art graphics and animations done by Paul Robertson, among the best in that field, are absolute eye-candy to look at. If you've ever played or seen
on consoles, you've seen some of this guy's work already. The basic gameplay works fine enough with you jumpin', runnin', knifin' and shootin' (not diagonally though) through an assortment of levels with a bunch of goodies hidden about. When you get into the groove and master the controls it can definitely trigger some nostalgia from cartridge/arcade cabinet days of yesteryear.
To deck out those guns and upgrade your gear, you're going to have to do quite a bit of grinding for ingredients (random drop or otherwise). Expect to revisit a bunch of areas for this purpose and have to deal with monotonous mission objectives, time-limits and silly boss fights where you have to worry about tracking them down across the whole map to fight them some more until they die if you take too long. All while the timer ticks down in the background. No pressure to find your way to one of those boss arenas scattered about the maze-like maps while the boss periodically shuffles around (leading to some particularly cruel instances where you can finally make it to a boss-zone where it's at and it just walks away after three seconds) or anything.
Even with this game's short-comings, there IS fun to be had. As such, there is definitely an audience or two to reccomend this to. Just be prepared to have a bit more Monster Hunter in your Metal Slug sandwich than you perhaps initially bargained for. Replace the Mission Complete jingle with the one from Metal Slug via files for maximum irony while you're at it, too.

It seems like this game had a ton of glitches before but I haven't come across any besides one problem I had with the resolution the first time I played it.
It's not perfect, but it is fun. Maybe not fun for a hundred hours, but it is fun. Get in on sale.

Overall, a very well done game, but Sanctum II is preferable.

Well, I have a feeling the verdict on this game will be quite in line with popular opinion, but
I have a couple complaints however that do affect the core nature of this game, that really shouldn't have.
First off, the class system is absolutely unbalanced for what a team requires for RAIDs. The War Cry abilities just don't give equal, varied buffs for the entire crew. Assault's regenerative health and lower ammo consumption is probably the only valuable team asset in most, if not all, situations. And that's honestly about it. Recon's (amateur) auto aim, Demo's damage resistance, and Insurgent's speed bonus are almost always outweighed in this regard.
The "profeciency" system honestly seems more like they tried making a ton of miniature buffs and shuffled them around for each class. It's not like PAYDAY 2 where you can choose any and all skills from the beginning, all being unique and highly valuable to a build. As for RAID, the classes try to be unique by getting some buffs earlier than others. Some get interaction damage resistance faster than others, despite both having them somewhere down the line. With the long grinding system for leveling, this becomes just absurd for what a player chooses as a class.
The leveling system for this game has become infamous for its grinding. Sure, you can reach levels quite frequently from 1 up until about level 20, then expect to have to play
10 missions before measly hitting the next. And it only exponentially increases from there. The mere problem here is just the innate repitition that is REQUIRED to progress. As well as this, the rewards for leveling (proficencies or the occasional weapon) make the venture absolutely worthless.
The main thing I would change wouldn't be the level requirements, but the XP distribution system rewarding more based on secured loot and difficulty (One thing that had to be changed in PAYDAY 2)
Some of the menu UI is also a bit inconveniet for what they should be. Biggest issue is the final ready up screen before a mission, where you can't change anything (class, weapon, etc) or anything without leaving the lobby altogether. It's a simple issue that will no doubt be fixed soon.
As for characters and level design, I personally found RAID interesting in this regard. The four main Raiders are quite enjoyable in their personalities, and similar to PAYDAY 1, they each have A LOT to say during each and every mission.
They aren't perfect, but I guarantee that LGL plan to expand more with them in the future.
Levels, from my view, are quite well done. The creativity in the objectives definitely shows, across the short RAIDs, and much longer, Operations. "Take down a truck convoy", "blow up an airship", "shoot down a bomber assault", "raid a Nazi treasury", etc. It never felt like a simple "Go here, defend this, escort that, escape" type deal, at least for me. It's one of the main things that kept me playing despite the lackluster aspects.
Gunplay is also unique. It's not as "guns-blazing" as PAYDAY, where you need almost no cover whatsoever. The Nazis themselves are simple, yet deadly, enemies. Successful RAIDs require lots of cover, patience, and prowess with your weapon, and more importantly, your team. This makes any difficulty over Normal quite a challenge, which is a nice breath of fresh air. However, it's easy to see how the sub-par mechanics (above) can make this more frustrating for players than it really should.
As for graphical issues and the sort, I have yet to experience anything particularly major. Yeah, the Diesel engine is pretty mucky at this point, but I think most of the landscapes were well handled by LGL, even if looking a little dated.
Overall, I don't want to hate this game. Yeah, it is on an old engine, with sub-par game mechanics of an older, more proficient 4-player action co-op shooter. I know that. However, RAID's concepts were distinct enough that I remained interested enough to purchase it. And I still am playing it frequently.
Lion Game Lion, in the time they've taken to fix the lauch bugs and game-breaking aspects, I genuinally believe the game will improve.  It IS, in its current form, quite playable, but will reasonably get stale by its disadvantages.
(TLDR) The game has a lot of good potential. However, the underlying flaws in the leveling, proficiecies, and class systems just bring the rest of the good gameplay components down with it in the final execution. The going price is just demanding too much for what is just too little of a so-called "complete" title. If you have interest in it, I'd give it some time for further updates. Or just buy it on sale. Or just buy a different game altogether.

I might change my recommendation to an yes ONCE the game will be fixed as, right now, it's in a Beta stage. Basically, the game involves tons of issues regardings rewards and achievements. It's a game that promotes itself as a game for COOP and yet, joining someone else's game doesn't register most of the stuff you have accomplished in your own game/save.
For example:
- If an host quit the game before any player have moved back to the "base", those unfortunate players gets no rewards and get kicked back to the main menu. (In fact, you get kicked back to the main menu whenever the host quit or disconnect.)
- It's almost impossible to gain gold without being an host because the loot bar (a gold-ish bar you fill up as you get valuable hidden in raids), while being filled visually, doesn't award any actual gold when filled. (Only the host gets his gold). (Gold is the in-game currency to unlock cosmetics such as upgrading your base or unlocking clothes.)
- If you're not an host, you get no recognition to your accomplishement. Trophees in your "base" aren't updated if you complete a mission on any difficulty when in someone's else game.
There's lot of issues with the allied AIs too. They are basically mobile turrets that are simply useless when shooting is not involved. They have issues with reviving you. They aren't able to do anything objective-wise except getting on your nerves by repeating the same "do X" every 30 secs while you're scavenging for loots and tags around. (Tags are hidden item that allows you to get a better reward at the end of the mission depending on how many you find).
If you think of buying this game because you like Payday 2 and would like to try a similar game set in World War II, don't buy this "for now". Is the game fun? Yes it is... but right now, you'll mostly playing to unlock "nothing". You play with friends, join their game, play for hours... and get nothing out of it while your friend (the host) get all the rewards. It's not a game ready for "coop".
