Rage is "Baby's first Fallout."
A post-apocalyptic outing with great gunplay and interesting, if derivative, setting hampered by anemic storyline and lackluster racing/vehicle combat controls. Buy this game on sale if you are just getting into the post-apocalyptic genre. Do not buy if you are a racing games fan.
I liked this game, all things considered, but I'd be lying if I didn't say there weren't some serious and concerning flaws that one should review before buying. First of all, let's start with the good: the gunplay is supremely satisfying. The game features a respectable variety of guns and gadgets and a decent number of upgrades, giving the shooting a meaty, cathartic feel. Enemies are intelligent enough to use the terrain and environments to their advantage, and each enemy type has a variety of death animations that really add to the immersion of the game. Also, the aesthetic finds a pleasing balance between the stark oppressiveness of Fallout 3, a game which RAGE is proudly inspired by, and the much cheaper and easier to render cell-shaded aesthetic of Borderlands. Also, apart from the main story, there is a middling amount of extra content, including side-quests, a card game, board game, and racing game. This is what I liked about the game.
On to the negatives: first and foremost, story. The game features several side characters who come and go and have little bearing on the plot and give you no reason to care about them. One sidequest sent me to rescue a character I never met or heard of and I found him dead. I might have cared a bit more if him being alive had meant anything at all. The villains of the story don't surface until later in the game and don't do anything that to motivate you to hate them. Also, there is NO final boss, no one taunts you, so there's no telling if there really is a villain at all, which the game never confirm or denies. Extrememly dissapointing. SPOILERS John Goodman voices a character in the game, one of the few with whom you share some sort of rapport, who goes missing halfway through the game. I thought it would mean the dystopic government forces had captured him, which would have been a motivating factor to destory said government, but no, just turns out he had to leave to do something elsewhere for the rest of the game. Extremely dissapointing. END SPOILERS.
There are sidequests, including timed deliveries, fetch quests, escort missions, horde modes, and several other standard modes that cause you to revisit game maps, which comes off feeling a bit lazy. I must say, however, that something about the sniper-guard escort missions really scratched my itch. Maybe it was the effective buildup of the scene and the fact that the people I guarded weren't completely incompetent at defending themselves against overwhelming odds, but other than that the side missions were boring at worst and bland at best.
The game makes pretenses of being Fallout 3, for example it features what wants to be an "open world map" but is so empty and inconsequential that it might as well not been added to the game. The game plays more like a linear FPS with a hub world that dispatches you to different levels, the overmap feeling like a vehicle combat minigame you play in between missions.
Let's talk about the vehicle combat. The game wastes a lot of potential and goodwill by featuring a variety of vehicles and upgrades for them, but instead of creating terrain or enemy types that would require different vehicles for different missions, the game, in linear fashion, requires you to pick up one vehicle, move to the next section, and upgrade to the next vehicle, rendering the previous vehicle and all of its upgrades useless. Furthermore, the vehicle combat is mostly auto-aimed, leaving the player to simply drive around while all of the shooting practically does itself. The driving controls are sluggish and slowly responsive for all vehicles, making driving a chore and the races barely servicaeble. I should add that all the race tracks are just preexisting parts of the overmap lazily cordoned off into a track. Maybe they were going for authenticity, but I was not impressed.
Lastly, the enemy types are based on the different gangs and their specialties, but the game handicaps it's own enemy variety. I can see how on paper that should vary the gameplay, but it ends up forcing you to fight one or two enemy types for an entire level instead of taking advantage of the numerous different enemies throughout the game as a whole. Essentially, you fight different mutants, diesel-punk Mad Maxian raiders, and cyber-punk robots and super-soldiers. Sounds cool, but you fight them all in different corridors.
All in all, there is enough to this game to recommend this game in spite of it's flaws and near misses, on sale, to a certain crowd. I would suggest first timers to post-apocalyptic shooters start here, then move up to Fallout, then finally graduate to the STALKER games.

Rage is a good solid shooter from id software that has fun gameplay and good aesthetic design but is let down by its mediocre story telling, non-existent characters and extremely lacklustre ending.
The actual gameplay is really solid - the guns are fun to shoot, they sound and look really good and enemies are fun to fight. They react to being shot and put up a decent fight; you have a wide array of options and tools that you can use to your assistence. When you're not fighting, there's driving in between zones but it's pretty fun as all of the vehicles you get are fast and handle relatively well. My biggest issue was the inability to look around whilst driving - there's also no manual aiming so you have to be facing any enemy vehicles before you can fire.
Visually the game is great; whilst it suffers from some of idtech 5's texture streaming issues (and also a lot of very ugly low-res textures in places) The actual aesthetic design of the game is fantastic. The animation of enemies is also good; NPCs are very vibrant as well but every single one of them has exagerated finger pointing animations and it kinda stands out. it's better than being stiff as planks like other AAA game NPCs however. The enemies look great, whilst a bit cliche - the main badguys, the Authority, look particularly fantastic and cool.
Rage's biggest issue is the story, or lack of it - you emerge from your Ark and then you basically just go forward and follow instructions for no particular reason. It feels really off; you don't feel motivated at all and the Authority has no presence in the game until about half-way through and even then you don't actually see them doing anything particularly bad. They make up for it by looking pretty sweet (as I already said) but plotwise, they don't have an impact. There's also no characterisation to speak of - you talk to NPCs, they give you jobs and it has that familiar problem where you do some missions for someone, they send you away and then they effectively disapear from the plot. It's not unexpected of an id game (it's something they improved on with DOOM, which despite essentially having 3 characters they were cool) but it is a let down to have a really good gameplay system but no plot to back it up.
Essentially, Rage is a mismash of classic id and newer gameplay mechanics. There's a lot of nods to previous id games and the game is a lot of fun over all (and a decent length to boot) Just don't go in expecting a good plot or a satisfying resolution to the story (or even a decent ending fight)

The epitome of tactical first person shooter video games, and unfortunately the last of its kind. The gameplay of Rainbow Six 3 focuses heavily on the careful formulation and execution of player-made tactical plans in hypothetical scenarios, having players designate specific waypoints and commands to squads of soldiers in the game world (of which they also play the soldiers themselves after planning) in order to complete various objectives. While this may seem tiresome and mundane for players wanting instant and intense action (planning is optional), the reward for having a tactical plan execute successfully is extremely satisfying, considering the difficulty of the scenarios and the respective time taken to fully plan for them. Throw in a completely seamless multiplayer component and the thrills of planning tactical missions together with friends become unforgettably fun.

Jedi Knight is perhaps one of the greatest Star Wars games ever created. Combining FMV cutscenes (with decent effects and acting, to boot) and adventurous first-person shooter gameplay from the late 90s, it's the rare old gem where graphics don't matter, and the atmosphere yanks you out of reality and into the world of the game. The addition of the lightsaber combat and the Force power and alignment system only adds to the immersion, and while its sequels may have improved on the saber combat, Jedi Knight's simple jousting is still remarkably engaging. Featuring a simple yet elegant plot and some of the more memorable characters to be produced by the Star Wars Expanded Universe, the game ensures that each level carries its own weight, and that nothing feels forced or stretched. Though the graphics have not aged well, a few fixes kindly provided by the community will have this baby up and running in no time.
If you're a Star Wars fan, an old-school adventure or FPS afficianado, or just looking for  a game with a solid balance between gameplay and narrative, Jedi Knight has you covered. Spend the five bucks and buckle up.

Star Wars: Fark Forces II is considered a classic to many from the gaming community.  Released in 1997, this game ushered in a new era of gaming, specifically for the first person shooter, that was predicated by games such as Quake and Wolfenstein where simply running and gunning was the only play style that counted.  Then came Dark Forces II and its ability to deliver gaming narrative, something that had not previously been seen in the shooter genre, with interactive storytelling through live action cut scenes and a storyline that could actually be influenced based upon your actions throughout the game.  While this aspect was great, the gameplay itself carrys Jedi Knight far as well.  With solid controls, impressive sounds and music that come direct from the Star Wars universe, great visuals for a game released in 1997, and an array of weapons and powers that create multiple play sytles and tactics, Star Wars Jedi Knight: Dark Forces II is a game that continues to stand the test of time.  Thanks to it, games such as Half-Life and the like (the story based shooter) were able to become a legitimized powerhouse in the gaming community and continue to rule the shooter community.  Very much worth the $4.99 Steam price tag.  May the Force be with you!

Fantasy wars is an underrated gem for those who like the genre.
This is pure turn based, strategic combat. This game is difficult, and especially in the later scenarios there is no shame in turning the difficulty down if it's too much (it can get brutal).
Good tactics are rewarded and the turn timer puts pressure on you and forces you to take chances. The progression system is actually surprisingly deep and if you try to play this iron man style - you'll find some of the less appealing abilities suddenly become far more useful (especially vision range).
Protecting your high level units while still making a gold level victory can be really intense, and if you pull it off, very satisfying.
My suggestion is - don't save scum. Play it straight up and give your brain a little exercise.

This is a fun game with some cool powers to help make gameplay even more interesting. It is fun to blink around and determine the best routes through an area to remain undetected.
A few issues stood out, namely the game is intended to be played in a "stealthy" or "full on combat" path, but the stealth focused powers all tend to be useful for combat too so it becomes more likely you will never use about half the skills in the game. Also, the "morality" aspect of the game is a bit suspect and a joke.
Regardless, I enjoyed it. It is neat how the levels all react to previous levels (if you clear a level without killing people, later levels will have less guards and vice versa). Combat can feel infuriating but fair and it's always fun to experiment with kills.
I enjoyed the art and world as well. It kind of reminded me of Bioshock, with a somewhat re-imagined Industrial Age. You'll get a bit sick of hearing "what do you do with a drunken sailor/whaler..." though.
It is like a less-serious-more-forgiving Hitman with supernatural powers and more linear levels.

I can recommend this game, but just barely. If you have time to play either Sanctum or Sanctum 2, please opt for the second in the series. The real issue with the original Sanctum, in my view, is just that there are just too many variables.  Sanctum is the free jazz of FPS tower defense, for my music fans out there. In the second game, your weapon stays the same, you can drop around 15 towers per map, and each tower can be upgraded 3 times. In Sanctum, you can upgrade your weapon up to 5 times, you can upgrade towers up to 5 times, and you can drop as many towers as you can afford. Secondly, the waves you fight each time you play a map are random. This led both me and my partner to fail maps repeatedly without really getting a feel for what our issues were. We completed all main game and DLC maps on normal, but had an extremely difficult time with a few on hard. An important aspect of any game is the sense of feedback the player is given. I feel that almost all of the changes made in the second game were positive. However, FPS tower defense is a unique and awesome genre, and the importance placed both on towers and the player's ability to place shots makes this series more engaging than typical tower defense.

This game is downright amazing. I didn't think much of it at first (like most indie games with little-to-no promotion), but the more I played it the more I fell in love with it. In my opinion, here's what makes it so great:
- It has the very uncommon trait of causing you to feel for the character(s). When they're sad, you're sad. When they're happy, you're happy. This helps so much in creating a bond between you and the main character.
- It has some of the coolest puzzle solving aspects (like making you solve puzzles with hints that it practically throws onto your desktop wallpaper or documents folder), while still maintaining a simplistic style of gameplay.
- The fact that the 4th wall is completely demolished is almost as amazing as both the way they put YOU in the game, and that it makes perfect sense how you're involved.
- The story seems pretty generic and cliche at first, but then slowly evolves into something much more amazing. Then, it somehow tops that as well.
- Practically half of what makes this game amazing, is it's wonderful retro/indie soundtrack. Every piece of this original soundtrack perfectly fits the environment or situation that you are in, and makes it memorable enough that I can easily remember the area I was in JUST from hearing the music alone.
- The little details that it adds each time you play it, make this game so amazing.
This game broke the 4th wall, broke my heart, and best of all broke my expectations. Without a single doubt in my mind, I give this a 10/10.

The story is gripping, the characters are vibrant and memorable, the puzzles extremely satisfying, if not a little convoluted at times.
I'd compare this to a game like Undertale, but I really don't think they are on the same plane. The music is beautiful, and the end is heart wrenching, no matter what you do. The innovation behind the computer manipulation is spectacular too. (Hey, that rhymes!)
TL;DR - It's a fun little indie game that's like Undertale, but better (IMO)

More than any other game I've played in recent memory RAGE feels like a relic of its time. Would you say that's a bad thing? Perhaps, but as I'll go into over the course of this review it becomes evident the game embodies so many of the video game fads from the turn of the decade when console FPS' were riding all-time high, with the notable exception of being wrapped in some of the finest threads technology can manufacture at the time.
Alright, gather around the fire for story time. Game makes use of a real life asteroid 99942 Apophis which it then exaggerates and employs as the catalyst for the game's premise - 99942 Apophis will hit Earth and humanity has to do something about it. Solution? Cryogenic Arks where humanity can escape to be awakened at a later date and restore civilization on whatever remains of the planet. 106 years after the asteroid hits Earth in 2029 our protagonist awakens and sees people in cryo units surrounding his own have been less fortunate. Having no idea what's happening he stumbles outside and almost gets accosted by a raving bandit before he gets rescued by Dan Hagar. He offers the confused sleeper ride back to the settlement and briefs him on the state of things.
Interesting thing is that, aside from the explanation where oppressive stratocracy/military dictatorship of some kind called the Authority and freedom-loving Resistance that fights it come from, life-that-was never really has a large role to play and seeing as our protagonist is mute he never really reminisces about his past life, either. Story of RAGE is firmly rooted in the post-apocalypse it inhabits with all the raving bandit clans, mutants hiding in the sewers and escaped experiments. Plot itself is disappointing simple and disjointed with developments you'll see from a mile away, but I won't pretend that's the main appeal of the game... and frankly characters don't fare much better. If you held me at gunpoint maybe I could remember someone from the game other than Hagar. That could be because he's voiced by John Goodman.
While I'm on the subject of good things I will say the game has rather insane production values all-around. Fact it still holds up so well six years later says more than I could probably put into these scribbles. That is, if megatextures feel like loading and you're not staring at a blurry mess. But design of pretty much everything, lighting and textures, as well as outstanding gritty and uncomfortable aesthetic really drew me in. Sound design is probably equally as good with phenomenal weapon effects that deliver just the appropriate amount of BOOM you want in your boomsticks. Soundtrack less so, but that might be because it pretty much employs atmospheric tribal and bombastic action tracks which is good for informing the player what's going on, but not really for being memorable and standout.
I also wish the ending was, you know, a proper ending instead of just setting up for a sequel that would never come. You could also excuse the following by saying “it was 2011, give id Software a break”, but ending your game with a gauntlet of enemies? No.
With story out of the way we can move onward to the actual divisive part – gameplay itself.
With that in mind I realize that may come off as some kind of sensationalist opinion when it really isn't supposed to be. RAGE is a good game, great even if it resonates with you on that specific level, but I had this constant feeling something was off as I played it. I'm specifically talking about to-kill ratio for enemies which only gets worse as the game goes on. I'll bounce back to that later on.
Structurally we have on our hands a tight mission-driven FPS that's interwoven with an open world section between missions. Now, keep in mind when I say “open world” I'm not really talking about modern idea of open world that has proliferated everywhere in video games – RAGE's take is more like couple of corridors and larger openings you drive through with your vehicle on your way to the mission entry point. That doesn't mean it's bad, though. In fact it was rather refreshing to go back to simpler days because I had little to no problem imagining how bloated this very aspect of the game would be had it been released today. There is still stuff to do here like pulling off jumps that reward you with materials for crafting, destroying enemies as part of repeatable missions, finding rare material, etc.
Wait a second, did you say crafting? Yessir. You see, RAGE is a bit of a kitchen sink in that it has a lot of everything, but none of it is really as fleshed out as I'd like it to be. Compared to modern titles that pretend to be more than just FPS' and water themselves down in the process, RAGE is perfectly aware of what it is. It just likes to two-time the missus with all these 20-something hotties like RPG inventory, weapon upgrades and quickslot items, varying the gameplay with vehicle races that have their own separate upgrades which carry over to Wasteland open world, etc. I may have mentioned this in one of my earlier review, but RAGE is one of those fully realized games we don't really see that much anymore when everything is so hyper focused and focus audience tested. Like I said earlier a lot of those additions are simple, but you'll also remember I mentioned this game knows what it is and that's shooting dudes with a variety of weapons. Which brings me full circle to my earlier point.
To-kill ratio. RAGE is a game where you MUST learn how to aim and make headshots. Which might seem kinda counteractive when you're dealing with enemies like agile mutants that close in on you in a second and actually do some genuinely impressive maneuvers like feigning dodges and bouncing all over the place. Hell, all enemies have a sort of expanded health system in a sense that you can wound them and they'll start crawling away, possibly even opening fire on you when you approach. As the game goes on you'll come across more advanced enemies like armored Authority guards that require you to get better ammunition and be aware what works best on which enemy because unless you get that right and unless you're aiming for headshot/weak spots it's no rarity to empty a clip into an enemy and see him walk it off. This is probably my sole notable annoyance with the game in its entirety, doubly so when this is the post-apocalypse and there's assumed to be some ammo scarcity yet you'll be swimming in it as long as you scrounge whenever you can.
And, of course, loot your enemies for money and ammo because this is that kind of game.
I touched on it already, but I really liked how there are proper settlements in the game and noticeable effort went into them. Like, we're talking actual quest givers and mini-games abound to pass the time. There's an entire collectible card game in, well, game where you collect cards in the world to play the game with. Not to mention the racing aspect of RAGE which offers its own staple of races/FFA if you want something more to do with your multiple vehicles, that's right – multiple for you acquire them over the course of the playthrough, in case just wasting some mutants in the Wasteland is not enough.
Maybe I should have dedicated more than a single paragraph to all of that, but that's exactly how it all comes across to me. Despite the insane production values that must have went into it when you look at the quality of assets it's still just an addition on top of the core shooter mechanics.
So how to end this? I'd recommend RAGE provided you can tolerate the brown & bloom that seems to have come to represent that era of FPS, but that goes almost goes with the territory. If you're into Mad Max and general post-apocalypse without frills you can have yourself a great time. I'd prepare myself for some repetition and missions that take you for a ride, literally or not.

OK... even though it's one of the more difficult war-strategy games i've played, i'm still going to recommend it because it really does do everything right, it's just frustrating sometimes when a group of orc riders come out of the fog-of-war, pinpoint your captain and end the game in one turn...... *sigh*.....
Pros:
-Dialog boxes have (cool role-played) speech.
-Tutorial doesn't just tell you to do a bunch of stuff while you fumble with the controls, it shows you how to do it, explains it, then lets you have a turn doing it yourself.
-lots of cutscenes.
-control and watch from far way with one-man icons or zoom in to see the whole troop and detailed (but simple) fight scenes with each battle.
-Magic is powerful but limited.
-Gives an "estimated outcome" of each battle before you commit to them so you know what to expect.  Similar to Advance Wars in this and many other respects.
Cons:
-It's difficult, even on easy mode expect to die and restart at least once per level either from a surprise attack or from being outnumbered and/or unlucky.
-The healing system is frustrating, yet still tactical.  Heal your wounded for free but it takes a full turn, and if you're close to any enemy units you won't heal as much.  Units dont heal when in a friendly town.
-Friendly cities do not generate gold.  In fact, i have yet to find a way to continuously generate gold except "find it" in newly taken towns.  This often mean that the units you start a level with are all you get, though you can build up and buy new units with the limited "found" money.  This makes the game very offensive-based by nature as there is no point to waiting around to build-up resources that don't exist.  This isn't really a bad thing, but i personally am not used to it.  Experementing with a powerful unit basically ends with "Ok, now i know not to do THAT.... restart...." because you cant rebuild resource and get another one.
-AND A BIG ONE- When your captain dies, level's over, regardless of how powerful/large your army is.  You're done.  Restart.  This wouldn't be that big of a problem normally, but 90% of the time your captain is your most powerful unit and if you leave him back to protect him there's a good chance you'll lose from lack of power.  But if you bring him the AI makes him the #1 target.  Frustrating.
All in all:
A REALLY good fantasy, turn-based strategy game.  Frustrating, but rewarding and still good.

At first glance, Mercenary Kings looks like a classic side scrolling shoot-em-up, a la Metal Slug. This is mostly due to Paul Robertson's (of Scott Pilgrim fame) beautiful pixel art. Though if this is what you're expecting, you may be disappointed. Instead, Mercenary King's hectic action is much more akin to classic Mega Man, requiring precise shooting and platforming. This is augmented with fully customizable weapons, allowing you to build custom killing machines. For example, you can attach a sniper rifle barrel and a submachine gun magazine to a magnum pistol and arm it with enemy-seeking missiles.
What starts out as an arcade-style excuse plot rapidly becomes a very compelling story. Including mindless clones, body horror, and a dog in power armor. The game is full of humor without relying too much on it's subtle 80's film and arcade references, and the characters are compelling enough to make you actually worry when they're imperiled.
The game can be played solo, but supports up to four player local and online co-op. I set the game up and got a few friends over to blast through the first 20 or so missions, and it's an absolute joy to strategize, team up against bosses, and explore the large and secret-laden maps.
Using a Monster Hunter style drop system for the materials to craft your knives, gun parts, and biomods, the game rewards replaying missions. If you get bored of seeing the same enemies and maps multiple times, this may not be a game for you. In classic arcade style, almost every enemy will have 'pallette swaps' that introduce new elemental attacks and strategies.
I've put a little over 50 hours into the game already, and I've been having a blast optimising my weapon builds, exploring and memorizing levels, and blowing away CLAW forces.
One of your guns is a cat with it's own tiny shotgun.

I have sort of conflicted feelings about Tales of Maj'Eyal. In short, if you judge it purely as a roguelike, I don't thing it don't hold up too well. Part of the reason I may think that may be my preference for NetHack influenced roguelikes, and my lack of familiarity or appreciation for Angband influenced or Ancient Domains of Mystery influenced rogelikes, but I am not sure how much Tales of Maj'Eyal's design is based on those games.
On the other hand, judged as a RPG Tales of Maj'Eyal does a lot of things right. It has a rather interesting tactical battle system, lots of different character creation options, many ways to tweak and customize your skills, any many items to find that offer a lot of tactical death. It's story, while perhaps presented in a way that relies too much on finding and reading lore text, is at least interesting and presents a few dark twists on the standard high fantasy setting.
No mater how you judge it, the interface is great, mostly easy to use but able to do a lot, the battles are fast-pasted and fun, and it can be very addicting. The graphics are simple but more then functional enough for what they are, and there are enough interesting special effects and visual flare to make up for the more static sprites. The music is generic but memorable and sometimes can actually be pretty fantastic, even if it is more or less all part of free game music packs.
I think that is all that really needs o be said, but here is some more detail about how I think about it as a roguelike:
The big problem with Tales of Maj'Eyal's design as a roguelike is simply that the game is too long, story heavy, and not random enough. There is variation in the loot you get and the monsters you face, but the over all world is basically set. Same world map, same town, same quests. The layout of a lot of the random zones are different but the basic themes of the zones are set, and each zone has a set rank for items, a set number of floors, a set list of enemies and possible bosses. Due to how the game is balanced and how enemies never respawn except in a few cases, it's basically required to repeat every zone and sidequest each run or you end up drastically underleveled very quickly, and due to each zone having fixed level requirements you can't even vary the order that much.
Although you actually have multiple lives before dieing in the default mode, permadeath still is a problem and when it happens you have to start over from he start and go through the same old stuff you already saw again. There is a mode where you can simply have infinite lives, but I kind of wish there was some kind of middle ground, perhaps a way to start over with a new character but with a number of story events that carry over and alter the world. There is a unlock system that adds new races, classes, skill trees, and other things, and that helps, but it still only adds so much and may of the unlocks are obscure or tedious.
I also have a problem with a lot of the streamlining or elimination of a lot of roguelike staples potions and scrolls are gone, and instead characters can equip a number of infusions or runes that can be used over and over again but have a cooldown timer between uses (actually every skill and magic spell in Tales of Maj'Eyal uses cooldown timers, I am not really a fan of them but it works). Wands and other tools work in a similar way as well. This eliminates stockpiling of consumable items, but also eleminates the sort of careful rationing of your resources you need to worry about in other roguelikes.
It's only logical because of this that the whole item identification game is gone and no items have overall negative effects, eliminating the kind of risk vs reward of using items in a panic. Many people may not like needing to worry about identifying stuff but the feature exists in roguelikes for a reason, the same reason randomized levels exist, to make sure you can't just win with rote memorization, and so every action you take has to be done very carefuly. Roguelikes since the original Rogue have always been about exploration and experimentation and the whole idea with unknown items was a big factor in that.
But again, despite all of these things I don't like about it as a roguelike, I still think it's a really good RPG. Maybe there isn't really that much of a difference, most roguelikes are basically RPGs after all, I just thought I would share my feelings on the subject.

Sniper Ghost Warrior 2 does the sniping aspect very well. There aren’t too many FPS games out there that focus on sniping, or at least, there aren’t any out there that have this much depth to sniping. The developers have done a superb job at creating a realistic sniping experience. Various measurements need to be taken before lining up the perfect shot and different locations mean different adjustments. Distance, wind, and even the curve of the bullet need to be taken into consideration. This makes sniping enemies very enjoyable and varied, depending on conditions.
Before starting to play Sniper Ghost Warrior 2, my expectations were very high. I was expecting it to at least match the original game in terms of gameplay features. Unfortunately it failed to do this, and ultimately failed to meet the standards of the Cry Engine 3 (one of the most powerful engines currently available).
Similar to the way I felt before and after I started playing the game, I’ll start with the good things and move on to the bad things and finish with the best part.
The developer, City Interactive seemed to have focused perhaps too much on the sniping aspects of the game, because that’s about all that’s good about it :/ I’ve noticed a lack of gameplay features that were present in the previous game such as, grapple hooking your way to high places, picking up enemy firearms, using throwing knives to take out enemies. The gameplay revolves completely around using your sniper rifle to well……..snipe, and using your P220 pistol if things get up close and personal. The P220 features in all three of the chapters as a sidearm, but the primary sniper rifle changes depending on what chapter you’re playing. Apart from finding the occasional enemy Dragunov rifle, you have no other weapons to find or interact with. This seriously upset me.
Level design is another issue with Sniper Ghost Warrior 2. The levels are detailed, but I feel this is just a way of disguising how painstakingly linear they are. Each chapter has you following a set path with a few open vistas to shoot enemies from a far. The vistas do offer fairly detailed locations to find and shoot enemies, but ultimately they just serve as complex shooting galleries and you never actually get to explore them. The levels are also too small. I find myself disappointed whenever I round a corner, only to realise that I’m in an even smaller house than the last one I was in. I was really hoping for a more open ended level design, but City Interactive has decided to play it safe and keep things way too simple.
Lastly, I’ll talk about the multiplayer. This is the most surprising part about Sniper Ghost Warrior 2. It’s actually a decent addition to the game. I was highly expecting an equally lack luster experience online as I did with my campaign experience, but it turned out better than expected. Sniping is really the only feature in multiplayer, but it’s easier to enjoy due to the lack of a forced story or other cheesy scripted events. The multiplayer levels are really well designed, plenty of places to hide, plenty of choices for rifles to use, and plenty of intensity that should have been more common in the single player. Looking around the maps for enemies is a long and tiring process, but once you find one and line up the perfect shot, it’s all worth it. Hearing the bullet whizz past your head as another sniper takes shots at you, forcing you to relocate before it’s too late, that’s an awesome feeling too. It’s a nice break from the normal run and gun shooters out there, where the SMG class is king. In this case, less is more.
All in All

I really don't know if i should recommend this game... It's a lotta fun, but some of the game mechanics are just so frustrating.
The negatives:
Not being able to fast travel to every checkpoint without placing a certain item there, it just makes backtracking annoying. When you wanna go back to an area because you just gained wall jumps or whatever, you sometimes can't. That's stupid. You'll have to teleport to a different checkpoint, walk to where you gotta go, and yada yada, that's 20 minutes you're never getting back. Also, as a bonus, you can get knocked off of edges by enemies or just get killed by them, making the walk even longer.
Also, some of the bosses, they just suck. A few are so easy you can't tell if you've stumbled into an earlier area since you just 3 shot it,
some bosses are so hard because of stupid attacks that one shot you or throw you off some dumb edge. I think it's safe to say i hated 80% of the bosses.
The positives:
Movement is fun, dashing and wall jumping makes it less tedious, if only a little, to backtrack to earlier areas. The regular monsters are a lot of fun to fight, with satisfying effects when you kill them.
The platforming is solid, for the most part, with clever intigration of the abilities you gain throughout the game.
Every weapon i've used has some fun combo's to learn and use in bosses. Not fighting game level complex combo's,
but more like a cross between fighting game and action game combo's.
I liked strategically placing things at checkpoints. (apart from that a fast traveler is one of them)
The bosses that i did enjoy were great, it was a lot of fun to learn to dodge them and go in for some hits before having to roll away.
(Almost) all the bosses had cool designs, even though their names were rather uncreative.
(I haven't played any co-op, so i can't give my opinion on that.)
Overall, I'm just sort of in the middle on this game. I don't hate it, but i don't think it's amazing, either. I'm a fan of the soulsborne franchise, and this is an interesting spin on those games. I think you should give it a try, for sure, at least if you enjoy the soulsborne franchise.

Imagine Contra, but this time, it was made by William Hanna, and Joseph Barbera, and the difficulty is dialled to 11.
In honour of keeping in theme of the game itself, I'll keep this review as G-rated as possible.
You take the role of Cuphead, an anthropomorphic teacup, who unwittingly made a deal with the Devil to sell his soul. But, he doesn't want to. So, to compensate, he must bring the souls of the characters that are still in debt to the Devil. Now, that sounds about okay, right? It sounds easy enough to do. Pretty straightforward. Very easy to understand. Just a few souls, how hard could it be?
I still haven't finished the story... I'll let you know if I do. Although, I'm not sure if I'll be alive by then. You ask me why? Well, keep reading.
It plays a lot like Contra. Since I play with the controller (and I recommend you play with a controller), it's fairly easy to grasp the controls. Directional buttons to move, X to shoot, A to jump, and so on, and so forth.
And the enemies come not in waves, they just come. They keep coming. And you shoot them. You jump over them. And you run through the level, and you reach the end. Some levels have you fight a boss. These bosses will either have some support with their minions, or they will go solo, and try their best to squash you.
But, hey... I'm sure you'll do just fine! It's easy! Just keep shootin', an' stirrin'! Yeah... you'll do just fine...
...
Actually, from the time I played the game, I've only done a few levels... I beat the first level I approached after 6 tries... then the next after about more than 6 times... then another level that I already had done with my friend a long time ago with his copy of
after 2 tries... and then I played another level that I kept dying in... ultimately, that was where I lost my cool, and I... well, I smashed my potato laptop's screen down. And then I lifted it back up to see if the screen wasn't damaged... and then I smashed it down again.
If you still find trouble in understanding what I'm trying to say here... then basically I raged. After the longest time ever... I actually raged. I haven't raged this hard in like a year.
Beware... you
suffer. Greatly. Both, physically, and mentally. This game tests both.
You thought Dark Souls was hard?
I mean, wow. It's so nostalgic. It's
the cartoons I used to watch. Tom & Jerry, Looney Toons... the moment I saw the screenshots of the game, it instantly reminded me of this episode I watched when I was a kid.

It's the same style of artwork! I heard about the difficulties faced by the artists working on this game. We really have to commend them for making it possible. It was grueling work, but it paid off in the end, and it's so beautiful and nostalgic.
And the music was the same. The jazz standard here is phenomenal! From the main menu, to the gameplay, it's just pure jazzy perfection.

I'm sure when Cuphead 6 releases, I'll finish this game! I'll be so proud when I do.
Buy it, guys. Just buy it. And here's hoping that a sequel happens. Or more games with this type of artwork happens. Pixel-art should step aside.

Plug & Play aims for the greater. You mindlessly trek through white space, waiting for the revelation, hoping for the sublime. You cut to scenes of innuendo: playing with a electric finger♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ crapping out the pins of a plug, etc... Beneath all the weird though, there ain't much meat (atleast projected into the game). It's an amalgam of ideas but doesn't have the words to commiunicate them. Frankly, it's intentionally eccentric, and a lot of times it blankets moments in pretension rather than elaboration. It asks the question, but it doesn't answer.
I'm giving this a postive review because it's makes an attempt. Navigating and expanding on the idea of human connection, especially in a video game, isn't easy. Developers jump through flaming hoops, burning themselves to find what we can and can't do in video games. I applaud that, and frankly, we need that. It's artistically curious, and that matters in itself. Either way, you're given something that's unfamiliar, and if you take a chance, you might find a nugget of something good.

The pacing of the game is hurt severely by a slow progression, grind for materials and lack of variety in combat - sure, there's some items you can use but they take up a slot in the inventory and its awkward to find a right moment to use them. It honestly feels like a chore - in Metal Slug games you had a few neat tools to fight the enemies (guns, grenades, tanks), big interesting levels with tons of unique hazards, plus the pacing of progression was fast and exciting.
MK managed to copy the face of Metal Slug to some degree, but not the core formula that made that series fun to play.

Fantasy Wars is a game with very good tactical turn-based battles. Nothing more nothing less.
The basic idea is this. You command a few heroes and other military units. You fight a lot of enemies and achieve some goal such as conquering a city. Then you move on to a new mission and do the same kind of thing. This is a lot of fun. Why? Because the tactical battles themselves are really good. For example thee are terrain bonuses that differ between military units and make perfect sense, e.g. elven archers may gain defence if hiding in the forest while knights will have a reduced charge attack score. Add to this a large number of different kinds of units to command, many of which are upgradable, several different heroes with unique skills and different skills to choose from for each type of unit when it levels up. Together it adds up to a challenging and fun to play turn based strategy game.
The story is the weakest element of the game. I cannot even remember what it was about and i just finished the game. But it doesn't really matter. This is not a game you play for the story anyway.
The interface is well designed and easy to understand and to use. There are three different campaigns, one of which is unlocked after you have beaten the other two (in either order). You can choose one of three difficulty level separately for each mission and there are also three different victory types depending on how quickly you finish the mission. This adds some replay value to what is already a long game.
Graphics are fairly good but nothing exceptional. Voice acting is okay, not bad but could have been better, although as with the story it doesn't make a big difference.
All in all I would highly recommend this to fans of turn-based strategy, but not really to anyone else. It offers great tactial turn-based battles if you like that. If you don't there is probably not really anything in it for you.

DISCLAIMER: the game is very much similar to an early access game. It is pretty rough around the edges, but all of the core is there. It is getting almost weekly updates improving upon the issues that are in the game.
So, with that disclamer out of the way, I can actually go somewhat into what I actually enjoy about the game.
The game is clearly taking a few notes off of payday's book, both games in fact. It takes the best aspects of both games and fits them together while also adding it's own flair to the soup. The combat is very much like it is in PD:TH, there are a lot of enemies, and they do a lot of damage but they go down after 1 or 2 headshots except for the select "Elite" unit which in this case is the flamer, and you very much know when a flamer is in the area just as you would a dozer. They aren't impossible to kill, they just require some good old fashioned teamwork to take down.
Speaking of teamwork, it is time to get into the class system. There are 4 unique classes and they can be summarised as Explody-man, Tank, Sniper, And Speedy-man. All of the classes have slight statistical variations and access to different weapons from one another, though most of the pool is shared. The Biggest difference in classes is the warcries, Which all give bonuses to you and your team for a short period of time after you kill enough people. The demo gives you a grenade back and allows all grenades thrown to be cluster bombs, assault gives you health and reduces his ammo consumption, the fast one gives wallhacks and increases his speed and chance to dodge, and recon gets probably the worst aimbot ever to exist in a video game and sightly increases everyone's damage.
The unique mechanics it throws in over the other 2 games are the way it handles stealth and the lockpicking. Much like PD:TH you are greatly rewarded for going as far as you can in stealth and you are already geared up to go loud should the situation go south, But the major difference is that you do not have a silenced weapon to shoot people with, you have a knife or knuckle dusters. There are no pagers, just guards spotting other guards or you, Stealth as it should be had. It is quite a refreshing change from Payday 2 since it is mostly about avoiding guards more than hiding. Lockpicking has become a short minigame now. Every time I see Mercenary Kings brought up online, people get warned away from it for various reasons. Despite that, I'm here to say that it's gone down as one of my favorite games. Seriously, it's one of those where I'll play it for 2-3 hours and then have to force myself to play something else because I want to keep doing missions. It might not be for everyone, but let me share the good parts with all of you for a change.
So if you've somehow glossed over this one, Mercenary Kings is a side-scrolling shooter in the vein of Metal Slug. Unlike Metal Slug, however, you have a persistent character that you upgrade with new guns and mods and stuff over the course of a hundred or so missions. And those missions take place in huge, wide-open levels with lots of paths and secrets to find. Missions range from beating bosses to saving hostages to recovering intel to gathering materials. Materials are very important, of course, because they let you build new guns and mods and stuff.
See, there's something like 300 guns in the game, and you build each one piece by piece, using money from missions and materials from exploring and shooting dudes to unlock components. Those pieces can be mixed and matched to create monstrosities like a 32-round caustic shotgun. It's kinda like Borderlands if you could custom-build each gun. You can also build mods for yourself that give you major advantages, like speed boosts and regenerating health, or guaranteeing material drops and finding more money. There's also melee weapon crafting, cooking, and decorating your tent!
There's also a surprising amount of goofy♥♥♥♥♥story, too. About half the missions are bookended with short character scenes like this that move the plot along. You have to rescue people to expand your camp, and once in awhile something will happen to them, like I had to go save my gunsmith at the start of the rank 4 missions. The design for the characters is by the same guy who did the Scott Pilgrim beat-em-up that sadly never made it to PC, and everything is beautifully animated.
When the subject comes up, I've seen three big complaints about the game. The first is the bosses, and they're definitely one of the weak points. You have to actually find them in the level (unless you use the mod that shows their location on the map), usually in one of four locations, and they move around. Worse than that, they can run away while you're fighting them, meaning you have to follow them, though they're marked on your map after you find them once. They're not like Metal Slug bosses, either... they tend to be invincible until they reveal their weak point, so you have to learn their attacks and patterns. Once you do, though, they're not that hard. Capture missions ♥♥♥♥ing suck, though... you have to weaken the boss to a certain point and then hit them with a special grenade you can only carry like two of. I won't fault anyone who got stuck on a Capture mission and quit because of it.
The second complaint is that you have to grind for materials, and I really don't get that one at all. The first few mods that open up let you control material drops; one guarantees a drop from every enemy but lowers the chance of getting rarer ones, and another makes rare drops more likely but reduces the cash you get from missions. There are no real rare drops, either. Each enemy has up to three items they drop, but they tend to be spread around so that almost every material is a common drop from something. The only hard to get ones are boss drops, but you can find those hidden on most levels in secret rooms, and they're always in the same boxes so you can get as many as you want during missions there.
The last is that it's repetitive, and really that's going to be entirely up to the player. There are ten ranks of missions, with 10-12 missions per rank. Missions tend to take place on the same 2-4 maps per rank, so if you get tired of doing different things on the same levels, then yes, it's going to be repetitive. After almost 30 hours I haven't really tired of any of the missions and still go back and replay old ones to get extra materials and try to beat the par times. It's not perfect, but I got absolutely addicted to it and I didn't even play it co-op. Honestly, it's not a Metroidvania game but it's scratching the same itch for me that the old GBA Castlevania games did. If you like item hunting and gear customization in your platform games, I think it's a blast.

The Good:
- I grew up playing NES and SNES platformers, and so I truly enjoy seeing this art style popularized again. For what Mercenary Kings offers in terms of gameplay, the art style matches up nicely and makes the game feel cohesive.
- Mercenary Kings offers a plethora of weapon customization options. The abundance of options enticed me to spend hours mixing and matching parts across different weapon categories in order to perfect a gun suited to my specific play style.
- Surprisingly, the game has a entertaining story with multiple twists. Mercenary Kings was definitely improved by this because it justified playing through the absurd amount of story missions (112 unique missions in total) in order to reach the conclusion.
The Bad:
- I loathed how Mercenary Kings portrayed their women antagonists and protagonists. The overt objectification only served to reflect that the designers are out of touch with where modern audiences are in terms of gender relations.
- The mission structures, goals, and levels in Mercenary Kings are extremely repetitive. While the goal might change between missions, you’re frequently placed in the same level to achieve this objective. Additionally, the objectives also lacked diversity - for example, often you’re collecting an object, neutralizing an enemy, or capturing a specific enemy.  Unquestionably, the central problem of Mercenary Kings is quantity over quality.
In order to acquire the necessary number of parts to construct banners, ornaments, gun parts, knife parts, and mods you’ll have to grind far too much.
Final Verdict:
Mercenary Kings looks like a Metal Slug clone (this is actually the reason I bought it without first researching the game), but it is far from that. The gameplay is much slower, and the RPG elements take center stage as opposed to a straightforward shoot ‘em up action adventure. I can’t recommend this game at full price. I purchased this game for 1.00 (humblebundle), and I had fun, but after the first ten to twenty hours it became an endeavor to simply complete the game. However, because of what I paid, I didn’t feel cheated.
6/10.

This game is an absolute abomination. I was considering writing a long review for this game, but I honestly can't be bothered. I'll cover some basic points though.
The Gameplay in this game is possibly the only positive / redeeming aspect of this game. A lot of quirky objectives in missions and the fast paced horde gunplay from PAYDAY is certainly embedded here. Mostly, these are enjoyable, and are the only thing that kept me coming back. For 50 hours. Still not sure how I have 50.
The Graphics in this game are simply AWFUL. The Diesel engine is terrible, but it's from 2001, so it's excusable. Even PAYDAY 2 has decent graphics, so it surprised me when this game, from 2017, with that sexy, shiny animated trailer had the worst graphics I've seen in recent years. But even at highest settings, the game undoubtedly looks awful.
This game runs terrible. Granted, I have an integrated graphics card (I know, I'm sorry), but I can indeed run PAYDAY 2 at 60fps, so this surprised me. Again, I know the Diesel engine is terrible, but it still makes little sense.
Of the 4 main characters, I only like one, and that's Sterling. Even so, I still find him largely unbearable to listen to. Overall, I think the quality of Sterling, Rivet, Mrs White and (even so it heavily pains me to say) Kurgan's vocie acting is very good. All other characters seem to be German. I don't know which idiot was made to do the German Voice Acting, but it's completely awful. I was convinced at one point that the Boat Driver was African. I'm serious. That's honestly what it sounds like.
The Soundtrack is alright, but very generic. It's the kind of music that sounds alright with the first few times you hear it, but gets pretty boring after a while. I can only recommend the track 'Strongpoint', which includes occasional good bits.
The Guns in this game are stupid choices, few, and mostly unrealistic. For example, the Sten and the MP40 are both held by the magazine in game. This is obviously something very little, but it annoyed me so much to see this stereotype play out. Holding a gun by a magazine is stupid. It's pretty obvious.
The Comedian John Clesse is hilarious. Why, or how he is in this game goes beyond me. His performance is, obviously, very good. For some reason, he is in only 4 cutscenes, 3 of which are about 4 seconds long. Yeah.
I found these funny at first, but they do get rather repetetive. I'm still not entirely sure why the guy looks so ludicriously unlike Hitler, but I don't think it matters. All I can say is that I'm glad these are skippable.
Conclusion:  I sort of like the game, but am still incredibly dissapointed with it. It is fun at times, but gets boring, and even on launch there was an incredible lack of content. This review is unfinished, but it's currently so late that I can't be bothered to finish it.

So... where to start?  This game, as far as I can tell, is Borderlands without the cell shading, humor, and great gameplay.   More annoyingly, though, are all the decisions that make you scratch you head.
1- They needed to hire a real interface designer.  There's a real deficit in the way the menus and skill are accessed in this game.  It's missing buttons that should say "OK" when appropriate.  From the splash page, you have to ENTER the game, just to QUIT.  There's a bunch of items like this, but hopefully you get the idea.
2- The game is ammo starved.  I assumed ID learned its lesson from DOOM 3.  It was everyone's least favorite part of DOOM 3, and they double downed here.
3- Monsters. bandits, and mutants are ammo sponges.  I can shoot someone in the leg or arm 4 or 5 times before they die.
4- I can PUNCH a mutant 3 times to kill him, or shoot him up to 5 times for the same effect.  The seeming trade off here is that punching things leaves you exposed to fire, and you die faster.
5- Automatic save points are rare and placed at nearly random.  It doesn't happen when you finish a quest or achieve an objective.  It happens when you get a loading screen, which is (to the game's credit) rare.
6- Invisible walls everywhere.  They shouldn't put the jump button in the game because railing will defeat you evertime.
7- LASTLY- Ladders are more dangerous than combatants.  I can go toe to toe with a bandit, mutant, or whatever.  I can engage in a fist fight with bullets whipping past my head.  I can survive doing a head over heels, 30 foot into the air ejection from an ATV, and I there's a mechanic in the game where if you get shot in the face, you can ressurrect yourself with some sort of nanite technology...  but if I accidently walk off a ten foot ledge with a ladder with a ten foot drop, I insta-gib in a shower of blood.
So in essence, this game should have been a triple-A title, but was seemingly abandoned to its fate.  EVEN RIGHT NOW, SO LONG AFTER ITS RELEASE, it's feels like a huge black eye to the devs and the company logos but on the front of the front of the game.  There's a lot to love here, but it's just so frustrating and confusing why so many issues are still here after so long.  For the love of god, hire a SINGLE INTERN to start fixing some of these issues.

Although I am writing this having played the sequel, Sanctum 2, I'm still going to recommend it. In fact, I'm recommending you to get both Sanctum and Sanctum 2. Get this: Sanctum and Sanctum 2, although not entirely different games, play different altogether. Read my review on Sanctum 2 for additional details.
Simply put, Sanctum puts more emphasis on maze and tower building, and has slightly less player interaction (e.g. you cannot change towers' targeting behavior) compared to Sanctum 2. I would say Sanctum is 90% tower defense and 10% hero defense, although based on many other players' calculations, and also depending on which stage you're playing, it could be classified as 75% tower defense and 25% hero defense. The hero defense number can be further increased if players themselves choose to actively participate in fights against enemies. In short, however, it is safe to say that there are more times in Sanctum when you can just leave your towers alone to do the defense than in Sanctum 2.
Gameplay aside, Sanctum is easily way ahead of its time for a game that was released in 2011. The graphics are impressive, and the developers spot-on exploited their advantage by designing an original world that is both beautiful and immersive. With its original characters and concepts, Sanctum deserves a whole lot more love than it currently does and that is doing it no justice.
Sanctum is a jewel of a game, a world record that has only been beaten by its sequel, which sadly had been born and crafted at the wrong time: Valve's own Portal 2 was released merely days later and everybody boarded the hype train for the more famous franchise. Sanctum, having barely wrestled gamers' attention from bigger titles such as Crysis 2, Dragon Age 2 and the PC release of Assassin's Creed: Brotherhood earlier that year, took a hit to its sales that persisted throughout 2011's Steam Summer Sale. Later that year, releases of games such as Dead Island, Dungeon Siege 3 and The Witcher 2: Assassins of Kings kept Sanctum from floating above the surface, while it struggled to race for sales before FPS competitors Battlefield 3 and Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 3 joined in for their share. However, it was when The Elder Scrolls 5: Skyrim was released in November that Sanctum drowned among the hype.
But is Sanctum dead? No, far from it. Like a ship filled with treasures, it had just sunk to the ocean floor, waiting for ambitious adventurers to come and retrieve it, and those who are looking for glorious gold would do well to pick it up. And good treasures should always be shared, and spent together. You can spread the word about the treasures to people you know, or pick up additional treasures to be given to them. Either way is a bargain for you as long as you are in possession of such a valuable artifact.
The paragon of Sanctum is the soundtrack. Perfectly composed to perfectly match the environment and mood, not many music composition can reach out to player's emotions as effectively as Sanctum. When you're done listening to the main menu theme on repeated loops while you sleep, play it one more time while you read the 2 or 3 paragraphs above. Leave a comment if you shed a tear or 2.

How do I even review this?
This game... Is SO amazing!
I started playing this game like any other game. Turn it on, see where I start off and go forward with whatever mission I'm given. This game isn't like that. It completely blew me away nearly right off the bat. I won't give anything away but I remember my eyes just shot open and I froze. *How did a video game know that?" Is what I asked myself. As I played, I started to feel empathy for the world and its inhabitants. When I got the original ending I felt a mixture of feelings but started again anyway to see what else I could do. When I got the *Special* ending, I cried so much! I cried for an hour after it was over, knowing that my journey with Niko was at an end. It didn't end because there wasn't more to explore, but because I decided to let things be as they were.

An interesting idea, I'll give it that. A combat-centric game that works to your own music. The bundled metalstep really works well, and I've found electro does the same. The game overall is a bundle of nice ideas, but the game lacks polish. I understand the minimalist style it aims for, but...graphical details? Backgrounds? In-game sound effects? Particles? Hello?
Again, the gameplay is unique. Each method of fighting back serves a purpose, but most enemies either shoot projectiles at you or run straight at you. Things only stop being a cakewalk around 70, at 100 I'm either dying in 2 hits or running into a pitfall. The fact that you can even accidentally veer off into a pitfall and have to end the stage is irritating, and the comments putting your low score to shame don't help either.
Earning points don't feel like they have any meaning; you're always more concerned about making it through a song entirely. If there was more to unlock with points other than actually interesting gameplay past the first 30 minutes, then I'd be pleased to use what downtime I have for colouring the board for extra points. This would've been a great place to include cosmetics or weapon upgrades, but it just lacks content. Most devs have the process backwards where they have a terrible idea ripped from a successful game and then expand on it too much, but Burst has the opposite problem.
One last thing is the requirement for .ogg files. I don't mind using them if it didn't mean having to pre-determine what songs you want to play before playing the game. This is definetly what sets Burst back over other games where you can blow through your music library in one sitting if you like.

I'm in a love/hate relationship with this game. I suppose that's the mark of an excellently crafted roguelike. Often when I die I'll want to exclaim how that was such bull puckey, that the game is unbalanced and it was totally unfair. That there wasn't any lesson I could have learned from dying that way. Yet somehow, I find I'm slowly getting an intuition about how to play the game. I play so that each time, I can get just a little bit further. That's the thing about roguelikes. They aren't about learning to play the game, and then playing it. You can't be said to know how to play the game until you've won.
For a game I've never gotten past the first third despite having played it for over 70 hours, I can't really claim that the sameyness keeps me from playing. I don't feel stuck or feel the need to consult strategy guides; the process of learning in ToME is rewarding. It'd be awesome if levels had more variety and the worldmap was randomized, but I don't think that would make it more replayable.

I waited a while before reviewing this game. I didn't want the "starting" excitement to overwhelm me.
After having played this game with several characters, I can say that every playthrough, I get more and more excited about this game. For me, this game is difficult and hardcore, I am not that experienced with rpg's but this game makes me want to be and every playthrough, I feel like I have learned new things.
For the first time, I carefully think about choices I make, what should I level up, how should I handle this enemy. For the first time, I take my time for every turn (usually with this kind of games, I rush through my turns as if it was real-time). The game makes me want to use my skills and intelligence and for me, this is a first-timer.
The funny thing is, I had this game marked as "Not Interested" originally, but came here by reading a review under another -not so good- game. That other game had much better graphics, but I don't care about graphics. On the other hand, because I had mostly been dissapointed by roguelikes with low-quality graphics (although TOME actually has relative good graphics for its genre) I had never looked at this game in detail. It was after that other review and seeing that people have actually spent a whole year in playtime on this game that I got interested.
That's sad... because this game is REALLY worth it. And it certainly is worth the price. I bought it at -30% and now I feel like they could easily charge 3x the price (and even more) and it would still be worth it. This game needs a commercial boost :-)
I am really enjoying this game, dying all the time and stuff like that. I prefer adventure-mode because I can die several times before it is game over, but I still don't want to die (like you could play through in exploration mode) so it still makes me try to play it roguelike (which is too hard for me at this time).
I also like how this game builds up unlocks: especially for me, being not that experienced, I like that in the beginning not all character types can be played and must be unlocked. It makes me build up my knowledge about the game and probably only when I am ready to learn about new types of character, they will be unlocked.
I wonder if I will stop buying other games on steam now for the next year because if I look at other people playing this game (2500 hours of playtime), it seems like I will never get bored with this game and will never need another game :-).
I think I can safely say that this game is for all kinds of RPG players: the beginners and the very experienced.
Buy it! Buy it now! :-)
Edit: I forgot to mention: it has a very very very good community. In game, you have chatrooms and when you have a question, you can ask it there and there's almost always someone who answers.

Short Version:
Like TDs? Definitely give this one a spin unless you heavily dislike FSPs.
Long Version:
Gameplay - The hybrid tower/FPS feels very good as you can single handedly wipe the some mobs yourself, let the towers do it for yourself or fine tune your defence in order to covers each's sides flaws or create true deathzones. There's a very decent number of maps with varied layouts and the possibilty to maze in your own style. Your typical towers/weapons are here with a few more original concepts in between. The difficulty feels fair, it takes good tower strategy and shooting in order to clear the more difficult maps. Multiplayer is there too and I had great fun playing with some friends, too bad they can't help you tackle the Insane difficulty ones so I could get those achievements T_T.
Story - Not much of it at first glance, there's material outside the game and some secrets to be found in some maps but overall it's not the selling point. It would eventually get greatly expanded in Sanctum 2 but I'll comment on that on it's review.
Sound - I surprinsingly love this game's tunes, I often listen to game ST's outside and people give me the looks but, listen to Sanctum's, and they praise it, they can't believe it's from a game, it's a different style. (Which I would love more of, if anyone know' more stuff like this PM me or something, I couldn't find more work by the same guy).
Graphics - The looks fit the futuristic style and everything is clean and slick. I personally tone some of it down because all the bloom and stuff makes the game so bright and vividly coloured it hurts my eyes but that's my preference.

An amazing tribute to the Souls genre and a worthy addition to that pantheon.
It understands the fundamentals that makes Dark Souls great and respects them.
It also adds it's own twists, this isn't a ripoff or a clone but an inspired production
+ Combat that blends deliberate stamina-based combat with combos and skills
+ Freeform playstyle, switch easily between weapons and styles to suit your needs
+ Nightmarish, interconnected world. Superbly done and easily comparable to any Metroid-vania
+ Implicit storytelling reveals a deep and mysterious world, look up The Drowned Tome for lore explanation
~Dodges can be a bit difficult to judge, and can result in some annoying deaths, but it isn't a major issue and you eventually get the hang of it.

Salt and Sanctuary is a true tribute to the Souls series. Everything that makes the Souls games great is there and intact in 2d form, though there are other elements that resemble games such as Castlevania more.
Therein, lies the root of the game's problems. A middling plot, a somewhat questionable art style, and some subpar design choices unfortunately mar the greatness of the game's vistas, sense of progression and variety, and absurdly tight and rewarding gameplay that'll just make you not want to put the game down until you've beaten it. Had this game been less -else, and more -souls, it would have been perfect in every sense. As it is, the pros more than outweigh the cons, and it's a must buy for fans of Dark Souls at any price range.

This game is an absolute abomination. I was considering writing a long review for this game, but I honestly can't be bothered. I'll cover some basic points though.
The Gameplay in this game is possibly the only positive / redeeming aspect of this game. A lot of quirky objectives in missions and the fast paced horde gunplay from PAYDAY is certainly embedded here. Mostly, these are enjoyable, and are the only thing that kept me coming back. For 50 hours. Still not sure how I have 50.
The Graphics in this game are simply AWFUL. The Diesel engine is terrible, but it's from 2001, so it's excusable. Even PAYDAY 2 has decent graphics, so it surprised me when this game, from 2017, with that sexy, shiny animated trailer had the worst graphics I've seen in recent years. But even at highest settings, the game undoubtedly looks awful.
This game runs terrible. Granted, I have an integrated graphics card (I know, I'm sorry), but I can indeed run PAYDAY 2 at 60fps, so this surprised me. Again, I know the Diesel engine is terrible, but it still makes little sense.
Of the 4 main characters, I only like one, and that's Sterling. Even so, I still find him largely unbearable to listen to. Overall, I think the quality of Sterling, Rivet, Mrs White and (even so it heavily pains me to say) Kurgan's vocie acting is very good. All other characters seem to be German. I don't know which idiot was made to do the German Voice Acting, but it's completely awful. I was convinced at one point that the Boat Driver was African. I'm serious. That's honestly what it sounds like.
The Soundtrack is alright, but very generic. It's the kind of music that sounds alright with the first few times you hear it, but gets pretty boring after a while. I can only recommend the track 'Strongpoint', which includes occasional good bits.
The Guns in this game are stupid choices, few, and mostly unrealistic. For example, the Sten and the MP40 are both held by the magazine in game. This is obviously something very little, but it annoyed me so much to see this stereotype play out. Holding a gun by a magazine is stupid. It's pretty obvious.
The Comedian John Clesse is hilarious. Why, or how he is in this game goes beyond me. His performance is, obviously, very good. For some reason, he is in only 4 cutscenes, 3 of which are about 4 seconds long. Yeah.
I found these funny at first, but they do get rather repetetive. I'm still not entirely sure why the guy looks so ludicriously unlike Hitler, but I don't think it matters. All I can say is that I'm glad these are skippable.
Conclusion:  I sort of like the game, but am still incredibly dissapointed with it. It is fun at times, but gets boring, and even on launch there was an incredible lack of content. This review is unfinished, but it's currently so late that I can't be bothered to finish it.

This game (right now) is fairly great in my opinion. It may have some ups and downs, have some glitchy (and funny bugs), but that doesn't mean its instantly horrible. You can compare the game to Payday 2, as some of the components from PD2 were used in RAID, as the jewelry store model was used, and then it was heavily detailed (especially on the inside). The game for me is well optimized, and I dont know why people are complaining about its bad optimization, I am able to run Medium Settings 60 frames with a GT 770, and that graphics card is garbage. Yes, I do have some if not all of the settings turned lower, but if its less laggy, than sure, use it. The only problem is the price for the game. Its 40 dollars, and thats honestly way too much for a game that looks like its still in alpha stages. If it was all done, diesel engine was removed and replaced, and everything was better, than sure, I would say 35-40 dollars is the amount for the game, considering there is a bunch of content in it. But, as of right now, it feels like it should be 15-20 dollars.
Theres another problem too. There is easy mode, its pretty "easy" obviously, allowing you to finish the mission in a cakewalk. There is then normal, its somewhat easy, and is still beatable. And then, there is hard. You click it and go into a mission, and you are instantly killed. It goes from normal mode, to omega difficult/ you are going to die in about 15 seconds difficulty. The enemies are extremely strong, and they pack a really strong punch. It definitely needs to be lowered so its still beatable. And I would say that very hard should then be nerfed to the "hard" difficulty thats out right now. It's still beatable, its just that if you step out of a bush for not even a second, you're instantly down. Wait 3 seconds and let hundreds of flamers and generals roll out, and you jump out of a bush, you are instantly killed. I don't have a problem with it, as its still beatable. But, please, nerf it. Other than those 2 problems (price tag and the hard enemies), the game is doing alright. It looks like its still in alpha state, but there is going to be amazing improvements to the game. Its only been out for 2 months now, and i don't know why its been recieving so much backlash. I won't compare the backlash to PD2's release, as one: I don't know what it looked like when it was released, and two: im not comparing the two games.
Thats all I really have, the game has (decent) optimization, difficulties that need a slight fix, and overall a fun game where you can pop nazi's heads off. Pretty fun, and people who say the EXP is too much (almost 5 millionEXP to get to level 40), you're correct. It's gonna be changed though, be patient.
