'Mercenary Kings‘ is an interesting recipe: You take a portion of 'Mega Man‘, add some elements of ‚Monster Hunter‘ and spice it up with a pinch of 'Metal Slug‘ or 'Contra‘. This may sound like a very odd combination and the reviews are quite ambivalent about the qualities of the game but especially in co-op this game is a blast.
The story itself can be told quite fast: The bad guys called „CLAW“ (they have the brilliant slogan „CLAW is law“) kidnapped a famoust scientist and conducted some evil experiments on a solitary island. To end this madness the military sends a super special unit – the KINGS. No, the story won’t win a creativity award, but it’s solid and full of humor. The crazy characters are quite likeable and several conversations are actually interesting and bring in some plot twists. But you can be honest: You won’t play this game for the story…
…you want these guns. And the knifes. And the ammo. All the good stuff. The gameplay can be compared mostly to a mixture of 'Mega Man‘ (jumping and shooting) and 'Monster Hunter‘ (crafting and grinding): First you have your own hub where you are able to buy items, upgrade your equipment and accept the missions. These jobs bring you into larger areas where you have to fullfill goals e.g. killing or capturing a boss, gathering materials or resucing some hostages. So you start running and jumping through the levels, avoiding obstacles on your way (like e.g. lava, needles and other evil stuff). Meanwhile you're shooting at everything that walks in front of your weapon while looking for hidden items and loot.
The level design is well done, the different areas and layouts allow for some nice exploration and the amount of traps and enemy types really brings some nice variety to the quite repetetive goals. Of course: at the end of several mission there's a boss waiting for you and these buddies provide some nice challenging moments. Most of the time simple button mashing ends in an early death and you really have to understand the patterns and to find a good strategy. Though when you’re finally able to defeat that annoying difficult boss (I look at you 'Metal Woof'!) and he drops the material you were looking for – that’s some pretty great feeling.
Talking about materials: On your journey you’ll stumble across many different ingedrients and materials that can be used to craft individual gun parts, knifes and bionic mods. The amount of different parts is tremendous and they can be combined to fit your playstyle, whether you’re the tanky dude with the shotgun or the spray’n run submachine-type. Crafting new guns, mixing the parts and farming for materials is the core element of the game – and it’s very entertaining.
In terms of the visuals and the sounds I have to admit that the design and the style is gorgeous (I’m a huge fan of well done pixel-graphics). The environment and the characters are detailled, the animations are perfectly fluid and the overall picture is simply great. And in addition there is an amazing soundtrack, that features some really catchy tracks.
I could go on talking about even more positive points, like the splitscreen multiplayer, the co-op mode or the omnipresent humor. But the negative points of the game can’t be hidden this way: the amount of different areas is very limited (there are over 100 missions but just like 8 different areas, so you will re-visit some rooms and places quite a lot) and after a short amount of time the missions can get quite repetitive (there are only like six different goals). Moreoever some time limits in the missions seem to be set totally random, sometimes you finish with half an hour left and sometimes with barely 3 seconds. That’s also due to the fact that some bosses 'escape‘ randomly after a short fight and then you have to search them again (probably not the brigthest gaming mechanic). Besides your characters appearance lacks some good customization aspects, aside from 12 different color schemes (approximately 75% of them look awful…) for the two characters there’s nothing more. Some unlockable characters (e.g. the 3 other members of the KINGS) and areas after finishing the main game would have been a huge plus.
________________________________________________________________________________
Yes, the reviews and opinions for the game have been quite ambivalent. I think the problem is that many bakers and players expected a ‚pimped up‘-version of 'Metal Slug‘ with all its core points and elements. And with these expectations the game may disappoint easily. I bought it in hope to get a mixture of 'Mega Man‘ and 'Monster Hunter‘ – and I’ve never regret buying it because the game entertained me instantly.
All in all I guess the game would be a solid 7 out of 10 (or maybe a 6 if you dislike good old Mega or grinding) due to all the negative points (that are clearly there), but… I love the game. Sure I would have loved to enjoy even more areas and to customize my character to look different than my partners, but hey... -  I had a machine gun that fired some caustic missiles, which bounced of walls, splitted in little pellets and exploded on impact. That was one hell of a weapon. And I’ll never forget my shark-shaped-knife that shocked enemies on contact.
These two things alone have to improve the score by at least two points. Because of… reasons! And explosions. And think of the knifes! And the dogs in mecha-dog-suits. Yeah, never forget mecha suit Doge – ‚Metal Woof‘ ready for action!

As much as I love Tribute Games' amazing pixel-art and audio, it's hard to recommend this game because of how repetitive it gets.
As per your standard "loot treadmill" loop, you will be exploring the same areas repeatedly while collecting crafting-goop that you use to craft better equipment. There's nothing inherently wrong with this formula, but I don't feel it worked for me in Mercenary Kings, because I got tired of the same 2-4 areas really quickly, and all the quests felt like filler. I also got really tired of picking-up crafting-material from everything, and didn't derive much joy from experimenting with various weapon/equipment combinations.
The first 2 hours of the game were really enjoyable for me, mostly because of the gorgeous aesthetics and good sound-design, but eventually monotony just took over and I had to stop.

I attempted to play this game based on the fun I had with another from the same developer.  The game itself is not all that bad.  It looks very dated, but I don't consider graphics an important part of a grid based strategy, as long as there is a consistent art style.  The story seems fairly generic for this style of game, but I did not progress very far to get that much depth from it.
The rules and game play are fairly straight forward, and it does offer some strategic depth, however, the game is not nearly as enjoyable or as polished as a game in this field needs to be to fully enjoy it.
The primary reason I do not recommend this game is because of the control scheme.  When selecting a unit, you use the left mouse button.  To move the unit, left mouse button.  To attack an enemy, left mouse button.  To select varying abilities, left mouse button.  Everything revolves around the left mouse button, which, in a 3-D hexagonal strategy game, often means you will be selecting or attack the wrong thing unless you've managed to position the camera perfectly for that encounter, something that takes some time if you need to complete it several times a turn.
If you are on steam for the sole purpose of playing and mastering every grid-based strategy, go for it, you will find something enjoyable here once you get past the difficult camera and controls, otherwise, skip this title.

Amazing game that really got me into the stealth genre.
Pros:
Large maps with various routes to objectives.
Multiple ways to complete a level.
Great skill/magic system (only one large problem which I will talk about in the cons).
Supports many play styles (whether it be rushing into a courtyard full of enemies and utilising various equiptment and skills to kill their opponents or sneaking past all the guards directly to the objective).
Nice artsy visuals.
Guards notice when you kill another guard near them (this is a common problem in other stealth games)
Good storyline.
Good/evil chaos system (though it could use improvements).
Cons:
Dated visuals
Guards cannot climb or jump which creates many problems for anyone looking for an intensly challenging stealth game:
Guards wont see you if you are two metres above them on a lamp post.
Easy to escape guards by climbing the side of a building and getting out of sight.
The magic power blink allows you to teleport short distances. This makes it possible to travel entire maps without being seen by guards.
If seen or locked in combat you can bink onto a ledge and run out of sight without guards following you.
Limited non-leathal takedowns.
Cannot hide in bushes, they are there for the visuals... crouching in bushes is just like crouching in plain view.
Note:
Assassins (an enemy later in the game) can travel three dimensially and follow you as they have a blink-like ability that is possessed by Daud.
You cannot always blink to escape as some enemies possess a device which does not allow the use of magic
Thankfully, the guards in dishonored two will be able to climb.
There will be more non-leathal takedowns in dishonored two.
Overall I would rate this game a solid 8.5/10 and definately worth any price below $20.

One of the most-polished MMO games I've ever played, RIFT offers everything a standard MMO does and then goes over the top to offer more, with collectible item hunts, custom player and guild housing, varied tweaks on standard character classes, and tight combat with beautifully rendered graphics. I grew up with a bad PC so it's rare for me to judge a game exclusively on its visual fidelity. I've dealt with a lot of poor framerates in my day, blurry textures, etc.
RAGE was a game billed on its "megatexture" technology. What do megatextures do? Well, they allow artists to provide more detail for less performance cost, or something like that. This was supposed to be a gorgeous game, one that pushed the limits of graphics technology in to new paradigms. Of course, that was five years ago, and I just built a system runs circles around the recommended PC hardware for RAGE.
But if that's the case, why does RAGE look so ugly? Why are textures so blurry? When this game came out, the newest, most expensive graphics cards had 2 gigabytes of memory. Mine has 6. I've dug in to console commands, custom configs, the whole nine yards, and there are places where it looks worse than games twice its age. iD Software and John Carmack, once regarded as the masters of amazing technology, and so much of this game looks grungy and compressed, even with the so-called "16K" textures "unlocked."
Lighting is beautiful. Everything looks very "expensive." Characters, at the very least, look very detailed. Taken as a complete picture, it can seem stunning, but put any individual piece under a microscope and it smears in to 1999. I also get occasional stuttering while driving around in the open world segments, and the entire time RAGE is running, my HDD is making more noise than I think I've ever heard come from a computer. It's obviously crunching megatexture data, because it's the most noticeable when I'm driving, but hearing it makes me uncomfortable. I'm actually worried that if I keep playing RAGE, it'll shorten the drive's lifespan.
Unfortunately gameplay also leaves a lot to be desired. You get a lot of really picturesque vistas, but all of it is artificial. This is a game about exploring a wasteland and scavenging for resources but you aren't really allowed to do much exploring or scavenging. The stuff you can loot is always just sitting on a table somewhere, there's no hunting it out. Dresser drawers don't open, you never dig through debris, you just pick up what's been set out for you to grab. The world feels like a movie set, where nothing is made to be used and just five feet off camera everything turns in to unpainted styrofoam. Invisible walls block off everything; you'll enter a room and half of it will be inaccessible for literally no reason because the game won't let you jump over a waist-high desk. Sure, there's probably nothing on the other side of that room, but that's the risk of scavenging, isn't it?
Similarly, the open world driving segments are all deep inside of valleys with cliffs on all sides so you don't really get the sense that you're actually out in a world. This is exacerbated by the fact that everything important seems to be a 2 minute drive from each other, all running along only a half dozen short roads. People will send you on supply runs like it's this big arduous journey when I'm pretty sure they could hike it on foot and be back in time for lunch.
And to be honest, I think after reaching the main town (Wellsprings) I've had my fill of RAGE. It's just not enough of anything I like or want.

I have never played Payday but I think RAID: WWII will feel similar to those who may have played Payday 2. The general premise is that you are one of 4 elite killers tasked with killing Nazi's and stealing their gold. Pretty straightforward stuff. The game is structured by various missions which can take the form of Raid's, operations or last orders.
RAID is bolstered by some pretty surprising production values. Visually the game won't knock your socks off but it gets the job done. Where the game shines however is it's video clips. The impeccable John Cleese plays the role of Mission control and he delivers a superb performance. Also of note is that after each mission you are treated to a video of an actor playing the fuhrer either upset by your success or pleased by your failure. Some of these can be quite humorous.
The missions themselves are varied enough, though some of the stealth sequences aren't as intuitive as they could be. It definitely feels a bit mismatched in that regard. Some maps have recently been patched to offer more hiding spots and make stealth more feasible.
Generally speaking the game is a series of horde mode encounters which can be a mix of tense and downright frustrating on higher difficulties. Some enemy spawns feel particulary malicious and vindictive when you have 2-3 flammenwerfers trying to roast you.
Some missions will have you stealing gold. Like Payday these feel a bit like "Trashbag sim" where you have to pick up bars of gold (1 at a time) and hurl them into a truck or transport.
The game can be played solo, though I wouldn't recommend it. The game is best played with a group of friends who can communicate.
After each mission you earn XP which allows you to level up, select perks and unlock weapon upgrades. The Xp gain and leveling process however can feel incredibly tedious once you get past lvl 15 or so.
If your looking for a good co-op game, Raid will fit the bill nicely.

Raid right now feels a lot like an early access title. It shows great potential to be something good but right now it lacks a lot of content. It also carries over bugs and glitches that were already fixed in a similar title, Payday 2. Every time I've started up Raid to play, I've encountered some kind of new bug.
Skill trees, aka "Proficiencies", have very little to be excited about. Only offering minor stat boosts until you reach a milestone of 5,10,15,20,25,30,35 or 40 in which you can slightly tweak your War Cry (think Overwatch's Ultimates) such as giving more of it's effect or gaining it faster by doing X. Some of the skills are even ripped directly from Payday 2 but split up between levels.
Classes minus their restricted weapons and War Cries all feel very samey. They all get access to a lot of the same skills but some can't max them out like others classes can. Currently, Assault and Insurgent are the best ones to use due to their usefulness at even lower levels. Demolitions and Recon need to be high level before they are even remotely useful compared to them.
Leveling both your classes and your weapons is nothing but a slow grind. Classes gain levels at decent pace until you hit around level 15. That's when you need to start doing multiple Hard or Very Hard raids to gain one level. It also doesn't help that you can't respec your skills freely. To do this, it requires you to pay a certain amount of gold (gained by finding loot in raids). You can also use gold to upgrade your camp but that's all.
Upgrading weapons can also be a chore when you have to repeatedly do challenges like "Kill X amount of enemies", "Kill X amount of enemies with hipfire", "Kill X amount of enemies Y meters away from you". These challenges only scale up each time you complete them and they can't be completed one after another because they are level locked. You also can't complete them then move on to the next one in line. You're forced to go back to your camp (think Payday 2's Safehouse) and start a new raid before you can continue to the next.
The raids (missions, heists, ect.) do all feel unique but they are also rather short. Objectives do feel different for each raid, which helps them feel less like the last one you played. However, they mostly rely on what Payday 2 has which is go somewhere, interact and/or defend the thing then leave. One thing that is rather nice compared to Payday 2 is that you're not constantly fixing drills or tossing bags around.
Some things unique to Raid are the Challenge Cards and Character Customization. Character Customization boils down to separate Tops and Bottoms for each Character.  During a raid, you will find dog tags scattered throughout the map. Collect enough of these and you might receive either a pack of Challenge Cards, a top or bottom clothing item for a character.
Challenge Cards are like modifiers that can slightly or largely change gameplay. Things like more player health, more enemy health, players can only use explosives and melee or players can only walk sideways or backwards. These can help make the game feel slightly different or offer a challenge. They can even give you an experience boost if they offer a negative effect. You can even trade these among friends but they aren't marketable, at least now right now.
Weapon selection is rather pitiful right now.
2 sniper rifles, 2 shotguns (1 at launch), 4 pistols (3 at launch), 3 Assault Rifles (4 if you count the pre-order exclusive golden variant of the M1 Garand), 4 SMGs and 3 LMGs (2 at launch). 5 melee weapons (2 locked behind the Special Edition) and 1 grenade (more coming soon).
The Raiders (characters) are all stereotypes, kind of like Payday 2 but not as good. You've got the swearing brash American, overly posh Brit, crazy Russian and German. Raiders act like Heisters did in PDTH (Payday the Heist) by interacting with each other. They will often comment on the current situation and comments made by other Raiders. However, these responses are very limited and you will hear all two variations they have within a short time of playing. They will also constantly remind you that you aren't doing the objective. This gets rather annoying while trying to sneak around, hearing "Isn't that the X? We should go interact with it!" "Yes, we should go X. Let's go do it!". Even when going loud it gets rather annoying if you for some reason can't do the objective, be it the wave of enemies in your way or you're just looking for dog tags.
The enemies you face have very little in the way of tactics. They will more often than not rush straight at you in massive hordes, overwhelming you. Lion Game Lion (LGL) are aware of this and trying to fix it but it's currently a major issue, especially on higher difficulties like Hard and Very Hard. There are four special enemies that you will also have to face. They are the Spotter, Sniper, Officer and Flamer. Officers will buff their allies and increase the spawns while also hiding the crowd of Nazis making it hard to kill them. Flamers feel slightly better balanced than Officers but can still kill you easily due to their fire they spread which ticks your health away pretty quickly. This is worsened when playing Very Hard and they are sent in groups of 2 or more.
Overall, I don't recommend RAID: World War II in its current state. As stated before, it feels so much like an early access game. A lot of content isn't there, it's full of bugs that need fixing, features that feel like placeholders and plenty of balancing issues that need to be addressed.
I do however have hope that LGL fixes the issues the game has. They seem very willing to listen to community feedback and are very involved with them. The only problem is that it will take months, at the very least it seems, to fix the core issues with the game.
TL;DR
If you've played Payday 2, there's not much you're missing out on. It's like a cross between Payday 2 and Payday the Heist. If you've never played a game like this, then I'd recommend Payday 2 Ultimate Edition instead. You'd get a lot more content for the same price and it has a lot more polish due to the four years it's been out.
The best option right now for anyone wanting this game, is to just wait. Wait for a sale, wait for LGL to fix issues and wait for the game to mature to what it should have been at launch.

Do not underestimate this game's difficulty just because it's in 2D; there are lots of traps, falls to death, dead ends, and deadly enemies that will easily kill you. The bosses are creatviely designed. Some of them take inspiration of Lovecraftian horrors.

It's one of the rare soulslike(sic) that actually understands why Dark Souls is good. Hard, but FAIR. It plays a lot like Dark Souls, but gave the mechanics its own spin, being a very statisfying ARPG. It's a great game, very fun to play with a lot of different possible builds, being worth a second playthrough, there's a lot of ways to advance and one journey can be completely different from the other, despite the game having a fixed order in which it wants you to progress (based on NPC questlines).
IMO, it improved the estus system a lot, by adding a mechanic that a % of the damage you take is taken from your max health, meaning you can't rely on chugging your way through everything, like you can in Dark Souls.

The Good:
Very well done retro 2D shooter
Very powerful gun customization system
Lots of stuff to craft
The Bad:
Poor tutorial, you really need to read the in-game manual on the main menu (which inexplicably is not accessible once you've loaded a charater).
Major pacing issues, especially at the beginning. The first part of the game is the most difficult since you haven't unlocked the good stuff yet and haven't memorized the maps yet.
Repetitive missions reuse the same maps over and over with slightly different objectives.
Enemies can be quite cheap at times (pinning you against a wall, attacking through a wall) and the retro gameplay means you can only shoot in 4 directions even though some enemies come right in on your blind spots.
Mission objectives are frequently unmarked and you have to scour the level to find what you're looking for (and hope you know where all the hidden areas are).
Reloading is annoying and slow for a run and gun type game.
The Ugly:
Endless instantly respawning enemies (they respawn as soon as you leave the screen) add a lot of frustration and annoyance when traversing a level for the nth time trying to find an unmarked objective.
This game is very close to being amazing, but suffers from a few fatal flaws. None of them would be particularly difficult to fix, but as it stands I can't recommend this game (especially at the asking price) unless you're willing to get past the initial difficulty wall and unlock the good guns.

NOTE: This review has been modified since posting. It was originally posted in January 2015 as ‘negative’, and is from March 2015 onwards rated as ‘positive.’ In addition, the content has been altered to reflect recent changes to the game.
First of all, know that this is not a ‘rogue-lite’. I have yet to see the final level, and there are others on the forums who have played for hundreds of hours and have yet to win the game.
For the TL;DR people: The game is amazing, but completing it on normal difficulty will take hundreds of hours because the learning curve is steep, and end-game balance depends on creating the most powerful build you can – theory crafting is a must, and if you don’t, the game will become unwinnable 30 hours before you realize it. For the rest of us, read on.
ToME has 26 classes at the time of this writing, all of which feel and play very differently. Like most RPGs, skill points are gained upon leveling and can be used for both active and passive effects. The skills for each class are unique and allow players to develop their own playstyles, though generally each class has its own style of combat and a playstyle that rewards sticking to their class-specific strengths. Summoners draw hordes of creatures to overwhelm opponents, archmages channel elements to great effect over an area, and rogues set traps and use stealth to outmaneuver or outwit opponents. There are even more creative classes in here, like a time warden (or time mage) that specializes in temporal effects and paradoxes.
The world has tons of surprises and interesting levels/areas to explore, acceptable story and interaction (for an old-school roguelike) and though nothing ever changes, the vast variety of mechanics assured that the game did not get old for me after 100 hours of gameplay, and likely will not for another 100 hours.
But Tales of Maj’Eyal does have its problems. The first and perhaps least bothersome is a learning curve that feels more like a cliff than a slope.
The tutorial explains a little of the game's mechanics, but understanding is better gained by blundering through the world and slowly learning what each of the many confusing formulas and statistics mean, and how important they are to the core gameplay. It takes dedication to keep coming back when mountains of unknown skills and abilities assail you from every side, and through trial-and-error, learn to slowly overcome that mountain. Perseverance does pay off – I actually enjoyed the game very much once I crossed the barrier between hopeless bungler and still-hopeless-but-educated noob.
The larger problem is that in order to win the game, the player’s character must be designed for perfection – built to optimal capacity with a full understanding of the many talents, stat formulas, status effects and saving throws present in the game engine. It’s not enough just to go with the most damage, or discover the best damage reduction, or center your build around strategic options – you must do all of these things, and do them with the dedication of a crazed League of Legends professional gunning for the gold.
This is where the game fell apart previously –it can become unwinnable very early on, and new players will never even know. They may even feel overpowered for a while, as they make one-strike KOs against hordes of enemies and pass tens of dungeons without a serious challenge in any of them. Rares, elites, and bosses fall without challenge - then suddenly, a belligerent abomination of a boss-class monstrosity strikes, and they find themselves hopelessly outmatched, their only recourse to grind for levels.
So they go to a new dungeon – and it happens again. Another new dungeon – wait, were the normals this hard before? And why can’t I use my spells? My abilities? Where did everyone go? And… how did I get one-shot by THAT?
Players be warned: No matter how many lives you have, you can make a mistake in your character build early on and not realize that your character is doomed until late-game, when you have already invested thirty-or-more hours into their development. With permadeath, obviously, you may not live long enough to realize your character build is impossible to win with. But even with unlimited lives, you will eventually reach the point where the bosses are impossible, and no matter how well you fight, how clever your tactics, you have no option but to die – or quit. Before the 1.3.0 update, this meant that you must start the game over again from the beginning.
This is why my review changed from negative to positive. While limited and full-permadeath players will still have to deal with the intense frustrations of sub-optimal builds, there is hope for those playing with unlimited lives after the 1.3.0 update: Full talent re-spec is available at all times, so if you’ve created a build that seems sub-optimal to your playstyle or eventually becomes self-defeating, you can easily change your skills to accommodate your newfound knowledge or equipment. Be warned, however, that stat points and category points are still permanent, so consider playing a Cornac (+1 cat points) your first time and keeping some stat points in reserve for future use while you learn the ins and outs of your chosen class.
Also, be warned that there is no way to carry multiple save files for your character in this game. The game will save on entering and exiting a dungeon, as well as upon making most major decisions, and you will have to live with the consequences of your actions.
So to recap: Tales of Maj'Eyal as it is an interesting game that supports a wide variety of skill sets and play styles, though impressive knowledge of the game mechanics that can only be acquired through vigilant study required to develop a successful playstyle. Full talent re-spec alleviates (but not eliminates) the steep learning curve, but if you like RPG roguelikes with unique classes and deep strategy, investing your time in this game will reward you with probably the best roguelike you’ve ever played. Just be prepared to invest heavily.
*Full disclosure here - I played the game on 'normal' difficulty for every playthrough. There is an easier difficulty that decreases the monsters' strength/abilities by 30%, but it does not give classes, races or achievements and so it does not appeal to those like me who want to feel they are accomplishing something while playing.

Rift is one of the best MMORPGs I know of. The Story is good. The character creator is GREAT! But the real juicy stuff is in the mechanics of the game (mainly the skill tree). It is free to play, however without the full version you can only have two characters per server, and two bag slots. But the main drawback for having a free to play version is not being able to use the auction house. Do not let that discourage you though. You can sell things from anywhere using the rift store, which helps with bag space and you don't really need more than two characters. I would recommend getting the full version, because it only costs $10 one time pay. Which gives you 3 extra bag slots, more character slots than you'll need, and access to the auction house. Back to the mechanics of the game. There are, Guardians and Defiants, the Defiants have 3 races, the Guardians do as well. Which all have fairly unique racial abilities. There are four classes, Warrior, Rogue, Cleric, and Mage. You can combine any race with any class. If you think that's cool, wait 'till you read the next part. Within all of your classes there are several branches of skills. Each branch is assigned a type of damage. For example: In a cleric class, Druid is DPS, Purifier is healing, and shaman is elemental damage. You can chose 3 branches of your skill tree and level them up how you desire. But here is the best part, you can have like 5 skill trees that you can flip flop in between outside of battle. Pretty sweet huh? On a scale of 1-10 I would give it a 10. Well, what are you waiting for? Start playing!

I DO recommend this for new players. I DON'T for old players, at least not until the studio changes stuff.
For people playing free-to-play for this, first time, Evolve Stage 2 is fine. It's a decent game, although it definitely has balancing issues and needs work. It says "beta" and they MEAN it.
For people who played this in the original beta, played it on a trial weekend, or (your poor wallets) bought it, this is NOT fine. I originally played this on a free-to-play weekend, put a fair amount of time in it, and watched my husband play it a lot. It was really good, but it was too expensive for our budget, so we had to pass up on it. (If you read the reviews, others felt similarly.) So here I am back again and this time I say: if they're proud they shrunk the size of the game (and comments online indicate they are) they shouldn't be. Too much is stripped out of the game. I hope this is because it's just a test run.
The game is faster paced and less nuanced overall, the game is missing a lot of game modes, and that poor souls who paid an arm and a leg need assurances they will get more stuff out of this than they're getting now. Since the studio has assured the "Founders" that they will get all their stuff back, they had better darn well do so. And if they are going to put in a lot more of the old content (maps, modes) later, they need to darn well say so.
As it is, this is a hollowed-out, incomplete beta that needs love so bad. I can't recommend it to anyone who saw Evolve before this unless the studio clarifies what the heck they're doing. I'd be happy to change my review if this improves.

Edit 8/4/16: Patches are adding things fairly quickly, and that's great.  Still missing my favorite game modes.  Still needs a lot more info on character abilities in places other than loading screens.  But it's improving.  Needs other modes.
TL;DR - All the game modes I liked are gone.  All that remains are the two game modes I liked the least.  If you've never tried it and don't know it well, download and play.  If you want what it was, don't get too excited just yet.
When I first heard about this game I was very excited.  It looked fantastic.  Sadly, it was a very expensive game on launch, and so I decided to wait.  Eventually, Steam had a free weekend, which I enjoyed immensely.  The game was just a blast to play.  I loved the story mode where you played a series of different maps with different objectives.  I loved all the modes where the goal was do something other than just beat on your opponent.  I loved the character interaction.  Overall, I loved the game.  I did NOT love the hefty price tag and the fact that even after that you'd have to pay a relatively high cost for every single new thing added from that time on to infinity.  In the end, it was purely financial.  As much as I enjoyed the game, I couldn't justify the cost.  Besides that, I'd always imagined it would be F2P like TF2, and thought it might go that way in the future.  If not that, then at least they'd have a huge bundle sale someday.
Months passed and I saw this tiny add on a wiki page that said Evolve was F2P.  I was downloading it within minutes, and very, very excited.  After it was all installed, I loaded it up with glee, and started trying to remember how to play the thing.  The interface and menus were different, and I couldn't find the nice animated character pictures that I remembered (I think they are gone), but that was a small thing.  I couldn't find how to join other game modes, but thought maybe I had to unlock them by finishing the tutorial or something.  It didn't take long to realize that what had happened was the game was a much reduced version of what I had played before.
I read a FAQ where the devs were proud that they reduced the size of the game massively.  Something like 43 gigs down to 20.  That is because they removed half of the game.  This is not a point of pride.  Anyway, I DO think the game is very fun, but I tried arena mode once and never liked it.  Hunt mode was ok, but a bit boring.  The other modes were great though.  Now, those are the only two left.  And more, there are only 4 maps.  I don't recall how many were there before, but it was a lot more than that.  I'm just baffled why they would remove so much of the game before doing a big relaunch.  I understand why they would do that if they were NOT going F2P, in order to pull all the remaining players into the same games.  But that wasn't the case.  So I'm a little confused.
My hope is that they plan to put them back in since this IS a beta afterall.  I can understand that after all the rebalancing they'd want to focus on the core gameplay at first.  But for now, it's a fun game.  It's a beautiful game.  It's a game full of character.  But it's repetitive and uninteresting with the two game modes that exist.  So, I'm going go play it for a week or a month before getting bored.  I truly hope the game gets those modes and maps back before that.
Side issues are only getting a pittance of silver keys for custom games since I prefer to just play with my wife and bots.  But I understand their reasoning.  Also, they currently have no way to make money in the game, and so I'm curious what they plan to do with that, and concerned as well. RAID: World War II is a continuation of the PAYDAY legacy set around seventy years earlier during the middle of the second world war. Choosing a class and nationality of a character, each player is given the ability to take up a specific role to help the raiders on their quest to stop the nazis (and pick up some cash on the side!)
Graphics are easily one of the weakest points of the game, if that kind of thing matters to you. They’re about a single step down from PAYDAY 2 in its current state. Much of the textures and environment actually doesn’t look half bad, however the shaders and other effects are quite mediocre. The experience feels like an early Source engine game sometimes, and this is probably the last game that can ever come out on the Diesel engine without being an immediate failure. The poor optimization and performance make this game run poorly and look even poorer sometimes.
The balance in this game is steep, challenging, and honestly kind of unique. Unlike its brother PAYDAY 2, not all of the guns in this game are going to be usable on every mission; some are just too specialized to a range. The sad thing about this is that they feature only a limited modification system, that is a onetime upgrade with no downsides. The only exception is that scopes are always available to true sniper rifles and can be detached. Melee weapons are a bit more clunky, having to be pulled out, but this is likely a choice to be more realistic. The choice of both kinds of weapons are limited, however this is not all that unexpected, and the list is expected to keep growing. The new feature, replacing deployables, are war cries. After getting a certain amount of kills, you can activate an ultimate of sorts tied to your class. These give you more powerful grenades, increased damage resistance, or even auto aim! This is a welcome addition and feels more fitting than deployables, especially as there are now enemy drops for health and grenades in addition to ammo.
The game during stealth is an enjoyable experience minus one aspect I will address later. Enemies spot you in a very similar way to PAYDAY or Far Cry before it, and you must kill enemies before they fully spot you and have a chance to shoot (alerting other enemies on the map) or hit the alarm (calling in the rest of Hitler’s forces.) In its current state the enemy’s cone of vision is glitchy, seeing you through walls as well as behind them, but this isn’t quite as bad as it has been in earlier builds of PAYDAY. Unlike PAYDAY there are no pagers, and instead of body bags you just heft the body up and throw them away. These are welcome changes making stealth a more valid approach except for one thing… There are no silenced guns. You HAVE to use melee to remain silent when there are enemies who can hit the alarm. This is a serious blow to the playstyle making it inviable sometimes, due to the fact two enemies stare right at each other from far enough away two people can’t rush and take them both down. This is expected to be remedied with a new gun in the future, but for now, stealth is sometimes just not a realistic possibility.
The game during loud features multiple varying difficulties. You clear out the existing nazi forces and prepare to complete your objective all while being hit by the oncoming nazi waves. On the lower difficulties most enemies only do a little bit of damage, but later on they hold harder-hitting weapons and do quite a bit more. Special enemies come in as well, such as the Officer and the Flamer, doing increased damage with specialized weapons. Being shot deals direct damage (except when you dodge) and there is no apparent armor; however, there are many crates scattered around you can use to find ammo, grenades, or health drops. Each player has a limited number of ‘down’ states where you fall to the ground and use a secondary to fight off the remaining enemies, and you must be revived. If you are not revived you are captured and must wait to respawn. Ammo is limited, but as earlier stated, can be picked up off of enemies, crates, or some mission stockpiles. The game emphasizes an objective based system, where you survive and do objectives until you can take your loot and leave; the only goal is to help the allies kill off vital nazi party objectives… as well as take as much bullion as you can carry. In addition to mission gold, dog tags and loot are scattered around the maps giving you some extra gold and other rewards after each mission.
RAID features a simplified skill tree system, where each class has their own tree with three branches. This allows you to focus on stealth, lockpicking, damage resistance, health, ammo conservation, and a whole lot of other bonuses. The trees sometimes do share effects, but in general, are focused on the respective weapons/skills of a class and their war cry, making them largely unique.
Servers are not really that; you join another person's locally hosted server for up to four player coop in the camp, a kind of virtual lobby, where you can change your various builds, guns, and characters. This suffers all the same fates of PAYDAY including desync, overpowered host powers, and slow load times.
The story here is that you take place of one of a few characters contracted by the allies to perform unique raid operations to cripple the nazi forces. You are instructed what to do by Mrs. White, a woman working as a middle man for you and your crew. The crew is made up of disgraced members of prominent factions in the war who share only one common thing: greed.
The maps in this game are easily the strongest point. Unique, atmospheric, and finely detailed by the map makers. Single or multi day missions take you across several of the nazi strongholds, camps, and even fortresses used during the war. The objectives of these maps are to destroy either nazis or nazi equipment, and therefore get paid for your efforts. In addition to just starting the map, you can also activate cards that give you extra xp and a buff at the price of a nerf that outweighs the buff. These can be fun and entertaining but I wouldn't quite call it a gameplay aspect.
The business model of this game is going to be the same as PAYDAY. Full price for the game and extra for a special edition, with more DLC on the way interspersed with free content updates. Currently there are no microtransactions or other things of note for the business model. I DO NOT recommend the special edition unless you purely want to support the developers.
Overall, this game has a lot of potential but just needs to get a good start. The quality, the time, the effort are all here. The game is a good base for a better game to come, it just needs the help of fans to inspire the developers to fix many of the issues and even add new and better content. This game can be fun solo, but becomes even more fun with an experienced team of raiders; burning the nazi flags never felt so fun.

Well, in all honesty, I have never beaten a Dark souls game or Bloodborne, and personally didn't like Dark Souls nearly as much as I've liked Salt & Sanctuary.
I have just beaten the game and entered NG+ and will now be moving on to play DS2, but will definitely be coming back to this game again.
Pros:
Nice Artstyle, Nice environments/areas to explore, cool enemies, cool bosses, good leveling system (Works on a skill tree system, but with some small twists), good platforming, fantastic area progression and a nice feeling of dread farther on in the game.
Cons:
-While the music is good, you tend to listen to most of the same songs or abience throughout the game and it's hard to recall any songs other than the Boss fight theme, Sanctuary theme, and Nameless God, while there's other songs, they just don't feel like they play as often.
-Enemies are cool and all that, but some of them are not fun or really engaging to fight. That number is really small, but the only enemy I can say for certain is a horrible enemy, is the main skeleton. They have an abillity where they can teleport and are invincible throughout the entire animation when beginning to teleport, and for a small opening when they finish, and that small opening is even smaller when you take into consideration most weapons have serious delay on them, and the chances of you reading them is nearly impossible because sometimes when they finish teleporting they just teleport off somewhere again, making you miss your shots. The little ♥♥♥♥ers will teleport ANYWHERE on the map and will sometimes *teleports behind you* nothing personnel kid and just get 5 free hits on you, and then another one will teleport to you and they will both poison you and probably kill you. Really just an unfair enemy to fight, and really annoying. There's only 2 of them that you will meet often, but even then you will hate them.
-For a game based on platforming, about mid way through the game when you start getting powers called "Brands", you get a lot more platforming (Wall jumps, air dashes) and this makes platforming fun and even sometimes really cool when you implement it into your actual fights, but when this starts to happen, you start to realize the game's platforming is well... a bit iffy. In an attempt to balance air dashes and wall jumps, once you fall a certain distance clinging on to walls and air dashes do almost nothing, as you will just fall while sliding down the wall, or just move forward with the dash. I understand this was a balancing thing, but sometimes that window to air dash or wall jump felt a bit small and you feel a bit cheated on your death.
-Ledge grabbing. Or for the love of god ledge grabbing in this game is slow and unresponsive on 15% of the walls you try to scale. Sometimes you want to grab a wall to jump, but you grab the ledge, you try to grab the ledge, but you just miss or fall to your death. Simple flaws but can be very annoying when the you got a lot of salt when just die cause the game's ledge was programmed a bit higher than the other's.
Now I'll just list some of my "Mehs" with this game.
-This game has a lot of back tracking and weird little secrets, which is nice when done right, but sometimes this game doesn't give you a set direction, and it gets confusing at times. Most other games will give you a hint, but this game just gives you an item, tells you to go wild and you just wander around wondering what do you with your life.
Overall, really good game, and I give it a 9/10
Even with it's good, but unmemorable soundtrack and flaws, it comes out to be a really good experience, due to most of the flaws being small issues that arise at only farther into the game, and by that point, you're already invested in this game and what it has to offer.
Recommend for full price, recommend even more on sale.

The positive:
-Really nice pixel art.
-Can be fun (mostly at first).
-Good variety of enemies.
-The concept of "secret objectives" is interesting, even though it's developed poorly.
The neutral:
-The story. It's kind of bland but it can be skipped without an issue (just keep pressing "next" everytime the dialog windows show up after some key missions).
The negative:
-Gathering materials is a chore. Even upgrading your armor requires grinding (example: one armor requires 2 of a material that's only dropped by one boss; to make matters worse, it's not a guaranteed drop)
-There are a lot of missions but they are really repetitive.
-Maps are quite big, which could be a good thing but you must check the map constantly to see if you are going to the right direction. Some missions actually don't tell you were the objectives are but luckily those are quite few.
-Crafting is kind of confusing but the worse thing is being constantly constrained by having to find materials.
-The food that can give you a boost on health (+ other temporary stats) must be grinded in the "hunting grounds" were you basically kill -mostly- harmless animals that provide no challenge. The whole thing looks like an unfinished featured that ended up being rushed.
-"Profencies" that you can get by crafting lots of stuff seem kind of nice but they are not worth the trouble of finding all the materials.
-The special "mods" that you can equip to your character are mostly kind of useless (although the one that assures that every enemy drops a material on death is extremely necessary to be able to craft weapons)
-Enemies have "strenghts" and "weaknesses" that you can learn about by talking to a guy in your camp and changing your bullets for each mission is so boring that you'll probably use the one with the higher attack number and disregard everything else.
-Weapons have a lot of different stats but they really don't change the playstyle.
-You can craft a lot of decorative stuff that serve no purpose except tempt you into wasting your materials. In my opinion it would have been better to see the base change as you completed missions.
Conclusion:
I can see a lot of potential in this game but it's full of really strange decisions that seem to be aimed at increasing the playtime of the game (but that's not the same as a game having a great replay-value).
in my opinion the game would have been a lot better without crafting and actually focusing in making combat and missions more varied.

This game is one of those kinds of games that says "Hey, you know everything you like about old-school sidescrolling shooters? We don't have any of that."
The game itself is a Borderlands style gameplay where you can play a level designed for multiple missions, but you are forced to play each mission one at a time, which seems to me like a lazy attempt to stretch out the gameplay. This also makes the only mission theme in the game grating and annoying pretty quickly.
Enemies have a chance to drop junk which you can use to craft items to customize your guns, barracks, mods among other things. So quickly this becomes a game that's all about the grind. But don't worry, because you're not actually grinding when you're doing missions one at a time on giant sprawling levels, right? Some of the things you can craft are ridiculous. For example, a hamburger, pinwheel and pizza ornament all have a huge recipe of collectables (some of which can only be found in a level called the hunting grounds where you hunt harmless wildlife specifically to grind for materials) and a $1000 price tag. Even for completionists, I don't know who would have enough spare time to grind for the materials and money necessary to place an ornament of a burger in their barracks.
Oh man, I haven't gotten to the best part yet. You like boss battles? How about boss battles that move around giant sprawling levels for no reason? That's right, if you take too long fighting a boss, he runs out of the arena and you have to go through more of the level to find him again, sometimes he wanders off straight after you arrive! Fun! Yes, I like fighting bosses with attention defecit disorder.
I'm a big fan of Metal Slug and I do somewhat moderately enjoy Borderlands, but this comes off as a horrible execution to combine the two. The deliberately stretched out gameplay and the need to grind to unlock items necessary makes this game pretty unenjoyable for me and I can't recommend it to anyone.

I enjoy this game, but there are a lot of caveats.
If you watch the trailers, it looks like a run and gun, a la Metal Slug. It's really not, though. It's more like Monster Hunter, where you gather materials and embark on quests with specific goals, as opposed to running through stage after stage and then beating the end boss. Mercenary Kings just happens to use 2D gunning/platforming instead of 3D action for its main gameplay mechanic.
The problem with its emulation of Monster Hunter is that it took the worst parts and made it the bulk of the game. Too many of the quests are boring "Kill 20 small minions, find 10 stupid items, reach this destination." It's repetitive and not interesting.
Even worse, Mercenary King's early boss fights are boring. They all follow the formula of duck, fire, roll under, repeat. There are 3 or 4 palette swaps per boss, who all receive the exact same new move. Why they chose to create 3 subspecies who all act identically is beyond me.
With that out of the way, let's get to the good stuff.
The late game bosses become much more interesting and varied. If more of the game were like this, I would give it a glowing review.
The gun design mechanic is good and forces the player to make meaningful choices and decide between tradeoffs.
Playing with friends is quite enjoyable.
In summary, I recommend the game, but if any of the above sounds unpalatable to you, then definitely skip it.

It seems odd to me that people didn't get what Mercenary Kings was before it was released. When I watched the gameplay footage, it was very clear that the game features mechanics as Monster Hunter such as collecting materials for crafting (a LOT of it), 3 lives per mission in total (especially important in multiplayer), and timed missions. Unlike Metal Slug, which is a really fast paced 2D game, MK is more tactical, forcing you to think your approach on enemies, or die and respawn at the start point of the mission (kind like Castlevania). This creates tension, and challenge. I don't understand why people complain about not being able to shoot in a diagonal direction, as you couldn't do it in Metal Slug either, but okay.
Gameplay variations come in bionic mods, which consist on equipping up to two ability enchaning mods, along with their respective penalties; then, there is the really extensive weapon crafting in both guns and blades. This is pretty much the core mechanic of the game. Gun parts will change your damage, ammo, firing speed, weight, element, bullet compatibility, etc. Properties for knives such as range, speed, element, and others also apply. Craft enough parts of the same weapon type, and you get proficiencies, which work as an additional mod, but with no penalties. If you have played Monster Hunter, Valdis Story or any other game which focuses a lot on defeating enemies to finally get the item you need, it's worth the time, because a new kind of weapon completely changes the way you approach enemies.
Mission types go from eleminating enemies in a certain area, to rescue missions, hunting missions, capture missions, material finding, etc. etc. Yes, you may feel that you have to replay maps a lot, but factors such as time, starting points, and even enemies will change as you progress through the game. Backtracking and respawing enemies work in a way that you have to very careful about not wandering mindlessly and be on your toes, as enemies will be there again, but you will encounter them from another angle, making you think twice about how to kill them once again. This also works in your favor for material collecting purposes. The fleeing Boss mechanic, I felt, works as a time and ability challenge. It can work for or against you. The thing about Bosses escaping, is that you can open the map, and you will see the skull icons where the boss actually is, so it's about how fast you can get there and finish the job.
Multiplayer is a blast, as you and your friends can tackle the missions from different points. You are not bound all together in the same screen, but can work individually when it comes to finding enemies or items in order to complete the mission. Also, if you pick up a material, all your friends will get it too, so it makes crafting a lot faster. If you hated going against a Boss solo, a multiplayer session will allow you and your friends to completely wreck those Steel Soldiers, Mechanic Hounds and many others. One thing of caution, though. I said that you have 3 lives in total per mission, not per player. So watch out for trigger happy companions, or loners, because if they day very far away from any support, "Mission Failed" is a highly likely scenario, so teamwork is never out of the question, and THAT'S the beauty of it. There are adrenaline shots to revive your comrades or yourself in these situations, but mind the inventory limit, as choices must be made, so once again, tactics is the word of the day.
There is also the platformer aspect of the game, so be careful about how hard you press the jump button. So, not only will you fight CLAW, but you will find the stages themselves. The reload mechanic is something you must master, as you must always be aware of how much ammo you got left before reloading. By reloading, you will see a black, yellow and green bar above you. If you time well your reloading and hit the green section of the bar, you will get a bonus damage for the amount of bullets your reloaded. If you miss, you'll be unable to shoot for a period of time, defined by the load time of the weapon you're carrying (So you better have a nicely forged knife to compensate). This mechanic adds even more tension to the game, because you won't always be standing still as you watch your reload bar, but you may be in a heated Boss battle, or sorrounded by enemies, so mastering your reload time for every weapon you carry is a must.
For the enemy part of the game, there is a nice variety of them. Not to mention that some enemies will level up in a way, and be stronger and change their attack patterns. The same goes for Bosses, and you will encounter some powered-up ones, which likely make your day harder (if you have played Monster Hunter, this if quite familiar). If you get into trouble at missions, you can always rest at the infirmary, which works both as a healing station (kind slow, so watch your times) and a spawn point, so if you die, you will respawn at the last infirmary you entered.
As I see it, people who really didn't like this game (and played for about 15 minutes of it), were expecting a super-fast paced shooting game, like metal slug. This is more tactical, as I said, like Castlevania, Metroid, Monster Hunter, etc. You can't be shooting endlessly or moving really fast with a full pleged machine gun in  your arms. Other were expecting things to be really casual and easy, but Mercenary Kings isn't that kind of game. If you can stand a challenge, and master the speed and mechanics of this game, satisfaction is a feeling that will get to you eventually. Also, after end-game, you can keep playing in order craft every weapon part there is, or just try the different kind of bullets and guns, just to see how you fare with them. Are you a revolver or hand-gun kind of person? Maybe shotguns are your thing. Maybe a Sniper Rifle, or a Machine gun. Maybe you like it close and personal, and your knife gets the best out of you. Changing a weapon type is pretty much changing your experiencie in the game, so give it a shot.
Design and artstyle-wise, the game is beautiful. If you like pixel art, the character designs are stylish, both friends and enemies. The game plays really smooth, and the map details are very well done. I'm not picky with graphics in videogames, so for me this really easy on the eyes.
When it comes to controls, I'm the rare kind of player who prefers the keyboard. The default keys are what I use, and at first they're kind of weird, but using your right hand as a second WASD actually makes sense in this game (at least for me). The thing to watch out for are the roll and the knife controls. If you don't want to trouble yourself with the roll button, you can enable the double-tap option to get that out of your way. Now you deal only with shoot, knife and jump. Of course, there is the reload button and how you handle your inventory, but all it takes is a button configuration or a controller set-up to better suit your needs.
Anyway, that's my way of covering how this game does what it does. I can see that it's not for the VERY casual players, or those who expect really fast paced 2D shooters (which I also love), but I wouldn't call it hardcore either. It's about letting Mercenary Kings grow on you if the general idea doesn't fully convince you yet, but I can't blame you if this isn't really the game for you. Just don't go with the "It's hard because I'm not super powerful" kind of reviews. This is a game that rewards your intelligence and your ability more than it rewards your farming for materials in order to craft the best equipment.
I hope this helps you out in that decisive "Yes or No" for this game in particular, and keep on playing.

Great game, very fun roguelike, and the fact that you unlock certain things for future playthroughs, without it changing the balance of the game is a great mechanic. It's fairly forgiving, in that you can start on easy mode, with unlimited lives (but no achievements) to figure things out, then once you've got the hang of it, you can change it up to a harder version.
If you're someone who has to get every achievemnt though, this game will take a LOT of your time. I first got it from DarGod's website, played it for a hundered plus hours, then heard it was on steam, so I bought it here too (on a friends shared account) and started playing it. I earned a hundred or so achievements before I just started playing under my account. And then I realized that I had to re-earn those achievements. I felt better when I realized that those hundred I earned? not even 15% of the total possible. Yeah, that's right, there's not 100, not 200, but over 1300 achievements for this game.
So like I said if you need to have EVERY achievement, this will take you some time, especially since at least one of the achievements is nearly impossible. You have to beat the optional boss, who is a super archmage/god (not kidding about that, it's part of the amazing in-depth lore of this game) on the hardest difficulty setting, with one life. Oh yeah, and she can come back to life a few times. Oh, and she gets stronger each time she does it. And she is in the middle of a town full of mages, who also attack you. But at least you can attack first, right?
So for those who don't want to spend the next 3 years trying to get that achievement, it's still an amazing game, with good graphics (for a roguelike) a great story, fun unlock systems, and interesting combat. All that, and it was developed by one guy! Props DarkGod, your minions salute you!

Lead a ball through mazes from an isometric perspective.
The controls are skewed and the ball's inertia is your biggest challenge (read: absolute BS).
It's playable and looks pretty but not my thing.

● Decent music.
● Simple but enjoyable art style.
● Extremely floaty & unresponsive controls.
● Confusing lack of visual depth.
● Near impossible later levels.
The ball movement seems sluggish yet it picks up a lot of momentum. Combine this with the unresponsive controls and not falling off the edge constantly becomes quite the challenge. While the art style is nice the game does a really poor job of conveying depth. This made navigating curves on skinny rails extremely hard and some levels basically involved trial and error to see if I was going to roll onto a moving platform or just fall off the world because the platform was actually on a different plane.
The first two and a half-ish worlds are fun, but then the game quickly becomes a chore.  In world 3 the game introduces skinny rails which are extremely difficult to traverse with the sluggish, unresponsive controls and confusing lack of depth. By the later levels these rails are so long and curvy that the levels become near impossible to complete normally, much less within the time challenge limits. I suffered my way through world 3 only to find that world 4 had more skinny rails, but now there was also some weird fire mechanic which can kill your ball and reset you. It was at this point I gave up. I enjoy a challenge, but by this point the game was so infuriatingly difficult that it was no longer fun. Unless you're a masochist I really can't recommend this game.

This is one challenging game, I'll give it that. First two sets of levels are easy/moderate, but once you get the third set your fingers are gonna get a workout. Fourth set, say good bye to them.

Feel some of the levels were TOO difficult though... especially the rail-heavy or -focus ones. It's also nearly impossible to turn well on  curved rail, which was the most frustrating aspect of the game.
It's an okay game though overall. Haven't had any huge issues with it.

I really like this game.
The animation is fluid and crisp which allows for precise gameplay. The platforming has tight controls and the action controls are also just as good. The music is on point with what the animation is trying to achieve in terms of period nostalgia. The boss fights (which comprise the bulk of the game) are all unique and interesting to me.
The game may seem really challenging at first but most of the game is about pattern recognition and getting better at reacting to those patterns. Some will not appreciate the attacks that cannot be dodged on a first attempt (and believe me there are plenty of those to go around) but since the game is built around you dying quite often it is to be expected. Having completed the game on Expert mode I feel comfortable in saying that you can and will be able to beat every boss if you practice. Some may need more or less than others but it is a game that requires your patience if you require more practice than others. For me it was fun to practice and improve which is why I kept on coming back. Another thing to consider is how quickly the game will load on your computer though when considering all this. Since I died plenty of times against the bosses I had to retry plenty of times and the retries began instantly which allowed for quick bursts and improvements.
In short:
If you like games where you may die a lot (which again your results may vary) then this is for you. If you don't then probably avoid this game. Patience and perseverance is key so if you want to see the ending don't give up and improve.

RAGE is a game that's all about scale. It has everything a good open world game has. Wastelands, Cities (well, 2 of them anyway), crafting, side-quests, races, a smash-TV style battle arena, stunt jumps, delivery jobs, gambling mini-games, a really awesome trading card game, and more.
And it fits all of this into a match box. This is the smallest "open world" you'll ever see. I swear that everything is within a minute distance of everything else. It's both ridiculous and amazing.
For the rest, it's pretty fun, the game doesn't take itself too seriously - I think there was a story but it's not that important - the combat plays a bit like borderlands minus the loot but with a nice variety of weapons, ammo, and sentrybots, and all in all it's definitely worth a playthrough. The game ends like it started: abruptly, not far from the start, and without getting boring.

A fun 2D platformer/shooter type deal with an amazing visual theme, good controls, and a decent amount of content.
Movement, controls, and weight mechanic are all well done and made this game a joy to play. The levels are full of impressively detailed pixel art animations which match the story to give the game a lot of character. The majority of the enemies and bosses are fun to fight, and learning the sprawling level layouts is rewarding. After you beat the game speedrunning levels adds a lot of content and is thankfully pretty achievable, dependant more on knowing map layouts and enemy patterns than raw skill. The multiplayer is also really nice, but due to random matching you can get groups of folks who are very different skill/progress levels, which sometimes doesn't work out so well.
The gun crafting system is interesting and allows one to customize for their personal playstyle, but there are some combinations which are just better than most others and so are more widely used. Farming for materials shouldn't be much of an issue during the game, but the rarer end game achievements (craftsmanship, etc.) will definitely require a bit of farming. Default keyboard controls are pretty weird, but I got used to it and now it feels natural. Can be remapped if desired anyway.
Overall a really well made game, certainly worth a try.

After six hours, it just makes me want to play Metal Slug.
There are a lot of cool ideas here that I want to like a great deal. The art and music is beautiful, and  the mechanics that they draw from Borderlands, Monster Hunter, and Metal Slug are very cool in concept. But, therein lies the problem. There is tons of character and tons of concepts, and they just don't really gel together in a satisfying way. The beautiful art is done injustice by how stiff the animations are, and by how creepingly slow variations in environments and enemies are introduced. While the music is good, the sound effects are flat, and don't provide any real sense of punch to the action. The guns are incredibly flaccid and static, feeling more like gussied-up number hoses than firearms. Customizing the guns doesn't really feel meaningful or fun. As in Borderlands, all the variety in the world ends up just being wallpaper for a different set of slightly different numbers. This is compounded by the fact that new weapons cannot even be found in the wild, reducing the excitement of their procurement a great deal. Action is plodding with neither the fast pace of Metal Gear nor the precision of Mega Man, but a muddy, fuzzy middle-ground that isn't satisfying. After playing through the same map for the fourth time, the massive list of missions begins to look more like a list of chores than a set of badass missions.

Having never played World of Warcraft makes comparing MMO's such as RIFT very difficult to do. As it stands, RIFT delivers an exceptionally well crafted world that's as diverse as it is gorgeous. Lore plays a huge part within RIFT's story, and content is implemented in such a way as to reduce an incessant grinding of monsters to close level gaps, content gaps, and so forth. Expansions are forthcoming and add a fair amount of content at each pass, shoring up the longevity of the title.
RIFT's biggest claim to fame currently is the players ability to have near complete control in class building, skill building, and content pathing. Any variety of class is up for grabs, and is subject to change if the player wishes it. The ability to switch between roles and create role-reversal classes is top knotch, and open to imagination. There is absolutely a huge array of variety to be had.
The combat system in RIFT is nothing spectacular, but more of the same - such is the case with most products of this type. The PvE content is a blast and is (in my humble opinion), what RIFT is really all about. PvP has its place, but unfortunately in its current state suffers from the "free to play" mentality. Trion, in its infinite "wisom", has decided to block defined access to most events, and now require Patron status to proactively pick and choose an arena, raid, or dungeon of the users choice. RIFT will undoubtedly continue to develop two flaws for every boon, as its age begins to show.
Now, along with Patron changes to the system, RIFT has been charging steadily for certain beneficial upgrades such as extra skill sets, class sets, and availability of equipable traits (such as foraging, mining, etc). While RIFT still maintains its "free to play" philosophy, it has also been funneling players into purchasing certain upgrades such as a mounts ability to traverse bodies of water, extra item slots, and generally items and allowances one would imagine to be free or, kindly, earned ingame. Now, generally speaking... these extra touches that cost a bit of money aren't of negative connotation, but if every progressive benefit costs an arm and a leg...
In the end, RIFT will continue to be an enjoyable experience tinged ever so slightly with the negativity of a free to play state, and is perhaps only worthwhile to those with ample change in their pockets (ironically), or as extremely casual players. RIFT is at present an entertaining title with slowly developing flaws, comprised of quality content, albiet a flawed ideology.

If this game were an RPG character, it'd have put all its skill points into game/mechanic design. Its basic story (despite stellar VA cast), single-track score, repetitive SFX, and somewhat brutalist environment art are all lacklustre, but Defense Grid can be carried by its gameplay alone, which is in itself pretty laudable.
The tower/alien interplay is very finely-tuned and pretty much every level is perfectly balanced. Most levels with the opportunity for mazing offer up an interesting extra puzzle layer. Though the HUD is a bit stark, the visual communication of alien/tower type and strength is impressively simple.
The game's takes on tower defence staples are clever and satisfying. Resource interest is earned in real-time instead of in waves, the life system takes the form of retrievable cores (which also affect interest), and these along with the existence of verticality and line-of-sight implementation makes tweaking solutions to improve high scores pretty addictive.
My main gripe mechanically is the length of each level, particularly the later missions which can take half an hour even on constant fast-forward. This isn't problematic for the campaign, but is daunting for completionists considering there are literally hundreds of challenge mode missions. Checkpoints can also sometimes occur at awkward moments. Luckily the length and aforementioned audio cons mean this game makes for a great podcast accompaniment.

As someone that buys FM every other year, I can truly say FM18 is an incredible game. It's hard for SI to add and upgrade significant features into a game annually, but I can definitely see the upgrades FM18 has made from FM16, as well as FM17.
To begin with, the new additions of the Dynamics system and Medical Centre is great. Dynamics adds a complete new dimension to FM, which takes into account even the smallest of press conferences, team talks, and individual discussions. While it's incredibly difficult and costly if not managed properly, a cohesive and united team plays far more better, and its implementation was incredible. The Medical Center goes far more in detail to the injury system in FM. FM has been notorious in having a lot of injuries which can plague a season, but by closely monitoring the Medical Center and adjusting your tactics accordingly, you can have a team that plays good football and remains injury free.
The new scouting system has been overhauled and has some great additions to it. The data analysts are great in FM18, and I hear a much better upgrade compared to last year. In addition, far more detailed scouting processes and recommendations are essential in trying to sign first-team players and hot prospects for the future. It's hard to get used to, but when you do get used to it, you can really use it to improve your team.
Compared to FM16, FM18 has increased the difficulty of the game, incorporating far more factors to success. However, if these are mastered, it'll lead to an overall better save. I can't speak for FM17 users, but FM18 is definitely a massive upgrade on FM16. To FM players that didn't buy FM17 and new players to the FM series, I would highly recommend purchasing FM18.

I have played Football/Championship Manager for many years and I buy the game every year (since 1997). The one thing that frustrates me hugely with the series is the annual addition of more fluff or features, which often don’t work as intended and which unnecessarily bloats the experience into more of an admin job rather than a fun game.
On top of this key fundamental areas of the game such as the transfer market fail to work properly and fail to see improvements year on year. With unrealistic transfers; great players rotting in the reserves and an AI which completely ignores player form in favour of hidden stats in the background. But further still, some of the newly developed features have taken a huge step backwards, this year the scouting system has over gone a huge overhaul to align the game more to real life, but it’s  really poorly explained to the player in game and doesn’t seem to work very well, it’s a mess.
I have over 150 hours in the game, I’ve played over 3 seasons in the lower leagues in England for my career save (and also 1 season in the Premier League in the beta) and I’ll admit I’m enjoying it, but that same familiar frustration of coming across the same problems I see year after year, game after game is too much.
+ Addictive as always and satisfying when you get success
+ I really like the new graphics engine, the stadiums CAN look great
+ Medical centre is a nice new addition, even if it’s rarely looked at
+ I really like new team dynamics/hierarchy feature
- Fundamental game systems such as the AI in the transfer market is still very poor. As stated above great players rot in the reserves with no interest from elsewhere, form is not taken into account at all, silly transfers
- More features added to further bloat the game with tedious, mundane, administrative tasks making the game feel more of chore
- The new scouting system is crap, poorly explained in game and doesn’t seem to work as intended, the interface is an absolute mess
- Animations in the match engine are still pretty bad, often destroying the immersion
- The design choices of the stadiums is terrible in the lower leagues, what’s the deal with the picnic tables?
- It’s yet another game in the series which fails to make big strides forward
I will play this game all year and no doubt get around 1000 hours out of it, but can I recommend it to others? If you really want an FM game and don’t own 15, 16 or 17 then maybe go for it. If you are hard-core fan then maybe go for it. But outside of that, overall I cannot recommend this game to other players. It suffers from the same old issues and has the same frustrations that all the previous games have seen. In my opinion Sports Interactive should freeze development on new features and get the fundamental game systems working correctly or at least move them forward. I’m sick of a broken transfer system and rushed poorly implemented new features like the new scouting. So with regret…
