It mainly involves stalking other players with your rifle scope, while not giving your position away. Only problem is that not so many people are playing multiplayer. The DLC maps, which are fairly impressive, had no one playing at all when I tried to find a game.
Sniper Ghost Warrior 2 is also surreal and ridiculous in a way that I really enjoy. I mean I don’t know if the developers intended for the voice acting to be so funny. The game appears to be a great example of ‘funny without meaning to be’. As I think they might of been trying to create a serious and realistic tone. However the Commander Wheeler character in particular sounds like a Thunderbird and his dialogue is ridiculous. The voice acting and dialogue, among other things, is pretty hilarious, throughout the whole single player experience.
This game is kind of an entertaining mix between guilty pleasure nonsense and genuinely engaging gameplay. Some of the areas can feel a bit empty and under developed at times. However, the focus here is primarily on the sniping mechanics, which are implemented quite well. I also played through the DLC campaign called Siberian Strike and I enjoyed that too.
I had a good time with this one overall and I would certainly recommend that you give it a try.

RAID: World War II is the first game of Lion Game Lion, formed mostly by Ex-OVERKILL members and having made DLC content for PD2 before this.
The Allies are losing the war, and a group of 4 prisoners of war have been freed by Control (John Cleese) as a last resort to turn the tables around. You will have to destroy the Nazi's weapons, resources, and men. And of course, stealing their gold to get paid.
The 4 characters are unique and very likeable. You have Sterling, the gentlemanly Brit who is calm and witty in every situation; Rivet, the rude American ex-gangster who cracks wise and is always looking for a fight; Kurgan, the crazy Russian who enjoys destruction and speaks in third person; and Wolfgang(my fav), the German ex-SS who is extremely campy and hammy.
The gameplay has the PAYDAY DNA, but it's different enough to be its own thing. Although considered a "PD2 reskin" by many, it's actually similar to PAYDAY: The Heist. The gameplay is challenging, and you will need your teammates to survive. Although the enemy AI is really bad, it's compensated by numbers, and the 4 Special enemies, who will give you trouble, the Flamer specially.
The raids are also varied and interesting in setting and objectives. You have a castle where you have to kill 2 ratting Russian generals, a bridge where you have to derail a train and rob its gold, a trainyard where you'll rob the Amber Room, a flakturm where you will destroy a blimp...
Apart from normal Raids, there's also one of the strong points of the game: Operations. Operations are a combination of modified raids with different objective, coupled with missions where you will have to drive around Berlin to complete multiple objective, all within a small storyline. There are 2 at the moment, Clear Skies, with 6 Raids, and Rhinegold, with 4.
Also, you can find intel during raids that will unlock one of the 2 Outlaw Raids, which are "consumable" raids unsanctioned by Control where the main objective is stealing gold. This is going to be your main source of gold.
These raids are also designed to be replayable, with most objective and item locations having RNG. Coupled with the leveling and the challenges, it's a game you will spend quite some time on.
You have 4 classes: Recon, Assault, Insurgent and Demolitions. They all have very similar skills, but they are largely based around their War Cries, basically the Ultimate Skill of each class.
The game has a great deal of customization, being able to change the clothing of your character (you get clothes by random drops after raids), and weapons have upgrades that you unlock by completing their challenges, you can also get gold bars after missions, which you can use to upgrade your camp with cool decorations.
On the technical side, it's pretty flawed, though. The graphics are bad, to be blunt. And on my personal opinion, while the game is fun, 40$ is too much of a price right now.. There's also quite a bunch of bugs, but these are being fixed at a rapid pace by the devs. Which brings me to my last point and one of the biggest reasons I recommend the game: the developers.
Lion Game Lion is full of nice people. They care about the game, and you can see the signs everywhere: not only are they listening to the feedback and fixing bugs swiftly, but they also communicate a lot. They respond to a lot of threads in the forums and are quite active in the Discord.
The game definetly has potential to be better, and looking at the devs, it definetly will be better, so if you are not interested in it right now, I recommend you to keep an eye on it, at least. On a sale, I definetly reccomend it.

First of all: I enjoy this game. A lot. I supported the developers (I preordered the special edition) and I think they did a great job and are still working hard on this game. I can happily look past all flaws and bugs, but can I recommend this game to a buyer that doesn't think like me? No, not at it's current state. Steam reviews are for customers, not for being supportive to companies I like. Of course I will adjust this review as soon as the major flaws are fixed.
In Raid: World War II you control one of four characters, Rivet, Sterling, Wolfgang or Kurgan to sabotage the German war machine behind enemy lines. Your missions mostly consist of search and destroy and you are attacking key locations/equipment. To accomplish this, you can select between four classes, Recon, Assault, Insurgent or Demolitions. Each class features it's unique war cry that grants you (and your teammates) a buff for a short time and can be replenished by killing enemies. Besides, you have a skill tree tied to the level of your character that offers various persistent perks, like faster reload time or more ammo.
Some of the raids start in stealth and can be stealthed up to a certain point, some start loud right away. Either way, your main goal is to fight off hordes of nazi soldiers and special units (Flamethrowers, Snipers and so on) to complete a series of objectives and win the raid. There are single day raids or operations, which go over multiple days. Your progress will save after each completed day.
You will get XP depending on the difficulty, number of players and challenge card (I will explain them later) active. If you level up, you can spend one skill point for one of three predetermined skills. And you can select only one, so choose wisely.
You will also get a lootbox, depending on the amount of dogtags you collected during the raid and your overall performance. They contain cosmetics, XP boosts, challenge cards or gold. You can use the gold for various things, buying cosmetics for your hideout or, more importantly, to reset your skills, if you want to change your playstyle. The challenge cards act as a mutator during the raid, having positive and negative side effects and a XP multiplier.
During the raids you can complete weapon challenges for your currently equipped weapon (e. g. score x headshots). When completed, they unlock different tiers of upgrades for damage, stabilty, accuracy or clip size.
Positive:

Negative:
Unfortunately I can't recommend it at the moment due to the technical issues.

RAID: World War II is an embarrassment of failed imitation of several year old games, Payday: The Heist and Payday 2; mostly losing the strengths of both and going further beyond their weaknesses to deliver a uniquely flawed game.
While Lion Game Lion is very good at level design as far as throwing more varied challenges and goals in a certain map than just waiting for a drill, they apparently have no one that understands the real draw of both Paydays is replayability and easy player customization that allows people to quickly shift between weapons and character abilities to craft different types of play. In RAID, you are expected to GRIND like this was a bot infested MMO to gather the maybe let’s say 4-5million XP from even Very Hard Raids that will deliver maybe at a maximum 10,000 or so XP, give or take if you actually can complete a heist with 2-3 other human participants, from level 1 to 40. The currently very small pool of weapons are locked behind specific classes and their challenges to unlock upgrades which are locked behind level specific tiers that maybe only one class has over another. If you wanted to play with shotguns in recon than too bad, start a whole nother profile. Which itself has to be GRINDed up from 1-40 too, making you wait to access the mods for a gun that you already completed the challenge earlier in a previous build, yet don't have the level to slap on a gun.
Then there is the♥♥♥♥♥♥show of a group lobby they have, you cannot change or add challenge cards if you ready up, the netcode makes Payday 2 look stable, and god help you if you can't even join because who knows what else is wrong with RAID today.
Hell, RAID expects you to do this across at least 4 profiles to "experience" every class, instead of utilizing something Payday 2 figured out back in 2014 to let you even just relevel several skill profiles very easily without an increasing amount of gold bars that you also have to grind, 1 to maybe 40 or 50 bars a successful Outlaw Raid, for the privilege of sculpting even one skillset.
And on top of all this, RAID asks about $10 more for a game with even less refinement than either of the paydays at launch. This as you could expect, limited it player base considerably to maybe 200-500 active players total. RAID is a Gordian knot of bad ideas that while not impossible to fix, with them all tangled together, they put the life of the game in jeopardy before even its first few months of release.  LGL is very open about wanting to adapt to the demands of the player base and fix this game, however, RAID was likely rushed maybe even years before it was actually ready to release to meet a deadline and has been seemingly left for dead by Starbreeze without the money and programming aid it desperately needs to course correct at this point.
If you are interested in a Payday like game, stick to the previous incarnations for now. I cannot in good faith recomend a game that likely will never get better to anyone.

Well, in all honesty, I have never beaten a Dark souls game or Bloodborne, and personally didn't like Dark Souls nearly as much as I've liked Salt & Sanctuary.
I have just beaten the game and entered NG+ and will now be moving on to play DS2, but will definitely be coming back to this game again.
Pros:
Nice Artstyle, Nice environments/areas to explore, cool enemies, cool bosses, good leveling system (Works on a skill tree system, but with some small twists), good platforming, fantastic area progression and a nice feeling of dread farther on in the game.
Cons:
-While the music is good, you tend to listen to most of the same songs or abience throughout the game and it's hard to recall any songs other than the Boss fight theme, Sanctuary theme, and Nameless God, while there's other songs, they just don't feel like they play as often.
-Enemies are cool and all that, but some of them are not fun or really engaging to fight. That number is really small, but the only enemy I can say for certain is a horrible enemy, is the main skeleton. They have an abillity where they can teleport and are invincible throughout the entire animation when beginning to teleport, and for a small opening when they finish, and that small opening is even smaller when you take into consideration most weapons have serious delay on them, and the chances of you reading them is nearly impossible because sometimes when they finish teleporting they just teleport off somewhere again, making you miss your shots. The little ♥♥♥♥ers will teleport ANYWHERE on the map and will sometimes *teleports behind you* nothing personnel kid and just get 5 free hits on you, and then another one will teleport to you and they will both poison you and probably kill you. Really just an unfair enemy to fight, and really annoying. There's only 2 of them that you will meet often, but even then you will hate them.
-For a game based on platforming, about mid way through the game when you start getting powers called "Brands", you get a lot more platforming (Wall jumps, air dashes) and this makes platforming fun and even sometimes really cool when you implement it into your actual fights, but when this starts to happen, you start to realize the game's platforming is well... a bit iffy. In an attempt to balance air dashes and wall jumps, once you fall a certain distance clinging on to walls and air dashes do almost nothing, as you will just fall while sliding down the wall, or just move forward with the dash. I understand this was a balancing thing, but sometimes that window to air dash or wall jump felt a bit small and you feel a bit cheated on your death.
-Ledge grabbing. Or for the love of god ledge grabbing in this game is slow and unresponsive on 15% of the walls you try to scale. Sometimes you want to grab a wall to jump, but you grab the ledge, you try to grab the ledge, but you just miss or fall to your death. Simple flaws but can be very annoying when the you got a lot of salt when just die cause the game's ledge was programmed a bit higher than the other's.
Now I'll just list some of my "Mehs" with this game.

Most other games will give you a hint, but this game just gives you an item, tells you to go wild and you just wander around wondering what do you with your life.
Overall, really good game, and I give it a 9/10

TL DR: Someone thought how Dark Souls would be as a metroidvania and made this game.
I played this game months ago and playing it for a few hours made me rage so hard that I was even going to delete it. I wanted to give it another chance and now, I saw the true potential in it.
Dark and pessimistic rooms, blood and gore, destruction, dead people in the background, old and scary environment is what you will see in this game if you want to play it. It really gives you the feeling that this game is properly designed for its purpose, which is making you feel vulnerable. It makes you feel like you are always in a danger, which you almost always are. Carefully designed traps and map design also boost this feeling. Overall the atmosphere is way too good considering that this is a metroidvania game. If you enjoy horror games or the atmosphere in horror games, you will enjoy the scenery.
General idea of the game is that you have to die in order to win. Dying is not an end, instead it is a step for you to both improve yourself and improve your character. You collect what's called salts in order to buy skills and items that help you kill your enemies. If you die, you lose your salts to the enemy that killed you and you have to kill that creature in order to obtain your lost salts. Returning to the place that you died usually gives you more salt than before since every creature resets if you die or if you save the game in a checkpoint. Which is also good because that means you can farm salts with killing creatures using checkpoints.
Most of the time actions are fluid and react really fast. Your characters reaction time changes with how much you carry and what weapon you choose which makes a great addition to the game and adds depth. If you want to be tanky and take lots of hits, you move like a truck which means you can't even swing your sword in time, however if you don't wear heavy armor or any armor whatsoever, you fly like a butterfly and sting like a bee. But don't forget that you also take so much damage so that even 1 hit might kill you.
Map is carefully designed so that every part of the game is connected without loading screens. Going left,right,up,down always takes you to new places. While this should make you feel like you lost your way, game somehow points you to the right direction without being obvious. Locked doors or unactivated elevators prevents you from going to the wrong places. Also there are candles in the background that lets you know that you are about to fight a boss. It is really helpfull considering that fighting with a boss requires preperation. Every part of the map is actually pretty smart. I didn't feel like getting swarmed by creatures or feel like something was wrong.
My only problem with the gameplay was that rolling left and right is not well designed, most of the time I found myself getting stuck in front of a boss or getting damage while rolling even if I manage to roll behind an enemy. It was the main reason why I raged so hard.
Overall the gameplay feels like a good rpg game, fast and responsive with any weapon. Hit register is also properly designed which is a huge plus.
The soundtrack of this game is really heavy, you can even say that it is psychologically heavy. It stresses you out as it should do, makes you feel the atmosphere even more. You always feel stressed while leaving safe zones because you constantly expect dying in every step, soundtrack of this game doubles that stres with sometimes heavy and sometimes fast musics.
There are many enemies created which are ranged and melee with a lot of different styles. You have to find a tactic for each of them since some of them have a heavy attack which you can foresee easily while some other creature uses magic that hits any floor in the visible screen. I overall enjoyed having a lot of different enemies in different areas, it made the game feel longer and harder to master.
Bosses are another topic that this game is pretty good about. All of them are different with their attacks, styles, damage types, weapons and sizes. You literally have to find a strategy to beat all of them because it really is not easy to kill them in the first time.
This game make you feel both stronger than everything and weaker than anything at the same time. You try to kill an enemy for an hour feeling rage and hatred, then eventually you beat it and feel like you are on the clouds. Also the depth that this game has is huge, it even has religions which I still couln't master. You can create lots of different game styles with different skill paths and you can even change the items that you use to completely change the gameplay of the game. Also just search its skill selection screen and you will understand what I'm talking about when I say depth. I found myself struggling to reach the outer circle of the skill tree because it is huge.
I think this game deserves 9/10 easily. That -1 point is for the fact that rolling is still♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥me off.
If you love games that are hard but rewarding and also have depth that will make you searching the internet every half an hour, don't even think about it, just buy this game and play it for many hours.
If you're a fan of the Souls' games, you MUST own and play this. There's just no better way to put it.

Probably the best received game of the original "trilogy"...
Assassins Creed was originally planned as a trilogy, through which is wound a modern-day thread to give it depth and meaning, and to tie the three ancestor's lives together with meaning. Assassins Creed 2 was the "Deus Ex" of the series, it set the standard for all that followed, but was never bested. "often copied, never equalled" as the saying goes, this was to set the theme and style for all that followed but they were mere "essays in the craft" as a famous author once wrote.
Set in Renaissance Italy, it tells the story of Ezio Auditore da Firenze, Ezio of the Auditore family of Florence. Renaissance Italy was a formative time for Italy and mainland Europe, and was an era where famous architects and artists abounded and marked their place in history. Here in this very city you can climb Florence Cathedral, designed by Giotto and engineered by Brunelleschi, wonder at the many re-created towers of San Gimignano and take in the beauty of Tuscany and it's many re-created landmarks.
This whole game is rich in history and has had entire regions of Italy, complete with it's famous people and landmarks, transplanted into it's very core, and this is your playground.
Following on from the original Assassins Creed, which introduced you to Altaïr Ibn-La'Ahad who was a member of a cult based on the real-life Ha-shi-shin, more correctly referred to in history as the "Asasiyun", Ezio continues the story-arc of Desmond Miles, a modern-day descendant of the original Assassins, on his unbidden quest to seek out the Piece of Eden, and to recover it and use it in defense against The Templars. A typical "them and us" scenario but beautifully executed, immersing the player into selected regions of real-life history, and merging it with a simple yet intricate fictitious concept.
Throughout the game you, the player, become Ezio, a rogue, a charmer and a parkour master... and possibly one of the most-loved characters of the entire series. You start off with nothing, but following the in-game death of your father and brothers, you very quickly learn the arts of stealth, stealing and most important of all, the deadly art of assassination. At fist it is only for revenge but surrounded by friends and family, you are slowly guided and "trained" to become an efficient killer in order to "take out" various city officials who are actually Templar Agents, bent on the domination of "the people".
As you progress through the game you learn more about the Templars and the Assassins, and the reason behind their long-term enmity, and the importance and urgency of trying to thwart them in their own deadly quest to dominate the entire earth.
All this content-rich plot is set in a beautifully recreated and innovative period of our own history when creativity was at it's peak and when famous people such as Leonardo da Vinci and Machiavelli actually lived and contributed to all that we know today.
Playing this game is more that just playing through a simple plot, it is an opportunity to experience  one of the most important periods of European history, and to virtually walk the very streets and admire the legendary architecture of Renaissance Italy, which has been an inspiration to us right down to this day.

One of the finest stealth actions games ever made. Story takes place in an alternate steampunk universe dominated by plague, death, and the supernatural. One of my main complaints about stealth games is their slow pace and often unforgiving trial/error gameplay. Dishonored solves this with a simple-but-genius mechanic of "Blink", an instant short range teleport, and piles on a series of fun abilities with unique situational uses. The open-level game design allows for multiple solutions to combat or story resolutions. A deep, dynamic game that tests your skill and moral compass. My only central complaint would be the story. Characters are stock tropes, and you can see the twists and turns coming a mile off, and it's a disservice to build such a lovely, grim dystopia and populate it with such a drab story. The few good character moments (mostly from supporting characters) are too few and far between.
PROS:
- Diverse set of stealth / action mechanics
- All stealth abilities feel useful, powerful, and synergize well. Fun to set up Rube Goldberg solutions.
- Strong sense of world through gameplay / discovered lore. A highlight.
- All missions have a non-lethal outcome, which affects world depending on choices
- Levels have open concept with multiple routes
- Can turn off individual HUD elements as desired! A welcome addition.
CONS:
- Default HUD is cluttered and too hand-holdy. Can adjust, though.
- Repetitive sound effects from powers get old fast.
- Obvious and not terribly interesting revenge-style story. A yawn.
- Can get overpowered easily in mid-game with runes
- Hand to hand combat is bland and all combat abilities worthless, thankfully discouraged

The Miami hotline left an indelible mark on the independent scene when it came to light, so it's no wonder it spawned many followers. "12 is Better Than 6" is one of them and probably one of the better ones.
It is remarkable how much the core of the game is reminiscent of Hotline Miami, even if its scenery and style are extremely different.
It's still a top-down game, but everything is black and white except blood
The action of the game is set in the second half of the nineteenth century on the unbridled border of America; classic western surroundings. You play as The Mexican, an infamous gunman.
That's what you do most of the time: you shoot a lot of bad guys. The fight is fast and deadly. Both you and your enemies are killed with a single bullet. Considering that the enemies are more numerous on each map, it forces you to take careful approach and thoughtful moves or sequences.
You have at your disposal a small, classic western arsenal: revolver, two-pipe, rifle, dynamite and occasionally a stationary Gatling, an additional bow and a knife for silent killings.
Unfortunately, there is not much diversity when it comes to enemies or maps, and after some time they become repetitive.
Dialogue at best is amateurish, and history is a terrible mess.
If you have never been interested in Western stereotypes, many times you wonder what exactly was the point of the mission.
Do not choose this game, expecting a fascinating narrative.
In conclusion, I recommend this game to Miami Hotline fans and similar games. Everyone else should think twice.

Hi all,
I bought this game years and years ago (not sure 6 or more?) I finally take the time to write a short review.
This is a Tower Defence (TD) game which I use to play on Warcraft/Starcraft Mods.
The game is actually fairly easy to understand as there are only 10 towers which can each be upgraded 2 times from basic (green) to level 2(Yellow) to max level (Red).
As always each tower has different strenghts and 2 towers are for pure support:
1) Temporals slows enemies down
2) Command Tower which gives you extra resources if an enemy is killed within their sphere of influence.
3) 1 Tower is for Flying enemies only (Missile)
The rest is a mixture from single Direct damage (Gun, Cannon, Laser) To AOE (Tesla, Inferno, Meteor, Concussion)
Using upgraded towers is usually a wiser choice then mass towers unless you play specific maps where you must shape the path of the enemy to ensure you have enough time to inflict maximum damage.
The favorite part for me is the AI which comments and advises you throughout the game and the community levels + expansions offered. The price , as far as I remember, was cheap and really worth it as now 6 years later I am still playing it and currently trying to get a golden medal high score on each map:-)
Addictive, fun and surpringly tactical as you can utilize many different strategies with enough room to build on most maps.
Fully recommended!
Kind regards,

Perhaps the most intense of simulators, following the world’s most popular sport, Football Manager 2018 throws you into the deep end for an immersive experience. This title mostly follows all the aspects of football that take place behind the scenes, touching on training, locker room atmosphere, contracting, scheduling, and press releases. I’m sure returning fans of the series may feel at home, but newcomers beware: this is not FIFA and is heavily emphatic on the “manager” part.
Before you do anything, the game allows you to create your very own avatar, which you can design. The graphics are not anything to get too excited about, but that was not where my attention was fixated. There are additional details, such as place of birth, favorite team, and age. These small things do have some impact on your development as a coach. For instance, I noted that I was from New York and was 23 years old, and the press acknowledged these things. They asked whether I felt intimidated by coaching a team with members that were older than me. They also asked if being a New Yorker would help with team solidarity, because that’s where my team is from.
The UI takes some time getting used to, mostly because you have multiple tabs dealing with different things, such as emails, social media, scouting, training, etc. It is very extensive. Thankfully, you can delegate tasks to the AI via your assistant coach to take care of things you may not have any clue how to work. I think the layout of things is well done and easy to navigate through, which is a plus. I think that shortcuts to certain pages would be helpful, because you tend to visit only a few specific ones per turn unless there is something you are specifically looking for. You can also subscribe to certain players, teams, and journalists like your own mini social media hub, which is very true to real life.
My team’s issues lay in leadership and unit cohesion (the game points it out to you under the “dynamics tab”), so I tried to remedy the issue via training and arranging friendlies/scrimmages with less reputable teams. That worked to an extent, but I found that the team’s members felt isolated from each other. This is where my love-hate relationship with the game starts. I think it is really cool that a simulator takes social groups into account, but the groups often refuse to intersect. I try to have the older members train the younger ones to improve their game, and they either agree or disagree, but they don’t seem to bond in any capacity. Building unity among players is a challenge, but I have only found results in the locker room atmosphere and leadership when we win matches.
Players are fascinating to interact with, but they can also infuriate you just as easily. They don’t really seem to take your instructions into account when they play (you only see highlights from each game, so I could be wrong) and they tend to get injured VERY easily. You may think you’re playing the wrong football because all these injuries. Players also tend to act like they deserve more than they actually do, which comes off as pompous on my part, but in my experience, I’ve found players wanting a lighter training regimen while their training is already light. I’ve also found players demanding first team chances even if they are still recovering from fatigue. Some players are still “considering their options,” straining your relationship with that player even further.
There are also some small things you can say to your players before matches, at halftime, and afterwards. Depending on your team, you may have players getting complacent on the field. Perhaps they are getting frustrated. You can make the difference with a few choice words. It is up to you to gauge the correct tone and wording to gain the respect of your team, often times having to be stern and candid about their performance. My advice: don’t get cocky, because somehow the AI will have more possession of the ball no matter which team you choose to coach.
I had a good time trying to see if I have what it takes to manage a professional football team. Aaaannndd the answer is a bit of yes and a bit of no. The game does teach you how to effectively delegate certain tasks, but you can learn how to manage them yourself. I would definitely say there is A LOT of content here and plenty of room for replayability. I think a fair rating for this game is an 8.5 out of 10.

I think ToME was the last big roguelike I hadn't tried yet. Every time I went hunting for a new roguelike, I'd find ToME, look at the screenshots, wrinkle my nose at the tileset, and move on.
A combination of peer pressure and exasperation at the four million half-baked early access games I'm waiting on finally tipped me over the edge to get it -- and I'm glad I did. Finally. I've been missing a lot of fun.
So! Here's what I'm digging about ToME:
1. Maybe this is mentioned in the reviews for it, and I've just somehow always glossed over it, but ToME has a really interesting set of skills that rely on various energy bars, cooldowns, and other variables. Even my very-straight-forward berserker has a hopping action bar that's a handful to manage. Honestly, it reminds me (pleasantly) of MMO combat. Just, you know, without the ganking, loot drama, time commitment, spouse aggro, RSI...
2. It's not early access. Invictus, I take back every eye-roll I ever aimed at you for avoiding the early access games I'd recommend to you, because I'm there now. Holy mother of pogo-jumping Christ, is it pleasant to play a game that's finished and working and not possibly maybe someday in the future going to not suck, honest.
3. There's a global chat where everyone currently playing ToME can talk with eachother. I'm really enjoying this, even though it's usually just a ticker for achievements and the new and exciting ways people are finding to die. Occasionally conversations or questions will spring up. Feeling like a single-player game has a shared community is a new thing to me, I guess.
I only have two quibbles with the game, and they're utterly cosmetic: some of the tunes aren't so hot (and all of them are short enough that the repetition wears on you very quickly), and I really don't like the tileset. It's what has put me off getting the game multiple times over the past years. They're too complex to hit my pixel-art happy buttons, and too amateurish to look good. It's some kinda tepid middle-ground, designed-by-committee tileset that makes Baby Jesus cry.
And I'm having so much fun with it that I can look past it. If you like roguelikes at all, get it. Seriously.

This game reminds me so much of the old arcade classic "Metal slugs, in regards to format, graphics, and even playstyle. But this genious game offers so much more with crafting, rank system, upgrades, multiplayer, mission types and even with enemy types.
When i first started playing, i fully expected to just run through a one direction level blasting everything without much thought, but it suprised me.
Firstly, each level can be "explored".  You can go up, down, left, right.. there is a full map to traverse!
Each enemy has vantages that can make you think as you approach it. It's not all mindless blasting ( well you can try, but you get beat up a fair bit ). Then there is the bosses. They each are challenging and have unique weaknesses.
Pro's:

Throw Metal Slug, Megaman, and a dash of Metroidvania in a blender and you have Mercenary Kings.  This was a Kickstarted game from the creators of the Scott Pilgrim Vs. The World beat 'em up and it shows in the art style big time.
It has a lot of levels to go through but many of them reuse the same areas, which honestly makes a lot of sense as some of them are quite huge and you can learn the level more, but it still feels really repetitive.
I also found the Boss fights more annoying and bullet spongey than actually fun to fight. Chasing them down all over the map was also kinda annoying. They're really the only kind of missions I didn't like though.
So if you really like Metal Slug, I cannot fathom why you wouldn't like this as well.

Hearts of Iron IV. I am almost certain that this game has been hijacked and tampered with by French nationalists. The reasoning for this is that, due to the horrible AI, the French rarely ever surrender (0/10 very unrealistic) as the Germans decide to declare war on the allies while stationing all of their troops on the danish border (Maybe they are trying to beat their previous world record of forcing the fastest capitulation, though 3 hours is pretty difficult to top).
In all seriousness though, as a huge Paradox fan and as someone who has spent over 1000 hours on their other games, I can sadly not recommend this one in its current state.
Pros:
-
I like how easy it has been made for alternative history to play out (with this being an option, so if you want everything to roughly follow its historical route you still can). In my very first game, I turned Australia nationalist and formed a faction with Japan where we reigned terror on Asia and the pacific.
-
Want to play as North Korea in 2016 and nuke the USA? Download the modern era mod and go for it. Want to try and hold back the zombie horde while the Allies and Axis trade fronts? Download the infection mod
Neutral:
-
Being able to play any nation in the world and take it in any direction you want gives you many opportunities. The focus trees (though only available for majors as of now) help this out even more. However, with the reasons listed below, you're not going to want to play for that long anyway in it's current state which is why this is neautral.
Cons:
-
They will often leave fronts completely unguarded while stationing all of their troops on some arbitrary border of someone they're not at war with. There will be many "what the hell" moments as you question the AI's choices and intelligence.
-
It's lost a lot of complexity that made the previous Hearts of Iron games great. It feels hollow. As usual, I'm sure they'll flush the game out with DLCs but that shouldn't be the case. Other paradox games take upwards of 100 hours to learn. I felt like I knew everything about this one after just 10 hours or less.
-
Due to the two above reasons, the game is ridiculously easy to play. Playing as one of the major powers is pretty much pointless as you will steamroll the world before 1941. This makes it no fun. There is no strategy needed and I'm sure a 10 year old could pull off a world conquest as Ireland.

RAID: World War II is an embarrassment of failed imitation of several year old games, Payday: The Heist and Payday 2; mostly losing the strengths of both and going further beyond their weaknesses to deliver a uniquely flawed game.
While Lion Game Lion is very good at level design as far as throwing more varied challenges and goals in a certain map than just waiting for a drill, they apparently have no one that understands the real draw of both Paydays is replayability and easy player customization that allows people to quickly shift between weapons and character abilities to craft different types of play. In RAID, you are expected to GRIND like this was a bot infested MMO to gather the maybe let’s say 4-5million XP from even Very Hard Raids that will deliver maybe at a maximum 10,000 or so XP, give or take if you actually can complete a heist with 2-3 other human participants, from level 1 to 40. The currently very small pool of weapons are locked behind specific classes and their challenges to unlock upgrades which are locked behind level specific tiers that maybe only one class has over another. If you wanted to play with shotguns in recon than too bad, start a whole nother profile. Which itself has to be GRINDed up from 1-40 too, making you wait to access the mods for a gun that you already completed the challenge earlier in a previous build, yet don't have the level to slap on a gun.
Then there is the♥♥♥♥♥♥show of a group lobby they have, you cannot change or add challenge cards if you ready up, the netcode makes Payday 2 look stable, and god help you if you can't even join because who knows what else is wrong with RAID today.
Hell, RAID expects you to do this across at least 4 profiles to "experience" every class, instead of utilizing something Payday 2 figured out back in 2014 to let you even just relevel several skill profiles very easily without an increasing amount of gold bars that you also have to grind, 1 to maybe 40 or 50 bars a successful Outlaw Raid, for the privilege of sculpting even one skillset.
And on top of all this, RAID asks about $10 more for a game with even less refinement than either of the paydays at launch. This as you could expect, limited it player base considerably to maybe 200-500 active players total. RAID is a Gordian knot of bad ideas that while not impossible to fix, with them all tangled together, they put the life of the game in jeopardy before even its first few months of release.  LGL is very open about wanting to adapt to the demands of the player base and fix this game, however, RAID was likely rushed maybe even years before it was actually ready to release to meet a deadline and has been seemingly left for dead by Starbreeze without the money and programming aid it desperately needs to course correct at this point.
If you are interested in a Payday like game, stick to the previous incarnations for now. I cannot in good faith recomend a game that likely will never get better to anyone.

I've played over 30 hours in the game as well as several hundred in Payday 2. I also have played many similar games way back into the 1990's. On top of all that I am a bit of a military history kind of person and an avid shooter. All of these things considered I like the game, not because the game fulfills what I want in each of these areas - it doesnt - but because I think I understand the aim and I support that. The first time you beat a RAID and see Hitler go insane it should dawn on you what the game actually is, not a true to history simulator with excruciatingly accurate weapons and uniforms or a hyper serious shooter along the lines of Payday where the slightest mistake in jut your loadout can fail the mission. This is a comedy game in a WWII setting. It's Hogan's Heroes meets Kelley's Heroes. As a shooter I absolutely cringe that removing the stock and shortening the barrel of the shotgun somehow reduces recoil and raises accuracy. As a historian I cringe that Kurgan is wearing a gas mask from over ten years after the war ended. As a gamer I get bored by the lack of variety in weapons, missions, and characters.
And yet, I love the game - I payed for the special edition on a pre-order and do not regret it. John Cleese reminds me so much of Rowan Atkinson as Captain Blackadder, and the Hitler in this game is almost exactly like Larry Hovis from Hogan's Heroes. I will continue to put up with the problems so long as that kind of content keeps coming.
The game is good, it's fun, it's a great way to kill some time and have a laugh. The problems will iron out over time and content will continue to be added, I payed my money to ensure that LGL has a chance to do that. This isnt Doom - it's Wolfenstein. It isnt Band of Brothers - it's Hogan's Heroes. It isnt Forgotten Weapons - it's FPS Russia. And it will only get better - if we support that.
I reccomend this game so that others will join me in supporting it to get better.
UPDATE: It's been a bit of time since launch and my original review. Content has been slow but is coming. The game has so much potential and I have high hopes that it will continue.

TL;DR Raid: World War 2 is an average game at best, hoping to succeed what PAYDAY 2 couldn't but fails to do so due to the engine and gameplay mechanics Lion Game Lion has chosen and agreed on.
Raid: WW2 is an Arcade-y FPS set in, shocker, World War 2. Your main plan in this game is to foil Hitler's plans and stop the nazis from winning. The game features 4 players, 4 classes, 11 raids (missions), 2 operations (multi-day missions), and around 16 firearms as of 10/11/17. Raid is very similar to a game LGL has also helped work on, PAYDAY 2. Both use the same engine and almost the same gameplay. Raid aims to be the successor of PD2, hoping to improve on what PD2 wanted to be. And in some regards, it did. However, there are things that Raid absolutely failed in.
PROS:
+Interaction between characters is great compared to PD2, it really feels like your character actually has a part in what's going on.
+The developers do seem to care about the community, and seem to do as much bug fixing as possible.
+Animations are mostly good, some could be improved however.
+Level design is good, it feels like I know where I am going in a map and know where each objective is.
+If you've played PD2, this game will feel right at home when it comes to gameplay.
+Killing Nazis.
MIXED:
+-Feels like a huge expansion to PD2. Some like myself would be fine with that, since I was expecting it to play extremely similar to it, however some people may not appreciate that and hoped that this game would go in a new direction. Specifically, the movement, looking around, options, driving, all of it feels like it was built from the foundations of PD2.
+-Graphics. Sure they don't look good, they could be better, but I'd rather focus on gameplay rather than graphics.
+-Voice acting could be better, plus some of the jokes they "crack out" get old really fast.
+-Health and the removal of Armor. Armor, if you are familiar with it in PD2, is removed. You only have a health bar now, which you need to constantly keep up with if you want to survive. Your health will not automatically regenerate, you need to find health kits on the ground or in set places to heal yourself.
CONS:
-Gunplay feels weak. When you are facing off against the nazis, you would think shooting a nazi in the head one time would be enough to kill him. However, in this game, enemies are spongy and absorb many of your bullets.
-Same engine. Diesel is a horrible engine, I have no clue why LGL used this engine anyway. It was first used in 2001 for a racing game called Ballistics. It is very outdated and needs to be replaced.
-The Level System. It is absolutely horrible. Within the first 10-15 levels it is acceptable, however after that it becomes a real grind. Doing a normal heist will probably only get you 1/20th of the way towards the next level. And I know what you are saying, "just do hard and very hard mode!" The difficulty spikes up easily when you jump to it from normal. "Get good," you're probably saying, and you might be right. "The easy way to do hard and very hard is to have a group!" My next con will talk more about this.
-The game is dead. Within the last 24 hours (3:41 PM as of 10/11/17), the game has had a 302 player count peak. The overall peak for this game has been 1,429 players. You'd think "oh but this a 4 player co-op game, surely there's enough people to fill THAT much!" but people need to remember this is worldwide, you have no clue how many are actually playing near where you live.
-AI is really horrible. Friendly AI isn't even helpful at all, in fact they're more of a chore. Enemy AI can also shoot your with their faces it seems.
Right now these are all the things I can talk about with some research. The game is fun, but really starts to suffer when you take the grinding and the optimization into play.
Overall, I give it a 5/10. It needs work.

It means it has a lot of fans, inspired other developers to making games and....it's old!
By old i mean outdated graphics, sometimes monotonous gameplay, inhospitable UI and other stuff.
Let's speak about gameplay. You need to defend the core in each mission. Core has 20 energy balls. When enemy comes to the core he takes 1 ball and tries to take it to the exit. If he dies, the energy ball will move back to the core slowly. If new enemy reaches the ball, it will take it. This is pretty interesting mechanic. I am wondering why i haven't met it in other TD games.
The story is nothing special. "Something" is commenting your actions and explaining what is happening. All you need to know that you need to protect the core in each mission against of aliens. There are l lot of aliens in the a lot of missions. So be aware. You have 10 towers to achieve your goal. Actually, there are only 3 at start, new ones will be unlocked later.
Each tower has 3 levels.
I found it very difficult to understand in the battle to understand in the battle which towers are good at the current level, because there are no exact numbers... just health bars. Because of you can't build the perfect defense. You can build only the best maze.
I liked the variety of levels. There were classic levels, maze levels. There were levels with 2 height levels
Pros
- A lot of levels. Some of them has really interesting design
- Each mission has a lot of mods. Story, Story challenge, 10 towers only and etc.
- Each mode of each level contains a special leaderboard.
- An interesting concept of lives. Enemies come from an exit to the core. Than they take Energy ball and go back to the exit. If the enemy dies, a ball flies back with slow speed, but if an new enemy reaches an energy ball it will take it.
Neutral
- All missions are available at start. it's pretty strange.
- There is a plot and voice acting which tells you about it. But I found what this voice tells nothing about the story. It just tells intro phrases at the start of the level and warn you about low core energy level
- Game was originalyl made for consoles. As a PC use i found it pretty uncomfortable.
Cons
- Low variety of towers. Only 10. Each has 3 upgrades which only improve parametres. No extra abilities, no tech tree and etc.
- There is no upgrade system between levels. Your power/tower power is same as at the level one and the last level.
- There are no exact numbers for health, attack damage, range and etc. There are bars. It's not enough for a TD game.
- It's unclear, which tower deals extra damage to which. Also, when there are a lot of enemies. It's unclear at all, you can't distinguish anything. It's just a big battle, where something happen.
- The sound effect of incoming message equals sound of Steam message in chat. It drove me crazy.

Anyway, it contains some good ideas, interesting levels and more than three hundred of gameplay time. So you are aware of flaws now and if you are OK with it, I can recommend this game for you with 70+% discount.

Jedi Knight: Dark Forces II is the second game in the Jedi Knight Series.  With some new tech in the engine, actually its a whole new engine.  Some keen ideas in the story, and a few role-playing game elements mixed in.  Jedi Knight is a visible step up from the path that Dark Forces paved.  But just how much of a step is it, and will it surpass its predecessors Breakdown?
Jedi Knight, in my opinion, has some of the best story telling I’ve seen in games of its era.  It uses what has almost become a lost art, full motion video.  So many games today are switching over to scripted sequences that are rendered right in the game with the engine carrying the load.  While this can be a great tool for the story telling, at times the better tool is a FMV sequence.  The other great thing about Jedi Knight’s FMV’s are that they use live actors.  Actual people interacting with the CGI characters at the CGI locations.  That does a great job of putting you in the world with a small graphic budget.
Jedi Knight had very little compatibility issues, I simply installed it within Steam and in minutes was playing.  At first I had some interesting graphical problems, but with a little help from the Steam Community I got things working in fine order.  The resolution is changeable, but 1280 x 1024 is the highest it goes.  Which was not issues for me, since that’s what I operate with these days.
The game does play full screen, but it goes windowed in between levels and to show the FMV’s.  This sometimes caused issues where the full screen shows a blinking or faded border.  Not a game breaker, but was just an eye-sore.
Controls were a bit clunky, especially the lightsaber combat.  Fighting Storm Troopers was easy enough, but once you had to fight another Jedi it became a real conflict.  There was a definite delay from mouse-click to saber-swing, which made fighting the more challenging foes that much more challenging.  Also Jedi Knight has a auto-aim feature, something akin to the games predecessors, like Doom and Quake.  You only need aim in the general direction and the game will make sure the target is hit.  There are times where this is great and brings the skill level of the game down a notch or two, and a couple points where its an annoyance.
The grenades, or Thermal Detonators as the game would call them, even though actual Thermal Detonators would be far more powerful than what appears in the game.  Either way, they are virtually useless.  A simple click while holding one will practically drop it at your feet.  You throw them at an odd arc that I was unable to get the hang of during my play.  By holding down the fire button you can throw the Det further, but the angles were too hard for me to master and I typically just threw it into the wall or ceiling.
Jedi Knight has a Light/Dark pseudo system.  There is a point in the story where you make the choice of Light or Dark.  This choice is made for you, based on your actions up to that point.  If you were bad and killed too many non-hostile NPC’s then you’ll go the dark route.  I was actually bummed when I got the dark route.  I’d known I had killed a few non-hostiles, but had hoped it wasn’t too many.  And unfortunately I had learned about the prospect of different endings too late into the game, and didn’t want to start it all over again.  So I had just been hoping for the best.
The levels are fairly par for the time.  Mostly inside buildings, with doors, switches, and decent lighting.   Most of the maps have you searching for a key or switch to unlock the other side of the map.  Often this is easy enough, however there were a couple times where the door or switch was annoyingly hard to locate.  In many cases doors are simply a different sheet metal looking texture, and have no marking to show its a door.  And switches can be found in some very strange places.  There was many a time where I strafed walk along a wall rapidly tapping the ‘Use’ key.  Jedi Knight also makes sure to fill the Star Wars cliche of massive bottomless chasms to fall into.
The maps are typicality very large, you can tell the developers were going for that classic Star Wars feel of large spaces.  Many times you can see out windows or over ledges to these vast expanses.   These must have looked nicer years ago.  Because now I feel a lot of the effect is lost in the lower end graphics.  You can clearly see the repeating textures and where the map surface ends and the skybox begins.  Sometimes this is hidden fairly well with fading, as a way to try and preserve the feel of distance.
Overall the game is pretty solid.  It has parts that have short comings, but they all fit together nicely.  Showing just how solid of a game it was back in its day.  It shows a good level of improvement from its predecessor, which raises hopes of a continues level of improvement into the rest of the series.  There are far worst games from the late nineties that you could play.
With a few exceptions, one of the biggest being the headaches some of these older games cause, I did enjoy my time with Jedi Knight.  It was nice to venture back in time with Kyle Katarn.  I know him well in many Star Wars novels, but finally get to take the time to really learn his backstory.

(This is my entry for the Old School Thematic Review Competition)
Quick Note:
People interested in buying Dark Forces II will probably be concerned about compatibility. So, does it work? The answer is no, probably not. If your hardware supports DirectX 9.0 or above, Dark Forces II will experience numerous graphical errors. However, there is a user-made patch that forwards broken functions to working DX7 functions, solving any graphical errors. This patch should have been packaged with the steam version, considering most people who use steam probably have a graphics card that is less than seven-ish years old.
Review:
In Dark Forces II, you step into the shoes of Kyle Katarn as he tracks down his father's murderers. He quickly discovers that Jeric, a Dark Jedi responsible for his father's death, has embarked upon a journey to find the "Valley of the Jedi", a source of power that would make him virtually invincible. Kyle travels home and is granted a lighsaber, and is then able to unlock and evolve his force powers as he confronts Jeric and other Dark Jedi. Your available powers and the game's story adapt to your choices. These choices will eventually lead you down the path to the dark or light side of the force.
The multiple endings are unparalleled even by more modern games, and this introduces a fantastic level of replayability. The replay factor is further increased by an array of secrets hidden in each of the levels that are quite fun to hunt down. You can use powers like speed and jump to reach previously unreachable areas, so upgrading your powers in different areas will yield different secrets, and a different overall gameplay experience.
The gameplay itself is very fun. Dark Forces gave people lightsaber control for the first time, and the level of immersion that it achieves ranks much higher than more modern Star Wars games, such as The Force Unleashed. You are also granted an arsenal of guns, crossbows, rockets, and grenades (along with special attacks on a few of them) to wipe out entire fortresses of enemies. The introduction of 3D graphics also allow you to move into third-person mode, which is a preferable viewpoint for control of your lightsaber. Later in the game, you can unlock powers such as force lightning, grip, throw, and more. The introduction of new elements through the entire game keeps combat exciting and non-repetitive.
There are cutscenes after most levels that feature live actors on pre-rendered backgrounds. Although the rendering was very good, some of the acting was pretty bad in my opinion. However, the actor playing Kyle, the protagonist, is fairly good, and I still looked forward to the cutscenes.
In terms of graphics and design, all of the levels are completely unique. I've played a few games from this same era, and a lot of them are quite brown and lifeless. The game designers did a very good job of incorporating different colors and worlds into the game, giving you an excellent sense of where you were. One level even takes place on a stinking ship, distorting gravity and allowing you to run up walls and elevator shafts (something that you probably saw in Episode III, however this was done many years before).
There was also 3D sound incorporated that game developers reportedly "tweaked extensively" to give whole new level to the immersion already present. This is something that a lot of gamers take for-granted today, but we have to remember that modern sound is "standing on the shoulders of giants", LucasArts undoubtedly being one of the giants in the industry.
Overall, Dark Forces II is a very good and innovative title. It introduced many concepts that were never before seen in gaming, and executed them perfectly. The amount of work put into this game is something we don't often see in the cash-cows of today's gaming industry, and it can be clearly seen in the game's immense success.
Dark Forces II is a timeless classic that will always be held close to the hearts of Star Wars fans. I highly recommend that you play it, it's an absolutely fantastic game!

Tales of Maj'Eyal is - albeit a tiny bit linear - a sub-randomly-generated roguelike adventure that relies more on tactics and availible active skills than any other
game I've played this far (if we don't take keyboard-mashing MMOs such as WoW, EVE and others).
The character progression offers vast customization and has decent impact on your playing style, and that's if you only take one single class into consideration, and there are maaaany various classes (which you have to unlock by playing out certain in-game events such as defeating bosses, gathering lore, completing sidequests or just as rewards for progression). The fact that you have so many options in such a (relatively) linear roguelike gives plenty of replayability, an I'm not even talking about unlockable difficulties and mods that add more challenge, randomness and options. Yes, this game has many, many mods.
If you like roguelikes, difficult games in general and good character progression, get this game!

Tales of Maj'Eyal is a descent of Angband and a great blend of classic rogue-like with modern UI, gameplay mechanics, and a lot of personality.  If you're into clearing dungeons, collecting loot, and leveling up, TOME is one of your best options, specifically if you don't mind complicated mechanics, tactically paced combat, and dying a lot.  The game has tons of replay value, and each playthrough can go from just a few to 40+ hours.  One of the key differences in this and other available recent 'roguelikes' is that this has a fleshed-out world and each playthrough keeps character progression interesting.  This is definitely worth picking up.

Oneshot is a puzzle adventure game where you, the player, are god and you must guide the messiah who is a(genderless cat...looking..person?)named Niko through a world that has lost its sun. The objective of the game is to restore the worlds sun and bring light back to the lands. There will come a time where you must make a vital decision, choose wisely because you only have ONESHOT.
Alright i want to start off by saying that this game absolutely blew my mind. For those of you who have played  UnderTale you may be able to somewhat compare the two but realistically they are very different. The game run's on the concept of breaking the 4th wall and connecting with its player. The world knows you exist and you are able to make a direct connection with Niko that you may not get with any other game which makes this game very special. Certain puzzles also require you to go into your own computer and look for certain documents to find passwords or hints(matrix muh dude).
Other puzzles also require you to obtain a certain item or combine other items in your inventory and find way's to reach a solution. I am not a heavy puzzle game person but i certaintly don't mind them. So if you like puzzle games then this is a good choice for you. Also the game will last a good 6-7 hours but i took my time and i have 13 hours lol. IMO its not as short as they really say just take your time and have fun.
The story is amazing and i highly recommend this game if you played other story heavy games like UnderTale, Lisa, Hyper Light Drifter, and others. As i have stated before you must guide Niko through the world on a mission to restore the sun. There are also multiple endings in the game(that sounds familiar) and your choice will effect the game heavily. Oh and i also forgot to mention that the sun is a lighbulb! which is cute. Very fair warning, THIS GAME WILL MAKE YOU CRY so make sure to have some tissues. There were times when i was playing and i had to stop to vent my emotional stress which is something that i really did not have to do with other games. The game also has unique and relatable characters that you will remember for a long time. Also there was recently an update to the game called Solstice which gives it a true happy ending so i highly recommend playing through that to really finish off the game. So again, if you like story based games then this is a good play.

Full disclosure, I got this free from a giveaway. I would be giving this a neutral rating if I could, but overall I'll fall on the side of Negative. This isn't an insanely indepth review, more like my first impressions.
The first thing to be addressed is that this game isn't really bad. I've enjoyed my time so far with it. However, I have to name three primary issues:
-The game is priced FAR too high. I would definitely only recommend it on sale. Either Payday game will give you better value- The Heist is suitably cheap, and 2 has an insane amount of content for the price. RAID is barely above Payday: The Heist in levels of content (it does have more weapons, but the increased number of heists is offset by half of RAID's being extremely short endeavours, while every heist from The Heist was in-depth and longer) and costs an insane amount more proportionally.
-The levelgrind is ridiculous. Worse than Payday: The Heist and release day Payday 2 combined, and then some. Not only will levelling a character to max take you hundreds of hours, but each new character you make must do this AGAIN! And on top of all that, there's 4 classes that cannot be changed after you've made your character, meaning that the effective "max level" will result in likely thousands of hours of investment to actually reach. I'm fine with this kind of stuff for cosmetic items, but not for the main skillsystem. The "characters" system is completely arbitrary padding (There is no reason they couldn't use Payday 2's system) and even discounting that levelling up still just takes too long. This will likely be modified in later updates, but I'm reviewing the game in front of me right now.
-As a result of Issue 1 (as well as the perception of the game being a payday reskin, the poor graphics and the generally bad impression people had from the game's closed beta), the game's playerbase is tanking more than a... Raging Kingpin with Maniac support? ♥♥♥♥, I can't think of a joke, you get the point. It's floating at around 300 from what I know, which is... Yeah. Make sure you have buddies to play with.
It feels like the game was padded out via levelgrind to attempt to justify the price. A game like Dead By Daylight can get away with that due to being PvP (therefore map variation don't matter much, as long as the PvP element is good enough people will play your game forever), but RAID only has so much gas in the tank, and it feels like it hasn't been fueled up yet.
I advise interested people to check back later for an updated version of the game. New content seems to be coming relatively fast for this game, which is good news. LGL, this isn't personal at all, but when your restaurant only sells appetizers, your customers always leave hungry. You need to ensure that this game has a longer lifespan through more methods than just pumping up the levelgrind- My advice is to utilise the Combo Cards you already have, and use them to make a new gamemode (much like payday 2 did with Crime Spree) in order to make a new way to play the game that's constantly changing every time you run through it, and is never predictable.

Jedi Knight was a day one purchase for me, and back when it blew my young mind and confused me. The story itself was a breathtaking focus back in '97, a landmark for storytelling in FPS games a year ahead of Half-Life--but in a more traditional sense, with a swath of cutscenes with acting and CGI reminiscent of the Beast Within. It was some seriously good♥♥♥♥♥♥ especially for Star Wars fans. (The Jedi Knight series has featured some of the more entertaining EU stories, which I admit to having a soft spot for.)
The level design returns from Dark Forces, this time with full 3D fancy. Occasionally impressive--visually speaking (of course)--and occasionally just balls-out confusing. Where the eff do you go half the time?
But still, man, outside of the sewer crap, I loved this game. The evolution of Kyle Katarn over the course of the story felt amazing to be in control of, even if the lightsaber combat was a huge, clunky letdown. And, as a youngster, the boss fights were the coolest thing ever to look forward to.

The sequel to Star Wars: Dark Forces, now with live action cutscenes, lightsabers, Force Powers and Jedi! This game is another nostalgic piece to my 90’s gaming history and once again, another classic in the Star Wars gaming lineup. Once again, it features Kyle Katarn and his journey to becoming a Jedi and stopping Jerec, the main antagonist from becoming all-powerful. The game also does what its predecessor did not do: gives you some moral choices which affect the ending. The cutscenes are fairly comical (especially Jerec), even though the story is once again, in my opinion, fairly dark. Another outstanding game in an outstanding series of games from LucasArts so I recommend you just buy the entire Jedi Knight series.
*The game requires DosBox however, with the Steam download, everything will be set up for you to enjoy as soon as the game is downloaded.
Story/Characters:
You continue to follow Kyle Katarn in his quest for continuing to kick♥♥♥♥♥and saving the galaxy. Characters are given live actors which is either good or bad as your mileage may vary. Looking back at the cutscenes, I find them enjoyable.
Gameplay:
For the first several levels, you will be doing the old shooting and scooting until you get your lightsaber. From there, its hacking and slashing to victory with Force powers mixed in. The actions you do in-game will affect the “path” you will go down, either with the Light or Dark Side. This includes saving civilians and making choices in the main storyline. As with the last game, you will be fighting mini bosses in the form of Jerec’s Sith cronies. The lightsaber fights are awkward in my experience, as the hit detection seems to be off so you will end up just flailing your weapon around like a madman hoping to get a hit. There are some cool Force powers available however, ones that were not seen in the movies which is a bonus!
Graphics:
Once again, your mileage will vary. Either you like the 2D pixels of Dark Forces, or the angular and stiff 3D appearance of Dark Forces 2… pick your poison. Regardless, it gets the job done as it is oddly satisfying to see sparks fly when you hit the walls with your lightsaber. I did get this extremely annoying color glitch and it seems many old games have this issue (Starcraft), where the colors all turn into a headache inducing, blinding neon such as bright teal and pink. I had to mess with the graphical options in-game which I believe was 3D acceleration and make sure the game ran with Admin powers with the compatibility options enabled.
Sound/Music:
Enemies make the appropriate noises as they are dismembered by Kyle’s lightsaber of justice or riddled with bolts from the Repeater Rifle. Guns and the lightsaber make their iconic sounds. Lightsabers make their crackling noises as they strike each other in the boss duels, or thermal detonators going off in that Rodian’s face. The music is excellent as it usually is in Star Wars games… the Imperial March is as good as it was in the 90’s, as it is now.
Controls:
The game allows you to use a joystick or the standard keyboard and mouse. I prefer the latter but I do believe I remember playing it with the joystick when I was a kid. (Note: I did not get very far.) You may also customize hotkeys from everything from moving to weapons to force powers.
Replay value:
You may play through the Dark and Light side paths and try out all the Force powers but there are no achievements or any real incentives to play over and over.
Online:
The ancestor to Jedi Knight Jedi Outcast’s multiplayer. Nowadays, there may be some group somewhere in a galaxy far, far away playing this multiplayer if you look hard enough but I have never played it.
---
***If there are any mistakes to the facts pertaining to the game, please let me know. Also, if you have further questions not covered by the review, or if something were unclear, I will try to clarify as best as possible. Thanks!

Star Wars Jedi Knight Dark Forces II is one of the great old gems. You can replay it to this day and still enjoy it. Strong gameplay, good graphics for it's time, great difficulty, well made maps and some of the best live action cutscenes you'll ever find.
It's funny replaying this old gem, a shooter from a time when level design was sprawling and non-linear, where enemies were numerous and survival was actually difficult you start to notice things about modern games. One strange observation I've made, playing this again after so many years, is that I can see the path from this game directly through Bioware's modern aRPG's, from Jade Empire to Mass Effect 3 so much of it have it's roots in Lucasart's Jedi Knight series. It is a shame that they took the simple RPG elements and basic morality system instead of the superb shooter and exploration elements. Such a shame.

The term 'Rogue-like' gets tossed around alot these days, however most games that are listed in this category aren't really like Rogue at all. This game is THE exception.
If you ever played NetHack, uMoria, Rogue, or any other classic Rogue-likes, you must purchase this game. As you can see from my collected play time, it has eaten a significant chunk of my life (literally my most highly played game).
I regularly buy both indie and AAA games, and this is, by far, the most fun I've had on Steam (well...except for maybe FTL).
Potential Positives:
+ Turn based world - Monsters move when you move. Take your time.
+ Not for the faint of heart - Remember when games used to be hard? So does this developer.
+ Unlockable races and classes - Replayability, anyone?
+ Dungeons combine randomness with structure - Key elements are always there, but many elements change between adventures.
+ The price is super low - You could buy this game 8 or 9 times for the price of one AAA game.
+ Active development - Last update was about 2 weeks before this review.
Potential Negatives:
- You're going to die - a lot. Some frustration will be had.
- Graphics are nothing special, although it does come in old-school @ style display (which I use).
- Not the best music, put on your favorite album instead.
TL;DR: A rich, impressive Rogue-like for fans of old-school games (no CoD 'bros' need apply).

A very traditional hard-as-balls roguelike. What sets this apart from other genrecompetitors like DCSS or nethack is the very accessible interface and overall decent presentation with a very good default tileset (that can be swapped out, if you feel like it).
Make no mistake, I have barely scratched the surface of what this game holds. But there is an insame amount of stuff in this, half a dozen races, several "sub"races, classes with subclasses and almost all of them come with a unique opening. Very impressive stuff. And everytime I die, even if its in the early stages due to some unfair RNG, I still keep rerolling thanks to the massive amounts of content, every run is different and you will always find another titbit of lore or a new quest.
Its hard to not miss the references to other fantasy worlds. This used to be set in the Tolkien universe, but for the sake of it being a commercial product, all of the connections had to be removed. Still it holds an interesting world with unique characters and well-written lore.
If you're into roguelikes, ToME is almost a mustplay. It takes a lot of time to get used to its "rogueiness" and I recommend changing some of the horrible default keybindings, but once you get out of that beginnerslump, you don't want to stop playing.

I'm a big fan of the Souls games, so have been keen to check this out for a while. It certainly lives up to its reputation as a 2D Souls-like; in fact, 80% of the time it feels like a complete cloning of those games. I don't have a problem with that. I actually welcome it.
Where Salt and Sanctuary has really fallen apart for me is in those Soul-like moments when the game's systems don't allow for the limitations of 2D space. The bosses I've faced are all in small arenas and, of course, they only move left and right. Therefore, your only real choices are to roll, and hope the hitboxes don't mess up (which they frequently seem to do), or use a shield. The problem with the latter is a lot of enemies hit so quickly that your stamina is drained almost instantaneously, making it an unviable option against bosses like the Queen of Smiles who often stops at the edge of the screen, meaning you have to throw yourself into the way of an attack just to continue the fight.
Tracking on enemy ranged attacks is overpowered, meaning that you'll often roll through attacks, only for an enemy to throw an axe or explosive bottle backwards to hit you. This is a real problem in a 2D environment.
I've died a lot in this game. I expect it. I love the challenge. But a lot of the time I don't feel like it was my fault, and that's a problem. I know most people will argue me on this point - when I started looking into these issues, most people who raised them received little in the way of response beyond 'get gud' - but I thought it important enough to mention.
I love the approach the developers have taken, but the execution has too many holes for me to recommend Salt and Sanctuary.

Oneshot is a puzzle adventure game where you, the player, are god and you must guide the messiah who is a(genderless cat...looking..person?)named Niko through a world that has lost its sun. The objective of the game is to restore the worlds sun and bring light back to the lands. There will come a time where you must make a vital decision, choose wisely because you only have ONESHOT.
Alright i want to start off by saying that this game absolutely blew my mind. For those of you who have played  UnderTale you may be able to somewhat compare the two but realistically they are very different. The game run's on the concept of breaking the 4th wall and connecting with its player. The world knows you exist and you are able to make a direct connection with Niko that you may not get with any other game which makes this game very special. Certain puzzles also require you to go into your own computer and look for certain documents to find passwords or hints(matrix muh dude).
Other puzzles also require you to obtain a certain item or combine other items in your inventory and find way's to reach a solution. I am not a heavy puzzle game person but i certaintly don't mind them. So if you like puzzle games then this is a good choice for you. Also the game will last a good 6-7 hours but i took my time and i have 13 hours lol. IMO its not as short as they really say just take your time and have fun.
The story is amazing and i highly recommend this game if you played other story heavy games like UnderTale, Lisa, Hyper Light Drifter, and others. As i have stated before you must guide Niko through the world on a mission to restore the sun. There are also multiple endings in the game(that sounds familiar) and your choice will effect the game heavily. Oh and i also forgot to mention that the sun is a lighbulb! which is cute. Very fair warning, THIS GAME WILL MAKE YOU CRY so make sure to have some tissues. There were times when i was playing and i had to stop to vent my emotional stress which is something that i really did not have to do with other games. The game also has unique and relatable characters that you will remember for a long time. Also there was recently an update to the game called Solstice which gives it a true happy ending so i highly recommend playing through that to really finish off the game. So again, if you like story based games then this is a good play.
