To summarize right away; 8/10, it's fun and is beautifully crafted. Defeinitely gets repetitive quickly, though.
Right away this game kinda jumps back to some older gameplay styles, it's highly intuitive. It teaches you some of the base mechanics right away in the intro, but it doesn't really give you the whole bag, it kinda makes you figure the rest out, which I personally enjoyed. There were a lot of "I can do that?!" moments throughout gameplay.
The platforming works really well, and the controls feel responsive enough. The design is a real eye catch, everything is gorgeous and so lovelingly animated. It's highly reminiscent of Metal Slug in a lot of ways. The actually gameplay feels a lot like MS, and the atmosphere is similar in a lot of ways too. I actually started to pick up a few silly references to MS, and other games similar, including Metal Gear Solid.
Boss fights at first were kind of a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥ though once I got the swing of things, they again became very intuitive and doable. They brought a Monster Hunter feel to it in how you had to track the bosses around the map.
Last good note I'm giving is the weapon crafting system. That♥♥♥♥♥♥s fun. Nothing gives a more personal feel to combat when you yourself had to scrounge up the pieces and put together your own weapon. Their are so many different pieces, and it's all together a very nice touch. It could have easily been replaced with weapon drops and no one would have noticed, and that shows the care put into making this.
Now onto the negative: It's REALLY ♥♥♥♥ing repetitive. You have set stages per rank of mission and you keep going back to those same maps continuously. This was kind of my deal on Peace Walker, though it wasn't nearly as bad there since the maps cycled more frequently. Here, you end up dealing with the same map per chapter.
Last thing I'm gonna mention, I saw a few rags on storyline. I kinda didn't feel like the story was all that important here, given you're a mercenary. The characters all had a bit of personality, and your actions felt like they mattered to the world, so it was good to me.
To conclude, 8/10 would recommend.

Very effectively blends a Dark-Souls-like aesthetic, world, and combat design into a 2D action-platformer.  The platforming is itself very satisfying, starting out simple before eventually becoming diabolically clever in forcing the player to combine acquired abilities to traverse puzzle-like gaps and obstacles.  The combat is also fairly tight, though sometimes rather brutal and demanding (see: Dark-Souls-like).  In addition, the game is quite the sight to look at, with a very detailed world of atmospheric environments and varied enemies.
This is one of two games (both 2D action-platformers with exploration mechanics) that I have played through from start to finish in one long sitting across two days (on a weekend), on account of not being able to stop.
(The inventory system could use a "sort" button, though.)

Star Wars: Dark Forces was a 2D 3D game in the vein of Doom and Wolfenstein 3D, and it was vastly inferior to both. Its main boast was having floors above other floors, and It suffered from confusing level design, irritating puzzles, and a spread-out control scheme. Dark Forces II, however, represents a major improvement. Level design is more intuitive, puzzles are handled far better, controls are mappable, and you can now save within the levels. The story is much more interesting this time around, dealing more personally with Kyle Katarn and expanding on some elements introduced in the backstory of Dark Forces. Also added is the use of a lightsaber and Force powers (spoiler: you're a Jedi, 'Arry!). Locations are varied, though the second half of the game is mostly spent in samey Empire structures, and boss battles all basically come down to frantic lightsaber duels. But for the most part, this is a very fun game that makes good use of the Star Wars EU setting.

Despite it's been years since its release, it's still a great game, and it still holds up pretty good.
If you, like me, enjoy great gameplay and don't have any problems with older graphics, there is no reason not to buy it.
If you're a Star Wars fan, but still haven't tried it, then you should click on the "buy"-button right away! You won't be disappointed.

The term 'Rogue-like' gets tossed around alot these days, however most games that are listed in this category aren't really like Rogue at all. This game is THE exception.
If you ever played NetHack, uMoria, Rogue, or any other classic Rogue-likes, you must purchase this game. As you can see from my collected play time, it has eaten a significant chunk of my life (literally my most highly played game).
I regularly buy both indie and AAA games, and this is, by far, the most fun I've had on Steam (well...except for maybe FTL).
Potential Positives:
+ Turn based world - Monsters move when you move. Take your time.
+ Not for the faint of heart - Remember when games used to be hard? So does this developer.
+ Unlockable races and classes - Replayability, anyone?
+ Dungeons combine randomness with structure - Key elements are always there, but many elements change between adventures.
+ The price is super low - You could buy this game 8 or 9 times for the price of one AAA game.
+ Active development - Last update was about 2 weeks before this review.
Potential Negatives:
- You're going to die - a lot. Some frustration will be had.
- Graphics are nothing special, although it does come in old-school @ style display (which I use).
- Not the best music, put on your favorite album instead.
TL;DR: A rich, impressive Rogue-like for fans of old-school games (no CoD 'bros' need apply).

Tales of Maj'Eyal is simply an amazing game. The sheer amount of content in this game is incredible.  The storyline and lore are deep and enjoyable while the gameplay, particularly the combat, remain consistently engaging.
Tales of Maj'Eyal does a good job of easing a new player into the world and game mechanics by restricting the initial race and class offerings and expands outward with a number of persistent unlockables including new races, classes, and items that will become available to your future characters as you progress forward through additional sessions.  The distinct classes (particularly with different race pairings) provide tremendously distinct play styles that will keep you on your toes and force you to adjust your gameplay to find success.

This is a hard one to describe. There are many complaints, but most of those complaints are about people thinking it's going to be similar to Metal Slug, which it's not. It takes inspiration from games like Monster Hunter and Megaman. And the reason I say a game like Monster Hunter is because the crafting system and online missions (Quests) are similar to Monster Hunter's. You have your sub missions and main missions, you must complete all the main missions to unlock your boss mission, or in Monster Hunter your "Urgent Quest," to move on to your next rank or "Hunter Rank."
As for Megaman, the game's enemies and precise shooting mechanics are very similar to the Megaman franchise. So close infact some enemies have the same gameplay mechanics, examples are the Floor Spiders acting the like Springers, and Riot Shields acting like the Sniper Joes from Megaman.
Since Monster Hunter and Megaman are two of my favorite videogame franchises of all time, I love this game, but I understand how some people might go into this game expecting a Metal Slug type game. If that's the case, Metal Slug 3 and X are available on Steam, which I highly recommend as well.

I don't play rogue-likes.
That was my starting point with ToME(4), aka Tales of Maj'Eyal.  I'm not really a fan of the genre, though I am a fan of tactical RPGs.  It was only after some interesting comments on another game forum (Grim Dawn, great game, look it up) that I decided to give ToME a try.
Unlike some other rogue-likes, ToME gives you the option to play softcore.  There are varying difficulty levels in addition to different degrees of 'rogue-like-ness' (multiple lives; from 1 to infinite).  The classes vary from basic and simple (Bulwark, Rogue, Archmage, etc) to surprisingly unique (Mindslayer, Oozemancer, Solipsist, etc).  The unlock system can be a pain, but it does encourage you to progress through the game, explore and play various archetypes.
The lore is great; the world has been excellently crafted (imo).  While it doesn't read like a AAA novel, the depth of the backstory is pretty astonishing considering it's been done primarily by one man (props Darkgod).
When it comes to the gameplay, everything is surprisingly newbie-friendly (for a rogue-like).  The UI is simple and easy, the controls are variable (keyboard and/or mouse, re-bindable) and the overly-complex item usage often found in the genre has been notably streamlined.
The graphics are solid.   Now, take that with a grain of salt; this is a 2d game of tiles and sprites.  If you're anticipating something like Dragon Age, you're going to be disappointed.  I know that I was unpleasantly surprised.  That being said, it has definitely grown on me and it certainly gives enough information on what's happening.
All that being said, this IS a roguelike.  You WILL walk around a corner/open a door/open a chest and get exploded.  Careful, cautious play is highly encouraged.
Overall, if you find yourself wanting to try out a roguelike but finding they are a little too 'hardcore' for you, give ToME a try.  It's the only roguelike that I have found myself returning to, time after time.

Please do not buy this game full price.
Allow me to explain: I am not saying this is a bad game, on the contrary, it is remarkable. The reason I say to not buy it full price is because this game does not lie. You only have one shot. You can only play the game once. Maybe twice if you're dedicated enough. The game jumps through many hoops to keep this intact. Not to mention, the game in itself is incredibly short, the entire thing taking about 8 hours. Buying this game for the full 10 dollars is like spending 10 dollars on a stack of pancakes, sure, the pancakes are delicious and well made, but you still spent way too much money on a thing you can never eat again.
This is where OneShot suffers most of all, but also where it gets its more intriguing elements: Everything you do has permanent consequences. This is not your little game of Undertale where even if you screwed up you can reset and try it all again, whatever you do is what you did and it will never be redoable. Ever.
I'm not saying don't get this game, please do. But maybe wait until the price drops during one of those big christmas sales or something. 10 dollars is a lot to spend on a thing you can only do once.
Thank you for listening.

turns a two stick shooter into a western on white canvas as disgruntled Mexican amnesiac, Jesús, trundles about greater Texas ricocheting through past and present, burning bridges just as quickly. Facing a stock cast of bandits, miners, injuns, chinamen, soldiers,, and barfolk, sardonic Jesús casts off the mantle of a neutral protagonist and doesn't hide his distaste for just about everyone.  Veterans of western games will find most characters rather boring if it wasn't for the occasional oddball to spice things up. Random white guy posing as an indian may offend some, but it at least shows some urge to stray from the strictures of western poetics and just have a whacked out dude because you can. But as the namesake goes, is this really a game about a great story?
No. It's for the combat, the best aspect of the game, letting players cut, shoot, or explode red splotches of blood all over the white background. Players must plan attacks using barriers like doors, buildings and livestock to conceal or cover. Gunplay is enjoyable with meaty hitboxes and a tasty-quick, reload, cuck-and-shoot (won't let me write♥♥♥♥♥♥), mechanic that are the bread and butter of the game. If rootin'-tootin'-shootin' isn' for you, luring enemies away and knifing them when they've turned their backs is also a valid  strategy. The amalgam of both styles, the bow, allows for silent and precise kills; with the only replenishable ammo of the game, slower rate of fire is but a small drawback. 3 big negatives make the game more difficult than it needs to be: ammo shortage and one hit player kills. In order to get ammo for most guns, you must swap the entire gun and trust that the new gun will have more, which it most likely won't.  The second problem, one hit player kills became immensely frustrating when clearing scores of bad guys to be undone by sleepy joe in the corner. Later you can acquire armor that puts death's theshold at two or three shots, but why not just make that standard? As fast as a reset may be it's still pretty jarring. The third problem is...well...If you're going to name a game after a dual pistol mechanic, it better be ♥♥♥♥ing good. I was so excited to use the dos pistoles that when I got them and realized it both canned the cuck'n shoot mechanic yet kept the ammo shortage I was pretty upset, and cursed when it seemed I had no other alternative but to use the clunker. Thumb-Click-Boom, Paint the West Red, Runny Gunny Western Funny, it could have been named anything but to be dubbed
means not only is it an eyesore when I think of it's clunky dual revolvers, but I have to see its name first whenever I go to the top of my Library. I only bought this because I wanted to play new games and I had fun ok, I HAD FUN. But on the cheap. Agh. Anyway....
The art of the game is enjoyable and though a little bright on the eyes, satisfies the desert aesthetic with a wash relentless white light. Interiors are clear from exteriors and a canyon segment even has a finely suited rain environment while you arrow natives. With each kill blood splatters did make me smile a bit knowing that guy wasn't gonna get up again and knife me while I'm scoping someone far away again. The music was a little strange though, tinny sounding and slightly too rock and roll for strict Westerns, but I kinda got into it as time passed.
While I'm not keen on playing the DLC I had some fun with 6 is better than 12 and look forward to more games that can make core combat as enjoyable as this was for the price.

Easily one of the best traditional roguelikes out there. It's more accessible than say Dungeon Crawl Stone Soup, Nethack, or other classics, but there's still tons of depth to be explored. TOME has decent looking (for roguelike standards) art, countless build possibilities (thanks to its in-depth character customization), and fun combat that actually involves the usage of skills as opposed to just bumping into enemies the entire time.

Like any roguelike worth it's salt, it's brutal. Death through hubris, through auto-exploring when you know there's a boss out there waiting to eat your liver with fava beans and rice, OOD (Out of Depth) Bosses waiting to do the same except with your soul, horrible and evil places to give out escort quests because it has no damn right to have you escorting the one class that can give you Providence in a place where giants throw lightning like Thor or that godforsaken hellhole in the dungeon where dreams go to die, and death is all around you. It wraps you in it's warm, suffocating embrace and there will be a next time. A new character, a retested combo, a new life that will die anew.
And you know what? You wield death itself and they will die by the hundreds by your power. Hell, take your pick form it's range of death dealers: Walking around as you fire beams of destruction that go off based on how suicidal your enemies are on getting close to you, stealing the lifeforce of your foes and slapping down plagues like an almighty pimp hand, the classic archmage that rains down fire or storms, sitting back as your summons tear and rip through throngs of foes and all manner of stabbings and slashy-slashy. It gives you the tools to stave off death for another encounter and when you finally kill that horrible wielder of lightning, masters of the arcane and life itself or The Horned Horror, it feels amazing. You will die, but it'll be after you create mountains of their dead.
Pure joy for us old guys who grew up on SSI gold box gameplay, difference is just one guy vs the world...

I like my RPGs like I like my coffee. Nice and deep, complex, with many different options with which to slay my enemies in any singular class, wait, what was I talking about again?
Tales of Maj'Eyal encompasses everything I love about roguelikes, everything I like about MMOs, and everything I LOVE about RPGs.
It has the typical roguelike grid-locked movement and combat system, plus projectiles have a fly speed, which means that you can dodge projectiles by sidestepping if they're slow enough that you can catch them midair. Every being has a global speed rating, too, so a slow mage with 75% global speed will often be double-turn-ed on by enemies often and won't be able to dodge many projectiles, whereas a rogue with 127% global speed will often be able to act twice in a "turn" and sidestep most projectiles! The speed system really does make such a big difference. Additionally, just like in roguelikes, if your character bites the dust they're gone... However unlike roguelikes you have three difficulty settings: Roguelike, Adventure and ...Endless, I believe? Whatever, the point is... Roguelike is roguelike: If your character dies, they kick the bucket for good. In Endless, you get to ressurrect every single time. However, Adventure is interesting. In Adventure, you work through lives--as you level and achieve things, you gain extra lives... but they're finite. So once you kick the bucket, the nameless cosmic tentacle-entity that keeps reviving you like a dunce for somehow loses interest and lets you fall into the void.
It borrows a few cool mechanics from MMOs too, namely the randomized loot system and many skill trees. Unlike MMOs, however, it ops for having many, MANY skill trees that are 100% linear with four steps, divided into two categories: Class trees, and Generic trees. Class trees are native to your class--a Rogue gets Trapitude, an Alchemist gets Golemancy, so on, so forth. Generic trees, on the other hand, you qualify for; being a Cunning-based class with high Cunning gives you access to the Survival tree; being a Wilder grants you access to the Wild Gift tree, so on so forth. On levelups you gain a Class point and a Generic point, as well as several Stat Points and, on particular levels, Category points. A Category point lets you unlock locked skill trees, or upgrade the potency of one you already had! Like I said: Deep and complex. Like coffee, I suppose?
And of course, from RPGs, it borrows the everything else. A vast world rich in story, with cool sidequests and enemy design and... this isn't RPG-native. what am i... i need to go sit down.

Alright, as a player of Payday 2, I am giving you what I think of this game and the review for it.
So, Raid: WW2, is much more like Payday 2, yet, it uses PayDay: The Heist technics. I'll give you details later. Let's talk about graphic first. The game uses Diesiel Engine 2.0. YES, THERE WILL BE ANNOYING BUGS, yet, those won't bugger much in the game. However, I must say, they should've used better engine to make this game, since the trailer just looks so beautiful. But everything in the game? Oh dear, who the hell turned off those spot lights? So yea, that's what I don't really like. But still won't affect me why I like the game. I mean, all of the "Do some robbery" games. Especially it has coop.
So, what's about PayDay: TH mechanic? Well, let's say you techinally has "4 weapons", from Primary (Main weapons, from Rifle to LMG), Secondary (Pistols), Grenade (Yes, you have to personally take out the grenades to give your foes some treats), and melee (Yep, a knife, mostly used if you want to go stealhy).
The reason why this game is (a bit) different is because of you're using WW2 weaponry. Yes, your weapons are garbages, and so are enemies' But that doesn't mean you can't tune it to be good. You will need to like perform certain kills, like killing 50 enemies by headshot to unlock parts that increase accuracy, or kill 250 enemies to get damage upgrade parts. Yes, your guns will have visual changes, NEAT HUH? Yea, it's cool. Very cool. Nah no, you can't upgrade your knife into a spear or sabre, (For now? I guess? Perhaps in the future they'll add more features)
About raids (heists), most of them are probably inside Berlin somewhere. You'll infiltrate bunkers, and gun and run on street, while shooting down god damned bombers. I kind of hated day and night mechanic, as you cannot choose when to attack, like, I prefer in the morning, yet, the game constantly put me into missions around noon and night. There are few exceptions where you really have to do at night or at day, so, you'll have to get used to it. BECAUSE THERE'S NO FLASHLIGHTS! So, just light up your "Brightness" via Video options.
About guns, well, a lot of guns are still missing. Like, do you love Bolt Action rifles? Well, sorry, if you're looking for KAR98s, they aren't here yet. What makes me sad is... THERE'S NO PPSH-41. (Sad violin, hope they add it soon, I really love that gun because of 71 rounds in a mag pew the crap out of Nazi) Italian Carcano, Swedish Mausker, perhaps... I asked too much, but PPSH-41 is kind of "A must" for me in any WW2-themed games. That's ok, not really bugging me too much, I am using BAR most of time so far.
This is my list of guns that any WW2 themed games must have which are missing. KAR98, Carcano, Lee Enfield for Bolt-action rifles (perhaps there are more, but I feel these are represting German, Italian, and British). Missing SMG is PPSH-41. Missing pistols are Luger, and AP38. Missing melee weapon is shovel (Why not? Increased range, dmg, but take a long time to charge attack and swing it)
Are there level systems and skill systems? YES,  THERE ARE! However, some guns are like "Taking forever to get" like my favorite LMG, MG-42, needs me to reach around level 30? or 40? I forgot, but you get the point. Some guns cannot be used until you reach the required level.
There are "currently" have only 4 classes, recon to do "Not so accurate" aimbot, and mostly using Bolt-action rifle, WHICH I DO NOT SUGGEST FOR PLAYERS WHO PLAY ALONE WITH 3 AIs, because your enemies will usually stick their guns into your nose trunk. Yes, they will swarm you. So I suggest you either go for Assault, Recon, or Demolition. Assault uses rifles, LMGs, and SMGs, The warcry can help you regen some lost hp, which can be kind of life-saving when you're in need ot health. Recon, well, it will just like Widow Maker's "No one can hide from my sight" Yea, it reveals every enemy and mark them as red color. NEAT HUH? Demolition, well, you don't get to be Demoman, just, your warcry can turn your grenade into Cluster grenade (ONLY CLUSTER WHEN WARCRY HASN'T WEAR OFF, IF ITS DURATION IS EXPIRED, IT IS NORMAL GRENADE AGAIN)., while you take "Slightly" less incoming damage.
Sad news is, you have to create characters, which means, yea, pick one of four classes, then choose one of four perks. You cannot switch them like in Payday 2. No, if you play as assault, you will level up as assault. If you want to play as recon, you have to create another character and apply Recon perk for the guy. AND GRIND LEVELS. Yes, they make this game feel much more like a RPG now. SO, MAKE YOUR SKILL CHOICES CAREFULLY, AS THE MORE LEVEL YOU HAVE, THE MORE GOLD NEEDED TO CHANGE YOUR SKILLS.
What about enemies? Eh... for me, they are all like the same, just..., with different guns, that's all. With exception there won't be LMG-Wielding gunner. HAHAHA, YAY? WRONG! There are flamethrowers who can down you in 3 seconds as full health if you don't take cover when they spew fire at your face. YES, THEY'RE MUCH MORE TERRIFYING THAN SKULL DOZERS! But... you can exploit them, since the fire will linger for a while, YES, FLAMER WILL LIKELY KILL THEIR OWNS. So make sure you plan out either to kill the flammer or exploit him. Oh yea, that's one special Nazi. There are 4 Specials in total.
Snipers, which of course, pews from high ground and long ranged, can be very annoying, since your guns are garbages, unless you're very close to them, it will take some effort to kill them, while you'll likely lose one third of your health. Spotters, they are dudes usually stand in high grounds, peeking at you with a binoculous. If you don't kill them fast, they'll shoot a flare at your location. PUT IT OUT OR RUN AWAY. Because it will summon 20 seconnds? I guess? 20 seconds of artillery strike at that area where the flare landed. Officer, uhhh, they're very rare to show up, in fact, I haven't seen any spawned for me, mostly are scripted to be there "To be assassinated". Perhaps, increase nearby Nazi's damage? or what? No idea.
Do I suggest it? UH, well. IT'S KIND OF HARD TO RECOMMEND THIS GAME. Currently, there aren't many raids to play with, Exp and gold bar are terrifying grind-fest. Guns granted on high levels aren't rewarding, like "STG-44 has only 15 rounds in a mag instead of 30, MG-42 only has 50 rounds in the drum instead of 100). A lot of "MUST HAVE" guns are missing for a game that uses WW2 as theme. And what's buggering me a lot are Desynch, glitches, and bugs. These are the 3 reasons why the game is ruined, plus one "Lack of content" consider this game cost around 40 USD. And they will add contents via DLCs, just... I know it will come this way. It will be.
However,  if you love to shoot Nazi in the face, or love to experience being swarmed up while using an awful gun with your friends? This game is for you. Why I bought the game? It's because I love WW2 theme games. Who the hell cannot like the "DING" from that amazing rifle? You know what it is! I don't have to spoil it for you! Hurry up and reach the requirement to unlock that rifle!
But uh... I would suggest only buy this game if you have friends to play with, since this game really needs some "Help" and "Updates" from developers. Otherwise, just play Payday 2. That is, I don't recommend the game for now, but maybe, in the future, after they added more stuff in the game and have all DLCs on discount.
You should go buy Payday 2 for now, and wait till Raid: WW2 got all it needed.

I am not a huge Payday fan, but I've put in 237 hours in PAYDAY: The Heist and 107 hours in PAYDAY 2. I am somewhat familiar with the gameplay, engine, and general feel of the game. I heard about this Raid game and was pretty interesting considering it was going to be set in World War 2. Granted I wasn't looking for histrocal accuracy because if I wanted that I would go read a book instead of depending on a video game. Before purchasing I did read many of the negative reviews and  the fans of the old payday series seem to be very adamant when criticizing this game. I believe that many thought that this was suppose to be the spiritual sucessor of Payday 2. It is a new direction and one I say only a few would like. This game has a very similar feel to PAYDAY: The Heist and if you enjoyed that game I say this game is quite enjoyable in that sense.
Now the first thing to point out about this game is the setting, it is during World War 2. You are not robbing people for your own personal gains. You are sabotaging, destroying key buildings, rescue, search and destroy, assasinations, etc. Pretty much anything you would imagine possible in a war would happen in this game. The objectives and mission really make you feel like you are doing some importance and making a change in the world fighting Nazi Germany Tyranny. I find the video clips before a mission starts and ends very enjoyable. Hitler would react depending on the sucess of the mission is pretty damn funny. The soundtrack is mediocre, some of the pieces are amazing while others are boring and repetitive. This game has a very similar feel to a film called Inglorious ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s. The way each character speaks and jokes around while slaughtering hundreds of nazis is fun. I really enjoy the voice acting, its entertaining and you can use specifc voice commands to let allies know what to do.
As for graphics and gameplay/gunplay goes, it really is no different from Pd 1 to pd 2. Lets be realistic here, if you are using the same game engine for all three games, you can't really make much of a difference in graphics. The payday series never had great graphics and we can all agree to that. There is noticeable frame drops during large battles, but runs mostly smooth. The same usual bugs I notice in previous titles is here, as ai would walk through walls and clip. The bugs are quite abundant right now, but payday is a buggy game too. I believe it is time for a new graphics engine for payday 3?  Right now the weapons feel and sound great in Raid. It makes it feel authentic to the setting. The downside is you won't have your precious red dots, laser sights, and a crap ton of attachments. That is totally fine for me though it feels like it gives a challange. However, shooting the weapons on my mouse and keyboard feels exactly the same as previous games. Hey a first person shooter what do you know?
All right overall I think it safe to say this game is totally fine and it is okay to buy it at 40 dollars. I spent roughly around the same for Payday:The Heist and its dlcs. Also when I purchased PD2 the month it came out I bought dlcs the month after and it was roughly around 40 dollars. Honestly 40 bucks is not even a lot, I've seen games trying to sell special editions for 79.99 or 99.99 or some ridiculous price lol. The devs have promise a lot of free content, Not a lot of dlcs and more so of Expansions. Hey Devs if you are reading this, if you guys do any expansions could you do something set in the Pacific theater!? :) Anyways the game just released and just like pd2 the vanilla game doesn't have much content. Give the developers some more time to release content.

Any game series that can spawn 3 sequels has to be doing something right;
is no exception. Offering a more traditional tower defense experience with solid & balanced game mechanics, there is
in total with some good map designs & waves that can challenge, throwing your planned strategy into turmoil!
For seasoned TD fans, initially the game does feel rather easy on normal difficulty level. Myself, I managed to get through to level 15 before running into any real progression-crushing issues, which resulted in me having to go back and replay levels to upgrade up my towers. Unlike TD games like

, the rewards for replaying are reasonable, which means although somewhat repetitive, you can progress at a reasonable pace even when you get stuck or continually loose at a level. Replaying earlier levels on hard or psycho difficulty will speed this up as well. For longer term replayability there is also
endless mode with Steam Leaderboards for some competition. There is no maze/pathing in
.
As the title implies, you also have a

that you can jump to certain locations on the map. They defend stronghold gates & support other fixed towers, allowing another layer to your strategy. As with the towers, your Sentinels can also be upgraded as they gain experience. Using these effectively can be the difference between success & failure. I really like the Sentinel feature & adds something different to what could be seen as a more generic TD game.
Graphically it's competent but not great; tower weapon effects are ok as is the environments/maps, but could have benefited from some higher quality textures for the PC version & some smoother animations. Alien types are easily distinguishable even when things get hectic which is always a plus with a TD game. The musical score was good, getting stuck in my head long after I have exited the game, but other sound effects were a bit bland, but this does add a bit of an ol' school flavor to it all.
There are a
that did lead to frustration though. Firstly, attacks from the air can happen from almost anywhere on the map & from multiple sources at once
. These are not highlighted in any way at the start of the level
often leading to restarts once you learn where they come from. It drove me nuts at times! It diminishes the strategic element of the game, instead changing it to memorising the specific waves & entry locations.
Also, what I believe is a new introduction to the series, is destructible towers. Without having a fully upgraded tower, most are very squishy especially versus certainly aliens & can completely demolish any attempt to complete a level sometimes within mere seconds. Later levels seem to have specific waves designed just for this purpose. I am not against towers taking damage or being destroyed, as it adds yet another layer of strategy, but it is not as well balanced as the rest of the game in my opinion. You can cash-in/recycle destroyed towers to help cover the cost of the rebuild, but that down-time generally means a restart anyways. Very frustrating to see your precious towers built up over the last
waves of the level destroyed so quickly!
is not perfect but does offer good value for money, refined gameplay & a reasonable difficulty curve that can keep you coming back for some time after your initial round.

Sentinel 4 is a tactical tower defense game. It's award-winning strategy gameplay expands explosively as the interstellar war moves to a mysterious alien world. Deploy devastating new towers and technology against an enemy that’s smarter and more deadly than ever before as you explore the mystery of the Dark Star. -  Recommended!

Probably one of the best SF tower defense games I have played: A lot of upgrades available through money earned in missions, good selection of different commanders to use; unique turrets to play with, allowing you to try out different strategies.  An excellent upgrade to Sentinel 3 in every way, as well as more leveling and upgrade or choice options compared to games like Defense Grid or Sole Survivor.

Sentinel 4: Dark Star:
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
You are in command of the dropship Sentinel and your mission is to repeal and destroy the fierce Alien onslaught by setting up your defence in a science fiction world.
At the start of each map, you will have a limited amount of money to spend, so choose wisely which turret you will place first and which position is the most appropriate on the map. The direction from which the waves come will give you a hint (look at the flashing arrows)! Each time you kill an enemy, you will earn $1; accumulate money to buy, upgrade or repair your turrets. You will also be able to buy traps (lava Pod), defence droids and others to deploy in the path of your foe and see them vanish!
Make sure to collect any credits that the aliens drop, you will need them to upgrade your turrets, sentinel and stronghold at your armoury in the pre-battle menu.
As you progress, you will be facing more and more waves of aliens per mission which will become hectic especially if you start losing several turrets and gates.
Sentinel 4: Dark Star is very fun, addictive, well designed and the graphics are good and polished. Mouse and keyboard for the control as you would expect. You will be able to play in campaign and endless modes with four levels of difficulty.
This game is a good tower defence game and I thoroughly recommend it.

Pretty much everything an RPG/Platformer hybrid should be.
Touted as the 2D version of Dark Souls (which I have yet to play) seemingly everywhere, this game is full of a wonderfully depressing and cold atmosphere from your character's trek from the shipwrecked shores to every withered and abandoned old location on the island. While the storyline itself may not be all that deep or full of details, the aesthetic will more than make up for the gaunt narrative and keep you very engaged in what's happening. The level design is fantastic, and the enemies (particularly the many bosses) all with distinct flavors restore faith that today's fantasy can still be dark, brooding, and heavy, and not just ridiculous scenes of elves skateboarding down elephant trunks while shooting orcs.
Despite falling victim occasionally to two of the cardinal "ways to make a platformer instantly not fun", the controls for the most part are very responsive and easy to learn, leaving most of the skill to timing and strategy, as platforming should be. The RPG elements are well placed as well, and find a good balance between build diversity without winding up a glorified rock-paper-scissors match.
A unique experience is rare in games today, and this one actually delivers. This game is a lot of fun, with memorable bosses. I recommend it strongly.

I like my RPGs like I like my coffee. Nice and deep, complex, with many different options with which to slay my enemies in any singular class, wait, what was I talking about again?
Tales of Maj'Eyal encompasses everything I love about roguelikes, everything I like about MMOs, and everything I LOVE about RPGs.
It has the typical roguelike grid-locked movement and combat system, plus projectiles have a fly speed, which means that you can dodge projectiles by sidestepping if they're slow enough that you can catch them midair. Every being has a global speed rating, too, so a slow mage with 75% global speed will often be double-turn-ed on by enemies often and won't be able to dodge many projectiles, whereas a rogue with 127% global speed will often be able to act twice in a "turn" and sidestep most projectiles! The speed system really does make such a big difference. Additionally, just like in roguelikes, if your character bites the dust they're gone... However unlike roguelikes you have three difficulty settings: Roguelike, Adventure and ...Endless, I believe? Whatever, the point is... Roguelike is roguelike: If your character dies, they kick the bucket for good. In Endless, you get to ressurrect every single time. However, Adventure is interesting. In Adventure, you work through lives--as you level and achieve things, you gain extra lives... but they're finite. So once you kick the bucket, the nameless cosmic tentacle-entity that keeps reviving you like a dunce for somehow loses interest and lets you fall into the void.
It borrows a few cool mechanics from MMOs too, namely the randomized loot system and many skill trees. Unlike MMOs, however, it ops for having many, MANY skill trees that are 100% linear with four steps, divided into two categories: Class trees, and Generic trees. Class trees are native to your class--a Rogue gets Trapitude, an Alchemist gets Golemancy, so on, so forth. Generic trees, on the other hand, you qualify for; being a Cunning-based class with high Cunning gives you access to the Survival tree; being a Wilder grants you access to the Wild Gift tree, so on so forth. On levelups you gain a Class point and a Generic point, as well as several Stat Points and, on particular levels, Category points. A Category point lets you unlock locked skill trees, or upgrade the potency of one you already had! Like I said: Deep and complex. Like coffee, I suppose?
And of course, from RPGs, it borrows the everything else. A vast world rich in story, with cool sidequests and enemy design and... this isn't RPG-native. what am i... i need to go sit down.

One of the best tower defence games ever made.

Pros
- Great looking game compared to other MMOs.
- Mechanics are solid, though it is action bar/button mashing, which may turn off more action oriented players.
- LOTS of content. Zone events, world events, dungeons, chronicles, raids, PvP (if you like that), instant adventures, etc etc.
- One of the better housing systems
- Really good F2P model, with pretty much all content being free aside from things like bag space, some of the souls etc.
- Can be a really casual or hard core game. It's pretty flexible in that regard.
- Soul system is one of the better "talent" systems in MMOs.
Cons
- The lore could use some work. It's got the GW2 problem in that the lore is there, just horribly horribly presented, which is sad because it has some pretty cool ideas and concepts.
- The shop is sometimes overpriced, and they do sell gear in the shop (albiet incredibly overpriced) which may turn off some people. Also they introduce new "lockboxes" all the time which I personally consider a lame version of gambling.
- The reputation system is horrible. Almost as bad as WoWs.
- The daily system the reputations are tied to get boring VERY fast, however if you want the best enchants for some slots, you need to do it.
- If you're a lore junkie, a lot of the world is unfinished. Stories and zones. You'll get disappointed staring at grey blobs on the map that sound cool, but just don't exist, or finishing a story quest chain with far more questions than answers.
It makes the world feel unfinished.
- The subscription fee is no where near woth paying for. You get some boosters and a weekly gift, along with a discount. It's pretty worthless. If you want to support the game just spend $5 to $15 a month on credits and get something worthwhile.
- Because tanking in this game is so unappealing like so many other MMOs, the old problem of tank shortages comes up a lot. It may be a turn off to some people who like to do dungeons.
In the end I would recommend the game. I consider it one of the best MMOs out right now. Definitely one of the best F2P ones.

When I saw the game on Steam, I had to get it. But there's a few problems I ran into.
You'll notice right away that the main menu is windowed. There is no way to make it full screen. The game itself has the opposite problem; It's full screen all the time with no way to make it windowed. If you want to change a setting while playing the game you'll have to do it through the small window. And it's not really an instant thing to do. The game will black out and you'll have to wait a second to do anything. It can be pretty annoying since it also does the same thing when you're done with the menu can go back to playing the game. You can change your display in-game but this is just for the game itself. And it's not recommended to have your game be something like 1920x1080 since it'll make the HUD really small.
The game runs just fine without any major problems that I noticed aside from wanting to make some adjustments to the controls. However it's noticable that there's no music. When you're in a bar or something, that has it's own little jingle. But the game has it's own music to play in addition which is absent in the steam version. So for the most part it's silence. You might not mind that though but it's worth mentioning.
There's lots of secrets to find and the levels each are pretty lengthy. You eventually do become a Jedi with force powers and that's alot of fun to use. There's a lightside and a dark side ending. I think some missions have differences depending on the route you're on but I forget the specific details.

The developers have removed options with updates, whether it is somethings as "rudimentary" as a brightness slider, to something as essential as difficulty options, it doesn't matter, it isn't here anymore...
The game isn't that long, about an two hours or so, although that's relative, depending on how you bode with the difficulty of the game, and how much patience can you have to withstand the terrible ammo management, and weapon system.
Basically, this game tries to create the illusion that you're holding, and using, an actual gun by making you &quot♥♥♥♥♥♥quot; the weapon before each shot, this is done by forcing the player to press and hold the right mouse button between each shot, it is as tedious as it sounds, and depending on how tolerant you are, it might be something that either makes your experience better, or "tears" it completely.
For me it was, sadly, the latter.
Not only that but you don't pickup ammo by walking on top of the weapons, nor by interacting with them while they're on the ground, the only way to aquire ammunition is by unloading each weapon manually, you do this by holding the right mouse button, before trading your weapon for another, of the same kind, or otherwise.
It is an utterly terrible system, that I can't stand, it slows down the action to a point where the tension, and adrenaline from gunfights turns into a tedious "micro-management" mess, it is completely unnecessary, and it doesn't contribute anything other than negative aspects to the gunplay.
It wouldn't matter nearly as much up until you began noticing the game at times doesn't provide weapons, instead in makes things a bit more diverse by having some later levels offer melee weapons such as shovels, axes, or pickaxes for you to kill your enemies.
All of which are useless against any kind of armed enemy, that can, and will, shoot you from afar.
Similarly to Hotline Miami what's really going to kill you in this game is your own unawareness to the enemy positions, and where exactly is it that they're coming from to begin with, as well as your own accuracy.
Difference being that in Hotline Miami each level was carefully revised to work in line with its own gameplay mechanics, whilst in this one, the game favors much more the concept, and the aesthetic of each level, while not caring in the least about how its own mechanics will work in conjunction with its level design, nor "black and white" aesthetic.
What ends up happening is that half of the times you will be confusing enemies for other objects around you, or alternatively, you'll grind your way through the game while trying desperately to actually see in other rooms that are covered by ceilings that don't allow you to see what's inside the actual buildings their sheltering to begin with.
Remember, this is a "top down shooter" meaning you will always be secluded to seeing the entirety of the game from that perspective.
Then there's the framerate, and the performance, I have a gtx 970, paired with an i5 6600k processor, and 24gb of ram, the game has a very limited graphics, and perfomance options, with only v-sync being the one that caught my eye (I personally hate input lag).
Besides that you have resolution options, and presets that go from high to low, that's it...
Even while going to the lowest setting, even while starting the game with the option to run it at a lower resolution, which it turn made things clearer, literally, I don't know why.
The game still at later levels drop to 40 fps, independently of the setting I chose.
I do not recommend this game, I finish it, but it was a "slog" to go through, at the last level, ironically, I chose to go to the "level select" screen to see how many more hours of grueling tediousness I was about to withstand by my own will.
I was happy to see I only had one level to finish.
And if you're asking to yourself why is it that I imposed myself the completion of this game.
Is simple.
This is a difficult game, but I'm not complaining because I die, I'm complaining because the game has inherent flaws in its design that end up going a long way in making it a difficult, and tedious experience to complete, even the "picking" of weapons doesn't work well at times, yet the game has created a context in which if you can't pickup a weapon fast enough, you'll get shot by the rushing enemies that are coming aggresively towards you.
Even then, some people will claim I'm bashing it because of its difficulty, yet I finished the game.
It is just like any other difficult game.
If you spend enough time, question what's killing you, and you can do something about it, you'll finish it through.
Because videogames, mechanically, don't require anything other than a "mechanical" effort, like the one from a machine that can learn patterns, amongst other things...
That process tho, doesn't mean it will be in every game a positive experience in the least.
And this is a perfect example of one it isn't.

I loved Sentinel 3, but I did not enjoy Sentinel 4 at all. Sentinel 4 tried to innovate upon a proven formula, but it was unsuccessful and made the gameplay worse.
While players overlooked Sentinel 3's graphics due to its well-designed gameplay, the amateurish-graphics were not updated at all for Sentinel 4; in fact, some of the new graphical addition in Sentinel 4 looks horrible, and the poor graphics now really stands out when combined with the game's poorly-designed gameplay.
Sentinel 4 tried to build upon Sentinel 3, but it completely went in the wrong direction. The main problem with Sentinel 4 is that they added destrutible turrets and completely changed the reason why players enjoy Sentinel 3. Tower Defense games with destructible turrets sometimes work, but Sentinel 4 is NOT one of them.
Sentinel 4 have a similar upgrade system from Sentinel 3, and players who have played Sentinel 3 would be familiar with the new UI and upgrade system. For Sentinel 3 players, Sentinel 4 is easy-to-pick-up, but will find it changed and overall unenjoyable.
The game starts off by throwing exploding enemies that takes big chunks off of player and barrier health, then not long after, the game introduces airborne enemies with no path indicator that fly past defenses to attack your turrets. If your setup is built for attacking ground units, and have no anti-air turrets setup, the defense that the player set up is completely ruined on a random wave that the game announces will contain airbourne enemies.
The combination of destructible turrets and airborne units is frustrating and not an interesting gameplay feature. It creates a lot of busy-work where the player have to micromanage to avoid having your mech destroyed and constantly monitor and repair turrets. Tower Defense lovers who enjoy finding perfect turret placement and watch waves run into their immaculate tower defense design will find this game to be frustrating having to fiddle with repairs and micromanagement.

- Abilites, more awesome ones unlocked playing campaign.

Pro/Con
- Interest gained for unspent currency each wave, subject to personal preference.

Con

This game will give you many hours of enjoyment and is most definitely worth it. I've played countless hours on my phone, and will continue to play on PC.

I got Payday 2 when it was in beta and put about four hundred hours in it.  I was excited for Raid, but didn't have massive expectations for it based on it still being on the Diesel engine, I pretty much expected a WW2 themed PD2-ish game, and that's pretty much what I got.  I have had problems with hit detection on a few weapons, mainly the shotgun (rarely) and the M1 garand (I was standing maybe 20 feet from a flamer, neither of us were moving, and only half of my shots hit, which was odd as I didn't have those issues with the M1 carbine).  Some of the level designs are too simple and too short, but given how quick they were to fix bugs during the beta I think the game will really shine over time with a few patches and some more content.  I really enjoyed the first operation I played (pretty much a multi-day raid), I hope they add more of those.  I also really enjoy how weapon upgrades are based on how much you use a certain weapon, it really rewards you for using a certain weapon a lot.
Edit:  I played the other operation which was surprisingly long, it was comprised of six various raids, but it felt weaker than the first operation with four raids which I felt had a stronger premise.  Honestly, these types of games are about killing lots of enemies and they need to find some way to make it seem longer.  PD2 had drills which could break and you had to repair.  Not a strong premise, but it's something, it takes a while to drill through all that metal, sure.  In Raid, they didn't really know how to tackle this.  On the plus side, they vary things up constantly, it's not drills holding you up 95% of the time.  On the down side, they have really weak reasons to hold you up.  Oh, this dynamite randomly takes a minute to explode.  Oh, this similar looking dynamite on a different raid takes a minute and a half to explode.  Hey, this door for this truck to get by takes a long time to close, then it's gotta stay closed for a bit, for reasons, before the other side can open up.  That, and escort missions, oh my gosh why escort missions, please either don't do those any more or do that very sparingly.  The missions that really shine for me are the ones that have a passable story for me, a good atmosphere, like Wiretap and Odin's Fall for example

Ok it's ID so no surpriss the FPS aspects are very much DOOM like and there are some creepy enemies mixed in with more traditional combatant ones The vehicle aspect varies the game up a bit and allows you to jump from one environment to another at your own choosing although the storyline is linear with optional challenges. Driving itself is reminiscent of Halo. More arcadeish than anything but at least you can get around quickly and as long as you take it for what it is, a game, you can have some fun karting around from A to B with your ridiculously powerful boost in hand. The engineering side of assembling gagdets makes combat varied as the gadgets are often quite effective and worth the investment in time. The aspect of employing your gadgets almost felt like playing Half Life 2 or Bioshock at times. For instance building a mobile sentry and letting it loose on the enemy may give you the ability to flank as the sentry does it thing. It aslo makes for a great guard dog to warn you of surprise company. There's quite a bit to build up and try out and for the most part the end results are rewarding. Initilally the game doesn't offer you much in terms of variety of gameplay but if you stick with it past a couple of hours of learning the ropes you start to obtain the items that make gameplay more varied and then are able to vernture further out to the various levels. Some repitiion exists in the levels as you may play a level in one direction and then be required to play through it in an alternative direction. Not sure if this is so much a negative as knowing the terrain somewhat helps you plan your strategy as the enemies undoubtedly will be more challenging the next time through.
If this were at the initial release price and I had to choose a game at that price I probably wouldn't have selectred RAGE. Now that it's sold at greatly reduced prices I'd say if you are a fan of the likes of DOOM or Wolfenstien (2010+ versions) you'll probably not want to miss this title. It's post apocalyptic earth stuff but it's ID's FPS vision of that and if your a fan of ID and you want to see how they envision it well here it is. I picked it up not expecting much and yeah the story should have been stronger given who it's from and the amount of effort it took to build the game in the first place but there's enough gameplay to keep you pressing on and wanting to see and do more regardless of storyline. Having said that the main characters you interact with can be engaging.
I think this game gets hit hard not for what it is but given the developer, what it could or should have been. That doesn't make it a bad game. Don't let dissappointment over missed opportunities that kept this game from being epic stop you from playing the game. It's an ID FPS in an alternative envirorment with added in gameplay features that some may or may not appreciate in ther ID FPS. All in all good fun for the buck that I'm glad to have experienced.

Good roguelike, technically an evolution of the old Tales of Middle Earth Angband variant but you won't notice unless you've played the old ToME.  It's quite forgiving for the genre.  It's not nearly as spoiler-heavy as Nethack or ADOM, and while it doesn't have the same "transparency" as Dungeon Crawl, it tends to be a little easier.  There is a multiple-life "adventure" mode which can be turned off.  There are essentially no consumables in the game; the roles typically filled by these are instead unlimited-use abilities subject to cooldowns after use.
One interesting feature is that if you log in to play, there is an in-game chatroom.  The online population rarely reaches above 200, so the chatroom isn't actually too cluttered.  I have frequently seen developers online answering questions/taking bug reports.
This game is available for free on the developer's website, but there is one class and a few other minor features that are only available in the paid version.

This game and its predecessor are simply not fun. First, most of your missions in both games are micromanaged by AI NPCs like your spotter or some bad voice actor over the radio."Hold your fire. Now walk forward. Now follow me. Now you may shoot the one on te left." YOu could almost play the games with your eyes closed. Sometimes you go through all that just to have your spotter kill the bad guy. The missions where you're on your own are a wee bit better. You still get excessive instructions over the radio on how to proceed but you have more freedom to figure out your own way through a situation. The dialogue between your character and the NPCs is triggered by certain events, and it' often referes to things they want you to see that you're not seeing, yet the dialog just continues like a recording as your character acknoweledges seeing something you the player have not seen. Sometimes, it's the exact opposite-- you can often clearly see a threat that your micromanaging NPC doesn't acknowledge, and they want you to comtinue into danger. Presumably this is to create SHTF scenarios, but it ends up working like a cheesy haunted house, where you can see the animatronic boogie man around the corner before it springs to action and "surprises" you. There are far too many cut scenes.Your character (in the first game, not this one) must be a 60 year old smoker....you can't do a breath hold for more than a few seconds without your heart rate jumping up to 130, making subsequent breath-hold shots impossible until your HR goes back down to 80bpm (which is apparently your resting HR). The game is short, the acting is bad, and the AI sucks, particularly in the first game. On more than one occasion the spotter just sits, waiting for something, and you cannot continue until it comes back to life. I've had to walk around and approach the spotter from just about every angle to eventually trigger him to start up again. On some missions I've had them just freeze and never come back. The game play is like watching a bad movie where every now and then you get to press a key to contribute to how the bland story unfolds. This game is slightly better than the first, but EVERY other sniping game I've played is way better than these.. Do not waste your time or money.

OneShot is... certainly something. When I first saw the game on Youtube, I instantly fell in love with the art, be it cutscenes or during gameplay, and it didn't take me long to get it myself.
Where I expected a simple, cutesy story, I instead took hold of the position of god, guiding a lost non-cat (honest!) person through unfamiliar world, all while carrying what was probably the most valuable thing in said world, their "sun". Game shot me straight through the heart, making literal emotional pancakes of it.
I found myself enchanted by the beautiful, yet dying world and connected to various people I met along the way, all while accompanied by one of better fitting soundtracks for each and every of the locations and events.
Not caring about the boundaries of a simple window, it expanded itself all allong my wallpaper and documents, effectively turning my entire computer into an active part of the game. (Maybe it's just personal kink, but I really love the 4th wall breaking in games.)
But most of all... I loved the interaction you were allowed to have with Niko. They really made it feel like I wasn't going through the game alone. Instead I had a companion all the way, who put their uttermost trust in myself. (Gladly they didn't follow me blindly, else the sun would end up smashed by a misfortunate missclick at the very beggining.) Just for their sole reason, I refused to ever quit the game, instead pushing forward trying to find beds, as to not leave them in the total darkness which follows the abrupt shutdown of the game by "X"-ing out.
...The game obviously finds a way to exploit the bond between the player and Niko, twisting that few additional needles into your heart at the very end...
I find it really hard to say anything else without spoiling, but if you have spare 10 bucks lying around, I'd honestly recommend to spend them here. The game is not as costly as other giants currently on the market, and I can promise you the experience is equally, if not more worth it.
I'll never forget you, Niko.

Hotline Miami left quite a mark on the indie scene when it came out and so it's no surprise that it spawned a number of imitators. 12 Is Better Than 6 is one of them and arguably one of the better ones. It's remarkable how closely the core gameplay loop resembles Hotline Miami even if its setting and art style are wildly different. It's still top-down but everything is in black and white, almost like it was drawn on paper. It's a bit of an acquired taste in that regard and one can certainly argue whether that is simply minimalistic or merely lazy.
Set in the second half of the 19th century on America's untamed frontier; a classic western setting. You play as The Mexican, an infamous gunslinger who starts the game escaping from the law. That's what you do most of the time: shoot loads of bad guys. Combat is fast and deadly. Both you and your enemies die with a single bullet. Given that you are also hopelessly outnumbered on every map, this makes a careful approach and smart positioning a necessity. You have a small arsenal of classic western firearms at your disposal: a six-shooter, a shotgun, a rifle and dynamite. Additionally a bow and a knife for silent kills. Unfortunately, there's not a whole lot of variety when it comes to enemies or maps, and it does tend to get repetitive after a while.
That's not the only downside, however. The dialogue is amateurish at best and the story is a mess. Plot threads and characters are picked up and dropped at seemingly random. When it doesn't drown in western clichés, including magical Native Americans, many times you will wonder what exactly the point of the last mission was.
Don't pick this game up expecting an enthralling narrative. Judging by the credits, the game was developed somewhere in eastern Europe. I don't know whether it's poorly translated or outright written by somebody whose grip on the English language is lacking but it has to be one of the two.
Recommended to fans of Hotline Miami and similar games. Everyone else should think twice.

Defense Grid: The Awakening is a Tower Defense game made in what reminds me as homage to old Starcraft TD maps put in to a modern more updated form. For perspective, it came out only a year after The Orange Box did. When it was first released, it was undeniably the best tower defense game in the world, but that's not surprising, because its only competition was Desktop Tower Defense and a handful of other shoddy flash games that were starting to ride the trend.
A lot of time has passed since then, and hundreds of weird and interesting tower defense games have been released. So, is Defense Grid still the best? No clue. I haven't played as many tower defense games with the exception of a few SC2 TD maps and WC3 maps.
The people who made Defense Grid understand where tower defense came from. Everything about this game is built to look, feel, and sound like retro StarCraft, from the isometric view, to the color choices, to the tower types and damage types. Gun towers are basically bunkers of marines, inferno towers are bunkers of firebats, cannon towers are bunkers of ghosts, and so on. They’ve even borrowed some classic towers from other games, like the tesla coils from the Red Alert series. Even today, it still hits me with that old 2002-era nostalgia of searching for tower defense maps on
and that pumped feeling of starting the map with a full lobby of people (because, of course, you needed a full lobby to even have a chance!)
Defense Grid also has a scoring system, which rewards even the tiniest improvements in performance with exponentially more money and score. It appeals greatly to the gamer's OCD, since the better you play the beginning of a mission, the more freedom you have to build deadly mazes for the remainder of the mission, the easier victory becomes, and the more often you can see your score skyrocket into the hundreds of millions. Fast-forward and checkpoint-rewinding controls make it simple to re-do every wave until it is perfect. It also creates an ultra-hardcore metagame with a massive curve of leaderboard scores, if you’re into that kind of competition. You’ll need to learn some really annoying advanced techniques if you want to break into the top 100 on any mission, or you could choose to compete in maps and game modes where the techniques don’t apply. Or you could simply choose to compete with yourself and your friends, or just aim for the pre-set gold medals.
This game is the sole reason why future tower defense games had to start trying new things, because it got the basics about as perfect as they can possibly get, at least for those of us who still occasionally see hordes of zerglings filing through mazes of bunkers in our waking dreams.
Pros:
+ Nostalgia TD map put into a modern form
+ One of the better TD games
+ Lots of customizability in gameplay and base formation
+ Scoring adds an element of competitiveness amongst friends and OCD min/maxing
Cons:
- TD is all the game is, if you're not into TD style games you won't like it
TL;DR:
7/10

This is a Dark Souls-inspired Metroidvania game that makes a good shot of trying to reproduce what made Dark Souls great in a 2D setting. In many ways, it succeeds. The atmosphere is suitably oppressive, the story is told subtly through item descriptions and brief encounters with random NPCs and everything like that. As a Dark Souls lover, I found this enjoyable.
I think the game has two problems:
1) It's easy.
I picked a Mage and went pure casting in my build, with enough endurance to have a quick dodge roll. For the first 3-4 bosses the game was appropriately challenging, but after I found one or two of the advanced spells that quickly melted away. My character could just bombard an enemy with magic from a screen away and then roll away well before they could retaliate. And when you add an air dash move to that equation it just felt unfair. Towards the end I would be walk into boss rooms and just blast the everloving♥♥♥♥♥♥out of the thing, often only stopping to sip one healing potion tops.
Maybe it's a different sort of game for a melee character, but the enemies just didn't feel like it had an answer for my character type. The fact that the game let me have 10 free mana potions at a time meant I was never going to run out of magic and so all the massive ranged DPS I was putting out came with no consequence. Even the final boss just couldn't close the distance with me to make things easier.
At least a few of the bosses needed to be changed to challenge casters more.
2) The soundtrack kind of sucks.
There's only one boss song for the majority of the game, while all the stages are either silent or has a generic guitar riff playing. The last boss' music sounds like someone fell asleep on an organ.
This game really needed to kick up the music game a bit and get some really evocative boss or area music going, just like Dark Souls or Symphony of the Night. The music in a game like this needs to play an active storytelling role. Think of Ornsteign and Smough or Sir Alonne in DS2. This isn't something you can just neglect.
I don't think that wouldn't have been impossible either. The Dark Souls community is pretty big with lots of creatives in there. Just cut Alex Roe a cheque and you'd have made this game 10x better.
Anyhow, those two quibbles aside it is a great game. Give it a go.

Salt and Sanctuary is an incredible 2D platformer developed by SKA studio. The game focuses on combat, puzzles and timing platform, but if you pay enough attention to everything around, you will slowly notice the insanely detailed story behind the lifeless world and its lore; It is very huge world put in a small simple 2D game and this makes S&S more valuable than anything i've ever played. For the price tag, this game is a steal even at full price because its the contents could be easily worth around $30 or more so don't hesitate if you want to pick it up, you can't go wrong with this price.
Let me explain it, the game was developed by a very small indie studio, only 2 people to be specific and it took them about two and a half years to develop; and the gameplay, well, it's tough, the first playthrough will take you around 25-30 hours. Its difficulty exceeds the standard videogame for sure so my advice, if you find some areas too hard, you will need to go back to the old areas and grind for some levels; trust me, being overleveled is one of the pleasure in this game but that's not all, when you backtracking and farming, you will propably find some secret areas as well as learning enemy's attack patterns and this is the key that help you survive. You will just barely scratch the surface of this game in the first playthrough, there are plenty of build combinations, secret areas, lore and hidden mechanics need to be explored; i still find out new mechanic even after 50 hours lol, for example: i didn't even know that you can counter with a pistol until my 3rd playthrough and it just showed me how crazily deep the combat system was. Now the level design, it's just simply genius, pretty much every area is interconnected, you can easily get lost and this will happen frequently since you don't know where to go and don't have any map or rada or gps like others moderm games; you just have to go with your instinct and when you reach some hardcore platforming sections, a single mistake or failed timing can wideout your entire grinded hour. My recommendation, check out
if you have hard time figuring out where to go next.
Now the most beautiful thing that makes S&S my all time favorite is the art style and its lore. Remember the first time i saw S&S, i thought it was a comedy game lol. But after playing it for couple of hours, the atmosphere hit me really hard; it's really dark and depressing, some areas could turn out really creepy. But everything you see propably has its own story,  you have to collect and connect informations in order to image the whole picture and trust me, the details of this picture will blow your mind. Make sure you check out
after finishing the game, it's a really well-written fan book which collects all pieces of information to explain the lore. Sure there are still mysteries and questions left unanswered. all these things will up to you and your theories.
The story, gameplay, art style, atmosphere ect just simply make S&S my all time favorite video game.
The only downside of this game is balancing, greatswords and greathammers are way too powerful compare to others weapon and this just make daggers, spears kinda poinless. But there's already a
to rebalance everything. Make sure you keep an eye on it if you're interested.

Sanctum is a tower defense game at its heart. You build towers and create mazes to stop the waves of enemies. All of this is in done in first person and when the wave starts you can use your 3 guns to personally attack the enemies. As the developers have said this is the first game ever to have this combination and it sure is fun!
GRAPHICS: 10/10
The graphics are pretty good all around. It can be taxing on older computers so it should be noted that the developers have thoughtfully allowed you to edit the engine files to reduce the graphics even further. To me this is a huge plus because if I couldn't do that I couldn't play this game. My only complaint is that the lower your resolution the fuzzier the text gets. I can barely read it at 800x600. The higher your resolution the harder the game is on your computer. That said this game lets you go down all the way to 320x200! So if your computer is real bad you can turn the resolution down that far and play with ease when you start the wave, then turn it up in between waves to build.
SOUND: 9/10
There are some nice sound effects when you build and do things like that. The gun sounds are kind of lackluster but this isn't heavily focused on that. Nothing bad about the monster sounds either. The music is actually really good and doesn't get repetitive or annoying.
STORY
No score because there isn't a story and tower defense games don't necessarily need one. I think they have released some lore and stuff in preparation for the sequel but I haven't read any of it. All I know is that you're a girl and you have something on your left arm that allows you to build towers. Your goal is to stop the invading monsters from getting to the giant blue core. What that core is I don't know.
TOWER DEFENSE ASPECT: 10/10
As I said this game is tower defense at its heart and it does not disappoint. There are several tower types, all useful to varying degrees depending on your play style. Something this game does that sadly few TDs do is allowing you to build a maze that the enemies are forced to run through. This allows for even more strategy than just simply building at certain spots outside of the enemies' route. On most maps you can create their route! You also have a set amount of towers equipped that you can then use to build on the level. This means even more strategy.
FIRST PERSON SHOOTER ASPECT: 9/10
This game is a shooter at a distant second. When you manually start the next wave of enemies you can then shoot them with your own weapons which you choose before the level starts. This part of the game is pretty basic as expected. The weapons are simple but each one does have an alternate fire which adds more variety. You can also upgrade them with your money to make them stronger. Despite shooting not being the main focus it's still essential for beating the levels.
What gives this a 9/10 instead of something lower is the fact that all enemies have a weak spot that can be exploited by you for a great increase in damage. Further, some enemies can only be killed by hitting them in their weak spot, something that isn't easy for your towers. There is an enemy that can only be hurt from its back. A tall enemy with a bobbing head that only takes damage from attacks to its head. Still another that has armor that greatly reduces damage to it and the only way to temporarily remove the armor is for a single concentrated shot (sniper) to hit it in the head. All this means a lot more strategy and player input is required than just simply shooting the enemy. Unfortunately if you have horrendous aiming skills you may have trouble, but there is an easy difficulty for you to enjoy.
ENEMIES: 9/10
There are more enemy types than the ones listed above, and they're all distinct. There are also flying enemies which pay no heed to your carefully made mazes. The designs are unique and interesting and follow a similar theme.
LENGTH AND REPLAYABILITY
There are several maps to enjoy including a few free ones and others you must pay for (worth it). Each map has 4 difficulties as well as various survival modes to play. On normal a map will take an hour or so to beat. There is also multiplayer but I never messed with that.
FINAL SCORE: 9/10
This is a must play for any fan of tower defense, if only to check out something new and unique in the genre. Even if you aren't into TDs check this game out (so long as you at least like FPSs) and who knows it just might get you into the genre. I got this game on a sale and it's worth it even at full price. There is a demo so if you aren't sure give it a spin.

On normal difficulty its a pretty fun time sinker with friends, On hard teamwork and coordination is neccasary. It gave me way more gratifacation than payday, where everyone can be doing something else and be winning.
