This is an awesome MMORPG that is slightly different then most. For example there are 4 classes and each class has 8 different skill trees(Reffered to as Soul Trees) for different play styles and each skill/soul tree is like a subclass.
CLERIC SUBCLASSES:
CABALIST- The Cabalist is an offensive Cleric who draws on powers that others fear. Using ritual and sigil to call forth seeping death and suffocating water, he devastates the battlefield with powerful attacks that catch all of his enemies in his grip
DRUID- Druids are melee Clerics who forge bonds with Fae creatures, strengthening their bodies, minds, and spirits by drawing upon the magical energies of their companions.
INQUISITOR- The Inquisitor is a cleric who no longer follows the doctrines of life or death alone; instead, they stand between these forces demanding purity from both. An Inquisitor passes judgment on those who are worthy, and damns those who are corrupt.
JUSTICAR- Justicars are healing clerics who fight shoulder-to-shoulder with their allies in close combat. Conviction builds with each swing of their weapon, bolstering nearby comrades and powering the Justicar’s potent healing magic.
PURIFIER- These Clerics draw upon a pact with their long-dead ancestors as the source of their offensive power. While Purifiers wreathe their allies in flames, they can unleash a spirit vanguard to visit wrath upon their foes.
SENTINEL- The Sentinel brings the blessings of light to all who do the will of the gods. Capable of healing many wounded at one time, Sentinels bolster their allies and protect themselves with divine wrath.
SHAMAN- The Shaman binds the power of the icy north to his very being, wreathing himself in pure elemental force. This power augments a Shaman’s attacks, making him a powerful melee combatant, and provides shields and reactive healing.
WARDEN- Echoing the soothing ebb and flow of the tides, Wardens specialize in slow healing that escalates over time, making them ideal for prolonged fights that would exhaust most healers.
MAGE SUBCLASSES:
ARCHON- Archons are support specialists who steal their opponents’ strength and convert that raw energy into beneficial magic. These mages bolster their allies and unleash potent kinetic blasts, quickly turning the tide of battle.
CHLOROMANCER- The Chloromancer is a healing specialist who draws on the vital energies of plants and nature to find a balance between life and death. They harness these energies into a devastating force, or recycle destructive magic to heal their allies.
DONINATOR- The Dominator is a support Mage who terrorizes opponents, leaving them unable or unwilling to act. Those who muster the courage to assault a Dominator will find themselves at the mercy of arcane shields that turn the fury of their own blows against them.
ELEMENTALIST- Elementalists are mages who specialize in manipulating and controlling the raw energies of the planes. Through fierce discipline and strict study, these mages dedicate themselves to commanding the harshest and most chaotic forces known to exist.
NECROMANCER- Necromancers are damage dealers who synergize with their pets. The majority of a Necromancer’s damage comes from a fully supported and buffed pet. In an emergency, Necromancers can also serve as secondary healers by sacrificing their own health to their allies.
PYROMANCER- Pyromancers are destructive mages whose sole focus is the mastery of fire, from launching massive incinerating blasts, to trapping their opponents behind a smoldering wall of flame. No other Ascended can match the sheer destruction at the Pyromancer’s fingertips.
STORMCALLER- Stormcallers are mages who channel the raw fury of the wind and water to command the battlefield, chilling their opponents to the bone or stopping their hearts with electric shock.
WARLOCK- Consummate practitioners of the dark arts, Warlocks embrace the grim forces of entropy and death. Protected within a cloak of shadows, they lurk on the edges of the conflict, as their deadly energies inevitably consume all that stand in their way.
ROUGE SUBCLASSES:
ASSASSIN- Masters of subtlety and subterfuge, an Assassin’s ability to walk in the shadows allows them to bypass obstacles and launch devastating surprise attacks. A rare few survive the initial assault, only to succumb to virulent poisons.
BARD- Singing the songs of battle and playing heart-stirring cadences, Bards embolden their allies and cripple their enemies through rhythm and rhyme.
BLADEDANCER- Blade Dancers are masters of wielding edged weapons. They specialize in ritualized combat movements that are lightning fast. Blade Dancers can overwhelm even an accomplished opponent's defenses, setting them up for a devastating coup de grace.
MARKSMEN- Marksmen are offensive sharpshooters trained to thin enemy ranks with ruthless efficiency. They combine swift hit-and-run attacks with devastating volleys, endlessly harassing targets, sowing the battlefield with dead and crippled foes.
NIGHTBLADE- Possessing deadly agility and mastery of the blade, the Nightblade can also draw upon the planar magics of fire and death to deal doom in a variety of ways. Favoring light armor, their ability to stalk and quickly eliminate their adversaries means the unfortunate quarry rarely has the chance to defend, let alone counterattack.
RANGER- Rangers are consummate hunters who know the strengths and weaknesses of every beast, taming animal companions to augment their considerable prowess in ranged combat. This synergy between bow and beast allows Rangers to handily overcome the most daunting obstacles.
RIFSTALKER- The Riftstalker is a defensive specialist who bends the planes to enhance his constitution and shift in and out of the physical dimension. These highly skilled and survivable combatants keep their opponents’ focus while easily evading incoming blows.
SABOTEUR- The Saboteur is a cunning Rogue who uses explosives and other incendiaries to cripple opponents and control the battlefield. With proper preparation, a Saboteur can destroy enemies without ever giving them a chance to join battle.
WARRIOR SUBCLASSES:
BEASTMASTER- This Warrior's journey begins by bonding to a spirit companion. The spirit beast fights beside the Beastmaster with speed and strength and sees him through his darkest trials.
CHAMPION- Champions are powerful Warriors who excel at melee combat. Wielding massive two-handed weapons, these battle-tested fighters find few equals in one-on-one battle. Champions strive to become one with their blade, constantly honing their fighting skills to win glory through warfare.
PALADIN- Righteous defenders of the weak, Paladins use heavy shields and divine blessings to stand as a bulwark against their foes. The Paladin’s large shield not only offers protection, but affords many opportunities to launch devastating counters in close combat.
PARAGON- The Paragon moves like a furious storm, never giving his enemy time to regroup. A master of dual-wielding, he uses parries and disciplined forms to build up power attacks and stay out of danger.
REAVER- Reavers are warriors who combine the art of combat with the entropic energies of death. The slightest touch of their weapon can spread disease, incite madness, and death to those unlucky enough to face them.
RIFTBLADE- Riftblades are Warriors who learn to enhance their attacks with elemental magic, allowing them to cast bolts of force across the battlefield and strike with boundless energies.
VOIDNIGHT- The Void Knight is a defensive Warrior who uses eldritch techniques to counter magic-wielding foes. Spells that would bring another Warrior low are shaken off by a Void Knight, reflected back at the caster, or stored in pacts the Void Knight can unleash to devastating effect.
WARLORD-A Warlord’s commanding presence expresses itself in auras that inspire her comrades to victory and cow her enemies into submission, allowing her to control the field of battle.

I hated this game for years, dismissing it as nothing but a total rip off of Deus Ex and Thief without any of the substance of each series, absolutely not the level design and absolutely not the story. Although that's still true,
even after spending so many hours on it trying to like it somehow eventually clicked for me. It's a truly great game. Not exceptional, and it has its issues, but I do rate it very highly now.
++Stealthing around is just a lot of fun
++Very replayable
++There are two levels in particular that I rate incredibly highly
+Decent art design by the same guy who did Half-Life 2 (you will see hanging mysterious pods)
+Performance is great. Well over 100fps at all times at 4K max everything on a GTX1060.
+Voice acting is good for the most part
+Writing is well done
+There's a specific mission so good and atmospheric I rank it as one of the best ever
+The powers are quite fun to use
+The world of Dishonored is pretty interesting and well built. Good setting.
+The 'pacifist' ways of taking out assassination targets are brutal and even more rewarding then outright murdering them, even if you have a bloodlust
+Game looks gorgeous, especially in later levels
+Later levels are tons of fun and are where the game really shines
+Sound design is decent
+-The whole idea of runes and bonecharms is cool, but they're not very helpful
-+Readables are pretty uninteresting for the most part, but I'm glad they're there
+-Average length
-There's a lot to explore, but there's no reason to do it as you already get a lot of money and there's nothing else really to be gained from it
-Somewhat forgettable music, besides a few tracks
-Stealth is a little basic being only line of sight in depth and that's about it. Oh, and running is noisy, but everything else is silent.
-Your gear is obviously made for a lethal playthrough as there are no non-lethal equipment besides sleeping darts and the ability to knock out people by choking them. This isn't that much of a problem if the game wasn't really made
for non-lethal, but considering how it lets you get through every mission without killing people, has a stat stating whether you did and allows you to find a way to get rid of every assassination target without truly killing them, the
game was obviously made to allow you to easily do it. Even the powers are made for lethal as all of the ones that don't just improve movement or sensual abilities are for getting better at killing.
-Despite all equipment tailoring to a murdering playstyle, the game gives you crap for murdering
--Combat is really quite bad. Swords reach further than it looks like they should, your hits always go through people even though it looks right on target, attacks are normally hard to counter due to shoddy animation work etc.
If you're going to play this killing everyone, swords wielded and gun in hand, don't buy this game. It doesn't work nearly enough to suit the playstyle despite being a game meant to suit both stealth and action.
--Everyone knows Arkane pretty much rip off everything from old Looking Glass Studios and Ion Storm classics. I mean, what hasn't been totally ripped off here? Like every gameplay mechanic has been ganked from Thief and Deus Ex,
the artstyle is Half-Life 2, all of your equipment is taken from Thief, the level design is very similar to Deus Ex etc. Everything that makes the game, the game, is taken from other stuff. Arkane have zero originality in-terms of gameplay.

Dishonored is a first person action game with some unique twists. You play the role of a loyal bodygaurd who is wrongfully accused of murder. You are granted supernatural powers by a god who enjoys watching your revenge. The story is good enough to give the player motivation to "get revenge", but it also puts you in a situation where that revenge isn't necesarily murder. While the plot is somewhat interesting the main features of this game are the stealth mechanics, the powers, and the choice to kill.
The stealth in this game is solid. You can stay out of sight and be quiet to avoid detection. The levels are designed so that there are multiple places to hide and different paths to take. You are highly encouraged to be sneaky. So you'll probably be lurking around a lot.
If you are detected, you'll be faced with a fight. Gaurds will call over other gaurds to help fight you. There are also other enemies, but gaurds are the main foe throughout the game. You have a few lethal weapons at your disposal, such as a sword, gun, and crossbow. There are also nonlethal options in a fight. Tranquilizer darts or choking a gaurd out can subdue an enemy without killing him. Running and hiding may also be an option. In fact you can play the entire game without killing a single person. You may also be able to use some of your supernatural powers to fight or evade.
The powers are the true highlight of the game. These seperate your character from the npcs. There are several powers to unlock, and they can all be upgraded into a more powerful version. My favorite powers are blink, time slow, and whirlwind. Blink is your bread and butter, it lets you teleport a short distance with extreme accuracy. Blink is great for stealth, combat, evasion, and navigating the level. Slowing time is a cool power that makes fighting easy. Upgraded you can basically stop time. Combined with blink, slowing time can let you sneak across an open room filled with gaurds because they won't have time to see you. Whirlwind turns you into the last airbender, letting you toss gaurds around and dominate combat. There's some other powers too.
The game isn't all good. It has some problems. First of all it is fairly short. It will likely take 8 hours or so to complete. That being said there is some replay value, because to can play sneakier or more violently. Also you can't get all the powers in a single game so you have to play multiple times to use them all. The levels are short but they are also fun and memorable.
Another problem with the "levels" is that you cannot go back and use unlocks from later levels on the earlier ones. In other words you can't get all the powers and then return to the first level to just have fun with it. I see why it's not in there, but it would have been fun.
The DLC isn't too great, I think the base game is much better. The DLC is completely seperate from the base storyline and only adds a different campaign.
Overall, the game plays very well. It is very fun and offers a lot of player freedom. The main downfall of the game is that there isn't more of it, it ends too quickly. The powers are very cool and fun. The stealth is fun. The combat is fun. It is simply a fun game.

Dishonored is one of those few single player games that you can play over and over again and never get bored of, and that is for a multitude of reasons. The kill chaining, the achievements, the dlc, the alternate endings. I could just go on for days, but the main reason I fell in love with this game was due to the lore. I would absolutely recommend that you get this game along with the dlc to anyone.

Salt and Sanctuary is an incredible 2D platformer developed by SKA studio. For the price tag, this game is a steal even at full price because its the contents could be easily worth around $30 or more so don't hesitate if you want to pick it up, you can't go wrong with this price.
Let me explain it, the game was developed by a very small indie studio, only 2 people to be specific and it took them about two and a half years to develop; and the gameplay, well, it's tough, the first playthrough will take you around 25-30 hours. Its difficulty exceeds the standard videogame for sure so my advice, if you find some areas too hard, you will need to go back to the old areas and grind for some levels; trust me, being overleveled is one of the pleasure in this game but that's not all, when you backtracking and farming, you will propably find some secret areas as well as learning enemy's attack patterns and this is the key that help you survive. This game, much like the roguelike ADOM, is a story driven game with setpiece and semi-random zones.  If you have played roguelikes in the past, dont let the trailers give you the wrong impression of its interface or themes.  The game is actually quite good.
A few technical details first.  The game is available for free on the creator's website.  Buying the game on steam unlocks some donator benefits such as a specific dotator only character class and item transfer between characters.  The game also has its own login, this is to use the site's statistics tracking features, cloud saves (IIRC), and also lets you access an official IRC channel from within the game client itself.  You do not need to login to play the game.  The game performs very well, no complaints.  The game has a great deal of accessibility features, such as a very functional tileset, mouse controls, hud rescaling, and some automation as well.  Overall, very accessible.
In terms of game design, I have a few things to comment on.  I very much enjoy roguelikes that have a storyline element such as this one, because it gives a good element of cohesion to the game with goals and progression.  This one actually has a number of class or race specific scenarios that help add to this as well.
The game's skill progression system is skill-tree based, with each class having at least two different themed trees with several branches along with more generic ones to give you a few options on how you want to play your character.  For example, a necromancer might have both minion summoning and debuff curses with two trees each to pick between.  Many skills intuitively synergize or benefit each other, and the play also has the ability to acquire out-of-class skills a few times per game for even more flexibility.  The last few skill points can be unspent while in towns if you dislike a recent skill choice, and skills also show the effect of adding an additional skillpoint before you spend them, as well as what character stats influence the variables of those skills.  I find this skill tree system more accesible than a train/abuse stat system present in many other roguelikes, and while the transparency is not perfect it is VERY welcome.
The game's combat, as in all perma-death roguelikes, is focused on limiting situations in which you experience risk.  As in all roguelikes this means things like bottlenecking enemies into more controlled environments and crown control, but more notably lies in escape skills for this game.  Being able to leave a situation you will not be able to survive is very crucial in this game, as you almost always cannot simly heal through or face-tank some enemies.  You will be fighting a lot of enemies in this game and the game is quite long, but the game gives you both difficulty and permadeath options so that you may play the game in a method that you enjoy.  The default setting for permadeath gives you a number of lives, and you can accrue a limited number of additional lives at certain milestones in the game, thus letting you maintain risk without letting a single careless mistake end a heavy investment of game hours.
The game's replayability more or less lies in two things.  First, many zones have an alternate version of their randomly maps which have varied enemies and difficulty from their originals.  These can be surprising to discover after your first playthrough.  The second is in trying out different race / class combinations, of which there are quite a few with a good variety of options.
There's quite a bit I could talk about, but more or less I'd reccomend this game.  It can be a pretty heavy time investment, as most traditional-style roguelikes can be, but its a pretty darn good one for a modern era!

I remember when Rage was a highly anticipated title. The follow up to Doom 3 that was years in the making. When Rage came out the reviews were pretty mediocre. At least for a shooter that took years of development by the guys that mastered the genre.  Nothing really appealed to me about Rage, I'm not the biggest fan of "open world" games and the post apocalyptic setting has been done to death. But on a whim I decided to install Rage and a couple hours I was still playing it. Needless to say it a huge surprise this was me.  The good? The game looks amazing (though less so with up close textures) and ran smooth as butter on my OK PC. The gunplay is awesome. Tons of weapons and each has a distinct and satisfying feel. There is tons of stuff to do. Take contracts, race for upgrades, minigames or build things to help you kill stuff. Rage has you covered. The bad? Yes, the abrupt ending is indeed terrible and screams for a sequel (which will probably never come). Apparently the game was designed with a controller in mind because selecting turrets, grenades etc is wonky and not explained to you how to do it (Hold the F1 key, mouse click what you want to use). The racing parts I thought were only OK. Overall though I had a ton of fun with Rage. The $9.99 MSRP is absolutely worth it. A sale makes it an even better value. And definitely get The Scorchers DLC. There you get an actual boss fight at the end which was really well done. Even with its imperfections, Rage gets an 8.5/10 from me.

I don't think that Steam version of this game can give new players a chance to understand why is it a great game. First, there is no music - and music is so important here. Second - to run it properly, one has to go at some lengths.
But this title was extraordinary at its time for numerous reasons, and the biggest advantage is immersive and addictive gameplay. Paradoxically so, because graphics are pretty bad. But not many people remember that this game was out when 3D accelerators were still not something to take for granted. I first played Jedi Knight in the software renderer mode, and believe me, without 3D accelerator it looked better than any other title of the time. But the biggest thing about this game, as I think of it now, is its silence. You know, modern games are afraid to leave you alone, there are always some NPCs yelling at you, your guide telling you where to go, hints, messages and directions pop up from everywhere... It doesn't let you sink deep into the story and feel like you're there. But JK is the opposite. You are always on your own, which is emphasised by the gigantic proportions of the levels. The classic John Williams' score is tastefully woven into the atmosphere and is changing dynamically to make it even more dramatic. The cutscenes tie the story together and it all makes sense, you are no longer wandering from checkpoint to checkpoint for some obscure reasons, killing people; you always know your mission. Plus to that you carry the responsibility for your actions - the way you play will define your fate - become a Jedi or be consumed by the dark side of the Force. Add to it a lightsaber, the Force powers, and you forget about the graphics, and feel like it is all happening to you.
If you're looking for cutting-edge graphics and unrivaled live-action cutscenes. Lucas Arts' Jedi Knight: Dark Forces II is the game for you.

Alright, it's been a while since I last tried doing a review, and last time I was insulted for my opinion. But hey, not everyone's an ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥.
So, on the topic at hand, I'll be blunt. Evolve isn't, never was, nor ever will be perfect. It has bugs. It has issues. It has all the things that a game has. But, that doesn't make Evolve a bad game... Not by a long shot. Yeah, I have to admit, some of the issues it's having right now are rather annoying, but with time and effort they Evolve team will smooth the rough edges, and make the actual edges sharper. It takes a block of metal to make a sword, and they're not done forging it yet.
Really ♥♥♥♥♥♥ analogies aside, I will make a suggestion. Play with friends. Whether they were friends you knew before playing the game, or ones you made because of the game, play with them and have fun. Just the other night I was playing with a group of friends, and I started laughing so hard I was crying. Not a thing you can really do with faceless, nameless a-holes who abuse the things in the game. And when your friends pull♥♥♥♥♥♥moves, you can laugh about it, rather than getting frustrated at the guy who just ruined your night.
Oh, and for those who really want to try something different, here's a suggestion... Play as Wraith. And don't go gung-ho like you would with another monster. Try taking the stealthy approach- Run, hide, sneak, and generally mess with the hunters. Wraith is the smallest, and sure, she has the least amount of health, but you can get to stage 2 without a single fight if you're careful. And it's always fun winnig a match with only one actual fight, and that fight taking thirty seconds or less. Well, I'll wrap this terrible, terrible review up and say this:
Try the game. Give it a chance. Play for a while, try different classes, hunters, monsters, and just enjoy the experience. If you don't like it, don't play it. If you do like it, tell your friends about it, have a blast, get those tear ducts worked up, that whole deal. And if you're gonna give someone problems, point that negative energy towards any jerks who tell you to never speak again when you're trying to be friendly, and then call you a queer after saying they were being rude. Looking at you, a-hole.
Well, I hope this review -and the suggestions therin- helped someone decide whether or not they were going to try the game. Despite my not having said anything about the actual game -it's really good-. And I hoped that my terrible attempts at sarcastic humor made someone smile. ♥♥♥♥♥♥ ending, away!

20 hours in, at the time of this review. Yep, there are a lot of comparisons to Dark Souls. Replace souls with salt, and it's basically the same mechanic.
It's fair enough to say it is a Metroidvania Dark Souls. And this one did it amazingly. It's been a while since I've enjoyed a platformer of this nature.
I put this one just below Symphony of the Night, in terms of 'Where did four hours just go? .... meh.... *tap* *tap* *tap*...
There's an expansive skill tree, so few builds will feel exactly alike. Want a pole axe maniac mage? Have at it, Brochacho! You can do eet!
The crafting system isn't terribly deep, but it's interesting. Bosses drop items which can be used to turn certain weapons into various stronger weapons. This can also be achieved with far more common items. It's neat.
There's no actual pause. The only safe places are sanctuaries you must claim in the name of a number of idols which have their own benefits. You'll have to claim sanctuaries in their name and kill their enemies to improve these semi-customizable sanctuaries.
You customize the sanctuaries by placing figures (cleric, fighter, leader, traveler, merchant, blacksmith, etc.) upon the altar of your chosen idol. The traveler in particular makes getting around the world easier, via an item he sells. Fast travel, gold is cheap!
Another thing I love about this game is that you can farm all you want and get totally OP. But you can still easily die if you forget about the various ambush situations throughout the game. Try being level 80, repeatedly without cancel, getting smacked around by an unfortunately effective sneak attack.
Now go back and git gud. Git u salt. Git rekd old man.

Exceptional title, embraces the core thinking of Dark Souls and brings a world to life with a compelling minimalist story, satisfying combat feel and rewarding gameplay.
I'll say that it feels like a distinctly "smaller" Souls world: for example, there's one greatsword available in the game world, additional obtainable through a not-immediately-obvious creed (covenant) uprank. This is fine for casual playthroughs, but I felt like my options for making boss weapons were a bit skewed by this: if I made something, I'd ultimately exchange it for another weapon down the line. This turned out to be less problematic as the upgrades carried over (partially, anyway). The achievements are nicely spaced, rewarding alongside the boss kills, but I don't think I have the patience for the second ending given less replayability - I started as a knight, enjoyed myself for
, but now find myself disinterested in replaying as a mage/cleric - the gameplay doesn't feel varied enough, and the options for equipment seems concentrated towards blades rather than spellbooks. ~
is however, something I'll be recommending for a while.

Salt and Sanctuary is better than it has any right to be--it is, in point of fact, terrific. While the great reviews and "Best of 2016" lists I read called this game a "2D Dark Souls," that description always sounds like a vague insult. Salt and Sanctuary borrows its RPG elements from Dark Souls, but it distinguishes itself through its tight, enjoyable gameplay.
So, let's get the similarities out of the way first. Yes, the leveling and RPG elements are basically re-skins of Dark Souls (i.e. salt = souls; creeds = covenants; bonfies = sanctuaries; levels buy points in attributes; weapons scale by letter, etc). The same could be said of the story and NPCs. Most of it feels like undersea/nautical/undead themed Dark Souls fan fiction--it's vaguely dark and slightly elliptical, but not nearly as opaque as Dark Souls' lore.
But, S&S takes this framework and turns it all into something really enjoyable: By mashing up Dark Souls' systems with the tight controls, action, and sense of exploration of a Metroidvania, it achieves something remarkable in the way the game actually plays. The controls are responsive and the action is fast-paced--jumping, blocking, rolling, dashing, slashing and bashing have an almost fluid joy to them. That's not to say the game is easy, as death comes frequently, with only two or three solid hits enough to kill you in most cases. But, I loved the thrill of rolling through an enemy's attack, executing a well timed combo, then juking, rolling, and jumping out of the way of their counterattack.
And while the combat is the biggest treat, the platforming and exploring are great, too. As you explore, your character acquires "brands," which serve the standard Metroidvania function of allowing you to access new places--you get a wall jump, an air dash, and the ability to go upside down in certain areas. These elements allow for some really interesting level design, and, once all the brands are collected,  eventually allows for the different areas to interconnect in surprising ways.
There are some nits to pick, but most are compensated for by other elements: While I generally loved the art style (especially for the bosses), the characters and NPCs I found odd. (Why doesn't anyone have a nose?!?!) The different weapon types didn't seem particularly interesting, but the different attack combos (including aerial combos) were pretty cool. Magic seemed underpowered. Overall, though, none of it detracts from an excellent, fun package.
So, while it might be easy to dismiss Salt and Sanctuary as derivative, it ends up taking Dark Souls' inspiration and doing something awesome with it. In fact, on a minute-by-minute basis, I had more fun playing Salt and Sanctuary than Dark Souls games. Praise the salt!

2d Dark Souls might sound like a reductive description, but it's entirely accurate: the degree to which you will enjoy S&S is directly related to how much you enjoy the Dark Souls series. There are some minor differences, but they share a huge amount of the same DNA, and all of the critical things that you love about Souls games are here: a big open world that you can explore in different ways, multiple ways to build your character, a big focus on gear and upgrades, and of course, punishing difficulty and huge boss fights.
Highly recommended.

This game, much like the roguelike ADOM, is a story driven game with setpiece and semi-random zones.  If you have played roguelikes in the past, dont let the trailers give you the wrong impression of its interface or themes.  The game is actually quite good.
A few technical details first.  The game is available for free on the creator's website.  Buying the game on steam unlocks some donator benefits such as a specific dotator only character class and item transfer between characters.  The game also has its own login, this is to use the site's statistics tracking features, cloud saves (IIRC), and also lets you access an official IRC channel from within the game client itself.  You do not need to login to play the game.  The game performs very well, no complaints.  The game has a great deal of accessibility features, such as a very functional tileset, mouse controls, hud rescaling, and some automation as well.  Overall, very accessible.
In terms of game design, I have a few things to comment on.  I very much enjoy roguelikes that have a storyline element such as this one, because it gives a good element of cohesion to the game with goals and progression.  This one actually has a number of class or race specific scenarios that help add to this as well.
The game's skill progression system is skill-tree based, with each class having at least two different themed trees with several branches along with more generic ones to give you a few options on how you want to play your character.  For example, a necromancer might have both minion summoning and debuff curses with two trees each to pick between.  Many skills intuitively synergize or benefit each other, and the play also has the ability to acquire out-of-class skills a few times per game for even more flexibility.  The last few skill points can be unspent while in towns if you dislike a recent skill choice, and skills also show the effect of adding an additional skillpoint before you spend them, as well as what character stats influence the variables of those skills.  I find this skill tree system more accesible than a train/abuse stat system present in many other roguelikes, and while the transparency is not perfect it is VERY welcome.
The game's combat, as in all perma-death roguelikes, is focused on limiting situations in which you experience risk.  As in all roguelikes this means things like bottlenecking enemies into more controlled environments and crown control, but more notably lies in escape skills for this game.  Being able to leave a situation you will not be able to survive is very crucial in this game, as you almost always cannot simly heal through or face-tank some enemies.  You will be fighting a lot of enemies in this game and the game is quite long, but the game gives you both difficulty and permadeath options so that you may play the game in a method that you enjoy.  The default setting for permadeath gives you a number of lives, and you can accrue a limited number of additional lives at certain milestones in the game, thus letting you maintain risk without letting a single careless mistake end a heavy investment of game hours.
The game's replayability more or less lies in two things.  First, many zones have an alternate version of their randomly maps which have varied enemies and difficulty from their originals.  These can be surprising to discover after your first playthrough.  The second is in trying out different race / class combinations, of which there are quite a few with a good variety of options.
There's quite a bit I could talk about, but more or less I'd reccomend this game.  It can be a pretty heavy time investment, as most traditional-style roguelikes can be, but its a pretty darn good one for a modern era!

Tales of Maj'Eyal (TOME) is a viciously addictive roguelike adventure which contains a number of key features that both improve the gaming experience overall and crucially distances itself from other run-of-the-mill roguelikes. It is 2D and turn based, preferring gameplay and depth over graphical wizardry.
One important distinction between TOME and other roguelikes is the lack of emphasis on procedural generation. TOME actually has a plot, one that spans continents and the void between worlds, a story of darkness, magic and of course world domination. Throughout each playthrough, the story is the same, albeit with some slight alterations/additions depending on the actions you take and the starting class you select. There is a world map, and the major story locations do not change. Although the layout of each dungeon is procedurally generated, this is not empasised as a selling point of the game - it is merely a tool used to highlight the other qualities this game possesses. And boy are there a lot of qualities.
First and foremost - the character classes. Good luck finding a more comprehensive, deep and exciting set of classes in any other roguelike, or any other GAME for that matter. TOME has over 15 of these, ranging from the stalwart Bulwark to the insidious Shadowblade to the righteous Sun Paladin, TOME has you covered for any kind of playstyle you wish to try. Each class then has a vast array of talent branches to follow, and the branches you choose to develop will essentially create a subset of the class you have chosen. The customisation possibilities are massive, resulting in a lot of replayability and tactical flexibility.
Combat is a highly tactical turn based affair, with a strong emphasis on positioning, cooldowns, and your innate knowledge of your own abilities versus your opponent's. Once within your view, every enemy you encounter can be right-clicked on to view their statistics, abilities (passive and active) and resistances. There are no consumables in TOME. The use of each of your skills and items works on a cooldown system, and managing these cooldowns effectively will make the difference between you slaying a boss or becoming a small stain on a tower floor.
And believe me, the latter will happen far more often than the former if you're not prepared, because TOME is HARD. Hard as in one-hit-kill hard. Hard as in the game gives you 3 options - Rogulike (1 life), Adventure (gain lives as you level up) and Exploration (infinite lives) - and taking the Roguelike option early on will result in tears. Hard as in some of the more powerful enemies in the game are comprised of two separate random character classes, and God help you if you face one with two even remotely synergistic classes under its belt.
And to be honest, if there's one thing that drives me nuts about TOME, it is the difficulty. No doubt this makes me a console casual, but I'm serious. The difficulty of TOME is not embedded within the general gameplay, such as a game like Dark Souls, but rather in its frightening inconsistency of enemy threat. The existence of enemies with randomly combined abilities, together with the fact that there are over 10 different damage types (Fire Cold Darkness Light Mind Temporal Blight Nature bleh) means that at some point (normally after you've spent 10 minutes breezing through a horde of useless trash mobs) you will suddenly bump into a Godlike terror that sends you screaming into the abyss of death with a single, sloppy blink, simply due to having the perfect storm of resistances, abilities and relative level that results in a big tick in the Rekt column. Despite my affection for this wonderful, deep and mechanically interesting game, it is also by far the game I have rage-quitted the most.
TL:DR Version....
Good - Excellent character classes, tactical combat and involving storyline.
Bad - Insane difficulty spikes
Overall - if you enjoy a good tough roguelike, you should already have this game!

Good game, but first part was better.

One bug almost finish the game, but I recommend this game anyway.

The bad:
- Controls are really clunky.
The response time from jump button pressed to actual jump happening takes a second. You literally need to see into the future in order to jump over bullets.
- Reload system is the bane of this game
Seriously, having a Guitar Hero "Press reload as the cursor hits green" system is just distracting. I have to dodge 4 bullets in a row and if I don't press the reload button my reload time will get longer, and if i press wrongly my gun jams? That's just punishing, no matter how you debate this. And this happened on the first mission already.
- Item pickup.
I see the need to share the crafting materials amongst friends but isn't trading after battle more intuitive? What's more, you have to go over to the item, press down to pick it up, and risk getting shot at from a one-eyed joe from far. It really is punishing to collect items for crafting.
- Confusing. Map. System.
Many of the rooms exist in the game to pad the gametime. Really. 6 rooms that exist for no good reason are there just so they can hide a hostage in one of them. And the map doesn't really help considering that the map doesn't indicate clearly which doorway links to the next map. It serves to confuse.
- Confusing. Objectives.
I know your testers have played this game a million times, but at least let a first timer know how a HOSTAGE looks like? When was the last time you saw a commando take off to save the President without knowing how he LOOKS like?
And while we are on the missions, why do I need to go over to the helicopter to start the mission when the Colonel already yelled at me to start the mission? Isn't that a wrapper within a wrapper of a candy? And its always a conensus in multiplayer that when someone starts a mission, everyone wants the mission to-go? You already did the "press A" confirmation at character select, you can always do it again for mission selection.
- Some scenary really stands out. Too much.
Some of the wooden pillars blend in too well with the foreground so much so that I mistook them as platforms. And died. This becomes a game of memory rather than a platformer reflex shooter.
The Good:
- Artstyle.
The lighthearted style gives you the remniscent Metal Gear nostalgia: Light hearted fun, run 'n' gun, nothing much to think about.
- The Gun.
The RPG style of upgrading your gun and your knife gives you the warm fuzzy feeling every RPG player has known and love. Though the ingredients farming can get grindy at times.
Overall, this game lacks the polish of Metal Slug that it clearly is inspired by. The gun upgrade adds flavour to the game but as a reflex Run'n'Gun player, this game fails to live up to my expectation mainly due to its lack of responsive controls and disruption of flow of the gameplay. Mainly, the reload mechanism. Seriously, remove it. The boost isn't even worth hitting the Green Area.

Strong word of caution: If you did not like Payday; The Heist, you will very likely not enjoy this game. Many of its mechanics feel more in touch with the original than with its successor. Fine, in my opinion.
Let's get this out of the way: Stealth is broken. It's nearly impossible to do any mission in stealth. THe stealth concept is there, but detection meters don't seem to work properly, enemies don't consistently die with knife hits, etc. THis game, like PD:TH feels like it is always meant to be played in a "loud" setting. I hope at some point they revamp stealth, and maybe give us some suppressed weapons; there weren't many, but I mean, the STEN is already in game, would it have been that much of a leap to add the MKIIS?
That said, I've seen many complaints of the game being grind-y. Well, I guess it is. It becomes really tedious to level up as you get later on in the game, meaning you'll get the first handful of weapons really quickly, then you'll be grinding for a while to get the rest.
The gunplay, I actually do like. It feels like a gory shoot-em-up sort of guns blazing commando-y game. Not historically accurate, but fun to play.
The characters are great, I'd like to see them developed more, and I have faith that LGL will do so.
All in all- I would honestly only reccomend buying this game to support the developers, who I think do good work, or if you are a fan of Payday and Payday 2, and are ready to interact with the RAID community, which has thus far actually been pretty good. The amount of content in the game so far is good, but it needs more for me to say, with certainty, that it's a definite good spend of money.
The variety of weaponry is also fairly underwhelming, but they've already announced three weapons they're dropping to the community for free in the near future- hopefully they follow through.
The cinematics after each mission are pretty humorous but eventually get a bit tiring. However, when having a bad day, seeing Hitler get angry knowing you've sold his paintings for safehouse loot is sometimes a bit nice.
Overall, 6/10. Too repetitive and not enough here to be perfect but the game has some really awesome fundamentals. I hate to only give it a 6 because we need more people to play the game!
PS- LGL give us customizable safehouse at release
UPDATE: With their first weekly patch, the game has already taken steps towards improving, with a rebalanced AI. Not a huge leap by any means, but certainly an indication of things to come, it seems like!

Rage is smi-open world FPS game. The main reasons to get this game is the gunplay, level design,ai and enemy animations.
The gunplay in the game is really good because if you shoot an enemy leg he will start to crawl to behind cover while at the same time try to shoot you, if an enemy charges you and you shoot him in one side of their body they will spin and at the same time go foward due to their momentum and headshots are truly satisfying where the enemies heads just explode in a really statisfying way.
You play as an ark soldier that has regenerating health and has an emergency defibrilator that creates an emp blast that stuns nearby enemies so it basically gives you a second chance but it has a fairly long cooldown.
A good portion of the game you spent going into bandit's hideouts and kill them and sometimes collect some quest related items and in that department the game has a fairly large enemy variety.
The second kind of enemies you fight are the mutants where the small common ones usually charging at you in wide angle so that way it is harder to shoot them instead of just going at you in a straight line, and then there is the large mutants that are kinda like mini bosses that are quite tough and deal a good amount of damage.
And finally the last kind enemies that you face are high tech soldiers with plasma guns and shields.
Besides that you also have races that give you tickets to improve your cars and change their appearance based on the upgrades that you get and also have a few diferent paintings to choose from.
And finally you have a decent variety of minigames that fit the game theme and one of them is a card game where you play with the cards that you collect throughout the levels, so in that way the game collectables are actually used for something and if you miss one that is in an area that you cant acess anymore the game shops will sell you that card for 1k dollars which is quite alot but the minigames can give you a decent amount of money so it isnt so bad if you miss one or 2.
The story is alright but it is good enough to fit the overall gameplay theme. The ending some people dont like it but in my opinion it kinda fits because the whole game you are just a lone wolf that deals with stuff that people ask you to do in exchange for armor, weapons, money and recipes that will help you make cool stuff. However if after the ending the game continued it would be just an all out war between 2 factions which would be pretty much a completely different game so in my opinion it ends where it is suposed to.
Rage is a pretty good FPS that i strongly recomend to play at ultra nightmare dificulty which is the highest if you just want  to have a truly great FPS experience however the only issue that I have with that dificulty is that the time trials are bit bs because they literally ask you to make perfect run in the first and last time trials but out side of that it is a quite enjoyable experience.

I thought that it was overall not a bad game, but it lacked depth. This game competes with Fallout 3 in terms of setting and mood.
The graphics are nice. The shading and lighting is a lot better than Fallout. It feels a bit low poly and some of the textures are washed out despite the otherwise impressive engine.
It is very smooth, even at highest settings.
The gameplay is nice, but not ground breaking. I severely disliked the feeling that you are on rails the entire time. You can not even jump over small obstacles. There is always only one way to get to where you need to be.
Everything is very scripted. Enemies will appear out of nowhere because of the way things are scriped. Your path will frequently close behind you, blocking your way back.
As a result there is no finesse to the combat. You can not sneak up on the enemy and take them out silently (forget about the boomerangs, they are worthless). This is something that games like dishonored did a lot better.
The engine would have provided the technology for an open world game like Fallout but they did not use it. It is a bit of a shame.
There is no way to advance your character and learn new things (it is just a shooter, alright). You can buy a few items to boost but that is about it.
There is the whole driving and racing element to the game. While it is fun, it feels like a separate game all together and very disconnected from the shooter part.
The story is very linear and is lacking depth. It is also quite short. Where do those mutants come from? Why did they mutate like that within 100 years? We never get to meet people behind the authority. Why are they doing all of this anyway? We meet a lot of characters but we never get to really know them.
Finally something for the game designers (and not just in this game but many post apocalyptic games): Why does no one clean up?! People occupy some ruins and install all sorts of traps and machinery but no one bothers to clean up and make the place livable?

This game is almost good, but even after only a couple missions, I can see where the bad reviews are coming from. The shooting mechanics are decent, but not perfect. For instance, you can't shoot upwards while moving, which feels unintuitive and confining. There are also some irritating things about the way the menus work that should clearly be changed, but this stuff is minor compared to the main flaws...
As much as I am growing sick of games about collecting and crafting, I think I would actually enjoy collecting materials in this game, if it weren't for the fact that enemies respawn in EXACTLY the same spot. And I don't mean the same spot every time you play the mission, or even every 30 seconds, I mean as soon as their spawn is off screen. This does two terrible things: it forces you to manage the screen's position or risk being mobbed by the same enemies repeatedly, and it makes material collection extremely trivial. For example, the first mission I played was in the hunting grounds, to acquire two pelts. This doesn't mean exploring the map like it should. What it means is knowing where one fox spawns, then repeatedly trying to kill it before it RUNS FIVE FEET AND DISAPPEARS FOR NO REASON. Then I move to one side and run back and do the same thing again until the mission ends.
If I can bring myself to continue the game, I can't imagine changing my opinion later on. As others have said, this is a game that's ultimately about grinding for materials and crafting, but that one single design choice completely undermines that. Enemies need to spawn in random locations, and they probably need to NOT RESPAWN AT ALL during a single mission. Even if the overall amount of content in the game is limited, I believe those two changes would make the game infinitely more playable than it is. As things stand, I wouldn't really recommend this to anyone.
If the game could be heavily redesigned from what it is, I could see it improving in one of two ways. The first would be to have more authored content, distinct levels that were meant to be played in a linear way from start to finish, but could be repeated to collect more ingredients, money, etc. In Metal Slug, I played those levels over and over for no reason except that they were fun. By comparison, I get bored of a Mercenary Kings level before I even finish it once, because it's so stagnant.
The second option would've been to move towards heavier randomization, perhaps procedural areas that would mean not repeating content at all, but could perhaps result in less interesting levels. But even in its current state, the only thing that needs to change to vastly improve this game is the enemy spawns, which seems like a totally doable change to me, though it'd be a fair amount of work to rebalance objectives and alter the enemy spawns to suit it. But IMO, it needs to be done or the game is not worth playing. Which is a shame, because there is a lot of stuff to like about it.

Cuphead is truly a piece of art. The game does a very good job on captivating the same kind of art style, that was used in cartoons back in the 1930's (also known as: "Rubber-Hosing"), and with filters covering the screen at all times, it really feels like you're playing through an interactive cartoon. And with the incredible jazz soundtrack, the gives off a sort of style you don't really see in a lot other games, TRULY a one-of-a-kind.
I love the story, because it captures the same thing you'd see in a 1930's cartoon. You follow the shoes of Cuphead and his pal Mugman, two troublemakers who find themselves in the Devils Casino one day. After losing a bet with the devil himself, they have to collect the souls of all the debtors in Inkwell Isle. It gets straight to the point, and you even encounter some cutscenes during the game, featuring the devil and his lackey King Dice.
The gameplay in this game, you'll find consists of run-and-gun style levels, where your goal will be to get from point A to B, while avoiding most damage and collecting coins to further upgrade your characters skills. The purchasable items either increase the amount of hits you can take, or give you an invincible dash for avoiding certain attacks. But one of my favorite parts about the gameplay, is the implementation of the "parry" move. The way the makes every pink object parry-able, makes it very useful in certain situations, like in boss fights.
But the kind of levels you'll encounter the most in this game, are the boss fights. It is essentially the core of the game, and you'll spend most of your time in the game, trying to defeat these bosses. But this however, is also where most of the games difficulty stems from. This has brought a lot of media attention regarding the games difficulty, from game reviewers and game critics alike.
Personally, I don't think it's right to compare the game to stuff like Dark Souls, as the two games difficulty is completely different. There is no punishment what so ever, when you die in Cuphead (other than becoming very frustrated).
In conclusion, (if you read the whole review, or just scrolled down to the last paragraph) I think Cuphead will go down as an Indie classic. With beautiful visuals, solid controls, and well made soundtrack to boot. Despite some few flaws, like unfinished bugs, and (some parts in the game) frustrating boss designs, I still think Cuphead deserves a 8/10 by far! During my 24 hours of playtime, I felt a feeling of accomplishment after each victory. Truly a game worth buying for platformer veterans.

12 is better than 6, a game where you play assome mexican who kills a lot of people for reasons I don't care to know.
Cons:
My main gripe with this game revolves around inconsistency. There are a few guns in this game but they all have different ways of firing them which frankly are annoying and hinder this games honestly very fun gunplay. For example the revolver has 6 rounds but to fire it you must hold rmb to♥♥♥♥♥♥it and then press lmb to fire, then there is the repeater whith i believe 6 rounds aswell but with this gun you only need to press rmb between each shot to load the next one. Then the double barrel shotty which has no need to press rmb at all. Then theres reloading which involves pressing R once to open the action of the gun then pressing R again to load each bullet in. While this is fine for guns like the double barrel which requires you to quickly press R 3 times for a full load it is very anoying with any other gun such as the revolver requiring a full 7 presses of the R button for a full load, this is annoying and makes it hard to move seeing as much of the game requires you to be always moving. In addition picking up a weapon requires you to press E when next to it but you have to be so close that its impossible to do on the fly. In summary of this section is that when in a heated gunfight and I run out of ammo in one of my guns I could pick up another one if I am lucky when spamming E but I would then have to know what I picked up so I know how to shoot it. In HLM for example I would either switch to my fist or easiliy pick up another weapon I know how to use no matter what with a simple forgiving press of rmb, The thing that seals the fate is how much to have to press R and E when in combat making you unable to press the movement keys at the same time.
Secondly is the art style, its a cool concept but very flawed for the fast paced action this game promotes. Everything and I mean EVERYTHING blends in. I can't tell the difference between a person, a sleeping person, a dead person, and a ♥♥♥♥ing hat on the ground because of the pencil art style.
Pros:
If you can get past the annoying mechanics slapped onto the games shooting it is actually fun to have a western shootout, the sounds are nice and the guns have a nice kick to them.
Honestly if you want an hour or two of slightly frustating fun then pick it up now while its 4 bucks.

I place my recommendation as a hesitant "no" for this game. Allow me to explain.
If you don't play with your friends, you shall be consistently frustrated as you are sent back to the main menu every time a host gets kick-happy and wants to speedrun every level for his 20th hour of grindfesting. You are sent back to the main menu EVERY time you disconnect for ANY reason. Pay Day 2 had a pretty decent and quickly-loaded menu system, you weren't forced to load your safe house (camp in this game) every time you wanted to just browse servers and missions. Prepare to see a lot of loading screens, to see a lot of disconnects as the host might kick you for being a mere three seconds too slow to reach the objective point. Remember, it's all about speedruns!
The game is a slog at the moment. Levelling does not feel rewarding, it feels like a job. I already have a job, my video games should not feel like a job. Developers, get this through your head. Pay Day 2 was fun because the ease of picking it up and being able to have fun with it. This isn't fun, this feels like work.
Enemies come in three flavors. They die rather reasonably on "easy" and "normal" difficulties. Then you dare to flip the switch to "Hard" or "Very Hard" and end up drowning in the torrent of kraut stormtroopers suddenly chewing down your health bar like a fat kid scarfing down a twinkie. What's that? You want MORE Nazis to shoot? Lets take the spawn-system's lever and break it off on the 'Hitler Clone Factory' setting. The density of a single mob of enemies was so thick that I stopped aiming with my weapons due to the suddenly target rich environment every level turns into. Iron sights? Why bother when you can literally LITERALLY close your eyes and shoot towards the guys softly shouting confused German at you.
Oh. Speaking of a grind. Lets pull out those exotic Malaysian Pink Salt grinders. Gold. This game is all about stealing GOLD. So you bust a train full of it. You steal eight to ten crates of gold, easily each one holding ten bars. That's a good pay for the crew, isn't it? Surprise! You don't get to keep it. You just get a "that a boy!" in the form of slightly increased XP on the already abysmal XP system that slows down more and more the higher level you reach. You managed to rob every crate of gold from the Nazi Treasury? Awesome! None of the OVER ONE-HUNDRED STACKS OF GOLD, not even a single bar is EVER, EVER seen again.
This game doesn't reward you. It doesn't feel like you succeeded in anything beyond shooting Nazis for a transitory and fleeting moment of nostalgia of games long gone. It literally feels as frustrating and unrewarding as a low-paying job. Only you don't get paid.
On a final note, I swear to whatever Cthulhu-grade dark gods that if the developers DARE to add in a damned micro-transaction system to this game. Or shell out five-dollar DLCs for tiny improvemets to the already lackluster armory the game provides. I will go on an active campaign to decry this game as a terrible cash-grab on peoples' nostalgia for a WWII shooter.
There are no real pros to this game that any other game can already provide. "Playing with friends!" Yeah, I can do that on Pay Day 2 already, and at least when I decide to hop on random games in Pay Day 2 I don't have to slog through infinitely long loading screens. Sure, this game is fun with friends. But what game isn't?
I won't praise this piece of garbage as it is for being mediocre. There is so much potential here that it's like watching a fat person scarf down twinkies all day while claiming they're trying. Put down the twinkies, roll up your sleeves, and make this game awesome. Not a fat-clogged arterial disaster it is at the moment.
I pre-ordered this, by the way. Yes, I pre-ordered this steaming heap of poorly put together crap.

Okay...I got this as a freebie, and based on the visuals and even the trailer vid, I kind of went into the game with a "meh" mindset. There's no denying I was pleasantly surprised with how the game worked: the UI works fluid and fast, and is not only pleasant to watch and intuitive to use, but makes a lot of sense theme-wise. This carries on in the puzzles: interaction is quick, level goals are immediately clear and even the 3D rotation is done as it should.
The main disadvantage, however, is in the gameplay section. I obviously can't thumb it down for achieving what it wanted to do (with flying colors, no less!). But this is the sort of game I hated as a child: those plastic slide puzzles  where you work towards something and invariably end up with ONE piece of the puzzle on the wrong end. It's frustrating and hard, especially since you know you can't solve it without breaking down what you've already put together.
This game has that very same frustrating feature: you can't finish it without having everything on the CORRECT spot, and until you're there it's mucking about. Perhaps sharp puzzle players can "see" what they've got to do to swap two pieces on thea board while having all the rest line back up where it was, but I never found it.
On top of that, it sure puts time and number of moves right in your face. Again: perhaps hardcore puzzlers can calculate in their head what they need to know where in a minimal amount of time, but I doubt it. Whether they can do that under time pressure is just insanity.
The time thing I could forgive, as it doesn't throw you off the board if you fail it within X minutes (at least not that I know). But the difficulty thing is so easily solved that it could almost be patched in: give a second 'hole' to work with on grids larger than 3x3. This ensures much smoother sliding of tiles and allows the player to more easily avoid these frustrations.
Yes, you can call me a filthy casual if you want. Yes, it changes A LOT to the way the game is played. But please...here you have this pretty decent puzzle game that is IMHO mostly ruined by it throwing you in the deep almost from the start. Let this be the hard mode...or call the mode with my suggestion in "baby mode" for all I care. Just...do something. Please?
Ahem...since I seriously doubt this will get picked up (the game is almost ten years old by now :P ), I can't but warn you readers: this is one tough♥♥♥♥♥puzzle game...but I leave it up to you whether you see this as a challenge or as an excercise in frustration. :-)

Not a bad game, but sometimes feels like the whole is much less than the sum of it parts. Mercenary Kings came dangerously close to being great but stumbled near the finish line and crashed hard. Maybe it's me. I'm going to recommend, because it's not a bad game in any way and it features a pretty cool concept. Ultimately it's fun and i've been playing it longer than i initially thought i would. And i still want more. If you're into pixel art, retro styled action platformers, this is a very solid, if very uninspired game.
Mercenary Kings has some good ingridients, but doesn't seem to click too well. It takes some pretty bland cliches of 80/90 over the top cartoons, villains and macho bs heroes but doesn't use them to create anything compelling. It rehashes cliches for the sake of rehashing cliches which is a shame because the game has some pretty good elements.
Ordinarily, i'd expect a game to come up with a cool concept then ruin it by being lazily half-arsed or rushed, but Mercenary Kings actually has good art and sound. I can't blame the developers for lacking effort because it's certainly there. The characters are drawn and animated with style and their dialogue fits the brash and cliched design. But they're unlikable and almost ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. I don't expect great depth but they're very "cookie cutter" and not very memorable, although i must begrudgingly admit the idiots kinda grew on me after a while. Animation and dialogues are well done, no complaints there. Maybe there's one too many generic clones of the generic villian soldier but that may well be intentional and it fits the theme.
The controls seemed pretty weird to me, but they can be remapped. A simple run 'n gun platformer shouldn't be confusing, but it took me a while to come up with a control scheme that i felt comfortable with. Which is the same one i got used to in Risk of Rain btw. The controls are responsive and other than there being too many of them, there's really nothing wrong so maybe just attribute my control discomforts to the fact the game just refuses to "click" for me.
Level design is, as has been noted in other reviews, very repetitive but once again, Mercenary Kings has many ingridients of a good game and while you're still interested in the RPG-like aspects of gameplay, or looking to concoct even weirder combinations of weapon parts to smash enemies with, you'll be able to forgive the repetitivnes. It may even help a little because the game is pretty difficult at frist, unless you're really good at action platformers.
Speaking of RPG elements, there's leveling up, acquiring extra skills and abilities, collecting resources to craft both usefull and useless upgrades but i was kinda uninterested in them at first. Maybe they were not presented the way i'd like or i was whiny and temperamental or whatever but it felt like a bunch of possibilities were dumped on me all at once, and then i was told to grind away and eventually unlock the stuff. Grind is a bit unkind because gameplay is pretty fun and the concept of mixing platforming, combat, RPG progression and crafting is promising. But then again repetitive levels do make it feel like a grind, so and the promise kinda falls flat. As with characters, i never felt any connection to any upgrade or whatever. It very much felt like i was doing whatever to kill whatever, in order to rescue whatever so i can whatever whatever...
Options are pretty sparse. There's volume controls, control remapping, windowed or fullscreen and... that's it. No resolution choices though reportedly you can scale the game down by using -windowed -scale=2 as a command line argument. It didn't work for me though.
Havent tried multiplayer but it seems like it's well implemented. There's co-op in either split screen or online and you can set players to join only if they're on your friends list or allow all. Or you can invite manually.
There is gore and violence but since it's done in a pixel art style, it isn't graphic in a way comparable to modern shooters or horror games. It is violent and over-the-top as much as the artstyle allows, so if you're concerned about that, then skip this game. It's fun and fitting and wonderfully old-skool and enemies explode in chunks of violence and gore. It's meant to be fun of course, but it definitely isn't to everyone's tastes.
Repetition is fine for as long as you're having fun playing. -Recommended.

It's like Monster Hunter and Metal Slug had a baby. And then you can play with your friends.

Here's how the game works, you load your character, spawn in the hub world, choose a mission, build your weapon, buy rations and grenades, test your weapon, go back to modifying your weapon, test your weapon again, become partially satisfied, check out the mods, become disappointed that you can't afford any of the good mods, test your weapon again, modify your weapon some more, leave the area via the chopper to perform the operation, roam the same map that you explored before on over ten previous missions, and then quit the mission because the reload speed on your weapon is terrible. That, and you ran out of rations.
And the whole thing repeats (figuratively).
I agree that it is repetitive, but that's what most of these Monster Hunter-style games are like.
Personally, I enjoy these kind of games where I drop myself into an open world, roam the map to find my objective, collect materials, build my own weapons, and then repeat the same process.
If you like games such as Metal Slug or Contra and are expecting this game to be similar, don't buy Mercenary Kings.
If you like games such as Monster Hunter or God Eater with 2D side-scrolling shooter aspects, then you might actually like Mercenary Kings.
I also recommend a controller.

The variety of towers available and how they work together is a strength of this game, and I appreciate how the developers put a good deal of thought into that. Tough to win without a well though out strategy and adapting your tower choices to the individual maps. Bravo for that. In some of the harder maps, it is amazing how the placement of just one or two towers is the difference between a win or loss.
A couple of tips. This game plays best with a mouse, I don't recommend using a controller. Also, the backspace and 'F' keys are very valuable. Backspace rolls back to the last checkpoint, and 'F' fast-forwards the play. Would have liked the option to save games individually at different point in order to pick up at various spots. Finally, as early as you can afford to, place a command tower close to your main killing zone to see the points add up.
Play the campaigns, study the maps and understand how the towers interact. There are some easy maps to get your feet wet and some really tough ones as DLCs.
All in all, a great game.

TLDR version
-----------------
Pros:

Cons:

In depth review:
I love strategy games, in the 90s there was an excess of these games and most of them were good or at the very least worth playing. Most people claim that Warcraft invented the tower defense game genre, but that is far from the truth. These kind of games already existed and Warcraft merely popularized it.
That being said, a tower defense game is a different take on the RTS genre. Taking in strategy and a finite amount of space that a player can actually use. I like tower defense games, however I have only played very few games that are ACTUAL tower defense games.
Most of games in this genre are nothing more than… how do I put it…. Glorified puzzle games. As in that only a preset combination of towers placed on specific spots will result in victory. Or that there isn’t even a fixed path leaving it to the player to figure out how to shape the way.
Don’t get me wrong, I don’t mind these things, but I do mind it when 80% of a tower defense game is like that. At that point it just stops being a tower defense game, because suddenly you’re not using strategy anymore but trial and error in order to win a level.
At first I liked the game, in fact I liked the campaign so much I even bought a few DLC packs. Which was a big mistake on my part, I don’t even know what exactly you’re supposed to do. None of the extra maps have a predefined path, none of them. It’s not nothing more than just replaying it again and again until you finally find out where you have to put the towers.
Another problem that I noticed is the fact that you have so many towers, yet you could finish most of the maps with nothing more than fully upgraded gun towers. Why even bother using the others? Why even bother playing this puzzle game?
So in the end, don’t spend your money on this, don’t even bother with the sequel.

This game gets compared a lot to Dark Souls, and not without reason, but it definitely doesn't feel like some cheap rip-off. It has a beautifully macabre atmosphere and mysterious mythos, and the animations feel very lively. It does a very good job of capturing the essence of what makes the Dark Souls franchise appealing, a learning curve so vast it seems insurmountable until you start to climb it, and applies it to 2D action platforming to considerable success. If you like RPGs, and especially if you like Dark Souls, and you're looking for something that demands more care and persistence than the stereotypical brainless AAA fare, you will almost definitely love this game.

Salt & Sanctuary ist ein Spiel, was jeder Fan der Dark Souls-RPGs mal gespielt haben sollte! Warum? Weil sich das gesamte Spiel sehr stark "anfühlt" wie ein Dark Souls-Ableger! Man spielt als namenloser Protagonist, und bewandert eine düstere Insel, die voll von kryptischen Hinweisen auf die eigentliche Rahmenhandlung gepackt ist - Den Rest an Story muss man sich wie bei Souls aus den detaillierten Item-Beschreibungen zusammenbasteln.
Auch gameplaymäßig ist das Spiel einem Dark Souls nicht unähnlich, so bedient es sich ähnlicher Heilungs und Kampfmechaniken. Bosse und auch normale Gegner sind sehr stark und man muss mit viel Bedacht an die Kämpfe herangehen um nicht in kürzester Zeit zu sterben. Ich sollte hier noch erwähnen, dass die Musik die Kämpfe episch untermalt und die Stimmung stehts gut unterstreicht.
Graphisch ist das Spiel für ein 2D-Spiel meiner Meinung nach auch recht hübsch, die Zeichungen sind schön und die Gebiete stark variabel! Es gibt sehr viel zu erkunden und auch das ein oder andere Geheimnis zu lüften, und das Spiel lädt zum (mindestens) 2-3maligen Wiederspielen ein!
Ein contra an dem Spiel sind meiner Meinung nach die Jump n' Run - Elemente, da diese teil sehr frustrierend sind und zum häufigen "plötzlichen Heldentod" führen. Auch hatte ich bei einigen Bossen das gefühlt, dass auf Balance und Anpassung verzichtet wurde...
Das ändert jedoch nicht mein Gesamturteil: Salt&Sancturay ist ein ziemlich forderndes und belohnendes 2D-RPG was einen in ein düsteres Universum entführt und potenziell das Herz eines jeden Soulsspielers höherschlagen lassen sollte! Wenn ihr gerne schwere RPGs mit gut pollierten Kampfmechaniken spielt sollte Salt&Sanctuary auch was für euch sein, also greift ruhig zu - ganz besonders wenn es im Sale ist!
Wenn euch das Gelesene gefallen hat, dann hört doch mal bei unserem Podcast-Channel rein! Wir sind zu finden unter:
, wo wir über Spiele diskutieren und reviewen.

Sanctum is a Tower Defense game which allows for a first person shooter perspective. Released in 2011, graphically it doesn't look bad at all. The object of the game is to lay blocks and outfit them with varying weaponry to direct the path of your enemy waves, lay down suppressive fire and take out as many enemies as possible, and have a varied amount of weapons as each wave has different enemies who have resistences to certain types of damage. Once you have done this, you go into initiate a wave, use your own personal first person shooter weapons and assist the towers with defeating waves before they reach your core. At the end of each wave you are given a number of resources which can be spent on upgrades both to the towers as well as your personal weapons.
I've played several tower defense games, but this one let's you get down in there and add a personal touch to defense, by combining the FPS experience with more traditional tower defense features. While I enjoyed Sanctum, I look forward to seeing what happens next in the series and how they upgrade our experience to another level. Sanctum features single player mode, a variety of different levels each with their own geography and challenges, as well as multiplayer mode. I recommend going through the tutorial phase, so you really get an understanding of what the weapons and enemies are capable of before diving right into the main game.

I have had Rage installed on my PC since 2011 and didn't play through it until 2016. My interest was only rekindled after finishing Doom (2016) and wanting to figure out why I gave up on Rage. I put about 1 hour into it at the time of release and then stopped. I remember, in that first hour, how impressive the world and animations were from the moment you set out. It felt like an expansive depart from other id software games, which was a good thing as well as bad. The world seems huge but you're actually more limited than you initially realize. A lot of invisible walls really ruin the experience and make you feel more like you are in a fishbowl than a big world. Because of this, I believe the world would have benefited from having the colonies closer together or having more direct paths. There is little to do out in the world and most everything is focused within the game's settlements. That is where the next big departure is - quests. All of the quests are essentially the same "clear out this area of enemies" or "scavenge these items" which gets boring when you have to run back to town in between each mission. If the game had a more organic progression I don't think I would have been bothered so much but the break of gameplay and running around is a bit tedious. This may be a result of Bethesda's publishing and the "Fallout" vibe the whole game kind of has. The salvage/crafting element also broke up the game's flow too much for my liking. If there was only 2 ammo types for each weapon, and they were more common to obtain, I think that would have improved the flow significantly. Stopping to craft or running to town to purchase ammo constantly put a delay in the fun. Additionally, the driving segments were very enjoyable and could even stand on its own as a racing game but my problem with it is that it's a requirement for progressing in a game that is a shooter. As enjoyable as the driving sections were, the game didn't really benefit significantly from having them. The 2nd "half" of the game also seemed incredibly rushed. I know I'm not alone in that way of thinking, either. (Without spoiling anything) Once you get to the final settlement the game just kind of falls apart and after doing "clear out this area" missions among the 3 major factions the game is suddenly over with a quick cut scene. Overall, I enjoyed the game and the addional goodies/missions from the available DLC are a surprisingly fun addition. If Rage 2 ever comes along I will definitely pick it up and hope that they trim the fat and stay focused on a solid shooter with a satisfying story.
