I hated the first Assassin's Creed but decided to give this one a try when it was on sale. I still hate it. Boring, repetitive, uninspired, bad controls, crashes at least once every two hours, etc. On top of that, you have to install Ubisoft's awful game service, make an account, and put up with its slow and poorly-timed updates. You have to be dedicated to play this game. First, you have to sit through up to an hour of pointless install. Then, it takes a good hour or two of very, very boring intro until you finally get to the meat of the game. For example, some of your first "exciting" missions include: watching yourself be born, walking around some cubicles in a drab office building, carrying a crate around for your mommy while she talks with another grown-up, climbing flights of stairs, and talking to everyone in the room to make sure that their feelings are heard. I am absolutely not kidding. These are your missions.
When you finally do get to assassinate people, the combat is so stupidly easy that it feels pointless. Yes you can fight with a sword, and the enemies will block, etc. But if you just switch to your hidden blade, pretty much every time you press the X button it instakills an enemy--no trouble at all. Once you get a double hidden blade, it instakills TWO enemies! It's not combat, it's just pressing a button. It was more difficult to pick up the crate for my mother the first time because the controls are bad. Killing people is much easier than picking things up.
But the absolute worst thing about this game is the stupid, stupid storyline. Despite their disclaimer, the people who made this game are clearly very hostile toward religion. Instead of real historical data, the game is filled with misinformation and twisting of facts that are told to you as though they were facts. Even Wikipedia is a better source of historical information than this game--and I am talking about the times when the game purports to be telling you historical facts, not about its fanciful storyline about the Knights Templar. I understand that when the game is being creative it does not have to be historically accurate. As for its creative storyline though, it may sound clever but honestly it's just Gnosticism all over again. Reversing the Fall, making Adam and Eve's sin into a good thing, this has been done already nearly two millenia ago. Secret societies, conspiracies... honestly, don't we have enough of this everywhere else?
Maybe I would like the game if it were just a bit more believable. For example, if the people in renaissance Italy actually spoke and acted like people in renaissance Italy and not just like horny, crude Americans today. A little research would have done the writers a lot of good. For example, they wouldn't say "Sunday service," they would say "Mass." Women would not be allowed in the cloister of the monastery. Instead of saying "priest" for a parish priest they would say "curate." But honestly all of this is superfluous; first and foremost, if you murdered two men in renaissance Italy--or even modern America, for that matter--and then picked up their bloody corpses and dragged them out into the street, tossing them in front of a crowd of people, I don't think those people would simply glance at you and then continue going about their business. But this is exactly what they do in this game.
Save yourself the frustration. Buy a better game, and avoid this over-hyped series altogether. They will continue to pump out worthless assassin games--three or so every two years--until the hype wears off.

Oh boy I was happy when I saw that Humble Bundle, but sadly the game dissappointed me.
I will make a comparision with Yoshi´ Island and Yoshi Story, because it reflects the best way, why this game doesn´t make any fun for me.
In Yoshis Island all the collecting is optional, the main goal is to reach the end. The collecting was fun and challenging, because it rewards you with a bonus level, but as I said, completely optional. People loved the game.
In Yoshi Story the collecting is mandatory to finish a level and it is just boring running around, searching for something, even if you reached the end of the level. People hated that game.
Mercenary Kings kinda is a mish-mash of these two in form of missions. The "Save X hostages" or "Kill X enemies" missions are damn boring. As soon as you overlooked one enemy it just running around while the time runs out. Ah and even worse, if you die, what you often will, your reward will be decreased, so your ambition to finish the mission is even lower. What kind of design is this? In Metal Slug the save the hostage thing was luckily also a optional thing.
As much as I like the mission idea for a platformer, collecting or finding  a dozen of something is one of the worst mechanics if you have to do it to finish a level. In all good games I know, collecting is always optional (and yeah in the Metroid Prime games collecting artifacts or batteries sucked pretty hard, never understood these decisions.) Maybe I´m too harsh on that, but it was the reason why i turned off the game, twice.
And the combat is pretty boring. Look at Metal Slug, Megaman or Towerfall Ascension how good combat is designed. It´s all about the timing, and here it isn´t pretty there.
Final Verdict: Awesome graphics and characters wasted in a mediocre designed game with pretty good ideas here and there.

As everyone seems to do so in their reviews to establish their 'creds' I've also been playing these games since the beginning and most years in between.
I'm really not sure what all the fuss is about with this iteration to be honest, I personally do not see all the catastrophic, sky is falling, game is broken issues that many reviewers keep talking about.
There are some new systems and in the main I find them to be useful and interesting additions. The chief outcome of much of the new content is to make the game more realistic - perhaps this is at the core of the issue with the complaints, many players maybe didn't want realism, they wanted to continue with their football fantasies as they were.
- the use of analysts adds a bit more depth to recruitment, I find it works well and has increased my fun when shaping and building my squad
- the new medical and sports science elements have helped me manage and avoid injuries more effectively than in previous versions
- the new match engine is pretty good, better than before but still not FIFA levels obviously
- the in game UI is pretty straightforward, it took a 'little' learning but it's perfectly easy to use (the feedback on this being horrible really confuses me to be honest, I don't see the problem here at all)
- the new dynamics system is fun, actually looking for players that will fit in with the rest of your team is entertaining, you can't just hire whoever you want and expect them to gel into the team (just like any team in any sport or professional setting anywhere in the world) - when your new star player starts as an outsider it gives you a sinking feeling of "oh no" until you see him blend in and join a social group "yay!"
There's a whole lot of negative comments which do not jive with my personal experience of the game. I have about 20 hours in on two different saves and so far I have to say this version is on balance a significant improvement over 2017 with some really fun new features.
I feel bad for those people who don't like the new features or are resistant to change on some revised features but if you're looking to try the game don't let some of the overly dramatic reviews and forum echo chamber put you off, give it a go, I personally think it's worth it.

Oh boy, what is there to say that hasn't already been said. Despite positive reviews from critics, which I find to be quite disingenuous and poorly constructed, Football Manager 2018 is one step forward and two jumps back. This will be a long review, as I have put a great deal of effort into figuring out this game and have been frustrated as a result. I am hoping this review will help interested parties make the correct choice in whether to buy this product or not. For those who do not have the time to read all of it, let me just say, right now; Do not buy this game.
Negatives:
- Crosses equals shots. For those who may not understand what this means, or have never played any previous FM, this phrase means simply this... Everytime your winger is wide and needs to play a ball into the box, his cross will turn into an unintended shot. Every damn time. The amount of times I have seen 'He certainly didn't mean that' is infuriating. Wingers with fantastic crossing ability, and composure, will continue to miss hit crosses and the keeper will palm it away for a corner. This repetitive animation will happen every single match, and that is not me exaggerating. I have seen this happen every goddamn match.
- Opposition, regardless of division or quality, will have terrifying shots to goal ration in comparison with your own team. You could be dominating a weaker side - Huddersfield for example - possession will be on your sides, the amount of shots you have had will be 10 to 1 at times. However, the amount of times I, as Liverpool, have had 20+ shots in comparsion to a weaker sides 2 or 3, with both teams ending in a 1-1 draw, is enough to tear your bleeding hair out. Possession will be around 60% in your favour and it makes no damn difference. This issue is commonplace and has been rampant in the series since its inception. I would understand this happening a few times during a season but this has happened to me, now, eight times in a row. This is simply unacceptable.
- Team and player Instructions still have no effect whatsoever. I have a ball playing centre back, Joe Gomez, with order to play from the back, clear instructions you would think, right? So, imagine my fury when, in every match I play him, Joe Gomez takes the ball, no opposition around him, and boots the ball to their opposing full back. Every goddamn time. Winger do not listen, I tell them to stay to the wing and when the match proceeds I see them collecting the ball centrally and cutting infield. This problem has existed for years. Explain to me how the developers are so incompetent that they cannot, one, identify the issue, and two, fix something that people have made them aware of. Get better programmers or coders if the current team cannot cope with this demand. They are clearly surplus to requirements.
- Frequent injuries. Frequent goddamn injuries. The players cannot control themselves, it is like my team is comprised of players with the injury persistance of Gareth Bale and Daniel Sturridge. I currently have eight injured players, minor to serious, and have no doubts that when I Continue the game, the next week, two more will be added. I have had to dip into my youth, the only problem, my best goddamn youth players are also injured. No matter what you do your players will pick up the dumbest injuries in training, I have risked glory in the league to ensure my players stay injury free, and guess what my reward was... MORE INJURIES.
-  The players demanding, or believing, they deserve first team chances are simply incorrect and painfully frequent. James Milner, one of my regular centre mids, demaded I give him more first team opportunities... The guy had played every single match before I decided to give him a 2 game break, due to match fatigue etc. 2 game break sounds reasonable after player seven consecutive matches, right? Right? Nope. After that 2 game break, Milner complained and I had to give him more game time. Then after allowing he to play, Milner was happy and with 2 days remaining appeared happy that I had fulfilled my promise. Then, a few hours later, Milner gets injured and it resets the goddamn timer to another month. Goddamn it! Also, rototation players, or those criminally underperfoming, will not shut up despite being played a decent amount. This problem existed before, and was considered by most to be the worst part of FM, AND THEY SOMEHOW MADE IT EVEN WORSE!!!!!!!!!
- Strikers, who have great finishing and composure ratings, will find themselves one on one with a goalkeeper, of low to mixed one on one stats, and the striker very rarely score. It happens so often and, considering this porblem exists with your side, you would expect the opposition to suffer the same consequences, right? Wrong. The opposition striker, no matter whether he is crap or simply created by FM gen system, are extremely deadly. This issue is most prevalent when playing ower league teams. This whole system is unbalanced and does not reflect a players true stats. What is the point of spending 40 million plus on a striker, with incredible stats, who scored many for his own side, when you know he will turn completely♥♥♥♥♥♥for you.
- The best players in my side, Coutinho, Salah, Firmino and Mane have a staggering consistency of recieving poor end of the match ratings. My best player are just♥♥♥♥♥♥ They are so poor in FM and do not impact the match despite prep being suited to each of their skill sets. Also, many players who can play in different positions and facilitate different roles are not able to in this game, even if they were able to previously. Salah is woeful at left wing, Mane is also useless there, which is not the case in real life. Coutinho cannot play as a CAM or CM despite having been played there often during his time at Liverpool. This stunts a managers means of playing them because, when you do, they are often playing out of position and poorly. Meaning they need to be dropped or you are forced to push other impressive players to the side to make room for them. What the hell are the developers doing!? Winger used to be a strong part of the game, OP in fact, and your response to this is to completely nerf them!? The hell!?!?!?!?
Positives:
-  Player Dynamics has added a much needed layer to squad building. I can't say much about its implementation on the pitch, but, players form social groups and support each other if they have issues. The social group system is very much appreciated and it is clear to see which players belong to each group, as well as the hierachy at the club. Fair to say, relationships with players has been much improved. I have to give the developers props on this one, seems like a very good foundation to build something that could be a new and strong component for the franchise.
- Data Analysts finally have a purpose in FM and complement the scouting team to a tee. Scouts discover a players ability and potential, analysts provide information on statistics as well as ratings during matches. Now, this is obviously a very minor improvement, as scouts in previous years would also serve the function of a data analyst. Instead, the roles have been split and new statistics have been added to cater to a data analysts strong points. This, for me adds to the experience, as it makes the experience of being a manager more realistic.
There a few minor positives like player potential being realised if they perform consistently early on, for instance, Ings and Woodburns current ability rose after a string of good perfomances. But, these are still inconsistent and a few bad performances will find these players back at their original stats by two or three games. Overall, I would suggest you wait and see how the game looks with updates because, as of right now, this game is unpolished and in need of serious attention. I hope this helps you and that I have been able to help you avoid spending money on a game that is simply, in its current state, not worth the price.

Picked this up on sale and I've already got almost 10 hours in the game in less than two weeks, and this is the first tower defense game I've ever played or owned.
Looks can be deceiving -- this game looks simple, but there's real depth to it, and each successive map opens up new possibilities in terms of strategy and playstyle. The brilliance of the game is how it nudges you out of your comfort zone to try new approaches, without losing what makes it fun.
For example, some maps are all about setting up brutal chokepoints that operate like murder mills, with all your firepower concentrated on the alien hordes as they pass through. Other maps require you to set up overlapping fields of fire and cover wide areas because aliens spawn in multiple locations. And some maps are all about closing off alternate paths and forcing the aliens to take the route you want them to take.
The towers all have their own strenths. Guns are weak but fire rapidly and can target flying aliens. Cannons pack a punch and can hit flying aliens, but fire slowly. Lasers are great at sapping aliens of hit points, but have a smaller targeting radius and can only harm land units. Inferno towers hit aliens with fire that leaves a DoT effect on them. Tesla towers electrocute aliens. Temporal towers send out pulses that slow aliens down. Missile towers provide air defense. Meteor towers have huge range but fire slowly. Concussion towers shred groups of aliens with AoE explosives. Command towers reveal stealthed enemies and help you recover more resources. And so on...
Bottom line: This game is a hell of a lot of fun, and on sale it's practically a steal.
Very good tower defense with a lot of content and a nice narrative to boot for such a low price? Yes please!

This is a very well done roguelike.
It's complex, yet doesn't ever leave the player wondering. Every detail has explanations that explain the effects; for example, leveling up primary stats (eg, vitality, strength, etc) will show the effects on secondary stats (eg, crit chance, health, etc).
Players are encouraged to play in order to unlock additional races, classes, game types, etc. In my first run, I stumbled across a zoo -- and died shortly after. However, I unlocked the summoner class because I had come across a zoo.
In another play through, I finished the first quest and headed to the town. In town, I agreed to fight 3 elite warriors in order to prove myself worthy of the arena. I was afraid that I would die again -- after all, I was doing so well in this run. It paid off because winning unlocked the Arena game mode.
I would add that he vast number of achievements also helps replayability, except that there are over 1300 achievements. This will be pretty frustrating for anyone looking for 100% achievement completion.
The only part of the game that is lacking is the graphics; though that comes with the territory in a roguelike. Despite every item, monster, spell icon, and basically the entire game fitting into a square-sized sprite, there is still a lot of variety: Player icons seem to change based on equipment and active spells.
I have played and loved this game for MANY years, it is an absolute joy.

Brilliant, the fact that a freeware game developed by one person has more customization and diversity than any multi-million dollar game I have ever played is mind boggling. To reiterate a free roguelike with myriad classes/builds (more being added regularly) and some theory craft for the price tag of 0.00$,

+: One of the best roguelikes on the market - easily top 3 alongside Dungeon Crawl Stone Soup and ADOM for me personally. What makes TOME so great is the way it is designed allows it to be incredibly easy to get into for a beginner but still have enough depth and complexity for an advanced player, and unlike traditiational Roguelikes where you try to survive through one really big hard dungeon this has you survive through many mini-dungeons with an overworld map you can explore.
+: Game mechanics are incredibly solid, stuff is for the most part well balanced and you can advance in the game well enough as any class really. It abandons the traditional roguelike mechanic of potion spam to heal and instead replaces it with a heal over time ability you can upgrade. There are no random deaths / mechanics that require you to have played the game already in order to know how to not die in this game either.
+: Personally I think the game has one of the better loot systems for a roguelike, it's almost Action RPG-esque really.
-: It's not really mentioned anywhere on the Steam page that this is normally a free game and the Steam version is just the donator version with Steam bonuses like Achievements & Workshop. By all means if you don't have the money for this game but are interested go download it on the official website. That said, I played the free version for a long time and finally donated when the Steam version came out since I wanted the steam benefits.
-: If you don't play often you need to set Steam to not download updates automatically or else major updates can break your saves and you will lose progress. Rarely happens but it did happen to me and it does kind of suck.
-: This is an
minor con here but the graphics aren't as good as other modern roguelikes like Dungeon Crawl Stone Soup. That said, if you really like roguelikes like I do graphics are probably one of the things you care about the least.

Pros:
1) Good Combat System - attacks flow together nicely and there is a sizeable variety of weapons
2) Unique Bosses - there are a few that are a little similar but they usually force you to use varied stategies against them.
3) Optional Bosses - Self explanatory
4) interconnected world - all one map that has secret passages all over that allow you to move back to earlier areas easier
5) Variety of Builds - from the quick light armored fighter, to the heavy armored warrior with a massive shield, down to spellcasters with a nice assortment of spells
Cons:
1) shift in art style from player character to enemies and environment (felt like mixing Salvador dali style art with something like the powerpuff girls)
2) Iron Rampart a sheild that exists and counters nearly everything once you get it (takes a lot of strategy out of the game)
3) Loss of 10% of current gold each time you die with no way to retrieve it. (this really limited the sense of exploration because it gave you an even greater punishment for dying) This becomes a problem later on in the game when the path forward isn't always clear.
4) Less skill based than dark souls, I think this is best shown as while you are blocking it blocks all sides rather than just the side the sheild is facing.
5) Storytelling - Lackluster storytelling, very little lore in game just item description that don't seem to come together very well.
6) Punishing Rather than Challenging - Often this game had trap rooms without a warning which makes you learn through repetition rather than learning and overcoming the obstacles by stategy (seems to use memorization for a challenge rather than a difficult puzzel)
7/10 worth a single playthough.

Assassin's Creed 2 was my favorite of the series. It introduced a dynamic, exciting new assassin in Ezio, the gameplay from the first game was much improved and the story was less repetitive. The game introduced a lot of new mechanics, such as money, building up your own Assassin base, bombs, hidden firearms, double blades, all kinds of things! It was a fresh new experience from the rinse and repeat gameplay of AC1.
AC2's biggest flaw was its ending, which ended up being really dragged out and repetitive. AC2 also still suffered from the control issues from the first game with Ezio randomly jumping off of or getting stuck on various things while climbing or doing parkour. While these created some frustration they didn't take away from the overall game.
If you are new to the AC franchise, I would recommend starting with AC2. Altair wasn't that great of a character and the gameplay of the first game was repetitive and boring. AC really begins to be its own unique game in AC2 and you start with a long, expansive story with Ezio spanning 3 games. This game provides hours of entertainment and lets you experience Renaissance Italy in a unique way.

I got this in the July 2015 "Humble Bundle" and was pleasantly surprised at how much fun this game packs in.  It's essentially a mix of Metal Slug and Mega Man with a crafting system thrown in.  The levels are fun, the RPG elements of upgrading and creating gear keeps things interesting, and the overall experience will keep you playing.  The missions are timed which turns off most new players... but you'll grow accustomed to it--and, ultimately, the timer provides a necessary sense of urgency to the game.

Mercenary Kings is an interesting game. It takes Metal Slug style graphics and gameplay, introduces an almost Monster Hunter style crafting system, and a fun skill-based reloading system that can jam your gun or give you extra damage. I love the soundtrack, sounding at times like a cross between Mega Man and Doom. I love the variety of guns and builds. I had a ton of fun playing this game and you may too if all this sounds appealing to you.
However, the game is not perfect. As many have stated, the levels and missions can be very repetitive. Much of the game consists of exploring the map, collecting items, saving NPCs, and fighting mini-bosses. There isn't really much storyline or variety in gameplay at all. The price is a bit steep for what you're getting here, but I personally love the game regardless. Wait until it goes on sale or goes in a bundle and try it out if you think the pros outweigh the cons.

First of all i played this game for like 50 hours now but Steam says 0.6 hours. Weird...
Let me say this; if you're looking for big improvements over the last year's game, you're gonna be disappointed. But still there are some upgrades and totally new features.
One of the new features is the Medical Centre that gives you information about players that are at high risk of injury and why. Accordingly you can make adjustments to your squad and may choose to rest some of the high risk players to prevent injury. Instead of rotating all the squad every 3 games, you now know exactly who to rest which helped me a lot.
The other new addition which i find so much fun and realistic is The Team Dynamics. It shows you the groups that your players divided into and hang around with. For example if there are, let's say 5 French speakers in your team and their personality is close too, they're likely to stick together and form a group. But these groups are not static also, players may get out of their group or get into the other groups later and i find following these relationships very much fun. There's another side of the dynamics, which is the hierarchy of your players. There's a hierarchy pyramid to order your players status. You're on the top as the manager and as you go downwards on the pyramid, your players are categorized based on their influence on other players. And this really makes you think twice before making certain moves such as selling the team leader or a high influence player. Because you always need leaders in your squad and now you can see who's seen as the leader by other players and who to replace him with if you need to. By the way an accepted and good captain is OP for you can make him talk to the players that are whining about their unhappiness and a good captain almost always calms them down.
One upgrade i noticed is the harmony of the players in the squad. When you play certain two players in certain positions for example two center backs, side by side for some time they will get used to playing with each other and get a little harmony bonus which you can see as a link between the two players on the tactics screen. I don't know exactly how much of an impact it has but it sure has quite a bit according to my experience.
There are some additional player roles in the tactics screen. I haven't get the chance to experience all of them, but the Mezza i like a lot.
There may be some new features and upgrades that i forgot to include here but these are the main things that i noticed. Of course the game has it's downsides too, like;
- Too many offsides.
- Too many of the crosses mistakenly going towards the goal and if not it's probably hitting the nearest defender and going out of the pitch for a corner kick which is most of the time a near post cross that gets cleared by the defender.
- Too many offsides.
- Goalkeepers are kinda stupid. They go out of the pitch with ball in hand, a lot.
- Did i say too many offsides?
These are all little things that i'm sure SI is working on so expect a patch for them.
All in all i say it's a good version of the FM series. Either you are a fan or a new FM player don't miss it. But since it's not much different than the old version you may as well wait for a sale.
8/10

Make no mistake:
is
made up of sliding puzzles. You know the kind where you slide around tiles numbered 1-15 and try to get them in order. The puzzles in
are more interesting than that, but the principle is the same all the way through. If you like that sort of activity, then you will love this. If not, it might change your mind, but don't expect anything too "exciting" here.
does have an unhealthy obsession with time-based objectives. Half of Challenge Mode involves solving puzzles in under 30 seconds, and half of the extra stars earnable in the main mode are granted based on solving speed. I find this is less a test of skill than a test of your memory or your patience to write down all your algorithms and then execute them from a list. Some of the puzzles require 100+ moves after all. Granted, this can all be ignored––all the puzzles can be unlocked and completed without caring a whit about time.
The visuals are polished and the sound design is immaculate. The difficulty of the puzzles is well-scaled and if you're an idiot like me, you'll be pleased with how this game will actually teach you to be better at sliding puzzles. Seriously, halfway through the game you will go back to some of the earlier puzzles and feel like a wizard. Overall, this is a deeply gratifying puzzle game and comes recommended.

Cuphead is an amazing game, and far better than almost every single game I've ever, EVER played. The inspiration of 1930's cartoon graphics, characters, maps, and many other things makes this experience even better for people who are either older or watch the old cartoons.
You may hear this game is very difficult. And you'd be right. It took me about a straight 8 hours to complete, which is average. Once you learn the controls, patterns of bosses, and other mechanics, the game gets easier...kind of.
Oh yes, now to the bosses. The bosses have cool little movements, and 2-4 phases to beat. Once you eliminate one phase of the boss, they shift to their second/third/fourth phase. Of course, they get harder. But, there is a way to make it easier to beat them, and that's to learn their patterns and signals. Before each of their attacks, the bosses will make a little movement to let you know, "Hey, I'm gonna do my attack, so you better act fast!" Once you fully learn these signals, they make the fight easier on you.
They also have patterns. Some phases do one attack, some do two, and some vary between attacks.
Though this game is boss-focused, there are 6 levels to run & gun in. You run around, collecting coins for stronger weapons, whilst defeating bad guys along the way. Every other one has a mini boss, but they're not that hard.
Finally, the story.
The story behind this game is pretty nice, and goes well with the game itself. Two boys named Cuphead and Mugman live with Elder Kettle, who is very wise. One day, the boys decided to wander off and do something else. However, they wandered onto the wrong side of town, where they find "Devil's Casino." They go in, and start playing gambling games, and they win every single one. Soon, the owner of the casino comes out and challenges the two boys. Of course, this owner is Satan himself. He makes a bet, saying that if Cuphead and Mugman win a game against him, they get the whole casino. However, if they lose, the Devil takes their souls. Blinded by easy riches, Cuphead goes for the offer, whilst Mugman sits back, worried. Of course, Cuphead loses. They beg the Devil, "Please, is there any way we can be spared?" The Devil then tells them if they want to be spared, they should go out and get soul contracts from the runaway debtors (bosses) around the Isles. So, of course, they go and do that.
There are 3 isles of awesome bosses, and, to be honest, my favorite is the third isle.
Anyway, this game is worth a lot more than 20 dollars, and it's DEFINITELY something to spend your money on. Cheers!

Raid: World War II is a fresh look to the Diesel engine (Payday 2 game engine). Despite critiques by people reusing "bad graphics", "literally a payday 2 reskin" and etc, this game is very different and is more mechanically interesting.
Raid: World War II is very different compared to Payday 2 in many different ways. For example:
Lock picking is now skill based rather than waiting for 20 seconds.
You have to manually pick up ammo and medical supplies off the floor.
Carrying and hiding bodies are now a challenge compared to hiding a small bag.
Stealth now has suspicion modes and individual detection meters.
Weapon upgrade challenges.
And much more.
There are still some negatives to the game however, although most of these issues were fixed, a majority of the issues mainly sit on balancing certain enemies and difficulty.
Overall, this game is different from payday 2 and brings a fresh feel to the gameplay. It's a good game and does some things payday 2 didn't do that is interesting. Give Raid: World War II a fair try.

I have nothing better to do so I'm going to review Dishonored. I'm not going to pretend I'm a
or anything. I'll just explain my favourite and least favourite parts of the game. You can decide from that if it's something you're interested in. This is also my first time writing a proper review, so expect it to be very disjointed and poorly written.
My number one favourite thing about it is that it makes you feel like you're good at video games. The game isn't easy, but it's simple. You don't need to spend much time planning out how you'll pass by enemies, but you spend just enough time to feel like you're engaging your brain. Evading enemies and taking them out stealthily brings an incredible sense of reward. Yet mowing through crowds of enemies as noisily as possible still feels gratifying.
You can tackle every level in multiple ways. I'd say at every point in the game, there's a second way to do whatever you're doing. This obviously means there's lots of replayability. I've played through the game somewhere around ten times and I'm still finding new things. There's an incredible amount of lore built around the world Dishonored is set in. Books of exposition and history are just lying around the game. I've yet to read them after all this time, so even now I have a reason to revisit the game.
There are two ways to play through the game, lethal and non-lethal. You can complete this game by killing practically everyone or literally no one. Through this you get the sensation of being an unstoppable killing machine or a merciful hero. Both of these are very fun and interesting in themselves, especially considering their effects on the story.
I'd recommend picking up the GOTY edition for a few extra quid as it includes DLC that fleshes out the story and some more DLC with some fun quick minigame challenge type games.
Those are the reasons I enjoyed the game. It's replayable, satifying and immersive. In terms of technical mumbojumbo it controls fine and runs great considering I play from a rubbish laptop. I'm sure the game would be very nice to look at too if I could run it above the lowest quality setting. This is THE game that made last year's remake of DOOM possible; DOOM 3 was good, but it still divides fans today.
Sure, RAGE may come off as more of the tired, but classic post-apocalypse setting cliches, but id made them fresh again, with their know-how, and from borrowing asteroid 99942 Apophis from the headlines of 2004. Wingsticks are one of the game's trademark weapons, a pity they didn't get quite the following I for one expected them to get.
Your rogues gallery of enemies consists of a fairly fresh take on the standard wasteland faire, including the Ghosts, who may or not be the unintentional forefathers of the Warboys from Mad Max: Fury Road. You are also up against the Authority, whose flag, weapons and red-and-black power armor evokes Hitler's SS; then there's the Mutant Bash TV gladiatorial show, hosted by the hilarious J.K. Stiles; RAGE's twists on After The End are the emphasis on vehicles, both to cross the wasteland, and to compete in racing and demolition derby mini games.
One of the last adjustments RAGE makes to the recipe is its weapon and vehicle customizations, bought here and there from merchants, or from mechanics with special credits earned from racing. Yes, id put in a version of the BFG from DOOM - and no, I'm not gonna tell you WHERE exactly!
Like a nice little bow atop RAGE's neat package, you also have bit roles of John Goodman voicing the first character you meet, and sexy voiced Steve Blum as John Marshall, the leader of those fighting the previously mentioned Authority.
Let's face it - without the Scorcher's DLC, RAGE is actually pretty damn short; but with the Scorcher's, you can keep your game going long after the credits, AND you have more reason to hope for a sequel or an HD re-release.
Fans of id Software's 26-year track record shouldn't pass this one up.

First and foremost: No, this is neither Contra nor Metal Slug. If you bought it thinking something like that, you might have a bad time with this game. But hey, at least you get to write a whiny review like everyone and their mother.
So if you think about buying this to get a quick action fix like aforementioned games, look elsewhere. " So Crawley you rapscallion of a squid, what kind of game is this?" I hear you ask. Well, it pretty much is Monster Hunter with Megamanesque mechanics.
It's rather slow paced compared to Metalslug or Contra and features a whole lot of gun and blade customization. You want your combat knife to look like a pizza cutter ? Done. You want a Revolver with a shotgun Barrel and an SMG Stock firing Acid Bullets? This game got you covered. You get annoyed quickly by playing mission-based on only a handful of maps? Well..
The thing is this: Like in Monster Hunter, you choose a mission and get dropped into one of only few maps, gunning down enemies and collecting different materials to upgrade or modify your Guns, Blades or  Body Armor. Yes there are not that many maps and yes, you have to grind for material. So if this easily irritates you, this might not be a game for you. However, I actually quite enjoyed my first few hours and because of this loot drops from enemies you make at least some progress, even if you fail a mission. Why? Because you get to keep everything you collected.
In addition to that, there is a little reload minigame, where you want to hit the sweet spot on a reload bar. Contrary to what some reviews imply, the gun does reload nonetheless, if you do not.  If you actually hit the sweet spot, you get a damage bonus for a percentage of your clip, indicated by glowing bullets.
So after talking about gameplay a bit: The music and artwork is superb. I instantly fell in love with it the first time I saw it, and after playing a while back then I was really disappointed, because I expected this game to be yet another Metal Slug inspired game.
And I am pretty glad it is not, because I like this way better.
TL;DR: No this is not Metal Slug. Its Mega Monster Hunter Man. It's obtainable via the Humble  Bundle for one Dollar right now. If you don't mind some grinding  or like either Monster Hunter or Megaman, it is definitely worth it.

This is my first ever review on Steam, as I think all the hate towards the game and developers is unfair, unreasonalble and totally undeserved. You may see that I played less than an hour, but don't let this fool you, I have 500 hours in beta. For those not willing to read long text, I will sum up right now - BEST FOOTBALL MANAGER EVER, if you are not dumb, blind or actually willing to tweak tactics (as you should). As to the price...It is for you to decide.
"I received this game for free, so I must be licking their♥♥♥♥♥quot;. Nope. You can't buy professionalism - you either have it or you don't. I am just against unfairness in reviews.
So, let's get started with common "cons":
- "Match engine keeps getting worse each year/AI is till pretty bad" - WRONG. I hated the match engine last year, was not satisfied with it in FM2016, but this...This is exceptional, nearly perfect. Why? Well, players now create combinations, use heal passes, hidden passes, move better, defend better, etc. I can spend an hour describing why this match engine is so great. The game became smarter, the players became smarter and it can't be denied by someone's inability to tweak tactics. It is not impossible like in FM17.
- "Awful cameras, replays, notifications, assists are credited to wrong players. no 2D" - Really? You have every angle you need and 2D view is in there, what's the problem? You can always disable replays, if you don't like them, or at least change the camera. In my opinion, notifications are much better placed now, as they do not block the field. The assist credited to wrong players issue never occured to me, but it may exist.
- "Predetermined simulation" - WRONG. Why would you expect to get a better result with the same tactic? Don't blame the game if your tactics suck. Better spend some time figuring our what's wrong.
- In-match lagging/game crashes. - TRUE/FALSE. Well, it happens. But this will be fixed, I am certain of it as this issue has occassionally occured throughout the beta and devs always fixed it. Be patient, these are early days of the release.
- "Graphics are still bad" - Graphics have improved significantly, especially stadiums and their surroundings, lights, etc. If you expect FIFA graphics - it will never happen and I hope it will not. This game can be played by anyone on any PC or laptop, which is why FM does not need even better graphics. It is accessible and should remain being such.
- "I have 60% possession and I can't score/keeper plays too good, etc." - FIX YOUR TACTICS. Yes, it is not always simple and easy, but since then possession equals goals? And why would you expect your every shot to be a goal? Think about it this way, not every shot is dangerous and not every shot on target is a goal-scoring opportunity. I can keep shooting from 30m range, but it is does not mean any of my shots will be dangerous.
- "They messed the scouting" - Some of it is not efficient, I agree (like getting reports once every X weeks insted of once it is compliled). BUT:
a) Now you have the packages, which is realistic.
b) Analysis report is useful and helpful.
c) Overview view is extremelly efficient, as it shows the positions, some stats, and asking price.
d) Default scouting is fairly good, as scouts actually travel around the world and watch games, instead of sitting on standby.
- "Hierarchy limits me in creating a team for future" aka DYNAMICS - Yes, you no longer can get rid off an aged and influencial player easily, but can you do so in real life? Did you forget all the noise around Totti, Casillias and others? Why should FM be any diffrent? And just as in real life, support of the dressing room is extremelly important or you will have De Boer's situation in Inter.
- "What do physios and sport scientists do? they are useless" - WRONG. They show you how much a player can handle before they get an injury. If your player is Diaby and you play 2-3 matches every week with high team training load plus individual training, he will get injured. So this tab helps you balance that out for each player. Reduce individual training load, tweak team training load, balance the playing time and you will not have as many injuries.
- Translation. - I can agree here, many languages require better translation. It is quite inaccurate and very academic (word to word translation, if you wish), resulting in loss of irony, sacrasm, and fun component or sense in some phrases.
- OTHER ISSUES:
- "They made me watch an intro" - Match intros can be skipped.
- No faces, logos, etc. - Licensing issues + space on the disk. You can easily download them on any forum.
- "Tactics screen is another mess" - It is not ideal, I agree, but think about about analysis feature and cohesion between players.
- THEY DID NOT IMPLEMENT THE 100 MOST REQUESTED FEATURES!!! - Yes, I would like to see some of them, I really do (such as managing u18/19/20/21 etc. regardless of how limited that experience would be). But here is a thing: how many of them would really make the difference in terms of the way game is played? Being an owner is not the same thing as being a tactician and it "kills" the true nature of the game. Family, cars, other stuff? What difference would it make? You would suddenly become a better tactician? I don't think so.
MY FAVOURITE:
- I can't score/I lose/my defenders are stupid, etc. - Your tactics suck. While in FM17 this was an issue for everybody, in FM18 tactics are fairly balanced and can be configured and tweaked, if you spend some time though.
- "I have been playing this game since the Roman Empire and I can't recommend it" aka "they took 'r jobs"  or "back in my days..." talk from your grandfather. - It is BETTER, stop denying it. Stop this unreasonable hate talk that you produce every year. The majority of your reviews are not even reviews, as they have no constructivity at all. The FM17 was an abberration in many ways, I agree, but FM18 is simply great.
Lastly, if you have an issue - LOG IT ON THE FORUM. Your whinning won't help (in majority of reviews it is whinning, not constructive criticism), unless you provide the neccessary info to the devs. No, it is not just "my player can't cross a ball". You have to provide supportive materials, which may include: a screenshot, a match itself, or even a save if you want the issue to be fixed.
I will update this review if I remember anything else.

And that's one of the things that I think works about this game, yes there is a route, but it doesn't feel like you're being pushed. The way forward is just there, you either find it, or you don't; the game doesn't really care.
That brings me nicely to a couple of other things - there's no map, why should there be? We are so used to being pushed in a direction, and told where we are, that people complain about "No Map WTF", but you don't need one; part of the point of the game - (aside from surviving) - is exploration, it rewards it. Besides, there are a multitude of games with no map. Standing in a labyrinthine ruin and trying to work out how to get an area you can quite clearly in the bottom right of the screen is all part of it, no?
Other things I've found: the atmosphere, it's gloomy and dark and oppressive but there's hope, scattered through it, and though some of the NPCs you meet have given up others seem to have retained what they can of their humanity and their resillience. Which brings me too...
...the dialog: I personally love it. The NPCs speak in Twitter-sized soundbytes, and this allows the dialog to be incredibly concise and actually really meaningful and in same cases quite touching.
The music is a little sparse, but what there is works I think, I like the guitar piece and to be honest on a long playthrough it's all in the background anyway. It's not Saints Row, you don't play it for the kicking soundtrack.
I could go on:
Graphically it's pretty much spot on, a kind of dark cartoon that reminds of paper cutouts, the color scheme really helps with that.
Grinding is a lot of in this game - (although clearly YMMV) - redoing an area for salt and cash is actually still challenging and you can die ridiculously if you take your eye off the ball...
In short, ignore comparisons, it's a game that stands on it's own and is incredibly impressive particularly given the size of the studio that made it.
Just get it, seriously.

ToME, in my opinion, is what combat-focused turn-based roguelikes ought to aspire to be since it has all the following (and more!):
-intuitive control scheme and ability to solely control the game with a mouse.
-many, many interesting classes, most of which can play very differently depending on how choose to build them.
-easy inventory management (throw all your potions and scrolls away!)
-great enemy variety, further made interesting by rare enemies that have skills seemingly beyond their scope of ability (that bone giant did just smite you with the power of the sun).
-excellent random loot generation system that makes other RPGs jealous.
-different difficulty and lives settings for players of different experience and skill levels.
-very extensive mod support, with some interesting mods that change up the game already in existence.
-a usually helpful in-game chat.
-fairly frequent and very substantial updates that keep classes interesting.
-basically infinite replayability.
I've beaten this game more than ten times and yet I still keep coming back to it every once in a while and get hooked all over again, every time.
In conclusion, buy ToME, enter a dragon's dream and kill it with your mind rays.

It has a well realised world, huge class depth and variety (with a bounty of class/race unlocks), and a punishing dungeon system that rarely makes you shake your head at the game design instead of your own mistakes. Permadeath in such a world is a rewarding experience. It challenges the player to be better, learn and achieve what at first seemed beyond reach. A special mention should go to the lore and world building. No large, tired, trope laden exposition exists here. Instead the world is littered with lore and item lore that slowly builds up a far greater picture through multiple playthroughs of a living, damaged world.

Wow, lots of hate for this game. Sorry RAID.
Before I start, I'd like to reinforce the fact that I don't search for flaws in games, and am bad at focusing on them most of the time. This review was written just after the very first update, and I have had 347 hours of prior experience to Payday 2, the chronological sequel after Payday: The Heist, which I'll get to in a bit.
So! You've decided to look at the reviews for RAID: World War II! More accurately, you've probably decided to check the box where you look for good reviews, buried under the heaping piles of negative reviews.
RAID: World War II is a game set in... you guessed it, World War II. The person who gives you new missions (John Cleese) later becomes the butler in Payday 2's safehouse, therefore placing this before Payday. Game mechanics wise, Payday and RAID are similar, but not the same. Allow me to elaborate. Raid is, instead of stealing from Banks, people, and stores like Payday, about stealing from or crippling the Nazi regime. The lockpicking mechanic is no longer "hold the button until the door opens" but instead a "Press the button when the circle rotates around, and the opening is over the lockpick." This can be quite challenging for some, especially if you have not put skills into increasing the size of the openings. Skills, right! Let's get into those.
The skill tree is overwhelmingly simple. Every level you are presented with three choices for where to put your skill point (sometimes only one), and you may cross over the same skills in later levels. Each point placed into something adds percentage to it, getting higher as you level it up. This is ludicrously different from Payday, where you either unlock or ace  skills, selecting from five different skill trees. To reset your tree, you use stolen Nazi gold. Now, gold is the main currency for Raid. It isn't used for buying weapons, as those are unlocked (and their modifications unlocked by getting kills with them) but instead used for resetting your skill tree, buying cosmetic items to equip onto your character, and purchasing various upgrades to your camp, your Payday safehouse. Gold is only obtainable through missions that you find the briefings to in other missions, meaning that you can't just redo the Treasury mission and get tons of gold. Instead, you must find special missions where your gold is not given to the resistence. As far as I know, you cannot unlock gold by paying for it with those hard earned dollars shoved inside that bank account.
But I'm rambling about the basic interfaces and game mechanics, let's go ahead and talk about the action!
In Payday 2, you were allowed to choose from a variety of different play styles, thanks to the skill tree. You could be a light armored character who ran to dodge bullets, or you could strap on every heavy object within reach and saunter around like a walking aircraft carrier, making Dozers cry as you dispenced anti-justice upon everything alive. In RAID, forget about armor. This was a more basic time in war, and as an undercover operative, you don't have a large, fairly angry rhinoceros to strap to your chest. You have the ability to equip different jackets or shirts, combined with different pants. There is no armor in this game, and no bonuses from clothing. (at this time, at least.) You are not allowed to bring equipment on heists either, making it an absolute necessity to carefully search the map for crates - that have a chance of being locked - for supplies. This also opens up new opportunities to grab dog-tags (the more you collect, the better your "Payday" will be, allowing better experience boosts or clothing items) and loot items. (Every loot item you collect gives progress to a bar that gives you ONE nazi gold upon being filled)
This can make a firefight challenging. As soon as you run out of healing items in the nearby crates, your health dips down more and more as waves of enemies crowd around with submachine guns, firing round after round into your poor, innocent face, who only wants to be loved. Have no fear, however, as you have an escape card!
Ever played Overwatch? That nice, shiny Q button that decimates the enemy team, or changes the tide of a battle if pushed at JUST the right time? Well, welcome to RAID, where you've got one too! My only experience with it has been the sniper class, as this is the one I've played the most. It immediately locks on to the first target your crosshairs pass over, and with a shot or two, they're dead. It lasts for a certain period of time, and allows perfect accuracy right on the chest of whoever you shoot. Of course, this is one of the four "Warcries" in the game, though I have no experience with the others.
In short, this is most certainly a Payday game. There is no shame in a company making a chronological sequel to their own game in the same way that Payday 2 was made. Driving, carrying bags, weapon modifications, and different heists are all there, just waiting to be experienced, and there's no shame in considering to support RAID. I consider it a game that is worth more than the negative reviews say, as its systems really are not the same, or inherently worse than Payday.
TL;DR (Because I know you really don't care what that entire mountain of text says)
Pros:
-Better Lockpicking!
-You gotta love those driving sequences!
-6 day missions, are you kidding me?!
-Epic Warcries
-Lots of roasted Nazi buns
-Promising base for a game that will undoubtedly be worked on even more overtime
-Much more challenging stealth (No silencers that I know of, get your knives out, though the alarms must be triggered personally by a guard, and there are no pagers or cameras. In a way, it may be a lot less challenging, but I know you loved throwing cards to kill guards, or shooting them with your pistol.)
-"I met a nazi fellow once. A bit shy at first, but then... he was all over me." -Sterling, occassionally upon killing somebody.
Cons:
-Not an overwhelming amount of missions, though I am positive that this will be expanded upon.
-Small amount of guns at the moment. (However, they're adding more, and each gun must be used a lot to get different mods. Do you want 55 guns that you have to work on each to make them good?)
-AI can glitch at times, though I've only had one scenario where the AI were stuck somewhere as I was downed.
Also, for those people who say enemies can't hit anything, I would like to restate that I have had 347 hours in payday, and I have been downed multiple times on the normal difficulty. They can, you just need to give the game more of a chance. Levels always start out slow, then get more involved.
Thank you for reading, or at least looking at the pros and cons!

Ignoring the graphical flaws (such as the textures not fully loading at first), this is one of the best-looking games of the 7th generation. The lighting details are amazing and the textures themselves are gorgeous. The gameplay has some of the most steady gunplay I've ever used and not one weapon feels boring. The maps feel a little cramped at times but they're never dull with even tight spaces being fair game for firefights, and the areas vary differently enough that it keeps things interesting. The sound design could have used a little improvement: its hard to tell where an enemy, particularly a mutant, is coming from because its only in mono. You hear the same sound from both speakers as though its right in front of you. Despite that, the guns, engines, explosions, and voiceacting are top notch. If there's one thing that drags the game down is that there's not much hiding from you: there are invisible walls everywhere, no secrets to be found besides cards for the Rage Frenzy mini-game, and each area is just a linear pathway connected by the open world driving area. Regardless of what few flaws there are, its obvious the good outweighs the bad and Rage is definitely worth playing through.

If RAGE had amazing gunplay, it would deserve a pass. But honestly, the gunplay in this game is mediocre at best. Enemies are unsatisfying bullet sponges, weapon switching is slow and unresponsive, and weapon reloads take far too long for how many bullets enemies can take. Not to mention iron sights are often annoyingly necessary on some weapons, yet the usage of them cause your weapons to stop firing until the aiming animation is completed.
The character animations are top notch, the environments are gorgeous (save for the ungodly megatexures), and the production values are excellent. However quest design is some of the worst i've ever seen, while level design is surprisingly decent in some places and shows the development team put alot of time into environmental work. Car combat is ok but feels ultimately tacked on and skippable, and overall the experience is aggressively mediocre. I guess for $3 I could say it was kind of worth it, but I will honestly never play this game ever again.
ID Software is one of the greats, new DOOM being proof, but this game is an exceptionally disappointing blunder on the resume of an otherwise great company.

Sometimes someone does something refreshing to an old staple, turning what other developers use as a tiny puzzle or distraction into an entire game.  Cogs does this to the old sliding-block 15-puzzle.
This game is, in general, much easier than the original 15-puzzle.  Rather than have to get all 15 blocks in exactly the right order, many of the blocks are interchangeable.  The different tiles will have gears or bell hammers or pipes on them.  Connect them up in the correct way to bring nifty steampunk contraptions to life.
Taking the sliding block puzzle into 3D was a bold decision, and it brings delightful puzzle possibilities. On some levels, you’ll be tinkering with 4 or 5 sides of a cube, each with its own mini-puzzle on it that all intersect on their edge.  Other times, you’ll need to work out two puzzles simultaneously, as the tiles are double-sided and you must spin the entire object around to see how your moves on one side affected the other.  There’s also a time-attack and move-limited mode.  It is fairly easy to skip ahead over difficult puzzles, as the game is generous with unlocks and you will rarely be left with only a handful of seemingly-impossible puzzles with no way to progress.
The music is pleasantly inquisitive and upbeat.  The steampunk aesthetic gives everything a clicky-clacky feel.   The UI will swing in on a gear-driven mechanism, you’ll press a button and it will fall away to lead you to the next puzzle.  This gives everything a physicality and weight that many games lack.  Steam will hiss out of pipes, and the tiles move with a satisfying chunk.  Some of the most interesting puzzles are built around sound, as you’ll have to figure out a way to play chimes not only in the correct order, but in the correct timing using just gears with different width.  These were some of the hardest, most rewarding puzzles in the game.  The visuals are simplistic but elegant. There are no widescreen options, however, but the graphics are crisp.
All the puzzles are well-designed and fair.  Some of the time and move challenges are a little tight, but they are all managable.  The machines you will be building are interesting and varied. The decision to not gate content behind difficult puzzles unnecessarily is a refreshing one, and the devs should be applauded for it.  Even if I didn’t complete every single puzzle, I still felt that I saw the whole game and all it had to offer.
Cogs is full of expertly-made puzzles that have a well-balanced difficulty curve.  If you’re looking for a few hours of sliding block relaxation, this is the game for you.

A true gem with only a couple of minor flaws.
Beautiful, atmospheric levels. Great voice acting and characters (even if a couple of minor characters appear to have their voices re-used within the game). Lots of options as to how to progress through the game, though the game seems to push the non-lethal method as more desirable.
If you like Half Life, Bioshock and Theif, I would definitely say give this a try. It can be a short game if you charge directly through, but for me the fun was in exploring. I spent a lot of time looking around and enjoying the scenery, but stil missed some stuff.
Once the player has the ability to 'blink' (short teleport), the levels open up incredibly. You find yourself scaling rooftops, looking for open windows and balconies to jump onto, and new possibilities appear. What began as a simple retrieval mission now has you finding new sub-plot points and new characters to interact with, all orbiting the main mission but in their own stories. These things expose themselves very naturally, and the player who chooses not to explore will likely never know what they missed out on.
I had the most fun hiding in shadows, blinking from cover to cover and stalking my adversaries until I found an opportunity to incapicitate them. There was the option to kill, but there are complications with that method. More deaths brings a more generally chaotic environment and sometimes it makes further progress more difficult.
The environments are gorgeous, the levels were created with an incredible attention to detail. Players with a teleporting ability can bring a lot of level designers to their knees, but it was handled well here. The architecture is used to create natural boundaries to keep the player in the 'arena' but still give you the feeling of freedom. There are multiple paths, in fact, it doesn't feel like paths at all, it just feels like I'm discovering my own route through the level.
Sound and music are top notch, the audio cues are wonderful and the feeling of sneaking in shadows is enhanced by the music and environmental sounds.
Free saving (not checkpoint based) allows you to experiment with ideas but it still remains fun and suspenseful to try to sneak through a level undetected.
The player has several lethal and non-lethal options to deal with enemies, and I used most of them throughout the game at one point or another, but nothing is more effective than sneaking up and choking somebody out from behind. Just be careful where you stash the sleeping victim or he may be discovered by another guard doing his rounds.
The AI is good. I played on easy because I'm generally terrible at games and I wanted to see it through, so the guards were pretty passive unless I really drew attention to myself or they had direct line of sight on me. Once a guard sees you, he must be dealt with quickly or he is going to alert others and things rapidly get out of hand. Plan B for me was the sleep dart if you could draw and fire quickly enough.
All in all, a very enjoyable diversion. I wish it were longer, but it was so well done, packed with detail that I appreciate it nonetheless. The ending seemed a little abrupt, considering the suspense and anxiety it built up, but the end game was tailored to my play style, so the game at least acknowledged the choices you made for the most part.
I think my biggest gripe would echo some of the other reviews here in that it allows you to play however you want, but you feel like it is silently judging you the entire time, and wishes you were a better person. I suppose that is the reality of being a bad guy though.. If you care about your reputation, maybe you really wouldn't act that way. I think I might play through again as an evil SOB just to see how bad things get.

In short, OneShot is scaled down Undertale on tons of chill pills.
What we are dealing with is a top-down adventure game built around exploration, simple puzzle solving and little expectation subversing. Just like in Undertale, the game is best approached without any information learned or gameplay seen before playing it yourself. That's why I won't go into details on many important aspects that OneShot tackles. What you need to know is that the game succeeds on this front and really delivers some clevel ideas here and there.
In opposition to Undertale, OneShot's atmosphere is quite heavy, melancholic and dark. Soundtrack and great visuals really sell us depressing, but in many ways beautiful, view on the dying world devoid of natural sunlight. Use of neon phosphorus colors really adds up and the game, despite using classic pixel art, still stands out from the crowd in a positive way. Creepy music nicely punctuates some more spooky moments filling all the important gaps in the presentation, which in return, benefits game's characters and world building in a great way.
On the topic of characters, there needs to be at least a small mention of Niko. If you didn't notice that yet, the main character really steals the show with his/her adorableness engines running on all cylinders. Niko ends up as one of the strongest points of the game and a character that you will grow fond of extremely fast. Obligatory
and
memes are quite valid here.
While OneShot is all around very polished and honest effort, in my judgment it feels somewhat small in scope and ambitions. The game can be finished in 4-5 hours and while there are some side activities to get more playtime, it ends quite abruptly without really unleashing its full potential. You travel through zones fast, meeting new people and experiencing events in quite swift pace. It really gives the impression that there should be at least one additional layer to the game: an additional area, more side stories or maybe a gameplay mechanic that could beef up the game a bit. Aside from that subjective complaint, the title lacks a bit in the variety department while in context of visited places. OneShot's world often consists of long stretches of fields without any landmarks or points of interests and because of that I found myself lost on several occasions. Nothing major, but I wanted to point this out.
All in all, OneShot is an adventure worth taking. While you shouldn't consider it your next "big" indie title, this little cuddly ball of game is priced accordingly and offers quite an interesting and satisfying experience with excellent presentation, good story and remarkable ideas. Without bigger hesitation, I can only leave a honest thumb up here,

I have seen many reviews, watch some gameplay and finally pulled the trigger on this game because I wanted some stealth based gameplay loop. And Dishonored provides that provided you want to play it that way (completed the game in full stealth gameplay so I cannot talk about the "violent" gameplay loop).
The story in itself is not the best, it's simply a means to make you go through with the experience, the levels are mostly open to your imagination as to your approach of the situation, want to go around the guards? Want to take some of them out before you try to run through? Want to posess a rat to go through the sewers? It's up to you.
Now I will also admit that the game is not perfect, as I noted above, the story is mainly a means to make you play it, I also have to say that the campaign is on the short side (9 hours to complete the story in stealth mode). The environment is also a bit dull: the color palette is always the same gray-brown tones and it can become a bit monotonous.
So in conclusion:
+Pros:
Good stealth mechanics
Many ways to approach one situation
Great level design
Replayability (different ending depending on your playstyle)
-Cons
Short and cliché story
Dull atmosphere in general
Little lore about the main character (please let us know mora bout Corvo!)
I would recommend the game mostly if you like the stealth mechanics and multiple approaches in a game.

Apparently 'Rogue-like' has been corrupted to mean "randomly generate unbeatable unexcapable bosses twice or more the dungeon level, until the player has no more resurrects left".
Some have taken issue with my concept of rogue-like because they played a much harder rogue-like and this is easy when compared to 'that game'.  To that I say, if you must use the No True Scotsman fallacy to defend your game from critique, you've already failed.
Escape options in this game are largely restricted to teleports; due to the level disparity that prompts a need for an escape, nothing less then escape in a single turn is fast enough. Unfortunately, the teleports are random and unreliable until late game, when they are finally targetable.
If you like a game where drinking a potion could kill you and there is no way to detect it is posion, you may find this game palatable.
If you like a game where just the act of entering a dungeon or changing a level may cause your character to slip and break their neck (die), you may find this game palatable.
Conversely, if you believe that no matter how hard a game is, the game should provide you the tools to handle risks like these and only punish you for not using those tools, then you will probably find this game to be 'fake hard'.  It randomly hits you with bosses that eyeroll at your escape attempt, giggle at your damage, ignore your debuff attempts and crush you.

This has become my favourite roguelike. Deep tactical combat built around activated talents and cooldowns makes this completely different from the traditional "walk towards things until they die" formula. It feels like a turn based action rpg rather than Nethack.
ToME has several gamemodes. Story mode has lots and lots of written original lore but it may get repetitive after several runs. You will die and have to start over many times and it is ♥♥♥♥ hard unless you know what you're doing. And that experience comes from dying enough times to learn how not to. Playing story mode is required to unlock other gamemodes and more than the few initial character classes and races.
In Arena you fight a set number of waves of increasingly difficult enemies, and if you win, your player character becomes the new final boss of the arena. It is not balanced for all character classes, some are significantly weaker because there's rarely time to rest your cooldowns, and most of the time there are lots of enemies on the screen.
Infinite Dungeon is just what it says. The challenge in it comes from the randomness. It is somewhat level scaled, but whereas in story mode you know what kind of monsters and bosses are in each area, here you can't really prepare for anything. It is the old school roguelike experience but the modern game mechanics still make it quite original.
Conclusion: Thinking man's roguelike with unique gameplay and diverse content. Tons of mods available. It is also completely free at
but buying it on Steam gets you some donator benefits.

A Payday 2 Veterans Honest Review of Raid:WW2
Hi guys TrustedCharl here a long time player of Payday 2 who loved that game since its Launch and bought every DLC including the completely overkill pack and experienced almost all the game had and has to offer.
So to the review....
Raid:WW2 is a Solo/Co-op experience similar to Payday 2 set in a world war 2 setting in which the nazi's are winning the war. John Cleese (Control) sets your gang the task of destroying the nazis one mission at a time via a set of Raids and Operations.
Raids are as follows:
Hunters
Odins Fall
Gold Rush
Bunker Busters
Wiretap
Rouges Gallery (Reskinned Jewellery Store from PD2)
The Amber Room
Trainwreck
Stronghold
Extraction
Tiger Trap
Last Orders
Outlaw Raids - Only Discovered Forest Raid atm
Operations are Clear Skies and Rhinegold.
This selection is quite a strong list to sink youe teeth into with the raids unlocking over time the more you play the game and with Outlaw Raids being randomly found by finding mission dossiers within the other maps. The selection is quite diverse and almost all maps apart from tiger trap, bunker busters and stronghold have stealth sections allowing for a variety of ways to complete the various missions.
Operations are long and arduous affairs which can feel like a bit of gentle anal with a sandpaper♥♥♥♥♥♥♥especially with how they are currently with stealth feeling very much like a bore to combat as enemies currently seem to have x-ray vision making stealth on some of these sections almost impossible.
Onward to the graphics, the games graphics arent anything to be amazed at they arent all lens blooms and HBAO+ shadows and all the fancy rubbish that we dont really need, but they do somewhat remind me of medal of honor 1 and rising sun with an almost purposely grainy and rough look to the game even on maxxed settings, not to say that is bad in this game but i know a lot of master racers will be put off by a game with OK graphics.
Now on to some of the major downsides to this game, the loot system is very poorly executed, it tried hard to seperate itself from payday 2 loot by making the drops based on whether you got awards at the end of a mission or how many of the dog tags (gage packages) you found on the map, this experience feels so tacked on and really needs some sort of refinement to be based more on the performance of the player rather than how many random collectibles i can find.
Secondly the whole GOLD system really needs looking at since the gaining of gold is almost too slow currently meaning that you cant really see the point of it till youre balls deep and 100's of hours in the game this is even taking into account the whole 20 bars you can obtain during a normal difficulty outlaw raid making the safehouse upgrade system a little useless for the playerbase until we actually get a better playerbase and dedicated players who want to invest time in the game.
And also sadly one major major major thing that pisses me off to the highest degree, the utter lack of John Cleese past a few minor videos after his tutorial masterpiece, in these videos he barely has time to speak let alone act or provide any semblance of the character of control, yet we do hear a hell of a lot of Mrs White without ever seeing her in a video, utterly shameful with how the game has been marketed to star John Cleese i expected more screen time.
Finally I just want to give my summarised/TLDR opinon, RAID:WW2 is a fun new take on the co-op horde heist mode shooter but is currently plagued with problems of its predecessors such as bugs galore and an overall lack of systems refinement making gameplay a little too clunky to be enjoyable. Overall a decent game for the price but needs to be shown some love by the developers and support from the Overkill/Starbreeze Fanbase otherwise we will see this game suffer an early death... then we will be stuck playing Payday 2 lootcrate edition till 2020.
Solid 7.5 out of 10 or B+ Average attempt with some exciting and excellent design work, just needs some refinement to be a solid 9/10 game.

When I first saw Mercenary Kings, I became very interested in the game and it looked very exciting to me. The graphics and the gameplay strongly resemble those of the Metal Slug series. There’s the side-scrolling and 2D platforming that old school gamers have appreciated.
The plot of Mercenary Kings is about a mercenary who is part of a resistance group that is doing battle with a villainous organization known as The Claw. The narrative quickly becomes irrelevant as you start off in camp and learn to customize your mercenary character. There is no voice acting, so you have to read the dialog text to understand what is really going on. The lack of relevance the narrative has does not bring the game down since gameplay tries to be the strength of the game.
Upon playing this game I first realized how awkward the keyboard controls are. There is no mouse to be used in the game, but the keyboard makes the gameplay feel like a drag. I firmly believe that fans of the Metal Slug series would be best advised to use a controller or gamepad to have any fun with this game. Another aspect of the gameplay that feels like a drag is the repetitive nature of the battles with The Claw. You have a limited number of lives and after each death you will have to face the same enemies and this feels quite tedious. Using keyboard controls is difficult when trying to press buttons to shoot, jump, and roll.
The graphics are pixelated, but that’s not too bad for a game that’s trying to be an old school, 2D side scroller. If the game had more variety in its levels, the replay value would be exponentially higher. I really wanted to like Mercenary Kings because of its concept of being of resistance fighter battling an organization of villains and the various characters to choose from and customize. Weapons can also be customized so that your mercenary can leave camp for battle with better gear.  I can only recommend this game to those with a game controller or gamepad and do not care much about the quality of the narrative. If you’re a gamer who is accustomed to using the keyboard/mouse combination, I would not recommend Mercenary Kings unless you are willing to commit yourself to playing with a game controller or gamepad.  I give this game a score of 6/10.
