TL;DR - "12 is Better Than 6" is a great addition to the top-down shooters genre, but unfortunately fell off short and became forgettable. Not worth the 10$ price, but is reasonable for half off. 6/10.
This game explains the story of a Mexican man named Juan, and his "on the run" from his past. The issue is that Juan seems to have a problem recollecting the things that have happened to him. Throughout the game, it’s your job to perform kill after kill and do favors for other men in order to fill the story on what happened to Juan.
Now, top-down shooters are notoriously known for being ambitious and difficult, with the player looking at everything from a bird’s eye view. Each level is packed full of enemies and it’s up to you to either take them all out or avoid them in order to proceed to the next level/world. What makes "12 is Better Than 6" distinctive is that it focuses much more on the stealth aspect than other games do. You’re given one weapon that you can change throughout the level by stealing from the corpses of enemies. Either a selection of guns like a pistol and shotgun, or a knife which you never drop. It can be used for silent kills to maintain your stealthiness. Dynamite can also be used to take out large groups of enemies – the downside being that you make noise and it alerts anyone in the area of your location. More often than not, I found myself either using my knife, or avoiding enemies altogether, because the gun is a nusiance that can make noise from all over the level. However, even the stealth aspect was hard to accomplish, and made it pretty difficult.
The controls took some getting used to, mainly having to make your gun ready to fire before each shot (Not what I'm used to). Your character is always holding their weapon in front of them, so it didn’t make sense to me that you would have to “aim” before you shoot each bullet. Even so, I decided to use the knife a lot more. However, stealth detection is not very fined in this game. I had some occurences where enemies see me, even though I'm either around a corner or behind a door. When an enemy does spot me, one shot is all it takes for me to die. There were some rage-inducing times. But, it wasn't impossible and I managed to go through levels smoothly in a challenging manner.
The game’s art style is what really drew me in to playing this game. It features a hand-drawn style where the environment, the weapons, and the people all look like they’ve just been written and sketched on a white piece of paper. One of the best parts about this is that when you kill an enemy or animal, the blood really stands out against the white background. It’s hard not to appreciate the game’s unique, yet charming style. One negative part about this though, is that everything blends together and things that are not moving are hard to perceive from things that are. On literally more than one occasion, I would be so close to finishing a level and I’d make a break for the exit, just to be shot down by a man in a cowboy hat sitting at a table a few feet away because I didn’t even notice him there.
Overall, "12 is Better Than 6" is a innovative take on the top-down shooter genre and, had it had more opportunities for me, it may have been my new favourite. The hand drawn art style is unlike anything I’ve seen before, and I would like the developers to make a new game with that sort of idea. If you’re looking for a game that will have you crying with rage one second and relieved the next, 12 is Better Than 6 is definitely worth a playthrough or two depending if you want to 100% this game. (I had to do two playthroughs to get 100% which all took me around ~7 hours). However, I would not buy this game unless if it's half off. Definitely not worth the $10.

Best FM installment, to date.
I get really frustrated when I read negative reviews based on one or two small issues/bugs (that will probably be fixed in updates in the near future). So here’s my first impression/game review.
The date is November 13th, 2017. The full game has now been out for 4 days and I have played it for 40+ hours. I’ve been playing Football/Championship Manager, since 2001/02. The last 3 or 4 FMs, I’ve racked up 1,200+ hours with each game.
At the end of the day… it’s the best management series around and ever made. It is unbelievably addictive, as normal. I bet most of the people that leave a negative review, still play it for hundreds of hours.
Graphically, the game looks incredible.
The new dynamics system is very cool, especially with the emergence of player power in the game. I haven’t had any team issues yet, but hopefully this isn’t just a feature to add even more player/team disturbances.
There’s loads of little cool new additions and extra options for different things, which I won’t ruin the surprise. New staff roles that actually play a part too.
The new tactics UI revamp is very cool. It looks different, but after familiarising myself with it, very good. This is very similar throughout a lot of the new features. Some people seem to struggle with change, then they get used to it and usually prefer it.
They’ve also come up with new ‘newgen’ (they’ll always be regens to me) faces, finally.
I have a relatively good machine to play the game on. There seems to be a lot less stress on my machine, with things that used to send my fans in to overdrive on FM17.
However, here’s a few small things that I’m having issues with or tweaks I would/wouldn’t have made. Not that this really effects an overall, positive review:
- First of all, it is way too expensive. However, pound to hours played for me, it’s still a bargain. Long gone are the days of £17.99 for the hard copy.
- I do miss getting individual scout reports in my inbox. The new scouting system is more realistic, but it seems you either have to wait for a high number of reports to be completed, before you get a notification in your inbox. Or you have to keep randomly checking the scouting page, which is frustrating. The scouting budget idea is cool, but it seems very complicated to scout players that are a specific role/position/age etc. A system that wasn’t broken, so it didn’t need fixing.
- Leading on from the scouting page… The player search UI has become so much more technical. I understand it means more players will appear on screen at once, but I miss having the search filters at the top. The amount you have to click is now over triple, to change a filter. Again, another system that wasn’t broken in the first place. I also quickly changed back to star ratings. The scout rating out of 100 seems to be very inaccurate most of the time.
- The pre-match meeting seems a bit pointless at the moment. A negative report of “7/13 goals you’ve conceded have been scored, near the penalty spot” doesn’t mean too much. And a lot of the things that you can speak to the team about, are already team instructions, within tactics anyway. ‘Retain possession’, for example.
- A small error from the transition from the beta… Tactics that I created and saved, were not carried over and I had to redo them all. A little annoying, but easily re-done.
- The new match engine:
- I miss the drop down headers at the top of the screen, when in a match. They’re now tiny little icons, that all look very similar. I’m having to pause and hover my mouse over them all every time at the moment. Bring back ‘Tactics’ (that takes you to the full tactics screen), ‘Instructions’, ‘Team shape’ (structured, fluid etc), ‘Mentality’ (attacking, counter etc), drop down menus. I also think they’ve removed the tone of the shouts? (Aggressive, calm, reluctant etc).
- I can’t get the match camera (TV), to look the same as it did previously, on FM17. Usually end up zooming in and out loads, every game. Great that it can be changed, but maybe there could be a ‘default’?
- The in match UI is a little annoying. You can’t have windows open, like you used to. Takes up much more of the screen now. The text needs to become smaller and the windows smaller.
- The pitch is still a little too bright, even after the update, after the beta complaints.
- Goalkeeper 1on1 save rate is WAY too high. I’m 8 games into my season and I’ve counted 12 1on1 saves, from 14 attempts.
- A lot of shots have no power what so ever, and seem to be like a light pass to opposition goalkeepers.
- A lot of crosses go out of play, over the bar.
- Players stood right next to the ball tend to stand still and leave the ball, whilst a player 10+ in game metres away, unnecessarily comes over and gets it. E.g. a RB stood by the ball, by the touchline, will leave it, whilst a CM/CB will run over from 10+ in game metes to get the ball. Especially frustrating when a CB leaves the ball for a CM to come and get it, when the opposition striker is quite obviously going to get it first, and they score. Even more frustrating when it’s a through ball, played past the CB and he lets it roll by him, instead of picking up possession.
- I play a ‘short passing’, possession based tactic. I still see a lot of long balls to no one, when there are multiple simple-pass options available.
It sounds like a lot, but it’s just a few tweaks that were due to happen, especially with the work of the new match engine. Everyone will always find something that they don’t like.
Overall, it gets an 8.5/10. A few adjustments will make it a 9. Definitely making the right movements to the perfect game.

Well, after +40 hrs and 1 season completed, it’s time to do a review of FM2018.
2018...one more year, one more FM, same addiction. The best football simulation and management game in world. You can not compare this game to anything, its essence is unique. And probably only your most faithful followers understand this. FM is a pure management game, in all aspects. A truly masterpiece.
Well, if you're a beginner player, visit my review of the previous edition. It will help you a lot. To be easier, here's the link:
This new edition have some key improvements, that include a newly implemented graphics engine that improves the detail of players, stadium and user interface elements. Scouting and transfer fees have also been altered to make for a more realistic experience. Let's look at each one of them.
Firstly, there is a totally new dynamics system implemented in this FM. In a nutshell, this system takes into account the relationship between players, the environment in the spa, and interactions with the coach, to determine morale and commitment in the field. More than ever, managing egos will be more important than ever. A squad like that of PSG will not be anything but easy to manage, where Neymar has caused many problems in real life, e.g.
The scout system of the game has changed, and will now work more realistically, approaching more and more of the reality currently experienced by the various football clubs.
Tactics are one of the most importante elements of FM. The redesigned tactics screen places analysis at its heart to give you a clear view as to whether your tactic is working. There’s an analysis overlay on the tactics display, which highlights the areas of the pitch where you’re currently and where you’re most exposed. You can also see which players are developing strong partnerships and a summary of the trends from the analysis of your recent matches.
The new pre-match briefing allows you to be better prepared for your upcoming fixture, while several new player roles make their debut in FM2018, giving you more ways to utilise your squad’s talents.
There’s a new dedicated “Sports Science” atribute for medical staff. You can view the feedback from your Sports Scientists on the new ‘Medical Centre’ section which is your one-stop shop for everything related to the fitness of your squad. There’re five panels within the section offering the most detailed insight and analysis of your team’s condition in the series’ history. The ‘Overview’ panel shows you who in the squad currently injured, which players have recently returned from injury and any players that are at increased risk of picking up na injury. If you want to see how you can reduce the likelihood of injuries occurring on the training pitch, you’ll want to go to the ‘Risk Assessment’ panel. This shows you your upcoming fixtures and current team training workload, allowing you to easily match the intensity of your training sessions to your upcoming matches.
There are diferences in transfers. In real life, we’ve seen a huge increase in the value of transfer fees over the last seasons and you’ll see these inflated fees and contracts reflected in FM2018. Several new transfer, contract and loan clauses have been added to reflect the volatile modern transfer market. The way you can make intalment payments on transfers had been changed to reflect real life better, with payments now being able to made to be made every 6 months rather than annually, with 3 instalments allowed. This is something that real clubs use to comply with Financial Fair-Play restrictions.
The FD user interface has been redesigned and optimised for streaming. The game icons that previously sat within the sidebar have been moved to the top of the screen giving more space to the centre of the screen. There’s also a range of new set-up options, including an increased squad budget and a Quick Start option which lets you tailor the FD experience to you. About the matchday, the edition of this year sees the debut of a new graphics engine that produces the best lighting, stadiums and player models in the series’ history. That’s alongside a new match interface and modernised pre- and post-match presentation, all of which helps to bring your fixtures to life.
As the experienced players knows, FM don't have the licenses of the teams and competitions. But there is a awesome community working to improve it.

Finally I can see the Football Manager series going into a positive direction, every year you get the 'fans' critiscing the game and pointing out how similar each game is but I would say this one is a fresh approach at the managerial football game. I skipped FM17 and played FM16 right until the release of FM18 beta and the change is drastic from the two. The updated graphics engine looks marvelous, the tiny little niche aestechic updates in the UI look very good too. Give this one a chance 10/10 highly recommend A****

But, I stuck trough, and altough some fights had random ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t, each victory felt incredibly rewarding.

A historic entry into the tower defense genre.
In many aspects Defense Grid has aged very well. The level design/variety is superb - Having very different levels is crucial for forcing the player to not get locked into certain strategies. The tower balancing is excellent compared to most entries in the genre - I think cannon towers are a tad overpowered, but not at all game-breakingly so.
Defense Grid incorporates my favorite Tower Defense mechanic - unspent resources earn you income (at least in a majority of the game modes). This encourages the player to keep their defenses as lean as possible to maximize the amount of available resources for later waves. With this, even "easy" levels are still very challenging for trying to achieve the highest score.
With a ridiculous amount of levels and score-keeping for them, you can compete with your friends' scores.
The biggest weakness Defense Grid suffers is that it feels too "vanilla". Not only was its design direction not particularly brave with any novel mechanics to begin with, but due to its age, later titles have been afforded the opportunity to duplicate its successful elements while also putting a more novel spin on their mechanics.
Still, what it lacks in novelty, it far surpasses in being an overall sleek optimized tower defense game.

If you're looking for a visually polished shooter and nothing more,
is your game. It's closer to
than anything else, which I think is somewhat disappointing compared to what could have been, but it's also by no means bad.
The game was obviously chock full of ideas. Multiple bandit clans, all with unique aesthetics and behaviors, unique settlements with their own cultures (though this tapered off heavily after the beginning of the game). Racing, RPG elements, sidequests. Unfortunately, it's all half-baked.
To begin, there's zero story to speak of. The writing isn't bad, it's just non-existent. You are the fetchiest of fetch boys and an incredible yes man without any need for would you kindlys. Your one desire seems to be fulfilling your master's wishes. Near the end you partake in some misguided attempt to save the world from some supposedly evil organization who doesn't particularly do anything evil, while meanwhile slaughtering entire tribes.
Weapon upgrades adjust spread and recoil and nothing else, and are a literal shop item. No questing necessary. In fact I think there was only one actual quest reward in the game, despite there being ~9 sidequests, and that was completed through item collecting. The vast majority of quests basically served as an excuse to respawn enemies in the latest dungeon you cleared out, with little backstory to speak of and no particularly new events to hold your attention.
Racing was... passable I guess though on the ultra-nightmare difficulty it was tedious more than anything. I imagine lower difficulties are more reasonable. Upgrades were plentiful and I enjoyed the damage model for the various vehicles.
So where does
shine? Gunplay, movement, animation, visuals. Guns are satisfying and varied, with multiple ammo types and plenty of unique use cases. Movement is tight and I never found any problems with the level design. What impressed me most was the way enemies travelled through the levels. They flipped, climbed, slid, and rolled in an attempt to close the gap and this made the shooting experience so much more pleasing than conventional point and click in other games. Typically in single player games you never need to track due to how static mooks are - this isn't the case for
.
Environment design was also great, at least for the dungeons. The overworld was bare, but in levels like Dead City there was a fantastic amount of detail that at times made the game look like concept art.
Overall, I think it's best to view
for what it is, not what it could have been. It's obvious the game had a lot more potential, but what's present provides a great experience regardless.

First off, I have never played the original version. I downloaded the game a day after it went free-to-play.

Just started playing at the release of Stage 2. So far, the game seams alright. It runs well on my computer (low settings 1080p) and the f2p component is fair and balanced. New characters range from 5000 to 9000 silver, but you earn between 100-1000 silver per game, depending on how well you do. There are also a bunch of perks that you can buy/upgrade for about 1000 silver a pop, and you can either buy skins or unlock them gradually. All in all, making the game f2p was a fantastic business decision for the developers, while also boosting the playerbase exponentially.
Be warned that this isn't your typical FPS, though. When it was first released, Evolve mainly drew controversy from its awful DLC design and confusing microtransations, but also garnered some criticism on the basis of gameplay. The game is essentially a game of Hide and Seek or Pacman, where four heroes chase a monster and attempt to kill it before it gets too powerful and kills them. That means that there's a lot of running, and not as much shooting for either side. A match can vary from 5-30 minutes each, depending team composition and individual skill, and most of that is the hunters chasing the monster around the map. Fortunately, traversal is fairly entertaining and skill-based, requiring from both sides a decent amount of resource management, however, if you want to shoot things, you will, but not as much as Overwatch or Call of Duty.
What this game really succeeds in is this sort of mood shift between each side. When you play as a hunter, you feel desperation as you struggle to keep the rest of the team alive while fighting this incredible monstrocity, whereas when you're playing the monster, you get incredibly annoyed at the continued persistance of these tiny things out to kill you like deadly mosquitoes. It's obvious that this is what they were going for, and the mechanics portray this conflict perfectly.
Overall, I'm glad I picked up this game for free, and I will enjoy playing a match every now and then. However, I'm also glad that I didn't buy it on release. It should have been free to play all along.

Featuring Paul Robertson's lovely artwork (you may recognize him from such games as Scott Pilgrim vs. The World), this game glows with a Metal Slug vibe.  However, it would be much more accurate to describe this game as something very similar to Mega Man or Cave Story that is wearing Metal Slug's clothes.
The plot consists of...  Um...  Mutant mandrake plants...  Some typical generic bad guys...  Doin' some stuff...  Bad stuff...  Something something elite team of super-juiced mercenaries are gonna kick some♥♥♥♥♥  Okay, so, the story isn't where the game shines.  That's really okay though.  The charm of the characters, the art, and various pop culture and gaming references is going to win you over in that department.
A typical session consists of gearing up at the games's hub, Camp Crown, and then selecting a mission to play.  There are several different objective types, however all missions are mostly identical in nature.  Roam around a lovingly-created level, back and forth, for the umpteenth TIME, shooting the same handful of baddies OVER and OVER, picking up endless crafting ingredients, leaping through somewhat sluggish platforming segments, and killing a boss you've probably already fought 3 times before.  All before the time limit runs out.
Then you come back to camp.  From here you get into the game's laborious crafting feature.  It is a straightforward collect-a-thon where you exchange various materials found from enemies and chests in order to build new melee weapons, armor, guns or bio-mods.  There is certainly a writhing mass of items to craft, more than I personally ever wanted.  You can create some pretty awesome guns by mixing and matching various parts (receivers, barrels, stocks, etc) and also...  Plenty and plenty of not-so-awesome guns.
Rinse.  Repeat.  And repeat.  And repeat.  And repeat.  And repeat.  AND REPEAT.

I don't think the game deserves so many negative reviews, even though I understand their overall issues, Mercenary Kings' pros easily outweigh it's cons.
Mercenary Kings is a load of fun, highly polished with much more depth than it appears at first glance.
The level design works through missions in 1-2 levels per rank (there's 10 ranks), with enough variation to keep you entertained, yet enough repetition so you can learn the levels and enjoy the benefits of improving with experience.
The game rewards your patience with a highly satisfying control system that gets better as you do, and a very enjoyable mechanic where you unlock weapon parts to customise your arsenal. As you progress, rarer hidden parts become vital to unlocking the best weapons, which offers great replayability.
It's fair to say taht the game does get a bit samey at times, and some of the levels can feel like a chore to replay, but overall I found this effect rather minimal to my enjoyment.
I should also add that I bought this game on sale, and would feel more comfortable recommending it around the $10 price range, rather than the $20. Also, I think you will enjoy the game a lot more if you have friends to play it with. While the single player is great, I think the game shines at sharing your mix of weapons and working together to explore the map and bring down the bosses.

My first impressions of Tales of Maj'Eyal...
First, I think it is important to point out that although Tales of Maj'Eyal is featured as a roguelike game with perma-death, it can also be played with limited lives as well as unlimited lives. So, even if you do die you can still advance through the entire game with all of your hard earned stats and gear! That's really like 3 versions of the game!  So far, it seems like a very solid and polished game. It's obvious that a lot of love went into the making of this game and it shows through the professionalism of the product. Everything is explained in great detail through text boxes.
It should also be noted that not all of the character races and classes are unlocked at the beginning of the game, and must be unlocked through playing the game. There are sub races and classes branching off of the main choices also.
When you die in Exploration mode, you can teleport back to the battle before you died, but must fight that same battle from the beginning again, or teleport a little further back out of harms way.  You also get the choice to retire your character roguelike style, so be extra careful when making one of these choices after dying!  That is the only penalty for death that I have seen so far, but this is only based on my experience playing on Easier difficulty and Exploration mode (unlimited lives).
Pros:
+3 game modes; Roguelike (perma-death), Adventure (limited lives) & Exploration (unlimited lives).
+5 difficulty settings.  Easier, Normal, Nightmare & 2 more locked settings.
+Generous level cap of 50.
+Extensive character customization with skill trees and infusions.
+No consumables.  You don't have to worry about food or water.
+Ammo is unlimited, but you will have to reload your quiver once in a while.
+Fast movement and strategic turn-based gameplay.
+Save feature. You can have multiple saves for multiple characters!
+Many towns, dungeons and creepy places to explore, and conquer!
+Can use both keyboard & mouse.
+Streamlined to play on many computer systems and configurations.
+Many races & character classes with sub races and classes to choose from.
+Randomly generated tactical battles and dungeons/maps. Both good & bad!
+Easy modding support with Steam Workshop integration.
+User friendly GUI with great explanations of everything!
+Great little tutorial provided.
+Cool sound track and sound FX.
+Smart AI.  Both character and monster AI.  Monsters will hunt you down!
+Options, options and more options!  The game is completely customizable!
Cons:
-Death comes too easy due to free roam exploration and randomly generated tactical battles & dungeons/maps.  You can encounter areas without warning, where you will die instantly.  Beware of dungeons you cannot exit because you activated a battle with monsters 30+ levels above yours!
-Randomly generated tactical battles and dungeons/maps. As I said, both good & bad!
-The game gets a little boring after a while.
-Once you beat Arena mode, your character is useless.
-You cannot play the regular game with Arena characters.
-The price is a little high for an indy game.  I usually get these kinds of games for $1 on my iPad.
You can use keyboard, mouse or a combo of the both. There are many key commands which most can be accessed with the mouse too. The keyboard commands are logical choices and easy to learn, but can be remapped to your liking. You'll be using the mouse most of the time though. I have not seen any In App Purchase (IAP) selections or buttons, so I assume most of the content so far is in the game.
Tales of Maj'Eyal seems like a nice little game that is very stable and polished with love for the genre. It's old school fun with a twist of 21st century ideas. Being able to set up the game with limited and unlimited lives was a very nice touch and gives the game some options to appeal to many other gamers! You even get your own set of achievements and recognition for playing with limited and unlimited lives! I'm happy with my purchase! :D Happy dungeon crawling! :)

Y'know, I actually REALLY like this game! All the time that this took was totally worth it because honestly it just feels like a complete experience! Honestly, this game is just TOO GOOD. So let me organise this review for you.
PROS:
-The price. The price is totally worth it for a game as amazing as this.
-It's really well balanced. each of the weapons are pretty balanced aside from the smoke bomb and the charge shot. Each charm and shot has it's own strengths and weaknesses, and it's really useful for fighting the bosses.
-The bosses are all really unique! While I'm on the topic of bosses, I would like to say that all of the bosses are pretty well balanced and the difficulty goes well with the time in the game in which you encounter them! Of course, I do have a lot of exceptions, which I'll mention later.
-THE BEAUTIFUL GRAPHICS AND ANIMATION. It just feels extremely fresh with it's high quality animation. It just feels really nice and smooth, and it just looks great.
-The run and guns are really nicely put out. I like how the run & guns just feel really fun and great and new, because none of the run & guns are very similar to eachother. They all feel very different with it's different enemies, layout, and minibosses.
-The music. I think the music is really good, because it's all hand-recorded and it sounds just like an actual cartoon!
-The secrets and unlockables. I think the remaining 10 coins and the special audio and visual modes are really fun to try to get and are well worth it.
-The sense of accomplishment you get. Yes, other reviews say it's really hard and I agree! But the sense of accomplishment after you beat a tough boss is GREAT.
Well, that's pretty much it. But no game is perfect so...
CONS:
-The difficulty curve. The difficulty isn't very well balanced. You have grim matchstick in the second area where it just feels too hard, and then you have captain brineybeard in the third area where he feels to easy. The tutorial and the first two levels are easy, the rest take a lot of hard work. Of course, it is supposed to be hard, and the bosses are supposed to be in the area where it fits for them to be, but the difficulty progression just feels so unnatural.
-Dr. Kahls's robot and Grim Matchstick. To me and a lot of other people, these two bosses were complete NIGHTMARES. They are so difficult at the time in which people encounter them. Dr. Kahl's a bullet hell and Grim matchstick is just unfair. A little bit too much to enjoy the rest of the cons when people are fighting these two. Please nerf them.
-When you're so close. The thing is, there is no health or progress bar AT ALL until you die or beat it. Which is good in some ways, but even more frusterating when you are TOUCHING THE END OF THE BOSS. It just feels AWEFUL. This is more about the players instead of the game, but it is still very frusterating.
-The weird little static things on the screen. I get that it's supposed to be like a 1930s cartoon, but it's just kinda annoying.
So to sum up, this is a great game. I highly recommend that you check it out. Of course, it does have it's cons, but I think the pros outweigh the cons by a landslide. But I recommend having a controller :-)

You don't need me to tell you that Cuphead is good, the game has already received a lot of positive revies from both critics and players.
I'd rather focus on the aspect of its difficulty: Cuphead received a lot of attention upon its release because people were waiting for it since 2014, and immediately became fodder for a lot of content creators on YouTube once it became clear that you die a lot in the game. There's a lot of rage videos on the net now, because a lot of viewers enjoy watching their favourite youtubers lose it after failing over and over again. Of course this sort of content is very popular and makes a lot of viewers.
I think that the idea that Cuphead is difficult has been blown out of proportion because of the way that the online community has treated the game. It's true that you die a lot in this game, but that does not necessarily mean that it's THAT hard. Almost every boss battle lasts 2 or 3 minutes, meaning that if you get killed it will only take you a very short period of time to recover the lost progress. Certain bosses will seem super hard the first time you face them, but you will constantly get better. Most importanly, regardless of how good you are, the game will never punish you. If you die against a boss in Dark Souls, you don't get to fight it again immediately, you lose resources and your character becomes weaker. None of this happens in Cuphead, yet you still feel a great sense of satisfaction when you finally manage to beat that one boss that kept you stuck for hours. Highly recommended!

This to me is THE tower defense game, that i compare every other TD to. Now, if that wasn't enough to make you buy this game, here's a bit more in depth analysis:
The real challenge in this game comes from the level design. The large open areas don't give you even grids like 10x10 to build your mazes, instead, they give odds like 8x7 etc. So most of the times i found myself thinking that:"Damn, if i put them this way, i could direct them to that area, but then the damage suffers pretty greatly..". Most other TD games just give your enemies a pre-determined path, that you put towers alongside of it, and usually one tactic works in every level.
Most TD games i've played give you usually a path of two that the enemies go, in this game, you can create a proper mazes on your own, on most levels. That increases the re-playability a lot, and often i find myself trying some level again just to test out a different strategy.
The towers are pretty basic ones, all with 3 levels. There's the gun tower, flamethrower which acts like "poison", heavy hitting cannon, laser, slower, air, concussion that does huge damage to land groups, and command tower that increases the money gained from kills/shows stealthed units better. So nothing too deep in that department.  But nothing more is even needed. In my opinion this game wuold be too much of a hassle with deeper tower system. Since the levels require thinking.
The levels itself, there are a good amount of them, and dlc's add a lot more. Every level also has different modes like 99 waves, lesser cores (that enemies steal), core's that stay where they're dropped by an enemy that's killed (these are challenging), restrictions that you must complete the level using only lvl1 towers, and many more different challenges.
if you're a fan of TD games, this is one of the must-play game of that genre. Really. I haven't encountered a single bug ever on these 134 hours that i've played this, runs perfectly on win 10.

Tower Defense. That's all you need to know. Think of your standard Tower Defense Game, Give it some sweet 3d graphics, a challenging difficulty curve and a soothing british voice as a narrator, and you'll have this game.
It doesn't do much beyond one new thing compared to the standard tower defense (TD). NO fancy gimmicks, no trick twists, no surprises. IT is as standard as you can get in terms of mechanics. In terms of graphics, this is where the polish comes in and boy did they polish it.
What id does add is a surprising bit of subtle story-telling through your AI Advisor. I won't spoil it but really, it's right up there with the Stanley Parable and the Bastion Narrator. Without this guy, the game becomes a well polished but soulless husk of a game.
As for negatives. Well  it has a crazy difficulty curve and is not advised if you OCD.. COmpleting the missions is not terribly difficult. COmpleting a mission with a gold star ranking on the other hand... Yeah. Plus each map has a plethora of challenge modes. Really it is the fun sort of game if you like a Tower Defense game that makes you think and plan.
About the only othe negative is that there's not really anything here for people who aren't already fans of the genre. If you know you like Tower Defense, give this game a shot. if you're not sure, give it a shot but be careful. YOu'll find the 2 hour limit goes by pretty quickly.

Again, the hard selling point of this game is the fact that it, like Undertale, demolishes the 4th Wall in a way previously unseen.  And it does it well.  Really well, actually.  So I recommend if you are into the more story based experience.

If you really like, in particular, sliding puzzles or the whole steampunk aesthetic, you'll probably like this game. However, looking at this in comparison to other puzzle games, it's just not quite as fun. The sliding puzzle mechanic is just unpleasant to interact with. Unlike some better puzzle games where the puzzles are about experimenting and discovering properties about each puzzle and having flashes of insight, these puzzles just feel like they're about sliding stuff around and remembering the patterns of moves you need to make to achieve a certain desired state. Particularly when you need to try to beat levels in a short time or with few moves, the game becomes entirely about memorization, which isn't a fun mechanic to people who like puzzle games, usually. It's not easy to describe, really, but the primary sliding block mechanics of this game just aren't fun to deal with unless you really like this particular sort of thing, and I'm a huge fan of puzzle games. As the levels get harder, you basically get into situations where you've come close to the final solution state for a given sliding puzzle, but in order to get a piece in place you need to temporarily "un-make" the solution to give yourself the mobility to get the final piece in place - so to do this well you just need to memorize the pattern of moves you need to do to get the final piece in place and to re-make the already solved part. I don't find this very fun, I find it more mentally exhausting than intellectually stimulating.
Again, if you like this sort of aesthetic or puzzle mechanic, you'll probably like this. Otherwise, if you're just looking for an all around fun game, probably skip this.

Cogs is a sliding tile puzzle game. That's all it is.
What makes it amazing is the theme, and the way that theme figures into the puzzles themselves. You're not just putting together a picture made of tiles -- you're positioning gears and steam pipes and all other sorts of steampunk gadgetry to make things work. The way everything comes together like clockwork upon completing a puzzle brings a joy that will enchant anyone who's interested in engineering and mechanical contraptions.
It falls short of Rube Goldberg-levels of absurd complexity (which I might have enjoyed!), but what's there will totally satisfy.

Tales of Maj'Eyal is a very rewarding Roguelike game.  Before you buy the game, though, you should consider whether the Roguelike genre appeals to you because this game is not a typical dungeon crawling RPG like Diablo II.  It seems that most of the negative reviews for this game have come from players who failed to consider their purchase.
The basic premise of a Roguelike game is randomly or semi-randomly generated dungeons with randomly generated monsters and randomly generated loot.  Luck is an integral part of the Roguelike genre, and most of them allow you only one life.  Skilled players can work with what they're given to create a powerful character, and get through very challenging randomly generated rooms/bosses/dungeons/etc.  Less skilled players might find that they die.  Often.  Tales of Maj'Eyal is unusually 'fair' for a Roguelike game, but you shouldn't mistake that to mean that it's easy, because it isn't easy at all.  It gives you extra lives, and most of the time the monsters are beatable for your level (even if they say that they're a much higher level).  The game even warns you when you're about to open a special room (rooms that often times have very numerous and/or difficult and/or high level monsters) or treasure chest (which usually spawns enemies).  Occasionally you'll run into a very difficult pack of mobs or a difficult boss, and if you lose all of your lives, then you die.  That's life, and that's how the Roguelike genre works.  Hopefully you unlocked something to explore for your next playthrough.
The appeal of this game is that there is a LOT of stuff to unlock.  You'll find yourself accidentally unlocking new classes, races, and even game modes all the time, unless you're using an unlockables guide, in which case you probably aren't having as much fun as you could be having!  There's also a great amount of class diversity, tons of classes, and even lots of depth within each class.  As a bonus, the game features a really cool world to explore and learn about.  There isn't so much of a 'storyline' but there is really a lot of lore to learn, and there are many things to discover about the current shape of the world, past events, and even letters and such from random adventurers or random people that give insight on a particular dungeon or event.  If you're anything like me, then you'll love that part of the game, but if you're one of those people who never read anything in a game, ever, then that's fine too because you can easily skip lore popups and keep playing.  If these things sound appealing to you, then great, you'll love the game.  If the Roguelike premise doesn't sound very appealing, then you may want to look elsewhere, but don't buy the game and then make a negative review if you can't even get past the first level (also here's a tip: don't play a Shalore on your first playthrough because they have a very difficult starting zone... I suspect that people who found the first level to be 'impossible' probably played a Shalore).
The UI definitely has its shortcomings, which is probably the worst thing about the game, but all-in-all I think it's a very impressive game for having been designed by one person, and well worth your 7 dollars to buy.  Also you can play it for free at
, so if you're on the fence about whether to purchase it, feel free to play for, well, free.

This is one of the few games I've ever reviewed without finishing, but honestly, I feel that I've seen enough to not recommend it.
You play as a Mexican outlaw who has no memory of why people are after him, yet he still wantonly murders a whole bunch of people. The story is told out of order and is quite frankly, all over the place, and for every thing it does right, it does something else wrong.
Take, for instance, the art style. It's gorgeous hand drawn pencil art that feels very Western. The monochromatic style makes all the blood you spill really stand out. If it was based entirely on how pretty it is to look at, it would be an absolute recommendation. But the thing is the art style makes enemies blend in to the environments. It's presented top down style, and every single enemy in the game wears a hat. It makes it very difficut to tell what's an enemy and what's not, meaning an enemy can very easily take you by surprise.
In another game, that may not necessarilly be a problem, but this game tries to imitate Hotline Miami. And you know what? Good for it. Hotline Miami is truly great. This game, though, fails to understand what made HM work. An enemy getting the jump on you means certain death because you die in one hit from just about everything. So do enemies, which mean precision shots are the name of the game. The thing is that this game has old weaponry, and you must manually♥♥♥♥♥♥your gun every time you fire. It requires a very deliberate approach versus HM, where you rush in and improvise. And another interesting wrinkle is that stealth is viable, as you can sneak up on enemies who are sleeping or have their backs turned to you and kill them silently, unlike in HM where ai is immiedately tuned in to your location. But it's very tough to figure out which way people are facing half the time.
It's constantly at odds with itself in just about every way. It wants you to throw caution to the wind, but the fact you need to manually♥♥♥♥♥♥your gun each time means you need to be very deliberate and choose your shots. It tries to have a surreal, strange story told in a fractured way like HM, but instead the story is underwritten, confusing as all hell, and contradicts itself. The point I stopped at was at an Indian camp. They said the Mexican needs to fight their warriors for story reasons and he says he doesn't just kill people for no reason even though on the way to the camp you kill a group of Indians for no real reason at all. Not one I could see, at least.
On top of all that, the game is buggy. Frame rate issues are very common (I only have a laptop but I've played more technically demanding games on it with nary a hitch). Hit detection feels inconsistent (the level I stopped on, I was peaking in and out of cover and kept on trying to hit a guy close to me, but it got caught on an invisible hit box for the box I was behind). And the game explains things very poorly, as well. Reloading your gun and getting more bullets in reserve is a pointlessly tedious task, one I had to consult a message board for. You can apparently purchase perks, but I guess only at predetermined sections?? There was no explanation for it, I was suddenly in an area where I could buy a perk that doubled my bullets but none of the other ones that are available. There are side missions you can take on, but also only at predetermined times, which means if you want to make extra money you have to do a bunch of side missions at once. I stumbled across something I think was a side quest (?) where I hd to defend a barbershop from bandits for seemingly no reason.
In other words, this game is an absolute mess. I really wanted to enjoy it. I LOVE Hotline Miami and it's clear the developers do too, but the thing is that the devs took a bunch of elements of HM without any understanding of what makes those work and the end result is a game that is simply all over the place. At the end of the day, though, I'm going to have to go with a no on this one. There are simply too many flaws to ignore and I felt absolutely no desire to push ahead because the story was a total cluster♥♥♥♥ (in a bad way), and the gameplay wasn't compelling or well executed enough for me to want to see what lay ahead.

1. The ammo mechanism is really annoying. I understand that it could be developer's intention for realism that you'll have to unload the bullet from current gun to add them to a newly picked gun. But the way this is done is very poor. You need to hold R for like 3s and you'll need to reload the gun fully first before you can unload them. It's annoying to the point that I gave up playing during one level because it makes my gameplay experience terrible.
2. The user interface is not very friendly. I got stuck for about three or four levels out of around 15 because I didn't know how to proceed to next level. There's no indicator where I should go or any mission briefing. Also trying to pick up a gun on the ground is like picking up a needle on the floor - you'll need to move to the precise spot in order to have the "E pick up" show up.
Because of these two really poor design choice in the game, I didn't have good experience despite the awesome game style and art.
Please note, I'm not saying this is a bad game though. I just don't enjoy the gameplay or the mechanism. I guess there could be someone who might enjoy the game.

Cuphead is a game I personally hadn't even known about until E3 2016, and while I thought it looked interesting at the time, I wasn't all that interested in it. Fast foward to its release just a couple months ago, I found myself more interested in it as I heard about how it was an amazing, challenging platformer. Now that I've played it, I've decided to weigh in: is Cuphead worth the hype? Short answer: Yes, and I'd go so far as to call it one of the top five games I've played all year.
Cuphead has a very simple plot: Cuphead and his friend Mugman went to a casino in their homeland of Inkwell Isles, only to learn that the casino was run by the Devil himself. The Devil offers them a bet: if they can win in a game of luck, they'll get his casino. If they lose, he'll take their souls. The two friends lose the bet and are forced into collecting souls for the Devil to repay their debt. It doesn't get much more complex than this, but Cuphead is a game that proves that a deep story isn't necessary to make a fantastic game. The premise on its own is fun and engaging, and the journey from start to end is a lot of fun.
As for gameplay mechanics, Cuphead takes the elements of classic platformers and bullet hell games and adds its own modern twist. The game is mainly focused on boss battles, with a few platforming levels mixed in. Most boss battles are fought in more of a traditional platformer style, but a few put Cuphead and Mugman into airplanes for some bullet hell action. Cuphead and Mugman have fairly simple actions: they can jump, shoot, dash, or use a special move after racking up enough damage. While this seems simple, there's a lot of depth to each mechanic. After a jump, you can parry off of pink objects to fill your special meter and protect yourself from damage.
There are multiple different weapons you can buy at a shop with coins earned in platforming levels, and charms can modify different stats or provide the player with additional abilities. Each weapon has its own special attack, and a full special meter allows players to use a powerful super move. The controls are tight and responsive, and the game design rarely, if ever, feels cheap. Make no mistake, this game is incredibly challenging: however, the challenge feels fair, and overcoming a tough boss fight is incredibly rewarding. Cuphead has some of the most solid platforming in any game I've ever played, and that alone makes it one of my favorites.
The bosses are all very unique in terms of playstyle and design as well. Each one of them is charming and a lot of fun to fight, and each one is also incredibly challenging. There are a few randomized elements in each fight to keep each attempt fresh, and these can get slightly annoying at times, but it isn't a big deal over all. Even as someone who is far from the best at platformers, I was able to beat the game in 14-16 hours, and that's with 100%. Even after beating the game, you unlock expert mode, which makes each boss even tougher. I've only scratched the surface on expert mode, but that adds plenty of replay value. In addition, each level gives you a score at the end based on your performance. Going for the highest rank in each level adds even more replayability, adding plenty of value for a game that's only $20. The game also has co-op, and while I haven't played a whole lot of it, that's fun and provides an opportunity for less experienced players to have a better shot at beating the game. Trying new combinations of weapons, super moves, and charms provides new ways to experiment with the game as well.
Of course, when talking about Cuphead, it's impossible to ignore the visuals and music. Cuphead was designed with classic '30s-era cartoons in mind. Everything in the game is hand-drawn for an authentic feeling, and the animation is incredibly fluid and detailed. The music is in the same style as well: everything in the game's aesthetic ties into an authentic feeling for the era that StudioMDHR tried to capture, and their desires and hopes for the game are clear. In an era plagued with lootboxes, incomplete games, and other business practices that harm fans, Cuphead is a game that shows that passion projects are still possible and incredibly fun to play.
Pros:
+Tight, rewarding gameplay
+Plenty of depth behind the seemingly simple mechanics
+Simple yet fun story
+Incredibly unique art style
+Catchy music
Cons:
-Random elements in some boss fights can get slightly annoying on rare occassions.
Score: 10/10. This game is absolutely worth the $20 it costs at full price.

I recommend this game for tower defense fans, and nobody else. Good balanced game; bit tedious; very bad presentation. In some respects this game is the best tower defense game I've played. I consider it to have flaws which diminish the fun.
Tower defense: waves of enemies come, and you build static defense weapons to counter them. Defense Grid is a pretty basic tower defense: despite the appearances, enemies seem to be considered one-dimensional dots on a path; weapons always hit. There's a line-of-sight mechanic though, by which towers can't shoot through other towers, and some towers are higher than others, and the levels are considered in 3D for targeting. It isn't immediately obvious what the barriers for targeting are (some towers are considered lower than their model suggests, many can shoot steeper downward than their models can bend).
That is the first weakness of the game: there isn't a direct correlation between what you see and what you get. Even the indicator for how far your towers can shoot seems not to precisely correlate to how far they can actually shoot. So now you can enjoy learning the actual capabilities of your weapons by heart.
In some stages Defense Grid let's you build towers in the way of your enemies, so that you can make them take a longer route. Often you need to find the longest route to get a good result on a level; the second longest route won't do. They obviously did a lot of balancing to get the stages to work like that. Also the different weapons are well balanced with their costs. So that's one strong point: very subtly balanced game.
Second strong point is the resource management. Keep your "money" in the bank and you get interest. Very simple, but works
for tower defense games. This is one of the points that makes it rewarding to go for a highscore.
The towers don't take any orders, tweaks, or diverging upgrade paths. They will however automatically target enemies they're strong against, which is nice on one hand, but isn't very rewarding. A special class of enemies flies and takes a shorter route. Countering them boils down to saving enough money to buy a special AA-gun on time. It all works, but it feels a bit artificially scripted.
For some reason you can't zoom out to see the entire stage at once. If an enemy slips by your defense, you will often not notice it immediately. The game has some checkpoints where it autosaves, so you can rewind the game as much as you like to one of those checkpoints. This is a must for getting good highscores.
The enemies are shapeless blobs that could have been somebody's first 3D project. The stages look like the part of the background that you can't actually interact with in other games. There's only one BGM (that interactively changes mood). The sounds of enemies dying is either muffled, or sounds like one of your cannons firing. And you have some posh computer companion with a tragic backstory who tells you what to do. Many people seem to be ecstatic about the voice-acting and humor of that character; I found him annoying and overly dramatic.
Nice voice acting, otherwise a totally standard tower defense game with no real interesting mechanics. It's well polished, but adds absolutely nothing new.
Classic! 8/10

Everywhere I went on the Internet, I was told this was the ultimate tower defense game, excellent in every single detail.
Don't get me wrong. This game has an amazing level of polish. It has everything good tower defense games should have. If you have not played many tower defense games, then it is probably going to be an amazing experience for you.
However, Grid is exactly that, and no more: a game that takes all the basics from tower defense games and make them work perfectly. There is nothing more. There is nothing new. You will play with the same basic boring towers you have been playing with since the very first TDs on Warcraft. No ambition, nothing new, nothing exciting. Even the strategic depth is minimal, leaving you sometimes with no choice on where to build your towers. It is a great production, but with no innovation. Frankly, some indie games or even some flash TDs are more innovative and addictive.
Grid, because it has NOTHING that makes it different from other super-classic TDs, will fail exactly where all the classic ones failed: it becomes quickly repetitive, boring and brainless. Such a shame when we think that a tiny bit of innovation would have made it a seriously great game.

Gave it another try and the game seems decent, but it makes me not want to play. You have to slowly sell towers at end of a level for higher score and the game doesn't tell you that you gain more interest when you have more resources. It's frustrating not to know this on early missions when you are going for gold medals.
I wouldn't have tried the game for longer if I didn't stumble upon this information when googling for "defense grid towers". Not only that, but comparing the game to other TDs that I've tried, it feels a little too slow or too basic.
I guess if you like mazing with basic towers (later in the game) or spending time on trying to understand how to beat a level without any knowledge on how to get a higher resource gain, give it a try.

The gameplay is similar to these type of games, four players who may choose different classes and characters with different weapons and special abilities. Especially compared to Payday 2 RAID lacks variety here though. Every class in RAID plays very similarly, whereas in Payday 2 you had basically infinite possibilities to create a build and playstyle that suits you the most. The skill system in RAID is pretty straight forward and does not offer a lot of options for personalization. Same applies to the weapon upgrade system, it's less complex than Payday 2's and provides less options when it comes to customization.
RAID still manages to transfer the awesome feeling of four people whiping out whole armys while stealing some nazi gold that Payday 2 had in its own setting. Boy, how do I talk about this game without really hurting what makes this game great?
A lot of people have called this a Undertale or Pony Island look alike, and... I don't think that's an unfair assessment but it's also not completely accurate as this is clearly it's own game. It is much more about the story it presents and the journey than anything else; you won't find much in the way of "real" gameplay here. If this sounds like a complete drag to you then that's fair and it may not be for you as this is more of an interactive book than a game in the traditional sense. For everyone else though, this game is extremely compelling and I really couldn't stop playing it until I saw the whole thing through.
Like games it has been compared to, it has a bit of a meta 4th wall breaking element that's hard to elaberate on without spoiling anything. The Steam synopsis, specifically "You are to guide a child through a mysterious world on a mission to restore its long-dead sun. The world knows you exist." does a good job of letting you know what sort of footing you're starting off with. Some of the story telling and puzzles will blow your mind when it comes to using this element to maximuim effect and I HIGHLY recommend going into this game blind. If you're curious about this game and it seems like it's up your alley, it is pretty much essential to go into this game knowing as little as possible to enjoy it to it's full potential. I'd say don't go looking up Let's Plays of the game to make sure if it's up your alley if you're considering buying it, it will really hurt what makes it so good.
Though minimalistic, the art and music are solid. The characters range from interesting and likable to downright adorable. I very rarely got stuck on a puzzle and when I did find the solution it was apparent that I just made a silly oversight or was just being dumb. The only negative thing I can even begin to think of saying about this game is it's value proposition may not look too alluring to someone who is gaming on a budget. With my regions price not on a sale being 10$, I can confidently say that I found it absolutely worth it. I have spent 9 hours on the game as of this review and honestly I do not think I'll be spending any more as I believe I've seen everything there is to, minus little side things for achievements... and I really took my time with this game, 9 hours may be longer than some people's play time or maybe shorter depending on how much of a completionist you are. It's a shame 10$ for 9 hours of entertainment can sound bothersome to some in this day in age of games, but the quality of the time I spent with this game is not something many games can match.
Really, how does one really review a game that's so story driven without ruining the story? I can't think of much else to say about this game that wouldn't be problematic so I'll end this on, if you're looking for a incredibly interesting and compelling story, this is one that would definitely make a top list for me. Although what makes a story good or not is subjective, the vast majority of people who have played this certainly agrees, and I really do think it's that good.

Man, this game is so close to being amazing, and still has so much potential...
The art and atmosphere are great, the characters are likable and are wonderfully designed, the worlds, lore and concept are all REALLY cool and the game's gimmicks admittedly surprised me more than a few times. Some more polish on the character interaction and sharpening their relationships to make their individual plights more relatable would be nice but its completely forgiveable.
There's one thing about this game that really, really, desperately needed more work on - and it really upsets me that it was overlooked so negligently:
The soundtrack.
It's pleasant, but is also so boring. It's all dismal, ambient, repetitive post apocalyptic mood music being played against a game that has an awesome world built with interesting characters that are TRYING SO HARD TO GET ME TO LIKE THEM AND MAKE ME LAUGH AND CARE ABOUT THEM AND RELATE TO THEM - But man, the music was literally lulling me to sleep. It's so frustratingly *boring*
I'm sorry, you really should not EVER take an existing track and slow it down multiple times to make separate area tracks. That is so LAZY  - which I don't really understand since the folks that worked on this game obviously put so much thought and love into so many other aspects of the game!
Man, I want to like this game SO much more than I do currently.
Here's a fun little experiment: For the factory area of the game (which features a track from the game used in like 3 other areas at varying speeds) - mute the game music and play something like core or another medium from undertale. Quite a difference, eh? suddenly this area is mysterious and intense and interesting!
I know it's unfair to compare the game to Undertale like that, but I doubt it's much of a stretch to suggest that the devs MIGHT HAVE PLAYED THAT GAME AT SOME POINT - AND MISSED THE PART WHERE THE SOUNDTRACK IS ONE OF THE MOST IMPORTANT AND CENTRAL ELEMENTS OF THAT GAME'S DESIGN.
I still recommend this game, it's a lovely little experiment about subverting the player's expectations and dabbling pretty hard in the meta... but, jeez. The soundtrack. It has about as much effect on the game if you just turned the music off. I know that's harsh, but it was true a lot of the time in my case.
That doesn't mean the music is poorly composed, mind. Just ill-fitting for a lot of areas of the game - which is a bit sad.

Tales of Maj'Eyal is a very rewarding Roguelike game.  Before you buy the game, though, you should consider whether the Roguelike genre appeals to you because this game is not a typical dungeon crawling RPG like Diablo II.  It seems that most of the negative reviews for this game have come from players who failed to consider their purchase.
The basic premise of a Roguelike game is randomly or semi-randomly generated dungeons with randomly generated monsters and randomly generated loot.  Luck is an integral part of the Roguelike genre, and most of them allow you only one life.  Skilled players can work with what they're given to create a powerful character, and get through very challenging randomly generated rooms/bosses/dungeons/etc.  Less skilled players might find that they die.  Often.  Tales of Maj'Eyal is unusually 'fair' for a Roguelike game, but you shouldn't mistake that to mean that it's easy, because it isn't easy at all.  It gives you extra lives, and most of the time the monsters are beatable for your level (even if they say that they're a much higher level).  The game even warns you when you're about to open a special room (rooms that often times have very numerous and/or difficult and/or high level monsters) or treasure chest (which usually spawns enemies).  Occasionally you'll run into a very difficult pack of mobs or a difficult boss, and if you lose all of your lives, then you die.  That's life, and that's how the Roguelike genre works.  Hopefully you unlocked something to explore for your next playthrough.
The appeal of this game is that there is a LOT of stuff to unlock.  You'll find yourself accidentally unlocking new classes, races, and even game modes all the time, unless you're using an unlockables guide, in which case you probably aren't having as much fun as you could be having!  There's also a great amount of class diversity, tons of classes, and even lots of depth within each class.  As a bonus, the game features a really cool world to explore and learn about.  There isn't so much of a 'storyline' but there is really a lot of lore to learn, and there are many things to discover about the current shape of the world, past events, and even letters and such from random adventurers or random people that give insight on a particular dungeon or event.  If you're anything like me, then you'll love that part of the game, but if you're one of those people who never read anything in a game, ever, then that's fine too because you can easily skip lore popups and keep playing.  If these things sound appealing to you, then great, you'll love the game.  If the Roguelike premise doesn't sound very appealing, then you may want to look elsewhere, but don't buy the game and then make a negative review if you can't even get past the first level (also here's a tip: don't play a Shalore on your first playthrough because they have a very difficult starting zone... I suspect that people who found the first level to be 'impossible' probably played a Shalore).
The UI definitely has its shortcomings, which is probably the worst thing about the game, but all-in-all I think it's a very impressive game for having been designed by one person, and well worth your 7 dollars to buy.  Also you can play it for free at
, so if you're on the fence about whether to purchase it, feel free to play for, well, free.

Unncessary complexities that might otherwise make a turn-based dungeon crawler tedious are streamlined using functionalities like auto-explore, auto-cast, and auto-sell. At the same time, the game retains all the complexities related character customization and strategy. There are 25 classes, and nearly all of them play very differently from the others. Adding to the strategic depth is the amount of effects the environment can have on a character, from vision blocked by fog to getting crushed by collasping walls to suffocated in water. The dungeon design makes great use of these elements. There is always something new to look forward to when you start a new game, which is a great news, because the game is challenging enough that it's only a matter of time before your first character runs out of lives.

I had sort of low expectations for this game due to the cluttered, amateurish look of the screenshots (it honestly reminds me of some of the janky Arcen games), but it blew away those expectations.
This is a roguelike, turned-based RPG with classes, races, stats, and abilities. The loot system is similar to Diablo and other ARPGs, with randomly generated loot of various qualities and special effects, along with unique loot. The art style is similar to old-school western RPGs like the Spiderweb games. An overworld map contains various towns and dungeons, the latter of which unlock gradually as you progress and complete quests.
Now, the part where this game really defied my expectations is that it provides a very streamlined experience, without a lot of the typical drudgery that goes along with games like this.
- First of all, the game itself is very intuitive to pick up and start playing without needing a tutorial. The interface is mouse-driven, no need to memorize keybinds (although it does offer fully customizable keybinds as well).
- The game seem to understand that the appeal of games like this is both the satisfaction of level progression, as well as the hunt for rare loot. Early on, you get an item that can recycle junk loot into gold, as well as a item with unlimited charges that basically provides a Town Portal effect that teleports you out of the current dungeon. This eliminates the trap that Bethesda games, for example, typically fall into, where you want to be a packrat and collect every piece of loot you come across, but are severely limited in the amount of weight you can carry.
- The game offers several difficulty levels, from unlimited lives, to several lives, to permadeath.
- The game has an "auto-explore" button, where your character will automatically move around the current dungeon floor until it finds an item of interest or an enemy. Movement can also be control via clicking on visible locations, and your character will move to the select square.

This game breathes life back into the metal slug side scrolling shooters that in my opinion we could all use more of.  This game not only brings it back, but adds an rpg element as well as the most in depth gun crafting system I've seen in awhile.  The game is not only pretty in its animations, the backgrounds and level design really give you a sense of going back to the metal slug days with its sprites. However:  The game feels almost too long for what it is, and that feeling will come when you notice alot of the enemies, levels, and mission types are reused.  In my opinion the game would be sweeter if the reskinned enemies, and missions were reduced to preserve the flavor.  That and the timelimit to each level. I played and beat this game on free weekend, and yeah, it's about as good as everyone says it is.
Because my reviews are always obnoxiously inconsistent, this time I'll write a list of pros and cons:
Pros:
-Excellent stealth level design as well as nonlinear design (For example, every level obviously directs you go to the same location- But how you get there is up to you. For example, when crossing a bridge, do you take the direct route? Do you climb up into the higher levels of the structure? Do you hide in the maintanence shafts and crawl under the guards' feet?)
-A pretty cool universe. While the story's just "Good", the actual universe the story takes place in is almost stunningly original. I'm not gonna act like I haven't seen steampunk before, but Dishonored is far more than just that.
-A large range of different playstyles
-Suitable recognition of all those different playstyles
-QUICKSAVING
-Excellently fun abilities
Cons:
-Too much stuff is clearly designed for non-stealth gameplay. Don't get me wrong, options are always better, but there's not enough stuff stealth players can upgrade compared to crazy, non-stealth players. This isn't that bad with Runes but with buying upgrades it's extremely glaring. The only thing that directly advantages pacifist stealth players are sleep dart upgrades (Which you won't need if you're doing a Ghost run and not being seen), and boot upgrades which you only get in the extreme lategame.
-It's also noteworthy that in my first playthrough I managed to buy every single money upgrade in the game- I did loot as much of the level as I can but it's a little ridiculous I was able to buy literally everything.
-Bodies despawn- Or rather merge into each other. This is a little hard to explain, but I noticed in my playthrough that leaving multiple bodies together would result in me coming back and finding only one body. Whatever the case I don't think this is acceptable for a stealth game, bodies despawning is a big deal.
-The Good ending is a bit anticlimatic. Obviously it's good, but let's just say you won't get the big battle you were hoping for. In the other endings you're put under significantly more pressure.
-There are boss fights, and I'm amazed that they're all optional- But I personally didn't like the way they played, unfortunately.
However, all these things are relatively minor marks on an otherwise unbelievably enjoyable game for the reasons I listed above. It's important to distinguish when a game's flaws does and doesn't overshadow the entire experience, and Dishonored's flaws certainly don't.

In terms of pure presentation, I cannot think of another game in 2017 as wholly confident and as singularly driven as Cuphead.  The animation, the art, the music, the film grain, the sound editing, the sounds themselves, hell, even the font, everything feels straight out of 1930s cartoons.
Well, everything but the gameplay.  That's the stuff of the 80s, without question.  With wicked attack patterns, reflex-hounding quickness, and a pitiably shallow health pool, its difficulty is all but guaranteed to make your heartbeat syncopated and thready.  Any error could put you back to square one.  But inch by inch, perhaps even unbeknownst to you at the time, you learn the patterns, find your openings to counterattack, and suddenly, somehow, you go from dying in the first minute to passing with an A-rank.  It's nothing short of miraculous.
You need this game.

I bought this game looking for something like the Hotline Miami games that I absolutely loved, but with 12 is better than 6 I got something different, which isn't a bad thing. The play style was similar to HM however the art and storyline made it feel like a completely seperate genre. It's a great old-style western revenge story that I grew to love. My favorite parts about the game were :
+The shooting mechanics which helped to prevent misfires.
+The AI having wicked fast reaction speed and movement to make the game more challenging.
+The settings were very well drawn and heavily varied.
+♥♥♥♥ing bomb rats.
+And of course, the BLOODSHED.

Now with every game, this one had quite a few flaws and slight bugs that I couldn't help but notice.
-Very little variety in weapons with only three hand held guns, a bow, and 3 melee weapons other than your knife.
-Enemies can't see through windows but they can see perfectly fine through doors and will often shoot you through them?
-As a person who uses heavy language and swearing quite often, even the dialogue was a bit over the top for me. I understand that the main character is supposed to be a badass Mexican but I feel like he could go one conversation without saying dropping an F bomb or calling people names(In Spanish of course)
-You can randomly get stuck on boxs or walls forcing you to restart the entire level.
-The bow is the strongest weapon in the entire game. It's completely silent, had no reloading time, and holds a ton of ammo. This is problematic because the ammo is completely reusable and you can take out tons of enemies from a distance without a problem.
-The only problem with the bow is that you can't shoot it when you're standing next to a wall?
With this information, even though there is an overwhelming amount of cons compared to pros in my opinion, I would still reccomend you play it, especially since it's currently on sale. Even if you're just searching for easy acheivements you might as well get a decent story and gameplay along with it.

Oh man...what can I say...this game...an indie game has been the most interesting adventure I had witnessed yet. Granted I couldn't wait for a YouTuber to actually finish his gameplay so I decided to find out myself. It is diffently worth the $9.99 for many reasons!
1. Self Involvement: Not only do you have the character interact with others but at times it will "contact" you at times with some options during the game. Most of them is basically finding out what type of person you are to the character Niko. But otherwise most of the time it is you that have to help Niko out by paying attention to the hints and tips that the "Entity" gives you to try and progress in the game.
2. Music: For me, music is always a big part in games as it sets the mood and makes the game more interesting to continue on the journey. For Instance I love the song "On Little Cat Feet" (Hint: The Catwalk where you find a way to the surface by finding a elevator button) got me to enjoy the rhythm and beat that I sometimes stay in that area just to listen to that song.
3. Storyline: This is one of the most interesting things I look at when it comes to single player games. How interesting is the storyline and what twists and turns does it has for me...this game has a lot of deep input as it has a lot of unexpected surprises I wasn't expecting to encounter during the game. And then playing the Solstice Update I realized this is entirely new and I didn't know what else to do until I found it. For me, it was sad at the very end and that I can always "replay" the game after playing the update but it will never be the same as playing it for the first time. Still the gameplay was great for me and happy for the new ending it provided.
I won't list much else as for me these are the important things to look at. And a bonus if you love cats, birdpeople, goats, and a demonic goat (you will know what I mean). I enjoyed the time I spent on this game and given the chance I would do a total reset to start the game from scratch again for enjoyment.

I had sort of low expectations for this game due to the cluttered, amateurish look of the screenshots (it honestly reminds me of some of the janky Arcen games), but it blew away those expectations.
This is a roguelike, turned-based RPG with classes, races, stats, and abilities. The loot system is similar to Diablo and other ARPGs, with randomly generated loot of various qualities and special effects, along with unique loot. The art style is similar to old-school western RPGs like the Spiderweb games. An overworld map contains various towns and dungeons, the latter of which unlock gradually as you progress and complete quests.
Now, the part where this game really defied my expectations is that it provides a very streamlined experience, without a lot of the typical drudgery that goes along with games like this.
- First of all, the game itself is very intuitive to pick up and start playing without needing a tutorial. The interface is mouse-driven, no need to memorize keybinds (although it does offer fully customizable keybinds as well).
- The game seem to understand that the appeal of games like this is both the satisfaction of level progression, as well as the hunt for rare loot. Early on, you get an item that can recycle junk loot into gold, as well as a item with unlimited charges that basically provides a Town Portal effect that teleports you out of the current dungeon. This eliminates the trap that Bethesda games, for example, typically fall into, where you want to be a packrat and collect every piece of loot you come across, but are severely limited in the amount of weight you can carry.
- The game offers several difficulty levels, from unlimited lives, to several lives, to permadeath.
- The game has an "auto-explore" button, where your character will automatically move around the current dungeon floor until it finds an item of interest or an enemy. Movement can also be control via clicking on visible locations, and your character will move to the select square.
