While a bit Short, Rage is a fairly solid gaming experience, with an ending that may come sooner than many were anticipating. With most of the side quests and most of the driving completed, I was still able to finish this in just under 30 hours. That said, I didn't bother with acheivments or the DLC (yet). However, for the price I paid ($10), it was worth the time spent.
The Positives:
Solid graphics
Generally free of bugs
Fun once I got into the gameplay.
Solid (albeit predictable) combat AI.
Decent item construction option, Although most items felt largely unneccessary at normal difficulty.
Attractive female NPCs. Ginny is mine. :D
The Negatives:
Little or no character development
Unengaging story/NPCs. Lacks much needed lore/backstory.
Typical weopens. Many of which feel overpowered. Honestly, you can get by with just the pistol and scope outside of a couple boss encounters. (A little advice: skip using the overpowered pulse rifle at the end)
Small, fishbowl type world. Extremely linear, and lacks a map feature.
A ton of fetch quests.
Mediocre driving mechanics with the keyboard and mouse.
Abrupt, unsatisfying ending. Despite nearly 30 hours, it makes the game feel short. Needed an epilogue.
While that does sound like a ton of negatives. it is a fun game. Just nothing you will likely be replaying. It lacks depth, character development, and varying styles of play. You're dumped into a scenario, told what to do and expected to do it without question. When the end comes, many like myself will undoubtedly feel a bit unsatisfied. It's like they ran out of the money needed to do a proper ending. Click--Done.
That said, I certainly recommend it at the right price.

EDIT: Ok, so my buddy figured out how to get it to work, I'm pasting his info down here for anyone who found they had the same issues I had:
RAGE Step 1
Creating cache file:
Enable invisible files to see Appdata, then go to:
C:\Users\UserName\AppData\Local\ create a folder called id software , new folder called rage.(C:\Users\UserName\AppData\Local\id software\rage).
Step 2 Ingame
Antialiasing: dont use 16x, it blurs the image, without AA wires looks bad or you cant even see it.
Vsync:off/on/smart, smart doesnt drop your fps to 30 when you cant maintain 60 fps and when it happens there is a chance to see screen tear.With off I have strong screentear when I look at the floor and move.
Texture Cache: set this allways to large,otherwise You will see texture "pop-in" streaming constantly with delay and lower quality textures also.Needs VRAM.After You enable 16k textures later on you will see small here displayed, but dont bother with that.
Texture Detail:Can affect fps a lot, also makes the game looking terrible and unnatural at close-mid range,long range textures are already unmatched dont need this.(rocks and road might look better for someone, but everything else is ugly, even the baked shadows)Experiencing huge fps drop with 16k textures or pop-in? disable this feature.
Anisotropic filter: keep at High or low, read below for more details
GPU transcode: this works only with Geforce cards with cuda,this helps to stream textures faster (faster GPU,faster streaming) otherwise CPU will stream the virtual textures.Can affect fps with weaker cards.Well this is pretty useless in someway.This option was made for geforce users with slow CPU back in the time I guess(remember long development time for RAGE), no wonder the newer Idtech5 games doesnt have it in the options(however could be enabled as hidden feature for both card manufacturer, but havent found any proof about this).We can play RAGE without texture pop-in with any CPU + any kind of VGA, it just matter of tweaks.64bit RAGE doesnt support gpu transcode, however cpu "transcode" is 1.5x faster.I set it off even if I have geforce.(measured by inbuilt benchmark)
Step 3 Go into Steam Properties and you can add Launch parameters (right click, properties, button in there about Launch Parameters):
Launch parameters:
+com_skipIntroVideo 1 +logfile 0 +fc_maxcachememoryMB 1024
these:skips the intro,reduce the loading times for 64bit,and use 1GB cache memory once you create the cache folder as well

Worse, is the fact that all those adverts suggesting that the game was littered with epic fights against these huge monsters, was in fact only ONE epic fight against ONE monster at the end of ONE particular quest. You always seem on the verge of getting caught, noticed, or accidentally killed by its random actions until you finally encounter him at the end and are forced to fight. Well, I guess it serves me right.
I read all the reviews... mostly good, but some bad.  And the ones that were bad were really pretty bad.  Some examples are:
- Bad optimization, so gameplay is laggy
- MAJOR crash issues for a significant number of people
- Severe graphical glitches that make the game completely unplayable
- Big time cheating and client sync issues in multiplayer
But, I really digs me some sniper action, so I went ahead & disregarded those warnings because I thought "Hell, I got a kickass pc that blows the recommended specs outta the water!  Maybe I wont be one of those guys that has those issues".
Riiiight.
<sigh>
Soon as I booted it up for the first time, I found out exactly what that whole "graphical glitch" thing looked like.  Just as everyone described; invisible characters, floating guns, and giant artifacts that take up most of the screen.  Surprisingly, I found a "workaround" for the problem.  Notice I didn't say a FIX for the problem.  No, it wont fix the issue, but I found out that if you cheat the video settings a bit, you can get the glitch to MOSTLY go away (still pops up here & there).
Alright, so now that's outta the way, should be good to go, right?
Riiiight.
<sigh>
About 2 mins into the game, right about the time you juuust start to finish that whole hand-holding "tutorial" kinda part at the beginning of the first mission....  "Sniper: Ghost Warrior 2 has stopped working".
OK, that's weird..  well lets boot 'er back up & get back into this thing!
Riiight.
<sigh>
Needless to say, I got to experience first hand the same crash issues that everyone else had talked about.  Happens randomly,  generally right when an insignificant action has taken place... like when you shoot a guy.  Cause, you know, you only do THAT once or twice a game, right?
Well, in my stubbornness, I continued to try & power through it, hoping that it would eventually go away & I would somehow get to enjoy me some good 'ol snipey action....  and I looked for solutions all over the place and tried different things, until finally I simply couldn't take it any more.  TWO HOURS I tried.  Loading the game OVER & OVER & OVER.  And every time I got going, for no reason (other than... you know... shooting a guy) it crashed every time.
SO, all I can hope at this point is that you will not be the stubborn dupe that I was, and you'll resist the urge to disregard the warnings as I did.  And that you will look elsewhere to satisfy that itch in your finger for some sniper action.  Cause let me tell you... the only itch that this game covers is the itch to bash your face into your keyboard.

However, one issue I did encounter was when I loaded up the game for the first time, my vision was blocked by strange squares on the characters. This was thankfully fixable, which if I recall correctly was done by changing from DX 11 to DX 9 shaders of all things. That's the only graphical bug I can think of actually encountering in my time of play. I will say there was a point where I thought I would have to restart a mission due to Diaz getting stuck, but continuing to the next area got him moving again. Rift is, in a sentence, the best hardcore fantasy MMORPG on the market. It's challenging, artistically stunning, and offers everything you could want in your hardcore MMORPG experience. The diversity of the soul system ensures that your character is never pidgeonholed into a single role; Clerics of other MMORPGS might be restricted to healing, but in Rift, they can heal, DPS, and tank if they so desire. The only thing your character is restricted to is a "calling," but within each "calling" are 9 classes, and at any given time, you can multi-class up to three of them. While it has little to offer in the way of players who enjoy casual or fluff gaming, Rift is truly the #1 hardcore MMORPG of this decade.

Pros: Easy to pick up and learn; has many similarities with other popular MMOs. You can change servers and recustomize your character (Excluding gender / race change) without having to pay real money. Changing servers is free, but recustomizing your character is expensive. (In game currency.)
-Only 4 classes, but many different souls (Specializations) to choose from, and can have 3 souls active at a time. You can play your character however you want to.
-PvP is fun in my opinion. Kind of reminds me of Unreal Tournament / Quake in the sense that it has an announcer that will announce events. "First Blood" "Killing Spree" "Unstoppable" etc. I found that pretty cool.
-Has an in-game video recorder, which is a first for MMOs. However, it does not record sound last I checked. Not for me anyway.
-UI Customization is good, you aren't too limited in that regard.
-Average playerbase is usually friendly and helpful.
-Can be played even on very bad computers. (Obviously your experience may not be ideal, but you should generally be able to play the game.)
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Cons: Only 6 races. 3 per faction. 4 of which are literally copy, pasted, and reskinned. There are only 2 unique races. Bahmi and Dwarves.
-Game is not incredibly populated.
-Only a few servers that I know of that have a decent playerbase, the rest are dead. For lack of a better word, the questing is, what I'd call, corridor questing. There aren't multiple same-level zones to choose from, should you decide you don't want to play in a certain. You have to level in a line of questing areas. No choice.
(No more cons come to mind at the moment.)
------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
There's more that can be said, but overall I enjoyed the game. It's certainly not bad by any means. It'd be better if it was more popular and had at least 1 more race for each faction that wasn't copy / pasted. If you get this game, it's certainly not a bad idea to bring a friend. I'd give this game a 7/10. It is subscription based. $15 per month. With new accounts, when you subscribe and set up a payment plan, your first month is free. (Your monthly billing will begin on the second month.)

Cuphead stands out for it's 1930's cartoon art-style, something that really hasn't been done in this fashion with such great gameplay complementing it. They really went the extra mile with the detail, implementing minor things that could be considered flaws, like the characters having yellow gloves on the scoring screen, all for the sake of authenticity.
Like the art-style, the music is also great, juxtaposing the difficult boss fights with smooth jazz that gives the game so much charm that dying relentlessly isn't as rage-inducing as it otherwise might be.
Bosses are challenging and each has variety with some putting you in a plane, and all bosses can mix up parts of their phases so that it isn't just about learning their patterns so much as it is about being prepared for every possible incoming attack. That keeps bosses feeling fresh, which goes along way if you plan on getting high grades.
Studio MDHR took extra time to make the game the best it could possibly be before releasing it. They added 'Run 'n Gun' which are essentially platforming levels where you can acquire coins to buy items to use against bosses. The games overworld map, full of NPC's add another level of charm to an already charming game, it's just a joy to explore.
I'm glad this game has gotten a lot of love, it absolutely deserves it, and it's one of the best indie titles I've played in recent years. Highly recommended; well worth the wait of its development, and well worth the asking price.

RAID: World War II is an ambitious game that is a spiritual successor to the Payday franchise.
I really enjoyed the beta when it was released and was looking forward to the full release very much with all the interesting features that it showcased. But sadly it is a pretty bland, grinding experience in comparrison to their previous games.
At this point I really can't reccommend this game, unless you fancy playing solo, because of points I will go into.
PRO
- Four interesting new characters
- Each class has a special ability unique to them
- Environment has things you can interact with such as mounted and AA guns
- Cards (not MT) give you strengths and weakness' on missions
- Customisable safehouse from the beginning
- Achievements and unlockables
- The game looks and feels nice, albeit optimisation could be a little better
- Missions are varied and not just robbing places. There are heists, assassinations, sabotage, defense and assaulting.
CON
- Game is dead on release. Payday 2, after 5 years, has over 32,000 current players and most of the time is on the top 10 list of whats being played on steam. While as of this moment RAID has 76.
- It feels a lot slower and more tedious than Payday and the hype isn't there
- Unlock progression is low, long and takes a lot of grinding
- Not much music to keep the moments alive (Far preferred electro music to wartime military marches)
- I know it's still early but there aren't a large variety of weapons (even after several updates there hasn't been a lot of additions, one or two guns and a grenade all of which don't seem to be all that great)
- Melee is pretty useless
- You don't automatically pick up ammo and health so many returning Payday players will have a little adjustment that can harm their experience (Little gripe)
- Stealth is hard and boring so loud is really the only way to go
- Enemy types have names that I can never remember (Small gripe I know but still its harder to identify them)
- Most of the enemies look the same so not clear on what their strengths and weakness' are (only one I can tell for certain is the flamer  because of the hulking armour and flamethrower)
- Since hardly anyone is playing you need to have at least one friend to go through the levels with
- the only updates that seem to come out recently are notication of dev streams, art competitions and minor fixes. There is a new silo level coming soon but it's too late for one level to save the game.
The thing that really bugs me the most about the game though is that after only TWO MONTHS of release it's already 75% off and is going for £7.74. Kind of a kick in the teeth to the people who paid full price for regular or special editions of the game.
As of this point I really can't reccommend it because of the sheer boredom of solo, long grindy sessions and dead playerbase. 4/10

All in all, it's somewhat like PD2 and PDTH had a child that kinda went off on their own to be different. There's a ton of improvements here and there (being able to equip your melee, much more engaging and well, skill-based lockpicking, enemies that aren't quite as braindead as the ones in PD2 etc), if play this game expecting something along the lines of a AAA take on payday 2 set in WW2, you'll be disappointed.
That being said, the game is essentially like payday 2 but it plays differently in a few ways (IMO more-so on the lines of PDTH, can be good/bad), as a whole if you enjoy payday 2 and/or payday the heist, you will enjoy this game a lot. Gunplay feels akin to payday 2's gunplay rather than PDTH (which IMO is a good thing - PDTH's gunplay felt.... light? more-so weightless), all in all I recommend this game to anyone that has in the past played PD2/PDTH or anyone who knows what to expect. You have to remember, this is a studio that has literally existed for like 2 years and whilst yes, they work closely with overkill, it doesn't necessarily mean they 'are' overkill. They're a small studio and this is their first ever game made as that studio, you can't expect AAA-tier graphics or, anything else AAA-tier really.
Regardless, a few negatives to take into mind.
Enemy skins are quite lacking, not in the literal manner of how they look but there's not all that many enemy skins, and since they're all unmasked it's a little weird seeing the same face countless times in one single raid.
Optimization. This is something I knew would be an issue since well, Diesel engine (before someone points out something like 'lol diesel engine in 2017', again, they're a new studio and this is their first game as that studio. Making a game on a new engine would be virtually suicide), all in all it's 'okay', better than I expected honestly but it needs work without a doubt.
Weapons. I feel like there needs to be more of them and IMO there needs to be more upgrades. Some weapons have very few upgrades and as a whole it makes it feel linear, the selection of weapons on launch is pretty good but I feel it could do with for instance a couple more bolt-action rifles, a couple more weapons akin to the M1 Garand etc, just more variety. Another thing, some weapon sounds are very dull, they just don't sound 'beefy' enough though I figure this'll be something that'll change at some point since quite a lot of people seem to share the same opinion.
Aside from that, there's a ton of positives compared to payday 2, the fact weapons and skills and even weapon unlocks are class-bound makes it like what I imagine overkill intended payday 2 to be like (rather than everyone running meta, using effectively the same builds), weapon unlocks are based per-class (e.g. assault unlocks rifles faster, recon(?) unlocks bolt-action snipers faster etc) which I thought was a nifty little change. Furthermore the things I mentioned prior, how you equip grenades instead of just throwing them (allowing quick spamming of grenades, avoiding the 'oh♥♥♥♥♥♥ moment when you accidentally throw a nade in stealth etc) and lockpicking is IMO one of the best changes. PD2's lockpicking was just so bland, no matter how good you were you quite literally couldn't make lockpicking any faster, it takes something that was incredibly bland and made it well, engaging. Levels visually IMO look much nicer than PD2's maps but this may just be bias speaking since I've spent a ♥♥♥♥load of time looking at the same maps.
TL;DR: It's like PD2 and PDTH had a child that veered off in it's own path with a lot of changes here and there that make it better than both games in different aspecs. If you like PD2/PDTH, you'll like this game.

This is hands down one of my favourite tower defence games of all time. Everything about it is on point. Mechanics are good, with lots of varied tower types, and many different aliens, the stages are also quite varied in design, within the limitation of the game mechanics. Graphics and sound are quite good, yet still playable on my tablet (Atom Z3775-based).
Which brings me to another point: it has touch support, and suffers little for it. Not quite as accurate as a mouse, which does result in some accidents, but it's mostly a matter of getting used to it.
The voice acted story is excellent, both in terms of voice acting quality, and writing. It was a particularly nice element of this game, actually. The player's AI ally is amusing and endearing, while also delivering the game's "tutorial" elements.
The gameplay is addicting, and the difficulty is fair, which led me to 100-percenting this game's achievements. Replay value is decent as well, with multiple strategies working well enough to pass most levels.
The only thing that feels "off" is the degree to which some towers are either useless in a given level, or basically mandatory. Missile towers in particular, and the flying enemies they shoot down, seem like they're only in the game to be a backdoor means of draining resources away from your other defences. This is easily the oldest Tower Defense on Steam, and is probably a bit of an obvious first choice for talking about them. But it's an obvious one for good reason, as Defense Grid is one of the best of them on Steam even being eight years old at this point. The premise is simple enough: aliens have invaded earth and are spreading chaos and destruction to...do something, they never really get around to saying what. Your player, an unnamed civilian, manages to escape the onslaught and reactivate an ancient defense system, as well as the AI operating it, the mind of the late General Fletcher. He serves as your mission control, and is pleasant enough to listen to even though it doesn't take very long to hear every line he has.
Together you set about using the grid to defend against the alien attacks, since the cores powering it are a far more appealing target for them than the Earth's population. Every level aliens will try to make their way to the terminal housing them. That's where things get complicated, as rather than taking health off you immediately, if one makes it there they'll grab up to 3 cores before turning around and trying to make off with them, either out where they came in or on a different path entirely. Kill it and the core will drop and float back toward the housing, but this also means another alien can pick it up themselves. Ideally this means you don't want them making it to the core at all, but in many instances this isn't possible, creating a tug of war.
You have quite a few tools to deal with this, of course, as you have all the usual tower types: the fast, low damage Gun tower, the high damage, slow Cannon tower, three different area of effect towers, and more. The campaign is 20 stages long and unlocks them at a good enough pace to keep letting you use new things. Every stage also has a great variety of places you can put them, too, and it's often crucial to alter the alien's path as much as possible, as the aliens have a lot of tricks of their own. Past the first ordinary enemy, there are extra-durable ones, extra-quick ones, ones shielded from most towers, and stealthy ones that won't ordinarily be targeted at long range are just some of the ones they'll throw at you. There are also bosses, and combinations of all of these can be pretty taxing at times. Luckily Defense Grid has what I wish other games in the genre would crib, a checkpoint system. If you mess up in a level you can simply go back a bit in the level and be more prepared, instead of doing the whole thing over again.
The game's campaign is easily enough to get your money's worth full price, and especially on a sale, but each level also has a bunch of alternate versions to it with various conditions, like not being able to upgrade your towers. If you want to give those a try you could easily spend a ton of hours watching aliens march to their doom. There are also the Containment and You Monster DLCs, which feature smaller campaigns (the latter of which swaps in Fletcher for none other than Portal's GLaDoS), and four map packs that contain two stages each. So for content, and good content at that, you can't really beat this game. To top it all off, every different level and variant on it has a scoring system to it, allowing a conservative player to compete with others. I haven't played the sequel to the game, but I've heard it's a bit lack-luster in comparison, which is a shame, since Hidden Path pulled it off so well here.

WARNING: NOT FOR THE WEAK
Tales of Maj'Eyal is an epic fantasy roguelike in a Tolkienesque universe in which your mighty heroes will die in great heaping mounds, alone and unremembered, and there's nothing you can do about it. While there IS a mode which allows infinite respawns, it rather defeats the point of the game, which is twofold:
1.) Death is permanant.
2.) Every world is randomly generated and different. (Within certain parameters, obviously. The Wood Elf's always gonna start in a randomly generated forest area and the Dwarf's always going to start in a randomly generated cave. This is because even the people who made this game realize that it would be a bit absurd to face down a level 1068 demon from hell when you start out in your underpants with a weapon stolen from the toy shop.)
Poor Jimmy the Dwarf Warrior never even made it out of the starter cave. But Mahariel, the Elf Archer chick I've  been running lately has consistently lived over an hour. This might sound a bit frustrating, but it also lends a fresh air of discovery everytime you play. And in that sense, it's probably the standard that all Fantasy RPGs should be held to. Not just indie ten dollar or less titles, but the big A-Listers like Elder Scrolls, Dragon Age, and the like. (If things feel mundane in a FANTASY game, something has gone terribly, terribly wrong.) With minimalist graphics and a shoestring budget, Tales of Maj'Eyal manages to remain engrossing and compelling throughout with evocative music and little smatterings of lore, alongside gameplay that rejects the handholding most games these days embrace. ToME does not hold your hand. It punches you in the testicles. That said, no game is perfect, so here is my criticism.
One of the general problems with the old school/minimalist vibe they're going for is that your character never really has their place in the world defined. You're just sort of there, playing around in this big sandbox with no real connections to it. You never have an uncle or a sister or a friend or whatever that serves as an anchor. The closest thing you get to party members are ineffective, personality-devoid asshats you have to escort to exit zones in repetitive sidequests you'll never pass up because the rewards are too damned good to turn down. But interpersonal interaction? Forget it. NPCs are just like "Hey ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, go do this for the XP and bonuses so you can do slightly harder stuff for the next ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥," and you're like "sure" and that's that. You just run around going on quests, killing stuff and getting loot because that's how pimps roll, I guess. Of course, one or two half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥excuses aside, Skyrim isn't much better in this regard, so I suppose it might not be fair to blame the presentation for this.
The thing is, with all this lore and stuff they dangle in front of your nose, explaining the truth behind the Orc genocide or the politics behind the human-halfling alliance, or the hatreds between the two elven peoples, the fact that none of it really has to do with your interactions with other people, who serve only as quest givers or static decoration, really gives one the off-putting feeling that you have shown up to a party five minutes after it ended.
Ultimately, the main character of the game is the world of Maj'Eyal itself and your interaction with it, and it is a compelling world which will be new everytime you play it. The immersive vibe you get from exploring a new bit of dark wilderness or dungeon with moody music playing in the background is excellent, and the lore documents encompass sad, hilarious, and terrifying without skipping a beat. It is a shame that the epic immersion Maj'Eyal offers is strained by the two-dimensional clods who inhabit it, but hey, it's a Roguelike, what were you expecting, War and Peace? Just get the damned game.

The story may be a bit bland (I have the feeling some parts of the story were just cut :/ ), but the characters are well designed. Each different faction has its own theme and culture ( 'fighting style' ), sadly you only come into contact with them once, one mission in their base camp and never to be heard of again.. except when some side quest sends you to the same area twice and it's inhabited with a different 'faction'.
This game isn't an rpg.. it's not your storytelling game that keeps you glued to your screen, but it is an amazing shooter. The weapons feel like actual weapons that pack a punch, the enemies have great animations (especially the melee ones that jump around like freaking ninjas and are sometimes a pain to hit), great level design, you take a break from the shooting to travel through this beautiful wasteland or join some races/minigames.
I wish this game had a larger world to travel through, more story, more quests,... You don't have a world map which makes the world feel big at first, but after awhile you know it already by heart. But this doesn't keep me from recommending this game to you! If you stick your head up against a wall and want to see crisp textures, this isn't the game for you. If you appreciate beautiful, unique scenery and fun gameplay you will appreciate this game!

Plug & Play is delightfully bizarre in ways that are as unsettling as they are endearing.
The playfulness of the vignettes that seem so mix matched and nonsensical trace intimate analogies into a collage of weirdness. It’s pulling from the darkest areas of failed relationships - denied feelings, refusal to communicate, meaningless sex to avoid complicated questions - but in ways that feel hopeful more than pessimistic. Plug & Play isn’t  about something falling apart, but learning to pick yourself up when things don’t work out.
I don’t know that I’d consider it especially adept or subtle in how it goes about this, but its sincere commitment to say something important while painting an amusingly offbeat, sex obsessed world is consistently entertaining and surprisingly considered. It might look like madness from the outside, and it is to a point, but it’s madness with a purpose but which also doesn’t get so caught up in showing how much life can suck that it forgets it can also be pretty fun sometimes.

Only played a few missions so far, but from my experience this game is pretty decent.
If you go into this game thinking its Payday 2, you're going to be disappointed.  It's NOT Payday 2.  There are surely some elements of it that are similar to Payday, but certainly not the same game in a WWII genre.  If you go into it comfortable with seeing some Payday aspects but realizing its a completely different experience, you'll probably like the game a whole lot more.
It has the same 4 player squad type play, doing missions that you can either go loud or stealth.  But the weaponry, perks, weapon modding, and all that are different.  Like I said, if you have an open mind and like this genre of games, you'll probably be pretty happy with the game.

RAID: WWII is a fun co-op experience, that is a bit rough around the edges. Things you should know going in, it runs on an outdated engine with performance and visual issues. This is the same engine that PAYDAY 2 runs on. In fact, this game takes quite a lot from PAYDAY 2, being made by Lion Game Lion, a company with close ties to PAYDAY 2's creators.
If you have played PAYDAY 2, you'll know how the general movement, weight and quirkiness of this game will feel. And while there are other similarities, such as objective types or gameplay elements, RAID has quite a lot to offer that PAYDAY 2 does not.
The gunplay is solid, weapons feel like they have kick and deal the damage they ought to. There are currently 15 firearms available, many of which are unlocked at later character levels, with more on the way in future content updates.
The level design is on point, with solid cover and creative objectives, that can vary based on player actions or randomly on different playthroughs. For instance, choosing to quietly sneak your way through the map and complete objectives, while difficult, will often pay out in the form of making your life easier later into the map.
The characters are fun, and well voice acted. They chatter with eachother quite a bit (this can be muted if one desires), and will point out objectives and items of interest aloud to other characters, and thus players, in game.
The loot is the most interesting aspect of the game to me. A random loot drop occurs at the end of every successful mission, and will grant more desirable rewards such as big experience bonuses or cosmetics provided the players collect enough "dog tags" throughout the game. These are found strewn across most maps, hidden out of sight.
This also goes for gold, which can be found and collected through most maps. After enough gold is collected, the player is rewarded a Gold Bar, currency used for cosmetic upgrades to the player's appearence and base of operation.
Occasionally players will find intel in a map, which unlocks an Outlaw Raid. These raids are designed specifically to earn the players gold, rewarding 20+ gold bars to players based on how much loot they secure during the raid. Joining the RAID: WWII steam group also grants the player 100 gold bars. The currency is exclusively kept to cosmetic additions in game. RAID: WWII does not and will not, according to the developers, have microtransactions.
Overall, it is a fun co-op shooter to play with friends. If you are going to be flying solo, or skeptical of the price point, perhaps wait for a sale. If you're a fan of PAYDAY 2, I'd recommend giving this game a shot.
(PS: I did NOT receive the game for free as many people seem to think. I paid full price for the special edition.)

Assassin's Creed 2 is my favorite game in the series to date, and the absolute crown gem when it comes to the series' best gimmick - throwing you into beautiful, well-researched historical worlds and just letting you do whatever you want with them.
Premise: Desmond Miles is being held captive by the Templars! Early in the game, he escapes with the help of their mortal enemies, the Assassins. To join the Assassins, Desmond trains by reliving the memories of one of his ancestors, Ezio. Ezio is an Italian living in the 15th century Renaissance. He is drawn into the life of the Assassins in order to discover the perpetrators of a political plot that threatens his family. Along the way, he assassinates dozens of people, and leaps off a lot of towers.
The Good: Almost any bad thing you could say about the first game in this series, AC2 cleans up pretty nicely. The sometimes awkward exposition and cutscenes of 1 are replaced by a sleek, modern story with high-quality cutscenes. The story is paced much better. The controls are simpler. Meanwhile, the strong points of 1 are even stronger here. Ezio is probably my favorite Assassin of the series, transitioning from a fun-loving Aladdin expy to a brilliant, manipulative and powerful one man army out for revenge on the Templar order. Ezio's family and friends are also fun and likeable, including a pretty unusual take on Leonardo da Vinci. It is easy to switch between playing the excellent main storyline and just tooling around Venice doing random sidequests and challenges. The side missions are very fun, but they also don't feel like forced side missions - if you aren't feeling them right now, you can come back to them later or not at all without any consequences. My favorite part of the game is the beautiful recreation of the cities. If you're anything like me, you could enjoy yourself a lot just running around without even doing anything. Most games in a setting like this feel like games in a setting - but I came away from this feeling a bit like I had honestly been to Italy and absorbed a little culture. This is the best roguelike on steam. Strikes a perfect balance between usability/user friendliness with depth and complexity. I'll review this game by highlighting what I think sets it apart from other games in the genre.
- TOME doesn't have potions, scrolls, or wands. You choose a limited number of abilities that give you the function that consumables play in other games - quick heal, regen, teleport, blink, fireball, etc. This eliminates the issues lots of people have with hoarding consumables, not knowing when to use them, the pain of having them destroyed, etc. Picking and choosing the right abilities adds a layer of depth that doesn't exist in other roguelikes.
- this game plays lightning fast and is very streamlined, thanks to the lack of consumables. Of course, it's turn based, so it's only as fast as you want...but I tend to play pretty fast, and lots of roguelikes feel sluggish in comparison.
- Lots of classes, from your standard mage and warrior to the cool weird things like Chronomancers and Wyrmics (dragon-fighters).
- The different classes feel distinct. In addition to the obvious (different skills and equipment), different types of classes have different types of resources (mana/stamina/equilibrium/hate/probably some other ones) that work in different ways.
- This is the only roguelike I've played where melee combat is actually fun. You get lots of buttons to push that do different things. In most roguelikes, the coolest thing about your melee character is the equipment you find. In TOME, you can actually do cool♥♥♥♥♥♥- charge, shout, whirlwinds, cleaves, etc.
- This doesn't mean easy and it doesn't mean shallow - it just means simple. Clean, streamlined design. The action bar is great - every option your character has is on it, so you always know what you can and can't do. No navigating labyrinthine menus, no checking your inventory after you died and remembering you could have used your blink, etc.
- Like ADOM and not like Crawl, TOME features a static overworld that's always the same and features the same dungeons/locations, which are themselves randomized. This isn't necessarily better or worse, just putting it out there.
This game is an absolute blast. If you liked Dungeons of Dreadmor, you owe it to yourself to take a step up to a more serious and more interesting game. :)

The break-out tower defence game that helped bring the genre into mainstream gaming, Defense Grid is still a stand-out example of TD done right. A clean interface and (relatively) smooth difficulty curve with a fiendish top-end make it an excellent introduction while ensuring perfectionists and score-chasers have an expansive leaderboard to climb as well. A combination of deeper mechanics such as interest-based resource generation and varying field-of-fire interactions across towers ensures things stay interesting for at least the duration of the campaign, and for those of us that get sucked in by a good system, a good many hours after its complete. Still worth the asking price nearly a decade from release, pick it up and give it a shot if your curiosity is piqued by the store page.

Rage Review.
I just beat the game a few minutes ago and my first initial reaction was...was that it? I beat the game and most side quests in about 12 hours and was left feeling like the game ended in act 2 when it should have had at least 4 acts, if that makes any sense. This review contains minor spoilers.
Overall storyline was a 5 out of 10. Definitely a fail. I didn't feel invested to any of the characters or even the faction I was fighting for, the Resistence.
Vehicle Combat again a 5 out of 10. It was horrible but it wasn't overly fun.  Very basic driving, and it felt like a mechanic that was added to the game just for a bit of filler.
Ground Combat 7 out of 10. The game does  a bit better here. At times the combat turned towards a very Serious Sam type feel as hordes of enemies bear down on you, which I've never been crazy about. The AI of the combat is poor and the only challenging parts of the ground combat was when they put hordes of enemy against you in a very close room, otherwise all other enemies could be fought every easily by simly moving backwards and having the enemies come to you.
Weapons 7 out of 10. Very basic weapons. The upgrades for the weapons were nice but not enough of them. The customized ammo was a nice addition but I felt like their could have big a bigger variety instead of just more powerful bullets (essentially). No weapon in particular stuck out as being really cool. They do have a mind control weapon but IMO they messed it up and it's not very fun with limited effectiveness.
Quests 6 out of 10. The have a very repetetive feel to it.  Quests didn't endear me towards certain characters.
Graphics  6-7 out of 10. When you think of this game, think Borderlands Graphics. Everything looks semi-painted on the screen and while I wouldn't give Borderlands a lower rating I would this game.  Borderlands has a very unique atmosphere, it has some very beatiful landscapes that add a sense of mystery to the game.  Rage for all it's painted landscapes doesn't offer anything really unique. And because effort wasn't put into making this stand out with interesting textures it gets a lower rating.
Other thoughts The game is incredibly linear. If you want to explore a new area, you pretty much need to quest to be able to interact with the environment. The game feels very similar to Borderlands without the funny jokes or interesting landscapes. Overall the game felt rushed, linear and very short.
Overall I'd rate the game a generous 6 out of 10.

Sanctum is an excellent blend of coop FPS and tower defense, with very good music and and excellent visuals, using a predominantly white color palette that sets it apart from most games. It's easy to pick up, enemy behaviors are clearly explained and the towers helpfully indicate their attack radius even before they are actually placed. The weapons in particular are very enjoyable to use, particularly the tesla rifle. The game's sound quality shows in said weapons: the shotgun makes a very satisfying bang, and it has a lovely animation in its telescoping barrel and heat-dispersing fins. You have the ability to switch away from a reloading weapon to a ready one without interupting the reload, an ability you will need to make use of often in later waves. Much like in other tower defense games, money is extremely limited and you will frequently have to juggle placing new towers, upgrading existing ones, and upgrading your own weapons, though I found that erring on the side of your own abilities often pays off, as in Orcs Must Die. The map layouts are interesting but at times haphazard, and Whirlpool, the map that won a user submission contest, has an absurd difficulty curve- I could not complete it even on easy, and I glided through it up until about wave 19, when it decided to drown me in a tide of Runners and Soakers, the latter being the most annoying enemies in the game. However, the multiplayer experince is quite solid, and adds the useful feature of sharing money between players. Whirlpool aside, this is a great game, and a bargain for its price considering the sheer time it took me to play each map at least once. It's by far one of my favorite tower defense games, a genre not always known for quality gameplay.

This game caught my eye a while back, but I put off buying it for some time. I see metroidvania games and they're usually alright, but not that satisfying. Well this seems to be the exception. Best game I've played in months.
The combat system is so close to Dark Souls that it'd be easier to list the differences than similarities, but it's not nearly as unforgiving as FROMSOFTWARE's series. And the map just keeps on going. I think this is the only game other than Symphony of Night where I felt like i was in danger of getting lost.
Anyway, it's fun and not nearly as frustrating as the dark souls games. There's lots of weapons and spells, but not quite as many as dark souls. The bosses seem to be a little on the easy side too, although I haven't finished it yet so I might be saying that too soon. Still, best metroidvania I've played since the 90s.

I'm no expert at games like this, and obviously I haven't put that many hours into the game yet since I just got it. However, I will try to explain why I fell in love with this game at first sight (from an analytical point of view).
: I'll be honest, I was reluctant to buy this at first simply due to the price and even found myself regretting the decision once I opened up that CC menu, but it was indeed worth it and I'll explain why later.
At first glance this game doesn't look like much. Just another dumb 2d flash game, right? That's what I thought. The first time I loaded up the game as a knight I wasn't expecting the damn near perfect swinging animations from my sword. Almost every good thing about this game took me by surprise. I was blown away by the amount of production value and time and effort that's just so apparent in every corner in the first few starting areas.

The combat is lovely and fluid and beautiful. It's everything I could ask for in a hack and slash rpg because unlike in Dark Souls you can perform Air Combos and finish off with a powerful downward strike which obliterates your enemies into a mesmerizing spray of red liquid. The enemy/boss ai works well to keep you on your toes and wastes no time punishing your mistakes and trying to put you in inconvenient positions. I got ♥♥♥♥ed up several times by The Sodden Knight (First boss)
yet, had I known that you could roll that probably wouldn't have happened quite as much.
Verticality is a must in 2d plat formers like SaS and it goes all out with the vast amount of detail packed into every area and the subtle creaks and croaks of old, moldy wood as you step on a board that may even give away underneath you due to pressure. The pick ups and drops are all easily attainable and don't divide into the action too much with long, tedious 'bend-over' animations. For once the developers decided to make it less of a fetching task to retrieve your lost currency (in this case 'Salt') in a Souls game. And, they did it by making a beast out of your salt which you have to kill every time you want to get your salt back. Otherwise, if you die again, as suspected, you permanently lose those piles of salt you worked so hard to attain and have to start all over from 0. Luckily to retrieve salt from a boss you don't have to kill him all the way. Just take his health down to a certain point.
Sound is a wonderful thing in this game, any game for that matter. It adds to the authenticity of being able to imagine these places. Hearing things adds levels of atmosphere to a setting. The rapid splashes of rain and mist and the sound of wind blowing through grassy fields gives the game that flavour; sells the vibe. I can't wait to get back into the world every time I hear that, it's amazing.
The music on the otherhand, even if there's little of it, is pretty good. Although it's very minimalist music, the background ost does well to add some tension throughout the areas you encounter. The boss fights are all made very epic with the addition of those fantastic chords. I believe there are like 2 boss fight tracks and 2 background tracks: In total 4 songs which shouldn't be too much of a problem given that the rest of the game is a masterpiece.
Last but not least we have the visuals. As I mentioned before, the visual effects of the blood spraying look absolutely mesmerizing. Some other visually stunning achievements would be the heat distortion near the torch flames and what not. It's always the little things like that which get my attention. Also, despite the mildy childish and cartoonish look of the world and it's characters, there is a certain level of realism to it all and I've come to like that a lot about it. Especially in the darkest areas is where the game's art direction can really stand out. It's so unique and interesting.
All in all this game is great because it was made well. A couple of glances on the surface don't mean much with gameplay this brilliant it will definitely have you hooked for hours no matter what your experience with rpg's is. I did my best to try and avoid references to Dark Souls and the like. Now I should probably stop typing because I've been typing this review for about an hour and a half now and I have exams.
If you ever wanted to play any of the dark souls games but wanted the game to be 2-D well look no further then this game.

Hotline Miami left quite a mark on the indie scene when it came out and so it's no surprise that it spawned a number of imitators. 12 Is Better Than 6 is one of them and arguably one of the better ones. It's remarkable how closely the core gameplay loop resembles Hotline Miami even if its setting and art style are wildly different. It's still top-down but everything is in black and white, almost like it was drawn on paper. It's a bit of an acquired taste in that regard and one can certainly argue whether that is simply minimalistic or merely lazy.
Set in the second half of the 19th century on America's untamed frontier; a classic western setting. You play as The Mexican, an infamous gunslinger who starts the game escaping from the law. That's what you do most of the time: shoot loads of bad guys. Combat is fast and deadly. Both you and your enemies die with a single bullet. Given that you are also hopelessly outnumbered on every map, this makes a careful approach and smart positioning a necessity. You have a small arsenal of classic western firearms at your disposal: a six-shooter, a shotgun, a rifle and dynamite. Additionally a bow and a knife for silent kills. Unfortunately, there's not a whole lot of variety when it comes to enemies or maps, and it does tend to get repetitive after a while.
That's not the only downside, however. The dialogue is amateurish at best and the story is a mess. Plot threads and characters are picked up and dropped at seemingly random. When it doesn't drown in western clichés, including magical Native Americans, many times you will wonder what exactly the point of the last mission was.
Don't pick this game up expecting an enthralling narrative. Judging by the credits, the game was developed somewhere in eastern Europe. I don't know whether it's poorly translated or outright written by somebody whose grip on the English language is lacking but it has to be one of the two.
Recommended to fans of Hotline Miami and similar games. Everyone else should think twice.

Obvious comparisons will be drawn between 12 Is Better Than 6 and Hotline Miami – with its unrelenting, hedonistic disarray of bullets and blood and death, shot from the lofty heights of a bird’s eye view – yet it’s more than a Wild West-set duplicate. The top-down, “kill everyone” shooter has blasted its way out..
While Hotline Miami more often than not requires deft tactics to best its levels, there’s always scope to tear through them reliant solely on luck and ammunition. 12 Is Better Than 6 doesn’t allow such recklessness. For one, the bad guys don’t miss. Ever. Which means planning two, three and four moves ahead quickly becomes essential. So too does making each bullet count, as the game’s shooting mechanics dictate the need to reload your revolver after every shot fired. At first this frustrated me, but, after I got used to it, it felt right. The baddies may’ve been freakishly good at hunting me down, but it rarely felt unfair. If I cocked up and found myself splayed out on the dirt with hand drawn blood oozing from my gaping wounds, that was on me.
“Wield the authentic weaponry: revolvers, guns, bows, knives, pitchforks and even ordnance,” reads the blurb for the game that scraped through a successful Kickstarter campaign with some eleventh hour high drama (a bunch of backers pulled out at the last minute, dropping its goal below its ask that it eventually made back up). “Rob trains, protect the innocents, collude with Sheriffs, and eradicate the gangs … Step into the dirty, lawless and cruel world of the North America land, 1873.”
Hang on a minute, that’s the same year ol’ RPS was founded. There’s only one winner there, pardner.

The Assassin’s Creed franchise is almost dead and buried at this point to some, but for me, a huge fan of the series, the franchises rest gives me a chance to go back and experience all the Assassin’s Creed games, before the eventual one to release next year in 2017. First, I started with Assassin’s Creed 2. I tried to get to part one, but for some reason it kept crashing every 15 minutes on my PC, and there was really nothing I could do that I didn’t already try. I do suggest however, that if you do go back to play the franchise, just stick with starting at AC2; AC1 is so far behind the technical curve of it’s sequels, that it feels like a PS1 era game compared to it’s contemporaries.
Assassin’s Creed 2 is often lauded as the best in the series and for good reason. After the simplistic and formulaic repetitiveness of Assassin’s Creed 1. AC2’s diversity is a breath of fresh air. And diverse missions and combat mechanics are the name of the game  in AC 2. However, there are some outstanding issues that have occurred in AC2 while I was playing, that is probably due to just the age of the game itself. First, when it comes to story, it’s great! Ezio’s story is engaging and often keeps you emotionally hooked, but I do have to say that I feel as far as Assassin stories go, I think Ubisoft got better at telling an Assassin's story as the series went along. My only problem with the story in AC 2 is that it tends to be exposition heavy, but what I do appreciate is that it does have some time for heartfelt moments. The other little nag is that the story overall raises far more questions than it answers. It’s a shame since everything about the lore is incredibly intriguing, but for it’s mysteries to be revealed in such a piecemeal manner (which is actually something the series becomes notorious for doing as it goes along) it tends to leave more of a pain to want to know just what the hell is going on. At last the reveal that comes near the end, while exciting and probably opens the series for amazing opportunities (opportunities that have seemingly been squandered in the sequels) is not entirely satisfying.
Now when it comes to graphics, the game is still a technical marvel. The environments and armors are so detailed that it makes them really feel real. Also another thing I’d like to bring up is the fact that people have started to complain recently that the series, in the more recent entries, has done all it can do to make it feel less like a real place and more like a game, but I’d quickly argue that AC2 feels like a game just as much as the others due to the fact that the Animus’ features cover up the screen in the same amount as the other later titles. Quickly, back to graphics, the game while still being beautiful in spots has terrible performance issues and some minor but irksome graphical glitches. When it comes to performance, it’s terrible across the board. Sometimes the game will drop below 60 to the 40’s for no apparent reason. I can output the game to 4k resolution and it still runs the same with the same inconsistent drops. It leads me to believe that it may be a CPU issue or something, but it is entirely annoying given that the game is pretty old. As for the graphical hitches, I fixed them with Nvidia Inspector which included better Anisotropic filtering, better VSync, and better anti-aliasing as all of the base features included in the game don’t work properly.
The gameplay loop of Assassin’s Creed is a kind of all over the place, since Ezio at this point for the next two titles isn’t as nearly as fast or agile as his successors it usually takes a while to reach place to place. This is  helped by the game providing horses and some minute way of fast travel. The fast travel works only if you go to a different city so it’s kind of useless and the horses unfortunately are only useful for the country sides. The good thing is that the horses are fast and not slow. However, if you come up near objects and obstacles you can slow down considerably as the game’s parkour system desperately tries to determine whether your horse is jumping off a cliff or jumping over a fence even when faced in front of the fence. Now when it comes to collectibles, it can be enjoyable since they are really easy to collect and are often in near proximity of each other, which makes the act of collecting them all into an activity that lasts for about 5-6 hours. However I’m glad that a couple of the future titles opted for a “kicking the chest to open” mechanic that makes treasure collecting far less tedious. The feathers are another collectible that you can’t find in a considerable amount of time without a guide, but also provide and emotional side activity. The feathers in AC 2 actually have meaning as Ezio’s mother who stops talking won’t communicate with her family. Ezio collects these feathers in hope that his mother changes. It’s a nice hook that gives collecting the things more meaning, something that the future entries fail to do.
The side missions are another part of the gameplay hook of Assassin’s Creed 2. They are enjoyable for the most part, but unfortunately ere on the side of repetitiveness a bit too soon, especially the assassination missions. In the main storyline the Assassination missions are quite diverse and unique, which set up a variety of ways to assassinate your foe, but the side missions which you collect from pigeon coops are not as consistent. There are some cool diverse situations, but unfortunately most of them turn into a simple run-to-this-location-and-then-assassinate-with-your-blade.
Is it the best game in the franchise? Yes and no, for the most part I think most people have rose-tinted glasses on when they compare the supposed “♥♥♥♥♥iness” of the future sequels with the greatness of AC2. AC2 is great, but the future games in the series eventually surpassed it on a gameplay level, and arguably on a story level. The one game I think that definitely improved from a combination of the two is AC 4. On a technical level AC2’s controls just pale in comparison with the other games. Recently in AC:Unity I actually felt that for the first time being an assassin was an actual viable option. In AC2 being an assassin usually comes down to dumb luck, at least from my experience. The soldiers FOV for instance just varies greatly. Sometimes I would jog to them and assassinate without a fuss, but other times when I’d jog to them they would turn around instantly and detect me in which would at times turn into an automatic desync, which is incredibly annoying, as the game pulls the camera out and shakes violently  in a way that almost feels like if it’s telling you, “You lost!, Stop you lost okay, Just shut up, you lost! Restart your checkpoint, you incompetent assassin!.”  While in my head I’m thinking, F**k you game, F**k you. It’s pretty safe to say that the game’s controls aren’t the best nor is it’s AI consistent. Thankfully these things aren’t incredibly annoying as to deter you from playing, but your mileage may vary depending on what kind of games you play.
When it comes to Assassin’s Creed 2, you can’t go wrong, you got a great story, detailed open-world, gameplay that is enjoyable, and a mythology to unravel. It may not be the best game in the franchise, but it’s pretty darn close. If you got $19 or better yet wait for a Steam sale, AC2 proves to still be an enjoyable experience that is still worth revisting.

Cogs is, in essence, a collection of 50(ish) sliding puzzles. WAIT, COME BACK HERE! It's also surprisingly fun and relatively varied.
Sliding puzzles are considered tedious because the aim usually is to reconstruct a picture, or a sequence of numbers, meaning every piece has to be at its exact place, and that may cause frustration. But here, you have to align cogs and pipes, and some of the tiles are definitely inter-changeable (with few exception a cog is the same as another cog), so that problem is considerably lowered in most puzzles. Variety comes from the shapes of the boards, the types of cogs or pipes present, the kind of contraption ultimately activated by all those trinkets, double faced boards, bells to ring... Cogs is quite effective at keeping your interest alive. And it must be, because the puzzles are clearly challenging.
Another nice touch, is that each of the 50 puzzles also has two variants, much shorter and easier but with additional constraints (one must be completed in less than 30 seconds, the other in less than 10 moves).
There isn't a story, even though there definitely is a Steampunk meets Da Vinci's codex theme.
Music is forgettable, graphics are nice and clean, but unspectacular. Also, it's a bit disappointing when a 2009 game forces you into a 4:3 screen ratio.
Overall, the puzzle difficulty lied just within my fun zone and the game's uniqueness makes it hard to not recommend to puzzle enthusiasts.

"Sanctum" is...okay.
The game's main interest lies in how it shows Coffee Stain's ability to iterate. The lessons that the team learned from "Sanctum" are very visible in "Sanctum 2," a noticeably more polished title. This entry in the series is a decent diversion for a day or two, but it never gets beyond that.
This is not to say that the original game is bad - it's just to point out that there are some very noticeable rough edges. In comparison to the sequel, the character handling in "Sanctum" feels clunky and imprecise. The tower building is much more of a chore, and just getting around the map feels a bit awkward.
The game pacing is also "clunky." Each map lasts for what feels like an extraordinarily long time, without really building much tension to keep things interesting. This feeling of things being overlong also tends to create outsize punishments for choosing a bad tower loadout or overall strategy. If you chase yourself into a situation that suddenly becomes unwinnable at a late wave, the reaction is NOT one of "Oh - I see what might work!" Instead, my feeling was "Ugh...I have to do all that again? *Sigh...*"
Part of the problem is that the game is so contextless. I feel that it's a perfect example of a multiplayer game that just happens to have a working singleplayer mode. Unlike its sequel, "Sanctum" has no worldbuilding, characters, or sense of purpose that makes you invest in the game's progression. It's just a collection of disconnected encounters that happen to you, and while some of the defense problems are interesting to solve, there's a lot of repetition. It might be better with multiplayer co-op, where some of the social aspects serve to spice things up independent of the software.
If the gameplay was truly a blast, the above wouldn't be as much of a liability. It doesn't make it to that point, though.
So, with all the apparent negativity, why would I still click "Yes" when asked if I recommend "Sanctum?"
Well, first, reviewers need a third option: A "Maybe" button. But beyond that...
I do feel that "Sanctum" is worth seeing as a curiosity. It provides a kind of window into how the series was formed and refined. Play time isn't everything, but in this case, I think there's a strong correlation. "Sanctum 2" was brilliant enough to keep me playing for almost 40 hours, which is more than four times longer than I was willing to spend with "Sanctum." It may be that "Sanctum" is only about 1/4 as good as its dramatically improved sequel. It certainly feels that way to me, and maybe that's just good enough to spend a few bucks on.
In other words, the game is pretty "Eh," but I don't hate it.

First of let me say this game is far from perfect. There are plenty of bugs, missing content and of course the plain stupid AI. However, none of those things stopped me from having fun in Hearts of Iron 4. This was the first Paradox Interactive game I really got invested in and I definitely did not regret it. I tried Victoria 2, but I failed to grasp all of its complex intrecacies and I heard HOI 3 was very complicated, so I was extremely relived to find that HOI 4 is relatively easy to learn. But once you learn the basics, there is so much more depth to explore, like the division designer.
The most fun that can be gotten from HOI 4 is if you enjoy roleplaying as various nations during WW2 and all the "what if" scenarios that can be had with this game. The modding community as well if flourishing, bringing so much more depth to the game. One of my personal favorites being The Great War mad and playing as Austria-Hungary. The amount of flavour mods add to the game also highlights one of the game's flaws. Paradox are again using their DLC centered buisness model, in which they slowly build on the base game until is finally becomes a masterpiece. Only the major nations and Poland have unique Focus Trees and flavoured units in the tech tree. All other minor nations are mostly the same, having the same research, National focus tree, etc.
The greatest flaw that people point out when talking about the game is the really bad AI. They get encircled all the time, expose vulnerbale flanks, fortify unimportant flanks and overall is just pretty useless. Hopefully after Paradox finishes the Together to Victory expansion they can focus on fixing the AI. Some other things that could be improved is the amount of lag the longer the game goes on due to the amount of units and the lack of a proper ending or score screen.
While far from finished, right now HOI 4 is a good base. There is a lot already to do and with some time it will undoubtedly become the best WW2 strategy game of this decade.
Final Score: 8/10

There is the monster. From a "weak" first phase you try to eat wildlife all over the map to evolve to your stronger phases 2 and 3. Meanwhile you are hunted by the hunters.
There are the hunters. 4 tough guys charget with hunting the monster. The assault, a tough guy focused on dealing out tons of damage while also being able to take some punches. The medic focuses on keeping the rest of the team alive by curing their wounds. The support trys to prevent the rest of the team from dying or does other things that help the team. And finally the trapper whose job it is to find out where the monster is, cut of his way and put it into the dome where the monster can't escape.
And oh my - the moment the dome appears you know there will be a tough battle. 4 against 1. The 1 could easily take out any of the four. But with perfect teamwork, good coordination and spreading out the 4 can deal damage to the monster.
It is hard. There is much learning involved in knowing how to play a member of each of the 5 classes. You have to know where to stand. Where not to stand. What weapon to use at a specific time. When to retreat.
After a battle has finished against a monster and the adrenaline slowly kicks back you know what you achived. Or did not when the monster stand over your dead bodies.
Evolve Stage 2 has a meta game besides the single rounds of playing. For each game you earn a bit of "silver keys". With those silver keys you can unlock perks to customize your characters (e.g. +5% movement speed, 3% less damage, 20% climbing speed), new characters, skins for your characters and weapons. You will undoubtly be able to pay for some of those unlocks later.
This is not a simple game. But a very rewarding experience that is very different from your classic school of Medal of Dutyfield kind of shooters. Try it.

When I first got this game from the Potato Sack I really liked it. It only took about fifteen levels for me to hate it. The problem stems from needing to complete previous levels to be able to play further ones. If one level is beyond your intellect, you're stuck. Either look up a walkthrough or replay previous levels again and again and again and again...
When the game introduced double-sided 5 by 5 slide puzzles into the mix, I knew that in order to better my score at all and get to the next level I would need a walkthrough, which is always an incredibly sad revelation for a puzzle game. I'm even good at slide puzzles, I can solve a 4x4 in literally seconds. But the game soon became about memorization and perfect execution, not a real winning combination in my book. To get more points to unlock another level I would have to complete levels in the absolute minimum amount of time and moves. I would have rather there been a little more leeway for me to find my own solution.
It's sort of appropriate that this game was bundled with Portal 2 as Portal has similar challenge mode mechanics where you have to execute your solution to a level with the least amount of time or the least amount of moves. The main difference is that in Portal, you usually remember the jist of the solution to a level and the trick is being efficient; while in Cogs, where solutions can be 100 moves minimum and take over 5 minutes, remembering the solution is a crap-shoot at best and executing it efficiently enough is near impossibility without outside help.
Worse yet, challenge mode in Cogs simply counts down your moves or time, so all it really can offer is a more punishing version of Inventor Mode, doing the exact same thing you already did for medals you might have already earned. The game even makes you play time and moves challenge mode in two separate tries. This isn't a problem in a game like Portal, where the least portals and least time solutions are usually mutually exclusive (or at least not the exact same thing); but in Cogs, least moves and least time are almost always the same solution, so it just feels like more pointless repetition.
A good idea for a puzzle game lies in this debris somewhere, but for all the frustrating and arbitrary progress gating, I can't recommend you play this game.

This game SEEMS like a great tower defense game, but I think there's a major flaw: It isn't FUN. The maps are big and there are so many ways you could lay out your defense.... yet, as each defense you try fails or barely succeeds, you get the feeling that there is actually only one or two ways to beat each challenge. That isn't fun to me. I think tower defense games need to choose whether the "solution" to a challenge is intuitive and you can find it after a few tries, OR whether you can decide how to build your defense and there are many ways to win. When a tower defense game gives you many options AND requires you to play a very specific way, I call that TEDIUM. You have to play the whole challenge (they are quite long) over and over until you find out the successful layout.
You could say I'm just not that great at the game, but I never consider "you're just not good enough" or "there are people out there who can do it" to be a strong defense (no pun intended) for a tedius and difficult game. I think if I play video games pretty often and I tend to be good at them, I should be able to achieve moderate success in a game without investing hundreds of hours. For that reason, I can't recommend this game. Non-hardcore tower defense fans will probably enjoy this game up to a point then realize that it's is either hopeless or way too time consuming and demanding.

The game takes elements from PD2 and PDTH. The gameplay is more akin to PDTH as you have to use actual cover believe it or not and dodge is basically non existant. It takes the skills from PD2 adds in Warcries and that gives you Proficencies, a quite unique way of doing skill trees. I just want to get this out of the way, I DO RECOMMEND this game, but not for the full the price. As of right now the price doenst justify the little bit of content. But the content we do have is great... the game is fun, it really is! The only problem is the price tag, if this game was say 20 maybe even 25 dollars, I think the current amount of players would be triple what it currently is.
-BUGS-
The game does have bugs, stealth right now is pretty buggy.. being detected when Germans arent facing you is strange. Maybe the players havent figured stealth out but, I killed a German on a floor beneath someone and when another player in the lobby picked up the dead body, the guard upstairs rang the siren? Stealth is weird and not fun since you have to be within♥♥♥♥♥♥distance of someone to kill them. Guns blazing is the way to play this game! A few other bugs I came across was objective markers staying on the map even after completing said objective. Detection meter staying on map after mission goes loud, key marker staying on map even after picking them up. Models are very strange, espically in the safe house and when driving, sometimes Rivet in particular will do that weird T model where his arms are straight out. There are alot of animation bugs but these are minor and dont impact GAMEPLAY at all, they are more so just unpleasant to look at.
-Audio-
Guns sound cheap when firing, grenades sound super cheesy when exploding... in fact ALL explosions thus far sound very cheesy. The voice acting for Kurgan(Soviet) and Wolfgang(German) CAN be cheesy at times. The hard R rolls are cringey in some voice lines, but for the most part the voices are fine... its a few lines that bug me but as a whole the characters do have great voice acting and awesome personality, its just a FEW voice lines that are eh, and its not so much the voice acting as it is the writing of the lines. Car sounds are boring and generic, but atleast the car drives decently.
-Video settings/options/graphics/optimization-
First thing is first, no option to remove HUD as of now. You can do basic things like adjust shadow quality, Anti Aliasing, head bobbing, there is an FOV slider, and obviously texture quality. At 60 fps in 1080p playing on MAX settings using a GTX 1070 8gb, i5 7600k 4.0ghz, 16gb ddr4 memory I was able to keep a stable 60 fps with a very few RARE drops and this was usually after alt+tabbing back into the game or directly after someone joined. So optimization seems to actually be good.... unlike a little game we all know of >.> . Graphics, well uhmmm... they are.. NOT good :/. Somehow managing to look worse than that little game I mentioned in the prvious sentence... Im not too caught up on the graphics because its pasable, graphics dont make a game imo.
-Gameplay-
I have tried not to mention Payday 2 in this review because it seems like the popular thing to do, but I cant help but mention it here in the gameplay portion. Is it payday 2 with a reskin? In short, no. It does feel alot like gameplay when it comes to mechanics, interacting with locks, running and jumping, shooting etc. But the core gameplay is alot different than payday 2, sure you have objectives that are I guess at the roots the same thing? Like defend this point for XXX amount of time, but this is not something only Payday 2 has. Wave styled games are universal across many games, not just payday 2. Maps in this game are ALOT larger, you have plenty of room to run around and explore. Speical units are alot less frequent and overall the units are lessend. The gameplay is still fast paced and action packed but overall the game is slower paced than Payday 2. Opening boxes to regen health and rarely finding it on the ground is nice, it doesnt allow that type of gameplay Payday 2 had where everyone just runs around 1 man army style and just kills everything.. never having to worry about health or downing. Speaking of downing, atleast on normal when in "custody" you automatically respawn after a certain amount of time. Fades (the point where no Germans spawn) seem to be about the same time as Payday 2 on Ovk. I enjoy the gameplay this game offers, it WILL punish those who are careless and rewards the careful strategic people. Shooting guns is great, so far there are no optional sights for weapons so if you are someone that doesnt like iron sights.. then good luck. There is a loot box system in the game but dont fear, its only in game. You get a loot box after every mission is complete 100% and depending on how many dog tags you find and how well you did will grant you a better loot box. In lootboxes you get cosmetic items and exp boosts (I have yet to get anything else after 7 hours of gameplay). At the end of each mission there is a MVP type of section showing who did the most kills, best accuracy, most headshots etc. If you get one of these 3 or all 3 you get a little boost in upping the chances of getting a better lootbox. Sounds great, but in my experience so far ALOT of players will just kill ♥♥♥♥♥ to get these MVP bonuses and just ignore the objective... (will update this portion later but I think ive covered most of it, the gameplay is fun!)
-Progression system-
You might be asking why I didnt inclue this in the gameplay section and thats because I feel like it deserves its own little space so it gets more attention. Lumping it in a wall of text it might get over looked.
The progression system is great, unlocking attachments for your guns by actually using them is much better than just being able to buy them outright. If you like a gun enough you WILL get everything you want for it by playing the game, if you dont like a gun well guess what.. you DONT have to use it. The guns dont have as much customization as they do in Payday 2, shotguns have one ammo type, no sight options, no suppresors. All you get is stability, extendo mag, and more damage. Given the time period it makes since that the options would be limited, so im not complaining by any means. As of right now there arent alot of guns, there are 13 primary weapons to choose from and 3 secondary weapons. Out of the 13p weapons 4 are class locked, 2 for recon only and 2 for assualt and demo only, insurgent as of now has no class locked weapons. Secondary weapons can be used across the board. You unlock guns by getting headshots, kills or hip fire kills for tier 1. To unlock higher tier attachments you need to reach a certain level tier 2 being level 15.
-Random input-
Live action cutscenes are corny.. sorry I HAD to say it. Also no one ever joins my server :/. Some missions feel like they should be done in singleplayer, almost as if this game was created as a singleplayer experience with coop added later.. its strange.
My final thoughts are, the game is awesome but the price tag isnt. I know I said alot of bad things but thats only because so many other reviews didnt. The game is great and over time with polishing and updates / new content I think it has the potential to compete with Payday 2. As of right now the game is more like Payday 1.

As of writing the game has mixed reviews, as for me I like the game alot. I enjoy the atmosphere more then its "predocessor" as well as its firearms. I am biased though considering I absolutly love the time line but anyway I would still recommend to all fps fans.
