This game is great, highly recommended if you like first person shooters.
The gameplay is a little different than past titles from id software, with regenerating health, aiming down gun sights and crafting supplies from scavenged materials. But the high body count and ubiquitous gore present in other id franchises (Doom, Quake etc.) is still here.
The visuals are fantastic, the character designs, animations and environments perfectly evoke a dirty, destroyed world. There is also some decent variety in the environments it is not just the junk yards and desert wastelands commonly found in post apocalyptic settings. The last level in particular is stunning. The graphics are very detailed and run fast and smooth. I never experienced any glitches or crashes but as you turn the camera and new objects come into view the texture resolution always starts out low and then the higher resolution details noticeably pop in.
The gameplay is more cover based than usual from this developer, with most enemies crouching behind things and taking pot shots at you rather than constantly charging your position. The animations on those few enemies that do charge at you are spectacular though with enemies dodging and flipping over stuff in a parkour-like manner. The weapon selection is generic FPS fare with pistol, shotgun, rocker launcher etc. but between alternate ammo types and craftable gadgets like turrets, bots and RC cars the arsenal does not feel lacking at all. The game is not very difficult on normal, a thorough explorer will always be able to scavenge more than enough resources to buy or craft whatever you want, whenever you want so you may want to start on hard. The Scorchers DLC is basically essential if you want a challenge as it adds another difficulty level and its missions are just harder overall than almost all of the core games levels.
While you can have multiple missions active at once and drive around large open areas the story is quite linear and unless you have an active mission, returning to previous areas will almost always be a walk through a ghost town with no enemies or items to collect.
This game also has some very fun minigames. In your car you can race on a few tracks both with and without weapons. There is also a checkpoint collecting mode that can get pretty frantic. In a bar there is a knife game that tests your reflexes, and a collectable card deck building game that uses cards found during missions. There is also a dice game that is basically just a slot machine but is much more fun to watch.

Does blasting an army of bad guys to smithereens Metal Slug-style sound like your idea of a good time? How about doing it with your own custom-made weapon using whatever mishmash of parts you can think of? If any of that appeals to you, then this is absolutely worth a shot.
Paul Robertson's handmade sprites and backdrops do a lot to give the experience that retro/fake-retro charm without coming across as just pixelated for the sake of it. The soundtrack's combination of metal and chiptune-like tones calls to mind things like Virt's compositions for Contra 4 and DuckTales Remastered.
Once you get some momentum going, it's lots of fun crafting gun parts, bionic mods and even substitutes for your trusty knife, to put together your own personal loadout and see how it performs.
There's a couple hitches though. To me at least, the system of equipment weighing you down seems out of place, and the Monster Hunter-type layout of missions giving you different objectives in the same areas means it can get kind of repetitive, especially if there's a gun part or something you REALLY want to get the materials for.
Trifles aside, it's a fine example of mashing together run-and-gun violence and strategic weapon crafting.

It never gets old to play a game like that with your friends ;)
Overall Rating, 8.5/10

Polished MMO launches are rare, but Rift pulled it off.  Since then, they've come out with a ton of content at a breakneck pace.  Between the content, the approachability of the dev team and the flexibility of the class system, I've been hooked on Rift since it came out in March 2011.

RIFT. Just as the word implies, the world of RIFT known as Telara is under constant war between two factions, the Guardians and the Defiant but also a third wheel, the armies of the all-powerful evil, Regulos who threatens all but spares none.
The interesting part of this game is how it starts, your world is on the verge of destruction and the only way you can save it is by dying. Not much for lore in an MMORPG? Besides the story, the game is an open-world, persistent MMORPG which has dynamic world events called Rift throughout all areas of the world so you'll never have a quiet moment through one area. Band together with other nearby players in a Public Group option which pops up and vanquish those minions of Regulos!

Evolve Stage 2. This is honestly what the game should have been in the first place, not the F2P aspect but the way the new system works is so much more rewarding and fun to use.
In the original game you got to pick one perk for a character and it was very grindy to level it up and it didn't feel worth it at all. Now the system let's you pick 3 different perks in different tiers all of which have 3 levels so you can create a very unique playstyle for your chosen hunter with a quick change of perks. It's a very nice change and one that the game sorely needed. The perk system is also there for the monster player.
As for the new gameplay mechanics, it definitely makes the game much more fast paced, everyone can now trap the monster and the new trapper scanner helps you locate it faster. It really helps make the game a lot more entertaining as there is more combat and less scoring for the sneaky monster. The monster player has to be extra careful and outplay the hunters if he wants to be stealthy now.
The maps are being redesigned now and they do seem a lot better to coincide with the faster gameplay mechanics. There are only 4 in the game at the time of writing this review but they all seem fairly balanced.
The only mode currently is Hunt or you can create custom games, I do hope that they add the multiple day career type mode back in, Evacuation I think it was called, as that was where the game was most fun.
There are a decent choice of weapon skins and hero skins to purchase using the new in game currency called silver keys. I do hope however that they add a lot more and much more frequently than they did when the game was originally released as the glacial development speed of content and patches were a huge part of what killed the game so fast.
The graphics and sound in the game is still great, I run it at max settings and it really does look amazing, especially with the dynamic weather system.
Overall I'd say Evolve Stage 2 is a great step in reviving this game which I am very glad with as I really did enjoy the original game. Good choice Turtle Rock Studios :)

Art, music and atmosphere are all fantastic and true to the theme. It does however feel like one of those "Newgrounds" flash-games from the early 2000's; You load a small area with a set number of enemies, you kill everything in the area and load the next one. Everything is tied together with a badly written story that checks most of the spaghetti western tropes.
By "badly written" I'm referring to everything from vocabulary and grammar to spelling, phrasing and dialogue as a whole; It all feels like it was written by a 15 year old. The language is not true to the theme, the references are far too modern and every bit of exposition and character development are right on the nose and seems to be written on a whim.

I usually don't care about these things and have no qualms about bad grammar (I make plenty of mistakes myself). However, the complete lack of voice acting in this game puts every bit of immersion on the art, music and dialogue, which becomes a problem. As previously mentioned, Ink Stains Games nailed the first two of these but whenever the game provides dialogue or exposition I'm thrown right out of the experience. In my opinion it makes the game far less enjoyable.
With that bit of criticism out of the way, I found other aspects of the game enjoyable, the combat as an example. It moves away from traditional top-down shooters and engages the player by making weapons a tad bit more complex: You have to reload the weapons one shell or bullet at a time and "ready" the hammer manually between shots. Though that's as far as it goes it's more than enough to enhance the immersion and make the gameplay a bit more interesting. Unfortunately there's no way of picking up ammo for the weapons, instead you have to repeatedly hammer the "Use"-key to pick up the weapons of fallen enemies to get a fresh supply of ammo, something that causes many unnecessary deaths. As does the fact that enemies can start shooting at you from outside the screen before you've had a chance to react.
To sum things up I found "12 is better than 6" to be a solid experience bringing some new mechanics and ideas to the table. This presented in a beautiful art style, in a nice environment with a great soundtrack. What takes my recommendation from a "Yes" to a "No" is the badly written dialogue and exposition as well as some minor gameplay issues caused by a lack of polish. When playing the game I never feel like it's a nice experience or that I'm playing a passion project, it feels like a flash-game from 2004. That in itself is a nice nostalgick throwback but not one I'd be willing to pay €7 for.

Moonfall brings a fresh take on the side-scrolling beat 'em up genre. A new era in the classic arcade game Golden Axe, but you have beautiful hand painted graphics, a Gothic industrial story, and RPG elements including 3 classes and character upgrades.
The intro has you fending off "savages" who do not agree with your expanding empire due to a new magic element called "Lunarium". Each level will have you hacking and slashing away at these savages with giant swords and axes. The combat feels shallow and repetitive as there is not much varying degree of strategy when you button mash the attack key, but the 4 available abilities like the shield charge -- stunning opponents, or power strike -- hitting multiple enemies, help to change things up. You get to explore branching paths through multiple levels in 2 main environments, which felt lacking considering the scope of the story and world, but the lore and Gothic steam-punk vibes will push you to see whats around the next corner.
Completing the campaign takes about 8 hours and I found the beautiful world of Terra Nihil is enticing enough to play with each class. Finding new weapons and armor with different stats helped mix up the repetitive combat and minor battle animations as enemies are stiff. The ending is open for the developers to continue this enchanting Gothic adventure.. and I sure hope they do because the detail of this world deserves to be expanded upon.

TLDR: Moonfall is an old school beat'em up with many modern twists that make this game feel fresh and fun for newcomers and veterans alike, making this well worth the $10. This game is a beat'em up set in a beautiful hand-drawn universe called Terra Nihil. Choose between 3 distinct characters and help the Empire fight against the Savages. This game has large open levels and the occasion boss. There's lots of enemy vareity and intesting weapons to acquire. The music is epic and the art style is awesome.
Moonfall is a beat'em up set in a fantastic gothic style environment. The visuals and setting are steampunk-esque which is really cool. You get to choose from 3 different classes, which have their own abilities and skill trees. They each excel in a different combat aspect (e.g. Vanguard is melee specialist, Elementalist relies on magic). The levels are open and quite large and there's also secrets and optional objectives.
- The visuals are one the strongest points of this game. The graphics are a nice painterly style and they're just gorgeous. They are beautiful, quality hand drawn graphics. The environments look fantastic and the levels are full of graphical detail. There's different settings such as the forest and a kind of castle place, which are vastly unique and add variety. I'm a big fan of Moonfall's visual style and it's quality is quite exceptional. However, the animations aren't quite up to par with the graphics. They're alright, but they're not terribly fluid and they could be better. The visual effects are decent but spells could have more visual flair and particle effects to improve the visual feedback. Overall, Moonfall delivers a beautiful visual experience which draws you into the world.
- The music consists of epic orchestral music which fits the game nicely. There's a bit of repetition but not to the extent that it gets annoying. The sound effects offer good feedback during gameplay and you won't have many quiet moments which is good.
- Moonfall is a side scrolling beat'em up, set over 13 open-ended levels. The game is linear but the levels are quite large and offer optional objectives and sometimes secrets with a nice reward for discovery. The core gameplay involves accomplishing a certain objective while beating up all the enemies on the way. The combat is decent, there's no combo attacks however, but you can block and use special abilities which are upgradable via a neat little skill tree. Since I'm playing as an Elementalist, which excels in using magic, I get to frequently use and juggle magic attacks which is fun. The skill tree is implemented well, and upgrading it actually makes a pretty discernible difference to your abilities. Levelling up allows allocating a point towards a base stat (such as health, mana, etc), but it's generally a good idea to upgrade your characters main stat (for example: Elementalist is mana) so that they can unleash their full capabilities.
In this game, your mana and health will regenerate naturally over time, however you can hold up to 6 mana and 6 health potions, which are frequently dropped by enemies. You can equip 2 weapons at a time, and switch between them with a button press. Sometimes you can come across loot chests, which can yield special weapons and armour. Weapons can have special abilities, such as a chance for environmental hazards to drop potions upon getting destroyed, or a chance to stun or bleed an enemy. There's a nice variety of weapons and armour but I found that they were too rare; even after 2 hours of playing I still haven't gotten all my armour slots equipped. Between levels is a hub, where you may buy weapons, armour and potions, as well as receiving your next mission. You only ever get missions from one particular person, no one else ever gives you missions or anything. Some missions contain bosses, which are surprisingly well done. They take a lot of effort and skill to take down and they're much more than just an enemy with a long health bar.
Overall, I found Moonfall to have simple, yet fun and engaging gameplay. It's certainly a very decent beat'em up game.
- I wasn't a fan of the storytelling in this game. It's only told through text, which I find boring to read. Voice acting would have made a big difference in this game. I wasn't really able to follow the story, but I do know that Moonfall is set in a fictitious place called Terra Nihil. You're part of the Empire, and there's evil enemies attacking, so you take on missions that will help the Empire. If the story was more audio-based then it would be much more compelling, but otherwise I just found it quite lacklustre.
- Functionally, Moonfall is especially great. I experienced no frame drops or bugs during my play time. Apparently it can even run on Windows XP, a 15 year old Windows OS. That is honestly quite surprising.
- The UX is probably one of the weaker points of Moonfall. Potions can be consumed even when you're at full health/mana which can be annoying. Navigating through menus is quite confusing and cumbersome, (I still have problems with it after a few hours) and especially more so with the strange lack of mouse support. I also found the text to be a bit too small and can be difficult to read. Other than those issues, Moonfall is easy to get into and simple and fun to play.
- I like the nice little touch where activating a switch/lever will show you a small screen detailing what occured.
- The game is ~6 hours long, but it offers new game+ and also 3 different classes with unique playstyles. There's also harder difficulty modes which offer a great challenge.
- The developers have been adding/modifying a lot of content in the game based on community feedback. They're active on the forums and they show willingness to continue improving their game.
Moonfall was thoroughly enjoyable. For only $9.99 I think it's certainly worth a buy. I'm not a big fan of beat'em ups, but Moonfall was simply enjoyable.
If you're looking for fun fantasy beat'em up then Moonfall is a great choice.
It may not be the game for you if you're expecting a deep and complex beat'em up, but otherwise you'd most definitely enjoy.
I give this game a 7/10 - A competent beat'em up set in an enthralling fantasy world.

Video Review here:
As it might be labeled as a brawler, this feels nothing like any of the beat’em ups I’ve played. My favorite series is Streets of Rage which has a solid style of slapping up thugs and showing them who’s boss. However in Moonfall it feels more stiff and with less impact from attacks.
Combat in general is what this game is said to be designed around but falls short in so many ways. Basic attacks do not cause enemies to stagger meaning they will strike you back as you strike them. You are able to combo attacks but even that can still be a bit clunky as you’re forced to finish the complete animations before moving. Using slow two handed weapons can result in you taking a lot more incoming damage since you cannot move out of the way. It would be nice to have some force behind your attacks that stagger enemies to help this feel more like a beat’em up.
Blocking feels completely useless as you can’t block majority of the incoming attacks and unless you have a shield you’ll still take damage. The best method is to simply dodge meaning you’ll end up running in circles to gather enemies and spam whatever spells you can. However, the issue is that the spells cost mana and if you run out you’ll need to keep running in circles until it regenerates enough for you to cast again.
This is all not mentioning the lack of indication that you’re actually taking damage. It is so subtle when your health starts to deplete that you’ll glance at your health bar only to notice that by swinging twice you’ve lost a good half of your health for reasons you probably can’t see. There are several environmental traps that will deal damage to you. Even the hit boxes from enemies can be really weird and strike you even when you think you’re out of range.
Overall the combat comes down to you dodging and using abilities to take enemies out regardless of your class. Speaking of classes there are a total of three which focus on giving you a different set of abilities and spells to use. Each class comes with four active spells and six passive abilities which typically enhance the four main spells.
Classes don’t feel too different as they typically use the same equipment. Equipment takes on a standard RPG style where you can find several bits of weapons with effects added on. Like diablo, you can find varieties of the same weapon with different effects and different tiers that show the strength of that particular weapon. Likely when you find a powerful unique weapon you’ll ignore the rest until the next more powerful unique weapon or armor piece comes along.
I never found myself really using a shop since I could never find anything that I could really use other than potions. I found all the best equipment while on the field which makes the lunarium currency useless since I never spent it on anything as potions drop quite often mid to late game.
There is a power bar is unique for each class but falls short as it does not provide a proper benefit that I can use in this game due to the wonky combat. The Elementalist, for example, can cast fire or ice to fill the bar to the respective side. As the bar is close to the end it adds that element of damage to your weapon. The problem you’ll notice is I’m not using my weapon. I can’t. If I were to start swinging back I’d end up taking more damage than I would be dishing out damage. So, this bar gets ignored the entire game. Same with the other classes I’ll just end up running around and ignoring the bar completely making it useless.
However, if you can get past this, the overall combat is mediocre. The game is very playable but then we fall to the story for a bit of help to cover the “RPG” elements of this game and oh boy is the story quite the trip. I do believe that the grammar and story writing issues comes from translation as the developers, Fishcow studios, are from Slovakia.
(For this paragraph specifically its taken fromt he video displaying the Prologue.)
Displayed here is the first screen of text that you get for the intro of the game. As walls of text don’t bother me, it’s the first paragraph that really cuts my immersion from this game. Terra Nihill is trying to be both a World and a Continent, which I’m not sure is really possible, and cultures birth lands. If you were to read the entire thing I still don’t know exactly what’s going on. In my summary of the game things called Savages, a group of random races, are taking down the Empire because some king died. From here we can get additional information from each quest and secret messages from the levels themselves, yet it’s hard to tell who even wrote the notes.
Not to mention the notes can be pretty funny as they’re written as if they’re actually talking. Including all the laughing, heavy breathing, and several exclamation points. It would be as if I were to write a love letter to my Fiancée and input ever grunt and breathing noise I made.
Without spoilers let me say that the ending is a bit confusing as it didn’t feel like much of an ending. The conclusion was pretty shocking mind you as I was unaware what the real goal was. However even with all this harping against the game it does have a few redeeming qualities.
The artwork and music is beautiful to be honest. The hand painted environments and characters look nice. Though limits some of the animations, it still works for what it is. Even if I were to complain while playing the game the entire time, the artwork makes up for quite a bit of it.
Overall I think Moonfall missed its mark as far as attempting to be a side scrolling beat’em up with RPG elements. With everything in the game, we ended up with a mediocre linear styled diablo game. It falls short on everything it’s trying to be without doing anything it wants to do well. If I wanted to play an RPG for the story I couldn’t go to Moonfall. If I wanted fun action oriented RPG styled combat, I’d have to look elsewhere. The most the game really has going for it is the beautiful art and environments.

If you like original games with clever mechanics and a protagonist that snags at your heart, this is the game for you. But remember: You only get One Shot.
Like I imagine many others are doing about now, I saw Markiplier pick up this game on a let's play. I looked up the reviews and overall synopsis about 2 minutes into his let's play and decided that I HAD to buy this and experience this for myself. One of my favorite games of all time is To The Moon. It was not beyond my ability to believe that another pixel style game could captivate me that way. Let me tell you a little about this, but overall, for concept and developer to player relationship, this is a 10/10 for me for the kind of game it is.
You find yourself in a strangely stylized world (for a pixel game!) with rich, satisfying colors, and your little protagonist, Niko, beginning his adventure. Your relationship with Niko [potential spoilers ahead] hinges on the concept that you, the player, are God of this world that you have both been thrown into, although as you play, you discover that you aren't exactly an omnipotent being. With Niko you fulfill a prophecy that heavily relies on the light-and-dark motif that is maybe too often used in games in general, but with a fresh twist. And then of course... there are the subtle, and occasionally not as subtle, prodding at the very core concepts of religion and God. Any game that makes me self reflect is a winner, period.
The game is also interactive. While not difficult,  when the game says "you have one shot" it means it. There's a satisfactory weight of consequence as a result of it's punishing "all or nothing" approach. This leads into this impressive level of immersion. I have never played a story game like this where the game itself, as well as the character, develops a relationship with the player, not to say there aren't other games like it. It's just very rare. The game challenges you to think outside of the box, use resources not necessarily part of its "programming," use environmental cues to find your next step and gently, creepily - riskily - leading you ever forward. The real joy in this game is its mechanics. And on this note, 100% I do recommend playing this in windowed mode. You won't regret it.
I love children and Niko's text captures that sense of innocence that often accompanies their ill-formed attempts to understand greater, abstract concepts. I knew I would enjoy Niko from the get-go, but when presented with a choice in my first play through, I was surprised to find just how invested I was in him. He snuck his way under my skin and became my little buddy, rather than the conduit, for the story. For how limited the game's dialogue had to be, the developers and writers did a phenomenal job of saying just enough.
I will be playing this more than once, absolutely. It is a sweet, meaningful story that I would recommend to anyone looking for a 1. unique 2. story rich or 3. RPG exploration game

This game is one of those rare gems that I would cherish forever in my hands or my heart for finding one like this.
This game isn't just a game... it's a game that you are actually in. Not a character that you control that supposed to resemble you.
What I mean is that you are guiding a character named Niko who is stuck in a world and must find a way home... but of course, the world that Niko is in, has a crisis... and who is guiding this little feline?
Don't overthink it... the guide... is YOU... that's right, you there reading this review on your PC with your actual eyes. That doesn't stop there with your own computer even taking part in this game.
And don't worry... that is not a spoiler, at least not overly major.
What this game does with knowing that "you exist" is remarkable. At some points the game seems to be talking to you at times and at other times... you have to use your actual computer outside the game to solve the puzzles that you'll encounter. An example would be the game
.
Everything about this game, the art style, the story, music, atmosphere... almost everything about it is excellent throughout.
I hope that other games in the future will follow the same concept that OneShot took. This "the game knows that you exist" is the key defining factor that makes OneShot one of my most favorite games of all time. Think about it... imagine playing a game, and the story has YOU as a major character. Not through some sort of "puppet" that you control, or a character that you are supposed to roleplay as in the story. I wish that other games has a story that involves... YOU... REAL LIFE YOU... the one still reading this review.
In conclusion, I recommend you buy this game and experience first hand playing through this. Don't even look at spoilers until you are finished playing this game to the end. I can guarantee, that you will not be dissapointed with your experience.

This game..... oh man where do I even start.... It all started when I watched markiplier play the game. I thought to myself "Oh this game looks intesting...  maybe I'll get it someday" After the video was over that I knew I had to play this game.
I'll start out by saying this game isn't perfect... no game is... but It comes really close. The stuning pixel art Is even more epic when It's next to the brilliant soundtrack. The gameplay is simualar to "Yume Nikki", with it being a exploritive puzzle game and to a sort of lesser extent "undertale"  both being inspired by the look and style of earthbound, showing that games with 2D pixel sprites and art can still be on par if not better then the games with next gen HD graphics we have today. The story is simple and strait forward you have to help your charater find your way home and save the world but the story is never as dull as it sounds because there is so much to explore, hidden rooms to find, and much more. Oneshot does something a bit different from the norm and this is where it's likeness to undertale kicks in... you and your main charater.... are not the same people.... you are a charater, you have to fill a role in the story and talk with the main charater and you begin to have a bond with the them, with this concept the game utilises your real computer to make puzzle solving have this huge extra layer and impact. Urgh, first of all, I thought a lot about this. I wish I could just give a "mixed but with a very low kick to the negative side", but that ain't possible and the closest thing is negative, although I don't really think it just deserves a negative.
So again, first of all, I want to say what really impressed me. Like many others I thought the game might be just Payday 2 in WW2. Well, the core is, sure, but we all knew that from the start. However, so many fresh and exciting ideas are worked into this game, it's kinda stunning. As a 1000+ hours Payday player, I knew what I expected. The mission objectives were fresh and new, and unlike in Payday 2 I was even able to see some of the action (Exploding an airship vs. PD2's blackscreen and Bain's "wow we blew that up!").
So I'd say it's more cinematic than PD2. I compare it to this game because it's the same engine and same core principle. About the engine: I get why they chose it, they got experience with it. The Diesel engine is what now, 15 years old or something? And it's stopping to work for Payday 2. And they need to step up for a newer game. Updates will be hard on performance, the engine is already at it's limits. Add the cinematic effects to this and we will surely have a crash incoming.
The graphics aren't neccessarily ugly, however they tried too hard to make realistic textures which just looks plainly bad in some places. It's especially bad for the overview of the whole gameplay.
Well, the gameplay. It's... hard to say, really. This game is full of bugs, most commonly clipping glitches, so NPC's walking through walls. About the gunplay itself, it's divided. Some guns like the shotguns feel just great and are fun to play, however the first pistol or the Insurgent's SMG just make me feel as if I never wanna look at them again, they felt simply... frustrating.
That all may be okay, however not for that price. This is a 15 buck game, not a 40 buck or even 60 buck game. Oh and while we're at it, I personally own the Deluxe Edition and it's a plain waste for me - none of these items are of interest, at all. Plus, I can almost guarantee incoming DLC, knowing Payday. So it tought me to not pre-order games anymore, which is good at least.
At the end, all this game got going for it are the cinematic effects, comical characters and clever ideas, but that just doesn't make it different enough from other genre-like games. I love the game's promise, just like I did with L4D, PD2 and even Killing Floor 2, however this just did not grab me, although I fully expected it to grab me.
As for the swastika and Nazi stuff: It's weird, really. I'm based in germany and concerning censorship, it's really finicky. Well all the swastikas are replaced with some other sign, good, who cares. Hitler just has a different moustache, also okay I guess. Now the real problem is the german version of the game being locked into german language, but devs promised to fix that, plus you can already change that in the game config outside the game. So concerning censorship, it's bearable. (Although they still say "Nazis" and "Hitler" however when John Cleese speaks he just says "Mr. Beep")

I'm going to avoid comparing this to PAYDAY 2, since I'm sure no one wants yet another review that literally just says "it's PD2 in WW2."
I'm also avoiding it because this game CAN'T be played like PD2. While still a tad derpy, the AI is actually smart enough to crouch and cover, and your health doesn't regenerate. Basically, it's harder and requires quite a bit of actual teamwork. The Nazis will definitely try to mob you, but it feels more like a tactical cover-to-cover rather than a suicidal death rush.
The graphics do feel a tad dated (the whole game, honestly, since LGL made the somewhat questionable decision to run it on the Diesel engine.) However, from a smaller dev you're not really expecting Battlefield 1; the textures aren't horrible except on a few ground elements (sonething I'm sure would be easy enough to update) and the character models, while not stellar, aren't by any means bad.
Gameplay is unique and interesting with the team elements, the characters are hilarious when reacting to each other, and John Cleese ('nuff said.) I don't see why the game is getting so much hate - the only bugs I've noticed are in one mission and I'm sure those will get patched out soon enough - the game only came out yesterday for crying out loud.
If you like a good challenging strategy-based team shooter, I'd definitely recommend.

This game is a roguelike with a modern UI (ascii tileset available if you prefer) that gets rid of all the annoying aspects of roguelikes and leaves you free to do your best until you die or beat the game (though as of this review I have not beaten it so I don't know if gameplay ends or continues at that point).
Some examples of things that have been annoying, but in this game are not: you can 'auto-explore' to make sure you haven't missed anything on a floor of a dungeon.   You can also use auto-explore to go from floor entrance to floor exit and vice-versa when navigating any floors you might have already cleared.  It can be played entirely using just the mouse (keystrokes are still available for most actions and mapped to keys by default but you can remap it all to whatever you want if you like).  You also unlock items that make inventory management easier, which you then will start with from 'birth' on future playthroughs once acquired (example: an item that you get early on during first playthrough which automatically picks up items in any tile that you run over, and anything auto picked up like this isn't counted against your weight allowance; you can take any item out and keep it in regular inventory)  You can use a "tag" feature to flag any item with whatever keyword(s) you type in, and the game will not sell/drop the item.  There are no cursed items.  All items are automatically identified once picked up.  You can "sell" items anywhere/anytime due to item spoken of above so "town runs" are not necessary for inventory management purposes.  There are HELPFUL tooltips for everything that you hover the mouse over.
There is a very well-done tutorial (accessible during character creation) which explains most aspects of the games' combat/magic system.  There is still a lot of detail left for you to explore/examine/ignore at your leisure/peril, but you're given a good gameplay explanation via the tutorial.  I feel it is worth mentioning and applauding, because unlike other roguelikes I could just start this one up and with the exception of 'dungeon order' (see end of review) I have not felt the need to seek help about gameplay from the internet yet.
You start the game with a couple of race choices, and a few more class choices (rough mix of melee and magic).  Through gameplay you unlock additional races and classes to choose from in future games.    There is a very high variety of loot, that can give you bonus abilities that are activatable or are used when you hit an enemy, or when you land a critical hit on an enemy (and even more than that that I haven't used yet, I've mostly played the 'melee' side of class choices).
You get various ability/skill points per level to assign to 'class' and 'general' skill trees, and a couple stat points per level to assign to your stats like strength, willpower, magic, constitution, cunning, dexterity as well.   Abilties in the skill trees have level and skill point requirements before they can be used, but if you are the min/max type, what is unlocked/available to put points into depends on your stat points from base points and equipment modifies "at the time you kill the enemy that levels you up".  This means you can plan ahead and stack your strength skill at level up time by wearing a bunch of equipment with +str on it, if you are playing a mage class but want to put points into a strength ability without sacrificing permanent points, to a degree.
Dungeons don't respawn; therefore, "grinding" isn't a gameplay consideration.  Dungeons are randomized in layout/monster placement but the monster types within each dungeon are the same every playthrough.  The world map/overview seems to be the same each playthrough but it's a small part of the overall gameplay and after a few playthroughs it's nice to know where the dungeons are each time.
Overall this is a very fun roguelike game that has great replay value due to skill/class/race combinations and the enormous variety of loot drops.

RAID:WWI is a game by Lion Game Lion, a small and quite new game studio based on Zagreb.  If you've played Payday 2, you might recognize Ilija ("This is Ilija, the sniper") who worked as their lead level designer.  After forming LGL, they did some content for PD2, such as the Bomb heists, the Dragan character pack, or the Golden Grin Casino.
This is the first game by LGL.
RAID puts you in the feet of a rogue-ish allied squad during WWII, allowing you to play as a German, British, Russian, or American soldier, each with their own background story.
There are four available classes right now:   Recon, Insurgent, Demolitions, and Assault, each with their own strenghts and weaknesses, and their very own warcry, which is a speciall ability that fills up with kills, and gives you and your team a temporary bonus for the duration of it.
The currently available weapon types are sniper rifles, ARs, SMGs, shotguns, LMGs, and pistols, as well as a melee weapon and hand grenades. As of right now, each class has one or two weapons that are restricted to them.  I'm not particularly a fan of this design decision, but we'll see if it gets changed in the future; the devs are really in touch with the players, constantly implementing changes that we ask for.  More on that later.
Back to the weapons.  Each weapon's got its own list of "challenges", which are usually about killing enemies with them, and making the most out of the gun's strenghts.  Upon completion, you can upgrade your weapon (stats-wise, and visually with some upgrades) and unlock the next tier of the challenge if you meet the level requirements.
You can level up your characters up to 40, gaining a skill point with each level, and being able to access some weapon upgrades at certain level thresholds, as well as unlocking more weapons.
Each level unlocks one "column" in the skill tree, which consists of 3 skills from which you must pick one in order to be able to pick a skill from the next column, and warcry-related abilities every 5 levels.
That's what you can expect in regards to playable characters.  You can mix any nationality with any class when creating your character, and each have their own set of clothes that can be unlocked.
The missions on this game are objective-based, rather than the "push hard and fast" that we experience in games such as Vermintide or L4D.
During the raids, you will encounter different objectives, ranging from killing high-value targets, to blowing♥♥♥♥♥♥up, protecting something, or escort/payload people or vehicles. You'll usually encounter a variety of these types of objectives during the same raid.
As of release, there are about a dozen raids, and two operations.  Operations reuse maps from standalone raids (although with different settings and objectives) to construct a multi-day raid.  As of now, we have a 6-raid op, and a 4-raid one.  Operation progress is saved and can be continued upon failure without having to reset the entire op.
There are 4 difficulties ranging from Easy to Very Hard, each featuring different enemies and granting you more experience upon completion.
The raids feature a decent ammount of randomness, mostly related to the location of the different objects, be it your spawning point, the location of an objective, the escape area, and so on.  It isn't Dwarf Fortress, but the difference is quite noticeable and certainly helps with the replayability value of the game.
The different maps will also spawn loot at random locations. It comes in two types; gold, and dogtags.
Gold turns into gold bars after you collect enough of it, and you can use them to  buy cosmetic upgrades for your base of operations, including a piano that you can actually play, if you are creative enough to compose a piece with all the missing keys.  The devs have mentioned that it will likely have other uses in the future.
Dogtags allow you to upgrade the loot crate that you gain at the end of the mission, depending of how many you find.  A better loot crate increases your chances of getting rewarded with clothes for your character, melee weapons, or most importantly; cards.
Cards are modifiers that you can apply to a raid or operation before starting it.  Some of them ar just boosts -such as 15% extra health for the team- and grant no extra bonuses other than that, while others work more like a challenge; giving you a bonus along with a set of constraints.  eg; there's one that increases your team's headshot damage, while making enemies immune to bodyshots.  These challenge cards will give you an experience bonus if you complete the raid.  Some will give a raw bonus, while others will multiply your gained experience by a set ammount.
Cards give a ton of replayability value to the game, and can result in some extremely fun situations.  There is one that only allows you to move backwards and sideways, for example.

About bad reviews and common complains.
Common rant 1:  It looks like a game from 2010.
See for yourself and decide.
The graphics are certainly outdated, and if that's a really important factor for you, then you'll likely not enjoy the game. That said, if you can look past them and can live with less than a FF-XIII cutscene, you'll quickly get used to them and even forget about it, because, you know, having fun and all of that jazz.
Common rant 2:  This is a Payday 2 subpar reskin.
Yeah, no.  Starbreeze/Overkill really screwed this game over by trying to force it as a PD2 successor, hijacking RAID announcements, and spamming the PD2 playerbase with it.
They are part of the same genre, and share many aspects that have proven successful on previous games, while implementing their very own thing.  That's how games work, otherway we'd all be playing Pong.
If you are coming from Payday 2 -which I assume is the case for many, due to the reasons stated above-, I guess you could get a feel of PD:TH, which had a greater focus on gameplay and murdering the baddies while trying to survive, rather than the ezmode  powercreep nonsense that PD2 turned into.  But still, I think RAID should be appreciated and judged by their own value, rather than by forced comparisons.
If you enjoy the current state of PD2, you'll probably not enjoy this game, or at least not prefer it over PD2.  On the other hand, those who enjoyed PD:TH, or early (pre-rogue update) PD2, you should probably give it a chance and judge for yourself.
Common rant 3:  y u no make game in unreel engin?!?!????!
I'm not gonna lie: ♥♥♥♥♥Diesel engine.  That said, and as someone who used to do programs for a living, expecting a new and small team to buy a new engine and learn it for their first project when they already have a working engine that they've mastered is just crazy.
If you've played PD2, you know what you can expect from Diesel engine and its limitations.  If you can't live with the engine's issues, that's fair and you should probably move on, else you know what it feels like.
Common rant 4:  The game is too expensive.
I know I'll get hundreds of hours from this, which will come as a few cents per hour if I had paid full price, which I didn't.  That sounds more than fair value to me, but then again; it's your money and decision.
Common rant 5:  Bad performance.
Sorry, but more like bad computer.   There are games which have awful performance and run badly in gaming computers, but in this case it's about people upset about not being able to run them on their portable potato.
The devs are in constant touch with us -be it in chat or during the QA sessions during live streams-, and really listen to our feedback and suggestions, and really care about the game.

Harsh, unforgiving, and addictive.
ToME is one of the few rogue-like RPGs that gets me frustrated over its unforgiving difficulty and harsh gameplay. And I love it because of it. The game gives a feeling of challenge and forces you to learn all of its mechanics and tricks. Fail to remember any and you will quickly lose all of your lives.
Did I mention that this game is a rogue-like? ToME is a game which has you create your own character picking one of the several races and classes. You can be a human warrior, an elven rogue, or even a halfling mage. The choice is yours. But don't get too attached to your character as they will very easily die. By default, your character is given only a few lives. Run out of them and it's game over. You either have to restart your character's entire story or make a new one. If perma-death or limited lives aren't your thing, there is an option to have infinite lives. But this removes a lot of the challenge in the game and you will not be able to get much of the game's NUMEROUS achievements.
While this game has very minimalistic graphics and mostly comprises of still images for characters and objects, it gives a very reminiscent feel of old rogue-like dungeon crawlers. The art-style is a very interesting one but might not appeal to all people. Overall, the game is very well design and made. It has the right amount of challenge and design put into it. The game even has its own lore set and a very interesting world to study and explore. And if you are worried about any lack of replayability, there is a ton of it. All of the dungeons are randomly generated. There are a wide variety of ways to play this game and interesting combinations of characters you can make. And the number of achievements will have completionists at their desks for days trying to get them all. If you feel that the game is lacking a certain something, this game does have Workshop support. So if you wish to make a Vampire race or even make one of the enemy races playable, then you can. This game is very open to mods and highly encourages it.
All in all, this is a very well-made game that will have on the edge of your seat as you try to keep your character alive. I recommend it to anyone who loves a good old fashioned dungeon crawler or anyone who is looking for something new in the swamp of games that is the Steam store.

Tales of Maj'Eyal is one of the bigger Roguelikes that along with Dungeon Crawl Stone Soup and Dwarf Fortress help set the standards for what makes a good Roguelike.
Unlike the two other roguelikes listed above you'll find an actual story being played out along with Lore and Monster Details that really tell you about the world your character is playing in; while not getting in the way of in-game play. Game Mechanics are plentiful but they are spelled out and not hidden from the player. User Interface for the most part is easy to get into and use.
There are a couple of hurdles one will need to commit to however in order to play this game - like any Roguelike there is the overall Game Depth and Learning Curve and Tales of Maj'Eyal is no different. Character skills sort of level up similar to what you might find in an MMORPG or Diablo-like, but skills themselves are also much like their counterparts - not descriptive enough to tell you what they do and requiring you have to test them out or read up on them.
For people coming from other Roguelikes, you may be thrown off by the sheer Tactical Nature of combat, Additionally it is worth noting that the game is meant to be played in Adventurer Mode - IE, Multiple Lives, not One. Lastly, the game is long - very long. A full run in the original Age of Ascendancy Campaign (The Main Vanilla Campaign that the game started with) from start to actual finish is probably going to be longer then most other Roguelikes bar a few.
All in all though, this is a very enjoyable game. Once you get past the couple tidbits that might hold you back or throw you off you'll likely have lots of fun playing with multiple races and classes in separate but distinct ways.

The art style, setting and characters capture the mid-90s shoot 'em up feel very well. Crafting your first machine gun after being stuck with the sub-par starter gun is hugely satisfying, as is completing a mission with all bonus objectives and enough resources gathered to buy several upgrades.
That said the gameplay turns out to be rather poor. On a regular basis players need to avoid enemy projectiles while firing at airborne enemies homing in on them and platforming, all at the same time. Sadly, the game lacks the silky smooth controls required to make this fun and instead just ends up being frustrating.
The actual gameplay takes the form of missions, each one with their own objective. Between them players can visit their homebase for upgrades and supplies. There are two major problems with this. First: missions take place in large locations which get recycled again, and again, and again. Secondly: no information is provided as to where in the freely traversable levels the current objective is located. As a result players are forced to scour the same places over and over again, often with endlessly looping background music, too. Combined with limited time for each mission things can become rather frustrating fast.
Other annoyances:
The camera is not overly intelligent.
Exponential grinding for better gear.
Jumping has a noticeable delay to it.
Jumping down larger heights leads to the character freezing for a moment upon landing.
Some enemies can fire diagonally, which players flatout can't.
Enemies may respawn the moment their spawn location is off screen.
Health items are few and far in between, making the gameplay rather unforgiving.
Health can be regenerated at field hospital, which act as save points. The health regen is slow enough to not be noticeable. The game doesn't bother mentioning that this health regen exists.
It's impossible to jump while crouching, making destructable platforms the player has to fire at while standing on them and exercise in patients.
Default grunt enemies on platforms above the players may randomly decide to drop down, giving no chance to walk away or kill them.
The first boss decided to leave once he was on low health. He came back eventually but not soon enough for there to be time to finish him off, leading to a failed mission. Who thought this was even a good idea?

A necromancer that flings fireballs? A cunning assassin who favours poison arrowed bow shots? A paladin in touch with his evil side? A viking-like brawler who can also heal with the power of fire? Moonfall is a genre hybrid (side-scrolling hack'n'slash) that has sadly failed to meet my expectations. It’s not inherently a bad game but I was unpleasantly surprised to realize that the decent looking visual style was hindered by the repetitive gameplay mechanics to a larger extent than in most video games I get to write about. Dev team’s second Steam project and their first one to be self-published. Suffice to say, Moonfall is a far cry from Fishcow Studio’s Steam debut which was a quirky point & click, named Gomo.
Only seemingly convoluted, the story isn’t properly handled. Once you start a new game, you are presented with a static page filled with words about a rapidly expanding Empire fighting against Savages with the help of magic (in-game referred to as “Lunarium”). Your foes are a combination of blue warriors and monsters. If the developer was aiming for an allegory in regards to the struggle between the Roman Empire and Celtic tribes, they missed the target. The savages look more like Smurfs, than blue dyed Celts and the “bestiary” is initially formed of zombie-wolves and bipedal fishmen drawn straight from Lovecraft’s writings. The Empire isn’t more fleshed out either since they seem to be a symbol of incompetence. You play as a mysteriously new recruit sent out on fetch quests which most of the time, include the rescue of your high-ranking superiors. Bare in mind that I haven’t met any cinematics so far and the dialogue between NPCs and you, is text-based. A far too silent experience indeed. It’s 2017 and there are still barebone RPGs like these being released?
2D nicely hand-drawn sprites and backgrounds which still suffer from repetitiveness. Enemy types are limited and they all look like clones of one another, while the static scenery just seems like one frame being rearranged after the previous one. It gets old fast and while this might have been a non-issue in the case of an indie platformer, role playing games are meant to be far more complex as a gaming genre by definition. It’s a pity, since the assets have been clearly created through actual effort. The way they are being “stitched together” though, makes it seem like a wasted opportunity. Performance-wise, at least Moonfall runs in a most stable manner as far as frame rate is concerned and no bugs or glitches were encountered.
Non-playable characters (NPCs) are mostly silent, with a single spoken (and random) sentence once you interact with them. The soundtrack is a repetitive tune which you might quickly wish to mute and replace with songs of your own choosing, while the other sound effects are just as “noteworthy”. I recommend some epic music which can surprisingly save the day in most cases. Even for an otherwise subpar video game.
I already mentioned the hybrid status but unfortunately the side scoller aspects are predominant over the hack'n'slash gameplay mechanics. You’d almost be temped to consider Moonfall a “street brawler” with swords and axes, if not for the inclusion of some spells and a ranged attack option. I always like to play my RPGs with an archer/stealth type since the beefy melee tank character which rips everything to shreds, has been a stereotype done to death. It’s the easy way out, folks. Plain and simple. Wizards are the exact opposite and they can be considered as glass cannons. A cakewalk to mop the floor with them, once they register a couple of hits. My stealthy archers represent the perfect compromise between being overpowered and vulnerable at the same time.
So naturally, I picked the Shadow class over Vanguard (fighter) or Elementalist (wizard). I was promised a fun time of “assassinating unsuspecting enemies from a distance, before they get a chance to return the attack”). Yeah, talk about promises you can’t keep. For starters, my miniature crossbow-wielding character gets spotted by the foes as soon as he sets foot during a frame (call it “battle scene” if you want). So much for the stealth option. You keep shooting bolts which have a curiously short range until the Savages drop dead and reveal collectible coins. The currency is being used to trade for potions or better equipment, which you’ll surely need since the loot that gets dropped by the enemies is disappointingly low tier. You level up eventually and can unlock skills that allow more powerful attacks or the ability to dash. You will be running away from the mob of gathering foes more often than you’d like to, trust me. Getting swarmed and killed won’t be a rare occurrence.
I never quite understood why the developer offers mouse support in Moonfall’s Main Menu but absolutely neglects this crucial PC peripheral once you are actually playing the game. This title isn’t even a console or mobile port, to warrant this game design issue. Having to use only the keyboard for both controlling the character and navigating the RPG menus, feels like an unnecessary chore. I can understand the attempts to emulate the old school feel, but try to do it with some minimal streamlining thrown in as well. At least the difficulty won’t leave you wanting for more. Despite being visually repetitive, the combat still shines far brighter than the generic storyline or clunky keyboard-dependent User Interface.
I still have mixed feelings about this game. I have certainly played worse role playing games in the past, on Steam or otherwise. Is Moonfall still worthy of being recommended by me now as opposed to my lower standards from one year ago, when I first started reviewing Steam games? Well, I reserve that final decision to you, as always. But I for one had my fill with it for a long time to come. I believe Moonfall should have been released as an Early Access stage and at a slightly lower price tag. It offers Cards and Achievements, which represent a saving grace at least for Steam collectors. Just buy it once it receives a discount or when it gets bundled along with a few other titles.
+ Steam Achievements & Trading Cards.
+ RPG elements, such as character classes.
+ Old school difficulty requiring quick reflexes.
- Core gameplay is far too repetitive.
- Limited mouse peripheral support.
- Next to no in-game sounds.
- Slightly overpriced.

Just under a year ago I reviewed
where I ultimately felt it was... alright... but multiple shortcomings and poor design choices held it back from true greatness. This time around, they've somehow managed to do almost exactly the same thing but in almost completely different ways. They've handled the story very differently, but still haven't improved it, they've tweaked the gameplay but inadvertently only served to highlight its flaws in the process, and they've given us lots of new toys to play with, but merely replaced one set of inconsequential features for a whole bunch of different ones. It's kind of both impressive and baffling how little actual progress they seem to have made from so much work.
The first time around, the story shifted constantly from a future setting to past, exploring a particular family lineage, but it was such a mess of writing, acting and mishandled plot that it was easily the least interesting thing the game ended up doing. This time, the future setting is pushed way into the background and largely just bookends the game and its story, coming across as baggage the developers grudgingly tried to deal with as little and as best they could. To that end, we play as Ezio in 15th century Italy as he is unwittingly drawn into the midst of a dangerous conspiracy, learning of the struggle between Assassins and Templars as they try to shape the players and politics of the day to take over the country, and ultimately the world. There's more to this as the game makes call backs to the mysterious artefact at the heart of the first game (among other things *wink-wink*), but it never feels as grand or as crucial as they probably mean it to be, and just as with the first game, I couldn't bring myself to care about the whys and found myself increasing checked out of the story, my interest having already long since departed way before the anticlimactic end. Only two games into a thirteen game series, I'm already done with the lore and wish it wasn't a thing anymore. The kernel of a good idea is tangible, but it frustratingly never seems to become anything more than that.
The gameplay fairs little better in its changes. The previous game had three large cities and a large hub area of towns, fields, canyons and various other sights connecting them. There was little to do here, though, so unless you really loved collectathons and sightseeing then you were bang outta luck and just had to endure the trip between main events. Thankfully, the hub area has been removed and we're instead given two very large cities, two small cities (with surrounding fields and swamplands) and your very own town to renovate. Once you're let loose to roam free in these places that's where the fun really begins, and also where the heartache hits, too, as what should be a simple joy becomes a near constant struggle and an increasing source of frustration.
My memories of traversal in the first game are good ones, always having a really nice sense of effortless flow to movement. Whether it was leaping across rooftops or scaling up walls, it just felt right, and very rarely did anything bad about it ever come to my attention. Here, however, I literally could hardly go a couple of minutes without encountering some kind of issue. Ezio seems magnetically drawn to damn near every object and you can barely run anywhere near a vertical surface without him trying to automatically leap onto it. Dislodging yourself from anything takes way too long, and he pretty much only jumps from anything in a 90 degree, X or Y axis direction. So, many times I wanted to jump one way but it was impossible because it wasn't aligned exactly with the limited directions he could jump. Add to this the camera that constantly insists on "helping" you into new angles or straight up removing your control of it completely, plus its annoying sensitivity that was never decent no matter how I adjusted it, or the frequent frame rate stutters, and the whole thing was a never-ending battle to control adequately, leaping to my death on several occasions because of the bad camera and jumping/climbing/grabbing system.
As with the previous title, the world itself and its scale is the star of the show which impresses most. The fact that there's only brief loading between main areas and cut scenes or missions is something I feel the games probably don't get enough credit for. Ditto with the sound design that really stood out to me on many occasions while they'd largely go unnoticed for me in other games. Visually, most of the areas are very "busy", which may make everything a bit of a blur of visual white noise, but I still greatly appreciated the effort once again in crafting such a fully realised world when they probably could have gotten away with less, between the overall layout, texture detail, and abundance of NPC models that fill the world. But, sadly, as with many other aspects, the busy-ness of the game also worked against it as there was a lot of what I can only think to describe as architectural clutter - basically lots of structures and pieces sticking out of every building in one place or another and getting in your way. It's clear they were placed with the intention of helping you get around faster or more gracefully, but it had the opposite effect on me as Ezio would continuously bump into stuff or grab on to out-of-the-way objects then take an age to let go of them. It just killed so much of the momentum and pace, and a lot of the fun along with it.
Like I said, there are many new features, like upgrading your small fortress town, but aside from some aesthetic changes that you probably won't even notice, rather than unlocking new things, they only generate more money for you. But since it's such a non-issue in the game and you'll rarely ever find yourself wanting for more, this seemed useless to me. As too where many of the additional weapons and abilities. Again, the combat is a chore. I never felt engaged or threatened, just like I'd hit a tedious roadblock to endure rather than enjoy. But one of the most notable additions were tombs, extra challenge areas of sorts where you had to test your agility across obstacle courses and receive a small reward at the end. But, really, all these actually did were remind me of the game's main influence once again, Prince of Persia, except not nearly as fun as that masterpiece.
For all my moaning about it, again, as with its predecessor, I'm rating it up not because I necessarily loved it, but because there isn't enough to truly hate on it. It never infuriates so much or for so long that it's ruinous, just occasionally annoying. And really, its worst crime isn't that it's bad, just that it's kinda dull and never becomes all that it could be. It has one trick that it repeats over and over, that makes it fun for the first five or so hours, but which I was completed done with by hour forty... go some place, climb some stuff, kill a guy, on to the next one. That's it. I wish every area was its own separate space, in its own time period and with its own character that only he or she would operate within independent of the others. Each would have their own skills or abilities (or lack of) and would require the player to play differently with each one, switching back and forth as preferred and completing every mission in whichever order they chose. It would mostly kill off the feeling of repetition and maybe even make the cities themselves have a greater sense of functional purpose rather than suspiciously coming across as filler impersonating content. Until that day comes, while I'm sure many will adore this, I ran out of enthusiasm for it far sooner than I ever should have. So, maybe don't read this as an endorsement of Assassin's Creed 2, so much as a recommendation for Prince of Persia. Seriously, those games are awesome.

if this applies to you, I would advise you, not to bother. The game throws you into the action and expects you to read, obvserve, learn and test stuff out for yourself. It also is crushingly difficult in some parts until you figure out what to do and not always is the challenge on the fair side. Trial and error are part of this game to a certain extent.
The first few hours in particular are very unwelcoming. You stand on a shore, get asked what gods you believe in, give a random answer, ask yourself, if this was something important(it was) and embark onto your salty journey. Everything is grey, it is hard to distinguish beween monsters, traps or chairs sometimes, enemies are cluttered everywhere and you begin to ask yourself, what you are trying to accomplish with aimlessly wandering about.
Because you also don't have a map. Then you level up for the first time and take a look at the skill tree. And holy mother of god, what a cluster♥♥♥♥ of skills it is. You decide to put points into random stuff. Might be useful at some point.
In short, the first few hours are a confusing mess and a mental state between satisfying monster killing and mild annoyance because yo do not seem to know anything.
And then you get further in. You leave the first 2 areas behind. You discover a weapon you find satisfying to use. You decide to level up you skill tree in accordance with that weapon and suddenly realize, that this abundance of perks to choose from is a really simple structure of classes and suddenly makes sense.
You find a few shortcuts and slowly begin to understand, how the world is structured and how to get around it.
You will meet a few NPCs and fragments of a story are beginning to form. There now is this sense of slow progression, the feeling, that everything is coming together bit by bit, the further you delve into the game. You are now hooked to Salt&Sanctuary.

Sanctum isn't the very first with this idea in mind, however it pulls it off with amazing gameplay and many viable options.  I don't have the DLC for this, but I can already recommend this game to people with a good group of friends for an online multiplayer romp of PvE.
Now, before we get to the core of this review, let me say this: Soul Masters was the first to attempt this style of gameplay with a mixture of magic, building, and minions.  In that game, you controlled a single character capable of building towers and upgrades, much like that of any tower defense game.  You can use your character to battle across the map and lead your minions to victory.  You build defense structures and upgrade your minions and yourself (if memery serves me well).  The only problem: the game was short-lived and free-to-play.  It's in development limbo, as it was set to re-release, correcting some of the more severe bugs.
Now then, on to the review.  The graphics definitely are limited, but get the job done beautifully.  THe enemy designs are a bit lacking, but at least the weak points are easy to spot.  By no means are they unique, but they work well, nonetheless.
On to the sounds.  I haven't messed much with the text to speech, but from what I hear, everything fits perfectly together.  The announcer lets you know what mode you're in and the sounds of weapons going off are adequet.  I just wish there was more to it than that, but the music is also adequet and fits the mood.
Gameplay: it's a tower defense game.  It's also an FPS.  It WILL get repetitive, but the beauty of it is that you can't favor one over the other.  Achieving balance is important to winning against the waves of enemies.  Some require heavy weapon fire while others require pin-point accuracy to their weaknesses.  Balance what you upgrade and you can make ith trhough.
Controls: Here, I have to dock it a little because there's no option to run, so you're moving kinda slow through the building process, but then again, you're building and you have unlimited time to build until you hit enter.  Still, the controls are solid and the aiming is what you'd expect from any FPS game.  Sniping is as easy as it is in most other FPS games, which is never a bad thing.
Overall: I'd give this game a definite 9/10, would like to see more people play this, but the sequel is already out there, so I suggest getting that over this, as long as the gameplay mechanics only improve over what this game has already done.  Still, if you can pick this one up, it's definitely a keeper.  I hope to grab the sequel someday soon.

Everyone making Metal Slug comparisons and judging it on those grounds went into this with the wrong expectations. Neither the steam page nor any gameplay video, now or prior to its full release, ever promoted this game as being similar to Metal Slug.
With that out of the way, let's come out and say what it is: this is Mega Man x Monster Hunter. The controls, level design, enemies, and gameplay are all explicitly cribbed from Mega Man, while the mission design, gear crafting progression, and boss mechanics are lifted from Monster Hunter. You accept a mission, from something as mundane as killing a couple mooks, to hunting two of a particular boss, and you're dropped into the level with the supplies you've brought with you. Certain supplies can be gathered in the field, as can materials, and you traverse the rather sizable level completing your objective, after which you return to base, where you resupply, craft guns, knives, and skills, and select a new mission. Much like Monster Hunter, this game encourages cooperative play, so rev up the online or bring along a friend, or you're quickly going to find yourself frustrated by how long later missions take to complete.
If that sounds at all appealing to you, by all means, pick it up. You could easily squeeze at least 20 hours out of it, and it's an excellent couch co-op title.

Hotline Miami poor mans edition.
Story:
12 is Better Than 6 puts you in the shoes of an Mexican who has amnesia. No matter where he travels he is followed by a rain of bullets, so he sets out on a journey to regain his memory and understand who he truly is.
The story of this game is a joke. I first started off enjoying the story and the random, but cringy jokes the characters throw around sometimes, but after a while the story started to get on my nerves. First of all most of the actions of the main character don't make sense, he acts like a complete idiot most of the time and is really unlikable and I realize that he was made that way, but his very aggressive attitude comes off forced and in the more serious moments you just can't help, but laugh at how bad his dialogue is.
It's also worth to note that the ending is one of the worst endings, I had the pleasure of seeing in any video game ever. It makes the entire journey seem worthless and sort of a massive slap to the face of the player.
Gameplay:
As Stated this game is basically a Hotline Miami rip off, but with way clunkier gun play. After every shot you have to manually load in the next bullet by clicking the right mouse button, which until you get used to, will get you killed many, many times.
Unlike Hotline Miami, the goal however is not to kill everyone in the level, but instead to get from point A to point B without dying, which is easier said than done as most of the levels are built the way where you have to pick off enemies from a distance behind a rock and hope for the best. Also it doesn't help that that the enemies have point perfect aim and can sometimes spot you through walls.
The game gives you many weapons, like shotguns, rifles, pistols, bows and dynamite to dispatch of your foes. Sadly the best weapon in the game is the bow as it's silent and doesn't attract enemies which makes it easier to pick them off from  a distance. Also the knife the game gives you is completely useless as when the enemies are alerted it does no damage what so ever.
Audio:
Most of the audio in the game is pretty bad, including the soundtrack. The Soundtrack is just generic western music, which sounds like it belongs in a very bad cowboy movie.
Graphics:
This is where most of the problems of the game start. The art style on the surface is really good and at one point I really enjoyed the hand drawn characters, but once I started playing I noticed one massive problem. From a top down perspective EVERYTHING LOOKS THE SAME. The colors you see most are purple and white and when everything looks the same it becomes really hard to track down enemies. In one of the hardest chapters in the game, I had gotten to the end of the level, to only die when I thought an enemy was a rock, that's how bad it is.
Verdict:
On most sales this game costs around 2 euros and will last you around 4 hours to complete the entire thing. For that money, it's not the worst game, but with the same money you can get Hotline Miami which is almost ten times better than this, so you should do that instead.
Final Rating:
4/10

- Soundtrack is terrible

Cuphead is a really well made game. The controls set a high bar for fluidity, and the art, music, and sound design are all outstanding.
A lot of reviews call out the game's difficulty, but it's really not THAT hard. I've been playing games most of my life, but my reflexes are far from amazing. That said, I was able to beat the game on normal after finding which builds work best against various bosses and what strategies to employ against them. This is a process that is difficult but rewarding, a success as far as game design goes.
This last part of the review contains spoilers.
There was, however, a point at which the game, for me, stopped being fun, namly the casino. The casino is the second to last level in the game. The setup is that you roll a three sided die, and move along the board fighting various mini-bosses until you reach the end and fight King Dice. Parts of this level are okay. Once you learn the patterns it's not too bad to beat the various minibosses without taking damage. That said, you need to roll properly on the die in order to pick up hearts along your path to gain life for the fight against King Dice. It's not terribly hard to pick the number you want on the die, but it's not easy and you will make mistakes. Sometimes poor dice rolls are enough to ruin a run. Moreover, it's incredibly hard to beat King Dice without taking a fair amount of damage, and it's difficult to practice against him because you have to beat the whole prior casino to do so. I got to the point where I was just throwing the dice at random because otherwise I would spend more time trying to roll correctly than actually fighting,and I mainly wanted to get reps in against King Dice. That said, I don't think I could have beat King Dice with fewer than 4 hearts so you do have to be somewhat careful about how you roll. You can dismiss some of these complaints by telling me to git gud, and you'd be right to an extent. I do think that the mechanics of this level, however, is enough to tilt off players who were otherwise willing to put up with the games (more 'fair') difficulty up to this point. The games penultimate fight is hard but more traditional, however, after the Casino, my enthusiasm for the game was so dampened that I grinded through the final fight more out of spite than pleasure and didn't really feel compelled to run it back in expert mode as much as I felt compelled to throw my desktop into a volcano.
All told, Cuphead is a fantastic game. It's well made, beautiful, and challenging. In my opinion, some of the choices made for the casino level (and really some of the side scrolling levels if we’re going to be picky) dampened the experience but certainly didn't ruin it. If this is the kind of game you can sink your teeth into, I would recommend you do so, but I think it's also important to know when to put it down if you want to enjoy it to its fullest.

I finished Cuphead recently and have to say, it's a wonderful game.
You take old-school side scrolling shoot 'em up games like Contra and Metal Slug and add in 1930's style animation and that's what Cuphead is. The game is hard. It is also a feast for the eyes. The soundtrack is also incredible with period appropriate big band and jazz style music playing over the cartoon action, as you would expect. Cuphead nails the aesthetic of everything but doesn't disappoint in the gameplay department. The game may be difficult, but jumping back in after dying on a level is made more palatable because of how good everything surrounding it is. The "one more run" mentality is in play here, and when you finally do beat that boss that was giving you so much trouble, you feel like you just climbed the proverbial mountain and came out on top.
If you are no stranger to difficult games, you cannot go wrong with Cuphead. Just be warned that it may be a turn-off if you do not have the patience to learn boss patterns while dying over and over again.
